days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: Two Airliners Had the Whole Sky Over the Grand Canyon. They Flew Into Each Other Anyway.
days.concept: Quantities with both size and direction, such as velocities, are vectors that add tip to tail or component by component. The relative velocity of two movers, one's velocity minus the other's, decides whether and when they will meet.
days.focus: Teaches vectors, components (via sine and cosine), vector subtraction and relative velocity. Then teaches the constant-bearing rule: if another craft's direction from you stays fixed while it gets closer, you are on a collision course. Explains why such a threat hangs motionless in a pilot's or driver's view.
days.model_or_equation: Components: vx = |v| sin θ (east) and vy = |v| cos θ (north) for a heading θ measured from north. Relative velocity of B as seen from A: v_rel = v_B − v_A. If v_rel points straight along the line from B to A, the bearing of B stays constant while the range shrinks, which is a collision course.

story.title: A crowded sky that looked empty
story.hook: On the morning of 30 June 1956 two airliners left Los Angeles about three minutes apart: TWA Flight 2, a Lockheed Super Constellation bound for Kansas City, and United Flight 718, a Douglas DC-7 bound for Chicago. Over the Grand Canyon they were in uncontrolled airspace, where pilots were responsible for seeing and avoiding each other. Both were flying at about 21,000 feet among towering cumulus clouds. In mid-morning they collided, killing all 128 people aboard, then the deadliest US commercial air disaster. The Civil Aeronautics Board could not determine why neither crew saw the other in time. Its list of possible reasons included intervening clouds, cockpit visibility, preoccupation with cockpit duties, efforts to show passengers the canyon, and the 'physiological limits to human vision.' The crash, followed by further midair collisions in 1958, led Congress to pass the Federal Aviation Act of 1958, which created the Federal Aviation Agency.
story.puzzle: Two crews with the whole sky to look at, in daylight: how could each fail to see an airliner on a course that would hit them?
story.payoff: Subtract one aircraft's velocity vector from the other's and you get their relative velocity. On a collision course it points straight along the line between them, so the other aircraft's bearing never changes. It sits at one fixed spot in the windscreen and simply grows, slowly at first. Human vision is tuned to motion, and a target that does not move across the field of view is easy to miss, especially behind a window post or a cloud. That is one documented reason see-and-avoid fails, though the CAB could not say which factor operated here. The fix that followed was a federal system of air traffic control, not better eyes.
sources: Civil Aeronautics Board, accident investigation report on the TWA Flight 2 / United Air Lines Flight 718 midair collision over the Grand Canyon, 30 June 1956 (1957)
Federal Aviation Act of 1958 (Pub. L. 85-726)
FAA 'Lessons Learned' entry on the 1956 Grand Canyon midair collision

days.application: Ships apply the same rule by law. Rule 7 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs, 1972) says risk of collision 'shall be deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.' It adds that risk may sometimes exist even with an appreciable bearing change, especially with a very large vessel or at close range. Worked example: your ship heads north at 12 knots. Another ship 10 nautical miles away (6 east and 8 north of you, bearing about 037°) heads due west at 9 knots. Relative velocity = (−9, 0) − (0, 12) = (−9, −12), a speed of 15 knots pointing exactly back along the line toward you. The bearing stays constant, and the ships collide in 40 minutes unless one turns.

builds_on.why: Velocity is Day 4's derivative of position. Once position has two dimensions, that rate of change has a direction too, which makes it a vector.

across.link: On Gemini 4 in June 1965, James McDivitt tried to fly up to the spent upper stage of his Titan rocket by thrusting toward it, and kept falling behind: in orbit, adding speed raises your orbit and slows your angular rate. Relative velocity still decides whether two spacecraft meet. Gravity bends their paths, though, which is where today's straight-line rule breaks.

days.apply_question: On a flat rural road with clear sightlines, two cars approach an uncontrolled crossroads at right angles and at the same speed: why might each driver fail to notice the other until very late, even in daylight?
days.evidence_note: The vector mathematics and the constant-bearing rule are settled. The CAB did not determine why the 1956 crews failed to see each other; constant bearing is a general mechanism consistent with its list of factors, not its finding. Crediting the 1958 Act to this crash alone oversimplifies, because further midair collisions in 1958 added pressure.

resource.title: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra (also listed as 'Vectors, what even are they?')
resource.creator: Grant Sanderson, 3Blue1Brown (2016)
resource.why: An animated introduction to vectors as arrows and as lists of components, with vector addition and scaling. It shows the geometry beneath relative velocity rather than describing it.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: Andrew Wiles Announced a Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in June 1993. By Autumn a Referee Had Found a Hole.
days.concept: A mathematical proof derives a claim step by step from axioms and previously proved results, so the claim holds in every case with a certainty that no finite number of examples or experiments can give. That certainty holds only if every single step is valid.
days.focus: Teaches what a proof is and is not: deduction versus evidence from cases, the role of axioms and lemmas, and proof by contradiction as Wiles used it. Explains why one gap breaks the whole argument and one repaired gap restores it. Sophie Germain's early-nineteenth-century partial results on the theorem belong in the history: Legendre published them in 1823 with credit to her, and she had earlier corresponded with Gauss under the pseudonym 'Monsieur Le Blanc'. The application turns proof on hardware: formal verification after Intel's Pentium division bug.
days.model_or_equation: Fermat's Last Theorem: for n > 2 there are no positive integers x, y, z with xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ. Structure of the proof, by contradiction: (1) if a solution aᵖ + bᵖ = cᵖ existed, the Frey elliptic curve y² = x(x − aᵖ)(x + bᵖ) would exist; (2) Ribet (1986) proved such a curve could not be modular; (3) Wiles, with Taylor, proved that every semistable elliptic curve is modular; (4) so no solution exists.

story.title: 'I think I'll stop here'
story.hook: On 23 June 1993 Andrew Wiles gave the last of three lectures at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge, England, under a deliberately unrevealing title: 'Modular forms, elliptic curves and Galois representations'. He ended by writing Fermat's Last Theorem on the board as a corollary of what he had shown, and said, 'I think I'll stop here.' Pierre de Fermat had claimed a proof in a book margin around 1637. In the 356 years since, mathematicians from Euler to Sophie Germain, who first wrote to Gauss under a man's name, had proved partial results, and computers had confirmed the theorem for every exponent up to the millions, but no one had found a proof. Wiles had worked in near-secrecy for seven years. Within months, while his roughly 200-page manuscript was being refereed, Nick Katz found a gap in one step. Wiles acknowledged the problem publicly in December 1993. On 19 September 1994, working with his former student Richard Taylor, he saw how to bridge it, and the corrected proof appeared in Annals of Mathematics in May 1995.
story.puzzle: If computers had already confirmed the theorem for millions of exponents, why did the world need Wiles's proof, and how could a single gap put seven years of work in doubt?
story.payoff: Checking cases is evidence; proof is deduction. Millions of confirmed exponents still leave infinitely many unchecked, and a counterexample could sit among them. A proof settles every case at once, through a chain of steps that each follow from axioms and earlier results. That is also why one invalid step undoes the whole chain, and why bridging that one step with Taylor restored all of it.
sources: Simon Singh, Fermat's Last Theorem (Fourth Estate, 1997)
A. Wiles, 'Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem', Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995): 443-551; R. Taylor and A. Wiles, 'Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras', same issue
Abel Prize 2016 citation for Sir Andrew Wiles (abelprize.no)

days.application: Intel's Pentium FDIV bug. In 1994 Thomas Nicely, a mathematician at Lynchburg College, found that the new chip sometimes divided wrongly: five entries were missing from a lookup table in its division hardware. Intel first called the error too rare to matter, then offered replacements, and in January 1995 took a $475 million charge. Testing had not caught the bug because no test suite can try every input. Chipmakers responded by investing in formal verification, meaning machine-checked proofs that a design meets its specification. For example, the division algorithm in AMD's K5 was mechanically proved correct with the ACL2 theorem prover in 1996. This is proof applied to hardware.

builds_on.why: Moore's straight line through a handful of points was induction, a pattern extrapolated from cases. A proof is the opposite: it needs no extrapolation.
Pearl and Reed's curve fit 120 years of census data and still failed. Agreement with every observed case does not prove that the next case will agree.

across.link: Legal 'proof' works differently. In In re Winship (1970) the US Supreme Court held that due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases. That standard is a threshold of confidence reached from evidence, not a deduction from axioms. The analogy with mathematical proof breaks exactly where mathematics claims certainty.

days.apply_question: seL4, an operating-system kernel used in defence research drones including an autonomous helicopter, comes with a machine-checked proof that its code implements its specification: what could still go wrong in a drone that runs it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Wiles's proof was refereed, published and accepted. Mathematicians and philosophers debate how far very long or computer-assisted proofs, such as the 1976 four-colour theorem and Hales's formal proof of the Kepler conjecture completed in 2014, change what 'certainty' means. A proof is only as strong as its axioms and its checking, and for hardware, as the match between the specification and reality.

resource.creator: Simon Singh (Fourth Estate, 1997)
resource.why: The best-known popular account of the 1993 lecture and the 350-year history behind it, written with Wiles's cooperation. Its opening chapter sets the scene and explains why mathematicians demand proof rather than evidence.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: In 1654 Pascal and Fermat Settled an Unfinished Game by Letter. Their Answer Became Expected Value.
days.concept: Probability puts weights on the possible outcomes. Expected value (each outcome's value times its probability, summed) is the long-run average that underpins decisions under uncertainty, though it is not the only thing a reasonable person may care about.
days.focus: Teaches probability as weights on a complete list of outcomes, the problem of points as Pascal and Fermat solved it, and expected value, which the law of large numbers makes a long-run average. Ends on its limits with Bernoulli's smallpox calculation and d'Alembert's objection: an average over a population is not the same as one person's choice about a risk faced now.
days.model_or_equation: E[X] = Σ pᵢ xᵢ. Problem of points: in a first-to-3 game with 64 pistoles at stake, A leads 2-1. A wins the next round with probability 1/2; otherwise the score is 2-2 and A wins with probability 1/2. So P(A wins) = 1/2 + 1/2 × 1/2 = 3/4, and A should take 48 pistoles and B 16.

story.title: How to split the pot when the game is cut short
story.hook: In the summer of 1654 Blaise Pascal, in Paris, was writing to Pierre de Fermat, a magistrate in Toulouse, about a gamblers' puzzle tied to the Chevalier de Méré. Two players each stake 32 pistoles, and the first to win three rounds takes all 64. Play stops with one player ahead two rounds to one. How should the pot be divided fairly? The problem was old. Luca Pacioli had proposed in 1494 to split the stakes in proportion to rounds already won, and later writers doubted his answer without settling it. Pascal's two long surviving letters are dated 29 July and 24 August, and the exchange ran through that summer and autumn. Fermat listed every way the remaining rounds could fall, while Pascal reasoned backward from each possible next round. They reached the same answer: 48 pistoles to the leader and 16 to the other.
story.puzzle: No one knows what would have happened in the unplayed rounds. How can there be a 'fair' share of a future that never occurred?
story.payoff: Fairness is defined over every future that could have happened, weighted by its probability. The leader wins in three of the four equally likely ways the game could finish, so a fair split gives the leader 3/4 of the pot, or 48 pistoles. That probability-weighted value of an uncertain prospect is expected value, the idea Pascal and Fermat made precise.
sources: Pascal-Fermat correspondence of 1654 (Pascal's letters of 29 July and 24 August 1654), in Pascal's Œuvres; English translation in D. E. Smith, A Source Book in Mathematics (1929)
Keith Devlin, The Unfinished Game (Basic Books, 2008)
Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica (1494)

days.application: Daniel Bernoulli's 1760 smallpox calculation. Variolation, deliberate infection with material from a mild smallpox case, was popularized in England by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen it in Constantinople and had her daughter inoculated in London in 1721. It killed roughly one in 200 of those inoculated, by the estimate Bernoulli used. In a paper read to the Paris Academy of Sciences in 1760 and published in 1766, Bernoulli modelled smallpox deaths by age. He calculated that universal inoculation would raise life expectancy at birth by about three years (from about 26 years 7 months to 29 years 9 months). Jean le Rond d'Alembert objected that an average gain spread over later life cannot simply be set against a 1-in-200 risk of dying within weeks. It was an early statement that expected value is a decision rule, not a fact.

builds_on.why: Bernoulli's calculation rests on a Day 6 kind of model: a differential equation for how the share of people still susceptible to smallpox falls with age.
Fermat's method was proof by exhausting the cases, listing every possible ending of the game, which is the complete reasoning Day 10 described. It is the same Pierre de Fermat.

across.link: Pascal himself applied expected value to religious belief. The 'Wager' in his Pensées (published 1670) argues that a finite stake against an infinite reward makes belief the rational bet. Critics from Diderot onward object that it ignores rival religions (the 'many gods' objection) and that belief cannot be chosen like a bet. It is a direct test of where expected-value reasoning stops.

days.apply_question: On an American roulette wheel (38 pockets, 18 of them red), a $10 bet on red wins $10 or loses $10: given that bet's expected value, why can the casino be indifferent to whether any one player wins tonight?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mathematics of probability and expected value. Value judgment: whether maximizing expected value is the right rule for a personal choice is a moral question. That is sharpest for a small risk of death now against a larger average benefit later, or when deciding for someone else. d'Alembert's objection, risk aversion and later evidence on how people actually weigh risks (prospect theory) mark the debate. Lady Montagu's role is documented. The 1-in-200 death rate is an eighteenth-century estimate.

resource.title: Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk, Chapter 4 ('The French Connection')
resource.creator: Peter L. Bernstein (John Wiley & Sons, 1996)
resource.why: A vivid history of how Pascal, Fermat and the problem of points turned gamblers' puzzles into the mathematics of risk, including Pascal's triangle and his Wager. It adds the human story around the arithmetic the lesson teaches. Bernstein was a historian of finance, so later chapters lean toward markets.
resource.verified_how: Not verified by web search (the session's shared search budget was exhausted, for writer and verifier alike). Book, author, publisher and year are certain; the chapter number and title agree with the verifier's recollection but are from memory. Confirm before use. No URL. Alternative: Keith Devlin, The Unfinished Game (2008), a short book on the 1654 letters.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Distributions: the bell curve and fat tails
days.headline_hint: Fukushima Daiichi Was Built for a 5.7-Meter Tsunami. The Wave That Came Was More Than Twice as High.
days.concept: A probability distribution's shape decides what 'typical' and 'extreme' mean. In thin-tailed (bell-curve) worlds extremes are vanishingly rare and averages rule. In fat-tailed (power-law) worlds the largest events dominate, so the biggest one on record is a poor guide to the next.
days.focus: Teaches distributions as the full map of outcomes, the normal distribution and why its tails fall off so fast, and power-law (fat) tails and why they make records and averages unreliable. Shows how to read a return period ('1-in-100-year') correctly. Uses Fukushima's design basis, earthquake statistics and Houston's floods, and flags that changing conditions can shift the distribution itself.
key_concepts: return period and annual exceedance probability
stationarity (whether the distribution itself is changing)
days.model_or_equation: Normal tail: P(X > μ + kσ) falls off roughly like e^(−k²/2), so a 5σ event is about 1 in 3.5 million. Power-law tail: P(X > x) ∝ x^(−α), which falls off only as a power. Gutenberg-Richter law: log10 N(≥M) = a − bM with b ≈ 1, about ten times fewer quakes per unit of magnitude. Return period T: annual probability 1/T, and the chance of at least one event in n years is 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ. A '100-year' flood has about a 26% chance in 30 years.

story.title: A seawall built for the biggest wave anyone had planned for
story.hook: The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, on Japan's Pacific coast, was licensed in the 1960s against a design tsunami of about 3.1 meters. In 2002 its operator, TEPCO, raised that to about 5.7 meters using the Japan Society of Civil Engineers' assessment method. The reactor buildings of units 1-4 stood on ground about 10 meters above sea level. In 2008 an internal TEPCO study, based on a 2002 government assessment of earthquake risk, calculated that a large offshore earthquake could send a wave up to about 15.7 meters. The company had not acted on it by 2011. At 2:46 p.m. on 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck offshore. Within the hour, waves of roughly 13-15 meters swept over the site, flooding emergency diesel generators and electrical switchgear. Three reactor cores melted.
story.puzzle: Engineers had planned for the largest tsunami they judged credible, and had then raised that number. How could the real wave be more than twice as high, and was it a once-in-a-millennium freak or a predictable kind of surprise?
story.payoff: If tsunami heights followed a bell-shaped distribution, a wave more than twice the design value would be almost impossible. But earthquakes and tsunamis have fat tails: the largest events are far bigger than typical ones, and the instrumental record is short. The biggest wave in a century of data therefore badly understates what a thousand years can bring. The region's Jōgan tsunami of 869 was the kind of evidence that pointed there. Designing to the largest event on record is designing to a sample, not to the tail.
sources: The National Diet of Japan Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission, Official Report (2012)
IAEA, The Fukushima Daiichi Accident: Report by the Director General (2015)
TEPCO, Fukushima Nuclear Accidents Investigation Report (2012)

days.application: Earthquakes follow the Gutenberg-Richter law (Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter, 1944): each step up of one magnitude brings about ten times fewer quakes, but each step releases about 32 times more energy. The largest quakes therefore dominate the total energy released. Houston had the Memorial Day flood (May 2015), the Tax Day flood (April 2016) and Hurricane Harvey (August 2017), each described as a '500-year' event in parts of the region. Worked example: a true 1-in-500-year event has a 0.2% chance each year, so three in three years at one place would be wildly improbable. The likelier explanations are that the labels applied to different places and measures, that the distribution shifted with paving and a warming climate, or that the tails were fatter than the estimates assumed. A '100-year' flood has about a 26% chance of occurring at least once during a 30-year mortgage.

builds_on.why: A distribution is Day 11's list of outcomes and probabilities extended to every possible value. The expected value of a fat-tailed quantity can be dominated by rare extremes.
A fat tail is a power law, which Day 3 showed is a straight line on a log-log plot, the standard way to spot one in data.

across.link: City sizes have a fat-tailed, roughly power-law distribution. George Kingsley Zipf noted in 1949 that a country's second-largest city tends to be about half the size of its largest, the third about a third, and so on (Zipf's law). 'The average city' therefore describes almost nobody's city. The fit is best among the largest cities and debated further down.

days.apply_question: The Thames Barrier, operating since 1982, was designed to protect London against a tidal flood with roughly a 1-in-1,000 chance in any year: what would have to be true of the tail of North Sea storm-surge heights, and of sea level over the barrier's life, for that number to stay trustworthy?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mathematics of distributions and return periods, and the heavy-tailed statistics of earthquake sizes. Debated: whether Fukushima's tsunami was foreseeable. TEPCO's own 2008 estimate and the 869 Jōgan tsunami are cited on one side, and Japanese criminal and civil courts have reached opposite conclusions on former executives' liability. Also debated is how much of Houston's run of floods reflects climate change, urban development or loose labelling; attribution studies found Harvey's rainfall made heavier and more likely by warming. Taleb's broad critique of bell-curve thinking is influential, and its sweep is contested.

resource.title: The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable, Chapter 15 ('The Bell Curve, That Great Intellectual Fraud')
resource.creator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb (Random House, 2007; 2nd ed. 2010)
resource.why: The most influential argument that bell-curve thinking misleads wherever extremes dominate, framed as his 'Mediocristan' versus 'Extremistan.' Read it as a named perspective: a polemic, sharper than the evidence in places, whose sweep statisticians dispute but whose core point about fat tails is standard.
resource.verified_how: Not verified by web search (the session's shared search budget was exhausted, for writer and verifier alike). Book, author, publisher and year are certain; the chapter number and title agree with the verifier's recollection but are from memory. Confirm before use. No URL.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Networks: nodes, links, hubs and small worlds
days.headline_hint: Milgram Mailed Folders to Strangers in Nebraska. The Ones That Reached a Boston Stockbroker Took About Six Steps. Most Never Arrived.
days.concept: A network's structure (how many links each node has, whether a few hubs hold most of them, how clustered neighbourhoods are, and whether a few shortcuts bridge distant clusters) decides how fast things spread across it and how failures cascade through it.
days.focus: Teach networks as nodes and links, then two surprises: a few random shortcuts make a highly clustered world 'small' (Watts & Strogatz 1998), and heavy-tailed degree distributions create hubs that speed spreading and concentrate risk. The angle: Milgram's chains show both how short the paths are and how fragile the search is, and the 2003 blackout shows structure deciding how far a local fault spreads.
days.model_or_equation: Idealized random network of N nodes, each with about k links: about k^L nodes lie within L steps, so the typical path length is L ≈ ln N / ln k. With N = 8 billion people and k = 100 acquaintances: L ≈ 22.8 / 4.6 ≈ 5. Watts and Strogatz showed that real networks can keep the high clustering of a lattice and still reach path lengths this short once a small fraction of links are random long-range shortcuts.

story.title: Folders from Nebraska for a Boston stockbroker
story.hook: In the mid-1960s the Harvard social psychologist Stanley Milgram sent folders to 296 volunteers, 196 in Nebraska and 100 in the Boston area, with one instruction: get this document to a stockbroker you have never met, who works in Boston and lives in Sharon, Massachusetts, but pass it only to someone you know on a first-name basis, who must do the same. 217 starters sent it on, and 64 chains reached him (Travers & Milgram, Sociometry, 1969; Milgram had described an earlier round of the experiment in Psychology Today in 1967). The completed chains needed 5.2 intermediaries on average, the seed of 'six degrees of separation', and nearly half of them reached him through the same three people in their last steps. Of the 296 folders, nearly four in five never arrived.
story.puzzle: Most people's friends also know each other, so a social world looks like a tight local cluster. How can strangers more than a thousand miles apart be linked in about six steps? And if the world is that small, why did most of the chains die?
story.payoff: Watts and Strogatz (Nature, 1998) showed that a handful of long-range ties, such as an old roommate in another state or a business contact, collapse the path length while leaving clustering high. Short paths therefore exist, and hubs like Milgram's three funnellers shorten them further. But a path that exists is not a path that gets found. Each forwarder sees only his own links, and every step risks a drop-out, so a chain's chance of surviving falls exponentially with its length. That is why most never arrived, a point Judith Kleinfeld (2002) pressed against the 'six degrees' legend.
sources: Travers & Milgram, 'An Experimental Study of the Small World Problem', Sociometry 32(4), 1969
Milgram, 'The Small-World Problem', Psychology Today 1(1), May 1967 (an earlier round)
Watts & Strogatz, 'Collective dynamics of small-world networks', Nature 393:440-442, 1998
Kleinfeld, 'The Small World Problem', Society 39(2), 2002

days.application: The Northeast blackout of 14 August 2003. FirstEnergy's control-room alarm software had failed, and several 345-kV lines in northern Ohio sagged into overgrown trees and tripped. Each trip pushed power onto neighbouring lines, and a cascade that began at about 4:06 pm cut power within minutes to about 50 million people in eight US states and Ontario (US-Canada Power System Outage Task Force, final report, April 2004). The network's structure decided how a local fault spread. Watts and Strogatz's own 1998 paper had analysed the western US power grid as a small-world network. In the chain, the grid is a recurring system at the physical-constraint and engineering links.

builds_on.why: Path length is a logarithm. If each person knows k others, about k^L people lie within L steps, so L ≈ log N / log k, which is exponential reach read with Day 2's logs.
Hubs come from heavy-tailed degree distributions. These are Day 12's fat tails, where a few nodes hold far more links than the average suggests and dominate how things spread.

across.link: The nervous system of the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, whose 302 neurons and their connections were mapped from electron micrographs by John White, Sydney Brenner and colleagues (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 1986). In the same 1998 Nature paper that analysed the power grid, Watts and Strogatz showed that this wiring diagram is a small world: far more clustered than a random network of the same size, yet with paths between neurons almost as short. The same clustering-plus-shortcuts mathematics describes a social network and a nervous system.

days.apply_question: In April 2010 ash from Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull volcano closed much of northern Europe's airspace for about six days, and roughly 100,000 flights were cancelled. Using degree, hubs and path length, explain why travellers were stranded on routes between cities nowhere near the ash.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mathematics of path length, clustering and shortcuts (Watts & Strogatz 1998), and that a local failure can cascade through a grid (2003 Task Force report). Debated: how small the world really is. Milgram's starters were not random and most chains failed (Kleinfeld 2002), though later studies by email (Dodds, Muhamad & Watts, Science 2003) and on Facebook (Backstrom et al., 'Four Degrees of Separation', 2012) also found short paths. Also debated: how common true power-law 'scale-free' networks are (Broido & Clauset, Nature Communications 2019, against Barabási and other defenders).

resource.title: The Science of Six Degrees of Separation
resource.creator: Veritasium (Derek Muller)
resource.why: A short, visual tour of Milgram's experiment and the network explanation of why short paths exist, with modern online measurements. It lets Logan see the clustering-plus-shortcuts picture that the lesson can only describe.
resource.verified_how: An earlier build pass's web search corroborated the title, the Veritasium channel and an August 2015 date through secondary listings (thetvdb.com; a glasp.co page carrying YouTube ID TcxZSmzPw8k; ScienceAlert). No youtube.com URL appeared, so there is no link. This verification pass could not search again (the shared search budget was exhausted, and WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here).
