days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Game theory: strategy when others choose too
days.headline_hint: The Program That Could Never Beat a Single Opponent Won the Tournament. Twice.
days.concept: When your payoff depends on what others choose, the stable outcome is an equilibrium in which no one gains by changing course alone. In the prisoner's dilemma that equilibrium leaves everyone worse off, unless the game repeats often enough for reciprocity to pay.
days.focus: Teach payoff matrices, dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium through the prisoner's dilemma, then show why repetition (the 'shadow of the future') makes reciprocal strategies like TIT FOR TAT viable. The angle: in Axelrod's tournament a strategy that can never outscore its partner wins on total points. Also teach the limits: TIT FOR TAT is not best everywhere, because noise favours more forgiving strategies.
key_concepts: repeated game and the shadow of the future
days.model_or_equation: Prisoner's dilemma payoffs satisfy T > R > P > S and 2R > T + S. Axelrod used T = 5 (temptation), R = 3 (reward for mutual cooperation), P = 1 (punishment for mutual defection) and S = 0 (sucker's payoff). In one round, defecting is dominant, so (1, 1) is the equilibrium even though (3, 3) is available. If the game repeats with probability w of another round, TIT FOR TAT resists invasion only if w ≥ max[(T−R)/(T−P), (T−R)/(R−S)] = max(0.5, 0.67). With these payoffs that is about 2/3 (Axelrod 1984).

story.title: A tournament won by the shortest program
story.hook: In 1980 Robert Axelrod, a political scientist at the University of Michigan, published the results of a computer tournament. Game theorists from economics, psychology, sociology, political science and mathematics had sent programs to play the repeated prisoner's dilemma against every other entry, 200 moves a match. Fourteen entries came in, plus a program that moved at random. The winner was among the simplest: TIT FOR TAT, submitted by Anatol Rapoport of the University of Toronto, which cooperates on the first move and then copies whatever its opponent did last. Axelrod ran a second round with 62 entries from six countries, and every entrant knew who had won the first; Rapoport entered TIT FOR TAT again, and it won again.
story.puzzle: TIT FOR TAT can never score more than the program it is playing. At best it ties, and against a defector it loses by a little. How can a program that never wins a single match win the whole tournament?
story.payoff: The tournament counted total points, not matches won. Against cooperative 'nice' programs TIT FOR TAT earned the mutual-cooperation payoff of 3 per move, while programs that tried to exploit others dragged themselves and their partners down toward 1. It is nice (never the first to defect), retaliatory, forgiving and clear, so cooperating is the best reply to it whenever future rounds matter enough. That is the repeated game's escape from the one-shot dilemma.
sources: Axelrod, 'Effective Choice in the Prisoner's Dilemma', Journal of Conflict Resolution 24(1), 1980
Axelrod, 'More Effective Choice in the Prisoner's Dilemma', Journal of Conflict Resolution 24(3), 1980
Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation (Basic Books, 1984)

days.application: The SUV 'arms race' on American roads. In 'The Arms Race on American Roads' (Journal of Law and Economics, 2004), Michelle J. White found that a heavier vehicle protects its own occupants and raises the risk to everyone it hits. She estimated that for every fatal crash avoided by the occupants of a light truck or SUV, several more fatal crashes involving others occur (her figure was at least four). Each household's safest individual choice pushes the fleet toward an outcome that is worse for all. The analogy to the prisoner's dilemma breaks where buyers want SUVs for reasons other than safety. In the chain this is the consequences link of the car, driven by choices made at adoption.

builds_on.why: A repeated game's value is Day 11's expected value. Each future payoff is weighted by the probability w that the game continues, so cooperation pays only when the future is likely enough.

Each player optimizes his own payoff, as in Day 8. Game theory shows that separate individual optima can combine into an outcome worse for everyone, so individual optimization does not guarantee a collective one.

across.link: The 'live and let live' system in the trenches of the First World War (Tony Ashworth, Trench Warfare 1914-1918: The Live and Let Live System, 1980), which Axelrod analysed as a repeated prisoner's dilemma in The Evolution of Cooperation (1984, ch. 4). Units facing each other for months held back their fire because they would meet again. High command broke the truce with raids and rotations, which shortened the shadow of the future.

days.apply_question: Each member of a cartel like OPEC gains by quietly pumping above its quota while the others hold back. Why can such a cartel hold together at all?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the game-theoretic results (mutual defection as the equilibrium of the one-shot dilemma, and the conditions for cooperation in repeated play). Debated: how far Axelrod's tournaments generalize. When moves are noisy or mistaken, more forgiving strategies such as generous TIT FOR TAT or win-stay, lose-shift (Nowak & Sigmund, Nature 1993) beat TIT FOR TAT, and how much real-world cooperation the model explains is contested. The SUV figure is one study's estimate (White 2004), not a consensus number.

resource.title: The Evolution of Trust
resource.creator: Nicky Case (2017)
resource.why: A free interactive explainer built on Axelrod's tournaments. Logan plays the repeated prisoner's dilemma himself and watches how repetition, payoffs and mistakes change which strategy wins, which a written lesson can only describe.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge: a widely cited free interactive piece by Nicky Case (2017). It could not be checked by web search (the session's shared search budget was exhausted, and WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited by title and creator without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know I: Bayes' theorem and base rates
days.headline_hint: An Expert Told the Jury the Odds Were 1 in 73 Million. He Had Answered the Wrong Question.
days.concept: Bayes' theorem says how much evidence should change a belief: multiply the prior odds by the likelihood ratio, which is how much more probable the evidence is under one explanation than under its rival. A rare event is strong evidence only if it is much rarer under the rival explanation.
days.focus: Teach Bayes in odds form and in natural frequencies, and show that the base rate (prior) and the likelihood ratio are both indispensable. The prosecutor's fallacy confuses P(evidence | innocent) with P(innocent | evidence). The angle: the Sally Clark case, where a tiny probability of the evidence under innocence was read as a tiny probability of innocence.
days.model_or_equation: Bayes' theorem in odds form: posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds, that is, P(H1|E)/P(H2|E) = [P(E|H1)/P(E|H2)] × [P(H1)/P(H2)]. Mammography in natural frequencies: a prior of 1%, sensitivity of 90% and a false-positive rate of 9% give P(cancer | positive) = 9 / (9 + 89) ≈ 9%.

story.title: 1 in 73 million at Chester Crown Court
story.hook: On 9 November 1999 a jury at Chester Crown Court convicted Sally Clark, a solicitor from Wilmslow, Cheshire, of murdering her baby sons Christopher (who died in 1996, aged 11 weeks) and Harry (who died in 1998, aged 8 weeks). The paediatrician Professor Sir Roy Meadow had testified that in an affluent, non-smoking family like hers the chance of one sudden infant death was about 1 in 8,543. Squaring it, he put the chance of two at about 1 in 73 million, and likened it to backing an 80-to-1 outsider in the Grand National four years running and winning each time. In October 2001 the Royal Statistical Society publicly stated that the figure had no statistical basis. In January 2003 the Court of Appeal quashed her convictions, chiefly because a pathologist had not disclosed microbiology results suggesting Harry had a bacterial infection; she had spent more than three years in prison, and she died in 2007.
story.puzzle: If the innocent explanation had only a 1-in-73-million chance, doesn't that make guilt all but certain? What exactly is wrong with that reasoning?
story.payoff: Two things were wrong. First, squaring assumed the two deaths were independent, but genetic and household factors make a second cot death in a family far likelier than the first. Second, and deeper, 1 in 73 million is P(two deaths | innocence), not P(innocence | two deaths): the prosecutor's fallacy. The jury needed to compare two rival explanations, both extremely rare: a double cot death, and a mother murdering two babies. The mathematician Ray Hill (2004) estimated that double SIDS was several times likelier than double murder. Bayes' odds form makes that comparison explicit.
sources: Royal Statistical Society, statement on the Sally Clark case, October 2001
R v Clark [2003] EWCA Crim 1020
Hill, 'Multiple sudden infant deaths - coincidence or beyond coincidence?', Paediatric and Perinatal Epidemiology 18(5), 2004
Nobles & Schiff, 'Misleading statistics within criminal trials: the Sally Clark case', Significance 2(1), 2005

days.application: Mammography read in natural frequencies (Gigerenzer et al., 'Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics', Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2007). Of 1,000 women screened, about 10 have breast cancer and 9 of them test positive, while about 89 of the 990 healthy women also test positive. A positive result therefore means cancer in only about 9 of 98 cases, roughly 1 in 10. When gynaecologists in Gigerenzer's training sessions were given the same facts as percentages, only about one in five chose the right answer. After a short training in natural frequencies, most did.

builds_on.why: Bayes extends Day 11's probability rules. Pascal and Fermat solved the problem of points by multiplying the chances of independent rounds, and that multiplication rule holds only for independent events, which is exactly the assumption Meadow's squaring got wrong. Conditional probability is the new step Bayes adds today.

across.link: The Bayesian search for Air France Flight 447, which crashed into the Atlantic on 1 June 2009. After three search phases failed, France's accident-investigation bureau (BEA) commissioned the US firm Metron to build a probability map: a prior from the aircraft's last known position and earlier crashes, updated by the likelihood that each past search would have missed the wreck, including the chance that both underwater locator beacons had failed. The wreckage was found in April 2011 after about a week of searching the most probable area (Stone et al., 'Search for the Wreckage of Air France Flight AF 447', Statistical Science 29(1), 2014). It is the same prior-times-likelihood update, used to decide where to look.

days.apply_question: In the Metropolitan Police's live facial-recognition trials in London, an independent University of Essex review (2019) found that only 8 of 42 computer-generated matches could be confirmed as correct. How can a system that is accurate on almost every face it scans still produce mostly false alarms?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Bayes' theorem is a theorem, and the prosecutor's fallacy is a recognized error (Royal Statistical Society, 2001). Debated: how probabilistic evidence should be put to juries (in R v Adams, 1996-97, the Court of Appeal disapproved of teaching juries Bayes' theorem), and how to interpret probability itself (degrees of belief or long-run frequencies). In fairness, Clark's convictions were quashed chiefly on undisclosed medical evidence, with the statistical testimony criticised alongside it.

resource.title: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs
resource.creator: 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), 2019
resource.why: It draws Bayes' theorem as areas, so updating a prior becomes something Logan can see rather than a formula to memorize. It reinforces the natural-frequency method the lesson uses.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge (3Blue1Brown, December 2019). It could not be re-checked by web search (the shared search budget was exhausted, and WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know II: Sampling and the margin of error
days.headline_hint: The Literary Digest Counted 2.4 Million Ballots and Called the Wrong President. Gallup Asked Far Fewer People and Called the Winner.
days.concept: A sample tells you about a population only if it was drawn at random. Then its error is predictable and shrinks with the square root of the sample size, while bias from who gets asked, or who answers, does not shrink at all.
days.focus: Teach random sampling, sampling distributions, the central limit theorem, the standard error and the margin of error (±1.96 SE for 95%), and separate them from selection bias and non-response bias. The angle: the Literary Digest's 2.4 million biased replies against Gallup's far smaller sample, then how the Current Population Survey turns about 60,000 households into the monthly unemployment rate.
key_concepts: standard error and margin of error
days.model_or_equation: For a proportion p estimated from a simple random sample of size n: standard error SE = √[p(1−p)/n], and the 95% margin of error ≈ 1.96 × SE. At p = 0.5, n = 1,000 gives about ±3.1 points and n = 2.4 million about ±0.06 points. Quadrupling n only halves the margin, and no value of n removes bias.

story.title: The poll that counted 2.4 million ballots
story.hook: In autumn 1936 the Literary Digest, whose mail-in straw polls had picked the winner of every presidential election since 1916, mailed about 10 million ballots to Americans, drawn largely from telephone directories, car-registration lists and its own subscriber rolls. About 2.4 million came back, and at the end of October the magazine forecast that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt with about 57% of the vote. On 3 November Roosevelt won about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of 48 states. George Gallup, polling a far smaller sample, had forecast a Roosevelt win, and months ahead he had even predicted roughly the wrong figure the Digest would publish. The Digest was gone within two years.
story.puzzle: How can 2.4 million answers lose to a sample a tiny fraction of the size?
story.payoff: Size controls only random error, and the Digest's error was bias. Its lists over-represented better-off households in a year when votes split sharply by income. Peverill Squire's 1988 analysis of 1937 survey data argued that Landon supporters were also more likely to mail their ballots back (non-response bias), and that this did more damage than the lists. A random sample of a few thousand carries a margin of error of a couple of points, while a biased sample of millions is precisely wrong. Gallup's sample was not truly random either (he used quotas): it underestimated Roosevelt by several points, and the same method failed outright in 1948.
sources: Literary Digest, final 1936 poll issue (31 October 1936)
Squire, 'Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed', Public Opinion Quarterly 52(1), 1988
Freedman, Pisani & Purves, Statistics (4th ed., 2007), chapter on sample surveys

days.application: The US Current Population Survey, run by the Census Bureau for the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It interviews about 60,000 households a month, chosen by a stratified random design and rotated in and out (four months in, eight out, four in), to estimate the unemployment rate for a labour force of roughly 170 million. BLS states that a month-to-month change in the rate must be about 0.2 percentage point to be statistically significant at 90% confidence. Response rates have fallen sharply over the past decade, so the main threat now is bias, not sample size.

builds_on.why: The central limit theorem is why Day 12's bell curve governs sampling error. Averages of many random draws are approximately normal, which is what lets a margin of error use the normal distribution's 1.96.
The margin of error falls as n to the power −1/2, a power law like Day 3's, so four times the sample buys only half the error.

across.link: Department of Commerce v. United States House of Representatives, 525 U.S. 316 (1999). The Supreme Court held that the Census Act forbids using statistical sampling to produce the population counts that apportion House seats, even though statisticians argued that a count adjusted by a well-designed sample could beat an enumeration that undercounts some groups. It is the sampling question decided as law.

days.apply_question: In the 2015 UK general election, final polls with thousands of respondents each showed the Conservatives and Labour roughly tied, but the Conservatives won by about six and a half points. The British Polling Council's inquiry (Sturgis et al., 2016) blamed unrepresentative samples. Why would doubling every poll's sample size not have fixed the miss?
days.evidence_note: Settled: sampling theory and the central limit theorem. Debated: why the Digest failed. The traditional story blames its mailing lists, while Squire (1988) argued that non-response mattered more. Also debated today: how well weighting can repair falling response rates in surveys like the CPS.

resource.title: Sampling Methods and Bias with Surveys: Crash Course Statistics #10
resource.creator: Crash Course (PBS Digital Studios), hosted by Adriene Hill (2018)
resource.why: A brisk visual survey of random, stratified, cluster and convenience sampling and the biases each invites. It gives Logan the vocabulary for judging any poll he reads.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the Crash Course Statistics series (2018), in which episode 9 is 'Controlled Experiments' and episode 10 this one. The episode number and length could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know III: Significance, p-values and systematic error
days.headline_hint: At Six Sigma, Neutrinos Outran Light. A Loose Cable Said Otherwise.
days.concept: A p-value (or 'sigma' level) is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if nothing but chance were at work. It measures surprise under random error alone, so it says nothing about systematic errors in the apparatus or about how plausible the claim was in the first place.
days.focus: Teach the null hypothesis, the p-value, sigma levels on the normal curve and significance thresholds (p < 0.05 is about 2σ; 5σ is about 1 in 3.5 million), the look-elsewhere effect, and the difference between statistical (random) and systematic error. The angle: OPERA's six-sigma 'faster-than-light' neutrinos, undone by a fibre-optic connector, and the prior from supernova 1987A that should have tempered the excitement.
days.model_or_equation: p = P(data at least this extreme | null hypothesis true). On the normal curve: 2σ ≈ 0.05 (two-sided), 3σ ≈ 0.003 (two-sided), 5σ ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁷ (one-sided, about 1 in 3.5 million), 6σ ≈ 1 in a billion (one-sided). Total error = statistical error (shrinks with more data) + systematic error (does not).

story.title: Neutrinos that arrived 60 nanoseconds early
story.hook: On 23 September 2011, at a packed seminar at CERN in Geneva, physicists from the OPERA experiment reported that neutrinos fired from CERN through 730 km of rock to detectors under Italy's Gran Sasso mountain had arrived about 60 nanoseconds sooner than light would have. The result rested on more than 15,000 neutrino events and was significant at six sigma, after months of internal checks, and the team asked other physicists to find the mistake. In February 2012 OPERA disclosed two suspect components in its timing system, one of them a fibre-optic connector that had not been fully plugged in. In March the neighbouring ICARUS experiment measured neutrinos travelling at light speed, OPERA's spokesperson resigned, and by June 2012 OPERA's corrected result agreed with Einstein.
story.puzzle: Six sigma means that if chance alone were at work, a deviation this large would turn up about once in a billion tries. How can a result that improbable under 'nothing is going on' still be wrong?
story.payoff: Six sigma measured only random error, the scatter of timing across thousands of events. A badly seated connector shifted every measurement the same way. That is a systematic error, which no amount of data averages away and no p-value can see. The prior was also low: neutrinos from supernova 1987A, about 168,000 light-years away, arrived within hours of its light, whereas at OPERA's speed they would have arrived about four years early. That is why physicists demand both five sigma and independent replication.
sources: OPERA Collaboration, 'Measurement of the neutrino velocity with the OPERA detector in the CNGS beam', arXiv:1109.4897 (2011)
CERN press releases, 23 September 2011 and 8 June 2012
ICARUS Collaboration, neutrino velocity measurement, Physics Letters B (2012)

days.application: The Higgs boson and the five-sigma rule. On 4 July 2012 at CERN, the ATLAS and CMS experiments each reported a new boson near 125 GeV at about five sigma, a threshold of roughly 1 in 3.5 million, while a typical medical study calls p < 0.05 (about two sigma, or 1 in 20) 'significant'. Physics demands more because of the look-elsewhere effect (a search across many mass windows will throw up chance bumps somewhere), because of systematic errors, and because of a history of three-sigma signals that vanished. Medicine accepts less because of the cost of delay, because biology supplies prior plausibility, and because it relies on replication across independent trials.

builds_on.why: A p-value measures the random scatter described by Day 16's standard error. The Literary Digest showed that error from a biased procedure does not shrink with more data, and the same was true of OPERA's connector.
Bayes explains why six sigma did not settle the matter. A p-value is P(data | no effect), not P(no effect | data), and a claim that contradicts relativity starts with very low prior odds.

across.link: BICEP2's announcement on 17 March 2014 of primordial gravitational waves, seen as B-mode polarization of the cosmic microwave background at high significance. A joint analysis with Planck's dust maps (2015) showed the signal was consistent with dust in our own galaxy. It is the same lesson in cosmology: high significance said nothing about a systematic source the analysis had underestimated.

days.apply_question: The ISIS-2 trial (The Lancet, 1988), which showed that aspirin cuts deaths after a heart attack, also split its results by patients' astrological birth sign: for those born under Gemini or Libra, aspirin appeared not to help. Why should no one believe that subgroup finding, whatever p-value it carried?
days.evidence_note: Settled: what a p-value means, and the cause of the OPERA error. Debated: where significance thresholds should sit and whether p-values should be central at all. The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement warned against bright-line use. Benjamin et al. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2018) proposed p < 0.005 for new claims, while Lakens et al. (2018) argued that each field should justify its own threshold.

resource.title: The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose
resource.creator: Ronald L. Wasserstein & Nicole A. Lazar (American Statistical Association), The American Statistician 70(2), 2016
resource.why: The statistics profession's own short, plain-language statement of what a p-value does and does not mean. It is the authoritative reference for the misreadings this lesson warns against.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge; it is open access, and some citations give the title as 'The ASA's Statement on p-Values'. It could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know IV: Correlation, confounding and Simpson's paradox
days.headline_hint: Berkeley Admitted 44% of Men and 35% of Women. Department by Department, the Gap Mostly Ran the Other Way.
days.concept: An association between two variables can be produced, hidden or even reversed by a third variable that affects both (a confounder), so a relationship seen in pooled data can point the opposite way within every subgroup (Simpson's paradox).
days.focus: Teach correlation versus causation, confounding, stratification (comparing like with like), and Simpson's paradox as an effect of weighted averages. Add Judea Pearl's point that the data alone cannot say whether to pool or split; that takes a causal story. The angle: in Berkeley's 1973 admissions the apparent bias lay in which departments women applied to, and in IIHS death rates the car and its driver are tangled together.
days.model_or_equation: An overall rate is a weighted average of group rates: p_overall = Σ w_i p_i, where the weight w_i is each department's share of a group's applications. If women's applications are weighted toward departments with a low p_i, their overall rate can be lower even when their p_i is equal or higher in every department.

story.title: Autumn 1973 admissions at Berkeley
story.hook: In autumn 1973 the University of California, Berkeley's graduate division looked at its admissions. Of 8,442 men who applied, 44% were admitted; of 4,321 women, 35%. The associate dean, the anthropologist Eugene Hammel, worried that the gap looked like discrimination, so with the statistician Peter Bickel and J. William O'Connell he broke the figures down department by department. In most of the large departments women were admitted at rates equal to or higher than men's, and in four of the six largest, women did better. Their paper in Science (February 1975) found, if anything, a small bias in women's favour.
story.puzzle: How can women be admitted less often overall, yet as often or more often in most of the departments that admit them?
story.payoff: Department was a confounder. Women applied disproportionately to the departments that admitted few applicants of either sex, while men applied more often to departments that admitted most. The overall rate is a weighted average, and the weights differed. Splitting by department compares like with like. The authors then pushed the question upstream and asked why women were steered toward the more crowded fields, a reminder that removing one confounder can open another causal question.
sources: Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, 'Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data from Berkeley', Science 187(4175):398-404, 1975
Freedman, Pisani & Purves, Statistics (4th ed., 2007), ch. 2
Pearl & Mackenzie, The Book of Why (2018)

days.application: Driver death rates by car model from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), measured as deaths per million registered vehicle years. The rates vary widely between models, but IIHS itself cautions that they reflect who drives each model and where, not only the car. Muscle cars, driven disproportionately by young men, show high rates, and minivans, driven largely by parents, show low ones. To isolate the car you must stratify or adjust for driver age, sex and road type. In the chain this is the consequences link of the car.

builds_on.why: An overall rate is a probability-weighted average, Day 11's expected value. Changing the weights (who applied where) can move the total against every group's own rate.
Simpson's paradox is about conditioning: P(admit | woman) differs from P(admit | woman, department). It takes the same care about what you condition on that Bayes demanded.

across.link: Kidney-stone treatments (Charig et al., BMJ 1986, analysed as Simpson's paradox by Julious & Mullee, BMJ 1994). Open surgery succeeded in 78% of cases overall and percutaneous nephrolithotomy in 83%, yet open surgery did better for both small stones (93% against 87%) and large ones (73% against 69%). Surgeons had reserved open surgery for the harder, larger stones.

days.apply_question: Early in the COVID-19 pandemic Italy's overall case-fatality rate was higher than China's, yet within every age group Italy's rate was lower (von Kügelgen, Gresele & Schölkopf, 2021). What explains the reversal?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the arithmetic of Simpson's paradox and the Berkeley figures. Subtle and debated: which table to trust is not a purely statistical question. If the third variable is a confounder, split by it; if it lies on the causal path (a mediator), splitting can hide a real effect (Pearl & Mackenzie 2018). Whether Berkeley's departmental pattern reflected earlier steering of women is a further, open question the 1975 authors raised themselves.

resource.title: The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect, chapter 6, 'Paradoxes Galore!'
resource.creator: Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie (Basic Books, 2018)
resource.why: Pearl uses causal diagrams to show when to split data and when to pool it. That is the step beyond today's lesson, and Logan will need it to judge causal claims in his book.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book (2018), whose chapter 6 treats Simpson's paradox alongside other paradoxes. The chapter title could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted). It is a book, so there is no link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know V: Regression and regression to the mean
days.headline_hint: Tall Parents Had Shorter Children, and Short Parents Taller Ones. So Why Didn't Everyone End Up Average?
days.concept: Whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated, cases that are extreme on one are, on average, less extreme on the other (regression to the mean). A change seen after picking out extremes can therefore be pure statistics rather than an effect.
days.focus: Teach the regression line and the correlation coefficient as Galton built them, show why regression to the mean follows from r < 1 (part of any extreme is luck that does not repeat), and show how it fools evaluations that select on extremes. The angle: in Galton's heights, children of tall parents were nearer the average, yet the population's spread did not change; and speed cameras are sited after a run of crashes.
days.model_or_equation: The regression line in standard units: predicted (y − ȳ)/s_y = r × (x − x̄)/s_x. With r = 0.5, a parent 2 standard deviations above average predicts a child 1 standard deviation above. Regression runs both ways: the parents of tall children are also predicted to be closer to average, so the spread of the population need not shrink.

story.title: Galton's 928 children
story.hook: In 1886 Francis Galton, Charles Darwin's half-cousin, a pioneer of weather maps and fingerprinting and the man who had coined the word 'eugenics' three years earlier, published 'Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature'. From family records gathered partly by offering cash prizes, he took the heights of 928 adult children of 205 couples. He multiplied women's heights by 1.08 to put them on the men's scale and averaged each couple into a 'mid-parent'. Tall parents had tall children, but not as tall: on average a child was only about two-thirds as far from the population mean as the mid-parent. Short parents had short children, but they too were nearer the average.
story.puzzle: If every generation's extremes are pulled toward the middle, why hasn't the human race converged on a single height? From one generation to the next, the spread of heights stayed the same.
story.payoff: Regression is not a force. Height is only partly predictable from parents (the correlation is well below 1), and the rest is variation that scatters children in both directions. The children of extreme parents are, on average, closer to the mean, but the children of average parents scatter out to fill the extremes, and average parents are far more numerous. Run it backwards and the same holds: the parents of very tall children are, on average, less tall than their children. Galton saw this himself, and from it statistics gained the regression line and, soon after, the correlation coefficient.
sources: Galton, 'Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature', Journal of the Anthropological Institute 15:246-263, 1886
Stigler, The History of Statistics (Harvard, 1986), ch. 8
Senn, 'Francis Galton and regression to the mean', Significance 8(3), 2011

days.application: Speed cameras in Britain. Fixed cameras were installed at sites chosen because of recent serious crashes, exactly the selection that guarantees some improvement by regression to the mean. The government's 2005 four-year evaluation reported a 42% fall in people killed or seriously injured at camera sites, a figure that did not fully remove the regression effect. Studies that corrected for it (Mountain, Hirst & Maher, 2004-05; the RAC Foundation's 2013 review by Richard Allsop) still found real but smaller reductions, about a quarter fewer fatal and serious collisions at fixed-camera sites in the RAC Foundation's estimate. In the car chain this is the regulation link, at enforcement.

builds_on.why: Regression turns Day 18's correlation into a prediction line. Regression to the mean is the same kind of lurking explanation as a confounder: something other than the treatment that moves the numbers.
Galton's heights followed Day 12's bell curve. Regression to the mean is what happens whenever two jointly normal measurements are imperfectly correlated.

across.link: Daniel Kahneman's Israeli Air Force flight instructors (Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011, ch. 17). Instructors believed that praising a good landing made the next one worse and berating a bad one made the next one better. Kahneman showed that both were regression to the mean in noisy performance, misread as the effect of praise and punishment.

days.apply_question: From 2010 the federal School Improvement Grants programme paid for turnarounds at each state's persistently lowest-achieving schools. If those schools' test scores rose in the following years, what comparison would you need before crediting the grants?
days.evidence_note: Settled: regression to the mean is a mathematical consequence of imperfect correlation. Debated: how large speed cameras' true effect is once regression is removed; UK estimates differ with site selection and method (the 2005 national evaluation against the RAC Foundation's 2013 review). Galton built these tools partly in pursuit of eugenics. The brief should state that plainly: the mathematics stands apart from his aims, and his aims are a matter of moral judgment.

resource.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow, chapter 17, 'Regression to the Mean'
resource.creator: Daniel Kahneman (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011)
resource.why: A Nobel laureate's account of how regression to the mean fools experts, told through the flight-instructor story and everyday examples; the next chapter, 'Taming Intuitive Predictions', shows how to correct for it. It carries today's concept into everyday judgment.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book. The chapter numbers and titles could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted). It is a book, so there is no link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know VI: Randomized controlled trials
days.headline_hint: Dozens of Studies Said Hormone Therapy Protected Women's Hearts. The Trial Found the Opposite.
days.concept: Assigning a treatment by chance makes the treated and untreated groups alike on average in every respect, measured or not, so a difference in their outcomes estimates the treatment's causal effect. Control groups, blinding and outcomes fixed in advance protect that estimate.
days.focus: Teach randomization as the cure for confounding (selection bias falls to zero in expectation), along with placebo controls, blinding, intention-to-treat and the hazard ratio. The angle: decades of observational evidence that hormone therapy protected the heart were overturned by the Women's Health Initiative trial in 2002 (the healthy-user effect), and in the 1954 Salk polio trial only the randomized arm gave a clean answer.
days.model_or_equation: Observed difference between treated and untreated = causal effect + selection bias. Random assignment makes the selection bias zero on average, leaving the causal effect plus chance, which Day 17's tests measure. In the WHI trial the hazard ratio for coronary heart disease was 1.29 (95% CI 1.02-1.63), meaning about a 29% higher rate in the hormone arm.

story.title: The trial stopped in 2002
story.hook: Through the 1980s and 1990s large observational studies, most prominently the Nurses' Health Study, which followed tens of thousands of American nurses, found that women who took estrogen after menopause had far lower rates of heart disease, by some estimates about half. Millions of women were prescribed hormone therapy partly on that basis. From 1993 the Women's Health Initiative tested the claim properly, randomly assigning 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50-79 at 40 US centres to daily estrogen plus progestin or an identical placebo. On 31 May 2002 its independent monitoring board recommended stopping the trial early, and in July 2002 the NIH announced why. Women taking hormones had more heart disease, not less (hazard ratio 1.29), along with more breast cancer, strokes and blood clots, though fewer hip fractures and colorectal cancers.
story.puzzle: How could dozens of studies, following tens of thousands of real women for years, get the direction of the effect wrong? And why should one trial outweigh them all?
story.payoff: The observational studies compared women who chose hormones with women who did not, and the two groups differed. The women who chose hormones tended to be wealthier, more educated, slimmer and more likely to see doctors and follow their advice. This is the healthy-user effect, a confounder that no statistical adjustment fully captured. Random assignment broke the link between who a woman was and which pill she received, so the only systematic difference between the arms was the hormone. Later analyses suggest the risk depends on age and time since menopause (the 'timing hypothesis', still debated), but the trial ended the practice of prescribing hormones to prevent heart disease, and the US Preventive Services Task Force now recommends against using them to prevent chronic conditions.
sources: Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators, JAMA 288(3):321-333, 2002
Stampfer et al., Nurses' Health Study, New England Journal of Medicine 325:756-762, 1991
Hulley et al. (HERS trial), JAMA 280:605-613, 1998
Rossouw et al., JAMA 297:1465-1477, 2007

days.application: The 1954 Salk polio vaccine field trial, directed by Thomas Francis Jr. About 1.8 million children took part. In some areas (in 11 states) children whose parents consented were randomly assigned, double-blind, to vaccine or an identical placebo; elsewhere every consenting second-grader was vaccinated, and first- and third-graders served as observed controls. In the randomized areas confirmed polio struck about 28 per 100,000 vaccinated children against about 71 per 100,000 given placebo (Freedman, Pisani & Purves's summary of Francis's 1955 report). The observed-control comparison was distorted. Its vaccinated group came only from consenting families, who tended to be better off, and in that era such families' children were more vulnerable to polio; its controls also came from other grades, and the doctors diagnosing them could know who had been vaccinated. The randomized arm is why the announcement of 12 April 1955 that the vaccine worked was believed.

builds_on.why: Randomization is the general answer to Day 18's confounding. It balances every lurking variable at once, including the ones no one thought to measure.
Once the arms are alike, the only question left is chance. Day 17's significance tests and confidence intervals (such as WHI's 1.02-1.63) measure exactly that.

across.link: Online A/B tests are randomized controlled trials run at software scale. Ron Kohavi and Stefan Thomke ('The Surprising Power of Online Experiments', Harvard Business Review, 2017) describe a minor change to how Bing displayed ad headlines that a randomized experiment showed raised revenue by about 12%. The idea had sat unprioritized for months because no one's intuition expected much from it.

days.apply_question: Observational studies linked higher blood vitamin D to less cancer and heart disease, but the VITAL trial (Manson et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2019), which randomly assigned 25,871 US adults to vitamin D or placebo, found no significant reduction in either. What most plausibly explains the gap?
days.evidence_note: Settled: in the WHI population (average age about 63), estrogen plus progestin did not prevent coronary events and modestly increased them. Debated: the 'timing hypothesis', whether women who start therapy near menopause face different heart risks, and how far trial results generalize; current menopause-society guidance treats hormone therapy as reasonable for symptom relief in many women under 60, and in November 2025 the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warnings added to hormone-therapy labels after the WHI, a move some specialists welcomed and others questioned. Also debated more broadly: RCTs estimate average effects in the people enrolled, and can be impractical or unethical (Deaton & Cartwright, Social Science & Medicine, 2018).

resource.title: Controlled Experiments: Crash Course Statistics #9
resource.creator: Crash Course (PBS Digital Studios), hosted by Adriene Hill (2018)
resource.why: A clear visual walk-through of control groups, placebos, blinding and random assignment, the trial machinery the lesson names, at Logan's level.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the Crash Course Statistics series (2018). The episode number and length could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know VII: Natural experiments
days.headline_hint: John Snow Couldn't Randomize London's Water. Two Companies' Tangled Pipes Did It for Him.
days.concept: When an accident of nature, history or policy sorts people into treated and untreated groups as if at random, comparing how the two groups change (before versus after, treated versus untreated: difference-in-differences) can reveal a cause that no one could ethically or practically randomize.
days.focus: Teach natural experiments and difference-in-differences, together with the assumption that carries all the weight: parallel trends, meaning the groups would have moved together without the treatment. Cover the threats to that assumption. The angle: John Snow's 1854 'grand experiment' in South London, where two water companies' pipes ran down the same streets, and the 1995 repeal of the federal 55-mph limit as a state-by-state natural experiment.
days.model_or_equation: Difference-in-differences: effect ≈ (treated_after − treated_before) − (control_after − control_before). The subtraction removes anything that changed for both groups alike. The estimate is valid only if the two groups would have followed parallel trends without the treatment.

story.title: Two water companies, one street
story.hook: In the summer of 1854 cholera returned to London, and the physician John Snow, who believed the disease spread through sewage-tainted water, saw a chance in South London. Two companies piped water there. The Southwark and Vauxhall Company still drew from the Thames at Battersea, downstream of the city's sewage outfalls, while the Lambeth Company had moved its intake in 1852 upstream to Thames Ditton, above the reach of the tide. Their pipes ran down the same streets, often to neighbouring houses, rich and poor alike, and Snow went door to door finding out which company supplied each house where someone had died, using a chemical test for salt when residents did not know. His 1855 tables show that in the first seven weeks of the epidemic, houses supplied by Southwark and Vauxhall suffered about 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses, Lambeth's about 37 and the rest of London about 59.
story.puzzle: Snow could not assign anyone to drink sewage. How could a comparison of households he did not choose prove that water carried cholera, when those households differed in a hundred other ways?
story.payoff: The companies' intermixed pipes did the assigning. As Snow wrote, more than 300,000 people were divided into two groups 'without their choice, and in most cases without their knowledge': groups alike in wealth, occupation and neighbourhood, differing in their water. There was also a 'before'. In the 1849 epidemic, when both companies drew from the polluted tidal Thames, their customers died at broadly similar rates; after Lambeth moved upstream, the rates diverged. Comparing before and after across treated and untreated groups is the logic now called difference-in-differences.
sources: Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed. (London, 1855), Table IX
Freedman, 'Statistical Models and Shoe Leather', Sociological Methodology 21:291-313, 1991

days.application: The 1995 repeal of the national maximum speed limit. Congress repealed it in the National Highway System Designation Act, signed on 28 November 1995, and states then raised their limits at different times, some not at all, creating a natural experiment. Friedman, Hedeker & Richter ('Long-term effects of repealing the national maximum speed limit in the United States', American Journal of Public Health, 2009) compared states and road types over 1995-2005 and attributed about 12,500 additional deaths (a 3.2% rise in road fatalities) to the higher limits. This is the regulation link of the car chain, and the second half of Day 8's 55-mph story.

builds_on.why: A natural experiment imitates Day 20's randomized trial, and its whole case rests on the assignment being as good as random.
Difference-in-differences subtracts out confounders that are fixed or shared by both groups, the lurking variables Day 18 showed can fake or hide an effect.

across.link: The Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944-45, when a German blockade cut rations in the western Netherlands to starvation levels for about six months, with sharp start and end dates and unaffected regions nearby. Ravelli, Stein & Susser (New England Journal of Medicine, 1976) found higher obesity rates at age 19 among men exposed early in gestation, and Heijmans et al. (PNAS, 2008) found epigenetic differences about six decades later. It is a natural experiment in prenatal development that no one could ethically run.

days.apply_question: On 1 April 1992 New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 an hour while neighbouring eastern Pennsylvania did not, and David Card and Alan Krueger surveyed about 400 fast-food restaurants on both sides before and after. What must be true of the Pennsylvania restaurants for this comparison to reveal the wage rise's effect on jobs?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Snow's data, and the design logic of difference-in-differences. Debated: the 'as-if random' and parallel-trends claims of any particular natural experiment. For speed limits the size of the effect is debated: Friedman et al. (2009) estimated about 12,500 extra deaths over 1995-2005, while earlier work on the 1987 rise to 65 mph on rural interstates (Lave & Elias, Accident Analysis & Prevention, 1994) argued that higher limits could lower statewide fatality rates by drawing traffic onto safer interstates and freeing police for other roads. The 2021 economics Nobel (Card, Angrist, Imbens) honoured these methods, and critics stress how much they rest on untestable assumptions.

resource.title: Natural experiments help answer important questions (Popular science background, Prize in Economic Sciences 2021)
resource.creator: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences / NobelPrize.org
resource.why: The Nobel committee's plain-language account of how natural experiments and difference-in-differences identify causes, using the New Jersey minimum-wage study and others. It is authoritative and free, and it shows the method beyond epidemiology.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the 2021 Nobel materials. The exact title could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know VIII: Replication and publication bias
days.headline_hint: Amgen Tried to Reproduce 53 Landmark Cancer Findings. Six Held Up.
days.concept: When journals and researchers favour striking, significant results and studies are small, the published record overstates effects: some findings are flukes and most are inflated. A finding therefore counts only once it survives replication, ideally preregistered, and a whole literature must be checked for missing studies.
days.focus: Teach publication bias (the file drawer), low statistical power and the winner's curse, flexible analysis (p-hacking), and the defences: replication, preregistration and registered reports, and funnel plots in meta-analysis. The angle: Amgen's 6 of 53 and the later Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, and then the lead-crime literature shrinking under a meta-analysis.
days.model_or_equation: Positive predictive value of a significant finding (Ioannidis, 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False', PLoS Medicine 2005): PPV = (1 − β)R / [(1 − β)R + α], where R is the prior odds that a tested hypothesis is true, 1 − β is the power and α is the significance threshold. With R = 1:10, power 0.2 and α = 0.05: PPV = 0.02 / (0.02 + 0.05) ≈ 0.29. Most 'significant' findings would be false even before any bias.

story.title: 53 landmark papers in an Amgen lab
story.hook: In March 2012 C. Glenn Begley, who had spent a decade running cancer research at the biotech company Amgen, and Lee Ellis of the MD Anderson Cancer Center reported in Nature what happened when Amgen's scientists tried to reproduce 53 'landmark' preclinical cancer studies, papers from respected labs and top journals of the kind on which drug programmes are built. The findings held up in 6. Begley told Reuters about one case: his team had repeated an experiment 50 times without getting the published result, and the lead author said his lab had got it once in six tries but published it because it made the best story. A year earlier, scientists at Bayer had reported that their in-house work fully matched the published data in only about a fifth to a quarter of 67 projects.
story.puzzle: Every one of those papers passed peer review with statistically significant results. If p < 0.05 means a fluke only one time in twenty, how could almost nine in ten fail to hold up?
story.payoff: p < 0.05 is a threshold for each test, not a guarantee about what gets published. Positive results get written up and accepted, while negative ones go into the file drawer. Small experiments that clear the bar do so partly by luck, so their effects are inflated (the winner's curse); flexible analyses let researchers find significance somewhere; and novel drug targets start with low prior odds. Together these can make a literature of significant results mostly unreliable, which is why replication, not a single paper, is the unit of evidence. In fairness to the critics, Amgen could not name the papers, so its own result could not be checked. The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (eLife, 2021), which did publish its targets, found that replication effects were on average about 85% smaller than the originals.
sources: Begley & Ellis, 'Raise standards for preclinical cancer research', Nature 483:531-533, 2012
Prinz, Schlange & Asadullah, 'Believe it or not: how much can we rely on published data on potential drug targets?', Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 10:712, 2011
Errington et al., Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, eLife, 2021
Sharon Begley, 'In cancer science, many discoveries don't hold up', Reuters, 28 March 2012

days.application: The lead-crime hypothesis under meta-analysis. Higney, Hanley & Moro ('The lead-crime hypothesis: A meta-analysis', Regional Science and Urban Economics, 2022) pooled 529 estimates from 24 studies. They found evidence of publication bias across several tests of the kind a funnel plot illustrates, and once they corrected for it the average effect was far smaller than the headline claims; on their reading, lead's decline explains at most a minority of the fall in US crime. It shows meta-analysis at work on a public debate that returns in Day 49's case on leaded gasoline.

builds_on.why: Publication bias is Day 17's p < 0.05 used as a gate. If only results that cross the threshold are published, the threshold no longer means what it says.
Ioannidis's argument is Bayes. The chance that a significant finding is true depends on the prior odds of the hypothesis as well as on the test, exactly Day 15's base rates.

across.link: The Open Science Collaboration's 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science' (Science, 2015) repeated 100 studies from three leading 2008 journals. 97% of the originals had significant results, but only about 36% of the replications did, and the replicated effects averaged about half the original size. Psychology's replication crisis follows the same mechanism as Amgen's.

days.apply_question: Ego depletion, the idea that exerting self-control uses up a limited resource, was supported by roughly 200 published experimental tests, and a 2010 meta-analysis found a medium-to-large effect. Yet a preregistered replication in 23 laboratories with more than 2,000 participants (Hagger et al., 2016) found an effect near zero. How can both results have been reported honestly?
days.evidence_note: Settled: publication bias and low power inflate published effects, and this is documented across many fields. Debated: how bad the problem is in a given field, since replication rates vary by field and by how 'success' is defined. For lead and crime, the true size of the effect is debated: Higney, Hanley & Moro (2022) found publication bias and a much smaller average effect, while other researchers maintain that lead contributed meaningfully to the crime decline.

resource.title: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
resource.creator: Veritasium (Derek Muller), 2016
resource.why: Shows with real cases how significance thresholds, p-hacking and the file drawer let false findings into print, and how preregistration and replication push back. It makes the mechanism easy to remember.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge (Veritasium, 2016). It could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know IX: Goodhart's law
days.headline_hint: Volkswagen's Diesels Passed Every Official Test. On the Road They Emitted Up to 40 Times the Limit.
days.concept: When a measure becomes a target, people optimize the number rather than the thing it was meant to indicate, so the measure drifts away from the reality it once tracked and can even move against it (Goodhart's law; Campbell's law).
days.focus: Teach why an indicator works only while no one is optimizing against it. A proxy captures only part of a goal, and pressure finds the gap through gaming, distortion or outright fraud. The defences are to measure outcomes directly and unpredictably, use several measures, and keep judgment in the loop. The angle: Volkswagen's defeat device as the extreme case, the legal gap between EU laboratory and road fuel figures, and NHS waiting-time targets that both cut waits and were gamed.
days.model_or_equation: Let the measure M equal the goal G plus a gap: M = G + gap. Before M is a target, the gap is small noise, so M tracks G. Once M is rewarded, effort flows to whichever of G or the gap is cheaper to move, and the gap is usually cheaper. Goodhart (1975): 'Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.' The popular wording, 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure', is Marilyn Strathern's (1997).

story.title: On the road, not on the rollers
story.hook: In 2013 a small team from West Virginia University's Center for Alternative Fuels, Engines and Emissions, hired by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), which expected the tests to show that US diesel cars ran clean, fitted portable emissions analysers to a Volkswagen Jetta, a VW Passat and a BMW X5 and drove them on US roads, mostly in California. The BMW largely met the limits, but the Jetta emitted nitrogen oxides at roughly 15 to 35 times the US standard and the Passat at roughly 5 to 20 times (report published May 2014). Volkswagen attributed the gap to technical problems for more than a year. On 18 September 2015 the US Environmental Protection Agency issued a notice of violation: about 482,000 VW and Audi 2.0-litre diesels from model years 2009-2015 carried software that recognized the official laboratory test and switched on full emissions controls only then, and on the road emitted up to 40 times the limit. Days later Volkswagen admitted that about 11 million cars worldwide carried the software, and its chief executive resigned.
story.puzzle: These cars passed every official test. How could a car be clean exactly when it was measured and many times dirtier the rest of the time? And why had the test, which was meant to stand for road driving, become so easy to tell apart from it?
story.payoff: The test had become the target. The official cycle is a fixed, published speed trace driven on rollers with the steering wheel still, so a car's software can recognize it. Once passing it was what counted, engineering effort flowed into passing it rather than into clean driving. Volkswagen's software was fraud, the extreme case, but the same pressure also produced legal gaming: the ICCT found that the gap between official and real-world fuel use of new EU cars grew from under 10% around 2001 to about 40% by the mid-2010s. That is Goodhart's law. Europe's answer was a real-driving emissions test, run on the road with portable analysers.
sources: US EPA, Notice of Violation to Volkswagen AG, Audi AG and Volkswagen Group of America, 18 September 2015
Thompson et al. (West Virginia University CAFEE), In-Use Emissions Testing of Light-Duty Diesel Vehicles in the United States, final report to the ICCT, May 2014
ICCT, From Laboratory to Road (2017 update)
Goodhart, 'Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience' (1975); Campbell, 'Assessing the impact of planned social change', Evaluation and Program Planning 2:67-90, 1979

days.application: English NHS targets of the 2000s: 75% of life-threatening ambulance calls reached within 8 minutes, A&E patients admitted, transferred or discharged within 4 hours, and GP appointments within 48 hours. They cut reported waits, and they were gamed. Bevan & Hood ('What's measured is what matters: targets and gaming in the English public health care system', Public Administration, 2006) documented response times bunched just under 8 minutes, patients held in ambulances outside A&E so the clock had not started, and GP practices refusing to book more than 48 hours ahead (a voter confronted Tony Blair with this on BBC Question Time in April 2005). Yet comparing England with Scotland, which lacked such targets, Propper et al. (Journal of Public Economics, 2010) found that the waiting-time targets did shorten long waits. The measure was both gamed and partly real.

builds_on.why: Goodhart's law is Day 8's optimization aimed at the wrong objective. An optimizer goes wherever the measured quantity is best, and if that quantity is a proxy, the optimum slides to where proxy and goal part ways.
Making p < 0.05 a publication target is Goodhart's law in science. Once significance was the prize, p-hacking optimized the number rather than the truth it was meant to signal.

across.link: Specification gaming in reinforcement learning, catalogued by DeepMind researchers (Victoria Krakovna and colleagues, 'Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity', DeepMind blog, April 2020). In one of their examples, from Popov et al. (2017), a simulated robot arm rewarded for the height of the bottom face of a red Lego block learned to flip the block over instead of stacking it on the blue one. The optimizer exploited the gap between the measured proxy (the face's height) and the goal (a stacked block), which is Goodhart's law with a machine as the gamer.

days.apply_question: In 1902 the French colonial government of Hanoi, fighting rats in the city's new sewers, paid a bounty for every rat tail handed in, and officials soon noticed tailless rats alive in the streets. What could the bounty have paid for instead that would have been harder to game?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Volkswagen facts, which the company admitted (it pleaded guilty in US federal court in 2017). Debated: the net effect of targets. Bevan & Hood (2006) documented gaming of English NHS targets, while Propper et al. (2010), comparing England with Scotland, found that the targets did cut waiting times, and both findings can be true. Value judgment: how much gaming is an acceptable price for a measure that also drives real improvement.

resource.title: The Tyranny of Metrics (chapter 1, 'The Argument in a Nutshell', and the chapter on medicine)
resource.creator: Jerry Z. Muller (Princeton University Press, 2018)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the two chapters
resource.why: A historian's short, case-rich argument about how measurement turned into target-chasing in medicine, schools, policing and business. It is useful for Logan's book as a sceptical counterweight to 'what gets measured gets managed'.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book (2018). The chapter titles could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted). It is a book, so there is no link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 1: Car I, the car by the numbers (spiral visit)
days.headline_hint: Bertha Benz Bought Fuel at a Pharmacy and Drove 106 Kilometres. How Did Her Husband's Noisy Toy Take Over the World?
days.concept: The car's rise can be read in numbers: an energy-density advantage, a price falling exponentially, adoption tracing an S-curve, and harms best judged as rates with confounders in view. But the numbers form a loop, not a line. Rules came before the car, the invention came before the need, and the car's consequences rewrote its rules.
days.focus: Walk the car through Logan's chain using only the mathematics just taught: energy density, log-scale prices, S-curve adoption, flat optima, natural experiments, Goodhart's law, rates and confounding, and the SUV game. Go deep on those links, preview the rest, and show the chain as a loop: Britain's road-speed law came about twenty years before Benz's car, the invention came before any need, and deaths fed back into law.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, reinforcing (adoption): more cars lead to more filling stations, paved roads and dealers, which make cars more useful, which leads to more cars (from one pharmacy in Wiesloch to a fuel network). R2, reinforcing (price): more output brings lower unit cost and price, which brings more buyers (the Model T; the mechanism is taught in Engineering). B1, balancing (saturation): as households acquire cars, the pool of new buyers shrinks, which is the S-curve's ceiling. B2, balancing (harm): more driving brings more deaths, which bring safety law and engineering and a lower death rate per mile, after a delay of decades (1920s death rates; the 1966 federal safety act). Reversals: regulation before invention (Britain's 1865 Locomotive Act) and invention before need (Benz's 1886 patent). Unintended consequences: the 55-mph limit saved little fuel because the optimum was flat, though it probably saved lives, and regulation by fixed test cycle invited gaming (Volkswagen).

story.title: Bertha Benz drives to her mother's, August 1888
story.hook: Early one morning in August 1888 (tradition gives the 5th), Bertha Benz, 39, left the house in Mannheim with her teenage sons Eugen and Richard and drove her husband Karl's three-wheeled Patent-Motorwagen toward her mother's home in Pforzheim, about 106 km away, without telling him. On the way she bought ligroin, a petroleum solvent, from the town pharmacy in Wiesloch, and had a shoemaker nail leather onto the wooden brake blocks. Family tradition adds that she cleared a blocked fuel line with her hatpin and insulated a bare wire with a garter. She arrived after dark and sent Karl a telegram. Some forty years later the United States alone had about 23 million registered cars.
story.puzzle: Why did a smoky, unreliable machine that needed a pharmacy for fuel and a cobbler for brakes become the machine of the century? And how much of that can numbers alone explain?
story.payoff: The numbers explain part of it. Hydrocarbon fuel packs roughly fifty times a battery's energy per kilogram; Ford's prices fell exponentially; adoption climbed an S-curve; and the harms, read as rates with confounding in mind, fell per mile even as totals rose. The numbers cannot explain why people wanted cars, how the engine was made to work, or how credit and streets were reorganized around them, and later blocks teach those. And the chain did not run in order: Britain had capped road locomotives at walking pace about twenty years before Bertha's drive.
sources: Karl Benz, German patent DRP 37435 (filed 29 January 1886)
Mercedes-Benz Classic archive and the Bertha Benz Memorial Route (Mannheim-Pforzheim)
US Federal Highway Administration, Highway Statistics Summary to 1995 (motor vehicle registrations)
World Health Organization, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023

days.application: The car, followed link by link from Bertha Benz's 1888 drive to the roughly 1.19 million road deaths a year today. This is Car I of four visits; Car II (Day 103), Car III (Day 216) and Car IV (Day 293) go deep on the links previewed here.

builds_on.why: Physical constraint: Day 1's order-of-magnitude comparison of gasoline (about 12 kWh/kg) and lithium-ion packs (about 0.15-0.25 kWh/kg) explains why liquid fuel won the first century.
Production: the Model T's price falls as a roughly straight line on Day 2's log scale, a near-constant percentage decline each year.
Adoption: US registrations from 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929 trace Day 7's S-curve, and the Depression's stall shows that the ceiling is an assumption.
Regulation: the 1995 repeal of the 55-mph limit is Day 21's natural experiment, the best evidence on what the limit did for safety.

across.link: Bertha Benz's fuel was ligroin, a light petroleum fraction sold as a cleaning solvent at Wiesloch's town pharmacy, which the town now promotes as 'the world's first filling station'. The energy-density advantage at the physical-constraint link is chemistry, the energy released when carbon-hydrogen bonds burn, which the Energy, Chemistry & Materials block takes up in Day 70, Combustion and energy density.

days.apply_question: Pew Research Center found that about 35% of US adults owned a smartphone in 2011, and about nine in ten by the mid-2020s. Read as an S-curve, as this case read car registrations, what does that predict about US smartphone ownership over the next decade?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the energy-density gap, the Model T's price fall, US registration growth, the fall in US deaths per mile, and WHO's estimate of about 1.19 million road deaths in 2021 (a modelled global estimate, not a count). Debated: how much of the falling death rate any single cause explains (road design, vehicle engineering, medicine, seat-belt and drink-driving laws all changed together); how large the effect of speed-limit changes was (Friedman et al. 2009 against earlier sceptics); and how far heavier vehicles raise net deaths (White 2004). Value judgment: who gained (mobility, livelihoods, freedom of movement), who paid (more than half of road deaths are pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, and over 90% occur in low- and middle-income countries, per WHO), and who consented (bystanders and children did not choose the risk). A utilitarian ledger sums lives, time and welfare, while the Christian and natural-law traditions stress duties of care to the vulnerable neighbour. The world without the car is an unknowable counterfactual.

chain.point: In 1888 the car met no pressing need that horses, trams and railways did not, and early buyers wanted novelty and status; by family accounts, Bertha's drive was partly meant to show that the car was practical. Here the invention came before the need. Psychology (Day 159, Motivation and human needs) and Sociology (Car III, Day 216) teach how mobility became a want and then a necessity.

Karl Benz's German patent DRP 37435, filed 29 January 1886, was for a vehicle powered by a gas engine; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach were working in parallel at Cannstatt. History II (Day 224, The invention of invention) and Engineering (Day 91, The internal combustion engine) teach how such inventions arise and how the engine works.

Gasoline stores about 12 kWh per kilogram (33.7 kWh per gallon in the EPA's MPGe convention), while a lithium-ion pack stores about 0.15-0.25 kWh/kg: roughly fifty times less per kilogram, or about fifteen to twenty times less once engine and motor efficiencies are counted. Liquid hydrocarbon fuel is why an 1888 car could carry its range in a small reservoir, and why batteries took a century to compete.

Bertha's repairs on the road, among them leather brake linings nailed on by a shoemaker and, by tradition, a fuel line cleared with a hatpin, were field engineering; after her report Karl added a lower gear for climbing hills. The Engineering block (Days 87-103, with Car II on Day 103) teaches design trade-offs, the engine and mass production.

The Model T touring car cost $850 at its 1908 launch; by 1925 a touring car listed at about $290 and a runabout at about $260. That is a fall of roughly three times in nominal dollars, about 6-7% a year and roughly a straight line on a log scale, and steeper after inflation; more than 15 million were built by 1927. Why the price fell (the moving assembly line, learning curves) is left to Engineering (Days 96-97). Financing is named only at CFA level: by family accounts Bertha's dowry had backed Karl's workshop, and mass ownership rode on instalment credit after GM founded GMAC in 1919, with most new cars bought on credit by the mid-1920s on most estimates. Car II (Day 103) returns to this.

Regulation came first. Britain's Locomotive Act of 1865 capped road locomotives at 4 mph in the country and 2 mph in towns, with a man walking ahead carrying a red flag, about twenty years before Benz's car; the 1896 Act raised the limit to 14 mph, which was celebrated by the London-to-Brighton 'Emancipation Run'. A century later the 1974 national 55-mph limit sat near a flat fuel-economy optimum, so it could save little fuel (Day 8). Its 1995 repeal became a natural experiment in road deaths (Day 21). And Volkswagen's defeat device showed regulation by test cycle failing under Goodhart's law (Day 23).

US automobile registrations rose from about 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929 (FHWA), the steep middle of an S-curve. The Depression then flattened them for several years, a reminder that the curve's ceiling is an assumption, not a law (Day 7).

WHO's Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 estimates about 1.19 million road deaths in 2021, more than half of them pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists and over 90% in low- and middle-income countries. In the US, deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell from about 24 in 1921 to about 1.3 in the early 2020s. That is a rate, and it must be read with confounding in mind, because roads, cars, medicine and drinking norms all changed together (Day 18). Meanwhile heavier vehicles protect their own occupants at others' expense, a prisoner's-dilemma-like arms race (Day 14).

Consequences fed back into rules and designs. Rising deaths and Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed (1965) were followed by the 1966 National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act. The 1973 oil shock produced the 55-mph limit and, in 1975, fuel-economy standards whose looser light-truck rules are often blamed, contestably, for the later SUV boom. Government (Day 243, How regulation works), Law (Day 254, Tort and product liability) and Engineering (Day 101, Crashworthiness) teach these loops.

resource.creator: Vaclav Smil (2020)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the transport section's short essays
resource.why: Smil's short essays lead with the numbers, several of them on cars, engines and transport, and they model exactly this case's method of reading a technology through energy, prices, adoption and risk as orders of magnitude and rates. Smil returns in the Energy block.
