days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Cape Town Set a Date for Its Taps to Run Dry. Then the Date Kept Moving.
days.concept: A stock changes only through its flows, so it keeps rising or falling until inflow equals outflow, and a steady inflow alone does not hold it steady.
days.focus: Teaches stocks and flows as the basic grammar of systems, using the integral (Day 5) as a modelling language. The angle is a well-documented failure of intuition: even highly trained people expect a stock to stop rising as soon as its inflow stops rising.
days.model_or_equation: S(t) = S(0) + integral from 0 to t of [inflow - outflow] dt; equivalently dS/dt = inflow - outflow. The stock is constant only when inflow = outflow. If net outflow is steady, time to empty = S / (outflow - inflow).

story.title: A city counts down to Day Zero
story.hook: In January 2018, after three dry winters, Cape Town's leaders warned its roughly four million residents that the city was likely to reach 'Day Zero': the day its supply dams fell to 13.5% of capacity and most household taps would be shut off, leaving people to queue for a daily ration at collection points. That month the city put the date in mid-April, at one point 12 April. From 1 February households were limited to 50 litres per person per day. As use fell, toward roughly half the 1.1-1.2 billion litres a day the city had drawn in 2015, the projected date slid back week after week into May, June and July. By March officials said Day Zero was unlikely to come in 2018, and the winter rains then refilled the dams.
story.puzzle: How could officials name the day a city would run dry months in advance, and why did cuts in daily use push that date back by weeks at a time?
story.payoff: The dams are a stock and Day Zero was simply usable stock divided by net outflow. With summer inflow near zero, every cut in outflow lengthened the time to empty disproportionately, and winter inflow then refilled the stock. The date moved because the flows moved.
sources: City of Cape Town dam-level and Day Zero updates, January-March 2018
Gina Ziervogel, 'Unpacking the Cape Town Drought: Lessons Learned' (African Centre for Cities, University of Cape Town, 2019)
Mike Muller, 'Cape Town's drought: don't blame climate change', Nature 559 (2018)

days.application: Atmospheric CO2 as a bathtub: emissions are the inflow and land and ocean sinks the outflow (roughly half of emissions are currently absorbed), so the concentration keeps rising while emissions exceed removal even if emissions stay flat. In Sterman and Booth Sweeney's experiments (Climatic Change 80, 2007), most of some 200 MIT graduate students drew CO2 trajectories that broke the rule of accumulation. The students were highly educated, most of them trained in science, engineering or economics. Many believed that holding emissions near current rates would stabilize the concentration, even though emissions would still exceed removal.

builds_on.why: A stock is the integral of its net flow; the fundamental theorem is the bathtub stated in calculus.
Net flow is the stock's derivative, so the sign of the net flow, not its trend, decides whether the stock rises or falls.

across.link: The clean-surplus relation (ending equity = beginning equity + net income - dividends) ties the balance sheet's stocks to the income statement's flows; it is the same bathtub identity.

days.apply_question: The 1922 Colorado River Compact gave 7.5 million acre-feet a year each to the Upper and Lower Basins. The split rested on river flows measured in an unusually wet early-twentieth-century period, and Mexico was later promised 1.5 million more. This century the river has averaged closer to 12-13 million. Using stock-and-flow reasoning, explain why Lake Mead fell to roughly a quarter full by 2022 even in years when the river ran at an ordinary flow.
days.evidence_note: Settled: stock-flow accounting is mass balance. Cape Town avoided Day Zero through a mix of household cuts, cuts to agricultural allocations and the return of winter rain; how much each mattered is debated locally. The Sterman results are robust across replications of the bathtub task, though exact percentages vary by sample, so the brief should say 'most' rather than quote a single figure unless it confirms one.

resource.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer, Chapter 1 'The Basics'
resource.creator: Donella H. Meadows (ed. Diana Wright), Chelsea Green, 2008
resource.why: The standard primer on stocks, flows and dynamic equilibrium, with the bathtub diagrams this whole block uses; it is the block's main text.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass: the shared search budget ran out and direct fetches fail here. Cited from knowledge of the book, whose Part One opens with Chapter One, 'The Basics'. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Two Cities, One Flu: Philadelphia Held a Parade, St. Louis Closed Its Doors, and Their Peak Death Rates Split Eightfold.
days.concept: A reinforcing loop amplifies whatever change it gets and a balancing loop pushes back toward a limit or goal, and most system behaviour comes from how the two interact.
days.focus: Teaches loop polarity: how to trace a closed chain of cause and effect and tell whether it amplifies or counteracts. The 1918 epidemic shows a reinforcing contagion loop meeting balancing loops (susceptibles running out, and deliberate closures), and the Matthew effect shows a reinforcing loop inside science itself.
days.model_or_equation: A causal-loop diagram marks each link with its polarity. A loop is reinforcing if it has an even number of negative (opposite-direction) links, including none, and balancing if it has an odd number. For the epidemic there are three loops. R: infected -> contacts -> new infections -> infected. B1: infected -> susceptibles depleted -> fewer new infections. B2: deaths -> closures -> fewer contacts.

story.title: A parade for 200,000 in a city already infected
story.hook: On 28 September 1918 Philadelphia went ahead with a Liberty Loan parade that drew about 200,000 people to Broad Street, although influenza had already reached the Navy Yard. Within days the city's hospitals were overwhelmed, and its closure order came on 3 October, after the epidemic was already exploding. St. Louis was hit at about the same time. It closed schools, theatres, churches and other gatherings on 7 October, soon after its first civilian cases. Richard Hatchett, Carter Mecher and Marc Lipsitch later reconstructed the weekly death data (PNAS, 2007). Philadelphia's peak excess death rate was about 257 per 100,000 a week; St. Louis's was about 31.
story.puzzle: The same virus struck two large American cities at the same moment. Why did one city's peak climb about eight times higher than the other's?
story.payoff: Each infection fed more infections, a reinforcing loop that the parade fed with contacts. St. Louis switched on a balancing loop early, cutting contacts while case numbers were small. Philadelphia acted only once its epidemic was exploding, so its curve climbed until closures and the slower balancing loop of running out of susceptible people bent it, at a far higher peak.
sources: Hatchett, Mecher & Lipsitch, 'Public health interventions and epidemic intensity during the 1918 influenza pandemic', PNAS 104(18), 2007
Markel et al., 'Nonpharmaceutical interventions implemented by US cities during the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic', JAMA 298(6), 2007

days.application: Robert K. Merton's 'The Matthew Effect in Science' (Science 159, 1968) drew partly on Harriet Zuckerman's interviews with Nobel laureates. Credit and citations flow disproportionately to scientists who are already eminent. That brings them more resources and visibility, and so more credit: a reinforcing loop in how science allocates recognition. Margaret Rossiter's 'Matilda effect' (1993) names the companion pattern, in which women's contributions were credited to men.

builds_on.why: A reinforcing loop with a constant gain is exponential growth; the doubling arithmetic of Day 2 is what the loop produces.
The logistic S-curve is a reinforcing loop handing dominance to a balancing loop as the ceiling nears; today names the loops behind that shape.

across.link: The Kessler syndrome (Kessler and Cour-Palais, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1978): debris collisions create fragments that cause more collisions. It is a reinforcing loop in low Earth orbit, and its only natural balancing loop is slow atmospheric drag.

days.apply_question: On 9 March 2023 depositors tried to pull about $42 billion from Silicon Valley Bank in a single day, and regulators closed it the next morning. Draw the reinforcing loop that drove the run and name the balancing loop that, had it been in place in time, could have broken it.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the loop mechanics and the 1918 differences in peak mortality. Debated: how much the 1918 interventions reduced total deaths rather than flattening and delaying the peak. Hatchett et al. and Markel et al. find real benefits, while Barro (NBER Working Paper 27049, 2020) found the short-lived measures did little to cut overall deaths. The eightfold gap is in peak weekly rates; the gap in total excess deaths was much smaller. The Matthew effect in citations is well replicated; its size, and how far it reflects merit as well as visibility, are debated.

resource.title: Public health interventions and epidemic intensity during the 1918 influenza pandemic
resource.creator: Richard J. Hatchett, Carter E. Mecher & Marc Lipsitch, PNAS 104(18), 2007
resource.why: The source of the story's numbers, with the Philadelphia and St. Louis curves side by side: you can see a reinforcing loop cut early and one left to run.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the paper; PNAS papers of this age are normally free to read. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Jay Forrester Held GE's Orders Constant on a Notepad. The Kentucky Plants Still Hired and Fired in Waves.
days.concept: A balancing loop with a delay overshoots and oscillates, because people act on old information and forget what is already in the pipeline.
days.focus: Teaches why delays turn a goal-seeking balancing loop into a cycle, and why the cycle is usually generated inside the system by its own decision rules rather than by outside shocks. The Beer Game and the bullwhip effect show it in supply chains.
days.model_or_equation: The stock-adjustment ordering rule: orders = expected demand + (desired inventory - actual inventory) / adjustment time, minus a correction for orders already in transit. Sterman (Management Science, 1989) found that players largely ignore the supply-line term, and dropping it is what turns a delayed balancing loop into overshoot and oscillation.

story.title: A factory that made its own boom and bust
story.hook: In the mid-1950s Jay Forrester, a computer pioneer, had just moved to MIT's new school of management. People from General Electric asked him a question about their household-appliance plants in Louisville, Kentucky: why did the plants sometimes run three or four shifts and then, a few years later, lay off half their workers? They blamed the business cycle. Forrester took the plants' own rules for hiring, production and inventory and simulated them by hand on a notebook page. Even with incoming orders held constant, employment rose and fell in waves. He later called this the beginning of system dynamics.
story.puzzle: If the orders coming in were steady, where did the waves of hiring and layoffs come from?
story.payoff: The oscillation came from inside the company. The plants corrected inventory gaps using information that was weeks old and ignored orders already in the pipeline, so each correction overshot and the next overshot the other way. The decision rules produced the cycle, not the market.
sources: Jay W. Forrester, 'The Beginning of System Dynamics', banquet talk to the System Dynamics Society, Stuttgart, 13 July 1989, reprinted in McKinsey Quarterly 1995 no. 4
Jay W. Forrester, Industrial Dynamics (MIT Press, 1961)

days.application: The 2020-21 automotive chip shortage. When the pandemic struck in spring 2020, carmakers cancelled semiconductor orders and chipmakers sold the capacity to electronics firms. Car demand rebounded within months, but new chip supply took many months to arrive, and the industry lost an estimated 7-11 million vehicles of output in 2021 (estimates differ by forecaster). It is a classic bullwhip: small swings in final demand were amplified upstream (Lee, Padmanabhan & Whang, Sloan Management Review, 1997). Real supply shocks compounded it, such as the March 2021 fire at Renesas's Naka plant.

builds_on.why: Today adds a delay to the balancing loop of Day 26; the delay is what converts goal-seeking into oscillation.
Inventory is a stock and orders in transit are a second, hidden stock; ignoring that supply-line stock is the decision error behind the waves.

across.link: Arthur Guyton and colleagues ('Basic oscillating mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes breathing', American Journal of Physiology, 1956) lengthened the blood's path from heart to brain in dogs. The dogs developed Cheyne-Stokes breathing, cycles of deepening and fading breaths and pauses. A delayed chemical feedback loop is one recognized reason the same pattern appears in heart failure, where slow circulation delays the brain's reading of blood carbon dioxide.

days.apply_question: In the late 1920s the German economist Arthur Hanau documented a regular 'pig cycle' in German hog prices. Farmers expand breeding when prices are high, but a decision to breed takes close to a year to become pork on the market. Explain, using a delayed balancing loop, why that arrangement produces repeated price booms and slumps even with steady demand for pork.
days.evidence_note: Settled: delayed balancing loops oscillate (control theory), and the Beer Game result replicates widely (Sterman, Management Science 35(3), 1989). Debated: how much of the 2021 chip shortage was bullwhip amplification and how much was genuine supply shock (the Texas freeze of February 2021, the Renesas fire, pandemic demand for electronics). Forrester's hand simulation held orders constant by design; it does not show that GE's real demand was flat.

resource.title: The Fifth Discipline, Chapter 3 'Prisoners of the System, or Prisoners of Our Own Thinking?'
resource.creator: Peter M. Senge, Doubleday, 1990 (revised 2006)
resource.why: Walks through a full play of MIT's Beer Game, round by round, so you see from the inside how sensible players produce a boom and bust nobody wants.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Jamaica's Reefs Flipped From Coral to Seaweed in a Decade. Getting Them Back Has Taken Far Longer.
days.concept: Some systems have two stable states separated by a threshold, so a push past it flips the system and undoing the push does not flip it back (hysteresis).
days.focus: Teaches alternative stable states: how reinforcing loops can lock in either of two conditions, why change can be sudden after long stability, and why the road back differs from the road in. It also teaches the limits: proving that a real system has two stable states is hard.
days.model_or_equation: Granovetter's threshold model: each person joins if at least r others have joined. With F(r) the share of people whose threshold is r or less, the crowd settles where the share joining equals F(that share). Shifting a single person's threshold can move the system from one equilibrium to another.

story.title: The urchins that vanished from the Caribbean
story.hook: In 1983 an unidentified pathogen swept through the Caribbean and, within about a year, killed most of the long-spined sea urchin Diadema antillarum, commonly more than 90% at a site. On Jamaica's north coast, decades of overfishing had already removed most plant-eating fish, so the urchins were the last major grazers. Hurricane Allen had already broken much of the coral in 1980. Terry Hughes's long-term surveys (Science, 1994) recorded what followed. Coral cover had been around half the reef in the 1970s; it fell to a few percent. Fleshy seaweed rose from a few percent to cover most of the reef.
story.puzzle: Reefs had survived hurricanes and disease before. Why did this combination flip Jamaica's reefs into seaweed, and why didn't the coral simply grow back once the storm damage passed?
story.payoff: With fish and then urchins gone, seaweed escaped grazing and occupied the bare rock coral larvae need. Each year of algae made coral recovery less likely: a reinforcing loop holding a second stable state. Recovery needed more than the passing of the original shock. Where urchins later returned, young corals began to reappear, but only partly and slowly.
sources: Terence P. Hughes, 'Catastrophes, phase shifts, and large-scale degradation of a Caribbean coral reef', Science 265, 1994
Lessios, Robertson & Cubit, 'Spread of Diadema mass mortality through the Caribbean', Science 226, 1984
Edmunds & Carpenter, 'Recovery of Diadema antillarum reduces macroalgal cover and increases abundance of juvenile corals on a Caribbean reef', PNAS 98, 2001

days.application: Mark Granovetter's 'Threshold Models of Collective Behavior' (American Journal of Sociology 83, 1978). Imagine 100 people whose riot thresholds are 0, 1, 2 ... 99. The person with threshold 0 starts, which triggers the person with threshold 1, and so on until all 100 riot. Change the single person with threshold 1 to threshold 2 and only one person riots. Two nearly identical crowds give two different outcomes, so the aggregate tells you little about the crowd's average temperament.

builds_on.why: Alternative stable states exist because reinforcing loops can hold a system in either condition; today is what Day 26's loops do when they compete.
Granovetter's result depends on the whole distribution of thresholds, not its average, the point Day 12 made about distributions.

across.link: Lenton et al., 'Tipping elements in the Earth's climate system' (PNAS, 2008), lists components such as the Greenland ice sheet that may have thresholds and hysteresis: once largely melted, it would not regrow at today's temperatures.

days.apply_question: On 3 September 1967 Sweden switched by law from driving on the left to driving on the right in a single morning (Dagen H). Using the idea of two stable states, explain why the change had to be made all at once rather than by letting drivers switch sides gradually as they chose.
days.evidence_note: Settled: threshold dynamics and hysteresis are well established in models and in some systems, such as shallow lakes (Scheffer et al., Nature 2001). Debated: how common true alternative stable states are on coral reefs. Mumby, Hastings & Edwards (Nature, 2007) support them for Caribbean reefs; Bruno et al. (Ecology, 2009) found coral-to-macroalgae shifts less widespread than claimed. Granovetter's model is a thought experiment, not an estimate of real thresholds.

resource.title: Catastrophic shifts in ecosystems
resource.creator: Marten Scheffer, Steve Carpenter, Jonathan A. Foley, Carl Folke & Brian Walker, Nature 413, 2001
resource.why: The standard short review of alternative stable states, with the ball-in-a-landscape and hysteresis diagrams and real cases from lakes, reefs and deserts.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the paper. It may sit behind Nature's paywall. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: Unintended consequences and fixes that fail
days.headline_hint: After the Big Burn of 1910, America Fought Every Forest Fire. Decades Later, the Fires Came Back Bigger.
days.concept: Purposive action produces consequences nobody intended, and a quick fix that relieves a symptom can, after a delay, strengthen the problem it treats.
days.focus: Teaches Merton's account of why consequences go unanticipated: ignorance, error, the 'imperious immediacy of interest', basic values and self-defeating prediction. It pairs that with the systems archetypes 'fixes that fail' and 'shifting the burden', in which a balancing fix carries a delayed reinforcing side effect. The angle is to respect the limits: hindsight makes every consequence look foreseeable.
days.model_or_equation: The 'fixes that fail' archetype (Senge, 1990) has two loops. A balancing loop: problem -> fix -> problem relieved. A delayed reinforcing loop: fix -> unintended side effect -> problem worse. For fire: fires -> suppression -> fewer fires now; suppression -> fuel accumulates over decades -> larger, hotter fires.

story.title: The two days that made fire the enemy
story.hook: On 20 and 21 August 1910, hurricane-force winds drove dozens of fires together across the northern Rockies of Idaho and Montana. In about two days the 'Big Burn' scorched roughly three million acres. It killed about 85 people, most of them firefighters, and burned a third of the town of Wallace, Idaho. Ranger Ed Pulaski forced some 45 men into an abandoned mine tunnel at gunpoint and held them there as the fire passed; all but a handful survived. The young US Forest Service drew a lesson: put out every fire. In 1935 it formalized the '10 a.m. policy': every fire controlled by ten the next morning.
story.puzzle: The policy worked for decades: burned area fell sharply. Why, by the 2000s, were many western forests burning in fires larger and hotter than anything the old foresters had fought?
story.payoff: Suppression was a balancing fix with a delayed side effect. Dry forests had been shaped by frequent low-intensity fire, and each extinguished fire left fuel that once would have burned off. The stock of fuel grew for decades, so the fires that did escape were more severe. How much of today's megafires this explains varies by forest type, and it competes with warming and spreading settlement.
sources: Timothy Egan, The Big Burn (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2009)
Stephen J. Pyne, Fire in America (Princeton UP, 1982)
US Forest Service history of the 1935 '10 a.m. policy'

days.application: The car's regulation link. The 1975 Energy Policy and Conservation Act set fuel-economy (CAFE) standards in which light trucks faced a looser standard than cars; the car standard rose to 27.5 mpg by 1985. Over the following decades light trucks, SUVs included, rose from about a fifth of new US passenger-vehicle sales to around half by the early 2000s (EPA Automotive Trends Report). Critics such as Keith Bradsher (High and Mighty, 2002) argue the rule helped create the market it exempted. Others give more weight to cheap fuel after 1986, the 1964 'chicken tax' on imported light trucks and changing tastes.

builds_on.why: The fire story is a delay at work: the side effect of suppression accumulated for decades before it showed, so the fix looked successful for a long time.
CAFE targets invited optimization of the measured category, a Goodhart response in which vehicles shifted toward the class the rule treated more leniently.

across.link: In his 1945 Nobel lecture Alexander Fleming warned that underdosing penicillin would breed resistant bacteria. Antibiotic overuse is a 'fix that fails': it relieves infection now while selecting for resistance later.

days.apply_question: In 1935 Queensland's sugar industry released cane toads imported from Hawaii to eat the beetles damaging sugarcane; the toads did little to the beetles and spread across northern Australia. Using Merton's sources of unanticipated consequences, explain which ones were most likely at work in that decision.
days.evidence_note: Settled: fire suppression increased fuel loads and fire severity in historically frequent-fire forests such as southwestern ponderosa pine. Debated: suppression's share in megafires elsewhere, where fire was naturally rare (high-elevation forests, chaparral), against climate warming and the spread of homes into wildland; and how much the light-truck rule caused the SUV boom. Value judgment: whether a policy is wrong because of consequences its makers could not reasonably foresee.

resource.title: The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action
resource.creator: Robert K. Merton, American Sociological Review 1(6), 1936
resource.why: The founding short paper on why consequences go unanticipated, with Merton's own list of causes, so you can test each fix in this lesson against it.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the article. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: The commons: Hardin, Ostrom and shared resources
days.headline_hint: Every Thursday at Noon, Eight Farmers Settle Valencia's Water Fights in Minutes. No Lawyers, No Appeal.
days.concept: An open-access resource tends to be over-used because each user gains the full benefit of taking and bears only part of the cost, but communities often govern shared resources well when the rules fit Elinor Ostrom's design principles.
days.focus: Teaches the commons as a structure: a shared stock that individually rational users over-use. It then challenges Hardin's conclusion that only the state or private property can save a commons, using Ostrom's evidence of long-enduring self-governed commons. The angle is the difference between open access and a governed commons.
days.model_or_equation: Ostrom's eight design principles (Governing the Commons, 1990): (1) clear boundaries of users and resource; (2) rules fitted to local conditions; (3) users help make the rules; (4) monitors accountable to users; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) cheap, quick conflict resolution; (7) outside authorities recognize the right to organize; (8) nested layers for larger systems.

story.title: A court that sits outside a cathedral door
story.hook: Every Thursday at noon, outside the Door of the Apostles of Valencia Cathedral, eight farmers in black smocks sit in a semicircle of chairs. They are the elected síndics of eight irrigation canals that share the water of the river Turia across the huerta, the farmland around the city. A bailiff calls the cases: a farmer who took water out of turn, a neglected ditch. Hearings are spoken, in Valencian, and decided on the spot, with no appeal. Tradition places the Water Tribunal's origins in the Moorish period, about a thousand years ago. Documents from after the Christian conquest of 1238 confirm the irrigation customs it enforces. UNESCO inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.
story.puzzle: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay predicted that a resource shared by self-interested users would be ruined unless the state or private owners took control. How has a farmers' court with no lawyers kept a scarce, shared river from being over-drawn for centuries?
story.payoff: The huerta is not open access. Its users are bounded, they make and enforce their own rules and watch one another, sanctions are graduated, and disputes are settled cheaply and fast: Ostrom's design principles. She studied these Spanish huertas in Governing the Commons (1990, ch. 3) as evidence against Hardin's fatalism.
sources: UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, 'Irrigators' tribunals of the Spanish Mediterranean coast', 2009
Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge UP, 1990), ch. 3
Garrett Hardin, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', Science 162, 1968

days.application: The Ogallala aquifer in western Kansas. Its groundwater is a stock recharged far more slowly than it is pumped. In 2013 farmers in Sheridan County created the state's first Local Enhanced Management Area (Sheridan 6 LEMA), voting to cap their own pumping for five years with a target cut of about 20%. Kansas State University and later remote-sensing evaluations report that water use fell by roughly a quarter to a third, with little reported loss of farm profit relative to neighbouring areas. It is a commons governed by its users with state backing.

builds_on.why: The commons is an n-person prisoner's dilemma: each user's dominant move (take more) produces a collectively worse outcome, and Ostrom's rules work like the repetition and enforcement Day 14 showed can change play.
An aquifer or river is a stock; over-use means outflow persistently exceeding recharge, the bathtub of Day 25.

across.link: Harold Demsetz's 'Toward a Theory of Property Rights' (American Economic Review, 1967) argued that private hunting territories emerged among the Montagnais of the Labrador peninsula once the fur trade made beaver valuable: property rights arising to manage a commons.

days.apply_question: Maine lobstermen have long defended informal fishing territories through 'harbor gangs' that cut the trap lines of outsiders (James Acheson, The Lobster Gangs of Maine, 1988). Which of Ostrom's design principles does that arrangement satisfy, and which does it lack?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Ostrom's large body of comparative evidence that many commons are self-governed for long periods; she won the Nobel Memorial Prize in 2009, the first woman to receive it. Debated: how well the design principles predict success in large, global commons such as the climate. Value judgment: Hardin's 1968 essay also argued for coercive limits on childbearing, a position many critics, Christian and secular ethicists among them, reject.

resource.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action, Chapter 3
resource.creator: Elinor Ostrom, Cambridge University Press, 1990
resource.why: Ostrom's own case studies of long-enduring commons, including the Valencia and Murcia huertas and Swiss and Japanese mountain commons, from which she drew the design principles.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link; the routine should confirm the chapter's case list if it can.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Brunel's Broad Gauge Won the Speed Trials. In May 1892, About 4,000 Men Narrowed It Over One Weekend.
days.concept: When the value of a choice rises with the number of others making it (increasing returns), small early events can lock a whole system onto one path, whether or not it is the best one.
days.focus: Teaches path dependence as a reinforcing loop of adoption, with network effects and switching costs creating lock-in. The angle is the contested part: how often lock-in actually traps us in an inferior technology, with QWERTY as the famous disputed case.
days.model_or_equation: Arthur's adoption model (Economic Journal, 1989), which works like a Polya urn: each new adopter picks technology A with a probability that rises with A's current share. Early random draws decide which technology takes over, and once one dominates, the outcome is effectively locked in.

story.title: The last broad-gauge train out of Paddington
story.hook: In the 1830s Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway on a gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch, chosen for speed and stability. Most other British lines used George Stephenson's 4 feet 8 1/2 inches, inherited from colliery wagonways. In trials for the 1845 Gauge Commission, broad-gauge trains ran faster. But standard-gauge track already ran several times as far. The Gauge Act of 1846 required new passenger lines to be built to standard gauge, except in broad-gauge territory. On Friday 20 May 1892 the last broad-gauge train left Paddington. Over that weekend some 4,000 platelayers converted the remaining main line through Devon and Cornwall, and standard-gauge trains ran on the Monday.
story.puzzle: If Brunel's gauge was faster, why was it the one that had to be torn out?
story.payoff: A gauge is worth what it connects to. Every mile of Stephenson gauge made the next line more valuable on that gauge, a reinforcing loop of adoption. The GWR's broad gauge became an island whose break-of-gauge transfers cost more than its speed gained. An early, almost accidental choice locked Britain in, whether or not it was the best gauge.
sources: Report of the Gauge Commissioners (UK Parliament, 1846)
Gauge Act 1846 (9 & 10 Vict. c. 57)
E. T. MacDermot, History of the Great Western Railway (1927), on the 1892 gauge conversion

days.application: QWERTY, the keyboard you type on, is Christopher Latham Sholes's layout, sold to Remington in the 1870s. Paul David's 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY' (American Economic Review, 1985) argued that QWERTY locked in an inferior design despite August Dvorak's supposedly faster layout. On his account, touch-typing on QWERTY spread after a famous 1888 typing contest in Cincinnati. Stan Liebowitz and Stephen Margolis replied in 'The Fable of the Keys' (Journal of Law & Economics, 1990). They argued that the evidence for Dvorak's superiority came largely from Dvorak's own studies, and that a 1956 US government test by Earle Strong found no clear advantage. Lock-in is real; whether it trapped us in something worse here is disputed. For contrast, over 31 May-1 June 1886 the US South re-gauged roughly 11,500-13,000 miles of track (sources differ) to join the northern network.

builds_on.why: Increasing returns are a reinforcing loop in adoption: more users make the option more valuable, which attracts more users.
Network effects follow from network structure: a connection standard is worth more the more nodes it links, which applies Day 13's mathematics to the choice of a standard.

across.link: United States v. Microsoft (D.C. Circuit, 2001) upheld the finding that an 'applications barrier to entry', the thousands of programs written for Windows, protected Microsoft's monopoly: network-effect lock-in recognized in antitrust law.

days.apply_question: Japan's electricity grid runs at 50 Hz in the east and 60 Hz in the west, because in the 1890s Tokyo bought German generators and Osaka bought American ones. After the March 2011 earthquake, converter capacity of only about one gigawatt limited how much power the west could send east. Using path dependence, explain why Japan has still not unified its frequency.
days.evidence_note: Settled: network effects and switching costs exist, and some standards persist for these reasons. Debated: how often lock-in leaves society with a clearly inferior technology. Arthur and David say it can and does; Liebowitz and Margolis argue that documented cases of inefficient lock-in are rare, QWERTY included. Railway historians also debate whether the broad gauge was superior overall once costs are counted.

resource.title: Positive Feedbacks in the Economy
resource.creator: W. Brian Arthur, Scientific American 262(2), February 1990
resource.why: The increasing-returns argument for lock-in written for general readers by its main theorist; read it as one side, with Liebowitz and Margolis as the reply named in the lesson.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the article, which may be paywalled at Scientific American. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Twenty-Two Cars, One Circle, No Bottleneck, and a Traffic Jam Anyway.
days.concept: Simple local rules followed by many individuals can produce large-scale patterns that none of them chose, so you cannot read individual motives or causes straight off an aggregate outcome.
days.focus: Teaches emergence: macro patterns generated bottom-up by interacting agents, and agent-based models as the tool for studying them. The angle is a double warning. Aggregate patterns may have no author, and a model that can generate a pattern does not prove that is how the real pattern arose.
days.model_or_equation: Schelling's rule: each agent on a grid is content if at least a set share (for example one-third) of its neighbours are like itself, and otherwise moves to a random empty cell. Repeating the rule produces near-complete clustering from mild preferences.

story.title: A traffic jam with no cause
story.hook: In a 2008 paper in the New Journal of Physics, a team of Japanese physicists led by Yuki Sugiyama reported a simple experiment. They put 22 cars on a circular track 230 metres around and asked the drivers to cruise steadily at about 30 kilometres an hour. There were no junctions, no lane changes and no merging. At first the cars flowed evenly. Within minutes small fluctuations grew: one car braked slightly, the one behind braked a little harder, and a stop-and-go wave formed. It travelled backward around the circle, against the direction of traffic.
story.puzzle: Nobody crashed, nobody merged and no driver wanted a jam. Where did it come from, and whose fault was it?
story.payoff: The jam was emergent. Each driver followed a sensible local rule, keeping a safe distance and reacting to the car ahead with a slight delay. Above a critical density, those rules amplify small fluctuations into a moving jam. No individual caused it, so blaming a driver misreads it.
sources: Sugiyama et al., 'Traffic jams without bottlenecks: experimental evidence for the physical mechanism of the formation of a jam', New Journal of Physics 10, 033001 (2008)

days.application: Thomas Schelling's 'Dynamic Models of Segregation' (Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1971; Micromotives and Macrobehavior, 1978). Working with coins on a checkerboard, he showed that people who would be happy as a minority in a mixed neighbourhood, wanting only a modest share of neighbours like themselves, can still produce near-total segregation. The model shows that mild preferences are sufficient to segregate, not that real American segregation came from them. Historians document laws and policies such as redlining and racial covenants (Richard Rothstein, The Color of Law, 2017).

builds_on.why: Each driver's reaction delay is a delayed balancing loop at the scale of two cars; emergence is what many such small delayed loops do together.
Day 18 showed that aggregating groups can reverse a relationship (Simpson's paradox at Berkeley); emergence is a second reason an aggregate can mislead about individuals.

across.link: John Conway's Game of Life, published by Martin Gardner in Scientific American (October 1970): four rules about each cell's neighbours produce 'gliders' that travel across the grid, though no rule mentions motion.

days.apply_question: On 6 May 2010 the Dow Jones index fell nearly 1,000 points within minutes and then mostly recovered; the joint SEC-CFTC report traced it to one large automated sell order interacting with high-frequency traders. Using the idea of emergence, explain why 'who decided to crash the market?' may be the wrong question to ask.
days.evidence_note: Settled: phantom jams emerge without bottlenecks (Sugiyama et al.), and Schelling's model reliably generates segregation from mild preferences. Debated: how much residential preferences, as opposed to law, lending policy and income, explain real segregation; the model shows possibility, not historical cause.

resource.title: Parable of the Polygons
resource.creator: Vi Hart & Nicky Case, 2014
resource.why: A free interactive version of Schelling's model: you drag the agents yourself and watch mild preferences produce segregation, then try rules that reverse it.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the piece. Cite without a link; a later run may add the creator-hosted URL only if a search result shows it.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Donella Meadows Walked to a Flip Chart and Ranked the Places to Change a System. The Numbers People Fight Over Came Last.
days.concept: Interventions in a system differ enormously in power: changing parameters such as taxes or quotas is usually weak, while changing feedback structure, information flows, rules, goals and the paradigm behind them is strong but harder and more resisted.
days.focus: Teaches Meadows's hierarchy of leverage points as a practical way to ask where a change will actually move a system. The angle includes its limits: the list is an experienced modeller's heuristic, not a tested law, and high-leverage changes can push a system the wrong way just as hard.
days.model_or_equation: Meadows's twelve leverage points, weakest to strongest: (12) constants and parameters; (11) buffer sizes; (10) stock-and-flow structure; (9) delays; (8) balancing loops; (7) reinforcing loops; (6) information flows; (5) rules; (4) power to self-organize; (3) goals; (2) paradigms; (1) the power to transcend paradigms.

story.title: A list written on a flip chart
story.hook: Donella Meadows was lead author of The Limits to Growth, a Dartmouth professor and the writer of a weekly newspaper column. In her 1999 essay 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System' she told how the list began. She was sitting in a meeting about the new global trade regime of NAFTA, GATT and the World Trade Organization, and grew frustrated as the discussion fixed on details. She got up, went to the flip chart and wrote out a list of places to intervene in a system, from weakest to strongest. In her experience as a modeller, she wrote, people almost always push the levers in the wrong direction and put most of their effort into the weakest ones.
story.puzzle: Why would the measures people fight over hardest, the tax rates, quotas and budget numbers, so often be the ones that change a system least?
story.payoff: Parameters adjust flows inside an unchanged structure, so the system's loops absorb the change. Rules, information flows and goals rewire the loops themselves. That is why Meadows ranked them higher, and why they are fought over less often but resisted harder.
sources: Donella H. Meadows, 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System' (Sustainability Institute, 1999); an earlier version appeared in Whole Earth, 1997
Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6

days.application: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments (Title IV) set a national cap on power-plant sulfur dioxide, about half of 1980 emissions, and let utilities trade allowances. Instead of a uniform technology mandate, it changed the rules and who had the information and incentive to find cuts. Emissions fell ahead of schedule and compliance costs came in far below early projections (Schmalensee & Stavins, Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(1), 2013). Cheap low-sulfur coal from the Powder River Basin, which rail deregulation made cheaper to ship, also helped. Later court rulings and new rules effectively collapsed the allowance market after about 2010.

builds_on.why: Several of Meadows's strongest levers act on feedback loops themselves, adding, strengthening or removing the reinforcing and balancing loops of Day 26.
Goals are high on Meadows's list, and Goodhart's law shows why: change what a system is told to maximize and its behaviour changes, sometimes perversely.

across.link: Meadows ranked paradigms as the second-strongest leverage point. On how paradigms change, she pointed to Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), the account of paradigm shifts in science that Philosophy I takes up.

days.apply_question: Singapore began charging drivers to enter its central business district in 1975 and moved to electronic road pricing in 1998, with charges that vary by time and place. Where on Meadows's list does that intervention sit, and what would have counted as a weaker or a stronger lever for the same traffic problem?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the SO2 programme cut emissions at lower cost than projected. Debated: how much credit belongs to trading itself and how much to cheap low-sulfur coal. Meadows's ranking is an expert heuristic that has not been tested systematically, so treat its order as a guide rather than a finding.

resource.title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
resource.creator: Donella H. Meadows, Sustainability Institute, 1999
resource.why: The essay itself, in Meadows's own voice, including the flip-chart story and her warnings that leverage points are counterintuitive and the list is tentative.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified in either the writing or the verification pass (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches fail here). Cited from knowledge of the essay, which the Donella Meadows Project distributes free. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: How systems models fail: the Limits to Growth debate
days.headline_hint: Paul Ehrlich Mailed Julian Simon a Cheque for $576.07. It Settled the Bet, Not the Argument.
days.concept: A model is a structured set of assumptions, so its scenarios are conditional 'if-then' statements rather than forecasts, and a model that leaves out adaptation, prices or feedback can be confidently wrong, or right for the wrong reasons.
days.focus: Teaches how to judge a systems model: what separates a scenario from a forecast, how structure and omitted loops drive results, and why a single outcome cannot settle a model dispute. The Limits to Growth debate, the Simon-Ehrlich wager and the dispute over RCP8.5 give three angles. Neither the 'doom was wrong' victory lap nor the 'Limits was right' one survives the evidence.
key_concepts: all models are wrong, some are useful
days.model_or_equation: World3 (Meadows et al., 1972) linked five sectors, population, industrial capital, food, non-renewable resources and pollution, through reinforcing growth loops and delayed balancing loops. With fixed assumptions its 'standard run' overshoots and declines in the 21st century. The structure, not the computer, produces the result.

story.title: A cheque in the mail, October 1990
story.hook: In 1980 the economist Julian Simon challenged the biologist Paul Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb, to bet on scarcity. Ehrlich and two colleagues chose $1,000 worth of five metals: chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten. They bet that their inflation-adjusted prices would rise between 29 September 1980 and 29 September 1990. During that decade the world added more people than in any decade before. All five prices fell. In October 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a sheet of price calculations and a cheque for $576.07.
story.puzzle: Simon won the bet. Did that prove that warnings of resource limits, such as The Limits to Growth of 1972, were wrong?
story.payoff: No single outcome tests a model. Kiel, Matheson and Golembiewski (Ecological Economics, 2010) found Ehrlich would have won in roughly three of five ten-year windows over 1900-2008. Graham Turner (2008) found data to 2000 tracking the Limits standard run fairly closely, though that run's decisive turns lay later. The bet showed price feedback, substitution and recession at work, which Ehrlich's view underweighted; it did not show that limits never bind. Both sides' victory laps outrun the evidence.
sources: Paul Sabin, The Bet (Yale UP, 2013)
Kiel, Matheson & Golembiewski, 'Luck or skill? An examination of the Ehrlich-Simon bet', Ecological Economics 69(7), 2010
Graham Turner, 'A comparison of The Limits to Growth with 30 years of reality', Global Environmental Change 18, 2008

days.application: The dispute over the IPCC's highest-emissions pathway, RCP8.5. It was designed as a high-end scenario but often described as 'business as usual'. Zeke Hausfather and Glen Peters (Nature, 2020) argued that with cheaper renewables and slower coal growth it is now unlikely, and misleading as a baseline. Christopher Schwalm and colleagues (PNAS, 2020) replied that it tracks cumulative CO2 emissions to date well. The argument is about which assumptions belong in a scenario, the central issue of this lesson.

builds_on.why: Pearl and Reed's 1920 logistic put a ceiling on US population that was an assumption, not a law; World3's limits and overshoot are the same lesson about structure deciding the curve.
One bet is one draw; Kiel et al. estimate the probability Ehrlich wins across many windows, the difference Day 11 drew between an outcome and an expected value.

across.link: Karl Popper's falsification criterion (The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1934/1959) meets a difficulty here. A scenario stated as 'if these assumptions hold' is hard to falsify by events, because a miss can always be blamed on the assumptions: the auxiliary-hypothesis problem philosophers of science call Duhem-Quine.

days.apply_question: On 16 March 2020 Imperial College's Report 9 estimated about 510,000 deaths in Great Britain if COVID-19 were left completely unmitigated. Actual UK deaths in the first year were far lower, and a national lockdown began a week later. Was Report 9 a failed forecast? Explain using the difference between a scenario and a forecast.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Simon won the 1980-90 bet, and all five metals fell in real price. Debated: how well the Limits standard run has tracked the data. Turner (2008) and later updates find a fair fit; critics such as Nordhaus, who in 1973 attacked Forrester's World Dynamics as 'measurement without data', reject the approach. The plausibility of RCP8.5 is also debated (Hausfather and Peters against Schwalm et al.). Value judgment: how much weight to give low-probability, high-cost scenarios in policy.

resource.creator: Paul Sabin, Yale University Press, 2013
resource.length: the chapters on the 1980 wager, about 40 pages
resource.why: A historian's even-handed account of the wager and how it hardened into a political divide, showing both men's blind spots rather than crowning either.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: Innovation as a system, not a pipeline
days.headline_hint: Bayer Sold Aspirin for Seventy-Two Years Before Anyone Knew How It Worked.
days.concept: Innovation is not a pipeline running from science to invention to production to use; it runs through coupled feedback loops in which practice often leads science, users and markets reshape inventions, and demand is built as much as found.
days.focus: Teaches Kline and Rosenberg's chain-linked model against the 'linear model' of innovation, and uses it to challenge Logan's own need-to-feedback chain directly: the chain is a useful checklist of domains, not a sequence of causes. The angle is balanced: science-led inventions are real too.
key_concepts: feedback between research, design and market
days.model_or_equation: Kline and Rosenberg's chain-linked model (1986) has a central chain: market need -> invent or design -> detailed design and test -> redesign and produce -> distribute and market. Feedback loops run from every stage back to earlier ones, and from the market to design. The chain also links to existing knowledge and to research, which is consulted when knowledge runs out rather than being the starting point.

story.title: A drug sold by the ton, explained in 1971
story.hook: For centuries people chewed willow bark for fever and pain, and in 1763 the Reverend Edward Stone reported its effect on agues to the Royal Society. In August 1897, at Bayer's laboratory in Elberfeld, Germany, the chemist Felix Hoffmann recorded a pure, stable synthesis of acetylsalicylic acid. Bayer registered the name Aspirin in 1899 and sold it worldwide, as powder and then tablets. In 1949 Arthur Eichengrün, Hoffmann's former superior, claimed he had directed the work; he was a Jewish chemist whom the Nazi years had written out of the story. For more than seventy years nobody could say how aspirin worked. Then, in 1971, the British pharmacologist John Vane showed in Nature that it blocks the body's production of prostaglandins, work that shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.
story.puzzle: If science comes first and products follow, how could one of the best-selling drugs in history be invented, mass-produced and sold for seven decades before science understood it?
story.payoff: Innovation does not have to wait for theory. Practice, chemistry, manufacturing and market feedback ran ahead, and science arrived later to explain what practice had found, then to improve it. Vane's explanation fed back in turn, toward low-dose aspirin for heart attacks and new anti-inflammatory drugs: the chain-linked model, with loops running in both directions.
sources: Edward Stone, letter to the Royal Society, Philosophical Transactions 53 (1763)
Walter Sneader, 'The discovery of aspirin: a reappraisal', BMJ 321, 2000
John R. Vane, 'Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis as a mechanism of action for aspirin-like drugs', Nature New Biology 231, 1971

days.application: Vannevar Bush's July 1945 report to President Truman, 'Science, the Endless Frontier', called basic research 'the pacemaker of technological progress' and helped lead to the National Science Foundation (1950). The 'linear model' was later read into it, though Benoît Godin (Science, Technology & Human Values, 2006) argues Bush never spelled it out. Policy then tested it. The Defense Department's Project Hindsight (Sherwin & Isenson, Science, 1967) traced 20 weapon systems and found that under 1% of the key research 'events' were undirected basic science. The NSF's reply, TRACES (1968), traced five civilian innovations further back and found a large role for earlier basic research. Both patterns are real. The transistor, a science-led invention taught in Computing, fits the linear story better than aspirin does.

builds_on.why: Car I set out Logan's chain and its first documented reversal, Britain's 1865 Locomotive Act regulating road vehicles before the car; today generalizes that reversal into a model of innovation as loops.
The chain-linked model is a set of feedback loops between design, market and research; Day 26's loop vocabulary is what replaces the pipeline.

across.link: In the late nineteenth century, German chemical firms such as Bayer and BASF built some of the first industrial research laboratories, organizing invention itself: the 'invention of invention' that History II takes up.

days.apply_question: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman reported modified-nucleoside mRNA in 2005 after years of rejected grant applications, and the BioNTech-Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines were authorized in December 2020. Does that story fit the linear model or the chain-linked model better, and what part of it would each model miss?
days.evidence_note: Settled among historians of innovation: the strict linear model does not describe most innovation, and practice often precedes theory. Debated: how much credit Eichengrün deserves for aspirin (Sneader 2000 supports his claim; Bayer has disputed it), and the long-run contribution of undirected basic research, where Project Hindsight and TRACES reached opposite emphases. Value judgment: how public money should be divided between basic and applied research.

resource.title: Science, the Endless Frontier (Summary of the Report)
resource.creator: Vannevar Bush, US Office of Scientific Research and Development, July 1945
resource.why: The founding text that the linear model was built on, in Bush's own words; read it as the view this lesson tests, noticing what it does and does not actually claim.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 2: The Grand Banks cod collapse
days.headline_hint: On 2 July 1992 Canada Shut a 500-Year-Old Fishery. Its Scientists Had Been Counting the Cod All Along.
days.concept: The northern cod fishery collapsed while being scientifically managed because a breeding stock, measurement that hid its decline, a commons, delays and a threshold combined into loops that no single decision-maker controlled, and its reopening in 2024 turned on a model as much as on the fish.
days.focus: The Systems Thinking block's case applies the tools of Days 25-34 to one real system. It asks how a watched fishery collapsed anyway and why recovery took 32 years and remains disputed. It goes deep on stocks, sampling, delays, thresholds, the commons and model failure, and previews biology, engineering, subsidies and regulation.
key_concepts: hyperstability of catch per unit effort
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, the technology loop: sonar and factory trawlers raise catch per trip as the stock falls, hiding the decline. B1, the intended balancing loop: stock assessment -> quota -> catch -> stock, weakened by delays and by biased catch-rate data. R2, depensation: below a threshold, fewer spawners -> fewer recruits -> fewer spawners. B2, ecosystem change: predators and competitors of young cod now dominate. Feedback in 2024: a revised model moved the stock's status. Surplus production: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K) - C, with maximum sustainable yield rK/4 at N = K/2. Catch per unit effort is roughly proportional to N raised to a power below 1 (hyperstability).

story.title: A minister, a microphone and a moratorium
story.hook: On 1 July 1992 Canada's fisheries minister, John Crosbie, met angry fishermen in Bay Bulls, Newfoundland, and shouted back that he had not taken the fish out of the water. The next day, 2 July, in St. John's, he announced a moratorium on fishing northern cod off Newfoundland and Labrador. Europeans had fished these waters since soon after John Cabot's voyage of 1497, and catches had peaked at about 800,000 tonnes in 1968. The closure put roughly 30,000 people in Newfoundland and Labrador out of work by common estimates, often called the largest layoff in Canadian history; figures run from about 19,000 at once to some 40,000 across Atlantic Canada as other cod stocks closed. The moratorium was announced for two years and lasted 32.
story.puzzle: Canadian scientists had managed the fishery with quotas since Canada claimed its 200-mile zone in 1977. How did a fishery watched that closely collapse anyway, and why did it take 32 years to reopen?
story.payoff: Every lesson of this block was at work. A breeding stock was drained faster than it could refill (stocks and flows). Catch rates stayed high as fish crowded into the last dense schools (biased sampling). Assessments lagged reality (delays). The population was pushed below a threshold where it no longer rebounded (hysteresis). Inshore and offshore fleets and foreign boats competed for a shared resource (the commons). And the models were too confident in their inputs (model failure).
sources: Jeffrey A. Hutchings & Ransom A. Myers, 'What can be learned from the collapse of a renewable resource? Atlantic cod, Gadus morhua, of Newfoundland and Labrador', Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 51, 1994
Carl Walters & Jean-Jacques Maguire, 'Lessons for stock assessment from the northern cod collapse', Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries 6, 1996
Fisheries and Oceans Canada, announcement ending the northern cod moratorium, June 2024

days.application: The case's own sequel. In June 2024 Fisheries Minister Diane Lebouthillier ended the moratorium with an 18,000-tonne commercial quota. Fisheries and Oceans Canada's 2023 stock assessment, using a revised model, had placed northern cod above the critical zone, by its reconstruction since about 2016. The fish had not suddenly surged; the model's estimate of where the stock stood relative to its reference points had changed. Scientists including Jeffrey Hutchings criticized the decision; the fishing industry and the province largely welcomed it.

builds_on.why: The cod population is a stock with births and growth flowing in and fishing and natural death flowing out; collapse is a persistent net outflow.
Commercial catch per unit effort was a biased sample: boats go where fish remain, so catch rates stayed high as the stock shrank (hyperstability).
After 1992 the stock failed to rebuild for years even with fishing stopped, behaviour consistent with a threshold and hysteresis.
Canada's 1977 200-mile zone turned an open-access commons into a national one but left competing fleets inside it and foreign fishing on the Nose and Tail of the Banks outside it.

across.link: Olsen et al., 'Maturation trends indicative of rapid evolution preceded the collapse of northern cod' (Nature 428, 2004): before the collapse, heavy fishing selected for cod that matured younger and smaller, an evolutionary response.

days.apply_question: Peru's anchoveta fishery, then the world's largest, landed about 12 million tonnes in 1970 and collapsed in 1972 during an El Niño. Anchoveta swim in dense schools. Using the loops of this case, explain why catches could stay high right up to the collapse and what an assessment would have needed to see it coming.
days.evidence_note: Settled: overfishing was the main cause of the collapse; commercial catch-rate data overstated the stock; the stock stayed very low for years after 1992. Debated: the roles of harp seals and colder water in the slow recovery, and whether the 2024 reopening was justified, with DFO's revised assessment on one side and scientists such as Hutchings warning of renewed risk on the other. Value judgment: who gained and who paid (offshore companies, inshore families, outport communities, future generations), and who consented. Consequentialist readings and stewardship readings, the latter shared by Christian and secular conservationists, weigh the moratorium's costs differently. Whether an earlier closure could have saved the fishery is a counterfactual and cannot be known.

chain.point: Salt cod fed Europe and the Atlantic world for centuries after Cabot's 1497 voyage; by 1992 the fishery sustained hundreds of outport communities in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Factory freezer trawlers, led from 1954 by Britain's Fairtry, together with sonar and fish-finders, let distant-water fleets fish winter spawning schools year-round; catches peaked around 1968.
A fish population refills only through births and growth. Logistic surplus production peaks at half the unfished stock, so catches above about rK/4 drain the stock year after year.
Northern cod historically matured at around six to seven years, so a stock fished hard loses its spawners before replacing them; fishing selected for earlier maturation (Olsen et al. 2004).

Government support for fleet and processing capacity, and seasonal unemployment insurance, kept effort high as returns fell. After the moratorium, adjustment programmes (NCARP, then The Atlantic Groundfish Strategy) paid income support; named here at CFA level.

Canada's 200-mile zone of 1 January 1977 ended open access inside it and brought quota management, but inshore and offshore fleets competed for one stock and foreign vessels fished just outside the zone.
Fisheries and Oceans Canada set total allowable catches each year; how quotas, enforcement and political pressure interact is taught in the Government block.

Assessments leaned on commercial catch per unit effort, which stayed high as fish concentrated in the remaining schools (hyperstability), a systematic error that no sample size fixes, while research-survey data were short and noisy.
Assessments described last year's fish with uncertain data, and cutting quotas took further time, so corrections lagged a falling stock: the delayed balancing loop of Day 27.
Spawning biomass fell to around 1% of 1960s levels by most estimates and stayed low for years after fishing stopped, as the ecosystem shifted toward shellfish and other species.
In 2024 the moratorium ended after a model revision, not a surge of fish, moved the stock out of the critical zone; the 1980s overestimates and the 2024 revision are both lessons in model structure.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Arguments: validity, soundness and hidden premises
days.headline_hint: Lincoln Was a Congressman and a Winning Lawyer When He Sat Down to Master Euclid. Most Bad Arguments Fail on a Premise Nobody Says Out Loud.
days.concept: An argument is valid when its conclusion must be true if its premises are, and sound when it is valid and its premises are actually true; most bad arguments fail on a premise that is left unstated.
days.focus: Teach validity as a property of form (test: can you imagine every premise true and the conclusion false?), soundness as validity plus true premises, and the working habit of reconstructing a hidden premise (an enthymeme) and sorting every premise into an empirical claim or a value claim - the move every later Evidence check in this course depends on.
days.model_or_equation: Validity test: an argument is valid if and only if there is no possible situation in which all its premises are true and its conclusion false. Valid form (modus ponens): If P then Q; P; therefore Q. Invalid look-alike (affirming the consequent): If P then Q; Q; therefore P. Sound = valid + every premise true.

story.title: A congressman with a copy of Euclid
story.hook: In June 1860, asked for campaign material by John Locke Scripps of the Chicago Press and Tribune, Abraham Lincoln wrote a short autobiography in the third person; among flatboats and the Black Hawk War it notes that he 'studied and nearly mastered the Six-books of Euclid, since he was a member of Congress' - his single House term of 1847-49, when he was nearly forty and already a busy lawyer. A reminiscence by the Rev. John P. Gulliver of a conversation with Lincoln in Norwich, Connecticut, in March 1860 gives a reason: in his law reading Lincoln kept meeting the word 'demonstrate', realized he could not say what it meant beyond 'prove', and went home and stayed until he could give any proposition in the six books of Euclid at sight. Gulliver's account is secondhand and places the study earlier, during Lincoln's law reading, so it is told as Gulliver's story. By his own account, then, a congressman who already won arguments for a living went back to a geometry book more than 2,000 years old.
story.puzzle: A successful trial lawyer already knew how to persuade juries. What could Euclid teach him that persuasion could not - what is the difference between an argument that convinces and one that demonstrates?
story.payoff: Euclid is validity in its purest form: every step follows necessarily from what came before and nothing is used that is not stated, so whoever accepts the axioms must accept the theorem. A persuasive argument often works by leaving a premise unsaid; a demonstration puts all its premises on the table, where they can be checked. Lincoln's Cooper Union address (27 February 1860) was built in that style: he quoted Stephen Douglas's premise that the founders 'understood this question just as well, and even better, than we do now', accepted it, and then checked it against what the signers of the Constitution had actually done.
sources: Abraham Lincoln, autobiography written for John L. Scripps, c. June 1860, in The Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 4 (1953)
Rev. John P. Gulliver, reminiscence of an 1860 conversation with Lincoln in Norwich, Connecticut (commonly cited as The Independent, 1864); discussed in Lincoln Lore, 21 November 1949
Abraham Lincoln, Address at Cooper Institute, New York, 27 February 1860

days.application: Logan's car chain, regulation link: reconstruct the slogan 'speed cameras are just about revenue'. Supply its hidden premises (if a device raises money, its purpose is money; if its purpose is money, it does not make roads safer), then sort them: empirical (do camera sites see fewer crashes once regression to the mean is removed - Day 19; how much fine income is net revenue) and value (would revenue-raising enforcement be illegitimate even if it saved lives?). The conclusion can be false even when cameras do raise money: a review for the RAC Foundation by Richard Allsop (2010) estimated that switching off Britain's cameras would mean roughly 800 more people killed or seriously injured each year.

builds_on.why: Proof: a mathematical proof is the model of a valid, sound argument - every step follows from axioms - and the gap found in Wiles's 1993 proof was exactly a step that did not follow.
Regression to the mean is the empirical premise the speed-camera argument usually hides: cameras sited after a spike in crashes would see fewer crashes even if they did nothing.

across.link: Checking validity can be mechanized: an argument is valid exactly when its premises together with the denial of its conclusion are unsatisfiable, which is what a SAT solver tests. In 2016 Marijn Heule, Oliver Kullmann and Victor Marek used one to settle the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem, producing a proof of about 200 terabytes.

days.apply_question: After Fukushima (March 2011) Germany decided to close all its nuclear power plants - the last three shut in April 2023 - on the argument 'Fukushima showed that nuclear power is unsafe, so Germany should phase it out': what unstated premise would make that argument valid, and is it a claim evidence could settle or one only values can?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the definitions of validity and soundness (standard logic). Debated: the size of speed cameras' safety effect once regression to the mean and diverted traffic are corrected; UK estimates differ by method and site. Value judgment: whether enforcement that raises revenue is illegitimate even if it saves lives.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Europe Had Seen Countless White Swans and Not One Black One. Then a Dutch Crew Rowed Up an Australian River.
days.concept: Inductive inference generalizes from observed cases to unobserved ones, and Hume showed that no number of past cases logically guarantees the next; science copes not by proving induction but by testing generalizations where they are most likely to break.
days.focus: Hume's argument (Treatise 1739, Enquiry 1748 section IV): any justification of 'the future will resemble the past' is either deductive (impossible, since its denial is no contradiction) or inductive (circular). Separate the logical problem (no guarantee) from the practical one (which generalizations deserve trust): many cases from one range of conditions are weak evidence about other conditions, and understanding the mechanism makes extrapolation safer.
days.model_or_equation: Hume's dilemma: to justify 'unobserved cases resemble observed ones' you need either (a) a deductive argument - impossible, because the denial is perfectly conceivable - or (b) an inductive argument - circular, because it assumes the very principle it is meant to prove.

story.title: Black swans on the Swan River
story.hook: For centuries Europeans used the black swan as a figure for the nonexistent: the Roman satirist Juvenal called a rare thing 'a rare bird in the lands, very like a black swan' (Satires VI.165), and every swan anyone in Europe had seen was white. In late December 1696 three Dutch East India Company ships under Willem de Vlamingh reached the coast of Western Australia, searching for a lost ship. On about 10 January 1697 a party rowed up a river near present-day Perth and found it crowded with black swans; Vlamingh named it the Swan River. The crew captured a few (accounts say two or three) and carried them to Batavia (Jakarta), where they died before they could be shipped to Europe. A Dutch mariner, Antonie Caen, had reported black swans off Bernier Island as early as 1636, but it was Vlamingh's report that ended the proverb.
story.puzzle: Europeans had millions of observations and not one exception. Were they reasoning badly - and if not, what was wrong with a generalization that every case anyone had ever seen supported?
story.payoff: By the standards of induction, nothing was wrong with the reasoning - which is Hume's point: no number of white swans could guarantee the next one. But the practical lesson is about the sample: all those observations came from one part of the world, so they never tested the generalization under the conditions in which it could fail. Induction becomes more trustworthy when cases are drawn across varied conditions and a mechanism is understood (plumage colour is a heritable trait that can differ between isolated populations), never certain.
sources: Juvenal, Satires VI.165
Gunter Schilder, Voyage to the Great South Land: Willem de Vlamingh 1696-1697 (Royal Australian Historical Society, 1985)
The Conversation, 'Friday essay: a rare bird - how Europeans got the black swan so wrong' (2021)

days.application: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge (opened 1 July 1940; collapsed 7 November 1940 in a wind of about 40 mph, killing no people but a dog). Its designers extrapolated from a run of successful, ever more slender suspension bridges: Leon Moisseiff's deflection theory held that a heavy deck hung from cables would be stiff enough without a deep truss, so Tacoma's deck was a girder 8 feet deep on a 2,800-foot main span - a depth-to-span ratio of about 1:350, more than twice as slender as the Golden Gate Bridge's (25 feet on 4,200, about 1:168). Every earlier success was a case; the extrapolation took the design beyond the range those cases covered, into aerodynamic instability - aeroelastic flutter, not the simple resonance of many popular accounts - that none of them had tested. Henry Petroski (To Engineer Is Human, 1985; Design Paradigms, 1994) argues that success itself breeds failure in this way.

builds_on.why: Sampling: a sample's value comes from how it was drawn, not its size - Europe's millions of white swans were an enormous but non-random sample of the world's swans, like the Literary Digest's 2.4 million replies.
Fat tails: Fukushima's 5.7-metre design basis was an inductive generalization from the historical record, and the largest event observed understated the next.

across.link: David Wolpert's 'no free lunch' theorems (Neural Computation, 1996) are a formal cousin of Hume's problem: averaged over all possible worlds, no learning algorithm predicts unseen cases better than any other, so machine learning succeeds only because real data have regularities that the algorithm's built-in assumptions happen to match.

days.apply_question: Before September 2008 only one US money-market fund had ever 'broken the buck', a small one in 1994; on 16 September 2008 the Reserve Primary Fund's shares fell to 97 cents after Lehman Brothers failed. What should an investor in 2007 have checked, beyond the long record of $1.00 share prices, to know whether that record was a sound basis for prediction?
days.evidence_note: Settled: no finite set of observations deductively guarantees a generalization; most philosophers accept this much of Hume. Debated: whether, and how, induction can be justified - Bayesian confirmation, inference to the best explanation, Reichenbach's pragmatic vindication, or Popper's rejection of induction (Day 39). Debated in engineering history: how regular Petroski's 'success breeds failure' pattern really is.
