days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Falsification: what makes a claim scientific
days.headline_hint: In 1919 Two Expeditions Photographed an Eclipse to See Whether Einstein Could Be Wrong. Then They Set Aside the Plates That Came Closest to Newton.
days.concept: Popper's criterion: a theory is scientific if it forbids something observable and so risks refutation - but a failed prediction never refutes a theory on its own, because the blame can always be shifted to an auxiliary assumption (the Duhem-Quine problem).
days.focus: Popper's 1919 contrast between Einstein's risky prediction and theories that could explain anything (Logik der Forschung, 1934; Conjectures and Refutations, 1963), the logic of refutation (modus tollens), and its limit: tests hit theory plus auxiliaries together (Duhem 1906; Quine 1951), so the real question is when rescuing a theory by changing an auxiliary is legitimate - answer: when the rescue makes new, independently testable predictions (Neptune) rather than merely patching (Vulcan).
days.model_or_equation: (T and A) implies O; not O; therefore not (T and A). Modus tollens refutes the conjunction of theory T and auxiliary assumptions A, not T alone. 1919 numbers: general relativity predicted 1.75 arcseconds of deflection for starlight grazing the Sun; a Newtonian calculation gave about 0.87.

story.title: Two eclipse expeditions and the plates that were set aside
story.hook: On 29 May 1919 a total eclipse of the Sun crossed the Atlantic, and two British teams photographed the stars around it: Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson at Sobral in northern Brazil, Arthur Eddington and Edwin Cottingham on the island of Principe off West Africa, where cloud cleared only partway through totality. General relativity predicted that starlight grazing the Sun would bend by 1.75 arcseconds; a Newtonian calculation gave about half that; no bending was the third possibility. On 6 November 1919, at a joint meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society, the Astronomer Royal Frank Dyson announced for Einstein, and the next day The Times proclaimed a 'Revolution in Science'. The published numbers carried a catch: Sobral's 4-inch telescope gave about 1.98 arcseconds and Principe about 1.61, but Sobral's main astrographic telescope gave about 0.93 - close to Newton - and that set was set aside on the grounds that the Sun's heat had distorted the instrument's focus.
story.puzzle: If you may discard the measurements that disagree with you by blaming the instrument, was it a real test at all - could Einstein's theory actually have lost?
story.payoff: It could have lost, which is what made it science by Popper's test: the theory forbade a deflection near 0.87 arcseconds or zero. The discarded plates show the Duhem-Quine problem at work - every result is theory plus auxiliaries (here, a telescope whose focus held steady) - and blaming an auxiliary is legitimate only with independent evidence for the fault. Historians still argue whether that evidence was enough: Earman and Glymour (1980) charged that the data were weak and selectively handled; Daniel Kennefick (2009, 2019) argues the focus problem was documented and that a 1979 re-measurement of the Sobral plates supported Einstein. Radio measurements since the 1970s have confirmed the bending far more precisely.
sources: F. W. Dyson, A. S. Eddington & C. Davidson, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 220 (1920) 291-333
John Earman & Clark Glymour, 'Relativity and Eclipses', Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences 11 (1980) 49-85
Daniel Kennefick, 'Testing relativity from the 1919 eclipse - a question of bias', Physics Today 62(3), March 2009
Daniel Kennefick, No Shadow of a Doubt: The 1919 Eclipse That Confirmed Einstein's Theory of Relativity (Princeton UP, 2019)
Karl Popper, 'Science: Conjectures and Refutations' (1953 lecture), in Conjectures and Refutations (1963)

days.application: Uranus and Mercury: the same logical move, opposite outcomes. When Uranus strayed from its Newtonian orbit, Urbain Le Verrier (and independently John Couch Adams) blamed an auxiliary assumption - that the solar system had only seven planets - and predicted an eighth; on 23 September 1846 Johann Galle found Neptune within about a degree of Le Verrier's position. Le Verrier then made the same move for Mercury, whose perihelion advances about 43 arcseconds per century more than Newtonian theory allows: he predicted an inner planet, 'Vulcan'; an amateur astronomer, Edmond Lescarbault, claimed to have seen it cross the Sun and received the Legion of Honour; no Vulcan exists, and general relativity accounted for the 43 arcseconds in 1915. The rescue is good science when the new auxiliary makes an independent prediction that comes true, and degenerating when it does not.

builds_on.why: OPERA's 'faster-than-light' neutrinos (2011) were explained by a faulty auxiliary - a loose fibre-optic cable - found by independent checking: the Duhem-Quine move done properly.
Falsification is Popper's answer to Hume's problem of induction: science need not justify generalizations from cases if it proceeds by bold conjecture and attempted refutation.

across.link: Trial preregistration makes a medical hypothesis falsifiable in Popper's sense by fixing the primary outcome before the data arrive. After the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute required it from 2000, the share of its large trials reporting a benefit fell from 57% (17 of 30) to 8% (2 of 25) (Kaplan & Irvin, PLoS ONE, 2015).

days.apply_question: Eugene Fama has argued that market efficiency can only be tested jointly with a model of what returns should be (the 'joint hypothesis problem'). When a study finds 'anomalous' excess returns, what does the Duhem-Quine thesis say it is entitled to conclude?
days.evidence_note: Settled: refutation strikes the conjunction of theory and auxiliaries (Duhem-Quine); light bending by the Sun has since been confirmed to high precision. Debated: whether falsifiability is an adequate test of what counts as science (Popper vs. Kuhn and Lakatos, Day 40; Laudan, 'The Demise of the Demarcation Problem', 1983); whether the 1919 team handled its data fairly (Earman & Glymour 1980 vs. Kennefick 2009, 2019).

resource.title: Karl Popper, Science, and Pseudoscience: Crash Course Philosophy #8
resource.creator: CrashCourse (host Hank Green; PBS Digital Studios), 2016
resource.why: Popper's own Einstein-versus-Freud contrast and the idea that a genuine test tries to refute rather than confirm, told briskly - the criterion in its plain form before today's lesson complicates it with Duhem-Quine.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: A Meteorologist Said the Continents Move. Geologists Rejected Him for Forty Years - and Some of Their Reasons Were Good.
days.concept: Kuhn: mature science works inside a paradigm - shared exemplars, methods and assumptions - solving puzzles and shelving anomalies until they pile into a crisis and a revolution replaces the framework; Lakatos answered that choosing between rival research programmes is still rational, by asking which one keeps predicting new facts.
days.focus: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962): normal science as puzzle-solving, anomaly, crisis, revolution, and the disputed thesis of incommensurability; why resisting a single anomaly is often rational (most anomalies turn out to be errors). Then Lakatos (1970): a programme's hard core is protected by a belt of auxiliaries, and the programme is progressive if its adjustments predict novel facts that are confirmed, degenerating if they only accommodate. Continental drift shows both: social resistance, and a settlement by new evidence.
key_concepts: Research programme (hard core and protective belt)
days.model_or_equation: Kuhn's cycle: normal science -> anomalies accumulate -> crisis -> revolution -> new normal science. Lakatos's test: a research programme is progressive when its changes predict novel facts that are then confirmed, and degenerating when its changes merely accommodate facts already known.

story.title: The meteorologist who moved the continents
story.hook: On 6 January 1912, at a meeting of the Geological Association in Frankfurt, a 31-year-old meteorologist and Greenland explorer, Alfred Wegener, argued that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart: the matching coastlines of South America and Africa, the same fossils (the reptile Mesosaurus, the seed fern Glossopteris) and rock formations on both sides of the Atlantic, the scars of ancient glaciers in lands now tropical. His book The Origin of Continents and Oceans followed in 1915. In November 1926 the American Association of Petroleum Geologists held a symposium on the theory in New York, to which Wegener contributed; most contributors rejected it, and the geologist Rollin T. Chamberlin is widely quoted as saying that if Wegener were right, geologists would have to forget what they had learned in the past seventy years (sources differ on the remark's exact wording and occasion). Wegener died on the Greenland ice cap in November 1930. In 1963 Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews showed in Nature that the ocean floor carries matching stripes of reversed magnetism on either side of mid-ocean ridges - new crust spreading outward - and within about five years plate tectonics was the new framework of geology.
story.puzzle: Wegener had real evidence. Were the geologists who rejected him for four decades being dogmatic - or were they reasoning well?
story.payoff: Both, which is what Kuhn and Lakatos together explain. Inside the fixed-continents paradigm there was still productive normal science, and Wegener had no workable mechanism: the forces he proposed, such as one arising from Earth's rotation, were far too weak, as the physicist Harold Jeffreys showed. What changed minds was not rhetoric but a programme that predicted something new and checkable - symmetric magnetic stripes - that then turned up. Kuhn explains why the switch was resisted and then abrupt; Lakatos explains why it was rational.
sources: Alfred Wegener, Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane (1915)
American Association of Petroleum Geologists, Theory of Continental Drift: A Symposium (1928)
F. J. Vine & D. H. Matthews, 'Magnetic anomalies over oceanic ridges', Nature 199 (1963) 947-949
Naomi Oreskes, The Rejection of Continental Drift: Theory and Method in American Earth Science (Oxford UP, 1999)

days.application: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren at Royal Perth Hospital. The reigning view held that stress and stomach acid caused peptic ulcers and that bacteria could not survive in the stomach; Warren had noticed curved bacteria in biopsies of inflamed stomachs, and in 1982 the pair cultured the organism now called Helicobacter pylori. Unable to infect laboratory animals, Marshall in July 1984 drank a culture himself; within days he had nausea and vomiting, and a biopsy showed gastritis (Medical Journal of Australia, 1985). Antibiotic trials showed that curing the infection stopped ulcers recurring; a US National Institutes of Health consensus panel endorsed antibiotic treatment in 1994; Marshall and Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. A Kuhnian anomaly long dismissed as contamination, and a Lakatosian win: the bacterial programme predicted a novel fact - antibiotics cure ulcers - that came true.

builds_on.why: Kuhn's chief objection to Popper: scientists do not abandon a theory at its first failed prediction, because blaming an auxiliary (Duhem-Quine) is the everyday tool of normal science.

Reinforcing loops inside science: Merton's 'Matthew effect' sends credit and attention to established figures - plausibly one reason an outsider, a meteorologist among geologists, struggled for a hearing (Oreskes stresses methodological reasons too).

across.link: Pierre Azoulay, Christian Fons-Rosen and Joshua Graff Zivin, 'Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?' (American Economic Review, 2019), tested Max Planck's quip that new truths win when their opponents die: after the sudden death of an eminent life scientist, articles by outsiders in that scientist's subfield rose by roughly 9% - Kuhn's social account, measured.

days.apply_question: In 1982 Dan Shechtman recorded a diffraction pattern with fivefold symmetry that crystallography said was impossible; Linus Pauling dismissed 'quasicrystals' for years, and Shechtman received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Using Lakatos's test, what evidence would have shown, during the 1980s, which side's research programme was progressing?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the historical sequence - drift proposed 1912-15, broadly rejected, vindicated by seafloor-spreading evidence in the 1960s; H. pylori causes most peptic ulcers. Debated: Kuhn's incommensurability thesis and how far theory choice is rational (Kuhn 1962 vs. Lakatos 1970 and Laudan 1977); whether the rejection of drift was dogmatism or a reasonable demand for a mechanism (Oreskes 1999 stresses American methodological habits).

resource.title: Thomas Kuhn (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
resource.creator: Alexander Bird, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (substantive revision 2018)
resource.length: about 20-25 minutes (the sections on the development of science and the concept of a paradigm)
resource.why: A careful, balanced account of normal science, paradigms and incommensurability and of the main criticisms - far more precise than popular 'paradigm shift' talk.
