days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Energy Kept Vanishing When Atoms Decayed. Rather Than Give Up the Law, Pauli Invented a Particle No One Could Detect. It Took 26 Years to Find.
days.concept: Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted between forms; work (force times distance) is how energy is transferred mechanically, and kinetic energy grows with the square of speed.
days.focus: Teaches conservation of energy as physics' strictest bookkeeping rule - work (force times distance) moves energy between accounts such as kinetic energy, which grows with the square of speed, potential energy and heat - through Pauli's 1930 refusal to abandon it when energy seemed to vanish in radioactive decay, and applies it to regenerative braking: an EV wins back only part of its motion because every conversion leaks some energy as heat.
key_concepts: conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics)
days.model_or_equation: W = F d; KE = 1/2 m v^2; energy in = energy out + change in stored energy. Heat is energy too: Joule's measurements of the 1840s fixed the exchange rate at about 4.2 joules per calorie (4.184 J by today's definition).

story.title: A letter to the 'radioactive ladies and gentlemen'
story.hook: By the late 1920s one measurement had put physics' most trusted law in doubt. Some radioactive atoms decay by shooting out an electron (beta decay), and each such decay should release the same, fixed amount of energy - yet the electrons emerged with a smear of energies, most far below the maximum. In 1927 at Cambridge, Charles Ellis and William Wooster trapped the decays of 'radium E' (bismuth-210) in a calorimeter and found the average energy deposited was only about a third of the maximum: the rest seemed simply to vanish. Niels Bohr was prepared to consider that energy might be conserved only on average inside the nucleus. On 4 December 1930, Wolfgang Pauli, aged 30, wrote from Zurich to a physics meeting in Tübingen - 'Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen' - proposing what he called a desperate remedy: an undetected, electrically neutral particle that carried the missing energy away. He could not come in person, he explained, because he was needed at a ball in Zurich.
story.puzzle: Was conservation of energy simply wrong inside the atom - and if it was not, where was the missing energy going?
story.payoff: Conservation of energy is a bookkeeping law tested so thoroughly that, when the books do not balance, the better bet is an account you are not measuring. Pauli bet on an invisible carrier; Enrico Fermi named it the neutrino and built it into his theory of beta decay (1933-34); and in June 1956 Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines, watching a reactor at the Savannah River Plant in South Carolina, cabled Pauli that they had detected it. The energy had never vanished - it left in a particle that barely interacts with matter.
sources: W. Pauli, letter of 4 December 1930 to the Tübingen meeting, in translation in Laurie M. Brown, 'The idea of the neutrino', Physics Today 31(9) (September 1978), 23-28
C. D. Ellis and W. A. Wooster, 'The average energy of disintegration of radium E', Proceedings of the Royal Society A 117 (1927), 109-123
C. L. Cowan Jr., F. Reines, F. B. Harrison, H. W. Kruse and A. D. McGuire, 'Detection of the Free Neutrino: a Confirmation', Science 124 (20 July 1956), 103-104
The Nobel Prize in Physics 1995 (Frederick Reines, for the detection of the neutrino), nobelprize.org

days.application: Regenerative braking: an EV's motor runs as a generator when slowing, turning kinetic energy back into battery charge instead of brake-pad heat. The US DOE estimates net regeneration recovers about 22% of energy on the EPA combined cycle (Fact of the Week #1360, Sept 2024) - not all of it, because every conversion (wheel to motor to battery and back) loses some energy as heat and part of each stop's energy has already gone to drag and rolling resistance.

builds_on.why: Work is the integral of force over distance - accumulation from a rate.
The work-energy theorem follows from F = ma: net work changes kinetic energy.
Pauli rescued a law by positing an unseen entity - the auxiliary-hypothesis move that found Neptune and failed with Vulcan; here the prediction was tested and confirmed in 1956.

across.link: The 'Calories' on food labels are kilocalories, the same unit Joule tied to work: 1 kcal is about 4.184 kJ, so a 250-kcal snack equals the work of lifting 70 kg about 1.5 km - before the body's low efficiency is counted.

days.apply_question: A cyclist coasts down a 100-metre hill without pedalling and reaches the bottom far slower than a frictionless calculation predicts; where did the 'missing' energy go, and why does conservation of energy still hold?
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Bohr's willingness (around 1929-32) to give up strict energy conservation in beta decay is documented in his writings; the neutrino's detection in 1956 settled the question. Pauli's often-quoted remark about having 'postulated a particle that cannot be detected' is second-hand and should be told as reported. Reported regenerative-braking recovery varies widely by definition and drive cycle (DOE's ~22% net figure versus 60-70% component efficiencies).

resource.creator: Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton and Matthew Sands (Caltech; free online edition)
resource.why: Feynman's famous 'Dennis the Menace' blocks explain what conservation of energy really asserts - an abstract number that stays constant - better than any summary.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Critics Said the World's Biggest Battery Could Run South Australia for Only Minutes. They Were Measuring the Wrong Thing.
days.concept: Power is the rate at which energy is converted or delivered - energy per second, measured in watts - so a kilowatt (how fast) and a kilowatt-hour (how much) answer different questions.
days.focus: Teaches power as the rate at which energy is transferred (the time-derivative of energy) and the kilowatt-versus-kilowatt-hour distinction that confuses most energy debates, through a grid battery that was small in energy but large and fast in power, then a charging EV and the roughly 100-watt human body.
days.model_or_equation: P = dE/dt (average P = E / t); E = P x t. Hornsdale at opening: 129 MWh / 100 MW is about 1.3 hours at full output, while 129 MWh against a state demand of roughly 1.5 GW is about 5 minutes. 1 hp = 33,000 ft-lbf per minute, about 745.7 W. Charging time is roughly battery energy / charging power: 75 kWh / 7 kW is about 11 hours; at 350 kW it would be under 15 minutes, but real fast charging tapers and takes longer.

story.title: The world's biggest battery and the Big Banana
story.hook: On 28 September 2016 a storm toppled transmission towers and the whole of South Australia went dark. In March 2017 Elon Musk bet on Twitter that Tesla could install 100 megawatts of batteries within 100 days of signing a contract, or the system would be free; the state government took up the offer. The Hornsdale Power Reserve, built for the French company Neoen beside its wind farm near Jamestown, was switched on at the start of December 2017 - well inside the 100 days - as the largest lithium-ion battery in the world: 100 megawatts of power, 129 megawatt-hours of storage. Federal Treasurer Scott Morrison had scoffed at the idea, likening it to the giant roadside attractions such as the 'Big Banana'. The sceptics' sums looked damning: at South Australia's typical demand of roughly 1.5 gigawatts, a full charge would run the state for about five minutes. Then, on 14 December 2017, a 560-megawatt coal unit at Loy Yang A in Victoria tripped off the grid, and the battery was injecting power within a fraction of a second - ahead of the coal plant contracted to respond.
story.puzzle: If its whole charge could keep the state's lights on for only minutes, why was the battery worth building - and what was it actually selling?
story.payoff: It was selling power, not energy. Megawatt-hours measure how much energy a battery holds; megawatts measure how fast it can deliver it. Holding a grid steady when a big plant fails takes a large flow of power for seconds to minutes, delivered almost instantly - a job a 100-megawatt battery does well even though 129 megawatt-hours is a tiny store. The sceptics answered 'how much?' when the grid was asking 'how fast?'.
sources: Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO), 'Initial operation of the Hornsdale Power Reserve Battery Energy Storage System' (April 2018)
Aurecon, 'Hornsdale Power Reserve Year 1 Technical and Market Impact Case Study' (2018)
AEMO, 'Black System South Australia 28 September 2016' final report (March 2017)
Neoen, Hornsdale Power Reserve project information (hornsdalepowerreserve.com.au)

days.application: EV charging: a home charger at about 7 kW and a highway fast charger rated up to 350 kW deliver the same kilowatt-hours to a battery at very different rates, which is why one takes all night and the other well under an hour (in practice charging slows as the battery fills). The same arithmetic shows why a human body, running on about 2,000 kcal a day, averages roughly 100 W - one bright old-fashioned light bulb.

builds_on.why: Power is today's name for the rate of the energy transfers taught yesterday.
Power is the derivative of energy with respect to time; energy is the integral of power (Day 5).

across.link: Robert Allen's The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009) argues that steam engines spread first in Britain because coal was cheap and labour dear there, so buying mechanical power from an engine undercut buying it from men and horses - a historical argument built on the cost of power.

days.apply_question: A household's electricity bill shows 900 kWh for a 30-day month; what is its average power draw in kilowatts, and why does the utility still have to build for a much higher peak?
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Hornsdale's figures (100 MW / 129 MWh at opening; expanded in 2020) and its sub-second response to the 14 December 2017 Loy Yang trip come from AEMO, Neoen and press reports; quoted response times and first-year savings vary by source and should be given as reported. Whether grid batteries are good value is an economic question beyond this lesson. The horsepower's definition (33,000 ft-lbf per minute) is exact; how Watt chose it is told differently in different sources.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
days.headline_hint: A 28-Year-Old Frenchman Proved No Engine Could Ever Be Perfect - Using Engines Britain Had Already Built.
days.concept: A heat engine turns heat flowing from hot to cold into work, and no engine can convert all its heat into work: the maximum efficiency is 1 - T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in kelvin), whatever the machine or fuel.
days.focus: Teaches the Carnot limit as a ceiling set only by temperatures, the reason most fuel energy in engines becomes waste heat, and why the hot-to-cold temperature gap - not cleverness alone - decides how good an engine can be.
days.model_or_equation: eta_max = 1 - T_c / T_h (kelvin). Example: a steam plant at 823 K (550 C) rejecting heat at 300 K: eta_max = 1 - 300/823 = 0.64; real plants get about 40%. A combined-cycle plant raises T_h by burning gas in a turbine first.

story.title: A book of 600 copies about fire
story.hook: In June 1824 Sadi Carnot, a 28-year-old French engineer and son of the revolutionary minister Lazare Carnot, published at his own expense about 600 copies of a short book, Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire. He began from a political fact: Britain's mines and factories ran on steam on a scale France could not match - to take away England's steam engines, he wrote, would be to dry up all her sources of wealth. Engineers were improving engines by trial and error, swapping steam for air or alcohol, raising pressures. Carnot asked a deeper question. The book was barely noticed; he died in the Paris cholera epidemic of 1832, aged 36. Émile Clapeyron revived it in 1834, and Thomson and Clausius built thermodynamics on it.
story.puzzle: Is there a limit to how much work fire can give - and does it depend on the working substance, the design or something else?
story.payoff: Carnot showed that work comes from heat falling from a hot body to a cold one, and that the best possible engine's efficiency depends only on the two temperatures. No working substance or design can beat it; the only route to a better engine is a hotter source or a colder sink - which is exactly what engineers have chased ever since.
sources: Sadi Carnot, Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu (Paris, 1824)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot' (St Andrews)
Larousse encyclopédie entry on Sadi Carnot (print run of 600)

days.application: The car's physical-constraint link: fueleconomy.gov estimates only about 12-30% of a conventional car's fuel energy moves it down the road, most of the rest leaving as engine heat - while Chubu Electric's Nishi-Nagoya Block 1 combined-cycle plant (GE 7HA gas turbines, with Toshiba steam turbines running on their exhaust heat) was certified by Guinness World Records in March 2018 at 63.08% gross efficiency, because it runs a far hotter source and recycles its exhaust heat.

builds_on.why: Conservation of energy says heat in equals work out plus heat rejected; Carnot's limit says how the split must go.
Carnot theorized engines that already worked: practice led science, the non-linear innovation pattern taught in Systems Thinking.
Day 1 discounted gasoline's energy density for engine efficiency; today explains why most of a fuel's energy is unavoidably lost as heat.

across.link: Muscle is not a heat engine - it converts chemical energy directly at body temperature, so the Carnot limit does not bind it - yet human muscles still convert only roughly a fifth to a quarter of food energy into mechanical work, the rest leaving as heat.

days.apply_question: Ocean thermal energy conversion plants try to run an engine between tropical surface water at about 25 C and deep water at about 5 C; use the Carnot limit to estimate their best possible efficiency and say why such plants must move huge volumes of water.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Real-world efficiency figures depend on the test cycle (fueleconomy.gov's 12-30% range spans city and highway driving) and on gross versus net measurement (Nishi-Nagoya's 63.08% is gross). Sources differ slightly on Carnot's final illness (cholera, possibly after scarlet fever).

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Entropy and why useful energy runs out
days.headline_hint: You Give Off as Much Energy as You Eat. So What Are You Actually Eating? A Physicist Answered in Dublin in 1943.
days.concept: Entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements are consistent with a system's state; isolated systems drift toward more probable, higher-entropy states, so what we 'use up' is not energy but low entropy - energy's capacity to do work (exergy).
days.focus: Teaches the second law statistically (Boltzmann's counting of arrangements), why heat flows from hot to cold and not back, and why the useful quantity in any energy system is exergy rather than energy - the point Schrödinger made about living things.
days.model_or_equation: S = k_B ln W (Boltzmann's formula, carved on his tomb in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof), where W is the number of microscopic arrangements; for heat Q flowing at temperature T, entropy changes by Q/T, so heat flowing from hot to cold raises total entropy.

story.title: What an organism feeds upon
story.hook: In February 1943, in neutral Ireland in the middle of the war, the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger - who had fled Austria in 1938 - gave a series of public lectures at Trinity College Dublin under the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, published in 1944 as What Is Life? He asked what keeps a living thing from decaying into inert equilibrium, and dismissed the obvious answer. Restaurants in some advanced country, he recalled, printed the energy content of every dish on the menu; but in an adult the body's energy content is as stationary as its material content - every calorie taken in eventually leaves again, mostly as heat - and if any calorie is worth as much as any other, a mere exchange cannot be what sustains us. His answer puzzled many readers and later inspired biologists: 'What an organism feeds upon is negative entropy.'
story.puzzle: If an adult gives back every joule it eats - and Earth, likewise, radiates to space about as much energy as it absorbs from the Sun - what are living things, and the planet, actually getting?
story.payoff: Energy in equals energy out, but its quality differs. Food and sunlight arrive as concentrated, low-entropy energy; bodies and Earth return it as diffuse, high-entropy heat (Earth sends out roughly twenty infrared photons for each visible photon it absorbs, a point Roger Penrose later popularized). Life runs on that difference: what is consumed is the drop in entropy - energy's capacity to do work - not the energy itself.
sources: Erwin Schrödinger, What Is Life? (Cambridge UP, 1944), ch. 6 'Order, disorder and entropy'
Walter Moore, Schrödinger: Life and Thought (Cambridge UP, 1989) on the Dublin lectures
Roger Penrose, The Emperor's New Mind (1989), ch. 7, on the Sun as a low-entropy source

days.application: Heating a home: a modern gas furnace may be 95% 'efficient' by the first law, yet it degrades high-quality chemical energy into 20 C air. An electric heat pump with a coefficient of performance around 3 moves about three units of heat from outdoors per unit of electricity - not free energy, but a way of spending far less exergy for the same warmth. The 1975 American Physical Society summer study 'Efficient Use of Energy' popularized 'second-law efficiency' to show how little of fuels' work potential such heating used.

builds_on.why: The Carnot limit is the second law applied to engines; today explains the law behind it.
Entropy is a probability argument: high-entropy states are overwhelmingly more likely because they have far more arrangements.
Boltzmann's formula uses a logarithm, which turns multiplying numbers of arrangements into adding entropies.

across.link: Landauer's principle (Rolf Landauer, IBM, 1961) says erasing one bit must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat; Bérut and colleagues measured this limit with a trapped colloidal bead (Nature, 2012) - entropy sets a floor under computation.

days.apply_question: A data centre's servers turn nearly all their electricity into warm air at about 35 C; using entropy and exergy, explain why that heat is hard to sell to a nearby town even though the energy is all still there.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The statistical reading of the second law is mainstream; Schrödinger's 'negative entropy' phrasing was criticized as loose (he later noted free energy was meant), and his book's biological speculations are historically, not scientifically, authoritative. The APS 1975 study's specific second-law efficiency figures should be checked before being quoted.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Thirty Men Ran Across the Vasa's Deck and the Test Was Stopped. The King's Warship Sailed Anyway - and Capsized Within a Mile.
days.concept: Pressure in a fluid grows with depth (P = rho g h); buoyancy equals the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes); and a floating body is stable only if its weight sits low enough relative to its centre of buoyancy that a tilt creates a righting moment.
days.focus: Teaches hydrostatic pressure, Archimedes' principle and floating stability (centre of gravity, centre of buoyancy, metacentre) through the Vasa disaster, and applies depth-pressure to why dams are thick at the bottom.
key_concepts: centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy
days.model_or_equation: P = rho g h (water: about 1 atmosphere extra per 10 m of depth); buoyant force = rho_fluid x g x V_displaced; a ship is initially stable when its metacentric height GM is positive.

story.title: The Vasa's 1,300 metres
story.hook: On 10 August 1628 the new warship Vasa, pride of King Gustavus Adolphus's navy, set sail from Stockholm with 64 guns, many on two gun decks high above the waterline. Within about 1,300 metres a gust heeled her over; water poured through the open gunports and she sank in Stockholm harbour, with the loss of some 30 people (estimates vary). Weeks earlier a stability test had been made at the quay: about 30 men ran back and forth across the deck, and after three runs the ship rolled so much that the test was stopped. She sailed anyway. Raised in 1961, she now stands in Stockholm's Vasa Museum.
story.puzzle: Why did a ship that floated perfectly well capsize in a light breeze - and what were thirty running men really measuring?
story.payoff: Floating is buoyancy; staying upright is stability. Vasa's heavy upper gun deck and too little ballast put her centre of gravity high relative to her centre of buoyancy, so when she heeled the shifted buoyancy produced only a tiny righting moment. The running-men test was a crude measurement of exactly that: a ship that rolls far under a small shifting load has little metacentric height.
sources: Vasa Museum (Vasamuseet), Stockholm: published history of the sinking and of the 1628 inquiry
Richard E. Fairley and Mary Jane Willshire, 'Why the Vasa Sank: 10 Problems and Some Antidotes for Software Projects', IEEE Software 20(2), 2003
Eric Kvarning and Bengt Ohrelius, The Vasa: The Royal Ship (1973)

days.application: Hoover Dam is about 660 feet thick at its base and 45 feet at its crest because water pressure rises linearly with depth: 500 feet down the water presses with about 15 atmospheres (over 200 pounds per square inch) more than at the surface, and the total thrust on the dam grows with the square of the depth.

builds_on.why: Floating and stability are balances of forces and of their turning effects.
The total thrust on a dam is the integral of pressure over depth, which is why it grows as depth squared.

across.link: The International Maritime Organization's 2008 Intact Stability Code, made mandatory through the SOLAS convention, sets minimum stability criteria (including a minimum initial metacentric height) for ships worldwide - Vasa's lesson written into treaty law.

days.apply_question: Cargo ships sometimes capsize after containers stacked high on deck shift in a storm; using centre of gravity and righting moment, explain why adding weight high up makes a ship less stable even though it still floats.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Vasa's death toll is uncertain (often given as 30, sometimes up to about 50); historians agree on the instability and the stopped heel test, and still discuss how far blame lay with the shipwright (Henrik Hybertsson, who died before launch), the admiral, or the king's demands.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: The Wright Brothers' Gliders Kept Failing. So They Built a Wind Tunnel in Their Bicycle Shop and Proved the Textbook Wrong.
days.concept: A body moving through air pays drag that grows with the square of speed (so the power to overcome it grows with the cube), and a wing makes lift by turning the airflow downward - both described by the same dynamic-pressure formula.
days.focus: Teaches the drag equation and lift as momentum given to air, through the Wright brothers' discovery that the accepted coefficients were wrong, and applies the v-squared and v-cubed laws to highway fuel economy and EV design.
key_concepts: lift as downward deflection of air
days.model_or_equation: F_drag = 1/2 rho v^2 Cd A; P_drag = F_drag x v = 1/2 rho v^3 Cd A; lift has the same form with a lift coefficient C_L. Going from 55 to 75 mph raises drag force by (75/55)^2, about 1.9 times, and drag power by about 2.5 times.

story.title: The bicycle-shop wind tunnel
story.hook: In 1901 Wilbur and Orville Wright returned from Kitty Hawk discouraged: their glider produced only about a third of the lift that published tables, built on Otto Lilienthal's data and the long-accepted 'Smeaton coefficient' for air pressure, said it should. That autumn, in their Dayton bicycle shop, they built a six-foot wind tunnel driven by a fan and tested some 200 small model wing shapes on balances made from bicycle spokes and hacksaw blades. They found the Smeaton coefficient, used for more than a century, was badly off: their value was about 0.0033 against the traditional 0.005, which had overstated the force of moving air by roughly half. Armed with their own tables, they flew the first powered, controlled airplane at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903.
story.puzzle: How could a coefficient used by engineers for over a century be wrong, and why did two bicycle makers need a box with a fan to design a wing?
story.payoff: Lift and drag depend on shape-specific coefficients that theory then could not predict, so they had to be measured. The Wrights' tunnel measured lift and drag directly for each wing shape and angle, exposing the bad constant and giving them coefficients that worked - the same equation, with honest numbers.
sources: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'The Wright Brothers: The Invention of the Aerial Age' (1901 wind tunnel)
NASA Glenn Research Center, 'Wright 1901 Wind Tunnel' (Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics)
Tom Crouch, The Bishop's Boys (W. W. Norton, 1989)

days.application: Highway fuel economy falls steeply above about 50 mph because drag power rises with the cube of speed (Day 8's flat optimum near 50 mph in DOE/ORNL tests), and it is why EV makers chase drag coefficients near 0.2: at highway speed, aerodynamic drag is the largest single draw on the battery, so a lower Cd directly buys range.

builds_on.why: The fuel-economy optimum near 50 mph is where rising drag losses meet falling fixed losses.
Drag is a power law in speed, a straight line on a log-log plot.
Lift is the reaction to momentum pushed downward into the air.

across.link: Chrysler's 1934 Airflow, among the first production cars shaped with wind-tunnel testing, flopped in the showroom - a case where the physics was right and adoption went the other way.

days.apply_question: Long-haul truckers can cut fuel use by fitting side skirts and trailer tails; using the drag equation, explain why these devices pay off on interstates but barely matter on city delivery routes.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The simple 'equal transit time' explanation of lift taught for decades is wrong; lift is correctly explained by flow turning and the pressure differences that go with it. Accounts of the Wrights' Smeaton result give it as about 0.0033 against a traditional 0.005 (sometimes 0.0054).

resource.creator: University of Cambridge, with Holger Babinsky (Department of Engineering), 2012
resource.length: a few minutes (exact length not confirmed)
resource.why: Smoke pulses in a wind tunnel show that air over a wing does not 'rejoin' the air underneath, overturning the common textbook explanation and showing lift as flow turning.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: In Deep Water the Tsunami Was Less Than a Metre High and Moving at Jet Speed. A Ten-Year-Old on a Phuket Beach Knew What It Meant.
days.concept: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the medium along, and its speed is set by the medium - for long ocean waves, the square root of gravity times depth.
days.focus: Teaches waves (wavelength, frequency, speed, amplitude) and superposition through the 2004 tsunami's speed and shoaling, then applies interference to noise cancellation.
key_concepts: wavelength, frequency and speed (v = f x lambda)
days.model_or_equation: v = f lambda; for waves much longer than the water is deep, v = sqrt(g d). In 4,000 m of ocean: sqrt(9.8 x 4000) is about 198 m/s, about 710 km/h; in 10 m of water, about 10 m/s (36 km/h).

story.title: The sea went out at Mai Khao
story.hook: On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1-9.3 earthquake off northern Sumatra lifted the seafloor along a rupture more than 1,000 km long. The tsunami it launched crossed the Indian Ocean at the speed of a jet airliner, barely a metre high in deep water, and killed roughly 230,000 people in about 14 countries. On Mai Khao beach in Phuket, Thailand, ten-year-old Tilly Smith, on holiday from England, saw the sea draw back and froth. Two weeks earlier her geography teacher, Andrew Kearney, had taught her class about tsunamis. She told her parents; the beach was cleared, and it was reported to be among the few on that stretch where no one was killed.
story.puzzle: How can a wave be nearly invisible to a ship at sea yet grow into a wall of water at the shore - and why did it travel at hundreds of kilometres an hour across open ocean?
story.payoff: A tsunami's wavelength is hundreds of kilometres, so the whole ocean depth moves and its speed is sqrt(g d): about 700 km/h over 4 km of water. As it reaches shallow water it slows, its energy bunches into a shorter distance and its height grows (shoaling). The receding sea Tilly saw was the trough arriving first.
sources: NOAA and US Geological Survey summaries of the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake and tsunami
BBC News, 'Girl, 10, used geography lesson to save lives' (1 January 2005)
Press coverage of Tilly Smith's 2005 award from the Marine Society (UK)

days.application: Active noise cancellation in car cabins and headphones: microphones sense low-frequency engine and road noise and speakers emit the same wave inverted, so the two superpose and largely cancel (destructive interference) - which works best for steady low-frequency hum and poorly for sudden high-frequency sounds.

builds_on.why: Fukushima's design-basis wave showed tsunamis are fat-tailed hazards; today explains how the wave itself moves and grows.
A sqrt(g d) estimate is an order-of-magnitude calculation that predicts arrival times across an ocean.

across.link: After 2004, UNESCO's Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission coordinated the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning and Mitigation System, operational from 2006; warnings work because seismic waves travel far faster than sqrt(g d).

days.apply_question: Ocean swell that approaches a beach at an angle offshore usually arrives breaking almost parallel to the shoreline; using the shallow-water wave speed, explain why the crests swing round as they come in.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The 2004 death toll is given variously from about 227,000 to over 230,000; the earthquake's magnitude is given as 9.1 to 9.3. The 'no deaths on that beach' detail comes from press reports and award citations.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Galvani Said Frogs' Legs Held a Living Electricity. Volta Stacked Zinc, Copper and Salty Cardboard to Prove Him Wrong - and Built the First Battery.
days.concept: Voltage is the energy per unit charge that pushes charge around a circuit, current is the rate of charge flow, resistance opposes it (V = IR, Ohm's law), and electrical power is current times voltage (P = IV).
days.focus: Teaches the circuit model - charge, current, voltage, resistance, power - and the I-squared-R loss that explains both thick starter cables and high-voltage transmission, through Volta's pile and his dispute with Galvani.
days.model_or_equation: V = I R; P = I V = I^2 R. For a fixed power delivered, current falls as voltage rises, and line losses fall with the square of the current: raising transmission voltage 10-fold cuts I^2 R losses about 100-fold.

story.title: The pile that answered a frog
story.hook: In the 1780s and 1790s the Bologna anatomist Luigi Galvani made dissected frogs' legs twitch when touched with two different metals, and argued for an 'animal electricity' residing in living tissue. Alessandro Volta, professor at Pavia, suspected the metals themselves were the source. On 20 March 1800 he wrote to Sir Joseph Banks, president of the Royal Society in London, describing a column of alternating zinc and copper (or silver) discs separated by cardboard soaked in brine: the 'pile'. It gave a steady, continuous flow of electricity - not a spark, but a current. Within weeks of the letter reaching London, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle used a pile to split water.
story.puzzle: What exactly did Volta's stack provide that a spark from a rubbed glass rod could not - and why did it matter that it kept flowing?
story.payoff: The pile supplied a steady voltage: a fixed amount of energy per unit charge, maintained by chemistry, which pushes a continuous current through whatever resistance is connected. That is the circuit model. And both men were partly right: the metals drove Volta's current, but nerves do run on electrical signals.
sources: Alessandro Volta, 'On the Electricity Excited by the Mere Contact of Conducting Substances of Different Kinds', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 90 (1800) - letter to Banks dated 20 March 1800
Marco Piccolino, 'Luigi Galvani and animal electricity: two centuries after the foundation of electrophysiology', Trends in Neurosciences 20 (1997)
IEEE / Royal Institution history accounts of the voltaic pile

days.application: Why a car's starter motor needs thick cables from its 12-volt battery: cranking can draw a few hundred amperes, and at that current even a few thousandths of an ohm wastes power as heat and drops voltage - so cables must be thick and short. Power lines face the same law at scale, which is why they run at hundreds of thousands of volts (Day 66).

builds_on.why: Electrical power P = IV is energy per second, the quantity defined in the power lesson.
Voltage is energy per charge; a circuit is energy conservation for moving charges.

across.link: Galvani was partly vindicated: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley measured the nerve impulse as an electrical signal in the squid giant axon (1952) and shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

days.apply_question: An extension cord rated for 10 amperes grows warm when a 2,000-watt space heater runs on a 120-volt circuit; using P = IV and I^2 R, explain why, and why the same heater on Europe's 230-volt mains stresses the cord less.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The Galvani-Volta dispute is usually told as Volta 'winning'; historians of neuroscience stress that Galvani's animal electricity was later vindicated in a different form.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Faraday's Needle Twitched Only When He Switched the Current On or Off. That Flicker Now Powers the World.
days.concept: A changing magnetic field through a loop drives a current in it (Faraday's law of induction), and a current in a magnetic field feels a force - so a motor and a generator are the same machine run in opposite directions, and a transformer only works with changing current.
days.focus: Teaches induction as the link between electricity, magnetism and motion, explaining generators, motors and transformers, through Faraday's 1831 iron ring and the electric car's motor.
days.model_or_equation: EMF = -N dPhi/dt: the voltage induced in a coil of N turns equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through it; a transformer's voltages scale with its turns ratio, V2/V1 = N2/N1 - but only while the flux is changing.

story.title: The iron ring, 29 August 1831
story.hook: Since Hans Christian Ørsted showed in 1820 that a current deflects a compass needle, physicists had looked for the reverse: magnetism making electricity. Steady magnets placed beside wires did nothing. On 29 August 1831, at the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday - a bookbinder's apprentice turned chemist - wound two separate coils of insulated wire on opposite sides of a soft iron ring. He connected one coil to a battery and the other to a galvanometer. The needle jumped when he closed the battery circuit, swung back, jumped the other way when he opened it - and stayed at zero while the current flowed steadily.
story.puzzle: Why did the needle move only at the instants of switching on and off, and never while a strong current flowed steadily in the first coil?
story.payoff: Induction responds to change, not to magnetism itself: only a changing magnetic flux through the second coil induces a voltage. That is why generators must keep moving magnets past coils, why motors are generators run backwards, and why transformers need alternating current - the physical fact that will decide the War of the Currents (Day 66).
sources: Michael Faraday, laboratory notebook entry of 29 August 1831 (Royal Institution); 'Experimental Researches in Electricity', Philosophical Transactions 122 (1832)
Royal Institution, Faraday's induction ring (museum object and history pages)
Frank A. J. L. James, Michael Faraday: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford UP, 2010)

days.application: The electric car's motor and the wind turbine's generator are the same physics in reverse: a car motor uses a rotating magnetic field to drag its rotor round, and runs as a generator during regenerative braking (Day 52). Tesla, Inc. took its name from Nikola Tesla, whose 1888 alternating-current induction motor is the ancestor of the AC induction motors that drove the company's first Roadster and early Model S.

builds_on.why: Induction drives currents through the circuits and resistances taught yesterday.
Faraday's law sets voltage equal to a derivative - the rate of change of magnetic flux.

across.link: Transcranial magnetic stimulation, cleared by the US FDA in 2008 for treatment-resistant depression, pulses a coil on the scalp so its rapidly changing magnetic field induces currents in brain tissue - Faraday's law used as medicine.

days.apply_question: Wireless phone chargers work only with alternating current in the pad's coil; using Faraday's law, explain why a pad fed with steady direct current would never charge the phone.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Faraday's discovery was nearly simultaneous with Joseph Henry's in the US; priority is usually given to Faraday because he published first.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Maxwell Calculated the Speed of an Electrical Wave From Lab Measurements. It Came Out as the Speed of Light.
days.concept: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are one phenomenon - electromagnetic waves - differing only in frequency, and the energy carried by each photon rises with frequency (E = hf).
days.focus: Teaches the electromagnetic spectrum as a single phenomenon, from Maxwell's unification to Hertz's radio waves, and the photon-energy rule that separates harmless non-ionizing radiation from DNA-damaging ultraviolet and X-rays.
days.model_or_equation: c = f lambda (c is about 300,000 km/s); E = h f (h is Planck's constant). A 77 GHz radar photon carries about 0.0003 eV; an ultraviolet-B photon (280-315 nm) about 4 eV; breaking a chemical bond takes a few eV and ionizing an atom roughly 10 eV or more.

story.title: A number that should not have matched
story.hook: In the summer of 1861, at Glenlair, his estate in south-west Scotland, James Clerk Maxwell was building a mechanical model of electric and magnetic fields out of imagined spinning cells and idle wheels. The model implied that the field could carry waves, at a speed fixed by the ratio between electrical and magnetic units - but away from his books he could not put a number on it. Back in London that autumn he found the ratio measured in 1856 by Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch in Germany, who had discharged a Leyden jar through a galvanometer - an experiment that had nothing to do with light. The speed came out at about 310,700 km per second; Hippolyte Fizeau had measured light at about 314,900. Maxwell told Faraday in October 1861 that he had worked out the formulae in the country before seeing Weber's number, and wrote in 1862 that 'we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.' In 1887 at Karlsruhe, Heinrich Hertz made such waves with a spark gap and detected them across his lab.
story.puzzle: Why should a speed computed from electrical measurements on a laboratory bench equal the speed of light from the stars?
story.payoff: Because light is an electromagnetic wave: a changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field, which makes a changing electric field, and the pair travel at a speed set by those electrical constants. Hertz's radio waves were the same thing at a lower frequency - the whole spectrum is one phenomenon.
sources: J. C. Maxwell, 'On Physical Lines of Force', Philosophical Magazine (1861-62), Part III
J. C. Maxwell, letter to Michael Faraday, 19 October 1861 (in P. M. Harman, ed., The Scientific Letters and Papers of James Clerk Maxwell, vol. 1, Cambridge UP, 1990)
Basil Mahon, The Man Who Changed Everything: The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (Wiley, 2003)

days.application: A modern car sees with the spectrum: automotive radar works at 76-81 GHz and lidar typically near 905 nm or 1550 nm in the infrared. A radar photon carries about ten thousand times less energy than the few eV needed to break a chemical bond, and lidar's near-infrared photons (about 1.4 eV at 905 nm, 0.8 eV at 1550 nm) fall far short of the roughly 10 eV needed to ionize - so neither damages DNA directly (lidar's real hazard is heating the retina, which eye-safety limits cap), while ultraviolet photons can, causing sunburn and skin cancer.

builds_on.why: Electromagnetic waves obey the same speed-frequency-wavelength relation (v = f lambda) as water and sound waves.
A changing magnetic field makes an electric field (induction); Maxwell added the reverse, which lets the pair travel as a wave.

across.link: The James Webb Space Telescope (launched December 2021) observes mainly in the infrared because the universe's expansion has stretched the visible and ultraviolet light of the earliest galaxies into infrared wavelengths.

days.apply_question: Airport body scanners use millimetre waves while hospital chest films use X-rays; using photon energy, explain why only one of them raises concern about ionizing radiation dose.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Claims that radio-frequency exposure from phones or 5G causes cancer are not supported by the mainstream evidence (IARC classed RF fields as 'possibly carcinogenic', Group 2B, in 2011, its weakest positive category, reflecting limited evidence rather than a demonstrated effect); this is a public controversy, not an expert one.

resource.why: NASA's illustrated tour gives each band - radio to gamma - its own short page with real instruments and images, the breadth the lesson cannot.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Two Physicists Bought Airline Seats for Four Atomic Clocks and Flew Them Around the World. The Clocks Came Back Disagreeing.
days.concept: Time is not universal: a moving clock runs slow relative to one at rest (special relativity), and a clock higher in a gravitational field runs fast relative to one lower down (general relativity) - small effects, but measurable and engineering-relevant.
days.focus: Teaches time dilation from motion and from gravity as two effects that can add or cancel, through the Hafele-Keating flights, and applies them to GPS, where ignoring them would ruin positioning within a day.
days.model_or_equation: Velocity: a clock moving at speed v ticks slow by about v^2 / (2c^2) (fractional, for v much less than c). Gravity: a clock higher by height h ticks fast by about g h / c^2. GPS satellites: about -7 microseconds/day from speed and +45 from altitude, net about +38 microseconds/day; light travels about 11 km in 38 microseconds.

story.title: Four clocks in economy class
story.hook: In October 1971 the physicist Joseph Hafele and the astronomer Richard Keating of the US Naval Observatory flew four portable cesium-beam atomic clocks around the world on ordinary commercial airliners - first eastward, then westward - booking seats for the clocks. Back in Washington they compared them with the Observatory's reference clocks. Relative to the ground, the eastbound clocks had lost about 59 nanoseconds and the westbound clocks had gained about 273, in line with predictions of about -40 and +275 nanoseconds within the stated uncertainties. They published in Science in July 1972.
story.puzzle: Why should the direction of a flight make clocks disagree - and why would the westbound clocks gain time rather than lose it?
story.payoff: Two effects were at work. Flying high, all the airborne clocks sat higher in Earth's gravity and ran fast (general relativity). Their speed relative to Earth's non-rotating centre made them run slow (special relativity): eastbound planes add to Earth's rotation and move fastest, so they lost more than altitude gave back; westbound planes move slower than the ground itself, so altitude's gain dominated.
sources: J. C. Hafele and R. E. Keating, 'Around-the-World Atomic Clocks: Predicted Relativistic Time Gains' and 'Observed Relativistic Time Gains', Science 177 (14 July 1972), 166-170
Neil Ashby, 'Relativity and the Global Positioning System', Physics Today 55(5) (May 2002)

days.application: GPS: satellite clocks orbiting at about 20,200 km run fast by about 45 microseconds a day from weaker gravity and slow by about 7 from their speed - a net gain of about 38 microseconds a day. The clocks are deliberately set to tick slightly slow before launch; uncorrected, ranging errors would accumulate on the order of 10 km per day.

builds_on.why: Special relativity is a theory of relative velocity: which frame the clocks move in decides the effect.
Eddington's 1919 eclipse test of general relativity was the first famous attempt to falsify Einstein; Hafele-Keating is a later test of the same theory.
The result is meaningful only against its stated error bars: predicted and observed agree within uncertainties.

across.link: On 6 April 1922 in Paris, Henri Bergson debated Einstein on whether relativity's 'time' is the time we live; Jimena Canales's The Physicist and the Philosopher (2015) traces how the clash split physics from philosophy of time.

days.apply_question: Physicists at NIST in 2010 measured an aluminium-ion clock running faster when raised by only about 33 centimetres; which relativistic effect is that, and why would a geodesist care?
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The original Hafele-Keating data have been criticized for their large uncertainties and clock behaviour; later, far more precise experiments (Gravity Probe A in 1976, NIST's optical clocks in 2010) confirmed both effects decisively, so the 1971 test is best taught as historic rather than definitive.

resource.why: A short, numerate walk-through of exactly how special and general relativity combine in GPS clocks - the lesson's application in an astronomer's own words.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: 'As If You Fired a 15-Inch Shell at Tissue Paper and It Came Back.' What Rutherford's Students Found Inside the Atom.
days.concept: An atom is a tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons that can occupy only discrete energy levels, so atoms absorb and emit light only at particular energies - the reason every element has its own spectral fingerprint.
days.focus: Teaches the nuclear atom (from the gold-foil experiment) and quantized energy levels (Bohr, 1913) as the explanation of spectral lines, then shows the same logic - a fixed energy gap sets the colour - at work in the LED.
days.model_or_equation: Photon energy = difference between levels: h f = E_upper - E_lower. For hydrogen, E_n = -13.6 eV / n^2. In an LED, photon energy is about the band gap: blue light near 450 nm needs about 2.7-2.8 eV.

story.title: The shell that bounced off tissue paper
story.hook: In 1909 at the University of Manchester, Hans Geiger and a 20-year-old undergraduate, Ernest Marsden, fired alpha particles from a radioactive source at thin metal foils, gold among them, counting the faint flashes on a zinc-sulphide screen by eye in a darkened room. Nearly all the particles went straight through or were barely deflected. But a few came back: by their estimate, about one in 8,000 was turned through more than 90 degrees. Their professor, Ernest Rutherford, recalled years later that it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.' The atom of the day, J. J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' of spread-out charge, could not do that.
story.puzzle: What could be inside a thin gold foil that turns back a fast alpha particle - and if atoms are mostly empty, why don't their electrons simply spiral into that centre?
story.payoff: Rutherford concluded (1911) that the atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus; a rare head-on approach turns the alpha particle back. Niels Bohr (1913) then proposed that electrons occupy only certain allowed energy levels and do not radiate while in them, jumping between levels by emitting or absorbing photons of exactly the level difference - which explained hydrogen's spectral lines.
sources: H. Geiger and E. Marsden, 'On a Diffuse Reflection of the α-Particles', Proceedings of the Royal Society A 82 (1909)
E. Rutherford, 'The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom', Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911)
N. Bohr, 'On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules', Philosophical Magazine 26 (1913)

days.application: LEDs: in a semiconductor the allowed electron energies form bands separated by a gap, and the light an LED emits has a photon energy close to that gap. Red and green LEDs existed by the 1960s-70s, but a practical bright blue LED needed gallium nitride, achieved by Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura around 1989-93 (Nobel Prize in Physics 2014); blue plus phosphors made white LED lighting possible.

builds_on.why: Photon energy E = hf is what links an atom's energy levels to the colour of its light.
The quantum atom is a textbook paradigm shift: the anomalies (back-scattered alphas, stable atoms) broke the classical model.

across.link: Electron shells explain the periodic table: Mendeleev ordered the elements by their chemical behaviour in 1869, and the quantum atom later showed that behaviour repeats because outer-shell electron arrangements repeat.

days.apply_question: Sodium streetlights glowed a single yellow-orange colour while LED streetlights look white; using discrete energy levels, explain why a sodium lamp's light comes out at essentially one colour.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Bohr's 1913 model is superseded in detail by quantum mechanics (electrons as standing waves, not orbits) but its core - discrete energy levels and photons equal to their differences - is retained. The '15-inch shell' line is Rutherford's own recollection from a late lecture, not a 1909 record.

resource.why: Explains band gaps, why blue was so hard and how gallium nitride was finally mastered - the quantum atom turned into the lighting revolution.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: On a Snowy Walk in Sweden, an Exiled Physicist and Her Nephew Did the Math on Scraps of Paper. The Uranium Nucleus Had Split.
days.concept: Mass is a form of energy (E = mc^2), and because nuclei are bound by energies millions of times larger than chemical bonds, splitting heavy nuclei (fission) or fusing light ones (fusion) releases millions of times more energy per atom than burning fuel.
days.focus: Teaches mass-energy equivalence and nuclear binding energy (the binding-energy curve peaking near iron) through Meitner and Frisch's interpretation of fission, and compares nuclear and chemical energy at the scale of a fuel pellet.
days.model_or_equation: E = m c^2. One uranium-235 fission releases about 200 MeV; burning one carbon atom releases about 4 eV - a ratio of roughly 50 million per atom (about 2-3 million per kilogram, since uranium atoms are about 20 times heavier).

story.title: Christmas in Kungälv
story.hook: At Christmas 1938, Lise Meitner, an Austrian-born physicist of Jewish descent who had fled Nazi Germany that July, was staying in the small town of Kungälv on Sweden's west coast. A letter from her longtime colleague Otto Hahn in Berlin reported that uranium bombarded with neutrons produced barium - an element of roughly half its mass - which seemed impossible. Walking in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch, who was on skis, she sat on a tree trunk and they worked it through on scraps of paper: the nucleus could split, and the two fragments together weighed less than the original by about a fifth of a proton's mass. Through E = mc^2, that missing mass came to about 200 MeV.
story.puzzle: Where would the enormous energy of a split nucleus come from - and how could two people in the snow calculate it on scraps of paper?
story.payoff: Meitner remembered the rule for nuclear masses, saw that the fragments were lighter than the uranium nucleus, and converted the missing mass with E = mc^2: about 200 MeV per fission, matching the electrical repulsion of the two fragments flying apart. Their paper appeared in Nature in February 1939; Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, an omission now widely regarded as unjust.
sources: L. Meitner and O. R. Frisch, 'Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction', Nature 143 (11 February 1939), 239-240
O. R. Frisch, What Little I Remember (Cambridge UP, 1979)
Ruth Lewin Sime, Lise Meitner: A Life in Physics (University of California Press, 1996)

days.application: Nuclear fuel: the US nuclear industry often says one uranium fuel pellet - about the size of a fingertip - holds roughly the energy of a tonne of coal (Nuclear Energy Institute comparison; the exact figure depends on enrichment and burnup), which is why a 1-gigawatt reactor refuels with tens of tonnes of fuel a year while a coal plant of the same size burns millions of tonnes.

builds_on.why: The million-fold gap between nuclear and chemical energy is an orders-of-magnitude comparison.
E = mc^2 comes from the same special relativity that slows moving clocks.
Conservation of energy now includes mass: the missing mass reappears as the fragments' kinetic energy.

across.link: The Einstein-Szilard letter of 2 August 1939 warned President Roosevelt that fission might make 'extremely powerful bombs', a path from the Meitner-Frisch result to the Manhattan Project and nuclear deterrence.

days.apply_question: The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second; using E = mc^2, estimate the Sun's power output in watts.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. The details of the Kungälv walk (skis, tree trunk) come from Frisch's memoir decades later. Meitner's exclusion from the 1944 Nobel Prize is judged an injustice by most historians (Sime; Crawford, Sime and Walker, Physics Today 1997), whose work in the Nobel archives found disciplinary and political reasons for it.

resource.length: about 30 minutes for the pages on Meitner, Frisch and Kungälv; about an hour for the whole chapter
resource.why: Rhodes tells the discovery of fission and the Kungälv walk from the primary sources, with the physics explained along the way.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.headline_hint: Radium's Alpha Rays Can't Get Through a Sheet of Paper. So How Did They Destroy the Dial Painters' Jaws?
days.concept: Unstable nuclei decay at a fixed probabilistic rate (half-life), emitting ionizing radiation, and the harm depends on the dose absorbed by tissue (measured in sieverts), on the type of radiation and on whether the source is outside or inside the body; how risk scales at very low doses is debated.
days.focus: Teaches alpha, beta and gamma radiation, half-life, activity and dose (gray, sievert), and the difference between external and internal exposure, through the Radium Girls; then compares radon and medical scans and presents the linear no-threshold debate fairly.
days.model_or_equation: N(t) = N0 x (1/2)^(t / T_half); effective dose (Sv) = absorbed dose (Gy) x radiation weighting (alpha about 20, gamma 1) x tissue weighting. Typical yardsticks: natural background about 2-3 mSv a year (US average about 6 mSv including medical); an abdominal CT about 8-10 mSv.

story.title: Lip, dip, paint
story.hook: From 1917, at the United States Radium Corporation's plant in Orange, New Jersey, young women painted luminous watch and instrument dials with a radium-based paint. To keep a fine point on their brushes they were taught to shape the bristles between their lips - 'lip, dip, paint' - and were assured the paint was harmless; radium tonics were then sold as healthful. By the mid-1920s former painters were suffering anaemia, bone fractures and disintegrating jaws ('radium jaw'); the county medical examiner Harrison Martland linked the deaths to radium in their bones. In 1927 Grace Fryer and four co-workers sued; the case drew national attention and was settled in June 1928.
story.puzzle: Radium's main radiation, alpha particles, is stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin. How could it destroy the women's bones from the inside years later - while radium on a dial in a sealed watch was a far smaller risk?
story.payoff: Radium is chemically like calcium, so swallowed radium was built into bone, where its alpha particles - harmless outside the body - deposited all their energy within a few cells' thickness of bone and marrow, year after year. Same source, completely different dose: internal emitters concentrate it where it does the most damage.
sources: Claudia Clark, Radium Girls: Women and Industrial Health Reform, 1910-1935 (University of North Carolina Press, 1997)
Kate Moore, The Radium Girls (Sourcebooks, 2017)
Ross Mullner, Deadly Glow: The Radium Dial Worker Tragedy (American Public Health Association, 1999)

days.application: Radon in homes: radon gas from uranium in soil decays to alpha-emitting products that lodge in the lungs. The US EPA recommends action at 4 picocuries per litre and estimates radon causes about 21,000 lung-cancer deaths a year in the US, second only to smoking (an estimate built on miner data and the LNT model). A year at the action level adds an effective dose of several millisieverts, on the order of an abdominal CT scan - which is why testing a basement is cheap insurance.

builds_on.why: Radioactive decay is the differential equation dN/dt = -kN; half-life follows.
Decay releases nuclear binding energy, which is why each emission carries millions of electronvolts.
Choosing a dose limit under uncertainty at low doses (LNT or not) is a textbook case of inductive risk.

across.link: The US Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (1990) compensates uranium miners and 'downwinders' of atomic tests - a statute that, like the dial painters' suits, turns a dose-response question into a question of legal causation.

days.apply_question: Airline pilots receive a few millisieverts a year more than the public from cosmic rays at altitude; using dose and the LNT debate, explain what you would need to know - and what you would need to value - to judge whether that is a meaningful occupational risk.
days.evidence_note: Settled: decay, half-lives, the dose units, and that doses above roughly 100 mSv raise cancer risk (atomic-bomb survivor studies). Debated: the shape of the risk curve below about 100 mSv - the linear no-threshold model used by regulators and supported by the US National Academies' BEIR VII report (2006), versus critics who argue for thresholds or that LNT overstates low-dose risk; the low-dose data are too noisy to settle it. Value judgment: how much precaution to buy against a possibly tiny risk. The Radium Girls' legal legacy (often said to have helped establish occupational-disease compensation and workers' right to sue) is real but often overstated when credited to a single case.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 4: The electric grid - why the world runs on AC
days.headline_hint: Edison Had the Bulb, the Patents and J. P. Morgan's Money. A Law of Physics Picked His Rival Anyway.
days.concept: The case question: how did a physical constraint - resistive losses that only transformers, and therefore alternating current, could beat - pick the winner between Edison's DC and Westinghouse's AC, and how did the grid's economics turn electricity into a regulated monopoly whose payoffs arrived decades late?
days.focus: Walks the electric grid round Logan's chain as a loop: deep on the physics (I-squared-R, induction and transformers, power versus energy), lock-in, S-curve adoption, delays and network cascades; previews fuels and grid balancing (Energy, Chemistry & Materials) and regulation and rural electrification (Government); financing named at CFA level.
key_concepts: load factor: peak kW versus kWh sold
natural monopoly and the regulatory bargain
days.model_or_equation: Line loss = I^2 R with I = P / V: for the same power delivered, raising voltage 100-fold cuts current 100-fold and resistive loss 10,000-fold. Utility economics: capacity cost scales with peak kW, revenue with kWh, so load factor (average / peak) sets cost per kWh.

story.title: Three o'clock at Pearl Street
story.hook: On the afternoon of 4 September 1882, at the Drexel, Morgan offices at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan, Thomas Edison's company switched on current from its new Pearl Street station a few blocks away. Steam-driven 'Jumbo' dynamos fed about 400 lamps for some 80 first customers, among them J. P. Morgan's bank and The New York Times, over copper mains laid under the streets - direct current at about 110 volts. Edison owned the patents, the lamp and the system, and had Morgan's backing. Within about fifteen years his direct current was in retreat: alternating current, championed by George Westinghouse with Nikola Tesla's motor patents, lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and sent Niagara's power to Buffalo in 1896, and Edison General Electric, merged into General Electric in 1892, built AC too.
story.puzzle: How did the side with the inventor, the patents, the first customers and the money lose - and why did the winners then ask governments to regulate them?
story.payoff: Physics set the terms: at 110 volts, I-squared-R losses confined each DC station to a district of about a square mile, while AC could be stepped up by transformers for long-distance transmission and down for safe use - and transformers work only with changing current (Faraday). Once AC's reach let one big plant serve a whole region, the economics of peak capacity and diverse loads favoured a single supplier, and leaders like Samuel Insull concluded that state regulation was the price of a protected monopoly.
sources: Thomas P. Hughes, Networks of Power: Electrification in Western Society, 1880-1930 (Johns Hopkins UP, 1983)
IEEE Milestone, 'Pearl Street Station, 1882' (Engineering and Technology History Wiki)
Jill Jonnes, Empires of Light: Edison, Tesla, Westinghouse, and the Race to Electrify the World (Random House, 2003)
Paul A. David, 'The Dynamo and the Computer', American Economic Review 80(2), 1990

days.application: Japan's split grid: eastern Japan runs at 50 Hz (Tokyo bought German generators in the 1890s) and western Japan at 60 Hz (Osaka bought American ones). After the March 2011 earthquake cut eastern generation, frequency-converter stations of only about 1 gigawatt limited how much western power could reach Tokyo, which faced rolling blackouts - lock-in with a real cost, now being eased by expanding converter capacity.

builds_on.why: I-squared-R losses are the physical constraint that limited DC distribution and drove the move to high voltage.
Transformers work by induction, which needs a changing current - the reason high-voltage transmission meant AC.
Power versus energy: a utility's costs follow peak kilowatts while its revenue follows kilowatt-hours, the load-factor logic behind Insull's monopoly.
AC, and the 50 Hz and 60 Hz standards, are cases of path dependence and lock-in.

across.link: New York and Wisconsin created state public-utility commissions in 1907, after Samuel Insull of Chicago Edison had argued in his 1898 address to the National Electric Light Association for exclusive franchises under state regulation - an industry asking to be regulated.

days.apply_question: A developer proposes a DC microgrid of rooftop solar and batteries for a new neighbourhood; using this case, explain which of Edison's 1882 handicaps no longer bind it and which still do.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the physics (I-squared-R, transformers need AC) and the broad timeline (Pearl Street 1882, AC's victory by the late 1890s, Niagara-Buffalo 1896). Debated: how large and how fast electrification's gains were - Paul David (1990) argues productivity gains waited decades for factories to be redesigned around unit-drive motors; today's micro evidence is mixed, with a randomized trial of rural grid connections in Kenya (Lee, Miguel and Wolfram, Journal of Political Economy 2020) finding low demand and no significant medium-run economic gains, while quasi-experimental studies such as Dinkelman (American Economic Review 2011, South Africa) found sizeable employment effects. Value judgment: the regulated-monopoly bargain - who gained, who paid in prices, who was left unserved (most US farms until public programmes in the 1930s) - and the War of the Currents' public animal electrocutions and the 1890 execution of William Kemmler, the first by electric chair, exploited partly as marketing; utilitarian, rights-based and Catholic social teaching's 'universal destination of goods' readings weigh universal service differently.

chain.point: In 1882 city lighting meant gas and kerosene, which fouled air and caused fires; Edison set out to match gas lighting on price with a safer, cleaner light. How needs and demand form is taught later, in Psychology (motivation and needs) and History.

Edison invented a system, not a bulb: high-resistance lamp, dynamo, meters, fuses and underground mains designed together to beat gas on cost - innovation as a coupled system, with the central station as the product.

At about 110 volts DC, losses grow as I-squared-R and copper costs soar with distance, so a Pearl Street-type station could serve only about a square mile; delivering the same power at high voltage cuts current and losses dramatically.

Transformers step voltage up for transmission and down for homes, but only with alternating current (Faraday's induction); Tesla's 1888 polyphase induction motor gave AC a practical motor; Westinghouse's AC lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and Niagara's Adams station sent power to Buffalo, some 20-26 miles away (accounts differ), in November 1896.
AC's installed base locked in, and so did early frequency choices: 60 Hz across North America, 50 Hz in most of the world, and a 50/60 Hz split in Japan that still needs converter stations.

chain.field: Physics (load factor); finance named at CFA level
chain.point: Pearl Street was financed through the Edison Electric Illuminating Company with Drexel, Morgan backing. Samuel Insull grasped that a plant's cost follows peak kilowatts while revenue follows kilowatt-hours, so mixing loads (factories by day, homes by night, streetcars) raised load factor and cut cost per kWh - the economics of one big supplier. His holding-company empire's 1932 collapse is named here at CFA level only.

Insull argued in 1898 for exclusive franchises under state regulation; New York and Wisconsin set up utility commissions in 1907, and the Public Utility Holding Company Act followed in 1935 - an industry that asked for its own rules. How regulation works, and how it can be captured, is taught in Government.

Household electrification traced an S-curve, fast in cities and slow on farms: by the mid-1930s most urban homes but only about one farm in ten had power, until the federal Rural Electrification Administration (1935) - a gap a single logistic curve hides unless the population is split.

Paul David (1990) argued electrification's productivity payoff came in the 1920s, roughly four decades after Pearl Street, because factories had to be rebuilt around individual electric motors rather than one steam shaft - a long delay between cause and effect; today's micro evidence on electrification's gains is mixed, including a randomized trial in Kenya.

Interconnection, which lets plants share load, also lets failures spread: the 14 August 2003 cascade cut power to about 50 million people in the US and Canada - the network structure taught in Mathematics.

Rooftop solar now sends power backwards through networks built for one-way flow, and long-distance DC has returned through power electronics (China's ±1,100 kV Changji-Guquan line, energized 2019). Fuels, variable renewables and second-by-second balancing are taught in the next block.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: The periodic table: why elements behave as they do
days.headline_hint: Mendeleev Told the Chemist Who Discovered Gallium His Measurement Was Wrong. He Had Never Seen the Metal. He Was Right.
days.concept: An element's chemistry is set by its outer (valence) electrons, so properties repeat in a periodic pattern that can predict elements nobody has yet found.
days.focus: Teaches the periodic table as a map of electron structure: rows are filling shells, columns share valence electrons, so behaviour repeats (the periodic law). The quantum atom (D63) supplies the shells; this lesson turns them into chemistry, and shows the table's power as a predictive model, not a filing system. Mendeleev found the pattern decades before electrons were known; the lesson says so plainly.

story.title: A letter from St Petersburg about a metal its writer had never held
story.hook: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev published a table that ordered the elements by atomic weight and grouped them by behaviour, and he left gaps. In 1871 he predicted the properties of the missing elements, among them 'eka-aluminium', with a density of about 5.9-6.0 g/cm3. In August 1875 the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran spotted a new violet spectral line in zinc ore (sphalerite) from the Pyrenees, and by the end of the year he had isolated the metal, which he named gallium. He reported its density as about 4.7. Mendeleev wrote that the figure must be wrong and should be nearer 5.9. Lecoq purified his sample, remeasured, and got about 5.9.
story.puzzle: How could a man in St Petersburg who had never seen the metal correct the measurement of the chemist holding it?
story.payoff: Gallium sits under aluminium because it has the same three valence electrons; the table encodes electron structure, so an element's neighbours fix its chemistry and roughly its physical properties. Mendeleev saw the pattern without knowing its cause (electrons were discovered in 1897; shells came with the quantum atom, D63), and his gaps were predictions from that pattern. Lecoq's first small sample was impure.
sources: Mendeleev, Zeitschrift fur Chemie 1869, and his 1871 predictions of eka-aluminium, eka-boron and eka-silicon
Lecoq de Boisbaudran, Comptes rendus 1875 (discovery of gallium)
Eric Scerri, The Periodic Table: Its Story and Its Significance (Oxford UP, 2007)

days.application: Why lithium dominates rechargeable batteries: the lightest metal (about 0.53 g/cm3), it gives up its single valence electron very readily; its standard electrode potential, about -3.04 V, is the most negative of any metal, which helps give lithium cells high voltage and high energy per kilogram.

builds_on.why: The quantum atom's discrete energy levels are the shells whose outer electrons set each column's chemistry.
Mendeleev's gaps were risky, falsifiable predictions, Popper's criterion in action; gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) confirmed them.

across.link: Mendeleev is philosophy of science's test case for whether a successful novel prediction should count for more than fitting known facts (prediction versus accommodation): Stephen Brush ('The Reception of Mendeleev's Periodic Law in America and Britain', Isis, 1996) and Eric Scerri and John Worrall ('Prediction and the Periodic Table', Studies in History and Philosophy of Science, 2001) argue that chemists credited his accommodation of known elements about as much as his famous predictions.

days.apply_question: Sodium sits directly below lithium in the table, and sodium-ion batteries are now being sold in China; using what the table says about the two elements, what would you expect a sodium-ion cell to gain and to give up compared with a lithium-ion cell?

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Two Physicists Peeled Graphite With Sticky Tape Until One Layer of Atoms Was Left. It Was the Strongest Material Ever Measured.
days.concept: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, and how they are arranged in space, explain why materials are hard or soft, brittle or ductile, conducting or insulating.
days.focus: Teaches the three bond types as different ways atoms share or trade valence electrons (D67), then shows that the arrangement of bonds matters as much as their type: carbon as diamond, graphite and graphene is the proof. Ends with why metals bend (dislocations glide through non-directional metallic bonds) and ceramics and glass shatter.

story.title: Friday-night experiments in Manchester
story.hook: At the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, both trained in Russia, ran 'Friday night experiments' on ideas too odd for grant proposals. Around 2003-04 they used ordinary adhesive tape to peel flakes off graphite, the material in pencil lead, again and again until some flakes were only a few atoms thick. Their October 2004 paper in Science reported these atomically thin carbon films, and by 2005 they were measuring single layers, graphene, a sheet that theory had long suggested could not exist stably on its own. In 2008 a Columbia University team measured monolayer graphene as the strongest material ever tested. Geim and Novoselov shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
story.puzzle: Pencil lead smears onto paper and diamond cuts glass, yet both are pure carbon, and one atom-thin layer of the soft one is stronger than steel. How can the same atoms be soft, hard and super-strong?
story.payoff: Within a graphite layer every carbon is covalently bonded to three neighbours, extremely strong; between layers only weak van der Waals forces hold, so layers slide (soft pencil). Diamond bonds every atom covalently in three dimensions (hard). Graphene is one layer, all strong bonds and no weak ones. Properties follow the bond type and its geometry.
sources: Novoselov, Geim et al., 'Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films', Science 306 (22 Oct 2004)
Nobel Prize in Physics 2010, press release and scientific background
Lee, Wei, Kysar & Hone, 'Measurement of the Elastic Properties and Intrinsic Strength of Monolayer Graphene', Science 321 (2008)

days.application: Why a car's steel door dents and its windscreen shatters: metallic bonds are non-directional, so planes of atoms can slip past one another by moving dislocations without the metal coming apart (ductility); glass has directional covalent and ionic bonds and no dislocations to move, so a crack, once started, runs (brittleness). That is why windscreens are laminated, two glass sheets bonded to a plastic interlayer that holds the pieces, and why crash structures are metal: deforming steel absorbs energy. This is the engineering link of the car chain at the level of bonds.

builds_on.why: Bond type follows from valence electrons: metals give them up easily, non-metals share or grab them.
The sea of free electrons in a metallic bond is what carries current, explaining why metals conduct and covalent solids like diamond do not.

across.link: On 16 January 1943 the new welded T2 tanker SS Schenectady cracked almost in two at its fitting-out pier in Portland, Oregon; the Cambridge metallurgist Constance Tipper showed that such ship steels turn brittle below a transition temperature, so a material that bends at room temperature can shatter in cold water. Engineers now specify fracture toughness, not only strength.

days.apply_question: Building codes in earthquake zones such as California favour steel frames and push owners to retrofit unreinforced brick buildings, even though brick is very strong in compression; using what bonding says about how metals and ceramics fail, why is a steel frame safer when the ground shakes?

resource.creator: Mark Miodownik (Viking, 2013; US edition Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2014)
resource.why: A materials scientist tells the carbon story from pencil to diamond to graphene, showing bond structure turning into everyday properties.
