days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Beirut's Port Stored 2,750 Tonnes of a Farm Fertilizer for Six Years. Then a Fire Reached It.
days.concept: Reactions release or absorb energy by breaking and making bonds; an activation barrier lets stored chemical energy sit safely until something lifts it over, and a catalyst lowers that barrier without being used up.
days.focus: Teaches reaction energy (exothermic versus endothermic, from bond energies, D52) separately from reaction rate (the activation barrier), and shows a catalyst changes the route, not the destination. Heat speeds reactions roughly exponentially, which is why a fire can trigger a runaway.
days.model_or_equation: Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(-Ea/RT): the rate constant k rises exponentially as temperature T rises or as the activation energy Ea falls (A a frequency factor, R the gas constant).

story.title: Hangar 12, Port of Beirut
story.hook: About 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate, unloaded in 2014 from the impounded ship Rhosus, sat in Hangar 12 at Beirut's port for six years, despite repeated warnings from officials. On 4 August 2020 a fire broke out in the warehouse, and shortly after 6 pm the store detonated, one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded. It killed more than 200 people (counts are about 218-220), injured around 7,000 and damaged homes across much of the city.
story.puzzle: Ammonium nitrate is a common fertilizer that farmers spread on fields, and this pile lay inert for six years. Why was it harmless for so long, and why did a fire turn it into a bomb?
story.payoff: Decomposing ammonium nitrate releases energy, but an activation barrier keeps it stable at room temperature. The fire supplied heat; because rates rise exponentially with temperature, decomposition sped up, released more heat, and ran away into detonation in a large, confined store. The energy was always there; the barrier was holding it.
sources: Reuters and BBC reporting on port and government records, August 2020
Human Rights Watch, 'They Killed Us from the Inside' (August 2021)
Rigby et al., 'Preliminary yield estimation of the 2020 Beirut explosion using video footage from social media', Shock Waves 30 (2020)

days.application: The car's catalytic converter: two-way oxidation converters, fitted to most new US cars from the 1975 model year, used platinum and palladium to burn carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons to CO2 and water at exhaust temperatures; three-way converters, standard from about 1981, added rhodium to turn nitrogen oxides back into nitrogen. Without the catalyst these reactions are far too slow in the second or so the gas spends in the exhaust. It sits at the regulation link of the car chain (the 1970 Clean Air Act's limits), and it needed unleaded fuel because lead poisons the catalyst (D49).

builds_on.why: Reaction energy is conservation of energy at the level of bonds: the energy released is the difference between bonds broken and bonds made.
Catalytic converters, fitted to meet the Clean Air Act's limits, were poisoned by lead, the requirement that pushed leaded gasoline out.

across.link: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation barriers so that reactions such as the breakdown of glucose run fast at body temperature, the mechanism behind metabolism as controlled, slow combustion.

days.apply_question: Lithium-ion battery fires in electric cars are hard to put out and can reignite hours later; using activation energy and the exponential effect of temperature on rate, explain why a battery that was stable for years can run away once one cell overheats.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the chemistry of activation barriers and runaway. Unresolved: what started the Beirut fire and who is responsible, because Lebanon's judicial investigation has repeatedly stalled; the brief should not assign blame beyond what Human Rights Watch and court records document.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: The Hindenburg Floated on the Fuel With the Most Energy per Kilogram. Nearly 90 Years Later, Airliners Still Burn Kerosene.
days.concept: Burning a fuel with oxygen releases bond energy, and energy per kilogram and per litre decide what a fuel can move.
days.focus: Teaches combustion as oxidation of carbon and hydrogen into CO2 and water, then the two energy densities (specific energy per kg, energy density per litre) and why liquid hydrocarbons win on both. Includes the chemistry of knock and octane briefly (why some molecules ignite before the spark), the chemistry previewed in the leaded-gasoline case (D49); compression ratios and engine design are Engineering's (D91).
days.model_or_equation: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O + energy. A rough table (lower heating values): hydrogen about 120 MJ/kg but about 0.01 MJ/L as gas at room pressure and about 8.5 MJ/L as liquid; gasoline and jet fuel about 43-46 MJ/kg and 32-35 MJ/L; lithium-ion cells about 0.5-1 MJ/kg.

story.title: Thirty-odd seconds at Lakehurst
story.hook: On the evening of 6 May 1937 the German airship Hindenburg, 245 metres long and lifted by about 200,000 cubic metres of hydrogen, was landing at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, after crossing from Frankfurt. Fire broke out near the tail and the ship was consumed in roughly half a minute, in front of newsreel cameras. Thirty-six people died: 13 passengers, 22 crew and one member of the ground crew; 62 of the 97 on board survived. The hydrogen was lifting gas, not fuel (the four engines burned diesel), and the disaster ended the passenger airship.
story.puzzle: Hydrogen holds nearly three times as much energy per kilogram as gasoline, so it should be the ideal fuel for flying. Why, nearly 90 years later, does every airliner still burn kerosene?
story.payoff: Hydrogen wins per kilogram but loses badly per litre: even liquefied at -253 C it holds only about a quarter of kerosene's energy per litre, and it needs heavy insulated tanks. Aircraft are limited by both weight and volume, so kerosene's combination wins. The Hindenburg shows the volume problem: its 200,000 cubic metres of gas weighed about 17 tonnes and held roughly the energy of 50 tonnes of kerosene, about a quarter of a Boeing 747-400's fuel load.
sources: US Department of Commerce, Bureau of Air Commerce, report of the Hindenburg accident investigation (1937)
Navy Lakehurst Historical Society, Hindenburg passenger and crew list
US DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center, fuel properties comparison

days.application: Why batteries cannot yet carry a 737 across the Atlantic: jet fuel stores about 43 MJ/kg against roughly 0.9 MJ/kg (about 250 Wh/kg) for good lithium-ion cells, a gap of about fifty times; even crediting electric drivetrains' roughly two- to three-times better efficiency, a transatlantic battery pack would weigh far more than the aircraft can lift, which is why electric aviation targets short hops.

builds_on.why: Day 1 compared gasoline's ~12 kWh/kg with a battery pack's ~0.15-0.25 kWh/kg; this lesson explains where those numbers come from.
Fuel energy only becomes motion through a heat engine whose Carnot limit wastes much of it, which narrows the battery's gap.

across.link: Animals face the same per-kilogram trade-off: fat stores about 37-39 MJ/kg against about 17 for carbohydrate, and glycogen is stored with several times its weight in water, so long-distance migrants fuel on fat; a satellite-tagged bar-tailed godwit flew about 11,700 km nonstop from Alaska to New Zealand in 2007 (Gill et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2009).

days.apply_question: Container shipping lines have ordered ships that run on methanol, and ammonia-fuelled ships are being designed, to replace heavy fuel oil; using specific energy and energy per litre, what would you expect those ships to give up, and why can a ship tolerate it when an airliner cannot?

resource.length: about 40 minutes for the chapter; the passages comparing fuels, batteries and aviation take about 15
resource.why: Smil sets fuels side by side by energy density and explains why liquid hydrocarbons are so hard to replace in flight and shipping.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Drake Struck Oil for Lamp Fuel, and Refiners Dumped the Gasoline. Today a Barrel Yields About 20 Gallons of It.
days.concept: Coal, oil and gas are buried photosynthesis cooked into hydrocarbons over millions of years, and refining separates and reshapes crude by boiling point into the products an economy wants.
days.focus: Teaches where fossil fuels come from (plankton and plants, burial, heat and pressure) and how a refinery turns crude into products: fractional distillation by boiling point, then cracking and reforming to shift the mix toward what sells. Explains why a fossil fuel is stored solar energy at enormous density.

story.title: The drive pipe at Oil Creek
story.hook: In 1859 Edwin Drake, hired by the Seneca Oil Company and styled 'Colonel' to impress the locals, was drilling beside Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania, with the salt-well driller William 'Uncle Billy' Smith. His key trick was driving an iron pipe down through the loose gravel so the hole would not cave in. On 27 August 1859, at 69.5 feet, the bit dropped into a crevice; the next day Smith found oil standing in the pipe. The product everyone wanted was kerosene for lamps; the light, volatile fraction we call gasoline was a near-worthless byproduct that early refiners often dumped.
story.puzzle: How can one black liquid yield lamp oil, gasoline, jet fuel and asphalt, and how did gasoline go from waste to the main product of the same barrel?
story.payoff: Crude is a mixture of hydrocarbons of many chain lengths; distillation splits them by boiling point (short chains boil low: gasoline; longer ones: kerosene, diesel, then residue). Refiners later learned to crack long molecules into short ones, so they can tilt the barrel toward whatever the market wants, and the car made gasoline the prize.
sources: Drake Well Museum and Park (Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission)
Daniel Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1
American Chemical Society National Historic Chemical Landmark, 'Development of the Pennsylvania Oil Industry'

days.application: What a 42-gallon barrel becomes: US refineries turn it into about 45 gallons of products (the extra is 'processing gain', because products are less dense than crude), of which about 19-20 gallons are motor gasoline, about 11-12 diesel and heating oil, about 4 jet fuel, and the rest petrochemical feedstocks, asphalt and other products (EIA, 'Oil and petroleum products explained'). For the car this is the production link: its fuel is one cut of a joint-product process.

builds_on.why: Fossil fuels are low-entropy stores of ancient sunlight; burning them releases energy that photosynthesis concentrated over millions of years.
Chain length sets both a hydrocarbon's boiling point and the energy density that made gasoline and jet fuel prized, so refining sorts fuels by the property Day 70 measured.

across.link: Oil's energy density turned a fuel choice into foreign policy: as First Lord of the Admiralty, Winston Churchill committed the Royal Navy's new battleships to oil (faster ships, refuelling at sea), and because Britain had no oil of its own the government bought a majority stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later BP, in 1914 for about 2.2 million pounds, making Persian oil a strategic interest.

days.apply_question: Europe's refineries are geared to produce more diesel than gasoline while US refineries make more gasoline; using what you know about distillation and cracking, why can't a refinery simply switch its whole output from one to the other when demand changes?

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: Resources versus reserves: why peak predictions fail
days.headline_hint: Hubbert Said US Oil Would Peak Around 1970. It Did. In 2018 It Broke the Record.
days.concept: Reserves are the part of a resource that is economic to extract with today's technology and prices, so reserves move when prices and technology move; the resource is what is physically there.
days.focus: Teaches the resource-reserve distinction (a definition, not a discovery) and the Hubbert curve as the derivative of a logistic (D7, D4): right when its ceiling holds, wrong when technology and price move the ceiling. Hedges both the peak-oil and the 'never runs out' views.
days.model_or_equation: Hubbert curve: if cumulative production Q(t) follows a logistic toward a ceiling URR (the ultimately recoverable resource), annual production dQ/dt = kQ(1 - Q/URR) is bell-shaped and peaks when half the URR is gone. The peak date depends entirely on the assumed URR.

story.title: A Shell geologist in San Antonio, March 1956
story.hook: In March 1956, at an American Petroleum Institute meeting in San Antonio, Texas, the Shell geophysicist M. King Hubbert presented 'Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels'. Fitting bell-shaped curves to US discovery and production, and assuming an ultimate total of 150-200 billion barrels, he predicted that crude output in the lower 48 states would peak between about 1965 and 1970 and then decline. US production peaked in 1970 at about 9.6 million barrels a day and fell for nearly four decades, making Hubbert famous. Then horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing opened shale rock, and in 2018 annual US crude production passed the 1970 record.
story.puzzle: Was Hubbert right or wrong? His curve called the peak, and yet the US now pumps more oil than at that peak.
story.payoff: Hubbert's curve treated the recoverable total as fixed; it was a model of reserves, and reserves are an economic and technological category. When prices rose and fracking made shale economic, part of the resource became reserve and the ceiling moved. His mathematics was sound; his assumed URR was a snapshot.
sources: M. King Hubbert, 'Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels', Shell Development Co. Publication No. 95 (1956)
US EIA, US field production of crude oil, annual series (1970 and 2018)
Kenneth Deffeyes, Hubbert's Peak (Princeton UP, 2001)

days.application: Lithium and cobalt: USGS estimates of world lithium reserves roughly doubled in a decade (about 14 million tonnes in the mid-2010s to about 28-30 million tonnes in the 2024-25 Mineral Commodity Summaries) as prices rose and exploration expanded, while identified resources are several times larger (over 100 million tonnes). 'Running out' claims depend on ore grade, price, extraction technology and recycling, not just tonnes in the ground; cobalt adds concentration risk, since most is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

builds_on.why: The Hubbert curve is the rate of a logistic: production rises and falls as cumulative output approaches an assumed ceiling, and the ceiling is an assumption, not a law.
Like Limits to Growth and the Simon-Ehrlich wager, peak forecasts fail when models omit price and adaptation.

across.link: Reserve estimates are bargaining chips between states: several OPEC members raised their reported reserves sharply in the late 1980s, which is widely attributed, at least in part, to quota talks that weighed reserves (members defend the revisions as reappraisals), an example of Goodhart's law (D23) in official statistics.

days.apply_question: Helium is extracted from a few natural-gas fields and is periodically declared to be 'running out'; using the distinction between resources and reserves, what would you need to know before deciding whether a helium shortage is geological or economic?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the definitions, and that reserves rise with price and technology. Debated: how much oil and critical minerals will ultimately be recoverable, and whether peak oil demand (from EVs) will arrive before any supply peak. Value judgment: whether to keep extracting what is economic, which turns on climate (D85).

resource.length: about 20 minutes for the oil sections
resource.why: Hubbert's own paper shows the logistic reasoning, the assumed ultimate totals and the dated forecast, so Logan can see exactly which assumption failed.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: At 57, John Goodenough Swapped One Powder for Another and Doubled a Battery's Voltage. Your Phone Still Runs on It.
days.concept: A battery is a controlled redox reaction that forces electrons to travel through an outside circuit, and the chemistry of its electrodes sets its voltage and its energy per kilogram.
days.focus: Teaches oxidation and reduction as electron transfer, how separating the two halves makes electrons do work in a circuit (D59), why voltage comes from the difference in the electrodes' appetite for electrons, and how lithium-ion 'rocking chair' cells shuttle lithium ions between graphite and a metal oxide.
days.model_or_equation: Energy stored = voltage x charge: E (Wh) = V x Q (Ah). Doubling cell voltage at the same charge capacity doubles the energy.

story.title: The cathode that changed the voltage
story.hook: In the 1970s Stanley Whittingham at Exxon built a rechargeable lithium battery with a titanium disulfide cathode; it worked at a little over 2 volts. At Oxford, John Goodenough, then 57, reasoned that a metal oxide would hold lithium at a much higher potential; in 1980 his group (with Koichi Mizushima and others) reported lithium cobalt oxide, giving about 4 volts. In 1985 Akira Yoshino in Japan paired it with a carbon anode, and Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion cells in 1991. In 2019 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Goodenough, at 97, was the oldest laureate ever.
story.puzzle: Both batteries shuttled the same lithium ions. Why did swapping the cathode powder nearly double the voltage, and with it the energy the battery could hold?
story.payoff: Voltage is the difference in how strongly the two electrodes bind electrons (and lithium). An oxide cathode holds lithium at a much lower energy than a sulfide, so each electron falls through a bigger potential drop, about 4 V instead of about 2; energy is voltage times charge, so the same shuttle carries roughly twice the energy.
sources: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019, press release and popular science background (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences)
Mizushima, Jones, Wiseman & Goodenough, 'LixCoO2: A new cathode material for batteries of high energy density', Materials Research Bulletin 15 (1980)

days.application: The car's battery pack: BloombergNEF's annual survey put average lithium-ion pack prices above $1,000/kWh around 2010 and about $115/kWh in 2024, a fall that plots as a straight line on a log scale (D2) and that Engineering explains as a learning curve (Day 97). Chemistry choices matter too: cobalt-free lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells trade some energy density (lower voltage, about 3.2 V) for cost, cycle life and safety, which is why many cheaper EVs use them. This is the physical-constraint and production link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: Volta's pile was the first redox battery; voltage, current and charge are the circuit quantities a battery supplies.
Pack prices falling by a steady percentage a year are a straight line on a log plot.

across.link: Battery supply chains are a chokepoint: China refines most of the world's lithium, processes almost all battery graphite and makes most cells, which is why the US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) tied its EV tax credit to where battery materials and components came from (that credit was ended for vehicles acquired after 30 September 2025).

days.apply_question: Grid storage projects increasingly choose lithium iron phosphate cells over the nickel-rich cells used in long-range cars; using what sets a cell's voltage and energy per kilogram, why might a battery that is worse for a car be better for a power station?

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: Steel: iron with just enough carbon
days.headline_hint: Bessemer Blew Cold Air Into Molten Iron. It Got Hotter.
days.concept: Steel is iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon; making it means first stripping oxygen from iron ore (reduction) and then burning excess carbon and impurities out of the iron (oxidation).
days.focus: Teaches the two-step chemistry of iron and steel: blast-furnace reduction with carbon monoxide, which leaves pig iron with about 4% carbon (brittle), then oxidation to bring carbon down to roughly 0.1-1% (strong and ductile). Shows why carbon content controls properties and why steel's CO2 is chemical, not just fuel.
key_concepts: iron ore, pig iron and steel
days.model_or_equation: Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2 (blast furnace); with hydrogen instead: Fe2O3 + 3 H2 -> 2 Fe + 3 H2O.

story.title: Malleable iron 'without fuel', Cheltenham, August 1856
story.hook: In August 1856 Henry Bessemer, a prolific inventor with no metallurgical training, read a paper to the British Association meeting at Cheltenham titled 'The Manufacture of Malleable Iron and Steel without Fuel'. His claim: blow cold air through a vessel of molten pig iron and, instead of freezing, the metal grows hotter, in a roaring shower of sparks, and in minutes becomes malleable. Ironmasters rushed to buy licences, and many got brittle, useless metal. Bessemer opened his own works in Sheffield in 1858 to prove the process, and with Robert Mushet's manganese additive and, from 1878, Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and Percy Gilchrist's fix for phosphorus, cheap steel became the material of railways and skyscrapers.
story.puzzle: Why does blowing cold air into molten iron heat it up rather than cool it, and why does that turn brittle iron into tough steel?
story.payoff: Pig iron from the blast furnace carries about 4% carbon plus silicon. Oxygen in the blast reacts with them, exothermically, so the impurities are the fuel. Burning carbon down to under 1% turns brittle cast iron into strong, ductile steel. The licensees' failures came largely from phosphorus in their ores, which the acid-lined converter could not remove (Bessemer's own trials had used low-phosphorus iron), and from over-blown, oxygen-laden metal, which Mushet's manganese corrected.
sources: Bessemer's British Association paper, reprinted in The Times, 14 August 1856
Henry Bessemer, An Autobiography (1905)
Thomas J. Misa, A Nation of Steel (Johns Hopkins UP, 1995)

days.application: Steel's climate problem is chemistry: carbon is the reducing agent, so CO2 comes out of the ore itself. Iron and steel produce roughly 7-9% of global CO2 emissions (worldsteel and IEA estimates). In August 2021 Sweden's HYBRIT venture (SSAB, LKAB, Vattenfall) delivered the first steel made from hydrogen-reduced iron to the truck maker Volvo Group; the by-product is water. It costs more, and scaling it has proved slow and expensive because it depends on large amounts of cheap clean electricity for the hydrogen. For the car, steel is the production link's largest material and its emissions part of the consequences link.

builds_on.why: Steelmaking runs on exothermic oxidation; the energy released by burning carbon and silicon keeps the Bessemer converter molten.
Small amounts of carbon pin the metallic lattice's dislocations, trading ductility for strength.

across.link: Cheap Bessemer steel replaced iron rails on American railroads from the 1870s; Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Works at Braddock, Pennsylvania (1875), was built to roll Bessemer steel rails, part of the second industrial revolution's surge in materials output.

days.apply_question: Electric arc furnaces make new steel by melting scrap with electricity rather than reducing ore; using the chemistry of reduction, explain why recycled steel has a far smaller carbon footprint than ore-based steel, and what limits how much of the world's steel can be made this way.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Rome's Pantheon Has No Steel Inside and Has Stood for 1,900 Years. Many Modern Concrete Bridges Are Designed for 50 to 100.
days.concept: Cement is made by baking limestone, which releases CO2, and hardens by reacting with water (hydration); the resulting concrete is very strong in compression and weak in tension, which is why it is reinforced with steel.
days.focus: Teaches clinker chemistry (calcination: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), hydration as a chemical reaction, not drying, and the compression-tension asymmetry. Explains why reinforcing steel both makes modern concrete possible and limits its life (corrosion), and why cement's CO2 is hard to remove.
days.model_or_equation: CaCO3 + heat -> CaO + CO2: about 0.5 tonne of CO2 per tonne of clinker comes from the limestone itself, before any fuel is burned.

story.title: The dome Hadrian finished
story.hook: The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian and finished around 125-128 AD, is roofed by a concrete dome about 43.3 metres across, with an open oculus about 8-9 metres wide at its crown. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, and it has stood for about 1,900 years with no steel inside. Its builders made the concrete lighter toward the top, grading the aggregate from heavy stone near the base to light volcanic pumice near the oculus. In January 2023 an MIT-led team (Linda Seymour, Admir Masic and colleagues) reported in Science Advances that lime lumps in Roman concrete samples, long dismissed as poor mixing, can dissolve and re-seal cracks.
story.puzzle: Modern reinforced-concrete bridges and car parks can need major repair within 50-100 years. How has a steel-free Roman dome outlasted them by nearly two millennia?
story.payoff: A dome carries most of its weight in compression, where concrete is strong. Near its base a dome also pulls outward (hoop tension), and the Pantheon's dome did crack there long ago, but the cracked segments still stand as a ring of arches, each carrying its load in compression, held by the massive drum and stepped rings at the haunches. With no steel inside, there is nothing to rust and burst the concrete from within. Modern concrete must carry tension in beams and slabs, so it relies on steel that corrodes when water and salts get in. Roman chemistry (and possibly self-healing lime) helps, but structure and the absence of steel explain most of it.
sources: Seymour, Masic et al., 'Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete', Science Advances 9 (6 Jan 2023)
Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson, 'On the Structure of the Roman Pantheon', The Art Bulletin 68 (1986)
William L. MacDonald, The Pantheon: Design, Meaning, and Progeny (1976)

days.application: Cement's climate weight: cement production accounts for roughly 7-8% of global CO2 (Chatham House, 'Making Concrete Change', 2018), more than half of it from calcination rather than fuel. Vaclav Smil's comparison (Making the Modern World, 2014): China used more cement in 2011-2013 (about 6.6 billion tonnes) than the United States in the whole twentieth century (about 4.5 billion tonnes), a measure of how fast urbanization consumes materials.

builds_on.why: The square-cube law: a dome's weight grows faster than the area that must carry it, which is why the Romans lightened the upper concrete with pumice.
Hoover Dam's thick base and the Pantheon's thick lower dome answer the same question: load builds up with what lies above, so material goes where the stress is greatest.

across.link: Cement consumption tracks urbanization: China's urban share rose from about 26% in 1990 to about 66% in 2023 (National Bureau of Statistics), the move of several hundred million people into cities that its 2011-13 cement surge built for.

days.apply_question: Some engineers propose building bridges with stainless-steel or fibre-reinforced polymer bars instead of ordinary rebar despite higher cost; using what you know about compression, tension and corrosion, what would you need to know to judge whether the extra cost is worth it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: calcination chemistry and the compression-tension asymmetry. Debated: how much the lime-clast 'self-healing' mechanism contributes to Roman concrete's durability in real structures, versus structural form and the absence of rebar.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Stephanie Kwolek's Solution Looked Like Something to Throw Away. It Led to a Fibre Five Times Stronger Than Steel.
days.concept: Polymers are long chains of repeating units, and the length of the chains and how they line up and grip each other set a plastic's properties, including the durability that makes plastics both useful and a lasting problem.
days.focus: Teaches polymerization, chain length, crystallinity and alignment, and the difference between thermoplastics (melt and reshape) and thermosets. Uses nylon (Wallace Carothers, DuPont, 1935) as background and Kevlar as the story; ends with why chains that resist breaking persist in the environment, and why recycling shortens them.

story.title: The cloudy solution at DuPont's Experimental Station
story.hook: In 1965 Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist at DuPont's Pioneering Research Laboratory near Wilmington, Delaware, was searching for a light, strong fibre to reinforce tyres. One polymer solution came out thin and cloudy, unlike the clear, syrupy solutions that normally spun well, and the technician who ran the spinning machine, Charles Smullen, at first refused to try it, fearing it would clog the spinneret. Kwolek persisted. The fibre that came out was extraordinarily stiff and strong. Developed further by DuPont colleagues, her discovery became Kevlar, launched in 1971 and about five times stronger than steel on an equal-weight basis. It now stops bullets and reinforces tyres and cables.
story.puzzle: Why would a watery, cloudy liquid that looked like a failure make a fibre stronger than steel?
story.payoff: These chains are rigid rods. In solution they spontaneously line up like logs in a river (a liquid crystal), which made it cloudy and runny; spinning locks that alignment into the fibre, and hydrogen bonds tie neighbouring chains together. Strength comes from long chains pointing the same way and gripping each other.
sources: Science History Institute, biography of Stephanie L. Kwolek
American Chemical Society National Historic Chemical Landmark, 'Kevlar'
Kwolek, US Patent 3,671,542 (1972)

days.application: Why recycling plastic is hard: Geyer, Jambeck and Law (Science Advances, 2017) estimated that of all the plastic waste generated up to 2015, only about 9% had been recycled, about 12% incinerated and about 79% landfilled or left in the environment. Mechanical recycling melts and reshapes the plastic, and each cycle breaks chains (chain scission) and mixes in other polymers and additives, so the recycled material is weaker and usually 'downcycled'. The same long, stable chains that make plastic durable make it persist for decades or more.

builds_on.why: Polymers combine strong covalent bonds along each chain with weaker hydrogen or van der Waals bonds between chains, the same split that made graphite soft.
Most plastics are made from refinery and gas-processing feedstocks such as ethane and naphtha.

across.link: Proteins and DNA are natural polymers: spider dragline silk, like Kevlar, gets its strength from aligned chains held by hydrogen bonds, which is why materials scientists study it.

days.apply_question: Clear PET drink bottles are among the few plastics recycled at scale, often back into bottles; using chain length and contamination, why does a PET bottle recycle better than a multi-layer crisp packet?
days.evidence_note: Settled: polymer structure-property relationships. Debated: the size of plastic leakage into the oceans and the health effects of microplastics, where measurement is still immature.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A Cracked Rod of Silicon Made Half a Volt in the Light, With No Battery Attached. Bell Labs Had Found the P-N Junction.
days.concept: Adding tiny amounts of impurities (doping) to silicon makes p-type and n-type material; where they meet, a junction lets current flow one way and turns absorbed light into a voltage.
days.focus: Teaches the band gap (from the quantum atom, D63), doping with boron and phosphorus, how a p-n junction forms a built-in electric field, and how that field separates electrons and holes freed by light, which is the solar cell. The transistor (D106) is left to Computing.

story.title: The rod with the crack, Holmdel, February 1940
story.hook: Russell Ohl, a Bell Labs researcher at Holmdel, New Jersey, was purifying silicon to make better detectors for short-wave radio. On 23 February 1940 he tested a rod that had cracked as it cooled and found that when bright light fell on it, it produced about half a volt, with no battery anywhere in the circuit. Early in March he demonstrated it to Bell Labs' research director Mervin Kelly and to colleagues including Walter Brattain, who later co-invented the transistor. With the metallurgists Jack Scaff and Henry Theuerer, Ohl traced the effect to impurities that had separated on either side of the crack as the melt froze, making two kinds of silicon that met at a sharp boundary.
story.puzzle: How can a lump of nearly pure silicon generate electricity from light?
story.payoff: One side of the crack held a trace of an element with one more valence electron than silicon (spare electrons: n-type), the other a trace of one with one fewer (missing electrons, holes: p-type); the culprits were traced to elements such as phosphorus and boron, silicon's neighbours in the table (D67). Where the two meet, a built-in electric field forms; light frees electrons, and the field pushes them one way and holes the other, so a voltage appears. Ohl had found the p-n junction, the heart of every solar cell and diode and, doubled up, of the junction transistor.
sources: Russell Ohl, US Patent 2,402,662 'Light-Sensitive Electric Device' (filed 1941, granted 1946)
Michael Riordan & Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire (W. W. Norton, 1997), the chapter on the p-n junction
Computer History Museum, 'The Silicon Engine' timeline, 1940: discovery of the p-n junction

days.application: Swanson's law: crystalline-silicon module prices fell from roughly $77 per watt in 1977 (an often-quoted figure) to about $0.10-0.15 per watt for Chinese modules by the mid-2020s, about a 20% drop for each doubling of cumulative shipments. The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2020 said that for projects with low-cost financing and good sun, solar PV 'is now the cheapest source of electricity in history'. Engineering explains the fall as a learning curve (Day 97).

builds_on.why: The band gap is the quantum atom's discrete energy levels spread into bands in a crystal; a photon must carry at least the gap energy to free an electron.
Photon energy rises with frequency, which is why only light above silicon's band gap (about 1.1 eV, near-infrared) makes current.

across.link: William Shockley's junction transistor (conceived in 1948, first made in 1951) is two p-n junctions back to back, the design that turned Bell Labs' 1947 point-contact transistor into a manufacturable device, so the solar cell and the microprocessor share a basic structure.

days.apply_question: Solar panels on Mars rovers and satellites use expensive multi-junction cells instead of cheap silicon; using band gaps and how p-n junctions turn photons into voltage, why might stacking junctions with different gaps capture more of sunlight's energy?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the junction physics and the price fall. Hedge: the 'cheapest in history' claim covers the cost of energy at good sites with cheap finance, not the system costs of using solar at large shares (Day 80).

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A Lake in Cameroon Released a Cloud of Gas One Night. About 1,700 People Died in Their Sleep.
days.concept: Reversible reactions and dissolving gases settle at an equilibrium, and a change in pressure, temperature or concentration shifts that equilibrium in the direction that opposes the change (Le Chatelier's principle).
days.focus: Teaches dynamic equilibrium (forward and reverse running at equal rates), the equilibrium constant as a description of where the balance sits, and Le Chatelier's principle as a predictor. Uses gas solubility under pressure as the clearest case and sets up the ammonia equilibrium for Haber-Bosch (D86).
days.model_or_equation: Le Chatelier applied to N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3 (exothermic): four gas molecules become two, so high pressure pushes toward ammonia; heat favours the reverse, so low temperature raises yield but slows the rate.

story.title: The night Lake Nyos turned over
story.hook: On the night of 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos, a deep crater lake in north-west Cameroon, suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide; estimates of its size run from about 100,000 tonnes to over a million. Heavier than air, the gas poured down the valleys and suffocated about 1,700 people (often given as 1,746) and some 3,500 livestock in villages up to about 25 km away, most of them in their sleep. The lake's water, normally blue, turned a rusty red as iron-rich water from its depths reached the surface.
story.puzzle: A lake is not a volcano. How could still water hold that much gas, and what let it all out at once?
story.payoff: Carbon dioxide seeping from volcanic sources dissolved into the lake's deep water, where high pressure held far more gas in solution than the surface could. When something (perhaps a landslide) lifted deep water upward, pressure fell, the equilibrium shifted toward gas, bubbles formed, the rising bubbly water lifted more water, and the release ran away like a shaken bottle being opened. Since 2001 pipes have been degassing the lake in a controlled way.
sources: Kling et al., 'The 1986 Lake Nyos Gas Disaster in Cameroon, West Africa', Science 236 (1987)
Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Oku Volcanic Field (Lake Nyos) reports
Lake Nyos degassing project reports (2001 onward)

days.application: Ocean acidification runs the same chemistry at planetary scale: the oceans absorb roughly a quarter of human CO2 emissions; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which shifts the carbonate equilibria, releasing hydrogen ions and consuming the carbonate ions that shell-builders need. Average surface-ocean pH has fallen by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times, roughly a 26-30% rise in hydrogen-ion concentration, because pH is a logarithmic scale (D2).

builds_on.why: Pressure rising with depth is what lets deep lake water hold so much dissolved CO2.
Nyos was a threshold system: once lifting water began degassing, a reinforcing loop flipped the lake from stable to erupting.

across.link: Divers' decompression sickness is the same pressure-solubility equilibrium in blood: nitrogen dissolved at depth comes out as bubbles if the diver rises too fast, which is why dive tables set ascent rates and stops.

days.apply_question: A sealed bottle of soda keeps its fizz while an open glass goes flat, and a warm glass goes flat faster than a cold one; using Le Chatelier's principle, what does the warm glass tell you about whether dissolving CO2 in water releases or absorbs heat?
days.evidence_note: Settled: equilibrium chemistry and the measured fall in ocean pH. Debated: the trigger of the Nyos release (landslide, cold rain-chilled surface water sinking, or a gradual approach to saturation) and how strongly acidification will harm particular species.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: French Uranium From Gabon Was Missing Some Atoms. Nature Had Run a Nuclear Reactor There Two Billion Years Ago.
days.concept: A reactor holds a neutron chain reaction exactly at balance, each fission causing on average one more (k = 1), using a moderator to slow neutrons, control rods to absorb them, and negative feedback and delayed neutrons to keep the balance stable and controllable.
days.focus: Teaches the multiplication factor k, why slowed (thermal) neutrons split uranium-235 more readily, enrichment, and the feedbacks that make a reactor self-limiting or unstable. Builds on fission energy (D64) and radiation (D65); risk perception and nuclear politics belong to Psychology and the nuclear case (D277).
key_concepts: chain reaction and multiplication factor k
days.model_or_equation: Neutron population after n generations: N = N0 x k^n. With k = 1.001 and prompt neutrons alone (a generation of roughly a ten-thousandth of a second in a water-moderated reactor), the population would grow e-fold in about a tenth of a second. But about 0.65% of U-235's fission neutrons are delayed, emitted seconds to about a minute later, which stretches the average generation to about a tenth of a second, so the same k takes on the order of a hundred seconds to e-fold: slow enough for feedbacks and control rods to keep up, as long as k - 1 stays below that delayed fraction.

story.title: The missing uranium-235 of Oklo
story.hook: In June 1972 an analyst at the French enrichment plant at Pierrelatte noticed that uranium from the Oklo mine in Gabon carried slightly too little uranium-235: about 0.717% instead of the 0.720% found in uranium everywhere else on Earth, the Moon and meteorites. A tiny gap, but in a business that tracks fissile material for fear of bombs, a gap means a question. In September 1972 France's Atomic Energy Commission announced the answer: about two billion years ago, parts of the Oklo ore body had run as natural nuclear reactors, on and off, for hundreds of thousands of years.
story.puzzle: How could a reactor start, run and switch itself off without engineers, control rods or a containment building, and why didn't it explode?
story.payoff: Two billion years ago natural uranium held about 3% U-235, like modern reactor fuel, because U-235 decays faster than U-238. Groundwater seeping into the ore slowed neutrons (a moderator) so the chain reaction reached k = 1. As it heated up, the water boiled away, moderation dropped, k fell below 1 and the reaction stopped; when the rock cooled, water returned and it restarted. Meshik's analysis suggests cycles of about 30 minutes on and 2.5 hours off: negative feedback holding k near 1.
sources: Meshik, Hohenberg & Pravdivtseva, Physical Review Letters 93 (2004); Meshik, 'The Workings of an Ancient Nuclear Reactor', Scientific American (Nov 2005)
Bodu et al., Comptes rendus de l'Academie des sciences (1972); IAEA symposium 'The Oklo Phenomenon' (1975)
Contrast: Chicago Pile-1, the first human-made reactor, critical on 2 Dec 1942

days.application: France's Messmer plan (announced in March 1974 after the oil shock) built a fleet of standardized pressurized-water reactors, essentially the Oklo recipe engineered: enriched uranium, water as moderator and coolant, and a design in which losing the water stops the chain reaction. Nuclear now supplies around two-thirds of France's electricity (about 65-70% in most recent years), one of the lowest-carbon grids in Europe. Its construction-cost history is Day 97's subject.

builds_on.why: Each fission releases about 200 MeV from mass turned into energy, and the extra neutrons make a chain reaction possible.
Oklo and modern water-moderated reactors are stabilized by a balancing feedback loop: more heat, less moderation, fewer fissions.

across.link: Chernobyl's RBMK reactor (26 April 1986) had a positive void coefficient: as cooling water boiled into steam, reactivity rose, a reinforcing loop where Oklo and Western water-moderated designs have a balancing one.

days.apply_question: US Navy submarines run for decades on highly enriched uranium while power reactors use fuel of about 3-5% U-235; using the multiplication factor and enrichment, why does richer fuel let a submarine's reactor be small enough to fit in a hull and run for its whole life without refuelling?
days.evidence_note: Settled: reactor physics and Oklo's interpretation. Debated (handled in Day 277): nuclear power's cost and the right level of regulation; its safety record per terawatt-hour is well measured, its place in policy is a value judgment.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Germany Had More Than Twice Its Peak Demand in Wind and Solar. One November Evening They Ran at a Few Percent.
days.concept: Capacity factor (average output divided by rated output) and the timing of output decide what a gigawatt of solar or wind is worth compared with a gigawatt of steady plant.
days.focus: Teaches nameplate capacity versus energy delivered, typical capacity factors (solar roughly 10-25% depending on latitude, onshore wind 25-35%, offshore 40-50%, nuclear about 90%), and correlation in time: when many wind farms are calm together, capacity does not add. Separates cheap energy from firm capacity.
days.model_or_equation: Annual energy = capacity x 8,760 hours x capacity factor. 1 GW of German solar at about 10% gives about 0.9 TWh a year; 1 GW of nuclear at about 90% gives about 7.9 TWh.

story.title: The dark doldrums of 6 November 2024
story.hook: By late 2024 Germany had installed roughly 170 GW of wind turbines and solar panels, more than twice its peak electricity demand. In early November 2024 a high-pressure system parked over central Europe: grey skies, almost no wind, and on 6 November the long November night falling by late afternoon. Wind and solar output sank to a small fraction of capacity, coal and gas plants and imports filled the gap, and the day-ahead price for the early-evening hour spiked to roughly 800 euros per megawatt-hour, many times normal. Germans have a word for it: Dunkelflaute, the 'dark doldrums'.
story.puzzle: How can a country own more than twice its peak demand in renewable capacity and still be short of power?
story.payoff: Nameplate capacity is the maximum, not the average or the guaranteed. German solar's capacity factor is around 10%, and on a November evening it is zero; wind output is correlated across the country, so on a calm day turbines idle together. What a gigawatt is worth depends on when it produces, which is why systems with much wind and solar still need storage, imports or dispatchable plants.
sources: Fraunhofer ISE, Energy-Charts: net generation and day-ahead prices, 6 November 2024
Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD data on installed capacity (end-2024)
Reuters and Clean Energy Wire coverage of the November and December 2024 Dunkelflaute price spikes

days.application: California's 'duck curve': in 2013 the grid operator CAISO published a chart forecasting that midday solar would hollow out net load (demand minus wind and solar) while leaving a steep evening ramp; the midday belly deepened faster than that chart projected. Each added gigawatt of solar is worth less when it all produces at noon (value deflation), so the system adds storage: California's batteries grew past roughly 10 GW by 2024, shifting midday solar into the evening.

builds_on.why: Capacity is power (GW); what the grid needs over a year is energy (TWh); capacity factor converts one to the other.
Correlation matters: wind farms' outputs are positively correlated by shared weather, so they do not average out as independent sources would.

across.link: Harry Markowitz's 'Portfolio Selection' (Journal of Finance, 1952) rests on the same formula: the variance of a sum shrinks only as far as its parts are uncorrelated, so spreading wind farms across distant weather systems smooths output only partly. The analogy breaks where a grid must cover every hour, not just earn a good average.

days.apply_question: An offshore wind farm of 1 GW at a 45% capacity factor and a solar farm of 2 GW at 20% produce similar annual energy; using capacity factor and timing, what more would you need to know to say which is worth more to Britain's grid in winter?
days.evidence_note: Settled: capacity factors and the arithmetic. Debated: the full system cost of high wind-and-solar shares (storage, backup, transmission), where studies differ widely by assumptions. Value judgment: how much reliability to buy, and at whose cost.

resource.why: MacKay, a Cambridge physicist, works through how much wind fluctuates and what storage it would take to cover lulls, with transparent arithmetic.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: The grid as a balancing act
days.headline_hint: Texas Came Four and a Half Minutes From a Blackout That Could Have Lasted Months.
days.concept: On an AC grid, supply must match demand every second; frequency (60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in Europe and Australia) is the signal of imbalance, and spinning inertia and reserves buy the seconds needed to fix it.
days.focus: Teaches why frequency falls when generation is short (generators slow down), inertia as stored rotational energy, the sequence of primary, secondary and tertiary reserves, and under-frequency load shedding as the last defence. Shows why inverter-based wind and solar need grid-forming controls or synthetic inertia.
days.model_or_equation: Swing equation, simplified: the rate of frequency fall is proportional to the power shortfall divided by the system's inertia; less inertia means a faster fall for the same lost plant.

story.title: Early morning, 15 February 2021, ERCOT control room
story.hook: As Winter Storm Uri froze Texas, gas wells, pipelines and power plants failed in the cold. Shortly before 2 am on 15 February 2021, generation in the ERCOT grid, which serves most of Texas and is barely connected to its neighbours, fell far below demand. Frequency dropped below 59.4 Hz and stayed there for about four and a half minutes; had it stayed there about four and a half minutes more, generators would have tripped automatically and the grid could have collapsed entirely, needing a 'black start' that ERCOT said could have taken months. Operators ordered rolling blackouts that left about 4.5 million homes and businesses without power, many for days; Texas officially counted 246 deaths, and independent estimates run higher.
story.puzzle: Why does a power shortfall show up as a falling frequency, and why does a few minutes below 59.4 Hz risk a months-long blackout?
story.payoff: Generators spin in lockstep with the grid; when demand exceeds supply, the extra energy comes out of their rotation and they slow, so frequency falls. Protection relays disconnect plants below safe frequencies to save them from damage, which deepens the shortfall: a reinforcing collapse. Shedding load restored the balance; the cascade it prevented would have required restarting the grid from nothing.
sources: FERC-NERC staff report, 'The February 2021 Cold Weather Outages in Texas and the South Central United States' (November 2021)
ERCOT presentation to its board, 24 February 2021 (the 4 minutes 37 seconds figure)
Texas Department of State Health Services, Winter Storm Uri mortality report (2021-22)

days.application: South Australia, 28 September 2016: storms with tornadoes toppled transmission towers; protection settings at several wind farms, which limited how many voltage dips they would ride through, cut about 456 MW of output within seconds; the interconnector to Victoria overloaded and tripped, and the whole state went dark. AEMO's final report (March 2017) blamed the settings, not wind's variability; the response included new ride-through standards, a 100 MW Tesla battery at Hornsdale (December 2017) that sells fast frequency response, and synchronous condensers to restore inertia.

builds_on.why: The AC grid case explained why the world runs on synchronous alternating current; frequency is that synchrony's heartbeat.
The 2003 Northeast blackout showed failures cascading through a network; protection that saves one plant can push the next over the edge.

across.link: Texas's grid is deliberately kept almost unconnected to interstate lines largely so that ERCOT stays outside federal (FERC) wholesale-market regulation under the Federal Power Act, a jurisdictional choice that limited emergency imports during Uri.

days.apply_question: Ireland's grid operator now lets wind and solar supply up to about three-quarters of demand at any moment but requires a minimum number of conventional generators to stay online; using inertia and frequency, explain why a grid might cap the instantaneous share of inverter-based power even when the wind is free.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the physics of frequency and inertia. Debated: the Texas death toll (official 246; independent estimates several hundred higher) and how far ERCOT's energy-only market design, versus failures to winterize gas and power plants, explains Uri.

resource.why: An independent university reconstruction of the night, with the frequency trace, the 59.4 Hz trip threshold and the load shedding, so Logan can see the near-collapse minute by minute.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: 347,000 Mirrors on 3,500 Acres of the Mojave, and an Average Output One Gas Turbine Could Match.
days.concept: Power density, the watts produced per square metre of land, differs by orders of magnitude between fossil extraction, solar, wind and biofuels, and so decides how much land an energy system needs.
days.focus: Teaches Smil's power density (Power Density, MIT Press 2015): fossil fuel extraction and thermal plants run at hundreds to thousands of W/m2, solar PV at roughly 5-20 W/m2 of land, wind at about 0.5-3 W/m2 of wind-farm area, biofuels well under 1 W/m2. Distinguishes land occupied from land excluded, and average from peak.
days.model_or_equation: Power density = average power / land area. Ivanpah: roughly 650-850 GWh a year is about 75-95 MW average, over about 14 km2 (3,500 acres): roughly 5-7 W/m2. Corn ethanol: about 0.2-0.3 W/m2.

story.title: Ivanpah opens in the Mojave, February 2014
story.hook: In February 2014 the Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System opened near the California-Nevada border: about 173,500 computer-steered heliostats, each carrying two mirrors, aimed sunlight at boilers on three towers some 140 metres tall. It cost about $2.2 billion, backed by a $1.6 billion federal loan guarantee, and was rated at 392 MW on roughly 3,500 acres of desert. In its early years it produced well below its projected output, and in early 2025 its main buyer, the utility PG&E, agreed to end its contracts early, with two of its three units slated to close as cheaper photovoltaics won.
story.puzzle: A plant rated at 392 MW and covering five and a half square miles delivers, on average, about what one mid-sized gas turbine on a site of a few hectares does. Why do the two differ so much in land?
story.payoff: Sunlight at the ground averages only about 250 W/m2 over day and night even in the Mojave, and after conversion losses, spacing between mirrors and night, a solar plant delivers single-digit watts per square metre. A gas plant concentrates energy that geology collected over millions of years and pipelines bring in, so even counting its gas fields its power density is tens to hundreds of times higher. Neither is good or bad in itself: power density tells you the land bill.
sources: US DOE Loan Programs Office, Ivanpah project page
US EIA Electricity Data Browser, Ivanpah annual generation
Vaclav Smil, Power Density: A Key to Understanding Energy Sources and Uses (MIT Press, 2015)

days.application: US corn ethanol: in recent years roughly 35-40% of the US corn crop has gone to ethanol (about a quarter once the distillers' grains returned as animal feed are credited; EIA, USDA), yet ethanol supplies only about a tenth of US gasoline by volume and less by energy (ethanol carries about two-thirds of gasoline's energy per litre). At well under 1 W/m2, biofuels are the least land-efficient energy source, which is why their climate and food-price effects are argued over.

builds_on.why: Power is energy per second; power density divides that rate by area, the unit that decides land needs.
Average output (capacity factor), not nameplate, is what goes into power density.

across.link: Photosynthesis stores only about 1% of incoming sunlight as crop energy over a growing season, which is why biofuels' power density is so low and why land for fuel competes with land for food.

days.apply_question: The UK's Drax power station burns several million tonnes of wood pellets a year, shipped mostly from North American forests; using power density, why must the land supplying a biomass plant be thousands of times larger than the plant itself, when a gas plant's is not?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the power-density figures to within a factor of about two. Debated: how to count land (panels alone or whole site, farmland shared with turbines) and whether biofuels cut emissions once land-use change is included.

resource.why: MacKay totals the power per square metre of each renewable against Britain's land area, the clearest worked example of power density deciding what is possible.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Watt's Engines Burned Far Less Coal for the Same Work. Britain Burned Far More. Jevons Said That Was No Accident.
days.concept: Making energy use more efficient lowers the effective price of the service it provides, which can raise use and eat part of the saving (the rebound effect); whether it eats all of it (Jevons's paradox, backfire) is an empirical question, usually answered 'part'.
days.focus: Teaches direct, indirect and economy-wide rebound, why efficiency still usually saves energy, and the cases where backfire is plausible (a new general-purpose technology). Assumes Logan's CFA-level price elasticity and names it in a clause.
days.model_or_equation: Rebound = (expected savings - actual savings) / expected savings. 0% means efficiency saves fully; 100% means no saving; over 100% is backfire.

story.title: A 29-year-old's warning about coal, 1865
story.hook: In 1865 William Stanley Jevons, a 29-year-old tutor at Owens College in Manchester, published The Coal Question, asking whether Britain's prosperity could last as its cheap coal was used up. He met the comforting reply that better engines would stretch supplies with a striking claim: 'It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.' James Watt's engines, far more efficient than Thomas Newcomen's, had not saved coal; Britain's consumption had soared. William Gladstone, then Chancellor of the Exchequer, cited the book, and it made Jevons's name.
story.puzzle: If each engine burns less coal per unit of work, how can better engines make a country burn more coal?
story.payoff: Efficiency made steam power cheaper per unit of work, which opened uses that had never paid before: mines, mills, railways, ships. Total coal use rose because demand for steam power was very responsive to its cost and steam was a general-purpose technology. Jevons was right about his case; whether efficiency backfires in general depends on how much a cheaper service raises demand.
sources: W. S. Jevons, The Coal Question (1865), ch. VII 'Of the Economy of Fuel'
Steve Sorrell, 'Jevons' Paradox revisited: The evidence for backfire from improved energy efficiency', Energy Policy 37 (2009)

days.application: Fuel-efficient cars are driven more: Small and Van Dender (The Energy Journal, 2007), using US state data for 1966-2001, estimated a direct rebound of about 4.5% in the short run and about 22% in the long run, falling as incomes rise; later studies range from near zero to about 30%. So a car that is 20% more efficient saves perhaps 15-19% of fuel, not 20%, and not zero. This is the consequences-and-feedback link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: Rebound is a classic unintended consequence: the fix (efficiency) changes behaviour and partly undoes itself.

James Watt, whose horsepower Day 53 defined, sold his engines on fuel savings (Boulton & Watt charged a royalty of one-third of the coal saved against a Newcomen engine), the very efficiency gain Jevons argued raised Britain's coal use.

across.link: Computing is the strongest modern candidate for backfire: computations per kilowatt-hour doubled roughly every year and a half for decades (Koomey's law, 2011), and total use rose with them; US data centres used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024).

days.apply_question: LED bulbs use roughly a sixth of the electricity of incandescent bulbs for the same light, and outdoor lighting has spread with them; using the rebound effect, what would you need to measure to decide whether LEDs have reduced lighting's total electricity use?
days.evidence_note: Debated: the size of economy-wide rebound; most estimates find partial rebound for household energy services, while some analysts argue backfire is common for general-purpose technologies (Harry Saunders) and others that it is rare (Gillingham, Rapson & Wagner, Review of Environmental Economics and Policy, 2016). Value judgment: whether more cheap energy services are themselves a benefit, as they are to the person who drives further.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Hans Rosling Called the Washing Machine the Greatest Invention of the Industrial Revolution. His Grandmother Watched the First One for the Whole Wash.
days.concept: Energy use per person rises steeply with living standards at first and then with diminishing returns, and energy transitions are slow because the system that supplies it is vast and long-lived.
days.focus: Teaches the energy ladder (from muscle and biomass to electricity and liquid fuels), the concave relation between energy per head and human development measures, and Smil's point that transitions take decades because of the size and lifetimes of the infrastructure. Keeps the empirical curve apart from the moral question of how much is enough.

story.title: Laundry day in Sweden, as Hans Rosling told it
story.hook: In a December 2010 TEDWomen talk, the Swedish physician and public-health professor Hans Rosling described the day, when he was about four years old in the early 1950s, that he watched his mother load a washing machine for the first time in her life. She had saved for years; his grandmother, who had washed laundry by hand all her life, heating water over a wood fire, sat watching the machine for the whole programme, mesmerized. His mother used the time it freed to take him to the library. Rosling called the washing machine the greatest invention of the industrial revolution, and pointed out that most of the world's people still washed clothes by hand.
story.puzzle: Why would a statistician of global health rank a laundry machine above the steam engine or the computer, and what does it say about how energy turns into human welfare?
story.payoff: The first units of modern energy, electricity and hot water replacing hours of human muscle, buy enormous gains: time, health, education, especially for women. Later units add comfort with diminishing returns. That concave curve means a kilowatt-hour does far more good at the bottom of the ladder than at the top, which is why access matters so much.
sources: Hans Rosling, 'The magic washing machine', TEDWomen, December 2010
Our World in Data, 'Energy' and 'Access to Energy' pages (Hannah Ritchie, Pablo Rosado and Max Roser)
Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (MIT Press, 2017)

days.application: The world's energy ladder today: the IEA estimates that roughly 700-750 million people still lack electricity, most in sub-Saharan Africa, and that over two billion cook with polluting fuels; commercial energy use per person in the richest countries is on the order of a hundred times that of the poorest (Our World in Data). Smil's warning: fossil fuels still supply about 80% of global primary energy, and earlier transitions (wood to coal, coal to oil) each took many decades.

builds_on.why: Day 53 put a working human body at about 100 W; a washing machine's heater and motor draw around 2 kW, the sustained output of many people, which is Rosling's point in watts.

Development indices rise roughly with the logarithm of energy use per person, so on a log axis the steep-then-flat curve becomes a rough line: each tenfold rise buys a similar step, and each step costs ten times more energy.

across.link: Household electrification shifted women's work: Taryn Dinkelman's natural-experiment study of rural electrification in South Africa (American Economic Review, 2011) found female employment rose by about 9 percentage points in newly connected areas.

days.apply_question: Some climate campaigners argue rich countries should cut energy use per head while poor countries raise theirs; using the concave energy-development curve, what would you need to know to judge where a cut costs the least welfare, and what would you need to value to decide whether it should be made?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the strong, concave correlation between energy use and development indices. Debated: causation (energy enables development, development raises energy use, or both) and how low rich-country use could go without welfare loss ('decent living energy' estimates). Value judgment: what level of energy use is 'enough', and who should cut.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: In 1856 Eunice Foote Put Carbon Dioxide in the Sun and Wrote That It Could Warm the Earth. A Man Read Her Paper Aloud.
days.concept: Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases let sunlight in but absorb and re-emit the infrared Earth radiates; adding CO2 raises the forcing roughly with the logarithm of its concentration, and warming per doubling (climate sensitivity) is likely about 2.5-4 C.
days.focus: Teaches why molecules with three or more atoms absorb infrared (their vibrations), the energy balance, why the effect is logarithmic and why the emission height matters, and the distinction between radiative forcing (physics, well measured) and sensitivity (includes feedbacks, still a range). The one home for the greenhouse effect in the path.
days.model_or_equation: Delta F = 5.35 x ln(C/C0) W/m2 (Myhre et al., 1998), the logarithm of Day 2: doubling CO2 gives about 3.7 W/m2 (IPCC AR6 revises this to about 3.9). Warming = sensitivity x (forcing / forcing per doubling); IPCC AR6: likely 2.5-4 C per doubling, best estimate 3 C.

story.title: Two cylinders in the sun, Albany, August 1856
story.hook: At the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting in Albany, New York, in August 1856, a paper by Eunice Newton Foote, 'Circumstances affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays', was read by the Smithsonian's Joseph Henry, not by Foote. She had filled glass cylinders with different gases, set them in sunlight and recorded their temperatures; the one with 'carbonic acid gas' heated most and cooled slowest. She wrote that an atmosphere of that gas 'would give to our earth a high temperature'. Three years later in London, John Tyndall measured how CO2 and water vapour absorb infrared radiation, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling CO2 would warm Earth by several degrees.
story.puzzle: CO2 is transparent to sunlight and makes up only about 0.04% of the air. How can so little of an invisible gas warm a planet?
story.payoff: Sunlight passes through, but Earth radiates heat as infrared, and CO2 molecules vibrate at infrared frequencies, so they absorb and re-emit that heat, some of it back down. More CO2 makes the air opaque higher up, where it is colder, so the planet sheds heat less efficiently until it warms. A trace gas matters because it acts on the one band of radiation that controls the energy balance. (Foote's sunlit setup mixed several effects; Tyndall's infrared measurements isolated the mechanism.)
sources: Foote, 'Circumstances affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays', American Journal of Science and Arts, 2nd series, 22 (Nov 1856)
Tyndall, Proceedings of the Royal Institution (1859); Bakerian Lecture, Philosophical Transactions (1861)
Arrhenius, Philosophical Magazine 41 (1896)
IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers (2021)

days.application: The Keeling curve and the carbon budget: Mauna Loa CO2 rose from about 315 ppm in 1958 to about 425 ppm by 2025 (D4). Because warming tracks cumulative emissions roughly linearly, scientists convert targets into a remaining budget: IPCC AR6 gave about 500 billion tonnes of CO2 from 2020 for a 50% chance of holding warming to 1.5 C, and the 2025 update of the Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster et al.) put the remainder at about 130 billion tonnes from the start of 2025, roughly three years of current emissions. Transport, including cars, emits roughly a fifth of energy-related CO2: the consequences link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: The greenhouse effect is about the electromagnetic spectrum: visible sunlight in, infrared out, and molecules absorbing at particular frequencies.
CO2 is a stock filled by emissions and drained slowly by oceans and land; stabilizing emissions does not stabilize the stock, the very error Sterman's students made.

across.link: The Paris Agreement (2015) turned the carbon budget into nationally determined contributions submitted every five years and a five-yearly global stocktake, a pledge-and-review design chosen because, unlike the Montreal Protocol's few CFC producers, CO2 has billions of emitters.

days.apply_question: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 but breaks down in about a decade, while CO2 persists for centuries; using forcing and stocks and flows, why might cutting methane slow warming quickly but not substitute for cutting CO2?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the greenhouse mechanism, the measured rise in CO2, that human emissions caused it, and that warming is under way (IPCC: 'unequivocal'). Debated: the exact climate sensitivity within the 2.5-4 C range, regional impacts and their costs, and tipping points. Value judgment: how fast to cut, at what cost, and who pays, which is policy, not physics.
