days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 5: Haber-Bosch - bread from air
days.headline_hint: A Tabletop Machine in Karlsruhe Dripped Ammonia in 1909. Nearly Half of Humanity Now Eats Because of It, and It Fed Germany's Explosives Factories in the First World War.
days.concept: How one reaction, fixing the air's nitrogen into ammonia, came to feed nearly half of humanity, and what that system has cost.
days.focus: Walks synthetic nitrogen through the chain as a loop: Crookes's 1898 warning (need), Haber's equilibrium and catalyst (invention), the pressure-temperature compromise (constraint), Bosch's scale-up (engineering), war (production), the fertilizer S-curve (adoption), population and pollution (consequences), and Haber himself (moral reading). Deep on equilibrium, catalysis, fossil feedstock, stocks and flows and ethics; previews engineering, the war and regulation.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops: (1) Reinforcing: more fixed nitrogen -> more food -> more people -> more demand for fixed nitrogen. (2) Reinforcing (war): the blockade of Chilean nitrate -> need for synthetic nitrate for explosives -> state-backed scale-up at Leuna (1917). (3) Balancing, delayed: excess nitrogen -> runoff -> dead zones and N2O -> nutrient rules and precision farming, decades later. (4) Energy coupling: ammonia depends on natural gas, so gas price shocks (2021-22) fed straight into fertilizer and food prices.

story.title: The drip in Karlsruhe, 2 July 1909
story.hook: On 2 July 1909, in Fritz Haber's laboratory at the Technische Hochschule in Karlsruhe, a tabletop apparatus built with his English assistant Robert Le Rossignol held nitrogen and hydrogen at about 200 atmospheres over an osmium catalyst. In front of BASF's chemist Alwin Mittasch it ran for hours, producing a steady drip of liquid ammonia, nitrogen pulled from the air. BASF's Carl Bosch then spent four years turning a lab bench into a factory: reactor tubes that hot hydrogen weakened until they burst, high-pressure compressors, and a cheap iron catalyst that Mittasch found after thousands of trials. In September 1913 the Oppau plant began producing ammonia at industrial scale.
story.puzzle: How did one reaction come to feed nearly half of humanity, and what has it cost?
story.payoff: Equilibrium said high pressure and moderate heat; catalysis made it fast enough; Bosch's engineering made it possible at scale; war paid for the scale-up; fossil gas made it cheap; fertilizer multiplied harvests. The same nitrogen now overloads rivers and seas, and the same chemistry made explosives. Every link is a reason it fed billions and a reason it costs something.
sources: Vaclav Smil, Enriching the Earth: Fritz Haber, Carl Bosch, and the Transformation of World Food Production (MIT Press, 2001)
Thomas Hager, The Alchemy of Air (Harmony, 2008)
Erisman, Sutton, Galloway, Klimont & Winiwarter, 'How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world', Nature Geoscience 1 (2008)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1918 (Haber) and 1931 (Bosch, with Friedrich Bergius)

days.application: The Gulf of Mexico 'dead zone': nitrogen and phosphorus washed down the Mississippi from Midwestern farms feed algal blooms whose decay strips oxygen from bottom water each summer, over an area that has averaged roughly 13,000-14,000 km2 (about 5,000-5,400 square miles) since NOAA-funded measurements began in 1985, against a federal-state task force goal of about 5,000 km2 (1,900 square miles) that has never been met.

builds_on.why: Le Chatelier sets the compromise: high pressure favours ammonia (four gas molecules become two), low temperature favours yield but slows the rate.
The iron catalyst lowers the activation barrier for breaking nitrogen's triple bond, making the reaction fast enough at 400-500 C.
Natural gas (or coal earlier) supplies the hydrogen and the energy, so fertilizer is fossil energy turned into food.
Reactive nitrogen is a stock with leaky flows: what crops do not take up leaches into water or escapes as N2O.

across.link: When the British blockade cut Germany off from Chilean saltpetre in 1914, synthetic nitrate from Haber-Bosch ammonia (oxidized to nitric acid) kept its explosives factories running; many historians argue Germany would otherwise have run short of munitions by about 1915-16, though captured stocks and other processes also helped and the counterfactual is uncertain.

days.apply_question: Green ammonia made with hydrogen from wind- or solar-powered electrolysis is being proposed both as fertilizer and as a ship fuel; using the loops in this case, what would you need to know to judge whether it could change the system's climate cost without changing its food benefit?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the chemistry, the global scale (synthetic fertilizer supplies roughly half the nitrogen in human food) and the nitrogen-pollution mechanisms. Debated: the exact share of humanity fed (Erisman et al.: 48% for 2008; Smil: about 40% for 2000) and the counterfactual, since without Haber-Bosch other routes (more legumes, more land, other fixation processes) would have been pursued; the counterfactual is unknowable. Value judgment: weighing billions fed against war use, pollution and fossil dependence; consequentialist and virtue readings of Haber himself differ sharply. Who gained (eaters, farmers, BASF), who paid (soldiers at Ypres and on every front, coastal fisheries, the future climate), and who consented: few of the downstream payers.

chain.point: William Crookes's September 1898 presidential address to the British Association in Bristol warned that wheat demand would outrun supply unless chemists could fix atmospheric nitrogen; Chilean saltpetre, the main nitrate source, was finite and controlled by a few exporters. Here need really did come before invention, though Crookes's forecast, like many resource warnings, assumed fixed yields and a fixed resource.

Haber and Le Rossignol's 2 July 1909 demonstration: N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3 at about 200 atm and roughly 500 C over an osmium catalyst, recycling the unreacted gas because each pass converts only a fraction.

Nitrogen's triple bond is among the strongest in chemistry; equilibrium yield per pass is modest at workable temperatures; hydrogen at high pressure and temperature attacks steel. Pressure and heat are energy costs: the best modern gas-based plants use about 28 GJ per tonne of ammonia, and the world average is higher.

Hydrogen first came from coal-derived water gas, now mostly from steam reforming of natural gas; ammonia production uses roughly 2% of world final energy and emits on the order of 1% of global energy-related CO2 (IEA, Ammonia Technology Roadmap, 2021).

Bosch's scale-up: double-walled reactors with a soft-iron liner that let hydrogen escape instead of embrittling the steel pressure shell, high-pressure compressors, and Mittasch's promoted iron catalyst found in thousands of trials. Engineering (the next block, Days 87-103) teaches the structures, fatigue and safety factors behind it.

BASF funded Oppau itself (1913); the far larger Leuna works (1917) were built under the Reich's wartime nitrate programme with state money, a war-financed scale-up. History II's World War I lesson (Day 230) teaches industrial war; the financing mechanism is named here, not taught.
Synthetic fertilizer use was small before 1950 and then followed an S-curve to roughly 110 million tonnes of nitrogen a year in the 2020s (FAO), with China the largest user.

Erisman et al. (2008) estimated that about 48% of the world's people were fed by Haber-Bosch nitrogen; it is the reinforcing loop of food and population. The crop side, semi-dwarf varieties bred to use fertilizer, is Biology's Green Revolution lesson (Day 146).

Humans now fix more reactive nitrogen than all natural processes on land; runoff creates coastal dead zones (a threshold in oxygen), and N2O is a greenhouse gas about 270 times as potent as CO2 over a century (IPCC AR6). A fix for hunger feeding a new problem.

Nutrient rules such as the EU Nitrates Directive (1991) and the Dutch nitrogen crisis after the Council of State's May 2019 ruling show regulation arriving decades after the harm; Government (Days 236-249) teaches how regulation works.

The same Haber directed the chlorine attack at Ypres on 22 April 1915 (History, Day 230); his wife Clara Immerwahr, a chemist, killed herself on 2 May. He received the 1918 Nobel Prize, and in 1933, Jewish-born though baptized a Lutheran in 1892, he resigned rather than dismiss Jewish colleagues under the new Nazi law and left Germany; he died in Basel in January 1934. A consequentialist tallies billions fed against war deaths; virtue ethics asks what his choices show about character and whether great benefit excuses them.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.topic: The design process: constraints and trade-offs
days.headline_hint: Apollo 13's Spare Air Filters Were Square. The Sockets Were Round. Houston Built the Fix From Plastic Bags, a Sock and a Flight-Plan Cover.
days.concept: Engineering design means meeting hard constraints while trading off goals that compete, so every design choice has a loser who pays a cost, and good design shows that cost openly.
days.focus: Design taught as constrained optimization in practice. Separate the hard constraints (must be met) from the goals (more is better), show the trade-off frontier where gaining one goal costs another, and show satisficing under pressure. The Apollo 13 'mailbox' and the car's weight, fuel and safety trade-off make 'every trade-off has a loser' concrete.
days.model_or_equation: Design as constrained optimization: choose a design x to do well on goals f1(x), f2(x) and so on, subject to hard constraints g(x) <= 0. When goals conflict there is no single best x, only a Pareto frontier: the set of designs where no goal can improve without another getting worse. Picking a point on that frontier is partly a value decision about who bears the loss.

story.title: Square canisters, round holes, and the air running out
story.hook: On the evening of 13 April 1970 (Houston time), about 56 hours into the flight, an oxygen tank in Apollo 13's service module exploded. Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise moved into the lunar module Aquarius. Its lithium hydroxide canisters, which strip carbon dioxide from the cabin air, were sized for two men on a short lunar stay, not three men on a four-day trip home, and the CO2 reading began to climb. The command module had plenty of spare canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's sockets were round. In Houston, crew-systems chief Ed Smylie's team worked out an adapter and tested it on the ground. Smylie later put the number of people involved at about 60. The adapter used only items on board: plastic bags, the cardboard cover of a flight plan, a spacesuit hose, a sock and grey duct tape. Mission Control read the crew the steps one by one, they built the 'mailbox', and the CO2 level fell.
story.puzzle: Some of the best engineers in the world built these spacecraft. Why did the lunar module carry so little air-scrubbing capacity, and why could two spacecraft on the same mission not swap canisters? And how do you design a fix when the only parts you may use are the ones already on board?
story.payoff: Design is meeting hard constraints while trading goals against each other. The lunar module's small scrubber capacity was the loser of an earlier mass trade-off: every kilogram landed on the Moon had to be paid for many times over at launch. The mismatched canisters partly reflect two contractors designing to separate requirements: Grumman built the lunar module and North American the command module. Houston's mailbox was not elegant. It met the hard constraints (CO2 limits, parts on board, crew time), accepted ugly trade-offs, and was tested before it was flown.
sources: NASA, Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, Apollo 13 'LiOH canister adapter' page (nasa.gov/history/alsj/a13)
Stephen Cass, 'Apollo 13, We Have a Solution', IEEE Spectrum, 2005 (Part 3)
Space.com obituary, 'NASA engineer Ed Smylie, who led carbon dioxide fix on Apollo 13, dies at 95' (May 2025)
Jim Lovell and Jeffrey Kluger, Lost Moon (1994)

days.application: The car's weight trade-off, at the engineering link of the chain. A lighter car burns less fuel, because accelerating and rolling a smaller mass takes less energy. But in a crash between two vehicles, the occupants of the lighter one take the larger change in velocity (Day 51). The National Research Council's 2002 report on fuel-economy (CAFE) standards had a majority view: the downweighting and downsizing of the late 1970s and early 1980s, partly a response to those standards, probably meant about 1,300 to 2,600 more traffic deaths in 1993. Two committee members, David Greene and Maryann Keller, dissented. They said the data could not support that estimate and that the net effect might be zero. Fuel savings are spread across everyone, while the added crash risk falls on whoever rides in the lighter car.

builds_on.why: Optimization under constraints: a constraint moves the optimum, and a flat optimum means small compromises cost little. Design trade-offs are this idea in practice.
Momentum and impulse explain the safety side of the weight trade-off: in a two-car crash the lighter car's occupants take the larger change in velocity.

across.link: François Jacob's 'Evolution and Tinkering' (Science, 1977) describes natural selection as a tinkerer that makes do with whatever is at hand under constraints, much like Houston building the mailbox from what was on board. The analogy breaks because evolution has no goal or foresight, and engineers do.

days.apply_question: Concorde flew from London to New York in about three and a half hours, but it carried only about 100 passengers and burned far more fuel per seat than a Boeing 747. Which of its requirements were hard constraints, which goals did its designers trade against each other, and who were the losers of those trade-offs?
days.evidence_note: Settled: design as meeting constraints and trading goals, and the Apollo 13 facts. Debated: how large the car weight-safety trade-off is. The NRC 2002 majority estimated 1,300 to 2,600 extra deaths in 1993 from downweighting and downsizing. Dissenters David Greene and Maryann Keller argued the data could not support that, and that the net effect may have been zero. Later NHTSA analyses (e.g., Kahane 2012) found the effect depends on which vehicles lose mass: taking weight out of the heaviest trucks and SUVs can save lives. Value judgment: who should bear the remaining risk when the fuel savings are shared but the crash risk is not.

resource.length: introduction and opening chapter, about 30 minutes
resource.why: Petroski, a Duke civil engineer and historian of design, uses everyday objects to argue that every design is a compromise among conflicting goals. That is today's concept, seen in things Logan handles daily.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: The Quebec Bridge Never Carried a Train. In 1907 It Fell Under Its Own Weight.
days.concept: Loads put each structural member in tension or compression, and a member's shape (how far its material sits from the bending axis) decides how well it resists bending and buckling, so every design must count both the structure's own weight (dead load) and what it carries (live load).
days.focus: How loads become stresses. Tension and compression; stress and strain; why the I-beam and the box section resist bending far better than their weight suggests; why slender members in compression buckle long before the steel itself crushes; and why dead load dominates large structures. The Quebec Bridge is the cautionary case and car body sections the everyday one.
key_concepts: bending moment and second moment of area
days.model_or_equation: Bending stress: sigma = M·y / I. Here M is the bending moment, y is the distance from the neutral axis, and I is the second moment of area. For a rectangle of width b and depth h, I = b·h^3/12, so doubling the depth makes a beam eight times stiffer. An I-beam puts most of its metal in flanges far from the axis. For a simply supported span carrying a uniform load w per metre, the maximum moment is M = w·L^2/8, so doubling the span quadruples the moment from the same weight per metre.

story.title: A bridge that fell under little more than itself
story.hook: Late on the afternoon of 29 August 1907, about fifteen minutes before the working day ended, the south half of the Quebec Bridge fell into the St Lawrence in roughly 15 seconds. It was being cantilevered out over the river to make the longest span in the world. Of the 86 men on it, 75 were killed (ENR's count is 74), among them about 33 Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake. No train had ever crossed it, and there was no gale and no earthquake: on it were only its own steel, the equipment building it, and the men. The consulting engineer, Theodore Cooper, had lengthened the main span from 1,600 to 1,800 feet. By 1906 the detailed drawings showed the steel weighed far more than the design had assumed, and work went on anyway. In August 1907 men on site reported that a lower compression chord, member A9L, was bending out of line. Cooper wired 'Add no more load to bridge till after due consideration of facts', but the message did not reach the site in time.
story.puzzle: How can a steel bridge built to carry trains collapse while carrying little more than itself?
story.payoff: A large structure's own weight is usually its biggest load. The bending it causes grows with the square of the span, and heavier members add still more weight. The Royal Commission found 'a grave error was made in assuming the dead load for the calculations at too low a value and not afterwards revising this assumption.' The overloaded compression chords buckled sideways. Slender members in compression fail by buckling well before the steel crushes, which is why shape matters as much as material.
sources: Royal Commission, Quebec Bridge Inquiry Report (Ottawa, 1908)
Pearson and Delatte, 'Collapse of the Quebec Bridge, 1907', Journal of Performance of Constructed Facilities (ASCE) 20(1), 2006
ENR, 'ENR's coverage of the 1907 collapse of the Quebec Bridge'
Legion Magazine, 'A bridge with two tragedies'

days.application: Car bodies and chassis. A car's sills, pillars and frame rails are closed box or hat sections, not flat plates, because material placed far from the bending axis gives stiffness and crash strength for little weight. A second application is the Canadian engineer's iron ring, conferred since 1925 in the 'Ritual of the Calling of an Engineer', with wording by Rudyard Kipling, as a reminder of professional fallibility. The popular tale that the first rings were made from the fallen Quebec Bridge is a legend: the bridge was steel, and the early rings were made elsewhere.

builds_on.why: Square-cube scaling: as a structure grows, its own weight grows faster than the strength of its members, so dead load dominates long spans.
Newton's laws applied to a body at rest: every force on a structure balances, so each member's tension or compression follows from equilibrium.

across.link: In Two New Sciences (1638), Galileo noted that hollow bones and reeds resist bending better than solid rods of the same weight. That is the same second-moment-of-area logic as the I-beam. The analogy breaks because living bone remodels itself to the loads it carries (Wolff's law, 1892), and steel does not.

days.apply_question: In a wooden house, floor joists such as 2x10 boards are set on edge, not laid flat. Using today's ideas, explain why, and say which loads the builder must count besides the people and furniture on the floor.
days.evidence_note: Settled mechanics. Label as legend that Canadian iron rings were first made from the Quebec Bridge wreckage. Sources differ on deaths (75 or 74) and on Kahnawake Mohawk victims (about 33, some say 35); give the range.

resource.creator: The Efficient Engineer (YouTube)

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.topic: Fatigue and the factor of safety
days.headline_hint: Britain's Jet Airliner Was Tested at About Twice Its Cabin Pressure. Then Two Broke Apart in Calm Air.
days.concept: Loads repeated many times, each far below a material's breaking strength, can grow cracks until a part fails (metal fatigue), so engineers design with factors of safety, avoid stress concentrations, and test whole structures through realistic load cycles, because calculation alone misses what repetition does.
days.focus: Why strength once is not strength forever. The S-N curve and its power-law shape, stress concentration at sharp corners, the factor of safety as cover for scatter and ignorance, and full-scale fatigue testing and inspection. The Comet is the founding case of fatigue in aviation.
key_concepts: metal fatigue and the S-N curve
days.model_or_equation: Factor of safety = capacity / expected load. Fatigue life follows an S-N curve, roughly the power law sigma_a = sigma_f'·(2N)^b (Basquin, 1910), with b typically about -0.05 to -0.12. Because the exponent is so small, a modest cut in stress multiplies life many times. Near an elliptical hole of half-length a and tip radius rho, the peak stress is about sigma·(1 + 2·sqrt(a/rho)) (Inglis, 1913): the sharper the corner, the bigger the multiplier.

story.title: The airliner that broke apart in clear skies
story.hook: On 10 January 1954 BOAC Flight 781, a de Havilland Comet, the world's first jet airliner, climbed away from Rome and broke up over the sea near Elba, killing all 35 aboard. Comets were checked and returned to service. Then on 8 April 1954 a second Comet, G-ALYY, flying Rome to Cairo for South African Airways, broke up near Naples, and all 21 aboard died. The weather had been calm. At the Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, investigators under Sir Arnold Hall put a whole Comet, G-ALYU, in a huge water tank and pumped its cabin up and down to simulate flight after flight. After about 3,060 pressure cycles (roughly 1,230 real flights plus about 1,830 in the tank), the fuselage tore open from the corner of a squarish escape-hatch cut-out.
story.puzzle: The cabin had passed a strength test at about twice its working pressure. How could it fail at ordinary pressure, and why did it fail at a corner?
story.payoff: Metal fatigue. Each pressurization cycle, though far below breaking strength, grew microscopic cracks where stress was concentrated: at the corners of cut-outs, where a tight corner multiplies local stress several times. A one-time strength test says nothing about thousands of cycles, and investigators concluded that earlier fatigue tests on a section that had already been proof-loaded flattered its life. Fatigue is why airliners now have rounded openings, full-scale fatigue tests and fixed inspection intervals.
sources: Report of the Court of Inquiry into the accidents to Comet G-ALYP on 10 January 1954 and Comet G-ALYY on 8 April 1954 (Cohen inquiry, HMSO, 1955)
P. A. Withey, 'Fatigue failure of the de Havilland Comet I', Engineering Failure Analysis 4(2), 1997
This Day in Aviation, '8 April 1954' (G-ALYY)

days.application: Fatigue in the car, at the engineering link of the chain. Springs, control arms and wheels see a new load cycle at every pothole and corner over hundreds of thousands of kilometres, so makers test them on rigs for millions of cycles and size them on the S-N curve, not on one-time strength. The same lesson explains why airliner windows are rounded ovals: no sharp corner is left to concentrate stress.

builds_on.why: Stress, tension and member shape: fatigue is what repeated stress does over time, and stress concentration is a local version of that day's stress formula.
Distributions and tails: fatigue lives scatter widely from one test piece to the next, and a factor of safety is a guard against the weak tail of that distribution.

across.link: Stress fractures (the 'march fractures' the Prussian military surgeon Breithaupt described in soldiers in 1855) are fatigue failures of bone under repeated loading. The analogy breaks because living bone repairs micro-damage between loads if it is given rest, and metal cannot.

days.apply_question: On 28 April 1988 Aloha Airlines Flight 243, a 19-year-old Boeing 737, lost a large section of its upper fuselage at 24,000 feet. It had flown nearly 90,000 short island-hopping flights. Flight attendant Clarabelle Lansing was killed, and the crew, including First Officer Madeline Tompkins, landed on Maui. Why does the number of flights, rather than the hours flown, govern a pressurized fuselage's fatigue life?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the fatigue mechanism, and the inquiry's conclusion for the Elba crash. The Naples cause was never proven because little wreckage was recovered; the inquiry said the Elba explanation 'appears to be applicable'. Popular accounts blaming 'square passenger windows' oversimplify: the cracks began at the corners of cut-outs (the roof ADF window on G-ALYP and an escape-hatch window in the tank test). Sources give about 3,057 to 3,060 cycles for the tank failure.

resource.creator: The Efficient Engineer (YouTube)
resource.why: Animates how fatigue cracks start and grow, and how S-N curves and endurance limits are read. These are the tools behind the factor of safety in the lesson.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: London's Millennium Bridge Lasted Two Days. The Crowd's Own Footsteps Shook It.
days.concept: Every structure has natural frequencies, and pushing it repeatedly near one of them makes small pushes add up to large motion (resonance), which only damping, the removal of energy each cycle, can limit.
days.focus: Resonance as the result of pushing in time with a structure's natural rhythm, the amplification factor and why it depends on damping, and the engineer's two fixes: change the natural frequency or add damping (including tuned mass dampers). The Millennium Bridge adds the twist of feedback: the people pushing respond to the motion.
days.model_or_equation: Driven, damped oscillator: m·x'' + c·x' + k·x = F0·cos(omega·t). The natural frequency is omega0 = sqrt(k/m). The steady amplitude is X = (F0/k) / sqrt((1 - r^2)^2 + (2·zeta·r)^2), where r = omega/omega0 is the frequency ratio and zeta = c/(2·sqrt(k·m)) is the damping ratio. At resonance (r = 1) the amplification is 1/(2·zeta), so a lightly damped structure with zeta = 0.01 magnifies a steady push about 50-fold.

story.title: The bridge that made a crowd walk like sailors
story.hook: On Saturday 10 June 2000, London's Millennium Bridge opened to the public. It is a slender steel footbridge across the Thames from St Paul's to Tate Modern, designed by Arup with Foster and Partners and the sculptor Anthony Caro. Tens of thousands of people crossed that day. With the deck crowded, it began to sway from side to side, enough that walkers splayed their feet and grabbed the handrails. It was closed on 12 June. Nothing had broken, and the bridge met its strength calculations. Arup spent many months on crowd tests and research, and fitted a retrofit of dampers costing about £5 million. The bridge reopened in February 2002 (sources give 22 or 27 February) without the wobble.
story.puzzle: A crowd walking at random should push a bridge left and right about equally, so the pushes should cancel out. Why did these footsteps add up instead, and why did the sway begin only once the crowd passed a certain size?
story.payoff: Resonance plus feedback. Each walker pushes sideways at about half their step rate, roughly once a second, which was close to the deck's lateral natural frequencies. Once the deck moved, people changed their gait to keep their balance, and that fed energy into the sway in time with it. This is a reinforcing loop, and it switches on above a critical crowd size. The fix added damping (fluid-viscous dampers plus tuned mass dampers) so the bridge sheds energy faster than walkers can feed it in.
sources: Dallard et al., 'The London Millennium Footbridge', The Structural Engineer 79(22), 2001
Strogatz et al., 'Crowd synchrony on the Millennium Bridge', Nature 438 (2005)
Tampa Bay Times archive, 'Two years later Londoners can use Millennium Bridge' (23 Feb 2002)

days.application: Taipei 101's tuned mass damper. A 660-tonne steel sphere about 5.5 m across hangs from the 92nd floor inside floors 87 to 92. It is tuned to the tower's sway frequency, so in wind it swings out of step with the building and soaks up energy; the maker claims it cuts sway by up to 40%. Its largest recorded swing was about 1 m, in Typhoon Soudelor on 8 August 2015. Car makers use the same physics on a small scale: engine mounts and dampers are tuned so the engine's vibration does not excite the body's natural frequencies.

builds_on.why: Differential equations: the mass-spring-damper equation is a differential equation, and resonance is a feature of its solution.
Feedback loops: at the Millennium Bridge, sway changed how people walked and their walking increased the sway, a reinforcing loop with a threshold.

across.link: Daniel Kirkwood showed in 1866 that the asteroid belt has gaps where an asteroid's orbital period would be a simple fraction (3:1, 5:2, 2:1) of Jupiter's. Jupiter's repeated tugs at the same point in the orbit add up, resonantly, and clear those orbits. It is the same physics of a periodic push in step with a natural period, acting over millions of years instead of seconds.

days.apply_question: In the Mexico City earthquake of 19 September 1985, many buildings of roughly 6 to 15 storeys collapsed, while many lower and taller ones survived. The soft old lake-bed soil shook with a period of about 2 seconds, and a building's natural period is roughly 0.1 second per storey. Using resonance, explain the pattern.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the bridge swayed because pedestrians loaded it sideways near its natural frequencies, and added damping fixed it. Debated: the exact mechanism. Strogatz et al. (Nature, 2005) model it as walkers falling into step with the bridge. Macdonald (Proc. Royal Society A, 2009) and Belykh et al. (Science Advances, 2017) show that walkers balancing on a moving deck can feed energy into it without true phase-locking.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: Rudolf Diesel's Engine Had No Spark Plug. It Was Roughly Three Times as Efficient as the Steam Engines of Its Day.
days.concept: A piston engine gets more efficient the more it compresses its charge before burning it, and knock (the fuel-air mixture igniting by itself) caps how far a spark-ignition petrol engine can go, which a diesel escapes by compressing air alone and lighting the fuel with the heat of compression.
days.focus: The four-stroke cycle, and why compression ratio sets efficiency (the Otto-cycle result, a cousin of Carnot). How knock limits petrol engines, and what octane measures. Why diesels run at far higher compression. How turbocharging and direct injection let small modern engines manage the trade-off.
days.model_or_equation: Ideal Otto-cycle efficiency: eta = 1 - 1/r^(gamma - 1). Here r is the compression ratio and gamma is about 1.4 for air. At r = 8 the ideal efficiency is about 56%, at r = 12 about 63%, and at r = 18 about 69%. Real engines reach roughly half of these figures because of heat loss, friction and incomplete expansion. A diesel's cycle differs in detail, but it gains for the same reason: a higher compression ratio.

story.title: An engine that lit its fuel by squeezing it
story.hook: On 17 February 1897, in the machine laboratory of the Technische Hochschule in Munich, Professor Moritz Schröter ran the official acceptance test of Rudolf Diesel's new engine. It was a single cylinder, 250 mm bore and 400 mm stroke, built at the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, the forerunner of MAN. It had no spark plug: it squeezed air until it was hot enough to ignite fuel sprayed into it. Schröter measured a net efficiency of about 26 per cent, roughly three times what a typical steam engine of the day managed. On the night of 29 September 1913, Diesel boarded the steamer Dresden at Antwerp, bound for Harwich. In the morning his cabin was empty. About ten days later the crew of a Dutch boat found a badly decomposed body in the North Sea; they kept items from its pockets, which Diesel's son identified, and returned the body to the sea. How he died has never been settled.
story.puzzle: Why should squeezing the air harder make an engine so much more efficient? And if it does, why don't petrol engines, which use spark plugs, compress as hard as diesels?
story.payoff: An engine's ideal efficiency rises with its compression ratio, because the burnt gas then expands from a hotter, higher-pressure start (the Carnot logic of Day 54). A petrol engine compresses fuel and air together, so above a certain ratio the unburned mixture ignites by itself. That is knock. It held 1920s petrol engines to about 4-5:1, set off the hunt for anti-knock fuels, and still caps modern ones at roughly 10-14:1. A diesel compresses only air, at about 15-22:1, and injects fuel at the top of the stroke, so it cannot knock in the same way.
sources: DieselNet, 'Early History of the Diesel Engine' (dieselnet.com)
IEEE Spectrum, 'The Diesel Engine at 120'
Deutsche Biographie, entry 'Schröter, Moritz'
TIME, on Rudolf Diesel's disappearance (time.com/4049401)

days.application: Why the 1920s octane race mattered, and why modern petrol cars use small turbocharged engines (the engineering link of the car chain). Tetraethyl lead (Day 49) let petrol engines raise compression without knocking, which is why GM wanted it so badly. Today a turbocharger forces extra air into a small engine for power when needed, and direct injection cools the charge so the compression ratio can stay high without knock. Downsizing and turbocharging are a way of living with knock rather than escaping it.

builds_on.why: Heat engines and the Carnot limit: no engine turns all its heat into work, and expanding from a hotter start raises the ceiling. Compression ratio is how a piston engine climbs toward it.
The leaded-gasoline case: tetraethyl lead was an anti-knock additive, so knock is the engineering reason that burden-of-proof fight happened.

across.link: In June 2012 the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified diesel engine exhaust as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1). It is the price side of the diesel's trade-off: the hot, lean, high-compression combustion that makes it efficient also produces nitrogen oxides and soot.

days.apply_question: Most piston-engine aircraft in the US still burn leaded '100LL' avgas, decades after lead left car fuel. Using today's concept, why has removing lead been harder for high-power aircraft piston engines than it was for cars?
days.evidence_note: Settled thermodynamics. Diesel's death is unexplained; most accounts lean to suicide amid financial trouble, and murder theories (German agents, business rivals) are speculation without evidence. Steam-engine efficiencies in the 1890s ranged widely, from a few per cent to the low teens for the best large engines, so 'about three times' is a rough comparison. Compression ratios are typical ranges, not limits: some modern petrol engines run near 14:1.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: Engineers Made Steam-Engine Governors More Sensitive, and the Engines Began to 'Hunt'. In 1868 James Clerk Maxwell Worked Out Why.
days.concept: Feedback (closed-loop) control measures the gap between a goal and the current state and acts to close it, with proportional, integral and derivative action trading speed against accuracy and stability, and too much gain in a loop with lag makes it overshoot and oscillate.
days.focus: The control loop: setpoint, sensor, error, actuator. What P, I and D each do: proportional action responds to the error now, integral action removes the steady error proportional action leaves, and derivative action damps overshoot. Why lag plus high gain causes hunting. Watt's governor, Maxwell's analysis and the car's cruise control carry it.
days.model_or_equation: PID controller: u(t) = Kp·e(t) + Ki·integral of e(tau) dtau + Kd·de/dt. Here e = setpoint - measured value and u is the actuator command (e.g., throttle). Kp sets how hard to push against today's error. Ki accumulates past error until none is left, which removes droop. Kd responds to how fast the error is changing, which damps overshoot. With lag in the loop, raising Kp too far makes the system oscillate.

story.title: The governors that hunted
story.hook: In 1788 James Watt fitted his rotative steam engines with a centrifugal 'flyball' governor adapted from windmill practice. Two iron balls on hinged arms spun with the engine. If it sped up, the balls flew outward and a linkage closed the steam valve; if it slowed, they dropped and opened it. Over the following decades, engineers built more sensitive governors with less friction to hold speed more tightly, and many engines began to 'hunt'. Instead of settling, they surged faster and slower in a steady rhythm. In 1868 James Clerk Maxwell published 'On Governors' in the Proceedings of the Royal Society. It wrote down the equations of engine and governor together, one of the first mathematical analyses of feedback.
story.puzzle: How could making a regulator more sensitive, so that it noticed errors sooner, make an engine run worse?
story.payoff: A feedback loop with inertia and lag applies its correction late. With high gain, the late correction overshoots, so the loop oscillates or becomes unstable. Maxwell showed that stability depends on the roots of the system's characteristic equation: every one must make disturbances die away. He also distinguished a 'moderator', which acts in proportion to the error and leaves a steady error when the load changes, from a true 'governor', which adds what we now call integral action and removes that error.
sources: J. C. Maxwell, 'On Governors', Proceedings of the Royal Society of London 16 (1868): 270-283
Otto Mayr, The Origins of Feedback Control (MIT Press, 1970)

days.application: Cruise control, at the engineering link of the car chain. It was invented by Ralph Teetor, a mechanical engineer blind since childhood who ran the Perfect Circle piston-ring company. Family accounts say the idea came from riding with a driver who sped up and slowed down as he talked. Chrysler sold it as 'Auto-Pilot' on its 1958 Imperial. A modern cruise control is essentially a PI controller on the throttle. Proportional action answers the speed error, and integral action removes the droop that would otherwise leave the car a few mph slow on a long climb.

builds_on.why: The integral as accumulation: integral action adds up past error until none is left, which is exactly Maxwell's difference between a moderator and a governor.
Delays, overshoot and oscillation: hunting governors are a balancing loop with lag, the textbook case of that day's lesson.

across.link: In September 2016 the FDA approved the first 'hybrid closed-loop' insulin system, Medtronic's MiniMed 670G. It reads a glucose sensor and adjusts insulin automatically, an engineered feedback loop standing in for the pancreas, whose insulin and glucagon normally hold blood glucose near a setpoint. Glucose control has its own lag: insulin takes time to act, so the same overshoot problem arises.

days.apply_question: A central bank raises interest rates in response to today's inflation, but its moves take a year or more to affect prices (Milton Friedman's 'long and variable lags'). Using today's concept, why can reacting hard to current inflation alone make inflation swing more, not less?

resource.creator: Brian Douglas, MATLAB Tech Talks (MathWorks), 2018
resource.why: A control engineer explains with a simple worked system what proportional, integral and derivative action each do, including why integral action removes steady error. It is the mechanism behind cruise control and Maxwell's governors.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: The 737 MAX Had Two Angle-of-Attack Sensors. Its New Software Listened to One.
days.concept: Parts in series multiply their chances of failure and redundant parts in parallel cut them, but only when their failures are independent and the design actually uses the spare, so a common-mode failure or a single unchecked input defeats redundancy.
days.focus: The arithmetic of reliability. Series systems fail if any part fails, parallel systems fail only if all fail, and common-cause failures dominate real redundant systems. Single points of failure can hide in software and in human assumptions as well as hardware. The 737 MAX shows each of these.
days.model_or_equation: Series: R_system = R1·R2·…·Rn, so ten parts each 99.9% reliable give about 99.0%. Parallel (any one is enough): P(all fail) = q1·q2·…·qn, so two independent sensors that each fail once in 10,000 flights fail together about once in 100 million. If a fraction beta of failures share a common cause (a bird strike, icing, one software path), then P(fail) is about beta·q + q^2, and the beta term dominates.

story.title: One sensor, two airliners
story.hook: On 29 October 2018, about 13 minutes after take-off from Jakarta, Lion Air Flight 610 plunged into the Java Sea, killing all 189 aboard. The plane was a Boeing 737 MAX 8 delivered to Lion Air only that August. On 10 March 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed about six minutes after leaving Addis Ababa, killing all 157 aboard. Among them was Samya Stumo, 24; her mother, Nadia Milleron, became one of the families' leading campaigners. In both crashes a new flight-control routine, MCAS, repeatedly pushed the nose down because a single angle-of-attack sensor wrongly reported that the wing was near a stall. Every MAX carried two such sensors, one on each side of the nose.
story.puzzle: The airplane carried two sensors. Why could one bad reading bring it down, and why did it happen twice?
story.payoff: Redundancy helps only if the design uses it. MCAS took its input from one sensor at a time, with no cross-check, so that sensor was a single point of failure in series with the airplane's safety. The design also relied on pilots as the backup layer, assuming they would recognize and counter MCAS within seconds. Amid simultaneous stall warnings and alerts, that layer failed in a way correlated with the very fault it was meant to catch. Boeing's fix makes MCAS compare both sensors, activate only once per event, and limits how far it can move the tail.
sources: KNKT (Indonesia), Final Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, Lion Air PK-LQP (October 2019)
Ethiopian Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau, Final Report on ET-AVJ (December 2022)
US House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, Final Committee Report on the Boeing 737 MAX (September 2020)

days.application: Split dual-circuit brakes, at the engineering link of the car chain. Since the late 1960s, US federal standards have required cars to have two separate hydraulic brake circuits (front/rear or diagonal). A single burst line or leaking seal then leaves half the brakes working, where an older single-circuit system lost them all. The design also shows the limit: both circuits share one pedal and one brake-fluid reservoir, so some common-mode failures remain.

builds_on.why: Probability: series and parallel reliability is multiplying probabilities of independent events, and common-mode failure is what happens when independence fails.
Lift and drag: lift rises with angle of attack until the wing stalls, which is what the MAX's sensors measured and what MCAS was designed to prevent.

across.link: Ireland's potato crop before 1845 relied heavily on one clonally propagated variety, the Lumper, so the blight Phytophthora infestans could strike almost every field at once. Genetic uniformity acted as a common-mode failure, and about a million people died in the famine that followed. The analogy breaks because crop diversity also trades away yield, and because the famine's death toll owed much to policy, not to the blight alone.

days.apply_question: On 1 June 2009 Air France Flight 447, an Airbus A330, crashed into the Atlantic, killing 228. Ice crystals probably blocked its airspeed probes, three separate probes of the same model sitting in the same icy air, within moments of each other. Using today's concept, why did triple redundancy fail to protect the airspeed reading?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the death tolls, MCAS's single-sensor input, and MCAS's role in both crashes (KNKT 2019; Ethiopian final report 2022; US House committee 2020). Debated: how much weight to give design, FAA certification and its delegation to Boeing, and pilot training and airline maintenance. The NTSB publicly disputed parts of Ethiopia's final report as underplaying crew performance. The House committee report emphasized Boeing's design and disclosure failures and weak FAA oversight. Value judgment: how much a design may rely on pilots as its last safety layer.

resource.creator: US House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure (majority staff), September 2020
resource.length: executive summary, about 20 minutes (full report about 240 pages)
resource.why: The congressional investigation's own account of how MCAS came to depend on one sensor, how its role was kept out of pilot training, and how certification missed it. It is a primary source for a single-point-of-failure decision.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: At Three Mile Island, a Light Said the Valve Had Been Told to Close. It Was Stuck Open.
days.concept: In systems that are both interactively complex and tightly coupled, several small failures can combine in ways nobody foresaw, so some accidents are 'normal' (Perrow, 1984), while high-reliability researchers argue that culture and structure can keep such systems safe, and the two schools still disagree.
days.focus: Perrow's two dimensions: interactive complexity (hidden, unexpected interactions) and coupling (how much slack exists). Why adding safety devices can add new ways to fail. The high-reliability answer from aircraft-carrier and air-traffic studies. What the debate means for choosing which technologies to run.
days.model_or_equation: Perrow's interaction/coupling chart, a 2x2 grid. Linear interactions with loose coupling: most assembly-line manufacturing. Linear with tight coupling: dams and rail transport. Complex with loose coupling: universities and R&D firms. Complex with tight coupling: nuclear power plants, chemical plants, space missions and nuclear weapons. Perrow argued that only the last quadrant breeds 'system accidents' that operator vigilance cannot reliably prevent.

story.title: A light that told the truth about the wrong thing
story.hook: Just after 4 a.m. on 28 March 1979, pumps feeding water to the steam generators of Three Mile Island Unit 2, near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, shut down. Pressure in the reactor rose, and a pilot-operated relief valve opened as designed. Then it stuck open, unnoticed, and vented cooling water. On the control panel a light went out, telling the operators the valve had been sent the signal to close; there was no direct indication of whether it had actually closed. Other instruments suggested the system was filling with water, so the operators cut back the emergency cooling. Over the next hours roughly half the reactor core melted. No one was killed and the radiation released was small, but it remains the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power.
story.puzzle: No single failure was exotic: a pump trip, a stuck valve, an ambiguous light and a reasonable-seeming choice by the operators. Why did ordinary small failures combine into a meltdown, and could better people or better rules have stopped it?
story.payoff: Charles Perrow's normal accident theory. Where interactions are complex and hidden and coupling is tight, with little slack and fast propagation, small failures will sooner or later combine in ways no one anticipated. Such accidents are 'normal', inherent in the design, and safety devices like the valve indicator can add new failure paths. High-reliability theorists reply that some organizations (carrier flight decks, air-traffic control) run complex, tightly coupled operations with remarkably few accidents, thanks to redundancy, training and deference to expertise.
sources: Report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island (Kemeny Commission), October 1979
US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, 'Backgrounder on the Three Mile Island Accident'
Charles Perrow, Normal Accidents (1984), chapter 1

days.application: US Navy aircraft-carrier flight decks, the classic high-reliability case. Gene Rochlin, Todd La Porte and Karlene Roberts studied carrier operations ('The Self-Designing High-Reliability Organization', Naval War College Review, 1987). They found that a crew of young sailors launching and recovering jets on a pitching deck kept accidents rare. Practices included constant on-the-job training, a formal chain of command that gives way during high-tempo operations to whoever holds the relevant expertise, and the authority of even junior crew to stop an operation. The deck is complex and tightly coupled, yet runs safely, which is the core of the challenge to Perrow.

builds_on.why: Reliability and redundancy: Perrow's point is that redundancy and safety devices add complexity. TMI's valve indicator was a safety feature that misled.
Unintended consequences: safety fixes that create new failure paths are 'fixes that fail' at the scale of whole technologies.

across.link: Diane Vaughan's The Challenger Launch Decision (1996) traced the 1986 shuttle loss to the 'normalization of deviance': an organization gradually redefining warning signs as acceptable. It is an organizational counterpart to Perrow's technical account, explaining how culture can produce the small failures that complexity then combines.

days.apply_question: Apollo 13's oxygen tank exploded at the end of a chain of small events. The tank was jolted in handling in 1968. Its heater's thermostatic switches were rated for 28 volts, but ground equipment used 65 volts. A long heater run while emptying the tank before launch damaged wire insulation, which sparked when the crew later stirred the tank. Using Perrow's two dimensions, was this a 'normal accident' or a preventable chain of errors?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the TMI sequence (Kemeny Commission, 1979). Debated: normal accident theory versus high-reliability theory. Perrow argued some technologies should be abandoned or radically redesigned. La Porte, Roberts and Rochlin, and later Weick and Sutcliffe, argued that organizational culture can achieve high reliability. Scott Sagan's The Limits of Safety (1993), which tested both theories on US nuclear-weapons safety, leaned toward Perrow. Value judgment: which high-risk technologies a society should accept, and on whose terms.

resource.title: Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies, chapter 1 ('Normal Accident at Three Mile Island')
resource.creator: Charles Perrow (Basic Books, 1984; updated edition Princeton University Press, 1999)
resource.why: Perrow's own minute-by-minute reading of TMI, which he uses to introduce interactive complexity and tight coupling. It is the founding text of the theory Logan is weighing against high-reliability research.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: NASA Launched Hubble With a Mirror Polished Almost Perfectly — to the Wrong Shape.
days.concept: Complex projects fail most often at the interfaces between parts and teams, so systems engineering manages requirements, controls interfaces and insists on independent verification that the whole system does what it is for.
days.focus: Requirements and the difference between verification ('built it right') and validation ('built the right thing'). Interface control between teams and suppliers. The V-model. Why the instrument that guides the work must not be the only one that checks it. Hubble and the A380 show two kinds of interface failure.
days.model_or_equation: The V-model. Down the left side, the mission need is broken into system requirements, then subsystem requirements, then component designs. At the bottom, the parts are built. Up the right side, each level is verified against its own requirements: components, then integrated subsystems, then the whole system, validated against the original need. Every horizontal pair is an interface where an assumption can go unchecked.

story.title: A nearly perfect mirror, ground to the wrong shape
story.hook: The Hubble Space Telescope went into orbit aboard Space Shuttle Discovery, launched on 24 April 1990. Within weeks its first images came back blurred: starlight that should have focused to a sharp point spread into a halo. The 2.4-metre primary mirror, made by Perkin-Elmer, was among the smoothest ever polished. Near its edge it was about 2.2 microns too flat, roughly one-fiftieth the thickness of a sheet of paper. The instrument used to test its shape during polishing, a 'reflective null corrector', had one lens about 1.3 mm out of position. Before launch, checks with other instruments had shown a discrepancy, and they were set aside in favour of the null corrector. In December 1993 astronauts on Endeavour fitted COSTAR, a set of corrective mirrors, and a new camera with its own correction built in.
story.puzzle: How did a team able to polish a mirror smooth to about ten billionths of a metre launch it with a shape error some two hundred times larger, one its own tests had hinted at?
story.payoff: Systems engineering says the checking must be independent of the making. The same flawed instrument both guided the polishing and certified the result, so the error was a common-mode failure of verification. The contradicting tests were never reconciled, and no end-to-end optical test of the assembled telescope was run before launch, partly to save cost and time. Systems engineering manages requirements, interfaces and independent verification so that one team's assumption cannot silently become everyone's.
sources: NASA, The Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report (Lew Allen, chair), November 1990
NASA, STS-61 first Hubble servicing mission (2-13 December 1993)

days.application: Airbus A380 wiring, 2006. Airbus announced repeated delays to A380 deliveries, eventually about two years, because wiring harnesses designed at its German sites would not fit airframes assembled in Toulouse. Hamburg used an older version of the CATIA design software (V4) while Toulouse used V5, and design changes did not carry cleanly across that interface. Each A380 carries roughly 500 km of wiring. The delays cost Airbus billions of euros, and its chief executive, Gustav Humbert, resigned in July 2006.

builds_on.why: Common-mode failure: using one instrument both to make the mirror and to check it is the verification version of two sensors that share a single failure.
Replication: independent re-checking is the scientist's defence against a lab's systematic error, and the engineer's independent verification plays the same role.

across.link: Ariane 5's first flight (4 June 1996) broke up about 40 seconds after lift-off. It had reused inertial-reference software from Ariane 4, and converting a 64-bit horizontal-velocity value to a 16-bit integer overflowed under Ariane 5's faster trajectory. The inquiry board (chaired by Jacques-Louis Lions) found the old software's requirements had never been checked against the new rocket: an interface failure between generations.

days.apply_question: In 2003, engineers building a road bridge over the Rhine between Laufenburg in Germany and Laufenburg in Switzerland knew that the two countries measure heights from different sea-level references, about 27 cm apart. The correction was applied in the wrong direction, so the two halves were heading for a mismatch of about 54 cm until the error was caught during construction. Which systems-engineering practice from today's lesson exists to catch exactly this kind of error before anything is built?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Allen report's finding that the null corrector's lens was mis-spaced, and the COSTAR fix. The A380 software-version mismatch was widely reported from Airbus statements in 2006. Figures for the delay's total cost vary with the accounting; give them as 'billions of euros'. The Hubble mirror's polishing accuracy is commonly given as about 10 nanometres; treat the 'two hundred times' comparison as approximate.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: Jefferson Assembled Interchangeable Gun Locks in Paris in 1785. America Needed About Forty More Years to Make Them for Real.
days.concept: Mass production depends on making every part within specified tolerances and checking it against gauges so that any part fits any machine, and achieving that takes a whole system of measurement, tooling and inspection, not a one-off demonstration.
days.focus: What interchangeability really requires: tolerances, go/no-go gauges, jigs and fixtures that put the skill into the tooling, inspection, and a patient customer to pay for it all. Then how tolerances add up in an assembly. The contrast between demonstrations (Blanc, Whitney) and the system built at the US armories carries the lesson.
days.model_or_equation: Tolerance stack-up. If n parts in a chain each vary by up to ±t_i, the worst case for the assembly is ±(t_1 + t_2 + … + t_n). If the variations are independent and centred, a statistical (root-sum-square) estimate is ±sqrt(t_1^2 + … + t_n^2). For five parts each ±0.1 mm, the worst case is ±0.5 mm and the RSS estimate about ±0.22 mm. That gap is why mass production relies on statistics as well as gauges.

story.title: Gun locks assembled from a heap of parts
story.hook: In 1785 Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in Paris, visited the workshop of the gunsmith Honoré Blanc, who was making musket locks so alike that their parts could be swapped. On 30 August Jefferson wrote to John Jay that he had put locks together himself from parts picked at random, and they fitted. In January 1801 Eli Whitney, already late on a federal contract for 10,000 muskets, gave a celebrated demonstration in Washington before President John Adams and Vice-President Jefferson, assembling locks apparently from mixed parts. Historians since Robert Woodbury (1960) have argued that the demonstration used parts prepared in advance, and examinations of surviving Whitney muskets found hand-fitted parts that were not interchangeable. In France, Blanc's methods were abandoned. Truly interchangeable firearms came only in the 1820s, at John Hall's rifle works in the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia.
story.puzzle: Two men had shown interchangeable parts by 1801. Why did it take a quarter-century of work in government armories to make them real, and why did France, which had them first, give them up?
story.payoff: Interchangeability is a system, not a trick. Every part must be made within tolerances and checked against gauges, using fixtures and machine tools that do the measuring. A patient customer must pay while the method costs more than craft work. Hall built that system with many gauges and specialized machines, backed by the War Department. Blanc's system lapsed when the French state stopped sustaining it; the historian Ken Alder argues the reasons were political as much as technical.
sources: Jefferson to John Jay, 30 August 1785 (Founders Online, National Archives)
Robert S. Woodbury, 'The Legend of Eli Whitney and Interchangeable Parts', Technology and Culture 1(3), 1960
Merritt Roe Smith, Harpers Ferry Armory and the New Technology (Cornell University Press, 1977)
Ken Alder, 'Innovation and Amnesia: Engineering Rationality and the Fate of Interchangeable Parts Manufacturing in France', Technology and Culture 38(2), 1997

days.application: From Cadillac's 1908 test to today's global supply chain (the production link of the car chain). In early 1908 at Brooklands, England, the Royal Automobile Club had three single-cylinder Cadillacs taken apart, their parts mixed (some swapped for parts from stock), reassembled, and driven 500 miles. Cadillac won the Dewar Trophy and adopted the slogan 'Standard of the World'. Today a car's thousands of parts come from suppliers on several continents. Each is specified with geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (ASME Y14.5 or ISO's equivalent), so a bracket made in one country fits a bolt made in another.

builds_on.why: Distributions: part dimensions scatter around their target, and when independent variations combine, their variances add. That is the root-sum-square rule for stack-up.
Innovation as a system, not a pipeline: interchangeability came from decades of accumulated practice, state funding and tool-building, not from one inventor's idea.

across.link: After British commissioners toured American armories and factories in 1853-54 and reported on what they called the 'American system of manufactures', Britain re-equipped its Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield with American-built machine tools in the mid-1850s. It is a checkable case of a production method crossing the Atlantic in the opposite direction from the usual story of the Industrial Revolution.

days.apply_question: An IKEA bookcase is assembled at home from panels whose holes were drilled by machine, often in different factories. Using tolerance stack-up, explain why the last cam bolt is so often the one that won't line up, and what the designer can do about it.
days.evidence_note: Debated: the Whitney story. Older accounts made him the father of interchangeable parts. Historians since Woodbury (1960) argue his 1801 demonstration was prepared or staged, and later work (Smith 1977; Hounshell 1984) credits the real achievement to the federal armories (Hall at Harpers Ferry, then Springfield) and to French precedents (Gribeauval's artillery system, Blanc). Why France abandoned the method is interpreted differently; Alder (1997) stresses politics.

resource.creator: David A. Hounshell (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1984)
resource.length: first part of chapter 1, about 30 minutes
resource.why: The standard history of how 'armory practice' (gauges, fixtures, special machines) actually produced interchangeable parts, and how that practice later fed Ford. It is the evidence behind the lesson's 'system, not a demonstration' claim.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: The First Liberty Ship Took About Eight Months. In 1942 One Went From Keel to Launch in Four and a Half Days.
days.concept: Unit costs tend to fall by a roughly fixed percentage each time cumulative production doubles (Wright, 1936), a straight line on log-log axes that is an empirical regularity of learning, not a law, and can stall or run backwards.
days.focus: Wright's law: the equation, what the learning rate means, and why cumulative output matters rather than time. What drives the curve (practice, tooling, redesign, scale) and what breaks it (bespoke designs, rising requirements, forgetting). Liberty ships, French nuclear construction, batteries and solar show steep, flat and reversed curves.
days.model_or_equation: C(n) = C1·n^(-b), where C(n) is the cost (or labour hours) of the n-th unit and C1 is the cost of the first. The progress ratio p = 2^(-b) is the cost multiplier per doubling, and the learning rate is 1 - p. An '80% curve' (p = 0.8, b ≈ 0.32) means each doubling cuts unit cost by 20%. The 1,000th unit (about ten doublings) then costs about 11% of the first. Taking logs gives log C = log C1 - b·log n, a straight line.

story.title: A ship assembled in less than a working week
story.hook: On 27 September 1941, 'Liberty Fleet Day', the SS Patrick Henry was launched at Baltimore. It was the first of a standard emergency cargo ship designed to be built quickly by workers who had never built ships, and it took about eight months from keel to delivery. US yards would build 2,710 Liberty ships by 1945. On 8 November 1942, at Henry J. Kaiser's Richmond Shipyard No. 2 on San Francisco Bay, workers laid the keel of the SS Robert E. Peary. Four days and about fifteen and a half hours later it was launched. It was a publicity stunt using sections pre-assembled in advance, but only a yard that had already built many hulls could have managed it. By 1943 the average Liberty ship was being built in well under two months.
story.puzzle: The ship's design barely changed, and the yards were not run by geniuses. Why did the same job get several times faster as the count went up, and is there a rule for how fast?
story.payoff: The learning curve (Wright's law). Unit labour and cost fall by a roughly constant fraction each time cumulative output doubles, as workers, managers and tooling learn. T. P. Wright found about 20% per doubling for 1930s aircraft, and Liberty-ship labour fell along a similar curve (Searle 1945; Rapping 1965). The Peary also shows that the curve has ingredients beyond practice: prefabrication, re-sequenced work and capital investment.
sources: T. P. Wright, 'Factors Affecting the Cost of Airplanes', Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences 3 (1936)
Frederic C. Lane, Ships for Victory: A History of Shipbuilding under the U.S. Maritime Commission in World War II (1951)
Leonard Rapping, 'Learning and World War II Production Functions', Review of Economics and Statistics 47 (1965)

days.application: Curves that fall, and one that rose. Arnulf Grubler found that the real cost per kilowatt of building France's 58-reactor fleet (the Messmer plan, Day 79) rose over the build-out ('negative learning by doing', Energy Policy, 2010), as reactors grew larger and more complex and safety requirements tightened. Lithium-ion battery packs, by contrast, fell from over $1,000 per kWh around 2010 to about $115 in 2024 (BloombergNEF; Day 73), and solar modules have fallen about 20% per doubling (Swanson's law; Day 77). The pattern: small, standardized, mass-produced units learn fast, while large, bespoke, site-built projects often do not.

builds_on.why: Power laws: a learning curve is a power law in cumulative output, which is why it is a straight line on log-log axes.
Nuclear fission reactors: France's standardized Messmer-plan fleet is the test case where costs rose instead of falling.

across.link: Newell and Rosenbloom's 'power law of practice' (1981) finds that the time an individual takes to do a task falls as a power of the number of practice trials, the same mathematical form as Wright's law. The analogy has a known weak point: Heathcote, Brown and Mewhort (2000) showed that individual learners are often better fit by exponential curves, and the power law can be an artifact of averaging, a caution that applies to industry curves too.

days.apply_question: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope cost about $10 billion and was built once. SpaceX has built thousands of Starlink satellites. Using the learning curve, explain why the cost per unit of these two kinds of space hardware has followed such different paths.
days.evidence_note: Settled: unit costs have fallen with cumulative output across many technologies. Debated: what drives the fall. Nemet (2006) found learning-by-doing explains only part of solar PV's cost decline, with scale and R&D explaining much of the rest. Thompson (2001) argued capital investment explains much of Liberty-ship productivity. Argote, Beckman and Epple (1990) found knowledge depreciated ('forgetting') in Liberty-ship yards. On nuclear, Berthélemy and Escobar Rangel (2015) found cost reductions within standardized reactor series, qualifying Grubler's picture of negative learning. Forecasting by extending the curve assumes it continues, which is a judgment, not a law.

resource.title: Why did renewables become so cheap so fast?
resource.creator: Max Roser, Our World in Data (2020)
resource.why: Plots solar, wind and battery prices against cumulative capacity on log-log axes, contrasts them with fossil and nuclear power, and explains learning curves in plain language. It is the lesson's equation in real data.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: GM's Worst Plant Reopened With Mostly the Same Workers. Within Two Years It Was Among Its Best.
days.concept: Lean production raises quality and productivity by treating every defect, delay and pile of inventory as waste that hides problems, stopping work at the first defect, pulling parts just in time and improving continuously, on statistical quality control's insight that most defects come from the system rather than the worker.
days.focus: Shewhart's and Deming's distinction between common-cause and special-cause variation, and the control chart. Toyota's pillars: jidoka (stop the line at a defect), just-in-time pull, and kaizen. NUMMI as the natural experiment of 'same workers, different system', and just-in-time's fragility when shocks hit.
days.model_or_equation: Shewhart control chart (first proposed at Western Electric in 1924). Plot a process measurement over time with a centre line and control limits at about ±3 standard deviations. A point outside the limits, or a non-random pattern, signals a special cause to find and remove. Variation inside the limits is common cause, built into the system, and only changing the system (methods, machines, materials, training) reduces it. Deming estimated that most quality problems, by one statement 94%, belong to the system rather than to individual workers.

story.title: Same workers, different system
story.hook: By the early 1980s General Motors' assembly plant in Fremont, California, was notorious for poor quality, heavy absenteeism (around 20 per cent on some days, by Paul Adler's account) and a long backlog of union grievances. GM closed it in 1982. In December 1984 it reopened as New United Motor Manufacturing, Inc. (NUMMI), a joint venture in which Toyota ran production and GM got a close look at Toyota's methods. Most of the hourly workers rehired had worked at GM-Fremont, and they were represented by the same union, the UAW. Toyota sent many of them to its Takaoka plant in Japan to learn the system. Within about two years, Paul Adler reported in the Harvard Business Review (1993), NUMMI's productivity and quality were close to Toyota's Japanese plants and better than any other GM plant.
story.puzzle: If most of the workers were the same people, what changed? And why couldn't GM simply copy it in its other plants?
story.payoff: Lean production. Standardized work is designed by the teams themselves. Any worker can stop the line at the first defect (jidoka, the andon cord), so problems are fixed at their source. Just-in-time flow exposes problems instead of burying them in inventory, and kaizen keeps improving the process. All of it rests on Shewhart's and Deming's statistical quality control. The gains came from the system and how it was managed, not from different people. Copying it meant changing management, which is harder than copying tools; GM struggled to spread it.
sources: Paul S. Adler, 'Time-and-Motion Regained', Harvard Business Review, January-February 1993
John Shook, 'How to Change a Culture: Lessons From NUMMI', MIT Sloan Management Review, Winter 2010
This American Life, episode 403, 'NUMMI' (26 March 2010)

days.application: Just-in-time's fragility, at the production link of the car chain. The Tōhoku earthquake of 11 March 2011 damaged Renesas Electronics' Naka factory, a major source of the world's automotive microcontrollers. Car plants in Japan and abroad cut output for lack of chips until Naka restarted about three months later. Toyota afterwards mapped its supply chain several tiers deep and, by widely reported accounts, asked suppliers to hold buffer stocks of critical chips. Those buffers reportedly helped it ride out the 2021 chip shortage better than many rivals (Day 27). Lean cuts waste, but some buffers are insurance, not waste.

builds_on.why: Distributions: control limits are set from a process's normal spread, and telling common-cause from special-cause variation is reading a distribution.
Delays, overshoot and the bullwhip effect: inventory buffers dampen supply shocks, and removing them makes a supply chain fast but brittle.

across.link: Virginia Mason Medical Center in Seattle adopted the Toyota Production System in 2002 as the 'Virginia Mason Production System'. It included a 'patient safety alert' that lets any staff member stop a process that threatens a patient, a hospital version of the andon cord (Charles Kenney, Transforming Health Care, 2010).

days.apply_question: In February 2010, after recalls of millions of vehicles over sticking accelerator pedals and trapped floor mats, Toyota's president Akio Toyoda told the US Congress the company had grown faster than it could develop its people. Using lean principles, how could a system built to surface defects at once still let a defect reach millions of customers?
days.evidence_note: Settled: statistical process control and its basic logic. Debated: how much of NUMMI's success came from the production system, versus selective rehiring and the shock of the plant's closure. Also debated: whether lean intensifies work ('management by stress', Parker and Slaughter, 1988) or empowers workers (Adler, 1993). After 2011 and 2021 many firms moved from pure just-in-time toward 'just-in-case' buffers, and the right balance is contested.

resource.title: How to Change a Culture: Lessons From NUMMI
resource.creator: John Shook, MIT Sloan Management Review (Winter 2010)
resource.why: Written by the first American manager hired by Toyota in Japan, who helped train NUMMI's workforce. It argues that changing what people do (the andon cord, standardized work) changed the culture, not the reverse. It is an insider's view of the lesson's natural experiment.
