days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.topic: Standards as infrastructure: the shipping container
days.headline_hint: Malcom McLean Shipped 58 Boxes From Newark to Houston in 1956. The Box Was Easy. The Standard Took Twelve Years.
days.concept: A shared standard turns separate technologies into a network: when every box fits every ship, crane, truck and train, the savings multiply across the whole system, and whoever sets the standard shapes an industry for decades.
days.focus: Why a container on its own saved little and a standardized container saved nearly everything. Interoperability and network effects, the fight over dimensions and corner fittings, complementary assets (cranes, ports, chassis, contracts), and who won and lost as the box spread.

story.title: Fifty-eight boxes on an old tanker
story.hook: On 26 April 1956 the Ideal X, a converted Second World War tanker, sailed from Port Newark, New Jersey, for Houston. Bolted to a deck built over its tanks were 58 truck-trailer bodies. Its owner, Malcom McLean, was a North Carolina trucking magnate who had bought a shipping line so he could send trailers by sea without their wheels. Loading loose cargo then cost about $5.83 a ton; by the figures Marc Levinson reports in The Box, McLean's cost came to about 16 cents. Yet containers spread slowly for more than a decade. McLean's 35-foot boxes didn't match Matson's 24-foot boxes on the West Coast, or anyone else's. Ports, cranes, railways and dock unions were all built for loose 'break-bulk' cargo.
story.puzzle: If putting cargo in a box cut loading costs by more than 90 per cent, why did containers take until the late 1960s and 1970s to transform world trade?
story.payoff: A box pays only inside a network. Ships, cranes, trucks, railcars, ports and contracts must all fit the same box. Once US standards bodies and then the International Organization for Standardization agreed dimensions and corner fittings (ISO standards from 1968), any box fitted any ship, crane or chassis anywhere. The standard, not the box, turned separate technologies into one system and cut costs along the whole chain from factory to shop.
sources: Marc Levinson, The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger (Princeton University Press, 2006)
ISO 668, Series 1 freight containers: classification, dimensions and ratings

days.application: The global supply chain that the box made possible (Day 31). Today one ISO container can travel from a factory in southern China by truck, ship, train and truck to a warehouse in Ohio without being opened. The cost of moving goods fell so far that firms could split production across continents, and the largest ships now carry more than 20,000 twenty-foot boxes. Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller (Journal of International Economics, 2016) estimate that containerization drove a large share of trade growth among industrialized countries. The costs were real too: tens of thousands of dockworker jobs disappeared, and old waterfronts such as Manhattan's and Brooklyn's emptied as cargo moved to Port Newark-Elizabeth.

builds_on.why: Networks: a standard turns isolated links (ships, ports, railways) into one connected network, and its value grows with the number of nodes that adopt it.
Path dependence: like the US South's 1886 change of track gauge, the container shows a standard winning because of network effects, then locking in.

across.link: On 1 January 1983 the ARPANET switched every host to the TCP/IP protocols (the 'flag day'), so any network that spoke them could join one internet. A shared interface standard turned separate networks into one, as the ISO container did for transport. The analogy breaks because a packet can be copied for free, while a container is physical and must be shipped back, often empty, when trade is unbalanced.

days.apply_question: The European Union's common-charger directive (2022/2380) requires new mobile phones sold in the EU to use USB-C, from 28 December 2024. Using today's concept, what does a standard set by law gain over one chosen by the market, and what does it risk?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the large fall in cargo-handling costs. The 1956 cost figures come from Levinson's sources and should be given as 'about'. Debated: how much containerization, as opposed to tariff cuts and cheaper communication, caused the growth of trade (Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller, 2016, find a large effect). Value judgment: weighing gains to consumers and exporters against the loss of dockworkers' jobs and of waterfront communities.

resource.title: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger, chapter 'Setting the Standard'
resource.creator: Marc Levinson (Princeton University Press, 2006; 2nd ed. 2016)
resource.why: Levinson tells how the dimensions and corner fittings were fought over by McLean, Matson, US standards committees and ISO, and why the winner mattered. It is the network-standard argument in its real history.
resource.verified_how: NOT verified by web search this session (the shared search budget was exhausted at drafting and at verification). Book, author and publisher are from prior knowledge. The chapter title is from memory (believed to be chapter 7 of the 2006 edition; numbering may differ in the 2016 edition). Cite by chapter title, without a link.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: For Two Years, Army Drivers Pounded Trucks Around Illinois Test Loops. Doubling an Axle's Weight Did About Sixteen Times the Damage.
days.concept: Pavement damage rises roughly with the fourth power of axle load, so a few heavy axles, not the many light ones, wear roads out, an empirical rule from the AASHO Road Test that shapes truck weight limits and road taxes.
days.focus: How the AASHO Road Test measured wear, and the equivalent single-axle load (ESAL). Why damage grows so steeply with load: pavements fail by fatigue, and stress grows with load. What the rule implies for truck limits, heavier EVs, road funding and seasonal restrictions, and why the exponent is an approximation.
days.model_or_equation: Relative damage per axle pass is about (W / W_s)^4, where W is the axle load and W_s is the 18,000-lb standard single axle (1 ESAL). A 2,000-lb car axle gives (2/18)^4 ≈ 1/6,561 ESAL, so one 18,000-lb truck axle does the damage of about 6,500 car axles. A 30% heavier car axle does 1.3^4 ≈ 2.9 times the damage, which is still tiny.

story.title: Two years of driving in circles near Ottawa, Illinois
story.hook: From late 1958 to late 1960, soldiers of a US Army Transportation Corps unit drove loaded trucks around loops of specially built test pavement near Ottawa, Illinois (six loops were built; five carried test traffic), logging more than a million axle passes. The AASHO Road Test, run by the American Association of State Highway Officials and costing tens of millions of dollars, assigned each lane a fixed axle weight, from light trucks to heavy tractor-trailers. It measured how fast each section lost 'serviceability', a score that began with panels of drivers rating how good the ride felt. The results were meant to set how thick to build the new Interstate highways.
story.puzzle: Cars outnumber trucks many times over on most roads. Who actually wears a road out, and by how much?
story.payoff: Damage rises roughly with the fourth power of axle load: the 'fourth-power law' fitted to the AASHO data and expressed in equivalent 18,000-lb single-axle loads. Doubling an axle's load does about 16 times the damage, so one heavy truck axle does the damage of thousands of car axles. Pavements fail by fatigue under repeated stress, and fatigue life is very sensitive to the size of each load.
sources: Highway Research Board, The AASHO Road Test, Special Reports 61A-61G (1961-62)
US General Accounting Office, Excessive Truck Weight: An Expensive Burden We Can No Longer Support (CED-79-94, 1979)

days.application: Truck weight limits and heavier EVs, at the regulation and consequences links of the car chain. US Interstate trucks are limited to 80,000 lb gross, 20,000 lb per single axle and 34,000 lb per tandem pair, limits set with this physics in mind. A battery adds hundreds of kilograms, and an electric pickup can weigh 25-40% more than its petrol version. By the fourth power that multiplies its pavement wear by roughly 2.5 to 4, which is still trivial next to one loaded truck axle. Heavier EVs matter more for crash compatibility (Day 51), bridges and tyre wear than for pavement.

builds_on.why: Power laws: damage proportional to load to the fourth power is a power law, a straight line of slope 4 on log-log axes.
Fatigue: pavements crack under repeated loads far below their one-time strength, and fatigue's steep stress-life curve is why damage climbs so fast with axle load.

across.link: Oregon charges heavy trucks a weight-mile tax, a rate per mile that rises with declared weight, instead of a diesel fuel tax. It is a rare road-pricing scheme that tries to charge trucks in line with the damage the fourth-power law says they cause.

days.apply_question: Michigan and Minnesota impose spring 'frost laws' that cut the allowed axle loads on many roads, by roughly a quarter or more, while the ground thaws. Using the fourth-power law and how pavements fail, explain why such a cut protects roads so strongly, and why it is needed only in spring.
days.evidence_note: Settled: heavy axles do far more damage than light ones. Debated: the exponent. 'Fourth power' is an average from one site's soils, climate and 1950s pavement designs, and later studies find exponents from about 2 to well above 4, depending on pavement type and how it fails. Weather and age cause much deterioration regardless of traffic. Value judgment: how road costs should be split among trucks, cars and taxpayers (highway cost allocation).

resource.title: Excessive Truck Weight: An Expensive Burden We Can No Longer Support
resource.creator: US General Accounting Office (GAO), report CED-79-94, July 1979
resource.why: The federal auditors applied the AASHO results to the national truck fleet and argued that overweight trucks were destroying roads that their taxes did not pay for. It shows the fourth-power law becoming a policy argument.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.headline_hint: People Have Fallen 150 Feet and Lived. Hugh DeHaven Asked Why — and Started the Science of Crash Survival.
days.concept: Injuries happen when energy reaches the body faster than tissue can tolerate, so they can be prevented or reduced before, during and after a crash by acting on the person, the vehicle and the environment, the nine cells of William Haddon's matrix.
days.focus: Injury reframed as an engineering and public-health problem, not 'accident' or fate. Energy transfer and human tolerance, packaging the occupant, crumple zones and restraints, and Haddon's matrix as a map of where to intervene. Vision Zero carries the same logic into road design and policy.
key_concepts: Vision Zero and the safe-system approach
days.model_or_equation: Haddon matrix: the rows are the phases (pre-crash, crash, post-crash), and the columns are the factors (human, vehicle, physical environment, with a social environment added later). Examples: pre-crash x human = sober, rested drivers; crash x vehicle = crumple zones, belts and airbags; crash x environment = breakaway poles and median barriers; post-crash x environment = emergency response time. Behind the crash cells: average force F = m·Δv / Δt, so stretching the stopping time or distance cuts the force for the same change in speed.

story.title: The survivor who studied survivors
story.hook: In 1917 Hugh DeHaven, a young American training as a pilot with the Royal Flying Corps, survived a mid-air collision. He was badly hurt, partly, he concluded, by the buckle of his own safety belt and the hard structures around him, while the cockpit itself held together. Decades later he collected cases of people who had fallen 50 to 150 feet and survived, and in 1942 he published 'Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet' in War Medicine. The same year he began crash-injury research at Cornell University Medical College. In 1966-67 William Haddon Jr., a physician and epidemiologist who built on this work, became the first head of the new federal traffic-safety agency created after Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed.
story.puzzle: A fall from 150 feet ends at about 65 miles an hour. Why do some people survive it, when others die in far gentler crashes?
story.payoff: Injury is energy reaching the body faster than tissue can take it. What kills is not speed but how abruptly the speed is removed and how widely the force is spread. DeHaven's survivors landed on yielding surfaces (soft earth, car roofs, awnings) that lengthened their stopping distance and spread the load, which is impulse (Day 51) applied to bodies. Haddon turned this into a matrix of the phases before, during and after a crash, by person, vehicle and environment, with each cell a place to intervene.
sources: Hugh DeHaven, 'Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet', War Medicine 2 (1942); reprinted in Injury Prevention (2000)
William Haddon Jr., 'Advances in the epidemiology of injuries as a basis for public policy', Public Health Reports 95(5), 1980

days.application: Sweden's Vision Zero, at the regulation and consequences links of the car chain. Adopted by the Riksdag in October 1997, it holds that no one should be killed or seriously injured on the roads, and makes the designers of the road system responsible for keeping crash energies below human tolerance. In practice that has meant '2+1' roads divided by cable barriers, roundabouts in place of signalled crossroads, and speed limits set by what a body can survive (about 30 km/h where cars and pedestrians mix). Sweden's road-death rate per person is now roughly a fifth to a sixth of the US rate.

builds_on.why: Momentum and impulse: lengthening the stopping time lowers the force for the same change in momentum, the physics of crumple zones, airbags and DeHaven's survivors.
Newton's laws: John Paul Stapp's rocket-sled rides measured what deceleration a human body can survive, and Stapp then campaigned for seat belts.

across.link: The National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, signed on 9 September 1966 after the uproar over Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed (1965), created the federal agency Haddon first led and the power to set vehicle safety standards. It is the point where crash-injury science became law.

days.apply_question: In frontal crashes, belted women have had about 73% higher odds of serious injury than belted men in comparable crashes (Forman et al., Traffic Injury Prevention, 2019). Meanwhile, regulatory crash tests long relied on dummies modelled on an average man. In which cell of the Haddon matrix does this gap mainly sit, and what kind of fix does that point to?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the biomechanics of injury and the energy-transfer model. Debated: how much of Sweden's fall in road deaths Vision Zero caused, compared with declines in other rich countries. Also debated: risk compensation. Sam Peltzman (1975) argued drivers offset safety regulation by driving more riskily; most later evidence finds the offset is partial and the net safety gain real. Value judgment: Vision Zero's ethic that the system's designers, not only road users, bear responsibility, and that no death is an acceptable price of mobility.

resource.title: Advances in the epidemiology of injuries as a basis for public policy
resource.creator: William Haddon Jr., Public Health Reports 95(5), 1980
resource.why: Haddon's own statement of injury as energy transfer and of his phase-by-factor matrix, with his ten countermeasure strategies. It is the founding argument for treating crashes as preventable engineering and public-health problems.
resource.verified_how: NOT verified by web search this session (the shared search budget was exhausted at drafting and at verification). Author, title, journal and year are from prior knowledge; it is believed to be free in PubMed Central. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Engineering
days.topic: The engineer's duty to the public
days.headline_hint: A Small Change on a Shop Drawing Doubled the Load on One Connection. 114 People Died at the Hyatt Regency.
days.concept: Engineers owe a professional duty to hold public safety paramount, above clients, schedules and costs, made concrete by sealing their work, checking every change to it, and a licence that can be taken away.
days.focus: What makes engineering a profession. The paramountcy clause of engineering codes, the engineer of record and the seal, shop drawings and change control, licensure and its enforcement, and the duty to warn when others decide. The Hyatt Regency is a load-path lesson that became an ethics lesson.
key_concepts: engineer of record and the professional seal
days.model_or_equation: Load path at the fourth-floor connection. In the original design, continuous rods ran from the ceiling past the fourth-floor walkway to the second, and the nut under the fourth-floor beam carried only that walkway's load, P. In the built design, two rods were used: ceiling to fourth floor, then fourth floor to second. The second-floor walkway now hung from the fourth-floor beam, so the same nut carried P + P = 2P.

story.title: Two rods instead of one
story.hook: On the evening of Friday 17 July 1981, more than a thousand people were at a tea dance in the atrium of the year-old Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri. Some watched from walkways suspended across the space. At about 7:05 p.m. the fourth-floor walkway, which hung directly above the second-floor walkway, tore loose, and both fell onto the crowded floor. 114 people were killed and more than 200 injured, the deadliest structural collapse in US history until the World Trade Center in 2001. The original design hung both walkways from continuous steel rods running from the ceiling through the fourth-floor walkway to the second. During construction the steel fabricator proposed two shorter rods instead, and the change went through on shop drawings that carried the structural engineers' seal.
story.puzzle: The change looked like a harmless simplification: the same rods, the same walkways, the same weight. How could it double the load on one connection, and whose job was it to notice?
story.payoff: Follow the load path. With continuous rods, the nut under the fourth-floor beam carried only its own walkway. With split rods, the second-floor walkway hung from the fourth-floor beam, so that nut carried both walkways, double the load. The National Bureau of Standards found the connection was already short of the building code's requirement even in the original design. The duty to check every change to a sealed design belongs to the engineer of record. Missouri's Administrative Hearing Commission found the engineers of record, Jack Gillum and Daniel Duncan, grossly negligent; their Missouri licences were revoked, and their firm lost its right to practise engineering in the state.
sources: National Bureau of Standards, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse (Building Science Series 143, 1982)
Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission, Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors v. Duncan, Gillum and G.C.E. International (1985)

days.application: Champlain Towers South, Surfside, Florida, partly collapsed early on 24 June 2021, killing 98. In October 2018 the engineer Frank Morabito had reported 'major structural damage' to the concrete slab beneath the pool deck, caused by failed waterproofing, and urged repairs. Work had barely begun when the building fell. The cause has been the subject of a National Institute of Standards and Technology investigation. Surfside shows the limit of an engineer's duty when owners decide whether and when to act, and Florida's 2022 law requiring 'milestone' structural inspections of older condominium buildings was the response.

builds_on.why: Structures: the Hyatt failure is a load-path error, the bookkeeping of which member carries which load taught with stress and beams.
Deontology: engineering codes state duties ('hold paramount') that bind regardless of client wishes or consequences for the engineer, a duty-based ethic in professional form.

across.link: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (Cal. 1976) held that a therapist owes a duty to protect identifiable third parties a patient threatens, a professional duty reaching beyond the client. The analogy breaks because the engineer's duty to the public is written into codes and licensure law and covers anyone at risk, while Tarasoff's tort duty is limited to foreseeable victims.

days.apply_question: On 15 March 2018 a newly installed pedestrian bridge at Florida International University in Miami collapsed onto a busy road, killing six people. In the days before, workers had reported growing cracks at a key joint; the bridge's engineer of record judged them no safety concern, and traffic kept flowing beneath while a crew re-tightened a member. Measured against today's concept, what did the engineer of record owe the drivers on the road below?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Hyatt load-path error (NBS, 1982) and the licence revocations. Debated: how responsibility should be divided among the engineer of record, the fabricator and the review process under schedule pressure (Gillum argued the change was never properly reviewed; the board held the engineers responsible). Also debated: whether occupational licensing improves safety or mainly restricts entry (Morris Kleiner's research). Value judgment: that public safety is 'paramount' over client interests is a professional norm stated in codes such as the NSPE's. Attribute it; do not issue it as the brief's verdict.

resource.title: To Engineer Is Human: The Role of Failure in Successful Design, chapter 'Accidents Waiting to Happen'
resource.creator: Henry Petroski (St. Martin's Press, 1985)
resource.why: Petroski explains the Hyatt walkways failure with his memorable image of people hanging from a knotted rope, and draws the lesson that small design changes need the same scrutiny as the original design. It is a classic for engineers and non-engineers alike.

The chapter title, and the claim that this chapter covers the Hyatt Regency, are from memory and should be confirmed. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 6: Car II — building the car, from Highland Park to the gigafactory
days.headline_hint: Ford Cut the Labour to Assemble a Model T Chassis From 12½ Hours to About 90 Minutes. Then It Had to Double Pay to Keep Anyone on the Line.
days.concept: How did engineering and mass production make the car cheap, safer and cleaner, and why was being the cheapest producer, riding the learning curve, necessary but not enough, now that the battery is replaying the same story?
days.focus: Walk the car's chain as a loop. Go deep on the links the path has now taught: physical constraints and materials, engine, control, redundancy and crashworthiness engineering, interchangeable parts, learning curves and lean production, adoption read as an S-curve, and emissions and safety consequences. Preview need, regulation, liability and battery geopolitics. Name financing at CFA level only (GMAC, 1919). The Model T's rise and fall against GM, and the EV battery's learning curve, carry the feedback.
key_concepts: annual model change and product variety
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, the mass-production learning loop (reinforcing): more output, lower unit cost along the learning curve, lower price, more sales, more output; the Model T fell from about $850 in 1908 to about $260 by the mid-1920s. B1, the human limit (balancing): a faster, more repetitive line meant monotony and about 370% turnover, which raised hiring costs, which forced the $5 day. B2, rigidity (balancing): specializing everything for one model cut cost but also flexibility, and when buyers wanted variety and credit, Ford's sales fell; Chevrolet outsold Ford in 1927, and Ford closed its plants for about six months to retool for the Model A. R2, credit (reinforcing): GMAC installment credit from 1919 brought more buyers, which brought more volume. B3, harm and regulation (balancing): more cars meant more deaths and pollution, then safety and emissions rules, then engineering changes that cut harm per mile, with a delay of decades. R3, the battery loop (reinforcing): more EVs, more cumulative battery output, cheaper packs, more EVs; its side effect is supply-chain concentration in China. Unintended consequence: cheap cars brought congestion and sprawl, Car III's subject.

story.title: The line that moved, and the men who wouldn't stay
story.hook: In spring 1913 at Ford's Highland Park plant in Michigan, workers assembling flywheel magnetos began passing each piece along a waist-high line instead of building whole units at a bench. That August Ford's engineers dragged a Model T chassis across the floor with a rope and windlass while men walked alongside fitting parts. By spring 1914 the moving chassis line had cut the labour to assemble a chassis from about 12½ hours to about an hour and a half. The work was relentless, and in 1913 labour turnover ran at about 370 per cent: Ford hired more than 50,000 people to keep about 14,000 on the payroll. On 5 January 1914 Ford announced the '$5 day', roughly doubling pay for workers who qualified. Within days thousands of job-seekers crowded the plant gates in the January cold, and on 12 January police turned fire hoses on them.
story.puzzle: Ford had just made each car far cheaper to build. Why did it then double wages, and why, barely a dozen years later, did it lose its lead to a rival with a less efficient factory?
story.payoff: Mass production was a system: interchangeable parts, the moving line, and a frozen design riding a learning curve. It drove the Model T's price down roughly threefold. But its human cost forced the $5 day, an efficiency wage that cut turnover, and its rigidity let General Motors' annual models, product variety and installment credit overtake Ford by 1927. Production efficiency was necessary but not sufficient, because demand, credit and taste fed back on the factory. The battery now rides the learning curve again; whether it also repeats the rigidity trap is still open.
sources: David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800-1932 (1984), chapters on Ford
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers, 'Did Henry Ford Pay Efficiency Wages?', Journal of Labor Economics 5(4), 1987
William J. Abernathy and Kenneth Wayne, 'Limits of the Learning Curve', Harvard Business Review, September-October 1974

days.application: The gigafactory and the EV battery. Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory, opened in 2016 to make cells with Panasonic, and its rivals were bets that battery packs would ride the learning curve. They did: packs fell from over $1,000 per kWh around 2010 to about $115 in 2024 (BloombergNEF). It is the logic of Highland Park again, but the volume leaders are now China's CATL and BYD, which moves the feedback loop from the factory floor into geopolitics.

builds_on.why: Car I read the Model T's price fall on a log scale and left the question of why it fell to Engineering; this case answers it.
Interchangeable parts: the moving line was possible only because Ford's parts, made to gauges, needed no fitting.
Learning curves: Abernathy and Wayne traced the Model T's price falling along a roughly 85% curve, and EV batteries now ride the same kind of curve.
Lean production: Toyota's system was the answer to mass production's rigidity and waste, and it became the industry's model.

across.link: China's dominance of battery manufacturing (the IEA's Global EV Outlook 2024 puts China at roughly three-quarters or more of global cell production capacity, led by CATL and BYD) turns the EV's learning curve into a question of supply-chain power and chokepoints.

days.apply_question: In 2007 Nokia was the world's largest maker of mobile phones, with a famously efficient supply chain, yet within about five years it had lost the smartphone market. Using Car II's loops, explain why production efficiency was not enough.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Ford's cuts in chassis assembly labour and the fall in Model T prices. US road deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell from about 24 in 1921 to about 1.3 in the 2020s (NHTSA), through vehicles, roads, laws and medicine together. The EPA estimates new cars emit roughly 98-99% less of the regulated tailpipe pollutants than uncontrolled cars did. Debated: whether the $5 day was mainly an efficiency wage (Raff and Summers, 1987, find large turnover and productivity gains) or also a tool of control (Ford's Sociological Department inspected workers' homes as a condition of the full pay). Also debated: how much of the Model T's price fall came from learning, scale or the design freeze (Abernathy and Wayne, 1974), and how large EVs' lifecycle emissions advantage is on different grids (most lifecycle studies find it substantial; the size varies). Value judgment: who gained (buyers, Ford, the workers who stayed), who paid (workers given monotonous, closely supervised work; those initially excluded from the $5, such as most women and young single men), and who consented. Catholic social teaching's just wage (Rerum Novarum, 1891) and a utilitarian accounting of cheaper mobility weigh this differently, and Marx's account of alienated labour offers a sharper critique; the counterfactual of slower, craft-built motoring cannot be known.

chain.point: People wanted cars for autonomy, access to jobs and markets, and status, which is more than one need. The Psychology block (Day 159) and Car III in Sociology take this up.

The car combined existing inventions: the four-stroke engine (Otto, 1876), the bicycle's pneumatic tyre, ball bearings and steel tubing. Diesel's compression-ignition engine (Day 91) later gave trucks and ships their workhorse. Innovation ran through combination and practice, not a single eureka (Day 35).

Petrol holds about 46 MJ per kg, against roughly 0.6-0.9 MJ per kg for lithium-ion cells (Day 70). Heat engines waste most of their fuel energy (Day 54), and drag rises with the square of speed (Day 57). These constraints shaped everything from engine size to body shape.

Ford advertised the Model T's vanadium steel. Pressed-steel bodies, plastics replacing metal (Day 76), and the EV's electrode chemistry (Day 73) followed. Steel's process emissions (Day 74) now count in a car's footprint.

The car as an engineered system: compression ratio and knock (Day 91); feedback control from cruise control to engine management (Day 92); redundancy such as dual-circuit brakes (Day 93); crashworthiness, with crumple zones, belts, airbags and the Haddon matrix (Day 101).

The production side is taught. Interchangeable parts and gauges (Day 96); Highland Park's line riding a learning curve, with Model T prices falling along a roughly 85% curve (Abernathy and Wayne, 1974; Day 97); lean production at Toyota and NUMMI (Day 98). Financing is named at CFA level only: GM founded GMAC in 1919 to finance dealers' stock and buyers' installment purchases, and by the mid-1920s most new cars were bought on credit.

Rules came after the harms. The 1966 Motor Vehicle Safety Act and federal standards from 1968; the 1970 Clean Air Act, whose catalytic converters needed unleaded fuel (the Day 49 case); fuel-economy rules from 1975; product liability from MacPherson v. Buick (1916) on. The Government and Law blocks teach how these work.

Price cuts widened the market. US registrations rose from about 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929, the S-curve read in Car I (Day 24) with the logistic model of Day 7. Why and through whom adoption spreads is the Sociology block's subject (Day 213).

Tailpipe pollutants were cut by catalytic converters (Day 69), while CO2 still accumulates (Day 85). On safety, US deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell from about 24 in 1921 to about 1.3 in the 2020s, through engineering (Day 101), roads, laws and medicine together.

Ford's design freeze locked the company into the Model T (path dependence, Day 31) while GM's annual models and credit reshaped demand. Chevrolet outsold Ford in 1927, and Ford closed its plants for about six months to retool for the Model A. The EV battery now rides its own learning curve (Days 97 and 73).

China's lead in battery cells, cathode materials and mineral refining (CATL, BYD) makes the EV transition a question of supply-chain power. The International Relations block's lesson on economic statecraft and chokepoints (Day 271) takes this up.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: To Say 'Moon,' Kele Drummers Beat Out 'The Moon Looks Down at the Earth.' Claude Shannon Later Proved Why the Extra Words Worked.
days.concept: Information is the reduction of uncertainty, measured in bits. Shannon's entropy sets how far a message can be compressed, a channel's capacity sets how fast it can be sent reliably, and deliberate redundancy is how you buy reliability over noise.
days.focus: Teach Shannon's 1948 definition. A bit is one yes/no answer between two equally likely options, and entropy is a source's average surprise (logarithms from D2, probability-weighted averages from D11). Then his two hard limits: no lossless compression below the entropy, and below a noisy channel's capacity error-correcting redundancy can make transmission as reliable as you like. The angle: the Kele drums show both halves at once, a channel stripped to two pitches and the redundancy that rescues it.
days.model_or_equation: H = -sum of p_i log2 p_i (bits per symbol). A fair coin gives H = 1 bit; a coin that lands heads 90% of the time gives H = -(0.9 log2 0.9 + 0.1 log2 0.1), about 0.47 bits, so a long record of its tosses compresses to under half. Channel capacity: C = B log2(1 + S/N) bits per second. A 3 kHz phone line with a 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio (S/N = 1,000) gives C = 3,000 x log2(1,001), about 30 kbit/s. That is the ceiling purely analogue dial-up modems ran into: the V.34 standard topped out at 33.6 kbit/s, on real lines with a little more bandwidth and a little less noise.

story.title: A drummer in the Congo takes a whole sentence to say 'moon'
story.hook: Along the upper Congo River the Kele (Lokele) people sent messages from village to village by drum, across miles of forest and faster than any runner. John F. Carrington, an English Baptist missionary who spent decades among them, learned to drum himself and described the system in The Talking Drums of Africa (1949). Kele is a tonal language, and the slit-log drum, with one high lip and one low, keeps only the pattern of high and low tones; it drops every vowel and consonant, so many words come out identical. Drummers therefore never beat a bare word. 'Moon' (songe) went out as a stock phrase rendered 'the moon looks down at the earth', and a call to come home became a long sentence about making your feet come back the way they went. Drummed messages ran several times longer than spoken ones; Gleick retells how a drummer summoned Carrington home from the forest for a meal with a whole string of such phrases.
story.puzzle: Why would a messenger with a slow channel make every message several times longer? And why did that make messages arrive more surely, not less?
story.payoff: The drum channel carries only tone, so each beat delivers at most about one bit, and many words share a tone pattern: the listener's uncertainty about which word was meant stays high. The stock phrases add redundancy. Each extra tone pattern rules out rival readings until only one is left. Shannon proved in 1948 that this is the general price of reliable communication over an ambiguous, noisy, low-capacity channel: redundancy can push errors as low as you like, but only by spending rate, and only up to the channel's capacity.
sources: John F. Carrington, The Talking Drums of Africa (London: Carey Kingsgate Press, 1949)
James Gleick, The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood (Pantheon, 2011), ch. 1 'Drums That Talk'
Freeman Dyson, 'How We Know', New York Review of Books, 10 Mar 2011 (review of Gleick, discusses the Kele drums)
C. E. Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', Bell System Technical Journal 27 (July and October 1948)

days.application: QR codes. Denso, a Toyota-group parts maker (the business now sits with its subsidiary Denso Wave), introduced the QR code in Japan in 1994 to track car components (the car chain's production link). Its Reed-Solomon error correction comes in four levels, L, M, Q and H, which can restore roughly 7%, 15%, 25% and 30% of the codewords. That is why a code with a logo printed over its middle still scans, and why the same-sized code holds much less data at level H: the redundancy is paid for in capacity.

builds_on.why: A bit is a logarithm: n yes/no answers distinguish 2^n options, so the information in one of N equally likely outcomes is log2 N bits.
Entropy is an expected value: the probability-weighted average of each outcome's surprise, -log2 p.

across.link: The genetic code. DNA's four-letter alphabet carries at most 2 bits per base, so the roughly 3.1 billion base pairs of a human genome hold at most about 6.2 billion bits (about 775 megabytes). The code's 64 codons specify only 20 amino acids plus 'stop', and that redundancy is why many single-letter mutations, especially in a codon's third position, are 'silent': the same error-tolerance the drummers built in.

days.apply_question: Zipping a long English text file often shrinks it to around a third of its size, yet zipping a JPEG photo saves almost nothing. Using entropy and redundancy, explain why.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Shannon's source-coding and channel-capacity theorems are proofs. The drum phrases are Carrington's 1949 records as retold by Gleick (2011). Retellings sometimes put the expansion at about eight drummed words per spoken word; treat any such ratio as a rough estimate and check it against Gleick or Carrington before quoting a number. Drum language was a living practice in Carrington's time that later declined; describe it in the past tense.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: Konrad Zuse Built a Computer From 2,600 Telephone Switches in Wartime Berlin. Not One of Them Knew Arithmetic.
days.concept: AND, OR and NOT, operations on true/false values, can be combined to compute any logical function, arithmetic included. Any device that switches (a relay, a vacuum tube, a transistor) can carry them out.
days.focus: Boole's algebra of true and false (1847, 1854) becomes circuitry. Shannon's 1937 MIT thesis showed that switches in series compute AND and switches in parallel compute OR, as Akira Nakashima at NEC in Japan found independently in the mid-1930s. Any truth table can be built from these gates, and NAND alone is enough (functional completeness). Binary addition is itself logic (sum = XOR, carry = AND), so chained gates add and shifted adds multiply. The angle: what closes the gap between a clicking switch and doing arithmetic is abstraction, since the same logic runs on relays, tubes or transistors.
days.model_or_equation: Half adder for one binary digit from each of A and B: Sum = A XOR B = (A OR B) AND NOT (A AND B); Carry = A AND B. For 1 + 1: Sum = 0, Carry = 1, giving binary 10, which is two. A full adder adds an incoming carry, and a row of them adds numbers of any length.

story.title: Telephone relays click through a multiplication in wartime Berlin
story.hook: On 12 May 1941, in his workshop in Berlin, Konrad Zuse, a 30-year-old civil engineer who had worked on aircraft stress calculations at Henschel, demonstrated his Z3 to an audience of scientists. The machine was made of about 2,600 telephone relays, electrically operated switches that are only ever open or closed. It read its program from punched 35 mm film, worked in binary floating point, and took about three seconds to multiply. Zuse had begun in his parents' Berlin living room with the mechanical Z1 (1936-38), driven by boredom with repetitive engineering arithmetic. The original Z3 was destroyed in an Allied air raid in 1943.
story.puzzle: A relay knows nothing about numbers. It is a switch, on or off. How can a heap of switches multiply?
story.payoff: Switches in series behave as AND, switches in parallel as OR, and a relay whose contact opens when energized behaves as NOT; Boole's algebra describes all three exactly, as Shannon showed in 1937. Adding binary digits is itself a logical operation (sum = XOR, carry = AND), so chains of gates add, and repeated shifted addition multiplies. Zuse reached binary relay logic largely on his own; Shannon and Nakashima turned it into a theory.
sources: Raul Rojas, 'Konrad Zuse's Legacy: The Architecture of the Z1 and Z3', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 19(2), 1997
Raul Rojas, 'How to Make Zuse's Z3 a Universal Computer', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 20(3), 1998
Konrad Zuse, Der Computer - Mein Lebenswerk (1970; English: The Computer - My Life, Springer, 1993)
C. E. Shannon, 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits', Transactions of the AIEE 57 (1938), from his 1937 MIT master's thesis

days.application: Railway interlocking. At a junction a signal may clear only if the route is set AND the points are locked in the right position AND the track ahead is clear AND NOT any conflicting route is set. John Saxby patented interlocking points and signals in Britain in 1856, and the UK's Regulation of Railways Act 1889, passed after the Armagh disaster, made interlocking compulsory on passenger lines. Relay interlockings use 'vital' relays that drop by gravity to the safe state (signal at danger) if power fails, so the logic fails safe.

builds_on.why: Day 37 showed that validity depends on an argument's form, not its subject matter. Boolean algebra turns that formal logic into calculation, and Shannon then turned the calculation into wiring.
A gate's inputs and outputs are bits. Today shows how bits are processed, not just measured.

across.link: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' (Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics, 1943), modelled a neuron as a threshold logic gate and showed that nets of them can compute logical functions. It is the ancestor of the artificial neuron. The analogy breaks because real neurons are analogue, noisy and change with use.

days.apply_question: A car's dome light should come on when either front door is open, but never when the driver has set the dome-light switch to OFF. Using AND, OR and NOT, how would you connect the two door switches and the dome-light switch, in series or in parallel, to get exactly that behaviour?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the logic and how circuits realize it. Debated by definition: 'first computer' titles. The Z3 (1941) was program-controlled and binary but not stored-program and had no conditional branch; Rojas (1998) showed it could in principle be universal. The Atanasoff-Berry Computer, Britain's Colossus (1944) and ENIAC (1945) hold rival titles depending on the criteria, so call the Z3 'one of the first'.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.topic: The transistor and the integrated circuit
days.headline_hint: Bell Labs' First Transistor Was Gold Foil, a Plastic Wedge and a Spring. By 2018 People Had Made About 13 Sextillion of Them.
days.concept: A transistor is a switch with no moving parts: a small voltage on one terminal controls the current through doped semiconductor. Because it switches and amplifies with nothing to wear or heat, it can be shrunk and printed by the billion on integrated circuits.
days.focus: From Day 77's p-n junction to the transistor. In a MOSFET the gate voltage opens or closes a channel, which is the physical switch behind Day 105's gates. Solid state beat relays and tubes on speed, power, size and reliability. Kilby (Texas Instruments, 1958) and Noyce (Fairchild, 1959) put whole circuits on one chip, and photolithography printed them like photographs. Shrinking made each switch cheaper, faster and more frugal at once (Dennard scaling), the loop behind Moore's law from Day 2, until in the mid-2000s voltage stopped falling, clock speeds stalled near 3-4 GHz and chips went multicore and specialized.
key_concepts: Dennard scaling and the power wall
days.model_or_equation: Dynamic switching power P is roughly a C V^2 f, where a is the fraction of transistors switching, C the capacitance being charged, V the supply voltage and f the clock frequency. Dennard scaling let V and C fall as transistors shrank, so power density stayed flat while f rose. Once V could no longer fall (leakage), raising f simply raised heat: the 'power wall' of the mid-2000s.

story.title: Two days before Christmas, a sliver of germanium makes a voice louder
story.hook: On 23 December 1947 at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, Walter Brattain and John Bardeen showed Bell Labs managers a crude device: a slab of germanium, a plastic wedge wrapped in gold foil slit by a razor into two contacts a hair's breadth apart, and a spring pressing it down. Speech fed in came out of the headphones audibly louder, as Brattain recorded in his notebook the next day. Nothing moved and nothing glowed. When Bell Labs announced the 'transistor' on 30 June 1948, the New York Times gave it a few paragraphs in its radio column. Weeks after the demonstration their group leader, William Shockley, devised the sturdier junction transistor, and the three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
story.puzzle: Bell already had amplifiers and switches: the vacuum tube and the relay. Why did this fragile lump become the most manufactured object in human history, about 13 sextillion (1.3 x 10^22) made by 2018 by the Computer History Museum's estimate?
story.payoff: A transistor is a voltage-controlled switch with no filament to burn out and no contact to wear, so it can be made very small, very fast and very frugal. Once Kilby and Noyce put whole circuits on one chip and lithography printed them, shrinking each switch made it cheaper, faster and lower-power at the same time. That reinforcing loop ran for decades, and one modern chip now holds tens of billions of transistors. The 13 sextillion is the product of that loop.
sources: Michael Riordan & Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire: The Birth of the Information Age (Norton, 1997)
Walter Brattain, Bell Labs laboratory notebook entry of 24 Dec 1947 (reproduced in Riordan & Hoddeson and on PBS 'Transistorized!')
Nobel Prize in Physics 1956, nobelprize.org (Shockley, Bardeen, Brattain)
David Laws, '13 Sextillion & Counting: The Long & Winding Road to the Most Frequently Manufactured Human Artifact in History', Computer History Museum, 2018

days.application: ASML's extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines are the only practical tools for printing the finest features of today's leading-edge chips. They make 13.5-nanometre light by hitting tiny droplets of molten tin with a powerful laser tens of thousands of times a second, and bounce it off ultra-smooth mirrors. A standard EUV system has sold for roughly $150-200 million and the newer High-NA systems for about $350-400 million (reported prices), and one Dutch firm is the sole supplier: a production bottleneck at the heart of the chip (chip geopolitics belongs to International Relations, Days 271-272).

builds_on.why: Doped p- and n-type silicon and the p-n junction are the transistor's raw material; today turns the junction into a switch.
Logic gates need switches. The transistor is the switch that implements AND, OR and NOT (a CMOS NAND gate takes four transistors).

across.link: Because lithography is concentrated in one firm, it became a lever of state power. The Dutch government has withheld export licences for ASML's EUV machines to China since 2019, so ASML has never shipped EUV to China, and the US export controls of 7 October 2022 restricted advanced chips and chipmaking tools further. Dense, cheap transistors created a chokepoint states can squeeze.

days.apply_question: Your phone's processor runs at roughly the same clock speed (3-4 GHz) as a desktop chip from 2005, yet it does far more work per second. Using the power wall, explain where the extra performance came from.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the device physics and the 1947-48 history. Debated: the state of Moore's law. Transistor density keeps rising (gate-all-around transistors, 3D stacking), but clock speeds stalled in the mid-2000s and cost per transistor at the leading nodes falls far more slowly than it used to; whether the law is 'dead' or 'alive' depends on which measure is meant. Credit is shared: Shockley's junction transistor (1948) and the Kilby and Noyce integrated circuits (1958-59) were separate inventions.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: ENIAC Could Do 5,000 Additions a Second. Giving It a New Problem Took Six Women Days of Rewiring.
days.concept: A stored-program computer keeps its instructions in the same memory as its data, so one fixed machine becomes any machine by loading a different program. The fetch-decode-execute cycle and the memory hierarchy follow from that design.
days.focus: ENIAC was programmed with cables and switches. The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (30 June 1945), under von Neumann's name but drawing on Eckert and Mauchly's team, put instructions in memory as numbers, and the Manchester Baby ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948. From that design follow the program counter and the fetch-decode-execute loop, and programs that write programs (assemblers and compilers; Grace Hopper's A-0, 1952). The cost is a single path between processor and memory, which John Backus in 1977 called the von Neumann bottleneck, and therefore the cache and memory hierarchy.
days.model_or_equation: The fetch-decode-execute loop: repeat { instruction = memory[PC]; PC = PC + 1; decode the instruction; execute it, which may read or write memory or set PC to a jump target }. Because instructions are just numbers in memory, a program can load, modify or generate another program.

story.title: The fastest calculator on Earth, and the six women who rewired it
story.hook: On 15 February 1946, at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School in Philadelphia, the US Army unveiled ENIAC: about 30 tons, some 17,500 vacuum tubes, about 5,000 additions a second. For the press it computed a shell's trajectory faster than the shell itself would fly. Jean Jennings (later Bartik) and Betty Snyder (later Holberton) had set that program up. They were two of six women, with Kathleen McNulty, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman, who programmed ENIAC by working out each problem on paper and then plugging cables and setting thousands of switches. They were not introduced at the unveiling or invited to the celebratory dinner, and moving ENIAC to a new problem could take days.
story.puzzle: ENIAC could add 5,000 numbers a second, yet changing what it computed took people days. What was missing, and why did fixing it turn a giant calculator into the universal machine in your pocket?
story.payoff: ENIAC's program lived in its wiring, outside its memory. The stored-program idea (written up in the EDVAC First Draft of 30 June 1945 from the ENIAC team's discussions, and first run on the Manchester Baby on 21 June 1948, where Tom Kilburn's 17-instruction program found the highest factor of 2^18 in 52 minutes) puts instructions in memory as numbers. A new problem then means loading new numbers in seconds, and programs can build other programs.
sources: W. Barkley Fritz, 'The Women of ENIAC', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 18(3), 1996
Jean Jennings Bartik, Pioneer Programmer (Truman State University Press, 2013)
Kathy Kleiman, Proving Ground: The Untold Story of the Six Women Who Programmed the World's First Modern Computer (Grand Central, 2022)
John von Neumann, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (Moore School, 30 June 1945)
University of Manchester and Computer Conservation Society accounts of the Small-Scale Experimental Machine ('Baby'), 21 June 1948

days.application: Why a phone can become a camera, a map, a bank and a game console: one processor fetching different instructions from memory. The same design sets the limit on AI chips. Fetching data from main memory costs far more energy than doing arithmetic on it (Mark Horowitz's ISSCC 2014 figures for a 45-nanometre chip: roughly 640 picojoules to read 32 bits from DRAM, against about 0.9 picojoules for a 32-bit floating-point addition and about 0.1 for an integer one), so AI accelerators surround the processor with stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to get past the 'memory wall' (Wulf & McKee, 1995).

builds_on.why: Gates build both halves of the machine: the arithmetic unit, and the decoder that turns an instruction's bits into control signals.
Transistors made memory and processors dense and cheap enough for programs to be stored by the thousand, then by the billion.

across.link: In his 1948 Hixon Symposium lecture ('The General and Logical Theory of Automata', published 1951), von Neumann argued that a self-reproducing machine needs a stored description that is both copied and interpreted: in effect a stored program for building itself. That was five years before Watson and Crick's double helix (1953) showed how DNA plays both roles. The analogy breaks because a cell has no central processor; genes are read in parallel by chemistry and regulated by feedback.

days.apply_question: Carmakers now add features to cars already on the road through over-the-air software updates. Using the stored-program idea, explain how a car built in 2020 can do something in 2026 that it could not do when it left the factory.
days.evidence_note: Debated (credit): von Neumann's name is on the First Draft, but Eckert and Mauchly had discussed stored programs earlier and Turing's 1936 universal machine supplied the theory. Historians such as Haigh, Priestley and Rope (ENIAC in Action, 2016) argue that the label 'von Neumann architecture' oversimplifies who did what. Settled: the Manchester Baby ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: There Are About 10^60 Ways to Tour 49 American Cities. In 1954 Three Men at RAND Proved Which Was Shortest Without Checking Them.
days.concept: An algorithm's cost is measured by how its running time grows with the size of its input. Problems solvable in polynomial time are tractable, problems that seem to need exponential time are not, and whether every quickly checkable problem is also quickly solvable (P versus NP) is unknown.
days.focus: Growth rates (big-O): why brute force on the travelling-salesman problem explodes factorially, and why that outruns any hardware (Day 2's exponentials). NP problems are easy to verify but apparently hard to solve, and NP-complete problems (Cook 1971, Karp 1972, Levin independently) are all equally hard. How practice escapes anyway: exact methods that prune vast families of answers at once (cutting planes, branch-and-bound; Concorde solved an 85,900-city instance in 2006) and heuristics that give near-best answers fast. Challenge the assumption that faster computers will eventually solve everything.
days.model_or_equation: Brute-force tours for n cities: (n-1)!/2. For n = 10 that is 181,440; for n = 20, about 6 x 10^16; for n = 49, about 6 x 10^60. Compare a polynomial n^2 algorithm: 100, 400 and 2,401 steps. A computer checking a billion tours a second since the Big Bang would have checked only about 4 x 10^26.

story.title: Three mathematicians, a road atlas and 10^60 possible tours
story.hook: In 1954 at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, George Dantzig, Ray Fulkerson and Selmer Johnson took on the problem every salesman and bus planner knows: visit every city once and return home by the shortest route. They picked 49 cities, one in each of the 48 contiguous states plus Washington, D.C. The number of distinct round trips is about 6 x 10^60, so checking them was hopeless. Instead they used linear programming, adding constraints by hand (later called cutting planes) until the best answer of the relaxed problem was itself a tour; they actually solved a 42-city version, because the other seven cities lay along its route and slotted in. They published the tour, and the proof that no shorter one exists, in the Journal of the Operations Research Society of America that year.
story.puzzle: If checking every tour is impossible, how did they prove theirs was the shortest? And why, seventy years later, can nobody guarantee to do the same quickly for every set of cities?
story.payoff: Brute force grows factorially, faster than any exponential hardware improvement. Clever methods can crack particular instances by proving that whole families of tours cannot win, without listing them, which is why Concorde later solved an 85,900-city instance. But no known algorithm solves every instance in polynomial time. The decision version of the problem is NP-complete, so a fast general method would settle P versus NP, which has been open since 1971.
sources: G. Dantzig, R. Fulkerson & S. Johnson, 'Solution of a Large-Scale Traveling-Salesman Problem', Journal of the Operations Research Society of America 2(4), 1954
William J. Cook, In Pursuit of the Traveling Salesman: Mathematics at the Limits of Computation (Princeton University Press, 2012)
D. Applegate, R. Bixby, V. Chvatal & W. Cook, The Traveling Salesman Problem: A Computational Study (Princeton, 2006)
Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Problems (2000)

days.application: UPS's ORION (On-Road Integrated Optimization and Navigation) system, rolled out across its US driver routes by about 2016, plans the order of a driver's 100-plus daily stops. UPS says it saves about 100 million miles and 10 million gallons of fuel a year. It does not find the provably best route. It uses heuristics to find very good routes quickly, honours constraints such as delivery windows and the company's preference for avoiding left turns, and lets drivers deviate when they know better.

builds_on.why: Exponential growth and log scales: polynomial and exponential running times separate dramatically on a log plot, and that gap is the whole tractable/intractable divide.
Optimization: Day 8's smooth optimum is found where the derivative is zero, but a tour is a discrete choice with no derivative to follow, which is why combinatorial optimization is hard.

across.link: Levinthal's paradox (Cyrus Levinthal, 1969): a protein chain has astronomically many possible shapes, so it could never find its folded form by trying them, yet real proteins fold in milliseconds. The resolution is that physics funnels the chain down an energy landscape instead of searching it. The analogy with intractable search breaks there: nature is not solving the general problem, only following a slope. Predicting the fold computationally stayed hard until AlphaFold.

days.apply_question: A wedding planner must seat 150 guests at 15 tables so that no two feuding relatives share a table. Checking a proposed seating chart takes minutes; why can finding one that satisfies every constraint become hopelessly slow as the guest list grows?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the growth rates, and that the travelling-salesman decision problem is NP-complete, are proofs. Open: P versus NP is unproved, and the Clay Institute's $1 million prize is unclaimed. Most researchers expect P to differ from NP (large majorities in William Gasarch's surveys of 2002, 2012 and 2019), but that is expert opinion, not evidence.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.topic: Computability: what no computer can do
days.headline_hint: A 23-Year-Old Proved in 1936 That Some Questions No Computer Can Ever Answer, Before Real Computers Existed.
days.concept: Some precisely stated questions have no algorithm at all. Turing proved that no program can decide, for every program and input, whether it will eventually halt, so some limits on computation are logical, not engineering, limits.
days.focus: Hilbert's decision problem (the Entscheidungsproblem, posed with Ackermann in 1928). The Turing machine as an idealized human clerk with paper and rules, and the universal machine that runs any machine's description: Day 107's stored program, in theory. The halting proof by self-reference and contradiction. Church's parallel result and the Church-Turing thesis (a thesis, not a theorem). Godel's incompleteness (1931) as the logical cousin, and Rice's theorem: every non-trivial question about what a program does is undecidable. The angle: impossibility proofs give certainty no engineering can.
days.model_or_equation: Proof sketch. Suppose a program H(P, x) always correctly answers 'halts' or 'loops forever'. Build D(P): if H(P, P) says 'halts', loop forever; otherwise halt. Now run D on itself: D(D) halts if and only if H says D(D) does not halt. That is a contradiction, so no such H can exist.

story.title: A runner lying in a Cambridge meadow takes on Hilbert
story.hook: In spring 1935 Alan Turing, a 22-year-old newly elected fellow of King's College, Cambridge, heard Max Newman lecture on David Hilbert's challenge: find a mechanical procedure that decides, for any mathematical statement, whether it can be proved. According to his biographer Andrew Hodges, the decisive idea came that early summer while Turing lay in the meadows at Grantchester after a run. To answer Hilbert he first had to define 'mechanical procedure', and so invented an imaginary machine that reads, writes and erases symbols on a tape according to a table of rules. In April 1936 he gave Newman his manuscript, and soon afterwards word came that Alonzo Church at Princeton had reached the same verdict by another route. 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem' was received by the London Mathematical Society on 28 May 1936; Turing was 23.
story.puzzle: Proving that something can be done takes one example. How could anyone prove that no procedure, including ones nobody has yet invented, can answer a question?
story.payoff: By making 'procedure' precise (the Turing machine), Turing could reason about every possible procedure at once. And because a program is itself data, a description one machine can read, he could hand any would-be halting-decider a program built to do the opposite of whatever it predicts. The contradiction proves that no such decider exists, so Hilbert's decision problem has no general solution.
sources: A. M. Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (2) 42 (1936-37)
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma (1983), ch. 2
Alonzo Church, 'An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory', American Journal of Mathematics 58 (1936)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Turing Machines' and 'The Church-Turing Thesis'

days.application: Why no antivirus can be perfect. Fred Cohen showed in the 1980s ('Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments', Computers & Security, 1987) that deciding whether an arbitrary program is a virus is undecidable, a special case of Rice's theorem (1953). Real security tools therefore trade false alarms against misses using signatures and behavioural heuristics. Verified software escapes the limit by proving properties of one specific program, as with the machine-checked proof of the seL4 microkernel (2009), rather than deciding them for all programs.

builds_on.why: Proof: the halting result is a proof by contradiction, and its certainty is the kind only Day 10's method can give.
Programs are data: the universal Turing machine is the stored-program computer in theory, and feeding a program its own description is the hinge of the proof.

across.link: The Lucas-Penrose argument: J. R. Lucas ('Minds, Machines and Godel', Philosophy, 1961) and Roger Penrose (The Emperor's New Mind, 1989) argued that Godel's theorem shows human minds are not Turing machines, because we can see the truth of a Godel sentence a given system cannot prove. Most logicians and philosophers reject the argument, chiefly because it assumes we know our own reasoning is consistent; it bears on later debates about consciousness.

days.apply_question: A vendor claims its tool can inspect any smartphone app and tell you, correctly every time, whether that app can ever freeze in an endless loop. Using the halting problem, which part of that claim cannot be true, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the undecidability of the halting problem and Godel's incompleteness theorems are proofs. A thesis, not a theorem: the Church-Turing thesis, that Turing machines capture every 'effective procedure', is near-universally accepted but cannot be proved. Debated: claims that Godel or Turing show minds are not machines (Lucas, Penrose); most specialists reject them. The Grantchester detail comes from Hodges's biography and should be attributed to it.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: The Screen Said 'Malfunction 54.' The Same Code Had Run Older Machines Safely for Years. Then an Experienced Operator Typed Quickly.
days.concept: Software does not wear out. It fails through design errors (untested states, race conditions, broken assumptions), so its failures can sit dormant for years, strike suddenly, and hit every copy at once.
days.focus: Contrast software with hardware, whose fatigue and wear produce spread-out, independent failures (Days 89 and 93). Software's failure modes: race conditions, untested combinations of inputs, code reused in a new context, and hardware interlocks removed because software was trusted. Testing can show the presence of bugs, never their absence (Dijkstra). Identical copies make every software fault common-mode. Defences: independent interlocks, defence in depth, staged rollouts, formal methods and safety standards such as IEC 62304 for medical software.
days.model_or_equation: Redundancy against independent faults: two units that each fail with probability p fail together with probability p^2 (with p = 0.01, 1 in 10,000). Two copies of the same software share the same bug, so the chance both fail is about p (1 in 100): redundancy buys nothing against a common design fault.

story.title: 'Malfunction 54' in a Texas cancer clinic
story.hook: On 21 March 1986 at the East Texas Cancer Center in Tyler, an experienced operator set up the Therac-25, a computer-controlled radiation-therapy machine built by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL), for Ray Cox's ninth treatment of a tumour on his back. She typed 'x' for X-ray mode, saw the slip, moved the cursor up, changed it to 'e' for electron mode within seconds, and started the beam. The console showed 'Malfunction 54' and 'treatment pause', with a dose reading suggesting almost nothing had been delivered, so she pressed P to proceed. Cox, alone in the shielded room with the video monitor and intercom out of action that day, felt what he described as an electric shock and tried to get up. He had received a massive overdose, estimated by Leveson and Turner at roughly 16,500-25,000 rads where about 180 was intended, and died about five months later. AECL could not reproduce the fault until the hospital physicist, Fritz Hager, worked with the operator and found that typing as fast as she had triggered it.
story.puzzle: The Therac-25's software was largely inherited from earlier Therac models that had treated patients safely for years, and nothing in the machine had worn out. So how could the same code suddenly kill, and only when an operator typed quickly?
story.payoff: The software had a race condition. If the operator edited the mode within about eight seconds, while the machine was still setting its magnets, the console accepted the change but the beam hardware did not, and the high-power beam could fire without the attenuating target in place. Earlier models had independent hardware interlocks that blocked the dangerous state (investigators later found the Therac-20 shared a similar flaw but merely blew fuses), so the bug lay dormant; the Therac-25 relied on software alone. Software fails by design, not wear: it is invisible until the exact state occurs, and then it fails the same way every time.
sources: Nancy Leveson & Clark Turner, 'An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents', IEEE Computer 26(7), July 1993, pp. 18-41
Nancy Leveson, Safeware: System Safety and Computers (Addison-Wesley, 1995), Appendix A
Nancy Leveson, 'The Therac-25: 30 Years Later', IEEE Computer 50(11), 2017

days.application: CrowdStrike, 19 July 2024. A faulty content update ('Channel File 291') to CrowdStrike's Falcon security sensor, which runs inside the Windows kernel, crashed about 8.5 million Windows devices within hours (Microsoft's estimate, under 1% of all Windows machines), grounding flights, delaying surgeries and taking broadcasters off air; Delta alone cancelled about 7,000 flights over several days. The update went to every customer at once, with no staged rollout. CrowdStrike's August 2024 root-cause analysis described a mismatch between the number of input fields the new template defined and the number the sensor code supplied, a design fault that testing had missed. Monoculture turned one bug into a common-mode failure across the world.

builds_on.why: Reliability and redundancy: Day 93's warning that a common-mode failure defeats redundancy is the default case for software, where every copy carries the same bug.
Normal accidents: the Therac-25 failed through an unforeseen interaction between operator speed, software timing and missing interlocks, exactly the interactive complexity Perrow described.

across.link: Whether software is a 'product' carrying strict liability long went unsettled; the Therac-25 lawsuits were settled out of court. The EU's revised Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853, adopted October 2024) now states expressly that software, including updates, is a product, so a defective update like CrowdStrike's can fall under strict liability in the EU once the directive applies.

days.apply_question: In 2015 the FAA ordered Boeing 787 operators to power-cycle their aircraft, because a software counter in all four generator control units would overflow after 248 days of continuous power and shut every unit down at once. Why did having four generators give no protection against this failure?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mechanisms of the Therac-25 accidents (Leveson & Turner 1993) and of the CrowdStrike outage (CrowdStrike's root-cause analysis, August 2024). Accounts differ on the Therac-25 death toll: Leveson and Turner describe six massive overdoses from 1985 to 1987, with at least three deaths attributed to them, and counts vary because some patients were already gravely ill. The Tyler accident of 21 March 1986 was the fourth of the six, so 'safe for years' applies to the inherited code on older machines, not to the Therac-25 itself; and the operator did nothing the interface forbade, so the brief should not blame her speed. The 8.5 million figure is Microsoft's estimate.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: Paul Baran Designed a Network to Survive a Nuclear War. AT&T Said It Couldn't Work. The Internet Runs on His Idea, Built for Another Reason.
days.concept: Packet switching breaks data into small, separately addressed packets that share links and find their own routes. Layered protocols with the intelligence at the endpoints (the end-to-end principle) let a network of unreliable parts deliver reliably and grow without being redesigned.
days.focus: Circuit switching (a dedicated path, as in a phone call) versus packet switching (store-and-forward, links shared statistically). Baran's distributed mesh, and Donald Davies at Britain's National Physical Laboratory, who reached the same idea independently in 1965 and coined 'packet'. Louis Pouzin's CYCLADES datagrams in France and Cerf and Kahn's TCP (1974). Layering, with IP as the narrow waist, and the end-to-end principle (Saltzer, Reed & Clark, 1984): keep the core simple and let the ends check, reorder and resend. Challenge the popular origin myth with the builders' own account.
days.model_or_equation: The TCP/IP layer model as a named model: application (web, e-mail) on top of transport (TCP: ordering, acknowledgement, retransmission, congestion control) on top of internet (IP: addresses and best-effort forwarding, the narrow waist of the 'hourglass') on top of link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, fibre). Each layer uses only the service of the one below, so new links and new applications can be added without changing IP.

story.title: A RAND engineer designs a network to outlive a nuclear strike
story.hook: In the early 1960s at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, Paul Baran, born in 1926 in Grodno (then Poland, now Belarus), worked on a question the Cold War made urgent: could US command communications survive a Soviet first strike? The telephone network ran through a hierarchy of central switching offices; destroy a few and much of the country goes deaf. In a series of RAND memoranda, On Distributed Communications (1964), Baran proposed a mesh of cheap, unreliable links and switching computers that chop messages into small 'message blocks', each passed onward 'hot-potato' style by whatever route is still open. His simulations suggested that a mesh with only about three or four links per node could survive heavy destruction. AT&T, which would have had to build it, rejected the idea (Baran later recalled being told it could not work), and when the Pentagon assigned the project to the Defense Communications Agency in the mid-1960s, Baran himself advised against going ahead, fearing it would be done badly, so the project died.
story.puzzle: How can a network built from parts that fail be more reliable than a network built from parts engineered never to fail? And why do the internet's own builders insist it was not built to survive a nuclear war?
story.payoff: Packet switching moves reliability out of the parts and into the structure and the ends: many paths (redundancy), routing around damage, and endpoints that check, reorder and resend. The ARPANET (1969) used the same idea for a different reason, to share scarce computers efficiently by letting many conversations share each line. Its builders (Leiner and colleagues, for the Internet Society) call the nuclear-war origin a false rumour that grew from Baran's separate RAND study. One mechanism served both goals, which is why the myth is so easy to believe.
sources: Paul Baran, On Distributed Communications (RAND Memoranda RM-3420 and following, 1964)
Paul Baran, oral history interview, Charles Babbage Institute, University of Minnesota (1990)
Barry M. Leiner et al., 'A Brief History of the Internet' (Internet Society, 1997; revised)
Janet Abbate, Inventing the Internet (MIT Press, 1999)

days.application: The Mediterranean cable cuts of 30 January 2008. Two submarine cables, SEA-ME-WE 4 and FLAG Europe-Asia, were damaged off Alexandria, Egypt. Egypt, the Gulf states and South Asia lost large shares of their international capacity (early reports put the losses for Egypt and India at roughly half or more), but traffic was rerouted around the break over other cables, slower and congested rather than cut off, while repair ships fixed the cables within about two weeks.

builds_on.why: Networks: Day 13 showed that structure (degree, hubs, shortcuts) decides how networks fail. Baran's distributed mesh against the hub-and-spoke phone hierarchy is that lesson as a design choice.
Reliability and redundancy: parallel paths cut the probability of losing a connection, the same parallel-redundancy arithmetic applied to routes.

across.link: The shipping container (Day 99) is a structural twin of IP. The ISO container standards of 1968 let any ship, train or truck carry any cargo, just as IP lets any link carry any application, and both turned many separate systems into one network. The analogy breaks because a lost container is gone, while a lost packet is simply sent again, which is why the internet can treat loss as normal.

days.apply_question: When the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption of 15 January 2022 cut the single submarine cable linking Tonga to the world, the country was largely offline for about five weeks. Why couldn't packet switching's routing around damage do for Tonga what it did for Egypt in 2008?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mechanism. Historiography: Baran's RAND work was explicitly about nuclear survivability. The ARPANET's builders (Leiner et al.; Bob Taylor) say the ARPANET was built to share computing resources and call the nuclear origin a myth; Donald Davies in Britain reached packet switching independently for time-sharing reasons. A dissent worth naming: Stephen Lukasik, ARPA's director in 1971-75, argued ('Why the Arpanet Was Built', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, 2011) that military command and control was part of ARPA's motive from the start, so 'only computer sharing' is also too simple. The AT&T dismissal rests mainly on Baran's own later recollections, so attribute it. The 2008 outage percentages varied by source and should be given as a range.
