days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: A 22-Year-Old at GCHQ Solved Public-Key Encryption in About Half an Hour in 1973. Britain Kept It Secret for 24 Years.
days.concept: Public-key cryptography rests on one-way functions, which are easy to compute and infeasible to reverse without a secret. They let two strangers agree on a secret, or sign a message, over a channel anyone can read.
days.focus: The key-distribution problem: ordinary (symmetric) ciphers need a shared secret first. One-way functions with a trapdoor: modular exponentiation is easy and the discrete logarithm hard (Diffie-Hellman, 1976); multiplying primes is easy and factoring hard (RSA, 1977). Digital signatures run the trapdoor in reverse. The security is assumed, not proved: it rests on Day 108's gap between easy and hard, and Shor's quantum algorithm (1994) would break both schemes, hence NIST's post-quantum standards of 13 August 2024.
days.model_or_equation: Diffie-Hellman. Public: a prime p and a base g. Alice picks a secret a and sends A = g^a mod p; Bob picks a secret b and sends B = g^b mod p. Both compute s = B^a = A^b = g^(ab) mod p. A toy run with p = 23, g = 5, a = 6, b = 15 gives A = 8 and B = 19, and both reach s = 2. An eavesdropper who sees 23, 5, 8 and 19 must solve a discrete logarithm to find a or b, which is trivial here but infeasible for numbers hundreds of digits long.

story.title: Half an hour of thought at GCHQ, then 24 years of silence
story.hook: In autumn 1973 Clifford Cocks, a 22-year-old Cambridge mathematics graduate, had just joined GCHQ, Britain's signals-intelligence agency in Cheltenham. His mentor, Nick Patterson, told him about 'non-secret encryption', an idea the GCHQ engineer James Ellis had argued was possible in 1970 but no one had made work: the receiver publishes how to lock a message, and only the receiver can unlock it. By Cocks's own account he thought about it at home one evening and found a scheme in about half an hour, using the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy but factoring the product is hard. He wrote it up in an internal note dated 20 November 1973, and it was classified. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published public-key exchange openly in 1976, and Rivest, Shamir and Adleman published essentially Cocks's scheme as RSA in 1977; GCHQ disclosed its priority only in December 1997, weeks after Ellis died.
story.puzzle: For all of history, two people needed a shared secret key before they could talk in secret. How can two strangers who have never met agree on a secret while an eavesdropper hears every word they exchange?
story.payoff: Through one-way functions. Each party keeps a private number and sends only a result that is easy to compute but infeasible to invert; the mathematics lets both arrive at the same key, while an eavesdropper would have to solve a discrete logarithm or factor a huge number. Cocks's trick is RSA's trapdoor: anyone can lock a message with the public product n, but only the holder of its two prime factors can unlock it.
sources: Simon Singh, The Code Book (Fourth Estate/Doubleday, 1999), ch. 6
J. H. Ellis, 'The History of Non-Secret Encryption' (written 1987; released by GCHQ/CESG 1997)
C. C. Cocks, 'A Note on Non-Secret Encryption' (CESG report, 20 Nov 1973; released 1997)
W. Diffie & M. E. Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), Nov 1976
R. Rivest, A. Shamir & L. Adleman, 'A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems', Communications of the ACM 21(2), 1978

days.application: The padlock in your browser. When you open your bank's website, TLS 1.3 runs an elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman exchange to agree a fresh session key and checks the bank's certificate, a chain of digital signatures from a certificate authority, before any password crosses the wire; bulk data then flows under a fast symmetric cipher such as AES. The threat: Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm would break RSA and Diffie-Hellman on a large enough quantum computer, and adversaries can record traffic now to decrypt later. NIST therefore published its first three post-quantum standards (FIPS 203, 204 and 205) on 13 August 2024, and major browsers began deploying hybrid post-quantum key exchange in 2024.

builds_on.why: Algorithms and complexity: public-key security exists only because some problems are easy one way and apparently intractable the other, and it would collapse if P = NP.

Exponentials and logarithms: the discrete logarithm undoes modular exponentiation as an ordinary logarithm undoes a power, except that 'mod p' scrambles the smooth curve that makes ordinary logs easy.

across.link: The 1990s 'crypto wars'. The US government's Clipper chip proposal (April 1993) would have given it escrowed copies of encryption keys, and US export rules treated strong encryption as a munition until they were relaxed between 1996 and 2000. Clipper was abandoned after a flaw was found and opposition grew. Once anyone can do public-key mathematics, governments must decide whether and how to seek lawful access, a question still argued today.

days.apply_question: WhatsApp says it cannot read your messages even though every one passes through its servers. Using public-key cryptography, explain how that can be true.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mathematics of Diffie-Hellman and RSA, given their assumptions. Unproven: that factoring and discrete logarithms are hard for ordinary computers; the confidence rests on decades of failed attacks, not proof. Debated: when, or whether, a quantum computer large enough to run Shor's algorithm will exist (estimates range from about a decade to never). Value judgment: whether governments should be able to access encrypted communications. The 'half an hour' is Cocks's own recollection.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.topic: Computing is physical: data centres and energy
days.headline_hint: Microsoft Signed Up for Every Watt a Restarted Three Mile Island Reactor Can Make. Software, It Turns Out, Runs on Electricity and Ends as Heat.
days.concept: Computing is a physical process. Every operation consumes electricity and ends as heat, with a theoretical minimum (Landauer's limit) far below what today's chips use, so at scale computing is limited by power supply and cooling.
days.focus: Landauer (1961): erasing one bit must dissipate at least kT ln 2, about 2.9 x 10^-21 J at room temperature (Day 55's entropy), confirmed in the laboratory (Berut et al., Nature, 2012). Real chips run many orders of magnitude above that, mostly moving data (Day 107's memory wall). By energy conservation essentially every watt a data centre draws ends as heat; cooling overhead is measured by PUE. Rack power density is climbing past 100 kW for AI hardware, forcing liquid cooling, and the round-the-clock load explains the demand for firm power. Challenge the image of a weightless 'cloud', and note that past forecasts of runaway IT power overshot.
days.model_or_equation: E_min = k_B T ln 2, about (1.38 x 10^-23 J/K)(300 K)(0.693), or 2.9 x 10^-21 J per bit erased. PUE = total facility energy divided by the energy used by the IT equipment itself. Google reports a fleet average near 1.1; the Uptime Institute's industry average is around 1.5-1.6, meaning half again as much energy for cooling and overhead.

story.title: A software company buys a nuclear reactor's whole output
story.hook: On 20 September 2024 Constellation Energy announced a 20-year agreement to supply Microsoft with the output of Three Mile Island Unit 1 in Pennsylvania. The reactor had been shut in 2019 because it could not compete on price, and its twin, Unit 2, suffered the partial meltdown of March 1979 (Day 94's story) that remains America's worst commercial nuclear accident. Constellation said it would spend about $1.6 billion to restart the roughly 835-megawatt unit, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, aiming for 2028 (it later said 2027). Microsoft's aim was to match its data centres' round-the-clock electricity use with carbon-free power.
story.puzzle: A data centre has no furnace and few moving parts; it just stores and moves information. Why would a software company need the steady output of a nuclear reactor?
story.payoff: Every bit operation dissipates energy as heat. Physics sets a floor (Landauer's limit) that is tiny, but real chips run vastly above it, and millions of processors running 24 hours a day turn hundreds of megawatts into heat that must then be pumped away, which takes more energy still. Because the load is constant, buyers value firm power from a high-capacity-factor source such as nuclear, not only intermittent sources, which is why technology companies are now signing nuclear contracts.
sources: Constellation Energy press release, 20 Sep 2024 (Crane Clean Energy Center agreement with Microsoft)
US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, 'Backgrounder on the Three Mile Island Accident'
R. Landauer, 'Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process', IBM Journal of Research and Development 5(3), 1961
A. Berut et al., 'Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics', Nature 483 (2012)

days.application: Ireland. Data centres used 21% of the country's metered electricity in 2023, up from 5% in 2015 and more than all urban households combined (Central Statistics Office, July 2024), and the grid operator EirGrid has effectively paused new data-centre connections in the Dublin area until about 2028. For US scale, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (December 2024) estimated that data centres used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 (176 TWh) and could reach 6.7-12% by 2028.

builds_on.why: Entropy: Landauer's limit is the second law applied to erasing information. Its kT ln 2 contains Boltzmann's k from Day 55's S = k log W.
Capacity factor: a constant 24-hour load values firm power, which explains why data-centre buyers seek nuclear and not only solar or wind by the gigawatt.

across.link: On 1 November 2024 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rejected, by 2-1, an amended interconnection agreement that would have let more of the Susquehanna nuclear plant's output go directly to an adjacent Amazon data-centre campus. The dissent and the commentary turned on who pays for the shared grid when big loads sit 'behind the meter'. Computing's physical appetite has become a question of utility regulation.

days.apply_question: Meta built one of its first European data centres at Lulea in northern Sweden, near the Arctic Circle and beside abundant hydropower. Using today's lesson, what physical problems does that site solve that a site in Phoenix, Arizona would not?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Landauer's bound (theory with laboratory confirmation), and that a data centre's electricity ends as heat. Debated: demand forecasts. LBNL's 2028 range spans nearly a factor of two (6.7-12%), and earlier predictions of runaway IT electricity use overshot because efficiency improved: Masanet et al. (Science, 2020) found global data-centre energy rose only about 6% from 2010 to 2018 while computing output rose about 550%. Whether AI demand will follow that pattern or a Jevons-style rebound (Day 83) is uncertain.

resource.why: The IEA's global, data-based estimate of how much electricity data centres and AI use now and could use by 2030, with the regional grid constraints and uncertainties. It adds the world picture the lesson's US and Irish figures cannot give.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.topic: Cybersecurity: attackers, surfaces and the weakest link
days.headline_hint: Ukrainian Grid Operators Watched Their Cursors Move on Their Own and Switch Off the Power. It Started With an Email Months Earlier.
days.concept: Security is a contest against an adaptive adversary. The attacker needs one way in while the defender must cover the whole attack surface, so defenders shrink that surface and layer independent defences (defence in depth) around the weakest links, which are usually credentials and people.
days.focus: Adversarial failure differs from Day 110's accidental failure: attackers deliberately seek out the rare bad state, a game (Day 14), not a dice roll. The attack surface and the usual sequence: phishing, foothold, credential theft, lateral movement, action. Defence in depth works only if the layers are independent (multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, least privilege, monitoring, offline backups). Colonial Pipeline (7 May 2021) is the one-clause example of the weakest link: a single unused VPN password without MFA, and a ransom of about $4.4 million. Kerckhoffs's principle ties back to Day 112: a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public.
days.model_or_equation: Defence in depth as probability. If an attacker must defeat three independent layers, each stopping 90% of attempts, the chance of getting through is 0.1^3 = 1 in 1,000. But layers that all accept the same stolen password are not independent (a common mode, Day 93), and an adaptive attacker keeps probing until he finds the layer that fails, so the real figure can approach the weakest layer's alone.

story.title: The cursor that moved by itself in Ivano-Frankivsk
story.hook: Late in the afternoon of 23 December 2015, in the control room of Prykarpattyaoblenergo, the power distributor for the Ivano-Frankivsk region of western Ukraine, an operator watched the cursor on his screen glide across the grid-control software and start clicking circuit breakers open, substation after substation. When he grabbed the mouse it would not respond, and he was logged out. Within about half an hour attackers had cut power at dozens of substations across three distribution companies, leaving about 225,000 customers without electricity, in winter, for one to six hours. They also flooded the utilities' phone lines so customers could not report outages, wiped computers, and overwrote firmware on network devices so crews had to restore substations by hand. Investigators traced the intrusion to spear-phishing emails with booby-trapped Office attachments (BlackEnergy malware) sent months earlier, and in 2020 the US Justice Department indicted officers of the Russian GRU unit known as Sandworm.
story.puzzle: The control systems sat on separate networks behind firewalls, and nothing had to be physically broken. How did attackers reach in from outside and flip the switches themselves, and why did one email months earlier matter more than any firewall?
story.payoff: The attackers did not break through a wall; they walked through doors. A phishing email gave them a foothold on the business network, and stolen passwords let them log into the remote-access link to the control network, which asked for no second factor. From there they used the operators' own control software. Every layer the defenders relied on shared one weak link, the password, so the depth was an illusion. Against an adversary, security means the whole attack surface and genuinely independent layers, because the attacker chooses the weakest path.
sources: E-ISAC and SANS ICS, 'Analysis of the Cyber Attack on the Ukrainian Power Grid' (18 Mar 2016)
Kim Zetter, 'Inside the Cunning, Unprecedented Hack of Ukraine's Power Grid', Wired (3 Mar 2016)
US Department of Justice, indictment of six GRU officers (19 Oct 2020)
Andy Greenberg, Sandworm (Doubleday, 2019)

days.application: The 2015 Jeep Cherokee hack. Security researchers Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek got in through the Uconnect infotainment system's cellular connection (a port left open on Sprint's network), then rewrote the firmware of a chip that bridged to the CAN bus carrying commands for the engine, brakes and transmission. With Wired's Andy Greenberg at the wheel on Interstate 64 near St. Louis, they cut his acceleration remotely (published 21 July 2015). Chrysler recalled about 1.4 million vehicles on 24 July, the first car recall for cybersecurity, and Sprint closed the port. On the car chain this runs from engineering (an infotainment unit connected to the drive network) to regulation: UNECE Regulation No. 155 has required certified cybersecurity management for new vehicle types in the EU since July 2022, and for all new vehicles since July 2024.

builds_on.why: Game theory: an attacker picks a best response to the defences, so the defender must anticipate strategy, not random faults.
How software fails: attackers exploit the same latent design faults, deliberately driving the system into the rare state that testing missed.

across.link: The Tallinn Manual (2013; 2.0 in 2017), written by international-law experts under the auspices of NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, sets out how existing international law, including the law on the use of force and on armed conflict, applies to state cyber operations. State-sponsored attacks like Sandworm's on Ukraine's grid are the cases it was written for.

days.apply_question: A hospital forces staff to change passwords every 60 days, has no multi-factor authentication, and lets one login reach both e-mail and the patient-records system. Using attack surface and defence in depth, which weakness matters most, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the technical sequence of the 2015 Ukraine attack (E-ISAC and SANS, 2016). Attribution: the US and UK attribute it to the GRU's Sandworm unit (US indictment, 2020); attribution relies partly on evidence not made public. Reported numbers vary: about 225,000 customers is the usual figure, and the outage durations ranged from about one to six hours. Debated practice: forced periodic password changes, which NIST's guidance (SP 800-63B, 2017) advises against.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Computing
days.headline_hint: 'Just a Hobby, Won't Be Big': A Student's 1991 Post Became the Code Running All 500 of the World's Fastest Supercomputers.
days.concept: Open-source software is commons-based peer production: volunteers and firms build shared code that anyone may use, study and change, coordinated by licences and reputation rather than ownership or command. It is enormously productive but prone to under-maintaining the unglamorous parts everyone depends on.
days.focus: Benkler's 'Coase's Penguin' (2002) names a third way to organize production, beside markets and firms. Why people and companies contribute: learning, reputation, their own needs, and profits from complementary products. Licences as Ostrom-style rules (Day 30): the GPL's copyleft, maintainers who review, norms that sanction. Code is non-rival, so the danger is not Hardin's over-grazing but under-provision of maintenance, a public-goods problem (Day 14): Heartbleed in OpenSSL (2014), run by a handful of people on about $2,000 a year in donations. Challenge the reflex that a commons must end in tragedy, and its mirror image, that 'free' means costless.

story.title: 'Just a hobby, won't be big and professional'
story.hook: On 25 August 1991 Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old computer-science student at the University of Helsinki, posted to the Usenet group comp.os.minix: 'I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones.' He asked what features people would like. He released the code that autumn, and in 1992 put it under the GNU General Public License, which lets anyone use and change the code on condition that they share their changes on the same terms. By November 2017 every one of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers ran Linux; it also underlies Android and most of the servers behind the web. Today most kernel changes come from engineers paid by companies, many of them rivals, who give the work away.
story.puzzle: No one owns Linux, no one can be ordered to work on it, and fiercely competing companies give their code away to it. Why did that produce some of the most reliable software on Earth instead of a tragedy of the commons?
story.payoff: Code is non-rival: using it does not use it up, so the classic commons problem of over-use never arises. Peer production works when work can be split into small modular pieces, when contributions are cheap to make and easy to check, and when rules (the GPL, maintainers' review, reputation) settle Ostrom's governance problems. Firms contribute because they profit from complements such as hardware, cloud services and support. The danger lies where those incentives are missing: dull, critical components looked after by one or two volunteers.
sources: Linus Torvalds, post to comp.os.minix, 25 Aug 1991 (Google Groups Usenet archive)
Linus Torvalds & David Diamond, Just for Fun (HarperBusiness, 2001)
TOP500 list, November 2017 (operating-system share)
Yochai Benkler, 'Coase's Penguin, or, Linux and The Nature of the Firm', Yale Law Journal 112 (2002)

days.application: The xz Utils backdoor. On 29 March 2024 Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer and PostgreSQL developer, reported that SSH logins on a test Debian system were using unusual CPU and taking about half a second longer. He traced the delay to a backdoor hidden in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 of xz Utils, a compression library maintained essentially by one volunteer, Lasse Collin. A contributor calling himself 'Jia Tan' had built trust since 2021 while apparent sock-puppet accounts pressured Collin, who had mentioned burnout and limited capacity, to share maintenance. Assigned CVE-2024-3094 with the maximum severity score of 10, it was caught before it reached most stable Linux releases.

builds_on.why: The commons: Hardin's over-use and Ostrom's design principles, applied to a resource that cannot be over-grazed but can be under-maintained.

Game theory: funding shared maintenance is a public-goods dilemma in which everyone gains if someone pays and each is tempted to free-ride; repeated interaction and reputation (Axelrod) help sustain cooperation.

across.link: Copyleft uses copyright law to guarantee sharing rather than restrict it. In Jacobsen v. Katzer (Federal Circuit, 2008) the court held that the conditions of an open-source licence (the Artistic License) are enforceable copyright conditions, not mere contractual promises. The legal rule is what makes the commons' boundary enforceable.

days.apply_question: Wikipedia, like Linux, is built by volunteers under an open licence. Using commons-based peer production, which kinds of Wikipedia articles would you expect to be well maintained and which neglected, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Linux's spread (TOP500 data) and the facts of the xz incident (Freund's disclosure, CVE-2024-3094). Debated: who 'Jia Tan' was (many analysts suspect a state-backed operation, but no attribution has been confirmed), and how open-source maintenance should be funded (foundations, corporate programmes, or public money such as Germany's Sovereign Tech Fund, launched in 2022).

resource.why: The report that brought the maintenance problem of open-source infrastructure to wide attention, explaining with real cases why widely used projects can rest on a few unpaid people. It adds the funding and governance side of today's commons.

days.phase: Computing: Information Machines
days.subject: Systems Case
days.headline_hint: The Internet's Ancestor Sent Its First Message in 1969. It Was 'LO.' Then the System Crashed.
days.concept: How did a four-node research network for sharing computers become infrastructure for about 5.5 billion people, and who governs it now that no single government does?
days.focus: Walk the internet through Logan's chain as a loop. The deep links are those this block and earlier ones taught: packet switching and end-to-end design, bits and bandwidth, network hubs, cryptography, security, the physical footprint and S-curve adoption. Public funding, Section 230, social effects and international governance are previews. Show the documented reversal, invention before need (e-mail, not computer sharing, became the ARPANET's main use), and the loop by which openness enabled growth and growth produced concentration.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, network effects: more users make the network more useful, which brings more users (Day 26). R2, permissionless innovation: open layers invite new applications (e-mail, the web, video), which bring more users and more investment in capacity. B1, congestion: more traffic causes delay and packet loss, TCP backs off, and operators add capacity. R3, concentration: preferential attachment makes the big hubs, networks and platforms bigger (Day 13), the internet's open design feeding its own centralization. R4, an attack-and-defence arms race: more value online draws more attacks, which spur encryption and security (Days 112, 114). Documented reversal: invention before need. E-mail (1971) was not in the plan.

story.title: 'LO' - and then the crash
story.hook: On the evening of 29 October 1969, in Boelter Hall at UCLA, the student programmer Charley Kline sat at a terminal connected to an Interface Message Processor, a ruggedized Honeywell minicomputer programmed by Bolt Beranek and Newman, which was linked by a leased 50-kilobit-per-second line to a second IMP at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, more than 300 miles to the north. Under Leonard Kleinrock's supervision, Kline began typing LOGIN while Bill Duvall at SRI confirmed each letter by telephone. The 'L' arrived, then the 'O'; at the 'G' the SRI system crashed. Later that night they got through, and the handwritten IMP log records 'talked to SRI host to host'. By December 1969 the ARPANET had four nodes.
story.puzzle: How did a four-node network built to share scarce research computers become infrastructure for about 5.5 billion people? And why, having been paid for by governments, is it governed by no single government?
story.payoff: Packet switching and end-to-end design (Day 111) let anyone add networks and applications without asking permission. Uses nobody planned, first e-mail and then the web, drove adoption up an S-curve (Day 7). Network effects reinforced growth while preferential attachment concentrated traffic into a few hubs and platforms (Day 13). Governance followed the architecture: open technical standards through the IETF's 'rough consensus and running code', and names and numbers through ICANN (1998), whose US government oversight ended in 2016, with states now pushing back.
sources: Leonard Kleinrock, accounts of 29 Oct 1969 (UCLA Samueli School of Engineering; Kleinrock Internet Heritage Site), including the IMP log entry
Katie Hafner & Matthew Lyon, Where Wizards Stay Up Late: The Origins of the Internet (Simon & Schuster, 1996)
Barry M. Leiner et al., 'A Brief History of the Internet' (Internet Society)
ITU, Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures 2024

days.application: The internet itself, traced through Logan's chain as a loop: from four ARPANET nodes at the end of 1969 to about 5.5 billion users (68% of humanity) in the ITU's 2024 count, with about 2.6 billion people still offline.

builds_on.why: Packet switching, layering and the end-to-end principle are the internet's architecture, the reason anyone could build on it without permission.
Networks: hubs and preferential attachment explain both the internet's robustness to random failure and its concentration into a few dominant nodes and platforms.
Logistic S-curves: internet adoption is a textbook diffusion S-curve, whose ceiling (the 2.6 billion offline) is the policy question.
Bits and channel capacity: the climb from 50-kilobit lines to fibre carrying many terabits per second is the physical constraint that every application rode.

across.link: Romualdo Pastor-Satorras and Alessandro Vespignani ('Epidemic Spreading in Scale-Free Networks', Physical Review Letters, 2001) showed, using data on computer viruses, that on networks with the internet's hub-dominated structure an infection can persist even when it spreads weakly: the epidemic threshold effectively vanishes. It is the same mathematics epidemiologists use for disease spreading through human contact networks, and it explains why internet worms linger and why protecting hubs matters most.

days.apply_question: Kenya's M-Pesa mobile-money service (launched 2007) was first piloted as a way to repay microloans. Using the chain as a loop, trace how M-Pesa, like the ARPANET with e-mail, found its main need only after it was invented.
days.evidence_note: Evidence check (mandatory). Settled: the 1969 timeline, the architecture, and the ITU's 2024 counts (about 5.5 billion online, about 2.6 billion offline, concentrated in low-income countries). Accounts differ on the exact hour of the first message: Kleinrock usually puts the 'LO' at about 10:30 p.m., while the IMP log's 22:30 entry records the successful host-to-host connection, so say 'that evening'. Debated, naming the sides: (1) how much credit public funding deserves (Mariana Mazzucato, The Entrepreneurial State, 2013, against critics such as Deirdre McCloskey and Alberto Mingardi, The Myth of the Entrepreneurial State, 2020); (2) the internet's net effects on well-being and democracy, including teen mental health (Haidt and Twenge against Odgers, Orben and Przybylski; taught in Psychology); (3) the often-cited 1973 finding that e-mail was about three-quarters of ARPANET traffic, which should be given as 'often cited'. Value judgment: who gained (users, platform owners, the economies that adopted early), who paid (taxpayers who funded the early research; victims of fraud, surveillance and harassment), and who consented (users to data collection under terms few read). A Rawlsian reading asks whether the digital divide leaves the worst-off behind; Catholic social teaching's universal destination of goods asks a similar question in different terms. Keep the counterfactual of a world without the internet marked as unknowable.

chain.point: In 1966 Bob Taylor, head of ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, had three terminals in his Pentagon office for three incompatible research computers. The need was to share scarce, expensive machines; by Taylor's account ARPA director Charles Herzfeld gave him about $1 million in a meeting of some twenty minutes.

Packet switching (Baran 1964, Davies 1965), BBN's IMPs (1969), TCP/IP (Cerf and Kahn, 1974; adopted network-wide on 1 January 1983), then Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web (proposed at CERN in March 1989, public in 1991, released by CERN into the public domain on 30 April 1993).

Bandwidth is bounded by channel capacity (Day 104): from 50 kbit/s lines in 1969 to fibres carrying many terabits per second, carried on infrared light (Day 61). Latency is bounded by light in glass, about 200,000 km/s, so a New York to London round trip through fibre can never beat about 55 ms. Energy and heat appear in data centres (Day 113).

Layering and the end-to-end principle keep the core simple. The resulting hub-dominated structure is robust to random failures but fragile to attacks on hubs (Albert, Jeong & Barabasi, Nature, 2000). Submarine cables carry the great majority of intercontinental traffic, redundant paths matter (Days 13, 93), and Tonga's single cable showed the cost of having none.

chain.field: Financing (named at CFA level; no block teaches it)
chain.point: Public money built the core: ARPA funded the ARPANET, and the NSF funded NSFNET (1985-95) as the backbone. Congress allowed commercial traffic in 1992, the NSFNET backbone was retired on 30 April 1995, and private carriers took over; today hyperscalers' capital spending funds the cables and data centres. Name the mechanism; do not teach finance.

Light-touch rules shaped what grew: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) shields platforms from liability for most user posts, a choice the Law block takes up with intermediary liability and the Collingridge dilemma.

A diffusion S-curve (Day 7): tens of millions of users in the mid-1990s, about a billion in the mid-2000s, about 5.5 billion (68%) in 2024 (ITU). The remaining 2.6 billion are concentrated in low-income countries, where only about a quarter of people are online.

Openness invited attack: from the Morris worm (1988) to state operations like Sandworm's (Day 114), with encryption (Day 112) spreading in response so that most web traffic now runs over HTTPS. The physical footprint grows with use (Day 113).

Effects on teenage mental health are contested (Haidt and Twenge against Odgers, Orben and Przybylski), as is how far false news outruns true news (Vosoughi, Roy & Aral, 2018). These are taught in Psychology's social-media case and Sociology's media-effects lesson.

Governance follows the architecture: the IETF sets open standards, and ICANN (1998) manages names and numbers, with US government oversight of IANA ending on 1 October 2016. States push back with national firewalls and Russia's 2019 'sovereign internet' law, the 'splinternet' that the International Relations block takes up with chokepoints and international institutions.

Ray Tomlinson's network e-mail (1971) was not in the ARPANET's plan, yet by an often-cited 1973 estimate it made up about three-quarters of the traffic. The users found the need after the invention, the reverse of the chain's textbook order, and openness then drove growth that ended in concentration into a few platforms.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: In 1774 the Astronomer Royal Camped on a Scottish Mountain to Weigh the Earth. The Mountain Tugged His Plumb Lines About 1/300 of a Degree.
days.concept: One inverse-square law of attraction between all masses explains the falling apple, the Moon's orbit and the tides, and it lets a small measured pull reveal a planet's mass.
days.focus: Teach F = Gm1m2/r^2 as one law covering Earth, Moon and tides, and show how comparing two pulls weighs whole bodies, from Schiehallion to the GRACE satellites. Tides come from the difference in pull across a body, which falls off as distance cubed.
days.model_or_equation: F = G m1 m2 / r^2 (G ≈ 6.674 × 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2); tidal acceleration across a body of radius R from a mass M at distance d ≈ 2GMR/d^3

story.title: A plumb line on Schiehallion that leaned toward a mountain
story.hook: In summer 1774 Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, camped for about four months on Schiehallion in Perthshire, a mountain chosen for its regular shape, to test whether a mountain's mass would pull a plumb line off the vertical. He fixed the true vertical from the stars at stations on the mountain's north and south flanks and found the plumb lines leaning toward the mountain by a combined 11.6 seconds of arc, about a three-hundredth of a degree. The mathematician Charles Hutton then turned a survey of the mountain into a volume by slicing it into horizontal layers, the method that made him an early user of contour lines. His result, read to the Royal Society on 21 May 1778 (printed in 1779), put Earth's mean density at about 4.5 times that of water.
story.puzzle: How can a sideways tug from one Scottish hill, too small to see without a star, tell you what the entire Earth weighs?
story.payoff: The same inverse-square law pulls the plumb bob down toward Earth's centre and sideways toward the hill, so the ratio of the two pulls, corrected for distance, gives the ratio of the two masses. Know the hill's volume and rock density and Earth's mass and mean density follow. Hutton's 4.5, far above the roughly 2.5 he assumed for the mountain's rock, led him to infer a dense, probably metallic, interior (the modern value is 5.5).
sources: Maskelyne, N. (1775) 'An Account of Observations Made on the Mountain Schehallien for Finding Its Attraction', Philosophical Transactions 65
Hutton, C. (1778) 'An Account of the Calculations Made from the Survey and Measures Taken at Schehallien', Philosophical Transactions 68 (read 21 May 1778; printed 1779)
Royal Society blog, 'Song of Schiehallion' (2022)
MacTutor Mathematical Gazetteer, 'Schiehallion, Perthshire' (University of St Andrews)

days.application: GRACE (2002-2017) and GRACE-FO (2018-) are twin satellites about 220 km apart whose separation, measured to micrometres, changes as each passes over extra mass. Rodell, Velicogna & Famiglietti (Nature 460, 2009) used them to show groundwater in Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana (including Delhi) falling about 4.0 cm of water a year (17.7 km^3/yr), a net loss of 109 km^3 between August 2002 and October 2008, with near-normal rainfall: irrigation pumping, weighed from orbit.

builds_on.why: Newton's second law turns the gravitational force into the acceleration that makes the apple fall and the Moon curve.
The inverse-square law is a power law, a straight line on a log-log plot, and the cube law for tides comes from the same scaling reasoning.

across.link: The La Rance tidal power station in Brittany (opened 1966, 240 MW) harvests tides raised by the 1/d^3 differential pull of the Moon and Sun; the energy itself comes mostly from Earth's rotation, which tidal friction very slowly brakes, a useful distinction between the force that drives a flow and the store that pays for it.

days.apply_question: The Sun pulls on Earth roughly 180 times harder than the Moon does, yet the Sun raises tides less than half as high as the Moon's. Using how gravity changes with distance, explain why.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Newtonian gravity is exact enough for everything in this lesson (relativity matters only for precise clocks, Day 62). Hedge: Hutton is often credited with inventing contour lines, but depth contours (isobaths) on maps predate him, e.g. Cruquius in 1729.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: Sputnik Fell Toward Earth for 92 Days Straight. It Kept Missing.
days.concept: An orbit is free fall with enough sideways speed that the ground curves away as fast as you fall (about 7.8 km/s near Earth); higher orbits are slower, and Kepler's laws follow from the inverse-square law.
days.focus: Use Newton's cannonball to show that orbiting is falling, derive circular speed from gravity supplying the centripetal pull, and read Kepler's third law as the rule that higher means slower. Explain why astronauts float where gravity is still about 90% of surface strength and why the geostationary belt sits 35,786 km up.
days.model_or_equation: v_circ = sqrt(GM/r); period T = 2π sqrt(a^3/GM), so T^2 ∝ a^3 (Kepler's third law)

story.title: An 83.6 kg ball that fell for three months
story.hook: On 4 October 1957 an R-7 rocket lifted off from Tyuratam in Soviet Kazakhstan and released Sputnik 1, a polished 83.6 kg sphere with four antennas, into an orbit roughly 215 by 939 km high. It circled the Earth every 96.2 minutes, and its radio beeps at 20.005 and 40.002 MHz could be picked up by amateur operators around the world until its batteries died about three weeks later. Most people who 'saw Sputnik' at dusk were in fact watching the rocket's much larger core stage, which travelled the same path. Sputnik had no engine once released, yet it stayed up until it burned up on 4 January 1958.
story.puzzle: With nothing holding it up, Sputnik was being pulled toward Earth the whole time. Why did it take 92 days to come down, and why did it come down at all?
story.payoff: Sputnik was falling every second, but at about 7.8 km/s sideways the curved Earth dropped away beneath it as fast as it fell: that is what an orbit is. It came down because its low point, about 215 km up, dipped through thin upper air: on each pass drag removed a little orbital energy, which lowered the orbit into denser air (and, paradoxically, made the satellite move faster), until it re-entered and burned up.
sources: NASA NSSDC Master Catalog, Sputnik 1 (COSPAR 1957-001B)
Roger D. Launius, 'Sputnik and the Origins of the Space Age', NASA History Office
Arthur C. Clarke, 'Extra-Terrestrial Relays', Wireless World, October 1945

days.application: Two real cases. On the ISS, about 400 km up, gravity is still roughly 89% of its surface value; the crew floats because station and crew fall together at the same rate (free fall), not because gravity is absent. And Arthur C. Clarke's 1945 Wireless World article proposed three relay stations at the one altitude, about 36,000 km (35,786 km) above the equator, where an orbit takes exactly one sidereal day, so a satellite hangs over one spot: the geostationary belt that now carries broadcast and weather satellites.

builds_on.why: The inverse-square force from yesterday supplies the centripetal pull that bends the path into an orbit and sets the speed at each altitude.
An orbit is two velocity components combined: the sideways speed and the fall; vector reasoning shows how the path curves while the speed stays the same.

across.link: Sputnik triggered the creation of ARPA (Department of Defense Directive 5105.15, 7 February 1958), the agency that later funded the ARPANET in the internet case (Day 116): a causal path from an orbit to a network.

days.apply_question: The Hubble Space Telescope has no engine of its own and slowly loses height to drag, so NASA has studied using a visiting spacecraft to boost it higher. Explain why giving Hubble extra speed would leave it in a higher orbit where it moves more slowly than before.
days.evidence_note: Settled physics. Hedge on priority: Clarke popularised the geostationary relay idea, but the orbit itself had been described earlier (Herman Potočnik, 1928), so the brief should not call Clarke its discoverer.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: The solar system: a disk, its leftovers and impacts
days.headline_hint: A Comet Hit Jupiter 21 Times in Six Days. The Biggest Blow Left a Dark Ring the Size of Earth.
days.concept: The planets formed from a flattened, spinning disk of gas and dust around the young Sun, which is why they orbit in one plane with rocky worlds inside and giants outside, and the disk's leftovers, asteroids and comets, still strike planets at rates that fall steeply with size.
days.focus: Explain the nebular disk (spin plus collapse flattens a cloud; the frost line splits rock from ice and gas) and then the leftovers: impacts as a power-law, fat-tailed hazard where small hits are common and huge ones rare but dominant. Close on how Earth's own record was read, from the Alvarez iridium layer to Chicxulub.
days.model_or_equation: Impact energy E = ½mv^2 at typical Earth-impact speeds of about 11-72 km/s; the number of impactors larger than diameter D falls roughly as a power of D, so each tenfold increase in size means far fewer, but far more energetic, impacts

story.title: Twenty-one fragments in a row, heading for Jupiter
story.hook: On films taken at Palomar Observatory in March 1993, Carolyn Shoemaker spotted a strange 'squashed' comet; with Eugene Shoemaker and David Levy she had found Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9, a comet Jupiter had captured into orbit, probably decades earlier, and had torn into a string of fragments during a close pass in July 1992. Between 16 and 22 July 1994 the fragments struck Jupiter one after another, 21 impacts in about six days, watched by the Hubble Space Telescope and observatories worldwide. The largest, from fragment G on 18 July, released energy Eugene Shoemaker estimated at about 6 million megatons of TNT and left a dark impact site whose outer ring was roughly as wide as Earth.
story.puzzle: The planets finished forming about 4.6 billion years ago. Why is there still enough debris flying around to hit a planet this hard, and how often should Earth expect the same?
story.payoff: Planet formation was never tidy: the disk left vast numbers of small bodies in the asteroid belt and in the icy outer reaches, and gravitational nudges from Jupiter keep sending some inward. Because impact frequency falls steeply with size, small strikes happen constantly and SL9-scale ones are rare, but over geological time the rare giants do most of the damage, which is why Chicxulub matters.
sources: NASA / STScI Hubble image release 1994-33, 'Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 Impact Sites on Jupiter' (1994)
The Moscow Times (July 1994), quoting Eugene Shoemaker's energy estimates (G about 6 million megatons; all fragments about 40 million)
Levy, D.H. (1995) Impact Jupiter: The Crash of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9, Plenum Press
Alvarez, L.W., Alvarez, W., Asaro, F. & Michel, H.V. (1980) 'Extraterrestrial Cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary Extinction', Science 208
Hildebrand, A.R. et al. (1991) 'Chicxulub Crater: A possible Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary impact crater on the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico', Geology 19

days.application: Luis and Walter Alvarez's team (Science, 6 June 1980) found iridium, rare in Earth's crust but common in meteorites, concentrated in the thin clay layer at the end of the Cretaceous, first at Gubbio in Italy, and argued an asteroid about 10 km across ended the dinosaurs. The idea was resisted for a decade until the buried Chicxulub crater, about 180 km wide, under Mexico's Yucatán, first noticed in oil-exploration data by Pemex geophysicists Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo, was identified as the impact site (Hildebrand et al., Geology 1991). Today the US surveys near-Earth objects under the George E. Brown Jr. Near-Earth Object Survey Act (2005), whose goal is to find 90% of objects 140 m and larger; its 2020 target date was missed, and NASA's NEO Surveyor telescope is being built to close the gap.

builds_on.why: Kepler's laws and gravitational nudges explain why leftovers stay in belts and how Jupiter can redirect them toward the inner planets.
Impact sizes follow a fat-tailed, power-law distribution, so the largest event on record understates the next rare giant.

across.link: The end-Cretaceous extinction about 66 million years ago, tied to Chicxulub, removed roughly three-quarters of species including all non-avian dinosaurs, after which mammals diversified rapidly: biologists treat it as a natural experiment in extinction and recovery.

days.apply_question: Asteroids about 20 m across, like the one that burst over Chelyabinsk, Russia, on 15 February 2013 and injured about 1,500 people, arrive far more often than 10 km giants. Using how impact frequency and energy change with size, explain why a 2005 US law set its survey goal at objects 140 m and larger, rather than at the smallest objects or only the largest.
days.evidence_note: Settled: formation from a disk in outline, and an impact at Chicxulub at the end of the Cretaceous. Debated: how much of the extinction the impact explains versus the Deccan Traps eruptions (Schulte et al., Science 2010, for the impact as primary cause; Gerta Keller and others for volcanism), and details of planet formation such as giant-planet migration.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: The New York Times Said Goddard's Rocket Couldn't Work in a Vacuum. It Apologized 49 Years Later, Three Days Before the Moon Landing.
days.concept: A rocket's change in speed equals its exhaust speed times the natural logarithm of its starting-to-final mass ratio, so extra speed costs exponentially more propellant, most of a rocket is propellant, and staging helps.
days.focus: Derive the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation from momentum conservation and show its tyranny: reaching orbit needs about 9-10 km/s with exhaust at 3-4.5 km/s, so a single stage would be over 90% propellant. Staging throws away dead mass; exhaust speed (specific impulse) comes from propellant chemistry.
days.model_or_equation: Δv = v_e ln(m0/mf), where v_e is exhaust speed, m0 the mass with propellant and mf the mass when it is burned

story.title: Two and a half seconds over a cabbage field
story.hook: On 16 March 1926, on his aunt Effie Ward's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard lit the world's first liquid-fuelled rocket, a spindly frame of gasoline and liquid oxygen about 10 feet tall. It flew for 2.5 seconds, rose 41 feet and landed 184 feet away in a cabbage field. Six years earlier, on 13 January 1920, a New York Times editorial had mocked Goddard's 1919 Smithsonian paper on reaching 'extreme altitudes', saying he seemed to lack 'the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools' because a rocket would have nothing to push against in a vacuum. On 17 July 1969, with Apollo 11 on its way to the Moon, the Times printed a correction: 'The Times regrets the error.'
story.puzzle: Grant that a rocket works in a vacuum. Why, then, did reaching the Moon take a roughly 2,900-tonne machine that sent only about 1.5% of its own launch mass toward the Moon?
story.payoff: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, which is why the Times was wrong (momentum, Day 51). But every kilogram of propellant must first be carried and accelerated by the propellant burned before it, so speed grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio: each extra km/s multiplies the propellant needed. That is why Saturn V was mostly propellant and was built in three stages, each discarded when empty.
sources: NASA History, '95 Years Ago: Goddard's First Liquid-Fueled Rocket' (2021)
Goddard, R.H. (1919) 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes', Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections 71(2)
New York Times, 'Topics of the Times' editorial, 13 Jan 1920, and 'A Correction', 17 Jul 1969

days.application: Saturn V: about 2,800-3,000 tonnes on the pad (NASA's nominal figure 6.5 million lb, about 2,950 t) to send roughly 45 tonnes (NASA's nominal 99,000 lb trans-lunar capability) of spacecraft toward the Moon. A worked example: with about 9.4 km/s needed to reach low orbit including gravity and drag losses and kerosene-oxygen exhaust near 3.3 km/s, a single stage would need m0/mf = e^(9.4/3.3) ≈ 17, so about 94% of it would be propellant, before any structure or payload.

builds_on.why: Momentum conservation is the rocket's whole mechanism: the exhaust's backward momentum equals the vehicle's forward gain, with or without air.
The equation is a logarithm; inverting it, the mass ratio grows exponentially with the speed you want.

across.link: Exhaust speed is set by propellant chemistry: hydrogen-oxygen engines such as the Space Shuttle's RS-25 reach about 450 s vacuum specific impulse against roughly 300-350 s for kerosene engines in vacuum, because the light water-vapour exhaust moves faster, yet liquid hydrogen's very low energy per litre (Day 70) makes the tanks huge.

days.apply_question: As planned for NASA's Artemis programme, SpaceX's Starship lunar lander is to be refuelled in Earth orbit by a series of tanker launches before it heads for the Moon. Use the rocket equation to explain why refilling in orbit can be worth many extra launches.

resource.why: An astronaut-engineer's plain-language account of why the logarithm dominates every design choice in spaceflight.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Reusability and the cost of reaching orbit
days.headline_hint: The Reusable Space Shuttle Cost About $54,500 a Kilogram to Orbit. In 2015 a Booster Came Back Standing Up, and the Math Changed.
days.concept: Launch cost per kilogram is the master variable of spaceflight, and reusing hardware lowers it only when refurbishment is cheap and flights are frequent enough to spread fixed costs.
days.focus: Build a simple cost-per-kilogram model (fixed costs per flight, refurbishment, expended parts, propellant) and use it to explain both the Shuttle's failure and Falcon 9's success. Show how cheaper launch changed what is worth putting in orbit, from constellations to small satellites.
key_concepts: fixed versus marginal cost per flight
days.model_or_equation: Cost per kg ≈ (fixed programme costs ÷ flights per year + refurbishment + expended hardware + propellant) ÷ payload mass

story.title: A first stage that came back standing up
story.hook: On the evening of 21 December 2015 a SpaceX Falcon 9 launched 11 ORBCOMM communications satellites from Cape Canaveral. About ten minutes later its roughly 40-metre first stage, the part that on every earlier orbital launch had been discarded (or, for the Space Shuttle's solid boosters, fished out of the sea and rebuilt), relit its engines, fell back through the atmosphere and landed upright at Landing Zone 1, a few miles down the coast from the pad. A month earlier Blue Origin's New Shepard had landed upright after a suborbital hop, but this was the first booster from an orbital launch to come back. The stage is most of a rocket's cost, while the propellant is a small fraction. Yet NASA had already flown a largely reusable vehicle for 30 years, and the Shuttle's cost per kilogram was among the highest of any launcher.
story.puzzle: If reusing the most expensive part is the obvious way to cut cost, why did the reusable Space Shuttle cost more per kilogram than throwaway rockets, and what made the Falcon 9 different?
story.payoff: Reuse pays only if the reused part is cheap to turn around and flies often. The Shuttle needed months of inspection and rebuilding per flight and flew about 4-5 times a year on a huge standing workforce, so fixed costs swamped any saving (Pielke & Byerly put the programme near $1.5 billion per flight). Falcon 9 boosters need little refurbishment and fly many times, at a high cadence, so fixed costs are spread thin.
sources: SpaceX ORBCOMM-2 mission and first-stage landing, 21 Dec 2015
Jones, H.W. (2018) 'The Recent Large Reduction in Space Launch Cost', 48th International Conference on Environmental Systems, ICES-2018-81
Pielke, R. Jr & Byerly, R. (2011) 'Shuttle programme lifetime cost', Nature 472

days.application: Harry Jones of NASA Ames (2018) estimated launch cost per kg to low orbit at roughly $54,500 for the Shuttle and about $2,720 for Falcon 9 (from list prices, inflation-adjusted), with Falcon Heavy lower still. Cheap, frequent launch helped make constellations of thousands of satellites, such as SpaceX's own Starlink, economically possible, and individual boosters have now flown more than 20 times each.

builds_on.why: The rocket equation is why stages are big and why landing propellant eats payload: reuse trades some payload for recovering the stage.
Learning curves: flying the same hardware often drives down unit costs, the effect the Shuttle's low flight rate never reached.

across.link: NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services programme (2006) paid SpaceX fixed-price milestone payments (about $396 million) instead of cost-plus contracts; a 2011 NASA cost-model study estimated that developing Falcon 9 the traditional way would have cost roughly $1.7-4 billion, a case of contract design changing incentives.

days.apply_question: An airliner flies several times a day for decades, while even a reused rocket booster flies a few dozen times. Using today's cost model, explain which costs airlines have nearly eliminated that rockets still pay, and what that suggests about how low launch prices can go.
days.evidence_note: Settled: launch prices per kg fell sharply in the 2010s. Debated: SpaceX's internal costs are private, so prices are not costs, and analysts disagree on how much of the fall is due to reuse versus vertical integration, fixed-price contracting and Starlink demand keeping cadence high.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: Kennedy Promised the Moon in 1961. Eighteen Months Later He Told NASA's Chief: 'I'm Not That Interested in Space.'
days.concept: Apollo was a mission-driven state megaproject chosen for prestige in a superpower contest; its technical success was real, while its wider economic payoffs are often exaggerated (spin-off myths), though careful studies find real if modest gains concentrated in space-related manufacturing.
days.focus: Show why Kennedy chose the Moon (after Gagarin and the Bay of Pigs, a goal the US could plausibly win first), what made the programme work (a single clear goal, urgency, money, a central agency) and how to judge its payoffs with evidence rather than myth. Contrast Artemis and SLS.

story.title: A president who said he wasn't that interested in space
story.hook: On 25 May 1961, six weeks after Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight and five weeks after the Bay of Pigs fiasco, John F. Kennedy told a joint session of Congress that the nation should commit itself to 'landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the earth' before the decade was out, warning that it would be costly. On 21 November 1962, in a White House meeting recorded on tape, Kennedy pressed NASA administrator James Webb to make beating the Soviets the top priority: 'Otherwise we shouldn't be spending this kind of money because I'm not that interested in space.' By 1966 NASA was taking more than 4% of the federal budget.
story.puzzle: Why would a president who was 'not that interested in space' commit the country to one of the costliest peacetime projects in its history?
story.payoff: Apollo was a political project first: a visible race the US could win, chosen to restore prestige in a Cold War contest of systems. That explains its shape (a fixed goal and deadline, money no object for a decade) and its sudden end once the race was won, with budgets falling and the last three planned landings cancelled.
sources: Kennedy, 'Special Message to the Congress on Urgent National Needs', 25 May 1961 (JFK Presidential Library)
Presidential recording, meeting with James Webb, 21 Nov 1962 (JFK Library; released 2001)
Logsdon, J.M. (2010) John F. Kennedy and the Race to the Moon, Palgrave Macmillan

days.application: Apollo cost $25.8 billion as reported to Congress in 1973, roughly $257 billion in 2020 dollars (Dreier, Space Policy 2022), with NASA peaking at over 4% of federal spending in 1966. Popular spin-off claims are mostly myths (Tang, Velcro and Teflon predate or came from outside NASA), but Kantor & Whalley ('Moonshot: Public R&D and Growth', NBER working paper 2023; American Economic Review 2025) use the Space Race spending surge as a natural experiment and find that NASA contractor R&D raised value added, employment and capital in space-related manufacturing, effects they describe as modest. Compare the Artemis programme: NASA's Inspector General (2021) estimated $93 billion through FY2025 and about $4.1 billion per SLS/Orion launch.

builds_on.why: Spin-off claims assume a one-way flow from a programme's research to consumer products, the 'linear model' Day 35 showed to be a myth of convenience.
Kantor and Whalley treat the sudden Space Race budget surge as a natural experiment, comparing places and industries that got NASA money with those that did not.

across.link: Mariana Mazzucato's Mission Economy (2021) proposes Apollo-style 'missions' for climate and health; critics reply that Apollo's conditions (one clear technical target, Cold War urgency, a decade of open-ended money) rarely recur.

days.apply_question: The Human Genome Project (1990-2003, about $2.7 billion) is often credited with roughly $800 billion of economic impact, a figure from a 2011 Battelle report that some economists criticise. Using today's lesson on spin-off claims, what evidence would you need before believing a number like that?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Apollo's costs and its political origin in Cold War competition. Debated: the size of its economic payoffs (spin-off myths versus modest measured gains, Kantor & Whalley). Value judgment: whether it was worth the money; at the Apollo 11 launch Ralph Abernathy's Poor People's Campaign protested spending on the Moon while Americans went hungry, and Gil Scott-Heron's 'Whitey on the Moon' (1970) made the same charge, while defenders cite knowledge, inspiration and peaceful competition.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: In 1962 Telstar Carried Live TV Across the Atlantic, but Only While It Was Passing Overhead.
days.concept: A satellite's orbit is chosen to fit its job: geostationary for broadcast and continuous weather watching, low orbit for sharp imaging and low delay, sun-synchronous for Earth observation under the same lighting each day.
days.focus: Teach the trade-offs between altitude, coverage, revisit time, delay and resolution, using Telstar's brief passes against later geostationary relays. Show satellites as quiet infrastructure: weather, communications, imaging, timing.
days.model_or_equation: One-way ground-satellite-ground delay ≈ 2h/c: about 0.24 s via geostationary orbit (h = 35,786 km) versus about 0.004 s via a satellite 550 km up

story.title: Live television, but only for minutes at a time
story.hook: On 10 July 1962 NASA launched Telstar 1, built by AT&T's Bell Labs, into an elliptical orbit about 950 km up at its lowest and roughly 5,600-5,900 km at its highest (sources differ). That night test pictures sent from the ground station at Andover, Maine, were received at Pleumeur-Bodou in Brittany, and less clearly at Goonhilly in Cornwall; on 23 July the first public live transatlantic broadcast showed Americans and Europeans each other's cities and part of a Kennedy press conference. But Telstar circled the Earth about every two and a half hours, so a transatlantic link existed only while it was above both horizons at once, about 20-30 minutes per pass by most accounts. It was also damaged by radiation from the Starfish Prime high-altitude nuclear test of 9 July and failed for good in February 1963.
story.puzzle: Why could the first TV satellite only broadcast in short windows, when the satellite dish on a house today points at one fixed spot and never moves?
story.payoff: Telstar's low, fast orbit meant it rose, crossed the sky and set, so ground stations had to track it and the link broke each time it set. A satellite 35,786 km above the equator orbits once per sidereal day and appears fixed (Syncom 3 relayed the 1964 Tokyo Olympics from there), so a fixed dish works. Orbit choice follows the job.
sources: Bell System Technical Journal, special issue on Project Telstar, July 1963
NASA NSSDC Master Catalog, Telstar 1 (1962-029A)
NASA, Syncom 3 and the 1964 Tokyo Olympics relay

days.application: Weather satellites combine orbits: geostationary GOES satellites watch a hurricane continuously, while polar sun-synchronous satellites pass over at the same local time each day with instruments that feed forecast models. The National Hurricane Center's annual verification reports show average Atlantic track errors at 24, 48 and 72 hours have fallen by more than half since 1990, measured progress, though satellites share the credit with better models, computers and aircraft reconnaissance.

builds_on.why: Kepler's third law fixes the one altitude where an orbit takes a day, and shows why low orbits are fast and short-lived over any spot.
Satellites talk by radio and microwaves, and the speed of light sets the delay of every link.

across.link: In the Bogotá Declaration (December 1976) eight equatorial states claimed sovereignty over the geostationary orbit above their territory; other states rejected the claim as contrary to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty's ban on national appropriation, and the ITU now coordinates orbital slots and frequencies.

days.apply_question: Three geostationary satellites can cover most of the inhabited Earth, yet Starlink needs thousands of satellites for continuous internet coverage. Using today's lesson, explain why.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the physics of orbit choice. Debated: how much of the improvement in hurricane forecasts is due to satellites versus models, computing and reconnaissance aircraft (attribution needs controlled comparisons such as data-denial experiments).

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Space debris and the orbital commons
days.headline_hint: Two Satellites Met Over Siberia at About 11.7 km/s. Nobody Aimed Either One.
days.concept: In crowded orbits, collisions create fragments that cause further collisions, a reinforcing loop (the Kessler syndrome) in an open-access commons that no single user has an incentive to protect.
days.focus: Explain why collision risk grows roughly with the square of the number of objects in an orbital shell, how fragments spread into clouds, and why low orbits clean themselves through drag while higher ones do not. Then treat debris as a commons problem, with deliberate anti-satellite tests as the worst polluters.
days.model_or_equation: Collision rate in an orbital shell ∝ (number of objects)^2 × cross-section × relative speed ÷ shell volume; above a critical density, fragments are added faster than drag removes them

story.title: An accident 789 km above Siberia
story.hook: On 10 February 2009, about 789 km above northern Siberia, Iridium 33, an active American communications satellite, and Kosmos 2251, a dead Russian military communications satellite launched in 1993, crossed paths at roughly 11.7 km/s and destroyed each other. It was the first accidental collision between two intact satellites, and it produced well over 2,000 tracked fragments. Two years earlier, on 11 January 2007, China had deliberately destroyed its weather satellite Fengyun-1C with a missile at about 865 km, creating more than 3,000 tracked pieces, the worst debris event on record.
story.puzzle: Space is vast and the two satellites were only metres across. How could they collide by chance, and why do experts worry that collisions could multiply even if launches stopped?
story.payoff: Satellites are not spread through space but concentrated in a few useful altitude bands, so the odds depend on density in those shells and grow with the square of the number of objects. Each collision makes hundreds or thousands of new objects in the same band, raising the odds of the next: a reinforcing loop. Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais warned in 1978 that past a critical density this cascade continues on its own.
sources: NASA Orbital Debris Quarterly News 13(2), April 2009, on the Iridium-Kosmos collision
NASA Orbital Debris Quarterly News on the Fengyun-1C debris cloud (2007 onward)
Kessler, D.J. & Cour-Palais, B.G. (1978) 'Collision frequency of artificial satellites: The creation of a debris belt', Journal of Geophysical Research 83(A6)

days.application: On 15 November 2021 Russia destroyed its defunct satellite Kosmos 1408 with a ground-launched missile at about 480 km, creating more than 1,500 trackable fragments; the seven people on the International Space Station sheltered in their docked spacecraft as the station passed near the cloud. In April 2022 the US announced a moratorium on destructive direct-ascent ASAT tests, and a UN General Assembly resolution calling on states to refrain followed that December.

builds_on.why: The Kessler cascade is a reinforcing loop, with atmospheric drag as the balancing loop that weakens with altitude.
Low orbit is an open-access commons; Ostrom's conditions (clear boundaries, monitoring, sanctions) are mostly missing in space.

across.link: Under the 1972 Liability Convention, after the nuclear-powered Soviet satellite Cosmos 954 scattered radioactive debris over Canada's Northwest Territories in January 1978, Canada claimed about C$6 million and the USSR paid C$3 million in a 1981 settlement, the best-known claim ever brought under the convention.

days.apply_question: In 2022 the US Federal Communications Commission required satellites it licenses in low orbit to be removed within five years of their mission ending, replacing a 25-year guideline. Using the reinforcing loop and Ostrom's commons principles, explain whether one country's rule like this can stop the Kessler loop on its own.
days.evidence_note: Settled: collision physics and that debris accumulates in some shells. Debated: whether parts of low orbit (around 800-1,000 km) are already past critical density, and whether megaconstellations with active deorbiting make things worse or better. Value judgment: whether destructive ASAT tests should be banned outright and who should pay to clean up debris made by others.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: A Five-Minute Flash on the Sun Made Telegraph Wires Spark in 1859. In 1989 a Smaller Storm Blacked Out Quebec in 90 Seconds.
days.concept: Solar flares and coronal mass ejections disturb Earth's magnetic field and induce currents in long conductors and drag on satellites, a rare, fat-tailed hazard whose worst case is far larger than the typical storm.
days.focus: Trace the chain from a coronal mass ejection to a changing geomagnetic field, induced geoelectric fields, and DC currents in power lines that saturate transformers; then treat the risk as fat-tailed, where planning must be for the extreme rather than the average.
days.model_or_equation: Faraday's law in the ground: a changing geomagnetic field induces a geoelectric field E (storms produce up to several V/km); across a line of length L that is roughly E × L volts, driving quasi-DC current through transformer neutrals

story.title: The morning Richard Carrington saw the Sun flare
story.hook: Just before noon on 1 September 1859, the English astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots projected from his telescope at Redhill, Surrey, when two patches of intense white light flared within the spot group and faded in about five minutes; Richard Hodgson saw it independently in London. About 17 hours later the most intense geomagnetic storm in the instrumental record, by most estimates, struck. Auroras were seen as far south as the Caribbean, and telegraph operators across Europe and North America reported shocks, sparks and, by some contemporary accounts, burning telegraph paper; some lines between Boston and Portland, Maine, reportedly ran on the induced current alone with their batteries disconnected.
story.puzzle: How did a brief flash on the Sun, 150 million km away, push electric current through copper wires on Earth a day later, and how likely is it to happen to today's far more wired world?
story.payoff: The flare came with a coronal mass ejection, a cloud of magnetised plasma that hit Earth's magnetic field and made it change rapidly; a changing magnetic field induces voltage in long conductors (Faraday). Telegraph lines then, power grids now. Because storm sizes are fat-tailed, a 'once in 150 years' storm is not an upper bound.
sources: Carrington, R.C. (1859) 'Description of a Singular Appearance seen in the Sun on September 1, 1859', Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 20
Boteler, D.H. (2006) 'The super storms of August/September 1859 and their effects on the telegraph system', Advances in Space Research 38
NERC (1990) report on the 13 March 1989 geomagnetic disturbance

days.application: On 13 March 1989 a geomagnetic storm induced currents that tripped protective equipment on Hydro-Québec's long transmission lines; the grid collapsed in about 90 seconds and some 6 million people lost power for about nine hours. Satellites face a different mechanism: in February 2022 SpaceX launched 49 Starlink satellites into a deliberately low orbit just as a modest geomagnetic storm heated and expanded the upper atmosphere, and the extra drag brought down up to 40 of them.

builds_on.why: Electromagnetic induction is the mechanism: a changing magnetic field drives current through any long conductor, telegraph wire or power line.
Storm intensities are fat-tailed, so the historical average says little about the extreme that does the damage.

across.link: After 1989 US regulators made geomagnetic storms a reliability requirement: FERC Order 779 (2013) directed NERC to write standards, leading to TPL-007, which requires utilities to assess their transformers against a benchmark extreme storm.

days.apply_question: An insurer asked to price cover against a Carrington-class storm has about 165 years of magnetic records containing one such storm, or two if the May 1921 storm counts. Using fat tails, explain why the historical record is a poor guide to the premium.
days.evidence_note: Debated: the chance of a Carrington-class storm per decade, from about 12% (Riley, Space Weather 2012) to roughly 0.5-2% in later statistical analyses, and the cost estimates (a 2013 Lloyd's study put a severe US outcome at $0.6-2.6 trillion), which depend heavily on assumptions about transformer damage. Also debated: whether 1859 was the largest storm on record or matched by May 1921. Settled: the induction mechanism and the 1989 Quebec collapse.

resource.title: Extreme space weather: impacts on engineered systems and infrastructure (summary report)
resource.creator: Royal Academy of Engineering (UK), 2013
resource.why: An engineering assessment of a reasonable worst case for grids, satellites, GPS and aviation, the planning view the lesson can only sketch.
