days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: A Graduate Student Found the Stars Are Made of Hydrogen. America's Leading Astronomer Called It Impossible, Then Confirmed It Himself.
days.concept: A star is a ball of gas in which gravity's inward squeeze is balanced by the pressure of gas heated by fusion in its core, a self-regulating balance, and its mass sets how brightly it burns and how long it lives.
days.focus: Explain hydrostatic equilibrium and the stellar thermostat (contract, heat, fuse faster, expand), hydrogen fusing to helium via mass-energy, and why more massive stars burn out far faster. Use Payne's discovery to show how spectra reveal composition.
days.model_or_equation: Hydrostatic equilibrium: dP/dr = −G M(r) ρ(r) / r^2; luminosity L ∝ M^~3.5, so main-sequence lifetime t ∝ M/L ∝ M^~−2.5 (about 10 billion years for the Sun)

story.title: The thesis that called its own result 'almost certainly not real'
story.hook: In 1925 Cecilia Payne, a British student of about 25 at Harvard College Observatory (her doctorate came from Radcliffe College, since Harvard did not then grant women PhDs), finished a thesis, Stellar Atmospheres, that applied new atomic physics, Meghnad Saha's ionization theory, to the spectra of stars. Her calculations showed that hydrogen and helium vastly outnumber every other element in stellar atmospheres, while astronomers then assumed stars had roughly Earth's composition. Henry Norris Russell of Princeton, the leading American astronomer, wrote to her that the result was clearly impossible, and her published thesis described the hydrogen abundance as 'almost certainly not real'. In 1929 Russell, by another method, concluded that hydrogen does dominate the Sun's atmosphere.
story.puzzle: If stars are mostly hydrogen, what are they doing with it, and how does a star burn steadily for billions of years without either exploding or collapsing?
story.payoff: Payne was right: stars are mostly hydrogen, and their cores fuse it into helium, turning about 0.7% of the mass into energy. Gravity squeezes the star; the heated gas pushes back; if fusion runs too fast the core expands, cools and slows it, and if too slow it contracts and heats. That balancing loop keeps the Sun steady for about 10 billion years.
sources: Payne, C.H. (1925) Stellar Atmospheres, Harvard Observatory Monographs No. 1
Russell, H.N. (1929) 'On the Composition of the Sun's Atmosphere', Astrophysical Journal 70
Moore, D. (2020) What Stars Are Made Of: The Life of Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin, Harvard University Press

days.application: Fusion on Earth must do without gravity's confinement. On 5 December 2022 the US National Ignition Facility focused 2.05 MJ of laser energy on a fuel capsule and got 3.15 MJ of fusion energy out, the first 'ignition' gain, yet the lasers drew roughly 300 MJ from the grid and the facility fires only a few hundred shots a year, where a power plant would need several shots a second. The Sun's core, by contrast, is held together by its own weight at about 15 million kelvin, converting about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy each second.

builds_on.why: Mass-energy equivalence and binding energy explain why fusing hydrogen to helium releases energy and how much.
Payne read composition from spectral lines, whose positions and strengths follow from the quantum atom's energy levels and ionization.

across.link: Margaret Rossiter named the 'Matilda effect' (Social Studies of Science, 1993), the under-crediting of women scientists; Payne, paid for years as a technical assistant, became the first woman promoted to full professor in Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences only in 1956, a frequently cited case.

days.apply_question: Betelgeuse has roughly 15-20 times the Sun's mass (estimates vary), yet it is only about 10 million years old and near the end of its life, while the Sun is 4.6 billion years old and about halfway through. Explain why a star with more fuel lives a much shorter life.

resource.title: The Sun: Crash Course Astronomy #10
resource.creator: Crash Course (host Phil Plait; PBS Digital Studios), 2015
resource.why: A visual tour of how our own star balances gravity against fusion and moves energy outward, the model case for every other star.
resource.verified_how: web search (drafting session): listings for episode #9 name #10 'The Sun' as the next episode; this episode's own page was not shown in any result, so cite without a link; runtime from prior knowledge, re-verify at build

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.headline_hint: Fred Hoyle Predicted a Nuclear Energy Level From the Fact That Carbon Exists. He Was Right to Within Half a Percent.
days.concept: Apart from hydrogen and helium made in the Big Bang, the elements were forged in stars, in exploding stars and in neutron-star mergers, with fusion building elements up to iron and neutron capture making the heavier ones (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle, 1957).
days.focus: Teach the binding-energy curve as the reason fusion stops paying at iron, the triple-alpha bottleneck to carbon, and slow and rapid neutron capture for heavier elements. Handle the Hoyle 'anthropic prediction' story with Kragh's historical correction.
key_concepts: triple-alpha process and the Hoyle state
days.model_or_equation: Triple-alpha: 4He + 4He ⇌ 8Be; 8Be + 4He → 12C* (the 7.65 MeV 'Hoyle state') → 12C + photons. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron and nickel, so fusion beyond it absorbs energy

story.title: A prediction made from the existence of carbon
story.hook: In 1953 the Cambridge astrophysicist Fred Hoyle, visiting Caltech, argued that stars could make carbon from helium only if the carbon-12 nucleus had an excited energy level near 7.7 MeV, a resonance no one had then established. Without it, he reasoned, the brief fusion of three helium nuclei would almost never happen and the universe would hold far too little carbon. He persuaded sceptical experimenters at Caltech's Kellogg Radiation Laboratory, where Willy Fowler worked, to look, and Ward Whaling's team found the level at about 7.65 MeV. Four years later Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, Fowler and Hoyle published a paper of about 100 pages explaining how stars forge most elements.
story.puzzle: How could the mere fact that carbon is abundant tell a physicist, in advance, where an energy level inside a nucleus must sit?
story.payoff: Making carbon needs three helium nuclei to meet, and the intermediate beryllium-8 falls apart almost instantly; only a resonance at just the right energy lets carbon form fast enough. Observed abundances are evidence about nuclear physics, so a correct theory of stellar nucleosynthesis had to include the level. That is the B2FH programme in miniature. Kragh (2010) shows the later telling of this as an 'anthropic' prediction from the existence of life is a retelling Hoyle did not make at the time.
sources: Burbidge, E.M., Burbidge, G.R., Fowler, W.A. & Hoyle, F. (1957) 'Synthesis of the Elements in Stars', Reviews of Modern Physics 29
Hoyle, F. (1954) 'On Nuclear Reactions Occurring in Very Hot Stars', Astrophysical Journal Supplement 1
Dunbar, D.N.F., Pixley, R.E., Wenzel, W.A. & Whaling, W. (1953) Physical Review 92
Kragh, H. (2010) 'When is a prediction anthropic? Fred Hoyle and the 7.65 MeV carbon resonance', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 64

days.application: On 17 August 2017 the LIGO and Virgo detectors recorded gravitational waves from two neutron stars merging about 130 million light-years away (GW170817); about two seconds later the Fermi satellite caught a gamma-ray burst, and telescopes then watched a 'kilonova' glow whose fading light matched freshly made heavy r-process elements. Estimates of the gold and platinum made run to several Earth masses but vary widely, and whether mergers make most of the universe's gold, or rare types of exploding star contribute heavily, is debated.

builds_on.why: Stars' cores are the furnaces; yesterday's mass-dependent life story decides which elements a star can reach before it dies.
The binding-energy curve explains why fusion releases energy up to iron and why heavier elements need neutron capture instead.

across.link: The Hoyle resonance is a standard example in fine-tuning arguments for design (Day 280 names it among the arguments for God's existence and their objections), and also in multiverse and selection-effect replies; Kragh's 2010 history is the check on how the example is told.

days.apply_question: Iron is one of the most common heavy elements in the universe and in your blood, while gold is so scarce that all the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 metres on a side. Using today's lesson, explain why the two are so unequal.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the B2FH framework of stellar nucleosynthesis and that neutron-star mergers make r-process elements. Debated: what share of the heavy elements comes from mergers versus rare supernovae (collapsars, magnetorotational explosions); and Hoyle's prediction as 'anthropic' (Kragh 2010 against the popular retelling). Philosophical, not settled by physics: what fine-tuning implies (design, multiverse or selection effect).

resource.why: A short review by the astronomer behind the widely shared 'where your elements came from' periodic table, giving each element's main cosmic origin.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Measuring the cosmos: the distance ladder
days.headline_hint: Edwin Hubble Crossed Out an 'N' and Wrote 'VAR!' The Milky Way Stopped Being the Whole Universe.
days.concept: Astronomers measure distances no one can travel by chaining methods, geometric parallax for nearby stars and then 'standard candles' of known brightness calibrated on them, so each rung inherits the errors of the rungs below.
days.focus: Teach parallax, the inverse-square dimming of light, and Leavitt's period-luminosity law as the key standard candle, then show how calibration errors propagate up the ladder, from Hubble's too-small Andromeda distance to today's Hubble tension.
days.model_or_equation: Parallax: d (parsecs) = 1/p (arcseconds); brightness falls as 1/d^2, so distance modulus m − M = 5 log10(d / 10 pc); Leavitt law: M = a log10(P) + b

story.title: A glass plate marked 'VAR!'
story.hook: In 1912 Henrietta Swan Leavitt, one of the women employed as 'computers' at Harvard College Observatory, reported in a circular issued under director Edward Pickering's name that in 25 variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, the brighter stars pulsed more slowly: period predicted luminosity. In 1920 Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis debated in Washington whether the spiral nebulae were inside the Milky Way or separate galaxies. On the night of 5-6 October 1923, at Mount Wilson's 100-inch telescope, Edwin Hubble photographed the Andromeda nebula and marked a new star 'N' for nova; comparing older plates, he found it brightened and faded on a regular cycle, crossed out the N and wrote 'VAR!'.
story.puzzle: Every star is just a point of light on a plate. How can one blinking point tell you how far away a whole nebula is?
story.payoff: A Cepheid's period gives its true brightness by Leavitt's law; comparing that with how faint it looks gives its distance through the inverse-square law. Hubble's variable put Andromeda roughly 900,000 light-years away, far outside the Milky Way, settling the debate. His figure was less than half the modern 2.5 million light-years because the calibration rung below was wrong: there turned out to be two kinds of Cepheid (Baade, 1952).
sources: Leavitt, H.S. & Pickering, E.C. (1912) 'Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud', Harvard College Observatory Circular 173
Carnegie Science, Hubble's plate H335H of M31 (1923)
Hoskin, M. (1976) 'The Great Debate: What really happened', Journal for the History of Astronomy 7

days.application: The Hubble tension: measurements from the early universe (the Planck satellite's cosmic microwave background, about 67.4 km/s per megaparsec) and from the distance ladder (the SH0ES team's Cepheids and supernovae, about 73) disagree well beyond their stated errors. Wendy Freedman's team, using other stars as candles, gets values in between, near 70. Either some rung hides a systematic error or the standard cosmological model is missing something.

builds_on.why: Astronomical magnitudes and the Leavitt law are logarithmic scales; a straight line in log period is what makes the candle usable.
Systematic error, not random scatter, is the ladder's danger: Hubble's factor-of-two error and possibly today's tension come from calibration, not sample size.

across.link: The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India (begun 1802) measured the subcontinent by chaining triangles from measured baselines, finally computing Peak XV (Everest) at 29,002 ft, announced in 1856; like the cosmic ladder, errors propagate up the chain, but surveyors could close loops and re-measure baselines, a check astronomers cannot make on distant rungs.

days.apply_question: The European Space Agency's Gaia mission measured parallaxes for well over a billion stars before it retired in 2025. Explain how a more accurate bottom rung changes every distance above it, including the Hubble constant.
days.evidence_note: Debated: the Hubble tension, about 67 versus 73 km/s/Mpc, with the sides split between hidden systematic errors in the ladder (Freedman and others) and new physics beyond the standard model of cosmology (a view taken seriously by Riess's SH0ES team among others). Settled: the ladder's logic and the extragalactic nature of Andromeda.

resource.length: about 25-30 minutes (over the usual 20; skip if short of time)
resource.why: A mathematician and a master explainer rebuild the ladder rung by rung, from parallax to Cepheids to the Hubble constant, with the geometry drawn.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: The expanding universe and the Big Bang
days.headline_hint: Two Bell Labs Scientists Cleaned Pigeon Droppings Out of Their Antenna. The Hiss Stayed. It Was the Afterglow of the Big Bang.
days.concept: Three independent lines of evidence, galaxy redshifts growing with distance, the cosmic microwave background and the abundances of the lightest elements, together establish that the universe was once hot and dense and has been expanding for about 13.8 billion years.
days.focus: Teach expansion as the stretching of space (redshift), the CMB as cooled light from about 380,000 years after the start, and light-element abundances as a third, independent test; show how the evidence defeated the steady-state theory and what remains unknown.
days.model_or_equation: Hubble-Lemaître law: v ≈ H0 × d; the CMB is near-perfect blackbody radiation at 2.725 K, light stretched about 1,100-fold since it was released

story.title: A hiss from every direction at Holmdel
story.hook: In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, radio astronomers at Bell Labs, set out to use a 20-foot horn antenna on Crawford Hill in Holmdel, New Jersey, for precise measurements and found a faint excess noise, equivalent to about 3.5 kelvin, coming equally from every direction, day and night, in every season. They checked their electronics, pointed away from New York City and evicted a pair of nesting pigeons, cleaning out their droppings (in the physicists' later joke, 'white dielectric material'); the hiss remained. A tip from the radio astronomer Bernard Burke led to a call to Robert Dicke's group at nearby Princeton, which was building an experiment to look for exactly such radiation; both groups published in the Astrophysical Journal in 1965, and Penzias and Wilson shared the 1978 Nobel Prize.
story.puzzle: What gives off a faint, perfectly even microwave glow from every direction in the sky at once?
story.payoff: The whole universe does. If space has been expanding from a hot, dense state, the light released when it first became transparent should still fill all of space, stretched by expansion from visible and infrared into microwaves at a few degrees above absolute zero. Penzias and Wilson's hiss was that light, and its discovery dealt the steady-state theory a blow from which, for nearly all cosmologists, it never recovered.
sources: Penzias, A.A. & Wilson, R.W. (1965) 'A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s', Astrophysical Journal 142
Dicke, R.H., Peebles, P.J.E., Roll, P.G. & Wilkinson, D.T. (1965) 'Cosmic Black-Body Radiation', Astrophysical Journal 142
Wilson, R.W. (1978) Nobel Lecture, 'The Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation'
Lemaître, G. (1927) Annales de la Société Scientifique de Bruxelles A47

days.application: The same precision cosmology that measures the CMB shows how little we understand: by the Planck satellite's 2018 results ordinary matter makes up only about 5% of the universe's content, dark matter about 27% (inferred from galaxy rotation, clusters and the CMB itself) and dark energy, which drives the accelerating expansion discovered in 1998, about 68%. Neither dark component has been identified.

builds_on.why: Distances from the ladder plotted against redshift gave the expansion; the Hubble constant is the ladder's top rung.
The CMB is microwave light on the electromagnetic spectrum, and redshift is the stretching of wavelength.

across.link: Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, proposed the expanding universe in 1927; in 1951 Pope Pius XII welcomed such cosmology as supporting creation, while Lemaître cautioned against mixing physics with theology, and Fred Hoyle, who coined 'Big Bang' on BBC radio in 1949, resisted it partly for philosophical reasons.

days.apply_question: If the universe were infinite, eternal and unchanging, every line of sight would end on a star and the night sky would blaze (Olbers' paradox). Using today's lesson, explain why the night sky looks dark to your eyes yet glows to a microwave antenna.
days.evidence_note: Settled: a hot, expanding early universe about 13.8 billion years ago, supported by three independent lines of evidence. Debated: what dark matter and dark energy are, and whether cosmic inflation happened. Not a scientific question: what, if anything, the Big Bang implies about creation; Pius XII (1951) and Lemaître differed on this within Catholic thought, and secular philosophers differ too.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Other worlds and the search for life
days.headline_hint: Theory Said a Jupiter Couldn't Circle Its Star in Four Days. In 1995 Two Swiss Astronomers Found One.
days.concept: Planets around other stars are detected only indirectly, mostly by the wobble they cause in their star's motion and the shadow they cast when they cross it, so every catalogue is shaped by what each method can see, and the Drake equation (1961) organises our ignorance about life elsewhere rather than resolving it.
days.focus: Teach the radial-velocity (Doppler wobble) and transit methods and the selection effects they create, and read the Drake equation as a list of unknowns. Use a contested biosignature claim to apply the standard for extraordinary claims.
days.model_or_equation: Doppler shift: v_r = c Δλ/λ; Drake equation: N = R* × fp × ne × fl × fi × fc × L, where only the first two or three factors are now measured

story.title: A planet in a four-day orbit
story.hook: On 6 October 1995, at a conference in Florence, Michel Mayor and his doctoral student Didier Queloz of the Geneva Observatory announced that the Sun-like star 51 Pegasi, about 50 light-years away, was being tugged back and forth by an unseen companion. Using the ELODIE spectrograph at the Haute-Provence Observatory in France, they had measured the star moving toward and away from us by about 55-60 m/s on a 4.23-day cycle, implying a planet of at least half Jupiter's mass orbiting closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun. Theory said giant planets form far out, as Jupiter did. Within days American astronomers Geoffrey Marcy and Paul Butler confirmed it; Mayor and Queloz shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
story.puzzle: How can you detect a planet you cannot see, and how could a giant planet be where theory said none could form?
story.payoff: The planet and star orbit their common centre of mass, so the star wobbles, and the wobble shows up as a tiny periodic Doppler shift in its light. Theory was wrong, most astronomers now think, about where giants end up rather than where they form: they can migrate inward through the young disk. And the wobble method finds massive, close-in planets most easily, so early catalogues overflowed with 'hot Jupiters' that turned out to be rare.
sources: Mayor, M. & Queloz, D. (1995) 'A Jupiter-mass companion to a solar-type star', Nature 378
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2019, press release (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences)
NASA Exoplanet Archive, confirmed planet counts

days.application: K2-18b, a planet about 8.6 times Earth's mass some 124 light-years away, was studied with the James Webb Space Telescope as it transited its star. In April 2025 Nikku Madhusudhan's Cambridge team reported a possible signal of dimethyl sulfide and/or dimethyl disulfide, which on Earth are made mainly by marine microbes, at about three-sigma significance; other teams reanalysing the data found weaker or no evidence, and abiotic sources of the molecule are known. The claim is unresolved and not accepted.

builds_on.why: Each detection method samples planets non-randomly, so the catalogue is a biased sample, like the Literary Digest poll: what is easiest to find looks most common.
A claim of alien life is extraordinary; its required evidence depends on the prior and on independent replication, not on one three-sigma signal.

across.link: Dimethyl sulfide was proposed as a biosignature because on Earth it comes overwhelmingly from marine phytoplankton; the debate turns on whether non-living chemistry can also make it, the same distinction biologists draw between a molecule's usual source and its only source.

days.apply_question: The seven Earth-sized planets of TRAPPIST-1 were found by the transit method. Explain why the transit and wobble methods each favour particular kinds of planets, and what that means for any claim about what a 'typical' planet is like.
days.evidence_note: Settled: exoplanets are common (about 6,000 confirmed by 2025). Debated: the K2-18b biosignature claim (Madhusudhan's team against several reanalyses), the details of giant-planet migration, and every factor of the Drake equation after the first few, which are unknown rather than merely uncertain.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 8: GPS, the invisible utility
days.headline_hint: An Airliner Strayed Into Soviet Airspace and 269 People Died. Two Weeks Later a Military Clock in the Sky Was Promised to the World's Airliners.
days.concept: GPS shows how a military system became global infrastructure: a constellation of orbiting atomic clocks whose free signals now time and locate much of modern life, with dependence that grew faster than its backups.
days.focus: Walk GPS around Logan's chain as a loop: Cold War need, invention by merger, the physics of orbits, light and relativity, engineering by four-unknown trilateration, free public financing, policy shaped by a disaster, adoption into timing and phones, consequences measured in trillions, and feedback through jamming, spoofing and rival constellations.
days.model_or_equation: For each satellite i: pseudorange ρ_i = |s_i − x| + c·b, with unknown receiver position x (three coordinates) and clock bias b, so at least four satellites are needed

story.title: Korean Air Lines Flight 007 strays over Sakhalin
story.hook: On 1 September 1983 (local time) Korean Air Lines Flight 007, a Boeing 747 flying from New York to Seoul by way of Anchorage, drifted far off its planned track, probably because of an autopilot setting, and flew over the Kamchatka Peninsula and Sakhalin Island in Soviet airspace. A Soviet Su-15 interceptor shot it down near Moneron Island, killing all 269 people aboard, including US Congressman Larry McDonald. On 16 September 1983 the Reagan White House announced that the Global Positioning System, then a handful of test satellites built for the US military, would be made available for civil aircraft once it was operational.
story.puzzle: How did a military navigation system, built to guide bombers and submarines, become a free utility that times power grids and phone networks and steers billions of people, and what happens if it fails?
story.payoff: The answer is a loop, not a line: a disaster made a promise of civil access; free, accurate signals then spread into uses no designer planned (above all, timing); dependence outgrew backups; and that dependence now feeds back as jamming, spoofing and rival national systems. Historians of GPS add a correction to the popular story: a civil signal had been planned since the 1970s, and the 1983 announcement made it a public commitment.
sources: ICAO (1993) report of the completed fact-finding investigation into the destruction of KE007
White House press statement on GPS civil access, 16 Sep 1983
Pace, S. et al. (1995) The Global Positioning System: Assessing National Policies, RAND MR-614
RTI International (2019) Economic Benefits of the Global Positioning System (GPS), report for NIST

days.application: GPS itself: about 31 operational satellites in six orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each carrying atomic clocks and broadcasting its position and time. Beyond navigation, its timing synchronises mobile networks, power-grid measurements and financial timestamps, and an RTI study for NIST (2019) estimated about $1.4 trillion in US private-sector benefits since GPS became available for civilian use in the 1980s, and losses of roughly $1 billion a day in a nationwide outage.

builds_on.why: Each satellite circles in a 12-hour orbit at about 20,200 km, set by Kepler's third law, so at least four are always above any spot.
Satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day (weaker gravity speeds them by about 45, orbital motion slows them by about 7); uncorrected, positions would drift by kilometres a day.
Solving for three position coordinates plus a clock error is a geometry of vectors from four known points.
Space weather disturbs the ionosphere that GPS signals cross, one of the system's natural failure modes.

across.link: In United States v. Jones (2012) the Supreme Court held that attaching a GPS tracker to a suspect's car and monitoring it for 28 days was a Fourth Amendment search, a ruling forced by the technology's adoption.

days.apply_question: In July 2019 Europe's Galileo navigation system went down for about six days because of a ground-station fault, yet most smartphone users noticed nothing. Using the GPS case, explain why, and what this says about where a navigation system's weakest link sits.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the physics (orbits, relativity, trilateration) and GPS's accuracy. Debated: the size of the benefits (RTI's $1.4 trillion rests on modelled counterfactuals of life without GPS) and how vulnerable timing-dependent systems really are. Value judgment: US taxpayers and the military paid, the world gained, and no other country consented to depending on a system one government can degrade. A consequentialist weighs the global benefit against that risk; sovereignty-minded states (Russia, the EU, China) answered by building their own; Christian common-good thinking can be read either way, as a gift freely shared or as a dependence no community chose. The counterfactual world without GPS is unknowable.

chain.point: In October 1957 William Guier and George Weiffenbach at Johns Hopkins APL worked out Sputnik's orbit from the Doppler shift of its beeps; inverting the idea gave the Navy's Transit system (operational 1964), so Polaris submarines could fix their position from a satellite's known orbit.

Over Labor Day weekend 1973 Bradford Parkinson's team at the Pentagon merged ideas from the Navy's Timation clocks and the Air Force's 621B project into one design; the first Block I satellite launched on 22 February 1978. GPS was assembled from existing parts by a systems-engineering decision, not discovered.

Light travels about 30 cm per nanosecond, so clocks must agree to billionths of a second; relativity shifts satellite clocks by about 38 microseconds a day; and signals arrive on Earth weaker than background radio noise, which makes them easy to jam.

Cheap receivers avoid carrying atomic clocks by treating their own clock error as a fourth unknown solved from four or more satellites; spare satellites and multiple clocks per satellite give redundancy in space, but the shared signal is a common-mode weak point.

Funded through US Air Force (now Space Force) appropriations and given away with no user fees, GPS is a non-excludable, non-rival public good in CFA terms; who decides to keep paying for such a good is a question for the Government block (Days 236-249).

After KAL 007 came the 1983 promise; a 1996 presidential directive committed to ending Selective Availability, the deliberate degrading of civil accuracy to about 100 m, which was switched off at midnight on 1-2 May 2000. How such executive and agency decisions are made and checked belongs to the Government block.

In 2011-12 the FCC moved to withdraw LightSquared's conditional approval for a nationwide network after tests showed interference with GPS receivers, a fight over spectrum rights the Law block can place in property and administrative law (Days 252 and 260).

Civil use climbed an S-curve from survey and aviation receivers to car navigation to every smartphone (helped by the FCC's E911 location rules), and timing users such as mobile networks adopted it quietly.

GPS became a hub in a network of networks: RTI estimated about $1.4 trillion in US benefits, but grids, telecoms and finance now share one timing source, so a failure could cascade across systems that look unrelated.

Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo (initial services 2016) and China's BeiDou (global system completed 2020) were built partly so their owners would not depend on a system the US controls; the International Relations block treats chokepoints and interdependence as statecraft (Day 271).

Widespread jamming and spoofing near conflict zones since 2022, which led Finnair to suspend flights to Tartu, Estonia, in spring 2024, feeds back into calls for backups (Executive Order 13905 on positioning, navigation and timing resilience, 2020): a balancing loop arriving decades after the reinforcing loop of adoption, with lock-in making alternatives slow.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: The cell: the unit of life
days.headline_hint: A Delft Cloth Merchant Saw Tiny Animals Swimming in Pepper Water. The Royal Society Asked for Witnesses.
days.concept: The cell is the smallest unit that is alive: a membrane that separates inside from outside, a metabolism that runs on energy, and a genome that carries instructions; and every cell comes from an earlier cell.
days.focus: Teaches cell theory as three claims (all living things are made of cells; the cell is the unit of life; every cell comes from a cell, Virchow 1855) and why cells are small, because surface area for exchange grows more slowly than volume. The application reads cancer as cells that escape the controls on division.
days.model_or_equation: Surface-to-volume for a sphere: A/V = 3/r, so doubling a cell's radius halves the membrane available per unit of cytoplasm.

story.title: Little animals in the pepper water
story.hook: On 9 October 1676 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft cloth merchant and town official with no university training, wrote a long letter to the Royal Society in London. Looking through single-lens microscopes he made himself, he described 'little animals' (animalcules) swimming in rainwater and in water in which he had steeped pepper. The smallest, he reckoned, were so tiny that a hundred laid end to end would not span a coarse grain of sand, so that a million of them would scarcely equal its bulk (as Clifford Dobell's 1932 translation renders it). Henry Oldenburg translated the letter, cut it to less than half, and an extract appeared in the Philosophical Transactions in March 1677. The Fellows were sceptical: nobody else could see what he saw. Leeuwenhoek sent signed testimonies from respectable Delft witnesses, and Robert Hooke was asked to reproduce the observation; his confirmation came in 1677-78 (sources differ on the date of his demonstration to the Society).
story.puzzle: If invisible living things were everywhere, swarming in every drop, what exactly makes them 'alive', and what do they have in common with a man, a tree or a whale?
story.payoff: What Leeuwenhoek saw were single cells, mostly bacteria and protists. Cell theory says each is a complete living unit: a membrane, a metabolism and a genome. A human is about 30 trillion such units cooperating, each descended from one fertilized cell, and the swimmers in pepper water are the same kind of thing living alone.
sources: Leeuwenhoek, letter of 9 October 1676 (Letter L-040), extract in Philosophical Transactions 12 (1677)
lensonleeuwenhoek.net chronology of the Royal Society's response and Hooke's replication
Hektoen International, 'Van Leeuwenhoek's discovery of animalcules' (2018)
Clifford Dobell, Antony van Leeuwenhoek and His 'Little Animals' (1932), English translation of the letter

days.application: Cancer as a cell-level failure: a cell that accumulates mutations disabling its division checkpoints (for example losing the p53 'guardian' protein, mutated in about half of human cancers) divides without permission, ignores signals to die and recruits blood vessels (Hanahan & Weinberg's 'hallmarks of cancer', Cell 2000). Every tumour obeys 'every cell from a cell': it is one lineage that broke the rules.

builds_on.why: The square-cube law explains why cells stay small: volume (demand) grows as the cube of size while membrane (supply) grows as the square.
A cell is a low-entropy, organized system that stays alive only by continually taking in usable energy, Schrodinger's point in What Is Life? (1944).

across.link: Battery cells face the cell's geometry problem: heat and current are generated throughout a cell's volume but must leave through its surface and terminals. When Tesla announced its larger 4680 cylindrical cell at Battery Day (22 September 2020), it said a new 'tabless' electrode, which shortens the path current travels, was what made the bigger cell workable thermally; the same surface-to-volume arithmetic that keeps living cells small limits how big a battery cell can grow.

days.apply_question: A single human motor neuron can stretch about a metre, from the spinal cord to the muscles of the foot; using the surface-to-volume idea, explain how a cell that long can still exchange enough material with its surroundings to stay alive.
days.evidence_note: Settled: cell theory and the descent of cells from cells. The exact date of Hooke's confirmation differs between sources (his letter is dated late 1677 or early 1678, and one chronology dates his demonstration to the Society to November 1678); say so rather than pick one.

resource.creator: Nick Lane, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 370 (2015), a commentary for the journal's 350th anniversary
resource.why: A biochemist rereads the very letter in today's story: what Leeuwenhoek actually saw, why the Society doubted him, and how his animalcules (bacteria and protists) became the starting point for understanding cells as the units of life. Free to read.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: Lavoisier Packed a Guinea Pig in Ice and Showed That Breathing Is Burning
days.concept: Cells release the energy in food by controlled, step-by-step oxidation, the same net reaction as burning, and store it briefly in ATP, so a living body is a slow furnace whose power can be measured in watts.
days.focus: Teaches metabolism as energy accounting: food is oxidized through enzyme-catalysed steps rather than in one flame, captured as ATP, and lost as heat. A resting adult runs at about 100 W (2,000 kcal a day is about 97 W). The angle is the continuity of chemistry: respiration obeys the conservation of energy exactly as a fire does.
days.model_or_equation: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O, releasing about 2,870 kJ per mole of glucose; resting power P = (2,000 kcal x 4,184 J/kcal) / 86,400 s = about 97 W.

story.title: A guinea pig, a basket and a shell of ice
story.hook: In the winter of 1782-83 Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace built an ice calorimeter in Paris: a wire basket inside a jacket packed with ice, insulated by an outer layer of ice and snow so that only the animal's heat could melt the inner shell. They placed a guinea pig in the basket for up to ten hours and weighed the water that melted. Separately they measured how much 'fixed air' (carbon dioxide) the animal exhaled, and how much ice melted when charcoal was burned to make the same amount of carbon dioxide. The two figures roughly matched (the animal melted somewhat more ice than the charcoal comparison predicted). In their memoir on heat, read to the Academy of Sciences in June 1783, they concluded that respiration is a combustion, slow but otherwise the same.
story.puzzle: An animal is not on fire and its body is barely warm, so how can it burn carbon at the same energy yield as charcoal?
story.payoff: Cells oxidize fuel through a chain of enzyme-catalysed steps, releasing energy in small packets captured as ATP instead of as a flame. The net reaction, and therefore the total energy, matches combustion exactly, as energy conservation requires; only the route and the rate differ.
sources: Lavoisier & Laplace, 'Memoire sur la chaleur' (1783)
Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Father of Modern Chemistry Proved Respiration Occurred by Freezing a Guinea Pig' (2017)
Ghent University Museum (GUM), Lavoisier-Laplace calorimeter collection entry

days.application: The food label and the marathon wall. Label calories come from Atwater factors (about 4 kcal per gram of carbohydrate or protein, 9 per gram of fat), descendants of burning food in a bomb calorimeter and correcting for what the body cannot oxidize. A trained runner stores roughly 400-500 g of glycogen (about 1,600-2,000 kcal), and because each gram is stored with about three times its weight in water it is a bulky fuel; a marathon costs a 70 kg runner roughly 2,600-3,000 kcal (about 1 kcal per kilogram per kilometre). When glycogen runs low, often around mile 18-20, the body must lean on fat, which it can burn only more slowly and which yields less energy per litre of oxygen, and pace collapses. Carbohydrate loading and in-race gels are metabolism managed as a stock and a flow.

builds_on.why: Combustion and energy density: respiration is the same oxidation of carbon fuel, and fat stores more energy per kilogram than carbohydrate for the reason fuels differ.
Power as energy per second turns a daily food budget into the body's roughly 100 W.

across.link: The same watts accounting compares two information processors: David Patterson and colleagues (Google and UC Berkeley, 2021) estimated that training GPT-3 used about 1,287 MWh of electricity, while a human brain, running on glucose at about 20 W, uses about 175 kWh a year, so that one training run equalled roughly 7,000 brain-years of energy. The comparison breaks where the systems differ: a model is trained once and then copied, and the two do different tasks.

days.apply_question: Many ruby-throated hummingbirds fly about 800 km nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico on migration, having nearly doubled their body weight beforehand; using what you know about fat and glycogen as fuels, explain why they store the energy for the crossing as fat rather than as glycogen.
days.evidence_note: Settled: respiration as oxidation and its energy accounting. Debated in detail: how precisely Atwater factors fit individual foods (fibre, nuts) and how much people's metabolic rates adapt to dieting.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: One Drought on a Galapagos Islet Killed Most of the Finches. The Next Generation Had Deeper Beaks.
days.concept: When individuals vary in heritable traits and those traits affect how many offspring they leave, the population's traits shift over generations; that is natural selection, and it produces adaptation without a designer of each step.
days.focus: Teaches the three ingredients (variation, heritability, differential reproduction) and the breeder's equation, which links today's selection to next generation's change through heritability, defined here simply as how strongly offspring resemble their parents (Galton's regression slope, Day 19; Day 136 treats heritability fully). The angle: evolution is observable and measurable, not only inferred from fossils; the evidence is settled science, even though its scope remains a subject of philosophical and theological discussion.
days.model_or_equation: Breeder's equation R = h^2 x S: the response R (change in the next generation's mean) equals heritability h^2 times the selection differential S (survivors' mean minus the original mean).

story.title: The year the seeds ran out on Daphne Major
story.hook: Peter and Rosemary Grant had been measuring the finches of Daphne Major, a volcanic islet of about 34 hectares in the Galapagos, since 1973. In 1977 the rains failed. Small, soft seeds were eaten first; what remained were large, hard seeds such as those of Tribulus. Roughly 85% of the island's medium ground finches died. The survivors were larger birds with deeper beaks, on average about 5-6% larger than those that died (Jonathan Weiner's account of the Grants' data). Peter Boag and Peter Grant reported in Science in 1981 that the selection was among the most intense then measured in any wild vertebrate. When the rains returned and the survivors bred, their offspring's beaks were about 3-4% deeper than the pre-drought average (accounts differ slightly on the figure).
story.puzzle: Not one finch grew a bigger beak during the drought, so how did the population's beaks get bigger in a single generation, and why only partly as big as the survivors'?
story.payoff: Selection did not change any bird; it changed who bred. Because beak depth is highly heritable, the survivors' offspring inherited much of their parents' advantage, and the breeder's equation predicts exactly a partial shift: response equals heritability times the selection differential. After the great 1982-83 El Nino left the island dominated by small, soft seeds, the next drought favoured smaller beaks: selection had reversed.
sources: Boag & Grant, 'Intense natural selection in a population of Darwin's finches', Science 214 (1981)
Jonathan Weiner, The Beak of the Finch (1994)
Quanta Magazine, 'Watching Evolution Happen in Two Lifetimes' (22 Sep 2016)

days.application: SARS-CoV-2 variants as selection in real time: Alpha, Delta and then Omicron (designated by the WHO on 26 Nov 2021, with more than 30 changes in its spike protein) each displaced its predecessor within months because they out-transmitted or evaded immunity, and genomic surveillance watched variant frequencies trace S-curves, the same variation-plus-differential-reproduction logic on a timescale of weeks.

builds_on.why: Heritability in the breeder's equation is Galton's regression slope of offspring on parents: offspring of extreme survivors regress partway to the mean, which is why the beak shift was smaller than the survivors' advantage.
Evolution makes risky predictions that could have failed (J.B.S. Haldane's 'fossil rabbits in the Precambrian'), the Popperian test the Grants' data passed.

across.link: Genetic algorithms copy variation-selection-inheritance in software; NASA's evolved X-band antenna, designed by an evolutionary algorithm, flew on the Space Technology 5 satellites in 2006, an odd shape no human engineer drew.

days.apply_question: During Mozambique's civil war (1977-1992) ivory poachers killed about 90% of the elephants in Gorongosa National Park, and among the females that survived the share born without tusks rose from about 18% to about 51% (Campbell-Staton et al., Science, 2021); using the three ingredients of natural selection, explain how a war could make tusklessness so much more common within a generation.
days.evidence_note: Settled: evolution by natural selection and common descent, supported by fossils, genomes and direct observation; this is the consensus of the relevant experts however loudly it is disputed in public. Debated within biology: the relative weight of selection, drift and development in particular cases. Many Christian scientists (for example Francis Collins, The Language of God, 2006) accept evolution; how it fits theology is a question for Philosophy II, not a reason to label the science.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Blurry X Helped Crack the Secret of Life. The Woman Who Made It Wasn't Told It Had Been Shown.
days.concept: DNA stores hereditary information as a sequence of four bases on two complementary strands, so each strand is a template for copying the other, and genes are read from DNA into RNA and translated into proteins (the central dogma).
days.focus: Teaches base pairing (A with T, G with C) as both the storage rule and the copying mechanism, the triplet code, and transcription and translation. The story corrects a myth: Franklin was not a passive victim who failed to understand her data; she was a co-solver whose data were used without her knowledge (Cobb & Comfort 2023).
days.model_or_equation: Information content: 4 bases = 2 bits per base pair; the roughly 3.1 billion base pairs of one human genome copy hold about 6.2 billion bits, about 775 MB.

story.title: Photograph 51 changes hands
story.hook: In May 1952 at King's College London, Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling recorded an X-ray diffraction image of the hydrated 'B' form of DNA after an exposure of many hours: a sharp X of spots. It was filed as Photograph 51. When Franklin prepared to leave King's for Birkbeck, Gosling passed the image to Maurice Wilkins, and in late January 1953 (historians usually date it to 30 January) Wilkins showed it to James Watson of Cambridge without Franklin's knowledge. Watson later wrote that the instant he saw it his mouth fell open. On 25 April 1953 Nature printed Watson and Crick's double-helix paper, alongside papers by Wilkins's group and by Franklin and Gosling.
story.puzzle: A single blurred X on film, and a structure that fits on one page of Nature: why did that structure instantly suggest how life copies itself, a question no one had been able to answer?
story.payoff: The X pattern says 'helix'; the chemistry says the two strands pair A with T and G with C. Pairing means each strand fixes the sequence of the other, so separating them yields two templates, which is how heredity copies itself, as Watson and Crick noted in their famous understated sentence. Franklin's measurements were essential; Cobb and Comfort (Nature, 2023) argue she was an equal contributor to the solution.
sources: Watson & Crick, Nature 171, 737-738 (25 April 1953); Franklin & Gosling, same issue
Cobb & Comfort, 'What Rosalind Franklin truly contributed to the discovery of DNA's structure', Nature (April 2023)
King's College London, 'The story behind Photograph 51'

days.application: DNA fingerprinting: in 1984 Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester found that repeated DNA segments vary hugely between people. In 1986 his test cleared Richard Buckland, a 17-year-old who had confessed to the murder of Dawn Ashworth in Narborough, Leicestershire; police then sampled several thousand local men (about 4,000-5,000; sources differ). Colin Pitchfork had a colleague give blood in his place, was caught when the swap was overheard, and in January 1988 became the first person convicted of murder on DNA evidence.

builds_on.why: DNA is a digital code in Shannon's sense: four symbols carry 2 bits per base, and copying errors are channel noise that repair enzymes correct.
A DNA 'match' must be weighed with Bayes: a random-match probability is not the probability of innocence, the prosecutor's fallacy of the Sally Clark case.

across.link: After the Pitchfork case the UK created the world's first national criminal DNA database (April 1995); in S and Marper v United Kingdom (2008) the European Court of Human Rights ruled that keeping the DNA of people never convicted violated the right to privacy, forcing Parliament to change the rules.

days.apply_question: In April 2018 investigators identified Joseph James DeAngelo, the 'Golden State Killer', by uploading crime-scene DNA to GEDmatch, a free genealogy site, and finding distant cousins; using the idea that relatives share long stretches of identical sequence, explain how uploads by a few third or fourth cousins, none of them a suspect, could lead investigators to one man.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the structure of DNA and the central dogma (with known exceptions such as reverse transcription by retroviruses). Debated in historiography: how to apportion credit for the double helix; the 'stolen data, wronged genius' story is being revised by archival work (Cobb & Comfort 2023), though the use of Photograph 51 without Franklin's knowledge is not disputed.

resource.title: What Rosalind Franklin truly contributed to the discovery of DNA's structure
resource.creator: Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, Nature (April 2023)
resource.why: Two historians of biology use a newly found letter and an unpublished 1953 news article to show what Franklin actually knew; it models how historians revise a famous story with evidence.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session: results from manchester.ac.uk, Chemistry World and ScienceAlert describe this April 2023 Nature commentary and quote it ('She was an equal contributor to solving it'). The Nature URL itself was not shown, so none is given.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Heredity and genetics: genes, ratios and heritability
days.headline_hint: A Monk's Pea Ratios Were Ignored for 34 Years, Then Called Too Good to Be True
days.concept: Inheritance runs through discrete genes passed on in pairs, which produce predictable ratios for single-gene traits; most human traits are polygenic, and heritability is a population statistic about variation, not a fixed destiny for any person.
days.focus: Teaches Mendel's segregation and the 3:1 ratio as probability, then the jump to polygenic traits (height involves thousands of variants) and what heritability does and does not mean. Huntington's disease is the rare clean single-gene case; height and IQ are the common, messy ones.
days.model_or_equation: For two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa): offspring AA : Aa : aa = 1 : 2 : 1, so dominant : recessive appearance = 3 : 1. Heritability h^2 = genetic variance / total variance in a given population and environment.

story.title: The peas of Brno, and a statistician's suspicion
story.hook: In February and March 1865 Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar at St Thomas's Abbey in Brno (Brunn), read two lectures to the city's Natural History Society on eight years of crossing garden peas: round against wrinkled seeds, yellow against green, tall against short. His 1866 paper reported ratios close to 3:1 across thousands of plants. It was cited only a handful of times until 1900, when Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently reached the same rules. Then, in 1936, R.A. Fisher, the founder of modern statistics, re-analysed Mendel's numbers and argued in Annals of Science that they fit the expected ratios too closely to be chance.
story.puzzle: How could a monk's counts of peas reveal invisible units of heredity a generation before anyone saw a chromosome, and if the data were 'too good', was the discovery itself doubtful?
story.payoff: Mendel's 3:1 is pure probability: each parent passes one of two copies at random, and a recessive trait shows only when both copies are recessive (1 in 4). That inference holds whatever happened to the counts. Whether the counts were unconsciously shaded, selectively reported or simply lucky is still argued (Franklin et al., Ending the Mendel-Fisher Controversy, 2008), but the laws were confirmed by every later geneticist.
sources: Mendel, 'Versuche uber Pflanzen-Hybriden', Verhandlungen des naturforschenden Vereines in Brunn (1866)
Fisher, 'Has Mendel's work been rediscovered?', Annals of Science 1 (1936)
Franklin, Edwards, Fairbanks, Hartl & Seidenfeld, Ending the Mendel-Fisher Controversy (2008)

days.application: Huntington's disease: a single dominant gene, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk. Nancy Wexler, whose mother had the disease, led expeditions from 1979 to villages around Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where the disease ran through an extended family of thousands; blood samples and pedigrees let James Gusella's team find a marker on chromosome 4 in 1983 (Nature), and the gene, with its expanded CAG repeat, was identified in 1993. Contrast height, about 80% heritable in well-fed populations yet shaped by thousands of genetic variants, each nudging stature by a millimetre or less: no single gene, and no fixed outcome for any one child.

builds_on.why: Mendel's ratios are probability: segregation is a fair coin per parent, and 3:1 is the expected value over many offspring.
Fisher's charge is a significance argument run in reverse: a chi-square fit that good would occur by chance only rarely.

across.link: Predictive single-gene tests like the one for Huntington's raised fears of genetic discrimination; the US Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), signed in May 2008, bars health insurers and employers from using genetic test results, but it does not cover life, disability or long-term-care insurance, a legal line drawn around what heredity can predict.

days.apply_question: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by inheriting two recessive copies of one gene and, untreated, causes severe intellectual disability, yet babies found by the newborn heel-prick screening test introduced in the 1960s and raised on a low-phenylalanine diet develop normally; using today's lesson, explain how a condition can be entirely genetic in origin and still not be a fixed destiny.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Mendelian inheritance, polygenicity of most traits, and the definition of heritability. Debated: whether Mendel's data were too good, and why; and in human behavioural genetics, how to interpret heritability estimates and polygenic scores across populations (Day 165 returns to this for intelligence). Value judgment: what, if anything, genetic prediction should be used for (embryo selection, insurance), which belongs to Philosophy II.

resource.title: The Gene: An Intimate History
resource.creator: Siddhartha Mukherjee (Scribner, 2016), Part One, 'The "Missing Science of Heredity"', the opening chapters on Mendel and his rediscovery
resource.length: the Mendel chapters of Part One, about 40 pages (roughly 1 hour)
resource.why: Tells Mendel's work, its neglect and its rediscovery as a narrative, and follows heredity's darker turn into eugenics, so the statistics arrive with their history.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge; the book is widely catalogued and Part One's title is recalled as 'The "Missing Science of Heredity": The Discovery and Rediscovery of Genes (1865-1935)'.
