days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Scientist in Shenzhen Edited Twin Embryos. A Court Gave Him Three Years. The Tool Itself Won a Nobel.
days.concept: CRISPR-Cas9 is a programmable DNA cutter, bacterial immune machinery repurposed so that a short guide RNA steers the Cas9 enzyme to one matching sequence, letting scientists disable or rewrite genes; editing a patient's body cells and editing embryos whose changes pass to descendants are ethically different acts.
days.focus: Teaches the mechanism (guide RNA, Cas9 cut, the cell's repair) and the somatic-versus-germline distinction that makes one approved medicine and the other a crime in many countries. The angle: the same tool can cure or overreach, so the ethics lives in what is edited and who consents.

story.title: The announcement in Hong Kong
story.hook: On 25 November 2018, two days before the Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing opened in Hong Kong, MIT Technology Review reported that a researcher at the Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen, He Jiankui, was running a trial to edit human embryos; the next day the Associated Press and He's own YouTube videos announced the result. He had disabled the CCR5 gene, which HIV uses to enter cells, and twin girls, given the pseudonyms Lulu and Nana, had been born. On 28 November he presented the work at the summit to an audience of stunned scientists. A third edited child was later confirmed. On 30 December 2019 a Shenzhen court sentenced him to three years in prison and fined him 3 million yuan for illegal medical practice.
story.puzzle: Gene editing was by then being tested to cure disease in adults, and within five years a CRISPR therapy would be approved. Why was this use a crime, when the scissors were the same?
story.payoff: The tool was identical; the act was not. He edited germline cells: every cell of the twins carries the change, and so may their children, without their consent, for a protection that safer means (avoiding infection, sperm washing) already offered, and with mosaic, unvalidated edits. Somatic editing changes one consenting patient's body cells and stops with them.
sources: Antonio Regalado, MIT Technology Review, 25 November 2018, and Associated Press, 26 November 2018, on the gene-edited twins
Reuters and Xinhua, Shenzhen court sentencing of 30 December 2019
Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing, Hong Kong, 27-29 November 2018

days.application: Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia: doctors remove a patient's blood stem cells, use CRISPR to switch back on fetal haemoglobin, and return them after chemotherapy. The UK's MHRA approved it first, on 16 November 2023, and the FDA on 8 December 2023; the US list price was about $2.2 million per patient, raising its own question about who can use a cure.

builds_on.why: CRISPR works by base pairing: the guide RNA finds its target by complementary pairing with the DNA, the same rule that copies genes.
Kant's formula of humanity and the consent principle bear on germline editing, whose subjects are future people who cannot consent.

across.link: The Council of Europe's Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (1997), Article 13, permits genome modification only for preventive, diagnostic or therapeutic purposes and only if it is not aimed at introducing a modification in the genome of any descendants, a treaty line drawn exactly at the somatic-germline distinction.

days.apply_question: Verve Therapeutics has tested a one-time infusion that uses a CRISPR-derived 'base editor' to switch off the PCSK9 gene in adults' liver cells and lower their cholesterol for life; using the somatic-germline distinction, what would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to judge whether offering such a permanent edit to people who are not yet ill is acceptable?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mechanism, and the approval of somatic therapies such as Casgevy. Debated: long-term safety and off-target effects; whether heritable editing could ever be justified (the 2020 international commission set out narrow conditions; many ethicists and religious traditions reject it). Value judgment: where to draw lines between therapy and enhancement, and how to price one-time cures.

resource.title: How CRISPR lets us edit our DNA
resource.creator: Jennifer Doudna, TED Global London (2015)
resource.why: The co-inventor explains the bacterial origin of CRISPR and, three years before the twins, called for a pause on clinical germline editing, so it shows the scientists' own ethical line being drawn.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of the TEDGlobal London talk (September 2015, about 16 minutes); confirm on ted.com at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Ecology: food webs and trophic cascades
days.headline_hint: Fourteen Wolves Came Back to Yellowstone. A Viral Video Says They Changed the Rivers. Ecologists Are Still Arguing.
days.concept: Populations grow toward the carrying capacity their environment allows and are linked through food webs, so removing or restoring one species, especially a top predator or keystone species, can cascade down through the web, though how strongly depends on the system.
days.focus: Teaches food webs, keystone species (Paine's starfish experiment, 1966; the term 1969) and trophic cascades, then uses Yellowstone to show how a famous cascade story grew larger than its evidence. The angle: ecology is systems thinking with real organisms, and its measurements are hard.
days.model_or_equation: Logistic growth with a predator term, informally: prey growth = rN(1 - N/K) minus losses to predators; removing the predator lets prey rise toward K, and their own food then falls.

story.title: The wolves of the Lamar Valley
story.hook: In January 1995 the first grey wolves captured in Alberta were released in Yellowstone National Park, about 70 years after the last resident pack was killed; 14 came that winter and 17 more in 1996. Elk had grown abundant without wolves, and willows and aspens along streams had been browsed low. Within a decade, some studies reported willows and aspen recovering in places, and in 2014 a short video, 'How Wolves Change Rivers', told millions of viewers that the wolves had reshaped valleys, birds, beavers and even the course of rivers.
story.puzzle: Could 31 predators really rearrange a whole ecosystem, down to its rivers, and if so, why do field ecologists disagree about how much they did?
story.payoff: A trophic cascade is real biology: predators reduce or move herbivores, plants recover, and other species follow. But Yellowstone changed in many ways at once (hunting, drought, bears and cougars, beaver reintroductions), and studies sampling the tallest willows exaggerated the effect (Brice, Larsen & MacNulty, Ecology Letters 2022). The cascade happened; its size is debated.
sources: US National Park Service, Yellowstone wolf restoration history (1995-96 releases)
Ripple & Beschta, Biological Conservation (2012), for the strong-cascade view
Brice, Larsen & MacNulty, 'Sampling bias exaggerates a textbook example of a trophic cascade', Ecology Letters (2022)

days.application: Why ecosystem interventions surprise their designers: in the 1990s Indian farmers began treating cattle with diclofenac, a cheap anti-inflammatory painkiller. Vultures that fed on treated carcasses died of kidney failure (Oaks et al., Nature, 2004), and India's Gyps vulture populations fell by more than 95%. Carcasses that vultures once stripped in hours rotted or fed growing packs of feral dogs, which carry rabies. Eyal Frank and Anant Sudarshan (American Economic Review, 2024) estimated that the vultures' collapse led to about half a million extra human deaths from 2000 to 2005. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. Nobody designing a cattle painkiller drew a path through scavenging birds to people; the food web had it.

builds_on.why: Carrying capacity is the logistic ceiling: populations level off where their environment, including predators, balances births and deaths.
Fixes that fail and unintended consequences: interventions in food webs routinely produce effects through paths nobody modelled.

across.link: The wolves were reintroduced under section 10(j) of the US Endangered Species Act (1973) as an 'experimental, nonessential population', a legal category that let ranchers kill wolves attacking livestock and made the reintroduction politically possible.

days.apply_question: Ransom Myers and colleagues (Science, 2007) argued that overfishing of great sharks off the US East Coast let cownose rays multiply and wipe out North Carolina's bay-scallop fishery, a textbook marine cascade that Grubbs and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2016) later disputed; using what Yellowstone teaches about trophic cascades, what evidence would you need to decide whether the sharks' decline really caused the scallops' collapse?
days.evidence_note: Settled: food webs, keystone species and trophic cascades as real phenomena (Paine's experiments; sea otters and kelp). Debated: the strength of the Yellowstone cascade, with Ripple and Beschta finding large effects and MacNulty, Hobbs and colleagues finding smaller, patchier ones; the river-reshaping claim is the weakest. The size of the human death toll from India's vulture collapse rests mainly on one recent study (Frank & Sudarshan 2024), so give it as an estimate.

resource.title: Some Animals Are More Equal than Others: Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades
resource.creator: HHMI BioInteractive (2016), short film based on Sean B. Carroll's The Serengeti Rules
resource.why: Free film showing the experiments behind the concept: Robert Paine prising starfish off the rocks at Mukkaw Bay to discover the keystone effect, and Jim Estes tracing sea otters, urchins and kelp; it gives the field evidence the lesson describes in words, before the Yellowstone debate.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of HHMI BioInteractive's 2016 film (it shares its title with a chapter of Carroll's book); confirm the title, runtime and free listing on biointeractive.org at build time. Replaces the earlier book-chapter pick with a free video on the same material.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: Billions of Passenger Pigeons Darkened the Sky. In 1914 the Last One Died in a Cincinnati Zoo.
days.concept: Extinction risk rises steeply as habitat shrinks and numbers fall, because small populations face chance, inbreeding and Allee effects (individuals that need company to feed and breed do worse when rare), so a species can be doomed while still numerous; and how to measure biodiversity decline is itself contested.
days.focus: Teaches extinction as a process with thresholds, not just a count of the dead, then teaches how an index such as the Living Planet Index aggregates thousands of populations and why its headline average invites misreading. The angle: both the loss and the measuring problem are real.
days.model_or_equation: Living Planet Index: an average of the logarithms of population changes across monitored populations; a few populations falling by 99% can move the average more than many stable ones.

story.title: Martha, Cincinnati, 1 September 1914
story.hook: Early in the nineteenth century, observers such as John James Audubon described passenger pigeon flocks passing overhead for hours or days; estimates of the population run to several billion birds, by some estimates a quarter or more of all the birds in North America. They nested in vast colonies. Market hunters, using the telegraph and the railway, shipped them by the boxcar, and eastern forests were cleared. The last confirmed wild bird was shot in Ohio in 1900. At about 1 pm on 1 September 1914, Martha, the last of her kind, died at the Cincinnati Zoo, aged about 29. Her body went to the Smithsonian in a block of ice.
story.puzzle: When the last great nesting colonies failed in the 1880s, birds were still left, in the wild and in a few captive flocks such as Martha's own, yet none rebuilt a population. Why didn't the survivors recover, the way white-tailed deer and egrets later did once hunting was curbed?
story.payoff: Passenger pigeons were colonial breeders whose feeding, predator swamping and nesting depended on enormous numbers. Below a threshold, the Allee effect turned smallness into further decline: small flocks bred poorly and were picked off, so the species was committed to extinction while birds were still alive, an extinction debt. This is the leading explanation; how much each factor (hunting, forest clearance, social breeding) mattered is still studied.
sources: Smithsonian Institution, 'Martha, the last passenger pigeon' (National Museum of Natural History)
Joel Greenberg, A Feathered River Across the Sky (2014)
Hung, Shaner, Zink et al., PNAS (2014), on passenger pigeon population history

days.application: WWF and ZSL's Living Planet Index 2024 reported an average decline of 73% in monitored vertebrate populations since 1970. That does not mean 73% of animals are gone: it is an average of rates across about 35,000 populations, and Leung et al. (Nature, 2020) showed the global trend is driven by a small cluster of extremely declining populations, while most are stable or growing. Both readings matter: the clusters are real crises, and the headline is easy to misstate.

builds_on.why: Thresholds and hysteresis: below a critical number, Allee effects flip a population into a self-reinforcing decline that removing the original pressure does not reverse.
Distributions: when a few extreme values dominate, an average misdescribes the typical case, which is the Living Planet Index's interpretive problem.

across.link: The US Lacey Act of 1900, the first federal wildlife-protection law, banned interstate shipment of illegally killed game, a direct response to the market hunting that had destroyed passenger pigeon and plume-bird populations.

days.apply_question: The vaquita, a small porpoise found only in Mexico's upper Gulf of California, has fallen to roughly ten animals after decades of drowning in gillnets set for another fish; using Allee effects and the risks of small populations, explain why even a complete end to gillnet deaths might not be enough to save it.
days.evidence_note: Settled: human-driven extinctions and steep local declines; the mechanics of small-population risk. Debated: how to measure global biodiversity change and how fast it is declining (Living Planet Index authors versus Leung et al. 2020 and other critics of its aggregation); claims of a 'sixth mass extinction' depend on definitions and rates.

resource.title: The Sixth Extinction: An Unnatural History
resource.creator: Elizabeth Kolbert (Henry Holt, 2014; Pulitzer Prize 2015), chapter 3, 'The Original Penguin'
resource.why: The great auk's extinction told through the hunters and naturalists who watched it, a second case of a once-abundant bird pushed past recovery; Kolbert writes from the view that a mass extinction is under way, which the lesson labels as debated.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge; the book and its 2015 Pulitzer are widely documented, and chapter 3 is recalled as 'The Original Penguin'. Confirm at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Doctor Made His Colleagues Wash Their Hands and Deaths Fell Fivefold. Vienna Let Him Go.
days.concept: Specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, which replaced the miasma theory of bad air and turned hygiene from a matter of smell and virtue into a science of breaking the paths microbes travel.
days.focus: Teaches germ theory through Pasteur's experiments (swan-neck flasks, 1859-62) and Koch's postulates (from 1884, after his tuberculosis work of 1882), with Semmelweis as the puzzle that came too early for the theory to rescue him. The angle: a correct finding was rejected because it lacked a mechanism and offended the profession.

story.title: Two clinics, one hospital, Vienna 1847
story.hook: Vienna General Hospital had two maternity clinics, admitting on alternate days. In the First Clinic, staffed by doctors and medical students who came straight from autopsies, roughly 10% of mothers died of puerperal (childbed) fever in the early 1840s; in the Second, staffed by midwives, about 4% did. Women begged not to be admitted to the First. In 1847 the young Hungarian assistant Ignaz Semmelweis watched his friend Jakob Kolletschka die of a similar illness after a student's scalpel cut him during an autopsy. In May 1847 Semmelweis ordered doctors to wash in chlorinated lime before examinations; the First Clinic's death rate fell to around 1-2%. Senior colleagues resisted, he lost his post, and he died in an asylum near Vienna on 13 August 1865, probably of an infected wound.
story.puzzle: The numbers were stark and the fix was cheap. Why did the medical world reject a fivefold cut in deaths?
story.payoff: Semmelweis blamed 'cadaverous particles' but had no theory of what they were, and he implied that physicians were killing their patients. Germ theory, from Pasteur and Koch in the 1860s-1880s, supplied the mechanism: specific living microbes, carried on hands and instruments, cause specific diseases. Only then did hand hygiene become doctrine (Lister's antisepsis from 1867).
sources: Semmelweis, Die Atiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861)
Loudon, The Tragedy of Childbed Fever (2000)
Best & Neuhauser, 'Ignaz Semmelweis and the birth of infection control', BMJ Quality & Safety (2004)

days.application: Checklists against hospital infection: in the Keystone ICU project, Peter Pronovost's team asked 103 intensive-care units in Michigan to use a five-step checklist for central venous lines (wash hands, full barrier precautions, chlorhexidine, avoid the femoral site, remove unneeded catheters). Bloodstream infections fell from a mean of 7.7 to 1.4 per 1,000 catheter-days at 16-18 months, about two-thirds fewer (Pronovost et al., NEJM, 28 Dec 2006): Semmelweis's lesson, made into a system.

builds_on.why: Semmelweis's comparison is a natural experiment: alternate-day admission assigned mothers to clinics as if at random, so the death gap pointed at the staff, not the patients.
Paradigms: a finding without a theory to house it was rejected until the germ paradigm arrived, Kuhn's anomaly story in medicine.

across.link: The pilot's checklist was born when Boeing's Model 299 bomber prototype crashed at Wright Field on 30 October 1935 because the crew forgot to release the control locks; Pronovost explicitly modelled the ICU checklist on aviation's, the high-reliability practice taught in Engineering.

days.apply_question: London's main drainage system, built by Joseph Bazalgette after the 'Great Stink' of summer 1858 to carry sewage away from the Thames, was designed to remove foul air under the miasma theory; using germ theory and the idea of a transmission route, explain why it nonetheless helped end London's cholera epidemics.
days.evidence_note: Settled: germ theory and the effect of hand hygiene. Debated in history: how much Semmelweis's own temperament, his slow publication and Viennese politics, rather than pure professional pride, explain his rejection.

resource.title: The Checklist
resource.creator: Atul Gawande, The New Yorker (10 December 2007)
resource.why: A surgeon's account of Pronovost's ICU checklist and the Michigan results, showing how germ theory's simplest rule fails in practice and how a system makes it stick.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of the New Yorker article (issue of 10 December 2007), later expanded into The Checklist Manifesto (2009); confirm on newyorker.com at build time (it may sit behind the magazine's metered paywall).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: An Enslaved Man Taught Boston to Fight Smallpox. Someone Threw a Bomb Through the Minister's Window.
days.concept: The adaptive immune system remembers pathogens it has met, so vaccination teaches that memory without the disease; and when enough people are immune, an infection cannot sustain itself, which happens once the immune share exceeds 1 - 1/R0, where R0 is the number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population.
days.focus: Teaches innate versus adaptive immunity, memory B and T cells, and the herd-immunity threshold as arithmetic, using inoculation (variolation) and vaccination as the historical path. The angle: immunity is both a personal biology and a shared good.
days.model_or_equation: Herd immunity threshold H = 1 - 1/R0. For measles with R0 = 15, H = 1 - 1/15 = 93%; with an imperfect vaccine of efficacy E, required coverage = H / E.

story.title: Boston, summer 1721
story.hook: In 1721 smallpox arrived in Boston on a ship from the West Indies. The minister Cotton Mather had learned years earlier from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man in his household, that in Africa people were deliberately infected with matter from a smallpox sore to give a mild case and lifelong protection. Mather urged the town's doctors to try it; only Zabdiel Boylston agreed, starting with his own son. The town's physicians, led by William Douglass, denounced it. On 14 November 1721 someone threw a lit grenade through Mather's window with a note cursing him; it failed to explode. By the end, about 2% of Boylston's inoculated patients had died, against about 14% of those who caught smallpox naturally.
story.puzzle: Inoculation gave people actual smallpox, and some died of it. Why did a deliberate infection protect so well, and why did the town see it as a danger to everyone else?
story.payoff: A mild infection trains the adaptive immune system, which keeps memory cells that respond fast enough to stop the disease next time. But variolated people were contagious, so it could spread smallpox to others, a real public risk. Jenner's cowpox vaccine (1796) gave the memory without contagious smallpox, and once enough people were immune, chains of transmission broke for everyone.
sources: Mather, letter to the Royal Society on African inoculation (1716); Boylston, An Historical Account of the Small-Pox Inoculated in New England (1726)
Harvard Library, 'Contagion: Historical Views of Diseases and Epidemics', on the 1721 Boston epidemic
Best, Neuhauser & Slavin, 'Cotton Mather, you dog, dam you!' BMJ Quality & Safety (2004)

days.application: Smallpox eradication: the WHO's intensified programme (from 1967) used ring vaccination, finding cases and vaccinating their contacts, rather than vaccinating everyone. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook in Merca, Somalia, whose rash began on 26 October 1977; the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980. Measles, with an R0 commonly given as 12-18, needs about 95% two-dose coverage, which is why small dips in coverage bring it back.

builds_on.why: Daniel Bernoulli's 1760 expected-value calculation for smallpox inoculation weighed a small immediate risk of death against years of life gained, the decision Boston faced in 1721.
Herd immunity is a shared resource with a free-rider problem: each person gains from others' vaccination, which is why coverage can erode when the disease seems gone.

across.link: In Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) the US Supreme Court upheld Cambridge's compulsory smallpox vaccination ordinance and its $5 fine, setting the constitutional baseline for public-health powers that courts still cite; Justice Holmes later leaned on it in Buck v. Bell (1927), the case in Day 43, which shows how a sound precedent can be stretched.

days.apply_question: Mumps has a basic reproduction number usually put at about 4-7, and two doses of MMR vaccine protect roughly 88% of people against it (CDC's median estimate); using the herd-immunity threshold and the coverage formula, explain why outbreaks still broke out on US campuses where about 98% of students had two doses, as at the University of Iowa in 2015-16.
days.evidence_note: Settled: adaptive immunity, vaccine-induced protection, the herd-immunity arithmetic in its simple form (real populations mix unevenly, so it is a guide, not a precise target). Value judgment: when communities may mandate vaccination, weighing individual liberty against protection of others.

resource.title: The Immune System Explained I - Bacteria Infection
resource.creator: Kurzgesagt - In a Nutshell (2014)
resource.why: Animates how innate defenders and adaptive B and T cells respond to an infection and build memory, the biology beneath the herd-immunity arithmetic.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of the Kurzgesagt channel's immune-system series (2014); confirm the title and runtime on the channel at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Toddler in a Guinean Village Fell Sick in December 2013. Two Years Later 11,000 People Were Dead.
days.concept: Whether an outbreak becomes a pandemic depends on four things: how many people each case infects (R0), how fast one generation of cases follows the last (generation time), how severe it is, and above all how much transmission happens before symptoms show, because only symptomatic spread can be stopped by isolating the sick.
days.focus: Teaches the Fraser et al. (PNAS 2004) framework, R0 together with theta, the share of transmission before symptoms, plus superspreading. The angle: deadly is not the same as dangerous; Ebola kills a large share of the infected but could be contained, while SARS-CoV-2 spread silently.
days.model_or_equation: Cases in generation n = R^n (from one case). With R = 2 and a 5-day generation, 10 generations (50 days) give about 1,000 cases; with R = 1.5, about 58.

story.title: Meliandou, December 2013
story.hook: In late December 2013 a small boy, Emile Ouamouno (usually given as 18 months old; some reports say two), fell ill with fever, vomiting and black stools in Meliandou, a forest village in southeastern Guinea near the borders of Sierra Leone and Liberia; he died within days, and his sister, mother and grandmother followed. Investigators later traced the epidemic to him, perhaps after contact with bats roosting in a hollow tree where village children played (the exact origin remains open). No one recognised Ebola until March 2014. By its end in 2016 the West African epidemic had caused about 28,600 recorded cases and 11,325 deaths, more than all earlier Ebola outbreaks combined.
story.puzzle: Ebola had erupted at least two dozen times since 1976 and burned out in remote villages. Why did this one explode across three countries, while for all its lethality Ebola still never became a global pandemic?
story.payoff: Ebola spreads mainly from visibly sick patients and the dead, so isolation and safe burial can stop it; earlier outbreaks were in isolated places where it ran out of contacts. This time it reached mobile border regions and capital cities with weak health systems, keeping R above 1 for months. But because almost no transmission happens before symptoms, tracing and isolation eventually broke the chains, which is why it never went global.
sources: Baize et al., 'Emergence of Zaire Ebola virus disease in Guinea', NEJM (2014)
CDC, '2014-2016 Ebola Outbreak in West Africa' (case and death totals)
Mari Saez et al., EMBO Molecular Medicine (2015), on the bat-tree hypothesis

days.application: SARS in 2003 caused about 8,100 cases and 774 deaths and was contained within months, because patients were most infectious after symptoms began, so isolating the sick worked. SARS-CoV-2 in 2020 had a large share of transmission before or without symptoms (estimates around 40-50%), so isolating the sick could not stop it: the Fraser framework predicted which virus would escape.

builds_on.why: R0, the number of people one case infects in a susceptible population, was defined with herd immunity; today asks what else besides R0 decides whether an outbreak explodes, and cases multiply by R each generation, the exponential growth of Day 2.
Networks: superspreading means a few highly connected cases drive most transmission, as hubs dominate spread on a network.

across.link: The Code Red worm infected about 359,000 computers in under 14 hours on 19 July 2001 (Moore, Shannon & Brown, 2002), and Staniford, Paxson and Weaver (2002) fitted its spread with an epidemic model; the analogy breaks where patching, unlike immunity, can be pushed to every machine centrally and overnight.

days.apply_question: Mpox spread worldwide in 2022 mainly through close sexual contact in particular networks; using R, presymptomatic spread and superspreading, explain why it grew quickly in those networks but did not become a general pandemic like COVID-19.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the framework of R0, generation time and presymptomatic spread. Debated: precise estimates for any one pathogen (COVID-19's presymptomatic share varies by study), and the origin details of the West African outbreak.

resource.title: Simulating an epidemic
resource.creator: 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), 2020
resource.why: Animated simulations of SIR models show how the infection rate, social distancing, contact tracing and undetected cases change an outbreak's curve, making the lesson's factors visible.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session (a cached result from another agent's query, reused because the shared search budget was later exhausted): the URL appeared on 3blue1brown.com titled '3Blue1Brown - Simulating an epidemic', described as covering SIR models and how behaviour changes an outbreak, with its YouTube counterpart (youtube.com/watch?v=gxAaO2rsdIs) also listed. Runtime from model knowledge, not confirmed. Not fetched.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: Of 649 Men With Lung Cancer, 647 Smoked. Convincing Washington Took Another Fourteen Years.
days.concept: When you cannot randomly assign a harmful exposure, epidemiologists build causal cases from observation, with case-control studies that compare the sick to the well, cohort studies that follow the exposed and unexposed forward, and Bradford Hill's 1965 viewpoints (strength, consistency, dose-response, temporality and others) for judging whether an association is causal.
days.focus: Teaches the two main observational designs, relative risk and odds ratio, and Hill's viewpoints as a structured judgment rather than a checklist. The angle: smoking was proven to cause cancer without a single human trial, and the reasoning that did it is the reasoning that also catches false alarms.
days.model_or_equation: Relative risk = (rate of disease in exposed) / (rate in unexposed). In the British Doctors Study, heavy smokers' lung-cancer death rate was more than 20 times that of non-smokers.

story.title: Twenty London hospitals, 1948-1950
story.hook: After the Second World War, lung cancer deaths in Britain had risen many times over, and the Medical Research Council asked Richard Doll, a young physician, and the statistician Austin Bradford Hill to find out why; Doll suspected road tar or car exhaust. From 1948 their almoners interviewed patients with lung cancer in twenty London hospitals and matched each with a patient of the same sex and age admitted for something else. On 30 September 1950 the BMJ published their preliminary report: of 649 men with lung cancer, 647 smoked, against 622 of the 649 comparison men, and risk rose with the amount smoked. Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham had published a similar US study in JAMA that May.
story.puzzle: Almost all the controls smoked too, and no one had randomly assigned cigarettes. How could a comparison like this establish that smoking causes cancer, rather than that some kind of person both smokes and gets cancer?
story.payoff: A case-control study can show a strong, graded association; causation needs more. Doll and Hill then followed about 40,000 British doctors forward from 1951 (the cohort design), found the same dose-response, and saw doctors who quit lower their risk. Strength, consistency across countries, temporality, dose-response and biological plausibility together made confounding implausible, the reasoning Hill codified in 1965.
sources: Doll & Hill, 'Smoking and carcinoma of the lung: preliminary report', BMJ (30 September 1950)
Doll & Hill, 'The mortality of doctors in relation to their smoking habits', BMJ (1954)
Hill, 'The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?', Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine 58 (1965)

days.application: Zika and microcephaly: after Brazil saw a surge in babies with small heads in 2015, CDC scientists (Rasmussen, Jamieson, Honein & Petersen, NEJM, April 2016) weighed the evidence with formal criteria: Zika infection in pregnancy preceded the defects (temporality), the virus was found in fetal brain tissue (plausibility), and a specific, rare pattern of defects appeared. They concluded Zika causes microcephaly without any trial.

builds_on.why: Confounding is the central threat to observational causal claims; Hill's viewpoints are ways of making confounding implausible.
Randomized trials are the benchmark; epidemiology explains what can be concluded when a trial would be unethical, as with assigning smoking.

across.link: The US Surgeon General's report Smoking and Health (released 11 January 1964), drafted by an advisory committee whose members the tobacco industry had been allowed to vet, used explicit causal criteria including strength, consistency and temporality to conclude that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men.

days.apply_question: Observational studies have long found that people who drink moderate amounts of alcohol live longer than lifelong non-drinkers; using Bradford Hill's viewpoints and the idea of reverse causation, what is the most likely alternative explanation for that pattern?
days.evidence_note: Settled: smoking causes lung cancer and many other diseases. Debated in method: how much weight to give observational evidence where trials are impossible, and how to apply Hill's viewpoints, which Hill himself said were not rules.

resource.title: The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?
resource.creator: Austin Bradford Hill, Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine 58 (1965): 295-300
resource.why: The original lecture is short, clear and modest: Hill walks through each viewpoint with examples and insists none is a mechanical rule, which is the judgment the lesson asks Logan to practise.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of the 1965 paper, freely available on PubMed Central; confirm at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Doctor Put Bleach in Jersey City's Water. A Court Had to Decide Whether That Made It Pure.
days.concept: Population-scale public-health engineering, with water filtration, chlorination and sewers, breaks the faecal-oral route by which waterborne microbes spread, and in many cities it cut typhoid and diarrhoeal deaths faster than any medicine of its time, though how much of the total mortality decline it explains is debated.
days.focus: Teaches sanitation as germ theory applied to infrastructure: the multiple barriers (source protection, filtration, disinfection, sewage separation), why chlorine works, and the dispute about its measured effect. The angle: the cheapest life-savers were pipes and chemistry, not pills, but the size of that claim must be measured.

story.title: Chloride of lime at Boonton Reservoir
story.hook: In 1908 Jersey City, New Jersey, was in court with the private company that supplied its water from the Boonton Reservoir, arguing that the water was not 'pure and wholesome' as the contract required; sewage from upstream towns still reached it after storms. The company's sanitary adviser, the physician John L. Leal, proposed something no American city supply had tried: add small, continuous doses of chloride of lime, a bleach, to the whole supply. With the engineer George Warren Fuller he built the plant in about three months, and continuous chlorination began on 26 September 1908, with the case still open. Critics argued that dosing a city's water with a chemical was itself a kind of contamination. A court-appointed special master later ruled that the treatment made the water pure and wholesome.
story.puzzle: How could adding a toxic chemical to a city's drinking water make it safer, and why would that do more for health than any doctor then could?
story.payoff: Chlorine at a fraction of a part per million kills bacteria such as the typhoid bacillus far faster than it harms people, so a cheap chemical in tiny doses cut the route by which one sick person's faeces reached thousands. Germ theory said what to kill; engineering did it for a whole city at once, and US typhoid deaths fell steeply as chlorination spread.
sources: Michael J. McGuire, The Chlorine Revolution: Water Disinfection and the Fight to Save Lives (2013)
American Water Works Association history of the 1908 Jersey City chlorination
CDC MMWR, 'Achievements in Public Health, 1900-1999: Control of Infectious Diseases' (1999)

days.application: How much did clean water explain? Cutler & Miller (Demography, 2005), using the timing of filtration and chlorination in 13 large US cities from 1900 to 1936, estimated that clean water explained about half of the fall in total mortality, three-quarters of the fall in infant mortality and nearly two-thirds of the fall in child mortality. Anderson, Charles & Rees (American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 2022), using more cities and data, found much smaller effects for filtration and little for other measures. Same question, same era, different methods, different answers.

builds_on.why: The staggered timing of filtration across cities is a natural experiment; Cutler-Miller and their critics both use difference-in-differences.
Germ theory told engineers what to remove from water and why chlorine, which kills bacteria, would work.

across.link: Flint, Michigan, run by a state-appointed emergency manager, switched its water source to the Flint River in April 2014 without the corrosion control federal rules required; lead leached from old pipes, the system also broke limits on chlorine by-products, and a Legionnaires' disease outbreak killed at least 12 people. Criminal charges against officials followed, though most were later dismissed: a public system failing at the multiple-barrier engineering this lesson describes.

days.apply_question: In spring 1993 an estimated 400,000 people in Milwaukee fell ill with Cryptosporidium, a parasite that chlorine at normal doses barely harms, after one of the city's two treatment plants let through cloudier water than usual; using the multiple-barrier idea, explain why a chlorinated supply still failed to protect them.
days.evidence_note: Settled: filtration and chlorination prevent waterborne disease. Debated: their share of the historic urban mortality decline, roughly half (Cutler & Miller 2005) versus much less (Anderson, Charles & Rees 2022). Value judgment: how to trade small long-term risks of disinfection by-products against acute infection risks.

resource.title: The Chlorine Revolution: Water Disinfection and the Fight to Save Lives
resource.creator: Michael J. McGuire (American Water Works Association, 2013), the chapters on Jersey City and the Boonton trials
resource.length: two to three chapters, roughly 1 hour
resource.why: A water engineer's history of Leal's decision and the court battle, with the documents; it shows how infrastructure decisions are made under legal and scientific uncertainty.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: Tuberculosis Deaths Fell for a Century Before There Was a Cure. So What Saved Them?
days.concept: Life expectancy at birth is a period statistic, the average lifespan a newborn would have if today's death rates held for life, so its doubling since 1800 came mostly from collapsing death rates in childhood, and why those rates collapsed (nutrition, sanitation, medicine, income, knowledge) is still debated.
days.focus: Teaches what life expectancy measures and what it does not, why child deaths dominate it, and the McKeown-versus-Preston-and-Szreter debate about causes. The angle: the best-measured gain in human welfare is not in doubt; its causes are, and that matters for policy and for Logan's book.
days.model_or_equation: Period life expectancy e0 = sum over ages of the probability of surviving to each age, using this year's age-specific death rates. A world where 40% of children die young and survivors reach 60 has e0 of roughly 0.4 x 2 + 0.6 x 60 = about 37 years, though no adult dies at 37.

story.title: McKeown's graph
story.hook: In 1976 Thomas McKeown, a professor of social medicine at Birmingham, published The Modern Rise of Population. His most famous graph showed the death rate from respiratory tuberculosis in England and Wales from 1838: about 4,000 deaths per million people a year, falling steadily decade after decade. Robert Koch identified the bacillus in 1882; streptomycin came in 1947 and BCG vaccination in the 1950s. By the time effective drugs arrived, most of the fall had already happened. McKeown concluded that medicine did little: better nutrition and rising living standards had made people resistant. The argument shaped public-health thinking for a generation.
story.puzzle: If doctors had no cure, what drove death rates down for a century, and does McKeown's graph prove it was food?
story.payoff: McKeown was right that drugs came late and wrong to infer that nutrition did it by elimination. Samuel Preston (Population Studies, 1975) had shown that the whole curve relating life expectancy to income shifted upward between the 1930s and the 1960s, so rising income explained only about 10-25% of the gain and better knowledge and public health most of the rest; Simon Szreter (1988) credited sanitation and municipal reform. Historians also point to isolation in sanatoria, less crowding and possibly changing virulence for tuberculosis. The mortality revolution had many causes, weighted differently by different scholars.
sources: McKeown, The Modern Rise of Population (1976)
Preston, 'The changing relation between mortality and level of economic development', Population Studies 29 (1975)
Szreter, 'The importance of social intervention in Britain's mortality decline c.1850-1914', Social History of Medicine 1 (1988)

days.application: Global under-five mortality: by reconstruction, roughly 4 in 10 children died before age five around 1800; by the early 2020s the global figure was under 4 in 100 (Our World in Data, from Gapminder and UN IGME). Because child deaths pulled the average down so hard, world life expectancy rose from about 30 years in 1800 to over 70 today, while many adults who survived childhood in 1800 already reached their fifties or sixties.

builds_on.why: Clean water and sewers are one of the candidate causes, with their own disputed share.
Several causes moved together over the same decades, so attributing the decline is a confounding problem, which is why McKeown's inference by elimination fails.

across.link: The demographic transition (Frank Notestein, 1945): falling child mortality is followed, after a lag, by falling fertility, so populations surge in between; the mortality revolution is the first half of that pattern.

days.apply_question: Russian male life expectancy fell by about six years in the early 1990s and then recovered; using the difference between period and cohort measures and what you know about causes of death, what would you need to know to decide whether a whole generation's lifespans changed or only a few years' death rates did?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the scale of the fall in mortality, especially child mortality, and what life expectancy measures. Debated: the relative contributions of nutrition and income (McKeown), public health and sanitation (Szreter), medical knowledge and technology (Preston and later work), and their mix by period and place.

resource.title: The Great Escape: Health, Wealth, and the Origins of Inequality
resource.creator: Angus Deaton (Princeton University Press, 2013), chapter 2, 'From Prehistory to 1945'
resource.why: A Nobel laureate economist weighs McKeown, Preston and the sanitation historians and explains life-expectancy measures with care; it is the book's own debate in one chapter.
resource.verified_how: From model knowledge; the book is widely catalogued. Not confirmed by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); confirm the chapter title at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: Borlaug's Wheat Seed Was Stuck at a Border During Riots, Then Shipped Into a War. Five Years Later India's Harvest Had Nearly Doubled.
days.concept: Grain yields multiplied in the 1960s-70s because plant breeders made short-strawed (semi-dwarf) wheat and rice that could use heavy doses of fertilizer and irrigation without falling over, so the gain came from a package of seed, nitrogen and water, and its costs (groundwater depletion, inequality, loss of crop diversity) are debated.
days.focus: Teaches the biology of the semi-dwarf trait (lodging, harvest index), why it needed Haber-Bosch nitrogen and irrigation, and the debate over who gained and what was spent. The angle: a genuine humanitarian success that drew down a hidden stock.
days.model_or_equation: Yield = biomass x harvest index; short straw raises the harvest index (grain as a share of total plant mass) and lets more fertilizer become grain instead of stalk.

story.title: Seed trucks, riots and a war, 1965
story.hook: In 1965 Norman Borlaug, an Iowa-born plant breeder working in Mexico for the Rockefeller Foundation, arranged to ship hundreds of tonnes of semi-dwarf Mexican wheat seed to Pakistan and India, both facing famine. The convoy of trucks was held up at the US-Mexico border; in Los Angeles, where it was to be loaded, the Watts riots broke out in August; and by the time the seed sailed, India and Pakistan were at war (September 1965). Some of the seed was damaged in fumigation and germinated poorly. Borlaug told the farmers to plant more densely and fertilize more. India's wheat harvest nearly doubled between the mid-1960s and 1970-71, and in 1970 Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize.
story.puzzle: Indian farmers already had wheat and fertilizer existed. Why did this particular seed make such a difference, and why did it need so much water and nitrogen to do it?
story.payoff: Traditional tall wheat fed heavily with nitrogen grew taller and fell over (lodging), wasting the grain. Semi-dwarf varieties, carrying Japanese Norin 10 dwarfing genes, put the extra nitrogen into grain instead of stalk, so the gain came only as a package: seed plus fertilizer plus reliable irrigation. That is why it transformed irrigated Punjab and largely bypassed rain-fed regions.
sources: Leon Hesser, The Man Who Fed the World: Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Norman Borlaug (2006)
Charles C. Mann, The Wizard and the Prophet (2018)
Nobel Prize official site, Norman Borlaug, Nobel Peace Prize 1970

days.application: Punjab's falling water table: the Green Revolution plus free farm electricity (from 1997) and guaranteed procurement prices pushed Punjab into a wheat-rice rotation that pumps far more groundwater than rain replaces. India's Central Ground Water Board classifies most of the state's assessment blocks as over-exploited, and the GRACE satellites (Day 117) weighed the loss from orbit across Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan at about 17.7 km3 a year in 2002-08 (Rodell, Velicogna & Famiglietti, Nature, 2009). The 2009 Punjab Preservation of Subsoil Water Act, which bars transplanting rice before a set date in June so that less water is lost in the hottest weeks, is a rule written to repair the gain's bill.

builds_on.why: Haber-Bosch: the semi-dwarf varieties were bred to use synthetic nitrogen, the other half of the yield package.
Groundwater is a commons: each farmer's pumping lowers everyone's water table, the Ogallala problem in Punjab.

across.link: USAID administrator William Gaud coined the phrase 'Green Revolution' in a speech on 8 March 1968, contrasting it with a 'violent Red Revolution like that of the Soviets', a Cold War framing of food aid and agricultural development.

days.apply_question: Much of sub-Saharan Africa's farmland is rain-fed, and fertilizer use there was so low that the 2006 Abuja Declaration set a target of just 50 kg of nutrients per hectare; using the seed-fertilizer-water package, explain why shipping Punjab's high-yield seed to a rain-fed African farming region would not by itself repeat Punjab's gains.
days.evidence_note: Settled: yield gains from semi-dwarf varieties with fertilizer and irrigation, and their role in averting famine projections of the 1960s. Debated: effects on rural inequality and smallholders, nutrition (less diverse diets), and environmental costs, with defenders such as Borlaug and Pingali against critics such as Vandana Shiva and some agroecologists. Value judgment: how to weigh lives fed now against stocks drawn down for later.

resource.title: The Wizard and the Prophet: Two Remarkable Scientists and Their Dueling Visions to Shape Tomorrow's World
resource.creator: Charles C. Mann (Knopf, 2018), the chapter on Borlaug ('The Wizard') in Part One
resource.why: Mann tells Borlaug's story alongside William Vogt's ecological warnings and takes neither side, which matches the lesson's balance of gain and cost.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge; the book is widely catalogued. The Borlaug chapter is recalled as 'The Wizard'; confirm the chapter title and page count at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Why nutrition science is so hard
days.headline_hint: A Dentist Found the Letters: In 1965 the Sugar Industry Paid Harvard Scientists to Point at Fat
days.concept: Diet studies face confounding (healthy eaters differ in many ways), measurement error (people misremember what they eat), small effects, and funding pressures, so a single nutrition finding is weak evidence and only consistent results across methods should move you much.
days.focus: Teaches why nutrition is a near-worst case for causal inference: no long-term blinded trials of whole diets, food-frequency questionnaires, many correlated exposures, and industry funding. The angle is calibrated scepticism, not cynicism: some nutrition findings (folate and neural-tube defects, trans fats) are solid.

story.title: The documents in the archive
story.hook: Cristin Kearns, a dentist who became a researcher at the University of California, San Francisco, spent years searching archives for sugar-industry papers. Among the files she found were letters showing that in 1965 the Sugar Research Foundation paid three Harvard nutrition scientists about $6,500 (roughly $49,000 in 2016 dollars) for a review of research on diet and heart disease, set its objective and saw drafts. The review appeared in two parts in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1967; it played down sugar's link to heart disease, emphasised dietary fat, and did not disclose the funding. One of the authors, Mark Hegsted, later helped shape the federal government's first dietary goals and guidelines. Kearns, Laura Schmidt and Stanton Glantz published the documents in JAMA Internal Medicine on 12 September 2016.
story.puzzle: If a funded review could tilt a field for decades, why were the underlying studies so easy to tilt, and how should anyone know which nutrition claims to trust?
story.payoff: Diet research rests on observational studies full of confounders and on self-reported food intake, so the evidence is ambiguous enough that framing and selection decide the conclusion. That ambiguity, not just the money, made the tilt possible; the defence is triangulation across trials, mechanisms and independent cohorts, plus disclosure.
sources: Kearns, Schmidt & Glantz, 'Sugar Industry and Coronary Heart Disease Research: A Historical Analysis of Internal Industry Documents', JAMA Internal Medicine 176 (2016)
McGandy, Hegsted & Stare, 'Dietary fats, carbohydrates and atherosclerotic vascular disease', NEJM 277 (1967)
New York Times, 'How the Sugar Industry Shifted Blame to Fat' (12 September 2016)

days.application: 'Is everything we eat associated with cancer?' Jonathan Schoenfeld and John Ioannidis (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2013) chose 50 ingredients at random from a cookbook and found studies linking 40 of them to cancer risk, many reporting both increased and decreased risk for the same food, with most effects weak and larger in single studies than in meta-analyses: publication bias and multiple comparisons at work.

builds_on.why: Confounding: people who eat more vegetables also smoke less, exercise more and earn more, so diet effects are hard to isolate.
Publication bias and replication: small, surprising diet findings are published, then shrink or vanish in larger studies.

across.link: The US Senate Select Committee on Nutrition and Human Needs, chaired by George McGovern, issued the Dietary Goals for the United States in February 1977, urging less fat; it became the basis for the first federal Dietary Guidelines (1980), turning contested nutrition evidence into national policy.

days.apply_question: A large study of about 400,000 older Americans (Freedman et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2012) found that coffee drinkers had lower death rates than non-drinkers; using confounding, measurement error and publication bias, what is the strongest alternative explanation for that finding?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the industry-funded 1967 review and its undisclosed funding (documented). Debated: how much the review actually shaped later guidelines, and the relative harms of sugar and saturated fat; nutrition scientists split over the reliability of nutritional epidemiology (Ioannidis's critiques against defenders such as Walter Willett).

resource.title: Sugar Industry and Coronary Heart Disease Research: A Historical Analysis of Internal Industry Documents
resource.creator: Cristin E. Kearns, Laura A. Schmidt and Stanton A. Glantz, JAMA Internal Medicine 176(11) (2016)
resource.why: The primary documents quoted, with the letters between the Sugar Research Foundation and the Harvard authors, show exactly how funding shaped the question and the conclusion.
resource.verified_how: From model knowledge of the 2016 JAMA Internal Medicine article; not confirmed by web search this session because the shared search budget ran out. Confirm access (free or paywalled) at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Chronic disease and the epidemiological transition
days.headline_hint: A President's Blood Pressure Hit 300 the Day He Died. A Town in Massachusetts Turned Fate Into Risk.
days.concept: As infections fall, chronic diseases such as heart disease, stroke, cancer and diabetes become the main causes of death (Abdel Omran's epidemiological transition, 1971), and prevention shifts to 'risk factors', measurable traits such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking that raise the probability of disease years before it appears.
days.focus: Teaches the epidemiological transition and the risk-factor idea, born from the Framingham Heart Study's cohort design. The angle: a risk factor is a probability shift in a population, not a verdict on a person, and treating risk factors became a new kind of medicine.
days.model_or_equation: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = risk without treatment - risk with treatment; number needed to treat NNT = 1 / ARR. A drug that cuts a 5% ten-year risk to 4% has ARR 1% and NNT 100.

story.title: Framingham, 1948
story.hook: On 12 April 1945 President Franklin Roosevelt died of a cerebral haemorrhage; his blood pressure had been very high for years, reportedly about 300/190 that day by his cardiologist's later account, but in the medicine of the day rising pressure with age was widely regarded as normal, even necessary, and no good drugs existed to lower it. Heart disease was the leading cause of death in the United States and was seen largely as fate. In 1948 the US Public Health Service began recruiting 5,209 men and women aged 30 to 62 in Framingham, Massachusetts, a town of about 28,000, to be examined every two years for the rest of their lives. In 1961 William Kannel and colleagues reported from Framingham the 'factors of risk' that predicted heart disease: high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking.
story.puzzle: Heart attacks strike suddenly and seemingly at random. How could watching healthy people in one town for years show that a disease 'of fate' was largely predictable and preventable?
story.payoff: A prospective cohort measures traits before disease appears, so it can see that people with high blood pressure or cholesterol in 1950 had more heart attacks by 1960, establishing temporality that case-control studies struggle with. The 'risk factor' turned prevention into managing probabilities, and US age-adjusted heart-disease death rates fell by more than half from the late 1960s on.
sources: Framingham Heart Study official history (NHLBI and Boston University)
Kannel et al., 'Factors of risk in the development of coronary heart disease: six-year follow-up experience', Annals of Internal Medicine 55 (1961)
Omran, 'The epidemiologic transition', Milbank Memorial Fund Quarterly 49 (1971)

days.application: GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide: in the STEP-1 trial (NEJM, 2021), adults with obesity lost about 15% of body weight over 68 weeks, against about 2% on placebo; in the SELECT trial (NEJM, 2023), among about 17,600 people with obesity and existing cardiovascular disease, heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths fell by about 20%. Here the risk factor (excess weight) is treated with a drug, and the right question is the absolute benefit and its cost.

builds_on.why: The mortality revolution's fall in infectious and child deaths is the first half of the epidemiological transition; chronic disease rises as people survive to older ages.

Absolute versus relative risk is the natural-frequencies point from the mammography example: '25% fewer heart attacks' and '2.5 fewer per 100 people' describe the same drug, and only the second tells a patient what to expect.

across.link: Risk-factor scores are prediction models, and the label chosen decides who is flagged: Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli and Mullainathan (Science, 2019) found that a widely used US algorithm measured patients' health risk by their past healthcare costs; because less had been spent on Black patients with the same illnesses, it under-flagged them, and changing the label would have raised the share of Black patients selected for extra care from about 18% to about 47%.

days.apply_question: A statin lowers the ten-year risk of heart attack for a moderately at-risk 55-year-old from 10% to 7.5%; using absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat, how would you explain that benefit to the patient in plain numbers?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the epidemiological transition as a broad pattern; blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking as causal risk factors. Debated: the limits of Omran's stage model (rich countries now see some infections return; poorer ones face both burdens), and the long-term balance of benefits, costs and side effects of GLP-1 drugs.

resource.title: Change of Heart: Unraveling the Mysteries of Cardiovascular Disease
resource.creator: Daniel Levy and Susan Brink (Knopf, 2005), the opening chapters on Roosevelt and the founding of Framingham
resource.why: Written by a later Framingham director with a journalist, it tells how the study was set up and how its findings changed medicine, filling in the story behind the risk-factor idea.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge; the book (Knopf, 2005), co-written by a later Framingham director, is catalogued by its publisher. Confirm chapter titles at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: For Forty Years the US Government Watched 399 Men With Syphilis Go Untreated. A Reporter's Story Ended It in Months.
days.concept: Research on people is governed by three principles, respect for persons (informed consent), beneficence (maximize benefit and minimize harm) and justice (fair selection of who bears the burdens and gets the benefits), as set out in the Belmont Report (1979) after abuses showed that good scientific goals do not justify any means.
days.focus: Teaches the three Belmont principles and the institutions built on them (institutional review boards, informed consent, the Common Rule). The angle: ethics written after scandal; and the long shadow of broken trust, measured.

story.title: Jean Heller's story, July 1972
story.hook: In 1932 the US Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, with the Tuskegee Institute: about 600 Black men, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without, were told they were being treated for 'bad blood' and given free meals and burial insurance. They were not told their diagnosis, and treatment was withheld, even after penicillin became the standard cure in the late 1940s. A PHS investigator, Peter Buxtun, raised objections inside the agency from 1966 and was rebuffed. He gave the documents to the press, and on 25 July 1972 the Associated Press reporter Jean Heller published the story. The study was ended that year, after 40 years; by then many of the men had died of syphilis or its complications, and wives and children had been infected.
story.puzzle: The study was published in medical journals for decades and reviewed by government doctors. How could so many professionals see it and not stop it, and what rule would have prevented it?
story.payoff: There were no binding rules of consent for US government research, and the subjects were poor Black men in the segregated South, which made their harm easy to discount. The scandal led to the National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report's three principles: consent (they were deceived), beneficence (treatment was withheld), and justice (the burden fell on a vulnerable group). Ethics review boards now must approve research before it starts.
sources: CDC, 'The U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study at Tuskegee' (timeline)
Jean Heller, Associated Press, 25 July 1972
National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects, The Belmont Report (1979)

days.application: Henrietta Lacks: in 1951 cells from her cervical cancer were taken at Johns Hopkins without her knowledge, and became HeLa, the first immortal human cell line, used in polio vaccine work and countless studies; she died in October 1951. Her family, who learned of the cells only decades later, settled a lawsuit with Thermo Fisher Scientific in August 2023 (terms undisclosed). The case raises consent, benefit-sharing and justice questions the Belmont principles name but do not fully answer for tissues.

builds_on.why: Kant's formula of humanity, treating people never merely as means, and the Nuremberg Code (1947) are the deontological roots of informed consent.
Randomized trials are ethical only under equipoise, genuine uncertainty about which arm is better, which Tuskegee violated once penicillin was known to cure syphilis.

across.link: In Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990) the California Supreme Court held that John Moore had no property right in cells taken from his spleen and commercialised, but that his doctor had breached a duty to disclose his financial interest, the legal line between consent and ownership that the Lacks family's case pressed against.

days.apply_question: During the COVID-19 pandemic, 'human challenge trials' in the UK deliberately infected consenting young volunteers with the virus to speed vaccine research; using the three Belmont principles, what would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to judge whether such a trial is ethical?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the facts of the Tuskegee study and the Belmont principles. Debated: Alsan & Wanamaker (QJE, 2018) estimated that the 1972 disclosure reduced Black men's use of medical care and their life expectancy, a careful but contested estimate. Value judgment: how to balance research benefits against risks, and who may consent for whom.

resource.title: The Belmont Report: Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the Protection of Human Subjects of Research
resource.creator: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research (1979), published by the US Department of Health and Human Services
resource.why: The founding document itself, short and readable, setting out respect for persons, beneficence and justice and how each turns into consent, risk assessment and subject selection.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge; the report is a public US government document hosted by HHS's Office for Human Research Protections. Confirm at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: An Iron Bar Went Through Phineas Gage's Head. He Talked on the Way to the Doctor. His Friends Said He Was No Longer Gage.
days.concept: Neurons signal electrically along their axons and chemically across synapses, brain regions specialize but behaviour comes from networks of regions working together, and connections strengthen or weaken with use (plasticity).
days.focus: Teaches the action potential, synaptic transmission, localization versus networks, and plasticity, before Psychology begins. The angle: the Gage case shows both what localization explains and how famous cases grow in the retelling.
days.model_or_equation: The resting neuron holds about -70 millivolts across its membrane; when input pushes it past a threshold (around -55 mV), an all-or-nothing spike travels down the axon at up to about 100 metres per second in insulated fibres.

story.title: Cavendish, Vermont, 13 September 1848
story.hook: On 13 September 1848, Phineas Gage, a 25-year-old railway construction foreman, was tamping blasting powder into a hole in rock near Cavendish, Vermont, when the powder exploded. His tamping iron, about 3 feet 7 inches long and 13 1/4 pounds, shot up through his left cheek and out of the top of his skull, landing many yards away. He was conscious within minutes and reportedly spoke on the cart ride to town. Dr John Harlow treated him and he survived. Twenty years later Harlow wrote that Gage had become fitful, profane and unable to keep to plans, so that his friends said he was 'no longer Gage'.
story.puzzle: A man lost a large piece of the front of his brain and could still walk, talk and remember. What had he lost, and what does that say about how the brain is organized?
story.payoff: The iron destroyed much of the left frontal lobe (reconstructions differ on whether the right was also damaged), a region that helps plan, inhibit impulses and regulate social behaviour; movement, language and memory depend on other regions and networks that were spared. But the story grew: Malcolm Macmillan's research (An Odd Kind of Fame, 2000) found Gage later worked for years as a stagecoach driver in Chile, suggesting substantial recovery, which plasticity and rehabilitation would predict. He died in 1860 after seizures.
sources: Harlow, 'Recovery from the passage of an iron bar through the head', Publications of the Massachusetts Medical Society (1868)
Malcolm Macmillan, An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage (2000)
Warren Anatomical Museum, Harvard Medical School (Gage's skull and tamping iron)

days.application: Brain-computer interfaces: in BrainGate trials, Matthew Nagle, paralysed from the neck down, moved a computer cursor using electrodes in his motor cortex (Hochberg et al., Nature 2006). In January 2024 Neuralink implanted its first device in Noland Arbaugh, paralysed after a diving accident, who used it to move a cursor and play chess; many of the implant's threads later retracted from the brain, reducing performance until software was adjusted. Both decode the electrical spikes of motor neurons that this lesson describes.

builds_on.why: The action potential is an electrical signal: charged ions move across the neuron's membrane, a voltage that obeys the same physics as circuits.
Networks: behaviour comes from connected regions, and hubs and shortcuts in brain networks shape what damage disrupts.

across.link: IBM's TrueNorth chip (Merolla et al., Science, August 2014) wired about a million artificial spiking 'neurons' and 256 million 'synapses' onto one chip that ran on roughly 70 milliwatts by copying the brain's event-driven signalling; the analogy breaks because its connections were fixed when programmed rather than rewired by use, the plasticity this lesson teaches.

days.apply_question: After a stroke damages the part of the brain that controls a patient's right hand, therapists may restrain the good left hand for most of the day to force use of the right (constraint-induced movement therapy, tested in the EXCITE trial, JAMA, 2006); using plasticity and networks, explain why forcing use could help the brain regain control of the hand.
days.evidence_note: Settled: neuronal signalling, regional specialization and plasticity. Debated: how much of the Gage story is accurate, since his personality change was reported mainly by Harlow and embellished later (Macmillan). Value judgment: questions raised by brain implants about privacy and agency belong to Philosophy II.

resource.title: Meet Your Master - Getting to Know Your Brain: Crash Course Psychology #4
resource.creator: Hank Green, Crash Course (2014)
resource.why: A quick, visual tour of neurons, brain regions and how researchers learned their functions, setting up the Psychology block that follows.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified at review (shared search budget exhausted; direct fetches blocked). From model knowledge of the Crash Course Psychology series (2014), episode 4, about 12 minutes; confirm the title on the Crash Course channel at build time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.headline_hint: A Misplaced Electrode Made Rats Press a Lever Thousands of Times an Hour. Was It Pleasure They Were Chasing?
days.concept: Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error, the difference between the reward received and the reward expected, which teaches the brain what to seek; drugs that hijack this signal can drive compulsive use (addiction).
days.focus: Teaches the reward prediction error (Schultz, Dayan & Montague, Science 1997), the move from 'dopamine is pleasure' to 'dopamine is a teaching signal' (and Kent Berridge's 'wanting versus liking'), and addiction as learning gone wrong. The angle: the brain learns from surprise, not from reward itself.
days.model_or_equation: Reward prediction error delta = (reward received) - (reward expected); the expectation is updated by a fraction of delta each time, so a fully predicted reward produces no dopamine burst, and a missing expected reward produces a dip.

story.title: The rat in the corner, McGill, 1953-54
story.hook: In 1953 at McGill University in Montreal, the young psychologist James Olds and the graduate student Peter Milner were implanting electrodes in rats' brains to study arousal. One electrode missed its target and ended in a different region near the septum. When this rat was stimulated in one corner of the box, it kept returning to that corner. Given a lever that delivered the stimulation, rats with such placements pressed it again and again, in later experiments thousands of times an hour, and in some studies hungry rats chose the stimulation over food. Olds and Milner published in 1954, and the press, and later Olds himself, spoke of the brain's 'pleasure centres'.
story.puzzle: If the rats were feeling pleasure, why did later research find that dopamine neurons stopped firing to a reward once it became predictable, even though it was still enjoyed?
story.payoff: In the 1980s-90s Wolfram Schultz recorded dopamine neurons in monkeys getting juice: they fired for unexpected juice, shifted to firing for a cue that predicted juice, and dipped when promised juice did not come. Schultz, Dayan and Montague (1997) showed this matches the prediction error in temporal-difference learning. Dopamine is a teaching signal about what to seek; the self-stimulating rats were in a loop of endless 'better than expected'.
sources: Olds & Milner, 'Positive reinforcement produced by electrical stimulation of septal area and other regions of rat brain', Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology 47 (1954)
Schultz, Dayan & Montague, 'A neural substrate of prediction and reward', Science 275 (1997)
Berridge & Robinson, 'What is the role of dopamine in reward?', Brain Research Reviews (1998)

days.application: The US opioid epidemic: CDC data counted about 108,000 drug-overdose deaths in 2022, roughly three-quarters involving opioids, increasingly illicit fentanyl; provisional data show a sharp fall in 2024. Opioids drive dopamine release and tolerance, so users need more to feel normal. Whether addiction is a 'brain disease' (the NIDA view, Volkow, Koob & McLellan, NEJM 2016) or a learned, choice-influenced condition (Marc Lewis, The Biology of Desire, 2015; Gene Heyman) is contested, and the answer shapes treatment and law.

builds_on.why: Dopamine neurons are neurons: their prediction-error bursts are action potentials releasing a neurotransmitter at synapses.
Expected value: the expectation in reward prediction error is a learned probability-weighted average of reward.

across.link: Gerald Tesauro's TD-Gammon (IBM, 1992) learned to play backgammon near world-champion level from self-play using temporal-difference learning, the same prediction-error algorithm (Richard Sutton, 1988) that dopamine neurons appear to implement.

days.apply_question: Some people with Parkinson's disease who take dopamine-agonist drugs develop compulsive gambling, shopping or eating they never had before (about 17% of agonist users in a 2010 study of more than 3,000 patients, against about 7% of non-users); using reward prediction error and the wanting-versus-liking distinction, explain why a drug that boosts dopamine signalling could produce this.
days.evidence_note: Settled: dopamine neurons encode reward prediction error in many settings. Debated: whether dopamine mainly drives 'wanting' rather than 'liking' (Berridge), and whether addiction is best called a brain disease (NIDA; Volkow) or a disorder of learning and choice (Lewis, Heyman). Value judgment: how law should treat addiction (crime, illness, or both).
