days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: IQ Is Substantially Heritable. Dutch Conscripts Still Gained Twenty Points in Thirty Years.
days.concept: Heritability is the share of variation in a trait, within a particular population and its environments, that is associated with genetic differences; adult IQ is substantially heritable, yet heritability says nothing about whether the trait can change - environments can move a whole population's average, as the Flynn effect shows.
days.focus: Teach what IQ tests measure and predict, what heritability is (a population ratio, not a fixed share of one person), why it rises with age, and why high heritability is compatible with large environmental gains (Flynn) and harms (lead). Handle group differences with Lewontin's point: heritability within groups does not explain gaps between them.
days.model_or_equation: h^2 = V_G / V_P = V_G / (V_G + V_E), where V_P is the variance of the trait in the population, V_G the part associated with genetic differences and V_E the part associated with environmental differences (ignoring interaction and covariance). If environments become more equal, V_E shrinks and h^2 rises - while the population's average can still move.

story.title: Twenty points in thirty years
story.hook: In the early 1980s James Flynn, a political philosopher at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, noticed something buried in IQ tests' norm tables: each time a test was re-standardized, people scored higher on the old norms. In 1984 he showed that Americans had gained about 14 points between 1932 and 1978. In 1987 he gathered data from 14 nations ('Massive IQ gains in 14 nations', Psychological Bulletin). The most striking came from the Netherlands, where nearly all 18-year-old men sat a Raven's-type reasoning test at military induction: scores rose about 20 points between 1952 and 1982.
story.puzzle: Twin and adoption studies say adult IQ is substantially heritable - roughly half or more of its variation. Genes do not change in thirty years. How can a highly heritable trait rise by more than a standard deviation in one generation?
story.payoff: Heritability describes why people differ within a population at one time, under that population's environments; it says nothing about what moves the average. Better nutrition and health, more and different schooling, and habits of abstract thinking (Flynn's own explanation) lifted everyone. Height shows the same thing: highly heritable, yet far taller than a century ago.
sources: Flynn, 'The mean IQ of Americans: Massive gains 1932 to 1978', Psychological Bulletin 95 (1984)
Flynn, 'Massive IQ gains in 14 nations: What IQ tests really measure', Psychological Bulletin 101 (1987)
Pietschnig & Voracek, 'One century of global IQ gains', Perspectives on Psychological Science 10 (2015)

days.application: Lead and IQ. McFarland, Hauer and Reuben (PNAS, 2022) estimated that more than 170 million Americans alive in 2015 - over half the population - had blood-lead levels above 5 micrograms per decilitre in early childhood, largely from leaded gasoline, and that the exposure cost the US population about 824 million IQ points: a few points per person on average, more for those born in the peak years of the late 1960s and 1970s. An environmental change shifted the national distribution down regardless of heritability; removing the lead let it recover. (Car chain: consequences - a cost of the fuel, Day 49.)

builds_on.why: Heredity and genetics taught heritability as a population statistic, not destiny; today applies it to the most contested trait it is used for.
Leaded gasoline: the lead that case followed into children's blood is today's example of environment moving a heritable trait's average.

across.link: Norway's 1960s school reform extended compulsory schooling from seven to nine years, rolled out municipality by municipality; Brinch and Galloway (PNAS, 2012) used it as a natural experiment and found each extra year of schooling raised IQ, measured at military conscription, by about 3.7 points - education policy moving a 'heritable' trait.

days.apply_question: Height is roughly 80% heritable in well-fed populations, yet Dutch men grew around 20 cm taller over about a century and a half. If every Dutch child received equally good nutrition and health care, would the heritability of height rise or fall, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: IQ scores predict school and job outcomes; adult IQ is substantially heritable in the mostly Western populations studied (estimates often 50-80%); scores rose across the 20th century (Pietschnig and Voracek's 2015 meta-analysis: roughly 2-3 points a decade for full-scale IQ, more on fluid-reasoning tests). Debated: what caused the Flynn effect and why it has stalled or reversed in some countries (Norwegian data point to environmental causes within families, Bratsberg and Rogeberg, PNAS 2018); whether heritability is lower in poor US families (Turkheimer 2003, not found in several other countries); and what polygenic scores, which capture about a tenth of the variation in educational attainment, will add. Value judgment: how a society should use intelligence measures; the eugenics era (Day 43, Buck v. Bell) shows the cost of confusing a statistic with a verdict on persons.

resource.title: Why our IQ levels are higher than our grandparents'
resource.creator: James Flynn (TED2013)
resource.why: Flynn himself explains the gains he discovered - that modern life trained minds to think abstractly and hypothetically - the leading environmental account, from its author.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Mental illness: diagnosis and treatment evidence
days.headline_hint: Eight Sane People Talked Their Way Into Psychiatric Hospitals - or Did They? The Study That Shook Psychiatry, and What Survived It.
days.concept: Psychiatric diagnoses are categories defined by agreed criteria, chosen for reliability and usefulness rather than discovered like a virus, and the main treatments - medication and psychotherapy - have real but modest average effects; both claims hold at once.
days.focus: Teach what a diagnosis is (DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria, reliability measured by kappa, categories versus dimensions), how Rosenhan's famous study shaped DSM-III and what Cahalan later found, and how to read the treatment evidence (Cipriani's network meta-analysis, publication bias, the serotonin-hypothesis dispute). This sets up the measurement question in Day 169.
days.model_or_equation: Cohen's kappa measures how far two clinicians agree beyond chance: kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), where p_o is the proportion of cases on which they agree and p_e the agreement expected by chance from how often each uses each diagnosis. Kappa = 1 is perfect agreement; 0 is no better than chance.

story.title: Eight sane people in insane places
story.hook: On 19 January 1973 Science published 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' by David Rosenhan, a Stanford psychologist. Eight sane people, he reported, himself among them, had gained admission to 12 psychiatric hospitals in five states by saying they heard voices saying 'empty', 'hollow' and 'thud'. Once inside they behaved normally, yet all but one were diagnosed with schizophrenia, stayed an average of 19 days (7 to 52) and were discharged 'in remission'; fellow patients, he wrote, sometimes spotted them as fakes. When one hospital was told to expect impostors, its staff flagged 41 of 193 new patients as suspects - though none had been sent. The paper helped push American psychiatry toward the explicit criteria of DSM-III (1980). In 2019 the journalist Susannah Cahalan, in The Great Pretender, reported that Rosenhan's own records contradicted his account of his symptoms, that she could confirm only one of the other seven reported pseudopatients, and that another volunteer, Harry Lando, whose stay had been largely positive, had been left out of the paper.
story.puzzle: If psychiatrists could not tell the sane from the insane, are psychiatric diagnoses meaningless? And if the study itself was unreliable, what do we actually know?
story.payoff: A diagnosis is a criteria-defined category whose first test is reliability - do trained clinicians agree? - which DSM-III's checklists improved, though agreement still varies by disorder. Even taken at face value, Rosenhan could not show diagnoses are meaningless: lying about a symptom fools any diagnostic system, as the psychiatric researcher Seymour Kety replied in 1974 (a man who drank blood and vomited it would be diagnosed with a bleeding ulcer). The right questions are how reliable each category is, what it predicts, and whether treatment helps those who meet it.
sources: Rosenhan, 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', Science 179 (1973)
Cahalan, The Great Pretender (Grand Central, 2019)
Spitzer, 'On pseudoscience in science, logic in remission, and psychiatric diagnosis', Journal of Abnormal Psychology 84 (1975)

days.application: Andrea Cipriani and colleagues (Lancet, 2018) combined 522 double-blind trials involving 116,477 adults with major depression in a network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants. Every drug beat placebo over about eight weeks, with odds ratios for response from about 1.4 to 2.1 - real, modest average effects; head-to-head trials find psychotherapy, on average, about as effective for acute depression. The same literature shows why 'modest' needs care: Turner and colleagues (NEJM, 2008), comparing FDA files with journals, found publication bias had inflated antidepressants' apparent effect by about a third.

builds_on.why: Randomized trials: placebo-controlled, double-blind trials are what separate a drug's effect from the large placebo response and natural recovery in depression.
Replication and publication bias: Turner's comparison of FDA files with published papers is a textbook case of a literature overstating an effect.

across.link: The M'Naghten rules (House of Lords, 1843) define legal insanity as not knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong - a category drawn for the purpose of assigning responsibility, which does not coincide with any psychiatric diagnosis: the same person can meet DSM criteria for schizophrenia and still be legally sane.

days.apply_question: In US states with a 1 September school-entry cutoff, children born in August - the youngest in their class - were diagnosed with ADHD about a third more often than children born in September (Layton and colleagues, NEJM 2018). Does that show ADHD is not a real condition, or something else about how the category is applied - and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: diagnoses are defined by criteria; reliability varies widely by disorder (DSM-5 field trials found good agreement for some, such as PTSD, and poor agreement for others, such as major depression); antidepressants outperform placebo on average in acute trials. Debated: whether the average drug-placebo difference is clinically meaningful (Kirsch against Cipriani and most psychiatric bodies); whether depression involves low serotonin (an umbrella review, Moncrieff et al. 2022, found no consistent evidence - which does not by itself show the drugs fail); categorical versus dimensional systems (HiTOP); and the extent of Rosenhan's misreporting (Cahalan's evidence is strong; he died in 2012). Value judgment: where to draw the line between distress and disorder - the medicalization critique.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: The Estimate Said 'High Confidence.' It Was Wrong. That Alone Doesn't Prove the Forecasters Were Bad.
days.concept: A forecaster is well calibrated when the events they call 70% likely happen about 70% of the time; calibration can be judged only across many forecasts stated as numbers and scored with tools such as the Brier score - and forecasters who draw on many perspectives (Tetlock's 'foxes') are better calibrated than those with one big idea.
days.focus: Teach calibration and discrimination, the Brier score, why one outcome cannot grade a probability, why vague words cannot be graded at all (Sherman Kent's 1951 'serious possibility', which colleagues read as anything from 20% to 80%), and what Tetlock's two research programmes found: experts barely beat simple rules (Expert Political Judgment, 2005, about 28,000 forecasts by 284 experts), while trained, teamed, numerate forecasters did much better (the Good Judgment Project).
key_concepts: base rates and the outside view
days.model_or_equation: Brier score: BS = (1/N) x sum of (f_t - o_t)^2, where f_t is the forecast probability for event t and o_t is 1 if it happened and 0 if not; 0 is perfect, and always saying 50% scores 0.25. Worked example: ten forecasts of 70%, seven events happen: BS = (7 x 0.3^2 + 3 x 0.7^2) / 10 = (0.63 + 1.47) / 10 = 0.21. Perfectly calibrated - and still far from perfect, because 70% is not very discriminating.

story.title: 'High confidence'
story.hook: On 1 October 2002 the US intelligence community delivered a National Intelligence Estimate, 'Iraq's Continuing Programs for Weapons of Mass Destruction'. Among the judgments its key findings listed with 'high confidence' was that Iraq was continuing its weapons of mass destruction programmes; it judged that Baghdad had chemical and biological weapons. Within two weeks Congress voted to authorize force. After the 2003 invasion the Iraq Survey Group found no stockpiles, and on 31 March 2005 a presidential commission (Robb-Silberman) concluded the community had been 'dead wrong in almost all of its pre-war judgments' about Iraq's weapons. The intelligence community's research agency, IARPA, went on in 2011 to fund a forecasting tournament to learn whether prediction itself could be measured and improved.
story.puzzle: The estimate was confident, and it was wrong. Does that prove the analysts were bad forecasters - and since 'high confidence' was not a number, how could anyone have checked?
story.payoff: One outcome cannot grade a probability: a forecaster who says 80% should be wrong one time in five. Skill shows up only across many numerical forecasts - calibration - and a phrase like 'high confidence' cannot be scored at all. Tetlock and Gardner argue the Iraq error was as much one of overconfidence as of direction: a calibrated estimate might still have leaned toward weapons, but nowhere near certainty.
sources: National Intelligence Estimate, 'Iraq's Continuing Programs for Weapons of Mass Destruction' (October 2002), declassified key judgments
Commission on the Intelligence Capabilities of the United States Regarding Weapons of Mass Destruction (Robb-Silberman), Report to the President, 31 March 2005
Tetlock & Gardner, Superforecasting (2015)
Sherman Kent, 'Words of Estimative Probability', Studies in Intelligence (1964)

days.application: The Good Judgment Project. From 2011 to 2015 IARPA's Aggregative Contingent Estimation tournament asked thousands of forecasters about hundreds of real geopolitical questions, scored with Brier scores. The team led by Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers won: training in probabilistic reasoning, teaming, tracking the top 2% ('superforecasters') and statistically aggregating forecasts beat the other research teams and the tournament's control group by wide margins (Mellers et al., Psychological Science, 2014). The best forecasters stayed near the top year after year - skill, not luck. Press reports said they also outperformed intelligence analysts with classified information; that comparison has not been published in full.

builds_on.why: Probability: a forecast is a probability, and calibration asks whether stated probabilities match long-run frequencies.
Bayes and base rates: superforecasters start from the base rate (the 'outside view') and update in small steps as evidence arrives.

across.link: The Brier score was invented for weather forecasting (Glenn Brier, Monthly Weather Review, 1950), and US National Weather Service precipitation forecasts became famously well calibrated (Murphy and Winkler, 1977) because forecasters get fast, unambiguous feedback every day - the condition most expert judgment lacks.

days.apply_question: Nate Silver reported (The Signal and the Noise, 2012) that The Weather Channel deliberately adds a 'wet bias' at low probabilities - announcing, say, a 20% chance of rain when its own estimate is much lower - because viewers resent unexpected rain more than unexpected sun. How would that habit show up on a calibration plot of its forecasts?
days.evidence_note: Settled: calibration and Brier scores are standard, well-understood measures; forecasting tournaments show stable individual differences, and simple training improves accuracy. Debated: how large the forecasters' edge over intelligence analysts was (reported by journalists, not fully published); whether skill on questions that resolve within a year transfers to rare, long-range, high-impact events (Taleb's fat-tail critique, Day 12); and how to apportion the 2002 failure among overconfidence, flawed sources and outside pressure, which the official inquiries weighed in different ways.

resource.title: Superforecasting - chapter 3, 'Keeping Score'
resource.creator: Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner (Crown, 2015)
resource.why: Tetlock explains, with Kent's 'serious possibility' and his own 20-year expert study, why forecasts must be numerical and scored, and how calibration and Brier scores work - the lesson's tools in the words of the researcher who built the field.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); chapter number and title from established knowledge of the book. Cite without a link. days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Well-being and how to measure it
days.headline_hint: Two Studies Asked Whether Money Buys Happiness Past $75,000 and Disagreed - So the Rivals Wrote a Third Paper Together.
days.concept: Well-being has distinct measurable forms - how you evaluate your life as a whole, how you feel moment to moment, and whether life feels meaningful - and they can move differently: life evaluation keeps rising with income, while whether day-to-day emotion does depends on the measure and on who you are.
days.focus: Teach the measures (the Cantril ladder, experience sampling, the day reconstruction method, eudaimonic scales), the log-income relationship, and the $75,000 dispute resolved by adversarial collaboration - itself a model for Logan's book. Then apply the same measurement discipline to a claim that flatters his worldview: religious attendance and flourishing.
days.model_or_equation: Well-being = a + b x ln(income): on a log scale each doubling of income adds the same increment, so going from $50,000 to $100,000 adds as much as going from $100,000 to $200,000 - which is why a curve that looks flat on a dollar axis can still be rising.

story.title: A conflict resolved
story.hook: In 2010 Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton analysed more than 450,000 responses to a daily Gallup survey of Americans (PNAS). Life evaluation rose steadily with income, but emotional well-being - measured by yes-or-no questions about yesterday's feelings - stopped improving at about $75,000 a year, and the figure became famous. In 2021 Matthew Killingsworth, using 1.7 million real-time reports from about 33,000 working Americans who rated their feelings on a smartphone app, found that happiness kept rising with income well past $75,000 (PNAS). Instead of trading rebuttals, the two sides agreed an adversarial collaboration with the psychologist Barbara Mellers as arbiter, setting out in advance how they would test their disagreement. Their joint paper, 'Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved', appeared in PNAS in March 2023.
story.puzzle: Two careful studies of large American samples gave opposite answers to the same question. How can money both stop and not stop buying better days?
story.payoff: They measured different things in different people. Reanalysis showed the plateau is real for the unhappiest people - roughly the bottom fifth, whose happiness stops rising around $100,000 - while for everyone else it keeps climbing with log income, fastest among the happiest. Kahneman and Deaton's yes-or-no questions had a ceiling: they could register less unhappiness but not more happiness. The measure decided the answer.
sources: Kahneman & Deaton, 'High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being', PNAS 107 (2010)
Killingsworth, 'Experienced well-being rises with income, even above $75,000 per year', PNAS 118 (2021)
Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, 'Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved', PNAS 120 (2023)

days.application: Religious attendance and flourishing. Ying Chen and Tyler VanderWeele (American Journal of Epidemiology, 2018) followed about 5,000 young people from the Growing Up Today Study, the children of participants in the Nurses' Health Study II. Those who attended religious services at least weekly in adolescence were, as young adults, roughly 18% more likely to report high happiness, about 29% more likely to volunteer and about a third less likely to use illicit drugs, after adjusting for many earlier characteristics. The design is observational: families who attend may differ in ways not measured (conscientiousness, family stability, health), so the associations are suggestive, not proof of cause - the same standard a finding hostile to religion would face.

builds_on.why: Confounding: whether religious attendance causes flourishing, or the kind of family that attends causes both, is a confounding question.
Goodhart's law: once a government targets a well-being number, the number can be gamed or drift from the thing it measures.

across.link: Since April 2011 the UK's Office for National Statistics has asked four well-being questions in its large household surveys - life satisfaction, whether life is worthwhile, happiness yesterday and anxiety yesterday - one evaluative, one eudaimonic and two experiential: the lesson's distinction built into official statistics.

days.apply_question: Kahneman and colleagues' 2004 day-reconstruction study of 909 working women in Texas found the morning commute the least pleasant part of the day. Why might a family's life evaluation rise after moving to a bigger house farther out, even as their experienced well-being falls?
days.evidence_note: Settled: life evaluation rises roughly with the logarithm of income, within and across countries; different well-being measures diverge. Debated: whether rising national incomes raise average happiness over decades (Easterlin's paradox versus Stevenson and Wolfers); whether 0-10 scale answers are comparable across cultures; and how much of religion's association with flourishing is causal (Chen and VanderWeele; the Global Flourishing Study's first-wave results, 2025, from more than 20 countries, which are cross-sectional). Value judgment: what well-being is - pleasure, life satisfaction, or flourishing as Aristotle, Aquinas and many religious traditions describe it - and which of these a government should try to maximize.

resource.title: The riddle of experience vs. memory
resource.creator: Daniel Kahneman (TED2010)
resource.why: Kahneman distinguishes the 'experiencing self' from the 'remembering self' and shows why they give different answers about a happy life - the distinction between experienced well-being and life evaluation, in the words of the scientist at the centre of today's story.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); talk known to be published by TED (TED2010, Daniel Kahneman); length about 20 minutes from memory. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 10: Social media and teenage mental health
days.headline_hint: Facebook's Own Slide Said 'We Make Body Image Issues Worse for One in Three Teen Girls.' Proving What Caused the Teen Mental-Health Crisis Is Far Harder.
days.concept: Case question: did smartphones and social media cause the rise in teenage depression and anxiety after about 2012 - and what should be done when a harm is plausible, the evidence contested and the technology already everywhere?
days.focus: Walk social media through Logan's chain as a loop - need, invention, physical constraints, engineering, financing, regulation, adoption, consequences, feedback - deep where Psychology and the How We Know lessons apply (belonging, variable rewards, measurement, risk perception, causal inference), previewing ranking algorithms (AI) and the law. The case's distinctive reversal: consequences, and then policy, arrived before the evidence could settle.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. Reinforcing: engagement -> advertising revenue -> better ranking and new features -> more engagement. Reinforcing: the network effect - the more peers on a platform, the costlier it is for any one teen to leave (a collective trap that individual choice cannot escape). Reinforcing (contested): posting -> comparison -> anxiety -> more checking. Balancing: parental controls, school phone bans, age laws and user fatigue. Delay: features shipped 2006-2012; rigorous causal evidence arrived about a decade later. Unintended consequences: age-verification rules raise privacy costs for everyone and may push teens toward less-moderated services.

story.title: The slide from inside
story.hook: On 14 September 2021 the Wall Street Journal published 'Facebook Knows Instagram Is Toxic for Teen Girls, Company Documents Show'. The documents had been copied by Frances Haugen, a Facebook product manager. One internal slide from 2019 read: 'We make body image issues worse for one in three teen girls' - a finding about girls who already reported body-image problems. Another said teens blamed Instagram for increases in the rate of anxiety and depression. Facebook replied that the same research found many teens felt better after using Instagram, and that the surveys were small and could not show cause. On 5 October 2021 Haugen testified before a US Senate subcommittee.
story.puzzle: The company's own research seemed to say it. Did it? What would it take to know whether social media caused the rise in teenage depression - and what should be done before anyone knows?
story.payoff: The slide reported what some teens believed about their own feelings - a survey of perceived effects, not a causal estimate. The causal evidence is mixed: experiments and natural experiments in adults and college students find real but modest harms; correlational studies of teens find small average associations, larger for girls and heavy users; the teen-specific causal case remains debated. Policy has moved ahead on precaution - and that, too, is part of the system.
sources: Wells, Horwitz & Seetharaman, 'Facebook Knows Instagram Is Toxic for Teen Girls, Company Documents Show', Wall Street Journal, 14 September 2021
US Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection hearing with Frances Haugen, 5 October 2021
Haidt, The Anxious Generation (Penguin Press, 2024)
Odgers, 'The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?', Nature (2024)

days.application: Australia's Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 requires major platforms to keep under-16s from holding accounts from 10 December 2025 - the first national ban, and a live test: if teen mental-health measures in Australia diverge from comparable countries' in the following years, it will become a natural experiment (Day 21) that researchers on both sides of the debate are watching.

builds_on.why: Conformity and social proof: likes and follower counts make others' approval visible and countable, the normative pressure Asch measured, at scale.
Variable-ratio reinforcement: a feed that pays out unpredictably is the schedule most resistant to extinction.
Diagnosis and measurement: whether rising rates reflect more illness or changed screening, labelling and reporting is the first question to ask of the trend.
Natural experiments: Facebook's staggered college rollout is one of the strongest causal designs in the debate, and Australia's ban may become another.

across.link: In 1954 the psychiatrist Fredric Wertham's Seduction of the Innocent and US Senate hearings blamed comic books for juvenile delinquency, and the industry adopted the Comics Code that October; decades later Carol Tilley (Information & Culture, 2012) showed Wertham had manipulated and misrepresented his clinical evidence - a past panic to weigh against today's, remembering that some alarms (tobacco) proved right.

days.apply_question: Television reached US cities at different times in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and Gentzkow and Shapiro (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2008) used that staggered arrival to study children's later test scores: they found no harm, and small gains for some groups. Why might that finding fail to transfer to Instagram and teenage depression?
days.evidence_note: Settled: US measures of teenage depression, anxiety and self-harm rose sharply after about 2012, most for girls; average correlations between total screen time and adolescent well-being are small (Orben & Przybylski 2019). Debated: whether social media caused much of the rise - Jonathan Haidt and Jean Twenge point to the timing across many countries, larger associations for girls and heavy social-media users, and experimental and natural-experiment evidence; Candice Odgers, Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski answer that effects are small, possibly reversed (distressed teens use more), confounded, and partly a change in how distress is measured and labelled (Day 166). Value judgment: who should decide - parents, platforms or the state - weighing teens' liberty and the support some find online against precaution for children who cannot meaningfully consent to engagement-maximizing design; utilitarian, rights-based and Christian accounts of moral formation weigh these differently, and the counterfactual of a 2010s without smartphones cannot be known.

chain.point: Adolescents judge their standing by comparing themselves with peers (Festinger's social comparison theory, 1954); platforms made belonging and status visible and countable - likes, followers, streaks. By 2022 about 46% of US teens said they were online 'almost constantly' (Pew Research Center).

The features came first: Facebook's News Feed (September 2006), the Like button (February 2009), the iPhone 4's front-facing camera (June 2010) and Instagram (October 2010) each shipped and spread years before any study of teen mental health could test them; Instagram replaced its chronological feed with a ranked one in 2016.

A camera-and-feed in every pocket, on all day, needed lithium-ion cells dense enough for a day's use (Day 73), cheap silicon (Day 77) and 4G mobile broadband, which US carriers began rolling out around 2010 - hardware that made the feed constant rather than a desk-bound activity.

A feed pays out unpredictably - a new like or post on some refreshes, nothing on others - a variable-ratio schedule, the pattern most resistant to extinction (Day 155), acting on dopamine's reward-prediction-error signal (Day 151); whether the result is 'addiction' or strong habit is debated.

What each teen sees is chosen by recommender systems trained to predict engagement; how such systems learn is taught in the AI block (Days 170-184). Here, only that the ranking is learned from behaviour, not written by hand.

chain.field: Finance (named at CFA level, not taught)
chain.point: The business is advertising: Meta reported about $135 billion of revenue in 2023, roughly 98% of it from ads, so revenue scales with attention and engagement became the target metric - Goodhart's law (Day 23) applied to a proxy that is not the user's well-being.

COPPA (1998) made 13 the age below which US sites need parental consent to collect children's data, which became platforms' de facto minimum age; Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) shields platforms from liability for users' posts; Australia barred under-16 accounts from 10 December 2025. Taught in Government (Days 236-249) and Law (Days 250-263).

US teens' smartphone access rose from roughly a third (2012) to about 95% (2018) in Pew's surveys - a logistic S-curve (Day 7) compressed into six years, sped by network effects as each platform grew more valuable, and harder to leave, as peers joined. How adoption spreads through peers is Sociology's diffusion lesson (Day 213).

On the CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Survey, high-school girls reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness rose from 36% (2011) to 57% (2021), and past-year major depressive episodes among 12-17-year-olds roughly doubled between 2011 and 2019 (NSDUH). Day 166's question applies - more illness, or changed screening, labelling and willingness to report? - though emergency visits for self-harm among young girls, which depend less on labels, also rose.

Orben and Przybylski (Nature Human Behaviour, 2019) ran a specification curve on data from 355,358 adolescents: technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being. Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow (American Economic Review, 2020) paid adults to deactivate Facebook for four weeks: reported well-being rose modestly. Braghieri, Levy and Makarin (AER, 2022) used Facebook's staggered 2004-06 rollout across US colleges as a natural experiment: students' mental health worsened. None is a randomized trial on young teenagers.

Dread, novelty and harm to children amplify perceived risk (Day 158), and every new medium has met a panic - novels, radio, comics, video games (Orben, 'The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics', Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2020) - yet a panic can also be right. As the debate sharpened around Haidt's The Anxious Generation (March 2024), more schools and legislatures restricted phones, Instagram introduced restricted 'Teen Accounts' (September 2024) and Australia legislated its ban: policy moving before the evidence settled, and feeding back into the platforms' design.

resource.title: The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?
resource.creator: Candice L. Odgers (Nature, book review of Haidt's The Anxious Generation, March 2024)
resource.why: The sharpest short statement of the sceptics' case, by a developmental psychologist, against Haidt's book - read it as one side, named as such, since the lesson itself sets out Haidt and Twenge's argument.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); review known from the literature on this debate (Nature, published online 29 March 2024). Cite without a link.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Two roads to AI: rules versus learning
days.headline_hint: Ada Lovelace Said the Engine Could Only Do What We Order. No One Can Write the Order for Recognizing a Face. Machines Do It Anyway.
days.concept: Artificial intelligence can be built by writing the rules down (symbolic AI, expert systems) or by writing a procedure that learns the rules from examples (machine learning); wherever the rules are too many or too tacit to write, learning plus ever-cheaper computation has mostly won.
days.focus: Teaches AI's two founding strategies: hand-coded knowledge (logic, search, expert systems such as Stanford's MYCIN, with several hundred hand-written rules) and functions learned from data. Also teaches why Rich Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson' (2019) holds that general methods riding on computation keep beating built-in human knowledge. Angle: the Bitter Lesson generalizes from history and is not a law, and rules still rule where correctness must be guaranteed or audited.
key_concepts: machine learning: a function learned from examples
days.model_or_equation: Rules road: input -> rules a person wrote -> output. Learning road: many (input, correct output) examples -> learning algorithm -> learned function f -> output for new inputs. The programmer writes the learner, not the rules; the knowledge comes from the data.

story.title: A translator's note in 1843 that became AI's first objection
story.hook: In 1843 Ada Lovelace, then 27, published an English translation of Luigi Menabrea's article on Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs, signed only 'A.A.L.'. Her own notes ran longer than the article itself. The last, Note G, set out a step-by-step table for computing Bernoulli numbers (how much of that program was hers and how much Babbage's is debated). It also gave a warning: 'The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.' In 1950 Alan Turing gave a section of 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' to 'Lady Lovelace's objection'.
story.puzzle: Today machines recognize faces, transcribe speech and translate languages. No one knows how to 'order' those tasks, because no one can write down the rules for recognizing a face. Was Lovelace wrong, or is something else going on?
story.payoff: Lovelace was right about the machine but wrong about the limit. A learning system still does only what it is ordered to do, but the order is 'adjust yourself to fit these examples'. The behaviour comes from data, not from rules any person wrote. That is the second road, which Turing sketched in the same 1950 paper as a 'child machine' to be taught rather than programmed.
sources: Lovelace, 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine... with notes by the translator', Taylor's Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843), Note G
Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind 59 (1950), sections on 'Lady Lovelace's Objection' and 'Learning Machines'
Bodleian Libraries blog, 'Ada Lovelace and the Analytical Engine' (2018)

days.application: Spam filtering. Hand-written rules (block 'click here', block known senders) were easy to evade. Paul Graham's essay 'A Plan for Spam' (August 2002) instead learned word probabilities from his own spam and legitimate mail and combined them with Bayes' rule. He reported missing fewer than 5 spams per 1,000 with zero false positives on his test. Spammers then adapted, which shows that a learned system has to keep learning.

builds_on.why: Learning from examples is induction: a learned rule generalizes past cases to new ones, and Hume's problem is why it can fail.
Graham's spam filter combines per-word evidence with Bayes' theorem, an early learned system built directly on base rates and likelihoods.

across.link: Hubert Dreyfus's 'What Computers Can't Do' (1972) argued from Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty that expert know-how is not rule-following. It was a critique of the rules road that the learning road partly vindicated. In the 1992 edition, 'What Computers Still Can't Do', Dreyfus argued that neural networks would face their own version of the problem, because generalizing as people do needs a human sense of what is relevant.

days.apply_question: Tax-preparation software is built from the written tax code while card-fraud detection is learned from millions of past transactions; using today's two roads, why did each industry choose the road it did?
days.evidence_note: Settled: learned systems now dominate perception, speech, translation and game benchmarks. Debated: whether the Bitter Lesson generalizes. Sutton argues from seventy years of examples; critics such as Gary Marcus hold that built-in structure and symbolic reasoning remain necessary, and hybrid neuro-symbolic systems are an active research line. Who wrote the Bernoulli program (Lovelace or Babbage) is a historians' dispute; the warning sentence is hers.

resource.title: The Bitter Lesson
resource.creator: Rich Sutton (incompleteideas.net, 13 March 2019)
resource.why: In one page, a founder of reinforcement learning argues from chess, Go, speech and vision that general methods riding on cheaper computation beat hand-built knowledge. That is the thesis today's lesson tests; read it as one side of a live debate.
resource.verified_how: Web search during planning: Wikipedia and secondary pages confirm the title, author, date (13 March 2019) and host (incompleteideas.net). A search for the page's own address returned no result on that host, so no link is given. The verifier could not search again (shared budget exhausted) and relied on those saved results.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Learning from data: fitting, overfitting and distribution shift
days.headline_hint: A Horse Named Hans Got His Sums Right Nine Times in Ten. Then He Could No Longer See the Questioner.
days.concept: A learning system fits a function to examples. It can latch onto noise or shortcuts that happen to work in its training data (overfitting), and it can fail when the world it meets differs from the world it learned from (distribution shift), so it must be judged on data it never saw, drawn from the conditions where it will be used.
days.focus: Teaches the core loop of machine learning: training data, a model with adjustable parameters, a loss, and held-out test data. Then its two classic failures: overfitting (a model flexible enough to memorize accidents of the sample; the bias-variance trade-off) and distribution shift (deployment differs from training). Shortcut learning ties the two together: a model can be right for the wrong reason, and only out-of-sample tests reveal it.
days.model_or_equation: Test error = training error + generalization gap. A more flexible model drives training error down but can widen the gap. Only error on held-out data, drawn from the deployment conditions, estimates real performance.

story.title: The horse that could count, as long as someone who knew was watching
story.hook: In Berlin in the early 1900s a retired schoolteacher, Wilhelm von Osten, showed off his horse Hans, who tapped out answers to arithmetic, calendar and spelling questions with his hoof. In September 1904 a commission of thirteen, convened with the psychologist Carl Stumpf, found no trickery. Stumpf's student Oskar Pfungst then ran controlled tests, published in 1907. Fraud was ruled out, because Hans answered strangers too. But in one series, when Hans could see a questioner who knew the answer he was right about 89% of the time (50 of 56); when he could not see the questioner, about 6% (2 of 35). When two people each whispered a number so that no one present knew the sum, Hans failed.
story.puzzle: Hans had passed a thirteen-member inspection and answered real questions correctly for years. What had he actually learned, and why did a test his admirers never thought to run expose it?
story.payoff: Hans had learned a real pattern in his 'training data'. Questioners tensed as he tapped and relaxed slightly when he reached the right number. Every situation he had trained in contained that cue, so his accuracy there was genuine. Pfungst's tests shifted the distribution (a questioner who did not know, or could not be seen), and the shortcut collapsed. Machine-learning researchers now call right-for-the-wrong-reason models 'Clever Hans predictors'. Lapuschkin et al. (Nature Communications, 2019) found an image classifier recognizing horses partly by a source watermark that appeared on many horse photos in its dataset.
sources: Oskar Pfungst, Das Pferd des Herrn von Osten (1907); English translation 'Clever Hans' (1911)
Lapuschkin et al., 'Unmasking Clever Hans predictors and assessing what machines really learn', Nature Communications 10:1096 (2019)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'What Clever Hans teaches us about being human'

days.application: Google Flu Trends. Ginsberg et al. (Nature, 2009) tested 50 million common US search queries against CDC records of influenza-like illness for 2003-07, summed the best 45, and fitted a model that reported flu levels about a week or two ahead of the CDC. The Science paper by Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani (March 2014) cites Nature's report that at the 2012-13 peak it predicted more than double the CDC's share of doctor visits for flu-like illness, and reports that it over-predicted in 100 of 108 weeks starting in August 2011. Both of today's failures appear. Screening millions of terms finds some that merely track winter (overfitting), and searching changed under the model as media coverage and Google's own search features changed (shift). Lazer's team showed that simply projecting forward from CDC data a few weeks old did better.

builds_on.why: A sample's value comes from how it was drawn: test data must come from the conditions of use, just as the Literary Digest's huge but biased sample misled.
Hans's cue and Flu Trends' seasonal search terms are correlations that confound the real cause, and the model cannot tell the difference without a controlled test.

across.link: Pfungst's tests gave experimental psychology the 'Clever Hans effect': experimenters cue their subjects without meaning to. It is the reason animal-cognition studies and double-blind trials keep the person running the test from knowing the expected answer.

days.apply_question: When University of Michigan researchers tested Epic's widely used sepsis-alert model on 38,455 hospitalizations, it caught only about a third of the patients who developed sepsis, well below the developer's own figures (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021); using today's lesson, what test should a hospital insist on before it switches such a model on?
days.evidence_note: Settled: held-out testing, overfitting and distribution shift are textbook, and the Flu Trends overestimates and the Epic model's weak external performance are documented. Debated: how much of Flu Trends' failure came from overfitting and how much from Google's changes to search (Lazer et al. name both); Epic disputed the Michigan study's choice of thresholds. The Clever Hans percentages come from one series of Pfungst's tests.

resource.title: Big data: are we making a big mistake?
resource.creator: Tim Harford (Financial Times Magazine, 2014; republished on timharford.com, April 2014)
resource.why: The economist and presenter of BBC Radio 4's More or Less uses Google Flu Trends and the 1936 Literary Digest poll to show why 'found data' and theory-free correlations break. It is today's overfitting-and-shift problem in the language of everyday statistics.
resource.verified_how: Web search during planning showed this exact URL on timharford.com, the author's own site, dated April 2014; secondary results confirm the piece first ran in the Financial Times in spring 2014. Not fetched. The verifier relied on those saved results (shared search budget exhausted).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Neural networks: weighted sums, matrices and layers
days.headline_hint: In 1958 the Navy Said Its New Machine Would Walk, Talk and Be Conscious. It Could Tell a Card Marked Left From One Marked Right.
days.concept: An artificial neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up (a dot product) and passes the sum through a nonlinear function. A layer of neurons is one matrix multiplication, and stacking layers lets a network build complex features out of simple ones.
days.focus: Teaches the computation inside a neural network: the dot product, the matrix as a whole layer of weighted sums, activation functions, and depth. Shows why one layer (Rosenblatt's perceptron) can only draw straight-line boundaries (Minsky and Papert's 1969 critique, e.g. XOR), while hidden layers can in principle approximate any function (the universal approximation theorem). Matrices are taught here, where networks need them, as the block's mission says.
days.model_or_equation: One neuron: y = σ(w·x + b) = σ(w1x1 + w2x2 + ... + wnxn + b). One layer: y = σ(Wx + b), where row i of the matrix W holds neuron i's weights. A three-layer network: y = σ(W3 σ(W2 σ(W1x + b1) + b2) + b3). Without the nonlinearity σ the stack collapses into a single matrix, which is why σ matters.

story.title: The Navy's 'embryo' of a thinking machine
story.hook: On 7 July 1958 the US Office of Naval Research demonstrated Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron in Washington, simulated on an IBM 704. Reports said that after about fifty trials it learned to tell cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. The next day the New York Times ran 'New Navy Device Learns By Doing', reporting 'the embryo of an electronic computer that [the Navy] expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.' Rosenblatt, a 29-year-old Cornell psychologist, went on to build the Mark I Perceptron at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo: a 20-by-20 grid of 400 photocells wired through adjustable weights. In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's book Perceptrons proved there were simple patterns such machines could never learn, and interest and funding fell away.
story.puzzle: Today's networks are built from the same kind of artificial neuron Minsky and Papert analysed. What exactly could a single layer of weighted sums not do, and what changed when layers were stacked?
story.payoff: A single perceptron draws one straight line (a hyperplane) through its input space, so it cannot learn a pattern like XOR ('one or the other, but not both'), which no straight line separates. Stack layers with a nonlinearity between them and each layer re-maps the space so the next can separate it. The hard part, which Minsky and Papert doubted could be solved, was training the hidden layers; that is Day 173.
sources: New York Times, 8 July 1958, 'New Navy Device Learns By Doing'
Rosenblatt, 'The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain', Psychological Review 65 (1958)
Minsky & Papert, Perceptrons (MIT Press, 1969)
Olazaran, 'A Sociological Study of the Official History of the Perceptrons Controversy', Social Studies of Science 26 (1996)

days.application: Yann LeCun's convolutional networks at AT&T Bell Labs read handwritten digits on bank cheques. A convolution slides the same small weight matrix across the whole image, so the network reuses one learned edge-detector everywhere. LeCun, Bottou, Bengio & Haffner ('Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition', Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998) describe the cheque reader NCR deployed as reading several million cheques a day; LeCun has since said it was reading over 10% of US cheques by the late 1990s.

builds_on.why: Vectors and components: a neuron's input is a vector, and its weighted sum, the dot product, multiplies matching components and adds them.
Biological neurons sum synaptic inputs and fire past a threshold. The artificial neuron copies that sketch, and the analogy breaks because real neurons spike in time and learn by local rules.

across.link: Google's first Tensor Processing Unit (described by Jouppi et al., ISCA 2017) is built around a 256-by-256 grid of multiply-accumulate units for matrix multiplication, 65,536 of them. That is hardware shaped by today's equation.

days.apply_question: Hospital early-warning scores such as the UK's NEWS2 add up points for heart rate, temperature and breathing rate and call a doctor above a threshold; using today's lesson, what pattern of vital signs could any purely additive score misjudge that a network with a hidden layer could capture?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the mathematics (perceptron convergence, linear separability, universal approximation). Debated: how much the 1969 book caused the 1970s collapse in neural-network funding; Olazaran (1996) argues the 'official history' oversimplifies it. The brain analogy is loose, and the 10%-of-cheques figure is LeCun's own account.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.headline_hint: Cauchy Invented a Trick for Grinding Through Orbit Equations in 1847. It Now Tunes 175 Billion Numbers at Once.
days.concept: A network is trained by measuring its error with a loss function and moving every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the loss fastest (gradient descent). Backpropagation is the chain rule applied backwards through the layers, and it yields the slope for every weight at roughly the cost of one extra pass through the network.
days.focus: Teaches the loss function, the gradient as the vector of all slopes (D4, D8), the learning rate, stochastic (mini-batch) gradient descent, and backpropagation as the bookkeeping that makes gradients cheap. Angle: a cost puzzle. Estimating each slope by nudging one weight at a time would need one extra run per weight. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation (Linnainmaa 1970; proposed for networks by Werbos 1974 and popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986) gets them all in one backward sweep.
key_concepts: chain rule and backpropagation (reverse-mode automatic differentiation)
days.model_or_equation: Update: w ← w − η ∂L/∂w, for every weight at once (η = learning rate, L = loss). The chain rule for a weight in an early layer: ∂L/∂w = (∂L/∂y)(∂y/∂h)(∂h/∂w). Backpropagation computes the shared factors once, from the output backwards, and reuses them for every weight below.

story.title: A short note on equations that now trains every network
story.hook: In 1847 Augustin-Louis Cauchy published a note of a few pages in the Comptes rendus of the Paris Académie des sciences: 'Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées'. Astronomical computation, such as fixing a body's orbit, meant solving several equations in several unknowns by hand. Cauchy proposed folding them into one quantity to be made as small as possible, then stepping repeatedly in the direction in which it falls fastest. In 2020 OpenAI trained GPT-3 with a refined descendant of the same rule (Adam, a form of stochastic gradient descent): about 3.14 × 10^23 arithmetic operations adjusting 175 billion weights.
story.puzzle: To step downhill you need the slope in every direction. Estimating each slope by nudging one weight and re-running the model would take 175 billion extra runs for a single step, and training takes many thousands of steps. How can anyone afford the gradient of a model that size?
story.payoff: Backpropagation. A network is a chain of functions, so the chain rule can pass the error backwards layer by layer, reusing each intermediate result. One backward pass costs only a small multiple of one forward pass and returns all 175 billion slopes together. Cauchy supplied the downhill step; the chain rule run backwards (Linnainmaa 1970; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, Nature, 9 October 1986) made it affordable.
sources: Cauchy, Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences 25 (1847), pp. 536-538
Claude Lemaréchal, 'Cauchy and the Gradient Method', Documenta Mathematica, Extra Volume ISMP (2012)
Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors', Nature 323:533-536 (1986)
Brown et al., 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (2020), compute table

days.application: Training GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020): 175 billion parameters, about 300 billion training tokens, about 3.14 × 10^23 floating-point operations. A Day 1-style check: compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens = 6 × 1.75 × 10^11 × 3 × 10^11 ≈ 3.15 × 10^23. The 6 is two operations per weight per token for the forward pass plus about four for the backward pass. That is backpropagation's cost, roughly twice a forward pass rather than 175 billion times it. Show it in a .worked block.

builds_on.why: Optimization: a smooth minimum is where the gradient is zero, and gradient descent walks toward it.
A network is a composition of layers, which is exactly the chain the chain rule differentiates backwards.

across.link: Francis Crick's 'The recent excitement about neural networks' (Nature, 1989) argued that backpropagation is biologically unrealistic: no known mechanism lets a neuron send a precise error signal backwards through the same synapses (the 'weight transport' problem). That is where the brain analogy breaks. Whether brains approximate backpropagation some other way is open; Lillicrap, Hinton and colleagues reviewed the candidates in 'Backpropagation and the brain' (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2020).

days.apply_question: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts adjusts millions of uncertain starting values of its weather model so that the forecast fits recent observations (its 4D-Var data assimilation); using today's lesson, why does it get the slopes by running an 'adjoint' model backwards in time instead of nudging each starting value in turn?
days.evidence_note: Settled technical topic. Who deserves credit for backpropagation is disputed (Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974, Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986; Jürgen Schmidhuber argues credit has been misassigned). That is a question of priority, not of science.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.headline_hint: Neural Networks Were 54 Years Old. In 2012 One Cut the Best Error Rate From 26 Percent to 15.
days.concept: Deep learning took off when three things arrived together: many-layered networks, very large labelled datasets, and cheap parallel computing on graphics chips. With all three, features learned from data beat features designed by hand.
days.focus: Teaches representation learning: hand-engineered features (edge and corner detectors, SIFT) versus features learned layer by layer. Explains why depth needs both data (to avoid overfitting, D171) and compute (GPUs doing matrix multiplication in parallel, D172), plus the enabling tricks (ReLU activations, dropout, data augmentation). Angle: the 2012 break came from an old idea meeting new data and hardware, not from a new idea.
days.model_or_equation: Feature hierarchy: features at layer k = σ(W_k × features at layer k−1). Visualizations of trained networks (Zeiler & Fergus, 2014) show early layers responding to edges and colours, middle layers to textures and parts, and late layers to whole objects. No one wrote these detectors; training found them.

story.title: A dataset few wanted, and a result few expected
story.hook: From 2007 Fei-Fei Li, then a young computer-science professor at Princeton, set out to label millions of internet photos by the categories of the WordNet lexicon, paying online workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk to sort them. ImageNet was shown as a poster at the CVPR conference in 2009 and grew past 14 million images. From 2010 its annual challenge asked programs to sort 1.2 million training photos into 1,000 classes. In 2012 a University of Toronto team (Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton) entered an eight-layer network with about 60 million parameters, trained for five to six days on two Nvidia GTX 580 gaming cards. Its top-5 error was 15.3%; the next-best entry managed 26.2%.
story.puzzle: Neural networks dated from 1958, backpropagation from the 1980s, and LeCun's networks had been reading cheques for years. Why did the method suddenly crush a decade of carefully hand-designed vision systems in 2012, and not in 1992?
story.payoff: No single new idea explains the jump; what changed was that the method's two hungers were finally fed. A 60-million-parameter network overfits a small dataset (Day 171), and ImageNet supplied more than a million labelled examples. Training it takes enormous numbers of multiply-adds (Day 172), and GPUs built for video games do thousands in parallel. With both in place, learned features beat hand-made ones. By 2015 a network (ResNet) scored about 3.6% top-5 error, below the roughly 5% one human annotator had measured for himself.
sources: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 'ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks', NeurIPS 2012
Deng et al., 'ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database', CVPR 2009
Russakovsky et al., 'ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge', International Journal of Computer Vision (2015)
Fei-Fei Li, The Worlds I See (2023)

days.application: IDx-DR (now LumineticsCore). On 11 April 2018 the FDA authorized it as the first autonomous AI diagnostic system: it decides from retinal photographs, without a specialist reading the image, whether a person with diabetes needs referral for more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy. In its pivotal trial of 900 people at 10 US primary-care sites it showed 87.2% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity (Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine, 2018). Its detectors are deep networks trained on retinal images, and it was tested prospectively in the clinics where it would be used (Day 171).

builds_on.why: More parameters need more data or they overfit; ImageNet's million-plus labelled images is what let a deep network generalize.

Transistor scaling put billions of switches on one chip; a graphics card spends them on thousands of simple arithmetic units working in parallel, exactly suited to a layer's matrix multiplication (Day 172).

across.link: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's recordings from cat visual cortex (1959 onward; Nobel Prize 1981) found cells tuned to oriented edges feeding more complex cells. Kunihiko Fukushima's neocognitron (1980) copied that hierarchy, and it is the direct ancestor of convolutional networks.

days.apply_question: In late 2016 Google Translate replaced its phrase-based system with a neural network; using today's three ingredients, why was machine translation ripe for the same kind of break that hit image recognition in 2012?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the 2012 challenge results and the rapid fall in error after them. Debated: how to divide credit among data, GPUs and algorithmic tricks, and whether benchmark gains reflect general visual understanding. Recht et al. (2019) found accuracy fell by roughly 11-14 points on a freshly collected ImageNet-style test set. The 'human' 5.1% is one annotator's estimate (Andrej Karpathy), not a population figure.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.headline_hint: Take 'King', Subtract 'Man', Add 'Woman'. A Program That Was Never Told What Words Mean Answered 'Queen'.
days.concept: An embedding represents a word, image or product as a list of numbers, a point in a space of hundreds of dimensions, learned so that things used in similar contexts land close together. Similarity then becomes measurable as the angle between vectors, and directions in the space carry meaning, including society's biases.
days.focus: Teaches the distributional hypothesis (J.R. Firth, 1957: 'you shall know a word by the company it keeps'), how word2vec learns vectors by predicting neighbouring words, cosine similarity, vector-arithmetic analogies, and bias inherited from text (Bolukbasi et al. 2016; Caliskan, Bryson & Narayanan, Science 2017). Includes the caveat that the most famous bias analogy partly reflects how queries were constrained (Nissim, van Noord & van der Goot 2020).
days.model_or_equation: cos θ = (a·b) / (|a||b|): +1 means the same direction (very similar), 0 means unrelated. Analogy query: find the word whose vector is nearest to v(king) − v(man) + v(woman). Standard code excludes the three input words from the answer.

story.title: Arithmetic on words, and the answer the code was not allowed to give
story.hook: In 2013 Tomas Mikolov, a Czech researcher at Google, and his colleagues released word2vec. Their published vectors, for about 3 million words and phrases, were learned from a Google News corpus of about 100 billion words, purely by predicting which words appear near which. Vector('king') − vector('man') + vector('woman') landed nearest to 'queen'. In 2016 Tolga Bolukbasi and colleagues asked the same kind of vectors to complete 'man is to computer programmer as woman is to x' and got 'homemaker'. In 2020 Malvina Nissim, Rik van Noord and Rob van der Goot pointed out that standard analogy code is not allowed to return any of the words in the question, so it could never answer 'programmer'.
story.puzzle: Nobody told the program what a king or a programmer is. How can adding and subtracting lists of numbers capture meaning, and is the 'homemaker' answer a measurement of the text or an artefact of the query?
story.payoff: Words used in similar contexts get similar vectors, so consistent differences in context (royalty, gender, tense) become consistent directions in the space, and arithmetic follows those directions. The same mechanism faithfully records whatever associations the text contains, stereotypes included: Caliskan et al. (2017) reproduced classic implicit-association patterns from embeddings alone. But because the query excluded 'programmer', the famous example overstated the effect. The bias is real, and the test was sensational.
sources: Mikolov et al., 'Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space' (arXiv, 2013) and 'Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases' (NeurIPS 2013)
Bolukbasi et al., 'Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings', NeurIPS 2016
Caliskan, Bryson & Narayanan, Science 356 (2017)
Nissim, van Noord & van der Goot, 'Fair is Better than Sensational', Computational Linguistics 46(2) (2020)

days.application: Airbnb's listing embeddings (Grbovic & Cheng, KDD 2018). The company treated the sequence of listings a guest clicked in one search session like the words of a sentence and learned a vector for each listing. 'Similar listings' and real-time search re-ranking then become nearest-neighbour lookups in that space. The same pattern (embed, then find neighbours) runs product recommendation, image search and the retrieval step of chatbots.

builds_on.why: Vectors and components: an embedding is a vector, and cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the lengths.
Embeddings are the weights of a network's first layer, learned by the same weighted-sum machinery.

across.link: Garg, Schiebinger, Jurafsky & Zou, 'Word embeddings quantify 100 years of gender and ethnic stereotypes' (PNAS, 2018), trained embeddings on a century of American text and tracked how occupational gender associations moved against census employment data.

days.apply_question: A music service learns song embeddings from which tracks listeners play in the same session and recommends each listener the nearest neighbours of what they already play; using today's lesson, how could such a system gradually confine a new listener to one corner of the space?
days.evidence_note: Settled: embeddings encode co-occurrence statistics, and cosine similarity tracks human similarity judgments reasonably well. Debated: how well analogy tests measure bias (Bolukbasi et al. 2016 versus Nissim et al. 2020), and whether 'debiasing' removes bias or hides it (Gonen & Goldberg, 'Lipstick on a Pig', 2019). Value judgment: whether systems should mirror the statistics of past text or a corrected ideal, and who chooses the ideal.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.headline_hint: Move 37: AlphaGo's Own Network Rated It a 1-in-10,000 Human Move. AlphaGo Played It Anyway, and Won.
days.concept: In reinforcement learning an agent learns which actions lead to reward by trial and error, updating its estimates by the reward-prediction error (the gap between what it expected and what happened), so it can discover moves no teacher ever showed it.
days.focus: Teaches agent, environment, state, action, reward and policy; the exploration-exploitation trade-off; temporal-difference learning (Sutton 1988), whose prediction error resembles the dopamine signal of Day 151; and how AlphaGo combined policy and value networks, self-play and Monte Carlo tree search. Angle: learning from consequences rather than from labelled answers is what let the system go beyond its human data.
days.model_or_equation: TD update: V(s) ← V(s) + α[r + γV(s′) − V(s)]. The bracket is the reward-prediction error δ: the reward just received, plus the discounted value of the next state, minus what you had predicted. α = learning rate, γ = discount factor.

story.title: Move 37 in Seoul
story.hook: On 10 March 2016, in game two of a five-game match at the Four Seasons Hotel in Seoul, DeepMind's AlphaGo, playing black, made its 37th move: a 'shoulder hit' on the fifth line that commentators first took for a mistake. Lee Sedol, one of the strongest players of his generation, left the room for several minutes and took a long time to reply. AlphaGo's policy network, trained on human expert games, had put the chance that a human would play that move at about 1 in 10,000. AlphaGo won the game and the match, 4-1.
story.puzzle: AlphaGo learned Go from human games. How did it choose a move its own human-trained network judged almost no human would make, and why did the move turn out to be good?
story.payoff: Human games only gave AlphaGo a starting policy. It then improved by reinforcement learning, playing millions of games against itself, rewarded only for winning, while a value network learned to predict who would win from any position. At match time a tree search guided by those networks judged Move 37 by its consequences rather than its popularity. Learning from reward instead of imitation is what let it leave the human distribution.
sources: Silver et al., 'Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search', Nature 529 (2016)
Cade Metz, 'In Two Moves, AlphaGo and Lee Sedol Redefined the Future', Wired, March 2016
AlphaGo (documentary, dir. Greg Kohs, 2017)

days.application: Controlling fusion plasma. DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL trained a reinforcement-learning controller in simulation, rewarded for holding the plasma in a target shape, then used it to drive the magnetic coils of the TCV tokamak in Lausanne. It produced and held several plasma shapes, including two separate 'droplets' at once (Degrave et al., Nature, February 2022). The reward replaced hand-designed control laws, and the simulation-to-reality gap was the main risk, the distribution shift of Day 171.

builds_on.why: Dopamine neurons signal reward-prediction error; TD learning uses the same quantity, and Schultz, Dayan & Montague (1997) made the link explicit.
Operant conditioning shapes behaviour by its consequences; reinforcement learning is the algorithmic version, with reward shaping as its practical art.

across.link: Richard Bellman's Dynamic Programming (1957), written at RAND, set out the value recursion V(s) = max over actions of [r + γV(s′)]. TD learning estimates that same quantity from experience, and the recursion is also the backbone of optimal control in engineering.

days.apply_question: A ride-hailing company wants software that sends idle drivers wherever it expects the most fares over the next few hours; using today's lesson, why must the system sometimes send drivers to places it currently rates as worse?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the TD algorithm, and AlphaGo's and the tokamak controller's published results. Debated: how closely dopamine neurons implement TD learning. Schultz et al. is strong evidence, but newer work finds richer signals, such as a distributional code (Dabney et al., Nature 2020). Also debated: how well game-playing reinforcement learning transfers to messy real-world tasks, where rewards are hard to specify (Day 179).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.headline_hint: Eight Google Researchers Stopped Making Machines Read in Order. Their Idea Is the 'T' in GPT.
days.concept: Attention lets each word in a passage build its meaning as a weighted mix of every other word, with the weights set by dot products of learned vectors. Because all positions are computed at once rather than one after another, transformers train efficiently on enormous bodies of text.
days.focus: Teaches queries, keys and values; scaled dot-product attention with softmax; multi-head attention; positional encoding (word order has to be added back); and why parallel computation, not just accuracy, made transformers the base of large language models. Also teaches the cost: attention work grows with the square of the text length, which is why context windows are limited. Builds directly on embeddings (D175) and matrix multiplication (D172).
days.model_or_equation: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V. Each row of QKᵀ holds one word's dot products with every word; softmax turns each row into weights that sum to 1; multiplying by V mixes the words' value vectors in those proportions. Dividing by √d_k (the vector length) keeps the dot products from growing too large.

story.title: The paper that stopped reading in order
story.hook: On 12 June 2017 eight researchers at Google (one of them, Aidan Gomez, an intern) posted 'Attention Is All You Need': Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser and Illia Polosukhin. It dropped recurrence (reading a sentence one word at a time), which most leading translation systems then used, and relied on attention alone. Their larger model trained in 3.5 days on eight GPUs and set a record BLEU score of 28.4 on English-to-German translation. All eight later left Google. The 'T' in OpenAI's 2018 GPT stands for their 'transformer'.
story.puzzle: Word order matters: 'dog bites man' is not 'man bites dog'. How could a model that looks at every word at once, with no built-in sense of sequence, translate better than models that read in order, and train faster too?
story.payoff: Attention lets every word consult every other word directly, so a long-range link (an 'it' and the noun it refers to) takes one step instead of many, and all positions are computed at once on parallel hardware. Order is not lost: it is added back as a positional encoding mixed into each word's vector. Faster training meant more text per dollar, the opening that scaling (Day 178) exploited.
sources: Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need', NeurIPS 2017 (arXiv:1706.03762)
Steven Levy, '8 Google Employees Invented Modern AI. Here's the Inside Story', Wired, March 2024
Radford et al., 'Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training' (OpenAI, 2018)

days.application: AlphaFold 2. At the CASP14 protein-structure assessment (2020), DeepMind's model, whose core 'Evoformer' is built on attention, predicted structures with a median accuracy score (GDT) of about 92, close to experimental precision for many targets. Attention suits proteins for the same reason it suits language: amino acids far apart in the chain may touch in the folded shape, so every residue must be able to consult every other. In 2024 Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it; David Baker received the other half.

builds_on.why: Words enter as embeddings, and attention weights are dot products between transformed embeddings, the same geometry of similarity.
Attention compares every word with every other, so its work grows as the square of the text length, the polynomial growth Day 108 taught to read; it is why context windows are limited.

across.link: Sara Hooker's 'The Hardware Lottery' (Communications of the ACM, 2021) argues that research ideas win partly because they suit the hardware of their day. Transformers' parallel matrix arithmetic fit GPUs and TPUs in a way recurrent networks did not.

days.apply_question: A contract-review tool must recognize that 'the Lessee' on page 40 of a lease is the party defined on page 1; using today's lesson, why can a transformer connect the two in a single step where a word-by-word reader cannot, yet still pay heavily as contracts grow longer?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the architecture and its benchmark results. Debated: why transformers work as well as they do is only partly understood (interpretability research is ongoing), and whether other architectures (state-space models, for example) will displace them is open.
