days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Wars of religion, toleration and the sovereign state
days.headline_hint: Three Men Were Thrown From a Prague Castle Window in 1618 and Lived. Thirty Years of War Followed.
days.concept: The wars of religion ended not with one faith's victory but in settlements, at Augsburg in 1555 and Westphalia in 1648. These strengthened rulers' control of their territories and, slowly and often reluctantly, made room for religious coexistence. The popular claim that 1648 founded the modern system of sovereign states is partly myth (Osiander 2001).
days.focus: Teach the Thirty Years' War (1618-48) as a stalemate. A Bohemian revolt widened into a European war in which Catholic France fought the Catholic Habsburgs for reasons of state. Perhaps 4.5 to 8 million people died, and some German regions lost a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia, negotiated at Münster and Osnabrück and signed on 24 October 1648, recognized Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, fixed 1624 as the 'normative year' for church property and confirmed the princes' rights within the Empire; a separate Peace of Münster, signed earlier that year, recognized Dutch independence. It did not invent sovereignty or non-intervention (Osiander; Krasner). Toleration came first as a truce between exhausted powers and only later as a principle: Castellio after Servetus was burned (1553), then Roger Williams, Locke and Bayle.

story.title: Out of the chancellery window
story.hook: On 23 May 1618, in Prague Castle, Protestant nobles of Bohemia were furious that the Catholic Habsburg government was breaking the religious guarantees of the 1609 Letter of Majesty. In the Bohemian Chancellery they cornered two of the emperor's regents, Vilém Slavata and Jaroslav Bořita of Martinic, together with their secretary Philip Fabricius, and threw all three out of a high window, a fall usually given as 15 to 21 metres (accounts differ). All three survived. Catholic writers said angels or the Virgin Mary had caught them; Protestant accounts said they had landed in a heap of refuse or dung in the moat, a detail that may itself be partly legend. Fabricius was later ennobled as 'von Hohenfall', 'of the high fall'. The revolt became a war that drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain and lasted thirty years.
story.puzzle: A war fought largely over religion ended in 1648 with three confessions recognized and no side victorious. Why did it end that way? And did it really give birth to the modern sovereign state, as textbooks long said?
story.payoff: No side could win, and thirty years of war had exhausted them all, so the bargain left was a negotiated settlement that let rulers decide religion in their territories, within limits. It stabilized the territorial princes inside the Holy Roman Empire, but sovereignty and toleration grew slowly over the next two centuries. The 'Westphalian system' is largely a label that 19th- and 20th-century writers read back into 1648.
sources: Peter H. Wilson, Europe's Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (2009)
Andreas Osiander, 'Sovereignty, International Relations, and the Westphalian Myth', International Organization 55(2) (2001)
Contemporary Catholic and Protestant accounts of the defenestration

days.application: Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1635 for arguing that magistrates had no power over conscience. In 1636 he founded Providence on land obtained from the Narragansett sachems, and Rhode Island's royal charter of 1663 promised a 'lively experiment' with 'full liberty in religious concernments'. John Locke's A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689) argued that belief cannot be compelled, so force is useless as well as wrong. Yet Locke excluded atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, and Catholics, whom he saw as owing allegiance to a foreign prince. Toleration grew by stages, and each stage had limits.

builds_on.why: The Reformation created the rival confessions, and Augsburg's rule that the ruler picks the religion set up the conflict that exploded in 1618.
Game theory: a costly war between sides that cannot win ends when a bargain beats continued fighting for all of them. Westphalia was a negotiated equilibrium, not a victory.

across.link: Stephen Krasner's Sovereignty: Organized Hypocrisy (1999) argues that powerful states have violated the 'Westphalian' norm of non-intervention whenever they found it useful. It is the international-relations side of Osiander's historical point that 1648 did not create the system named after it.

days.apply_question: Henry IV's Edict of Nantes (1598) gave French Protestants freedom of worship in defined places and fortified towns of their own. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, after which perhaps 150,000-200,000 Huguenots fled. Using the difference between toleration as a truce and toleration as a principle, why did the edict fail within a century?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the defenestration and its survivors; the war's devastation; the 1648 treaties' recognition of Calvinism and confirmation of the princes' rights. Debated: the death toll (roughly 4.5-8 million); how far Westphalia created state sovereignty (Osiander 2001 and Krasner 1999 against the conventional IR story); how much toleration came from principle rather than exhaustion. Value judgment: whether toleration rests best on religious grounds (Williams's liberty of conscience, Locke, Bayle's rights of the erring conscience) or on secular ones (Mill's On Liberty, 1859), which is still argued.

resource.title: Sovereignty, International Relations, and the Westphalian Myth
resource.creator: Andreas Osiander, International Organization 55(2): 251-287 (2001)
resource.length: about 37 pages; the introduction and conclusion take about 20 minutes
resource.why: The standard scholarly demolition of the idea that 1648 founded the sovereign-state system. It sets what the treaties actually said against what later international-relations textbooks claimed: a model of checking a myth by reading the primary text.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search (the session's shared search budget ran out for the planner and for this verifier). Citation agrees with the verifier's own knowledge. Usually paywalled (JSTOR), so a library copy may be needed; no free alternative could be verified this session.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Scientific Revolution and the Christianity-and-science question
days.headline_hint: Galileo Knelt in Rome and Recanted in 1633. Historians Now Call the 'War Between Science and Religion' Mostly Myth. Mostly.
days.concept: Historians of science have largely replaced the 'conflict thesis' of Draper (1874) and White (1896) with a 'complexity thesis' (Brooke 1991; Numbers, ed., 2009; Harrison 2015): relations between Christianity and science varied by time, place, institution and question. The opposite claim, that Christianity uniquely gave birth to modern science (Stark 2003; Hannam 2009), has its critics too, and some scientists still defend a conflict view (Coyne 2015).
days.focus: Teach the Galileo affair in context, then the historiography. The sequence: Copernicus (1543); Galileo's telescope discoveries (1610); the 1616 decree against Copernicanism; the Dialogue (1632); the trial (1633). The evidence was not yet decisive. No stellar parallax had been detected (Bessel first measured it in 1838; D128 teaches parallax), and Tycho's hybrid system, with the earth at the centre, fitted the observations. The deciding issues were who had authority to interpret scripture after the Council of Trent, Pope Urban VIII's sense of betrayal, and Galileo's combative tactics; Kuhn's paradigm change (D40) was also a fight about authority. Then the historians. Draper and White wrote amid the 1870s battles over papal infallibility and Darwin. Brooke, Numbers and Harrison replaced their account, and Heilbron (1999) documented how heavily the Church funded astronomy. Stark and Hannam push on to a pro-Christian thesis that critics such as Noah Efron reject. Coyne's argument is philosophical, not historical.

story.title: A kneeling astronomer at Santa Maria sopra Minerva
story.hook: On 22 June 1633, in the Dominican convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, Galileo Galilei, 69 years old, knelt before the cardinals of the Holy Office. He read a formula abjuring the opinion that the sun stands still at the centre of the world and that the earth moves. He was sentenced to imprisonment at the Inquisition's pleasure, soon commuted to house arrest, served from late 1633 at his villa at Arcetri near Florence, and his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632) was banned. The story that he muttered 'Eppur si muove' ('and yet it moves') first appears in print in 1757. Twenty-two years before the trial, in 1611, the Jesuit astronomers of the Collegio Romano had confirmed his telescope discoveries and honoured him at a gathering in Rome.
story.puzzle: If science and religion were at war, why were the Church's own astronomers among the first to confirm Galileo's discoveries? And why did the Church condemn him anyway?
story.payoff: Because the affair was not a timeless war between faith and reason. It turned on who had authority to interpret scripture after the Council of Trent, on a pope who felt mocked in the Dialogue, on Galileo's tactics, and on evidence that was not yet decisive. The complexity thesis explains both facts. It does not excuse the verdict, which was the coercion of a scholar.
sources: Maurice A. Finocchiaro (ed.), The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989)
Ronald L. Numbers (ed.), Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion (Harvard, 2009)
J. L. Heilbron, The Sun in the Church (1999)

days.application: The Merton thesis. In 'Science, Technology and Society in Seventeenth-Century England' (Osiris, 1938), the sociologist Robert K. Merton argued that Puritan values — glorifying God through useful work and the study of creation — helped drive English science, and he noted how many Puritans were among the early members of the Royal Society. Critics reply that many founders were Anglicans and royalists and that 'Puritan' is hard to define. The thesis is still argued: a careful pro-religion hypothesis that remains unsettled.

builds_on.why: The conflict thesis is Whig history, reading the past as a march toward the present's victors, and its stock stories, the flat earth among them, are the myths D185 taught you to test.
Kuhn's account of paradigm change — rival frameworks, unresolved anomalies, a fight over authority as well as evidence — fits the Copernican dispute better than a story of reason against faith.

across.link: James Bradley's discovery of the aberration of starlight (1729) and Friedrich Bessel's measurement of the parallax of the star 61 Cygni (1838), about a third of an arcsecond, supplied the direct evidence of the earth's motion that Galileo did not have in 1633.

days.apply_question: In the 1920s and 1930s the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître proposed that the universe is expanding from a 'primeval atom'. In 1951 Pope Pius XII praised the idea as consonant with creation, and Lemaître is reported to have urged that it not be used that way. Which facts of Lemaître's story would a conflict historian, a complexity historian and a Stark-style historian each be tempted to leave out?
days.evidence_note: Settled among historians of science: the Draper-White conflict thesis fails as a general history; Galileo was tried and abjured in 1633; 'eppur si muove' is legend. Debated: whether Christianity positively caused modern science (Stark 2003, Hannam 2009 and subtler versions in Harrison, against Efron and others); the Merton thesis; whether science and religion are philosophically compatible (Coyne 2015 against, for example, Plantinga's Where the Conflict Really Lies, 2011), which is a philosophical question for D282, not a historical one. Value judgment: what the Church owed Galileo, and whether John Paul II's 1992 acknowledgement of error settled it.

resource.title: 'Myth 8: That Galileo Was Imprisoned and Tortured for Advocating Copernicanism', in Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion
resource.creator: Maurice A. Finocchiaro; Ronald L. Numbers, ed. (Harvard University Press, 2009)
resource.why: The leading documentary historian of the Galileo affair separates what happened from what the myth says, in a volume that also takes apart pro-Christian myths. The complexity thesis, demonstrated on one case.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search (the session's shared search budget ran out for the planner and for this verifier). The verifier's own knowledge places Finocchiaro's Galileo essay as Myth 8, between Myth 7 (Bruno) and Myth 9 (Efron on Christianity and the birth of science); confirm on the contents page.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: Systems Case
days.headline_hint: Gutenberg Borrowed 1,600 Guilders and Lost the Lawsuit. His Machine Remade Europe Anyway.
days.concept: The case's one question: did printing cause the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution, or only make them possible? And what evidence could tell the difference?
days.focus: Walk the press around Logan's chain as a loop, not a pipeline: needs (universities, churches, merchants); invention as combination; the materials and engineering of type; Fust's financing; adoption on an S-curve; consequences for religion and knowledge, measured by natural experiments; regulation that followed adoption; and feedback. Two pieces of feedback stand out: printed indulgences funded the Church before printed tracts attacked it, and in the Ottoman Empire the rulers' dependence on religious legitimacy delayed adoption. The verdict to teach: printing was an enabling condition with measurable causal force, not a sufficient cause. East Asian movable type shows that the machine alone did not remake a society.
key_concepts: movable type and the hand mould
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, cheap books: more presses → cheaper books → more readers and schools → more demand → more presses. R2, the pamphlet war: controversy sold, so printers sought it out, which spread the controversy further (Luther became the best-selling author of his age). B1, control: heretical print → licensing decrees and the Roman Index of Prohibited Books (1559) → printers self-censored or moved to friendlier cities. Reversals: the press served the Church (printed indulgences, 1454-55) before it served the Church's critics, and regulation and copyright (1710) came after adoption, not before. Unintended: the witch-hunters' manual Malleus Maleficarum (1486-87) spread through many printed editions.

story.title: A notary's record in a Mainz refectory
story.hook: On 6 November 1455, in the refectory of the Franciscan friary in Mainz, the notary Ulrich Helmasperger recorded the end of a lawsuit. The merchant Johann Fust had lent Johann Gutenberg 800 guilders around 1450 and another 800 around 1452 for 'the work of the books'. With interest, Fust claimed about 2,026 guilders. Gutenberg sent representatives instead of coming himself, and Fust swore an oath about the interest he had paid to borrow the money he lent. The ruling went largely Fust's way, and he appears to have taken over much of the printing equipment. Peter Schöffer — Gutenberg's skilled assistant, a witness that day, and later Fust's son-in-law — worked with Fust to print the Mainz Psalter in August 1457, the first book with a printed date and the printers' names. Gutenberg's great Bible had just been finished: about 180 copies, of which some 49 survive. He died in 1468 without a fortune.
story.puzzle: Within fifty years presses were working in more than 250 European towns. Within seventy, printed controversy had split Western Christianity; within ninety, printed books were carrying Copernicus's astronomy and Vesalius's anatomy (both 1543) across Europe. Did the press cause those revolutions, or only make them possible?
story.payoff: The chain shows a loop, not a push. Printing answered demand that already existed, spread fastest where trade and literacy were strongest, and was turned to whatever purposes its users had: indulgences first, then the Reformation's pamphlets, then science. Natural experiments show it had real causal force, since printing towns grew faster and turned Protestant more often. But Korea's and China's movable type show it was not sufficient. 'Made possible, then amplified' is the answer the evidence supports.
sources: Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, 6 November 1455 (Göttingen State and University Library)
Elizabeth Eisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
Adrian Johns, The Nature of the Book (1998)
Jeremiah Dittmar, Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(3) (2011)
Jared Rubin, Review of Economics and Statistics 96(2) (2014)

days.application: Venice. By 1500 the city was Europe's largest printing centre, with scores of firms competing for an international market. In 1501 Aldus Manutius's press introduced italic type and small, portable octavo editions of the classics. This is the production link at its most commercial: competition drove design forward and prices down.

builds_on.why: The Reformation's spread is the main consequence this case asks the press to explain.
The Eisenstein-Johns dispute is a source-criticism argument about what early printed books could be trusted to carry.
Dittmar's and Rubin's estimates use distance from Mainz as a natural experiment, the only way to move from correlation to cause here.
Type cast to one gauge in the hand mould is the interchangeable-parts principle that makes the machine work.

across.link: Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities (1983) argues that 'print capitalism' — printers selling in vernacular languages to widen their markets — created reading publics who imagined themselves as one nation. It is a proposed long-run consequence of the press, and History II meets it again with nationalism (D228).

days.apply_question: In 1377 Buddhist monks at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, Korea, printed the Jikji with movable metal type, decades before Gutenberg, and Bi Sheng had made movable ceramic type in China around the 1040s. Neither made movable type the main way of making books, as it became in Europe. Which links of today's chain — physical constraints, financing and markets, or regulation — best explain the difference?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the 1455 lawsuit; the spread of presses to more than 250 towns by 1500; the statistical associations between early printing and later urban growth and Protestant adoption. Debated: how to read those associations (Dittmar 2011 and Rubin 2014 use natural experiments, with the usual doubts about instruments); Eisenstein against Johns on whether print fixed knowledge; why the Ottoman Empire delayed printing in Arabic script (legitimacy, scribes' interests, the script itself); whether print was a cause or an amplifier. Value judgment: who gained (readers, reformers, printers, states), who paid (Gutenberg himself, scribes, the victims of printed witch-hunting manuals and of confessional wars), and who consented. A consequentialist tally, Catholic and Protestant readings of the Reformation, and Mill's defence of free expression against the Church's case for protecting souls weigh these differently. A Europe without print is an unknowable counterfactual.

chain.point: Demand existed before the machine. Universities (D192) needed standard texts, the Church needed liturgical books and indulgence forms, and merchants and lawyers needed documents. Paper, brought west through the Islamic world (D191), had already made a cheap writing surface, while a scribe might take months over a single book.

Gutenberg's press was a combination of existing parts: the screw press of wine and oil makers, oil-based ink, paper, a type metal and, his key contribution, the adjustable hand mould for casting type. Innovation as recombination, not a lone leap (D35).

Type metal had to melt at a low temperature, flow into fine moulds and wear well. Lead alloyed with tin and antimony became the standard (Gutenberg's own recipe is not known), an alloy whose properties are set by its bonding (D68). Paper beat parchment on cost: by a common estimate, a vellum copy of the Bible needed the skins of about 170 calves.

Movable type was an early system of interchangeable parts. Every piece of type was cast in the hand mould to the same height and body, so any letter fitted any line: the tolerances and gauges of D96, three and a half centuries before the armories.

chain.field: Finance (named at CFA level; no lesson teaches it)
chain.point: Debt, not equity, financed the Bible: Fust's two interest-bearing loans of 800 guilders, secured on the equipment. After the 1455 lawsuit much of the collateral appears to have passed to the lender, who then ran the business with Gutenberg's foreman. Early printing was hungry for capital, and many printers failed.

An S-curve (D7): from Mainz around 1455 to presses in more than 250 towns by 1500, with roughly 28,000-30,000 known editions printed before 1501 (the incunabula). The press spread first along trade routes and to commercial cities, and Venice became the largest centre.

The Reformation's pamphlet war (D197): Luther's writings dominated German printing in the early 1520s. Using distance from Mainz as a natural experiment (D21), Rubin (2014) found that towns with a press by 1500 were markedly more likely to have turned Protestant by 1530, by his estimates tens of percentage points more likely.

Eisenstein (1979) argued that print fixed and standardized texts and so made cumulative science possible. Johns (1998) answered that early print was unreliable and pirated, so trust in printed knowledge had to be built. Theirs is a source-criticism dispute (D185) about the Scientific Revolution (D199). Separately, Dittmar (2011) found that towns adopting print by 1500 had no earlier growth advantage but grew substantially faster than similar towns between 1500 and 1600.

Print spread error and cruelty as well as knowledge: the witch-hunting manual Malleus Maleficarum (1486-87) ran through many editions. How media effects and misinformation work is the Sociology block's subject (D214).

The rules followed adoption. Church licensing decrees and the Roman Index of Prohibited Books (1559) tried to control content, and England's Statute of Anne (1710) created the first statutory copyright, vested in authors for 14 years, renewable once. The Law block teaches how such rules work (D256, intellectual property).

The loop ran both ways. The press first served the Church — printed indulgence forms appeared in Mainz in 1454-55 — before it served the Church's critics, and the authorities then answered with censorship. In the Ottoman Empire, Jewish printers worked in Istanbul from 1493, and Armenian (1567) and Greek (1627) presses followed, but printing in Arabic script waited until İbrahim Müteferrika's press, licensed in 1727. Coşgel, Miceli & Rubin (2012) argue that the rulers depended on religious authorities for legitimacy: the church-state bargain of D192 in another form.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Suicide Is the Most Private Act There Is. So Why Did Durkheim Find Each Country Producing Almost the Same Rate Year After Year?
days.concept: Some patterns - rates, norms, levels of integration - belong to the group rather than to any individual and constrain individuals from outside: Durkheim's social facts.
days.focus: Teaches the social fact as sociology's founding move: a group-level rate can be stable and explainable even when every single case is unpredictable. Angle: the same logic as emergence (D32), plus its trap - the ecological fallacy of reading individual motives off group rates.
days.model_or_equation: Durkheim's two axes as a 2x2: integration (too little = egoistic, too much = altruistic) and regulation (too little = anomic, too much = fatalistic); suicide rate rises at both extremes of each.

story.title: A Bordeaux professor counts the most private act there is
story.hook: In 1897 Emile Durkheim, a professor at Bordeaux in his late thirties, published Le Suicide, built on official statistics from across Europe that his nephew Marcel Mauss helped him organize. The tables showed something unsettling: each country's suicide rate barely moved from year to year, as if each society had a definite 'aptitude' for suicide, and Protestant states such as Prussia, Saxony and Denmark ran well above Catholic Spain, Portugal and Italy, with Jewish communities lower still. More than a century later Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann re-tested him with 452 Prussian counties (1816-21 and 1869-71): Protestant suicide rates were roughly three times Catholic rates, and the gap survived an instrument based on distance from Wittenberg.
story.puzzle: Every suicide is a private act with its own reasons - so how can the rate be so steady, and why should it track something as collective as which church a region attends?
story.payoff: The rate is a social fact: a property of how strongly a group binds and regulates its members, not the sum of private motives. Durkheim's answer was integration - Catholic communities bound people more tightly - and Becker and Woessmann's evidence favours that social-cohesion channel over a theological one, while van Poppel and Day (1996) warn that part of the old gap may reflect how deaths were recorded.
sources: Durkheim, Le Suicide (1897); Britannica on Mauss assisting with Le Suicide
Becker & Woessmann, 'Social Cohesion, Religious Beliefs, and the Effect of Protestantism on Suicide', Review of Economics and Statistics 100(3) 2018, 377-391
Warwick press release and VoxEU column 'Religion matters, in life and death' (roughly three times higher)
van Poppel & Day, American Sociological Review 1996

days.application: 'Deaths of despair': Case and Deaton (PNAS 2015) found all-cause mortality of white non-Hispanic Americans aged 45-54 rose from 1999 to 2013, driven by drug and alcohol poisonings, suicide and liver disease and concentrated among those with a high-school education or less; had the 1979-98 rate of decline continued, about half a million deaths would have been avoided. Their 2020 book, Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism, draws explicitly on Durkheim's account of suicide and anomie - a social-fact explanation of a mortality rate.

builds_on.why: Emergence: a macro pattern no individual chose, and the warning that you cannot read individual motives off aggregate outcomes - Durkheim's rate is the sociological version.
The Reformation: the spread of Protestantism outward from Wittenberg is the very variation Becker and Woessmann exploit.

across.link: Geoffrey Rose's 'Sick individuals and sick populations' (International Journal of Epidemiology, 1985) argues that the causes of a population's incidence rate differ from the causes of individual cases - the same rate-versus-case distinction Durkheim drew, now basic to public-health strategy.

days.apply_question: Japan's suicide rate has risen and fallen with economic crises and policy campaigns over recent decades; using the idea of a social fact, what group-level change would you look for first to explain a sustained shift in that rate, and what would it be a mistake to infer about any single person who died?
days.evidence_note: Settled: suicide rates differ stably across groups and places. Debated: how much of the historical Protestant-Catholic gap was real versus recording practice (van Poppel & Day 1996), and whether 'despair' or the opioid supply drives the post-1999 US midlife mortality rise (Case & Deaton against Ruhm and others).

resource.title: Emile Durkheim on Suicide & Society: Crash Course Sociology #5
resource.creator: CrashCourse (Nicole Sweeney), 2017
resource.why: A clear, fast walk through social facts, collective conscience and the four types of suicide, so the vocabulary is fixed before the lesson tests it against modern data.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Thirty-Five Women Vowed to End a Custom in Their Village. A Neighbouring Imam Said One Village Could Not Do It Alone - and Set Out on Foot.
days.concept: A social norm is a rule people follow because they expect others to follow it and to approve or sanction them, so it is self-enforcing - and it can collapse quickly when enough of the people whose expectations are linked move together.
days.focus: Teaches norms as interlocking expectations (Bicchieri; Mackie's convention account) rather than as private beliefs, which explains both their stubbornness and their sudden tipping (D28). Angle: why coordinated, public change works where individual persuasion fails - and the evidence that the convention model fits only part of the facts.
days.model_or_equation: Bicchieri's conditions: a person follows norm N if she expects most others in her reference network to follow N (empirical expectation) AND expects most of them to think she ought to (normative expectation); change one person's beliefs without changing these expectations and behaviour stays put.

story.title: A press conference in Malicounda Bambara
story.hook: On 31 July 1997, 35 women of Malicounda Bambara, a village in western Senegal, told about 20 Senegalese journalists and government officials that their village would stop cutting its daughters. They had reached the decision in a Tostan education class and had asked their imam, who told them the practice was not a religious obligation. Neighbouring villages were not on board, and the women faced criticism. Demba Diawara, imam and village leader of nearby Keur Simbara, saw the problem: his village married its daughters into a wide network of villages, and families feared an uncut girl would be unmarriageable. He spent months travelling, much of it on foot, to the villages of that network, and on 14 February 1998 representatives of about a dozen villages (some 8,000 people by one count) declared together at Diabougou.
story.puzzle: If the women of Malicounda had genuinely changed their minds, why was their declaration not enough - and why did Diawara insist the change had to be made by many villages at once?
story.payoff: Cutting was sustained by expectations in a marriage network, not only by private belief; a family that stopped alone paid the price while everyone else's expectations stayed the same. Mackie's 1996 convention account, modelled on how Chinese 'natural foot' societies ended footbinding by pledging not to bind daughters or marry sons to bound women, predicts exactly this: the intermarrying group must move together.
sources: Tostan, 'Celebrating the movement to abandon FGC in Senegal'
Malicounda Bambara and Demba Diawara pages (31 July 1997; Diabougou, 14 Feb 1998)
Mackie, 'Ending Footbinding and Infibulation: A Convention Account', American Sociological Review 61(6) 1996, 999-1017
Shell-Duncan et al., Social Science & Medicine 73(8) 2011

days.application: How drunk driving became shameful in the United States: MADD (founded 1980 by Candace Lightner after her daughter's death) changed laws and penalties, and from 1988 the Harvard Alcohol Project under Jay Winsten persuaded TV writers to show 'designated drivers' in more than 160 prime-time episodes (Cheers, L.A. Law) - modelling a new empirical expectation. Alcohol-related traffic deaths, above 23,000 a year in 1988, fell by more than a quarter over four years, though laws and enforcement changed at the same time, so the norm's own share is not separable.

builds_on.why: Thresholds and hysteresis: Granovetter's threshold model is the mechanism by which a norm tips once enough people move.
Game theory: a convention is a coordination equilibrium - the footbinding pledge works by moving a whole group to a new equilibrium at once.

across.link: Corruption as a norm equilibrium: Bo Rothstein (2011) argues honesty does not pay where everyone expects bribes, so escapes tend to be 'big bang' resets of expectations - the logic behind Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (1974), which the Government block examines on Day 246.

days.apply_question: Japanese law has long let fathers take extended parental leave, yet for years only a small share did, and survey research (Miyajima & Yamaguchi, Frontiers in Psychology 2017) found that men underestimated how much other men supported taking it; using the idea of a self-enforcing norm, why might a government campaign telling fathers they are entitled to leave change little, and what kind of coordinated, public change would have a better chance?
days.evidence_note: Debated: how well the social-convention account fits female genital cutting - Shell-Duncan et al. (2011), with 300 interviews and 1,220 surveyed women in Senegambia, found marriageability mattered mainly indirectly and proposed a peer convention among circumcised women instead; Tostan's figures on abandoning communities are the organization's own claims, and how fully public declarations change practice is contested. Value judgment: that the practice violates girls' bodily integrity is the position of WHO and most human-rights bodies, which practising communities have contested.

resource.creator: Cristina Bicchieri, Ryan Muldoon and Alessandro Sontuoso
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the opening sections; the full entry is longer
resource.why: The standard careful statement of what separates a norm from a custom or a convention, by the scholar whose expectations-based definition this lesson uses, including the game-theoretic view that links back to Day 14.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: A Top Journal Rejected It Outright. It Found That Close Friends Were Rarely the Ones Who Passed On the Job.
days.concept: Acquaintances (weak ties) are more likely than close friends to bridge separate social clusters, so they carry new information - which is why they matter disproportionately for finding jobs and spreading ideas.
days.focus: Teaches Granovetter's argument from network structure (triadic closure makes strong ties redundant; bridges are almost always weak) and its 2022 experimental test. Angle: an idea from a rejected paper, confirmed fifty years later by randomizing the networks of 20 million people - with the twist that the best ties were moderately weak, not the weakest.
days.model_or_equation: Triadic closure: if A has strong ties to B and to C, B and C are likely to be at least weakly tied (Granovetter's 'forbidden triad' rules out B and C as strangers); it follows that a bridge - the only path between two clusters - cannot be a strong tie.

story.title: Job changers in Newton, Massachusetts
story.hook: In the late 1960s Mark Granovetter, a Harvard PhD student, surveyed 282 professional, technical and managerial workers in Newton, Massachusetts, who had recently changed jobs, and interviewed 100 of them. Of those who found their job through a personal contact, only 16.7% saw that contact 'often'; 55.6% saw them 'occasionally' and 27.8% 'rarely'. His paper on what this meant was rejected by the American Sociological Review in 1969 without even an invitation to revise; a shortened version appeared in the American Journal of Sociology in May 1973 and became one of the most cited papers in social science.
story.puzzle: Close friends care more, know you better and want to help - so why did the decisive job leads come mostly from people the job-seekers hardly saw?
story.payoff: Close friends move in your own circle and know what you know; acquaintances sit in other clusters and are the bridges through which news of an opening reaches you. The value of a weak tie is structural - it is new information, not affection.
sources: Granovetter, 'The Strength of Weak Ties', American Journal of Sociology 78(6), 1973, 1360-1380
Granovetter, Getting a Job (1974)
economicsociology.org (2014) on the 1969 ASR rejection; Stanford News (2023) on citation counts

days.application: Rajkumar, Saint-Jacques, Bojinov, Brynjolfsson and Aral (Science, 15 Sep 2022) analysed LinkedIn experiments that randomly varied how many weak-tie suggestions 'People You May Know' showed to more than 20 million members over five years, during which 2 billion ties and 600,000 new jobs were created. Moderately weak ties (about ten mutual connections) did most for job mobility - an inverted U, not 'weaker is always better' - and the effect was strongest in digital industries. The study also drew criticism for experimenting on users without explicit consent.

builds_on.why: Networks: clusters, bridges and the small-world shortcut are exactly the structure Granovetter's argument rests on.
Randomized trials: the LinkedIn study converts a 50-year-old correlation into a causal test by randomizing exposure to weak ties.

across.link: Network science: Onnela and colleagues (PNAS 2007) studied a mobile-phone network of about 4.6 million users and found that deleting weak ties first shattered the network into islands, while deleting strong ties first did not - Granovetter's bridge claim confirmed in percolation terms.

days.apply_question: A hospital wants a new infection-control practice developed in its intensive-care unit to reach the surgical wards; using the strength of weak ties, whose relationships would you map and use to spread it, and why might relying on the ICU nurses' closest friends be slow?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the structural argument and the LinkedIn causal evidence for job mobility. Debated: how far the effect generalizes beyond online professional networks and digital industries, and the ethics of large platform experiments run without explicit consent.

resource.title: Networks, Crowds, and Markets, Chapter 3: Strong and Weak Ties
resource.creator: David Easley and Jon Kleinberg (Cambridge University Press, 2010; free draft on Cornell site)
resource.why: Draws the triadic-closure argument with diagrams and shows why a bridge must be weak, then tests tie strength on large-scale data - the formal version of the lesson's logic.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: In 1970 Italy Built Fifteen Regional Governments From One Blueprint. Twenty Years Later, Some Worked and Some Barely Did.
days.concept: Social capital - networks, norms of reciprocity and generalized trust - helps communities solve shared problems, but how to measure it and whether it is truly declining are debated.
days.focus: Teaches social capital as a community-level resource - networks, norms of reciprocity and generalized trust - with bonding and bridging forms, and trust as its most-measured trace. Angle: Putnam's Italian study, where identical institutions performed very differently, and his later 'Bowling Alone' decline thesis for the US, each alongside its critics - a concept whose importance is widely accepted while its measurement and history are contested.

story.title: Fifteen new governments, one blueprint
story.hook: On 7-8 June 1970 Italians elected the first councils of fifteen new regional governments, all set up under the same national framework with the same formal powers - Emilia-Romagna in the north on the same terms as Calabria in the south. Robert Putnam, then a young political scientist at the University of Michigan, began interviewing the new regional councillors that year and, with Robert Leonardi and Raffaella Nanetti, kept returning for about two decades. They scored the regions on twelve measures of performance, from cabinet stability and on-time budgets to how many day-care centres and family clinics they actually opened and how promptly their offices answered citizens' enquiries. The gap that emerged was stark: governments such as Emilia-Romagna's were efficient and innovative, while Calabria's lagged far behind.
story.puzzle: The institutions were the same on paper, so what made some of them work and others stall - and why did a region's wealth account for the difference less well than one might expect?
story.payoff: Putnam's answer, in Making Democracy Work (1993), was the 'civic community': regions dense with horizontal associations - choral societies, football clubs, cooperatives - and with high newspaper readership and referendum turnout had citizens who trusted one another, expected reciprocity and pressed government to perform. That stock of networks, norms and trust is social capital. He traced it to the medieval communal republics of the north, a historical claim critics such as Sidney Tarrow (1996) dispute; in 1995 he turned the same lens on the United States in 'Bowling Alone'.
sources: Putnam, with Leonardi & Nanetti, Making Democracy Work: Civic Traditions in Modern Italy (Princeton University Press, 1993)
Tarrow, 'Making Social Science Work Across Space and Time', American Political Science Review 90(2), 1996
Putnam, 'Bowling Alone: America's Declining Social Capital', Journal of Democracy 6(1), 1995, 65-78
Skocpol, Diminished Democracy (2003); Paxton, American Journal of Sociology 105(1), 1999

days.application: Congregations as social capital: in American Grace (2010) Putnam and David Campbell found regular churchgoers volunteer and give more, including to secular causes, and that the strongest predictor was having friends at church - belonging more than believing. Because people choose whether to attend, the link may partly reflect who joins (compare Day 168's self-selection caveat).

builds_on.why: Game theory: Putnam explains civic regions with the logic of repeated play - dense associations make reciprocity (TIT FOR TAT) the rational strategy.
Weak ties: bridging social capital is built from the cross-cutting acquaintances Granovetter studied, and Putnam's horizontal networks are made of them.

across.link: Kawachi, Kennedy, Lochner and Prothrow-Stith (American Journal of Public Health, 1997) found that across 39 US states, lower generalized trust and sparser group membership in the General Social Survey went with higher age-adjusted mortality - social capital as a population-health variable, though as a state-level correlation it carries Day 201's ecological-fallacy warning.

days.apply_question: Most German towns rely on volunteer fire brigades (Freiwillige Feuerwehren) that also run village festivals and youth groups; if a town replaced its brigade with a professional, tax-funded service that responded faster, what might it lose that does not show up in response times, and how could you tell whether it really was lost?
days.evidence_note: Debated: whether Italy's civic gap really has medieval roots and how much it explains (Putnam against Tarrow 1996 and historians of the South); whether US social capital declined (Putnam 1995, 2000 - his emblem: between 1980 and 1993 the number of bowlers rose about 10% while league bowling fell about 40%) or changed form toward professionally managed advocacy groups (Skocpol 2003) and informal or online ties. The GSS 'most people can be trusted' share has fallen from roughly 45% in the early 1970s to about a third or less in recent surveys, but trust measures are coarse. Settled: high-trust communities tend to cooperate more, though the direction of causation is hard to establish.

resource.why: The short essay in which Putnam carried the social-capital idea from his Italian study to the United States, with the bowling statistic and the evidence on falling membership as he first put it - worth reading in full before reading his critics.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Born Poor in Charlotte, a Child Had About a 4% Shot at the Top Fifth. In San Jose, About 13%.
days.concept: A child's chance of rising out of poverty varies sharply by place, and randomized evidence shows that moving to a better neighbourhood raises adult outcomes in proportion to how young the child was when the family moved.
days.focus: Teaches intergenerational mobility as a measurable rate that differs by place, and the step from geography-as-correlation to neighbourhood-as-cause through the Moving to Opportunity experiment. Angle: an experiment first judged a disappointment turned out to hold its biggest effect in the children too young to be measured.
days.model_or_equation: Rank-rank model: child's adult income percentile = a + b x parents' income percentile; b (about 0.34 nationally in Chetty et al. 2014) measures persistence, and the chance a bottom-fifth child reaches the top fifth summarizes upward mobility for a place.

story.title: The map that put Charlotte last
story.hook: In July 2013 Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Patrick Kline and Emmanuel Saez released mobility estimates built from anonymized tax records on more than 40 million children and their parents, with the core measures based on children born in 1980-82 (published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2014). For children whose parents were in the bottom fifth of incomes, the chance of reaching the top fifth as adults was about 4.4% if they grew up in the Charlotte area and about 12.9% around San Jose. Charlotte - a booming banking centre - ranked last of the 50 largest commuting zones, and local leaders responded by convening the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Opportunity Task Force, which reported in March 2017.
story.puzzle: Is the place doing it, or do different kinds of families simply live in Charlotte and San Jose - and how could anyone tell?
story.payoff: Geography alone cannot separate place from people; the Moving to Opportunity experiment, which randomly offered families vouchers to move, can. Its long-run data show that children who moved young gained the most, so a large part of the place effect is causal and works through years of childhood exposure.
sources: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez, 'Where is the Land of Opportunity?', Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(4), 2014
Chetty, Hendren & Katz, American Economic Review 106(4), 2016
Leading on Opportunity, Charlotte-Mecklenburg Opportunity Task Force report (2017)

days.application: Moving to Opportunity (HUD, 1994-98): about 4,600 low-income families in Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York were randomly offered vouchers to move to low-poverty neighbourhoods. Early evaluations found little effect on adults' earnings (better adult mental health and mixed results for youth); Chetty, Hendren and Katz (2016) followed the children and found those who moved before about age 13 earned roughly 31% more in their mid-20s and were more likely to attend college, while moving as a teenager brought no gain.

builds_on.why: Randomized trials: MTO's lottery is what separates a neighbourhood's causal effect from the kinds of families who live there.
Development and sensitive periods: the age gradient in MTO is an exposure effect consistent with childhood as a period when environments matter most.

across.link: Hills v. Gautreaux (US Supreme Court, 1976) led to Chicago's Gautreaux programme, which moved public-housing families to suburbs and whose striking but non-random results inspired Congress to fund the randomized MTO test.

days.apply_question: A city plans to spend the same budget either on vouchers that help families with teenagers move to low-poverty areas or on vouchers targeted at families with children under eight; using the MTO evidence, which would you expect to change adult earnings more, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: mobility varies widely by place, and MTO shows that moving young children to low-poverty areas raises adult outcomes. Debated: what about places causes it (segregation, school quality, family structure, social capital), whether results transfer to other cities and eras, and how to reconcile MTO's small adult effects with the children's gains. Value judgment: how much inequality of opportunity a society should tolerate, and whether to move people or invest in places.

resource.title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment
resource.creator: Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren and Lawrence F. Katz (American Economic Review 106(4), 2016)
resource.length: about 20 minutes for the introduction and main results
resource.why: Shows how the authors reopened an experiment judged disappointing and found the age-at-move pattern - a model of why the right outcome and subgroup matter.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before both the drafting and the verification pass reached this lesson, and reference sites cannot be fetched from this environment; citation from established bibliographic knowledge (American Economic Review 106(4), 2016, pp. 855-902). The routine should confirm before citing.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Same Résumé, Different Name: 'Emily' and 'Greg' Got About 50% More Callbacks Than 'Lakisha' and 'Jamal'.
days.concept: A group disparity is not by itself proof of discrimination; audit and correspondence experiments isolate discrimination by changing only one attribute and holding everything else equal.
days.focus: Teaches the measurement problem - disparity versus discrimination, omitted variables, the 'unexplained gap' - and the experimental fix. Angle: the cleanest designs answer a narrow question (callbacks), while the big historical questions, like redlining's long-run effects, force researchers back to harder causal inference.
days.model_or_equation: Correspondence-test estimate: discrimination = callback rate with name A - callback rate with name B, on otherwise identical randomly assigned résumés; e.g. 9.65% - 6.45% = 3.2 points, a ratio of about 1.5.

story.title: Five thousand résumés sent to Boston and Chicago
story.hook: From July 2001 to May 2002 economists Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan answered more than 1,300 help-wanted ads in the Boston Globe and Chicago Tribune with about 5,000 fictitious résumés. They randomly gave each résumé either a distinctively white name such as Emily Walsh or Greg Baker or a distinctively Black name such as Lakisha Washington or Jamal Jones. White-named résumés drew callbacks about 9.65% of the time, Black-named ones about 6.45% - roughly 50% more. A white name was worth about as much as eight extra years of experience, and better résumés helped white-named applicants more.
story.puzzle: Employment gaps between groups had been documented for decades, but every gap could be blamed on differences in schooling, experience or skills; what made this result so hard to explain away?
story.payoff: Because the résumés were identical except for the randomly assigned name, no difference in qualifications could explain the gap. The design isolates discrimination at one decision point - the callback - which is exactly what a raw disparity cannot do.
sources: Bertrand & Mullainathan, 'Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal?', American Economic Review 94(4), 2004, 991-1013
Quillian et al., PNAS 2017 (meta-analysis of field experiments since 1989)
Kline, Rose & Walters, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2022

days.application: Redlining: in the late 1930s the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded neighbourhoods in more than 200 cities, colouring many Black neighbourhoods red. Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder (AEJ: Economic Policy 2021) compared streets on either side of grade boundaries and found lower homeownership, house values and more segregation for decades on the worse side; Fishback and colleagues (NBER 2021) counter that HOLC lent heavily in red areas and that the maps largely recorded segregation that already existed. The causal step from a map to today's outcomes is where the dispute lives.

builds_on.why: Confounding: a raw gap mixes discrimination with every other difference between groups - the reason disparities alone do not settle the question.
Randomized trials: the correspondence study randomizes the name, the one attribute of interest.

across.link: Reuters reported in October 2018 that Amazon scrapped an experimental résumé-screening model after it learned to downgrade résumés containing the word 'women's' - discrimination absorbed from historical hiring data, the machine-learning version of the problem audit studies measure.

days.apply_question: A ride-hailing platform finds that drivers cancel more often on riders with certain kinds of names; what experiment, changing only one attribute, would show whether the names themselves cause the cancellations, and what would it still not tell you about the platform's overall fairness?
days.evidence_note: Settled: correspondence experiments repeatedly find callback gaps by race-signalling names; a meta-analysis (Quillian et al., PNAS 2017) found no decline in hiring discrimination against Black Americans since 1989. Debated: whether names also signal class (Fryer & Levitt on name choice), how much callback gaps translate into final hiring and wages (Heckman's critique of audit methods), and redlining's long-run causal effect (Aaronson et al. versus Fishback et al.).

resource.title: Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination
resource.creator: Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan (American Economic Review 94(4), 2004)
resource.length: about 20 minutes for the introduction, design and main table
resource.why: The design is the lesson: reading how the names were chosen and validated shows why the method is persuasive and where its limits are.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before both the drafting and the verification pass reached this lesson, and reference sites cannot be fetched from this environment; one of the most cited field experiments, cited from established bibliographic knowledge (American Economic Review 94(4), 2004, pp. 991-1013). days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: In 1968 a Leading Sociologist Predicted Believers Would Be 'Huddled Together' in Small Sects. Thirty Years Later He Took It Back.
days.concept: Secularization theory predicted that religion would decline as societies modernize; religious-market theorists reject it, Norris and Inglehart revise it around existential security, and Voas and Chaves argue that US decline now follows Europe's generational pattern.
days.focus: Teaches secularization as three different claims (Casanova: institutional differentiation, decline of belief and practice, privatization) and the evidence for each. Angle: a famous prophecy, its recantation, and data suggesting both the prophet and the recanter were partly right - a contested theory to be weighed, not a verdict.

story.title: A prophecy in the New York Times
story.hook: On 25 February 1968 the New York Times quoted the sociologist Peter Berger: by the 21st century, 'religious believers are likely to be found only in small sects, huddled together to resist a worldwide secular culture.' Berger was no village atheist - he was a Lutheran and the author of The Sacred Canopy (1967), a classic of secularization theory. Three decades later, editing The Desecularization of the World (1999), he wrote that the assumption that we live in a secularized world was false: most of the world was 'as furiously religious as it ever was'.
story.puzzle: Western Europe's churches emptied much as Berger predicted, yet religion boomed across Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia - so was secularization theory wrong, right, or right only somewhere?
story.payoff: 'Secularization' bundles separate claims. Institutional differentiation of church from state, school and science happened almost everywhere modern; decline in belief and practice happened where life became secure and spread by generations, not by individuals losing faith; privatization did not. Berger's 1968 forecast overgeneralized one pattern; his recantation over-corrected for places like Western Europe and, increasingly, the US.
sources: New York Times, 25 Feb 1968 (Berger quotation)
Berger (ed.), The Desecularization of the World (1999)
Voas & Chaves, 'Is the United States a Counterexample to the Secularization Thesis?', American Journal of Sociology 121(5), 2016
Norris & Inglehart, Sacred and Secular (2004); Stark & Finke, Acts of Faith (2000)

days.application: Pew Research Center's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study (released February 2025, about 37,000 adults): about 62% of US adults identify as Christian, down from 78% in 2007 and 71% in 2014, with about 29% religiously unaffiliated - and the Christian share roughly stable since about 2019. Whether that is a plateau or a pause depends on cohort replacement: each younger generation is less religious than the one before.

builds_on.why: Social facts: religious integration was Durkheim's own example of a group-level force, and religiosity rates are social facts that change by cohort.
The rise of Christianity: Stark's market-style explanation of early Christian growth is the same author's supply-side theory applied to today.

across.link: Charles Taylor's A Secular Age (2007) proposes a third sense of secularity - not fewer believers but a changed condition of belief, in which faith is one option among others - the philosophical side of the change these data measure; Philosophy II takes up faith and reason on Day 282.

days.apply_question: South Korea saw rapid Protestant growth during its industrialization and has since seen rising numbers of the religiously unaffiliated; which version of secularization theory - Berger's 1968 forecast, the religious-market view, or existential security - fits that sequence best, and what evidence would you need to choose between them?
days.evidence_note: Settled: church attendance and affiliation have fallen across Western Europe and, since the 1990s, in the US, and the fall follows birth cohorts. Debated: whether modernization causes decline (Norris & Inglehart; Bruce) or religious supply and regulation explain it (Stark & Finke), and whether global religiosity will rise through higher religious fertility. Value judgment: whether secularization is loss, liberation or neither - a question for Philosophy II, not this data.

resource.title: Is the United States a Counterexample to the Secularization Thesis?
resource.creator: David Voas and Mark Chaves (American Journal of Sociology 121(5), 2016, pp. 1517-1556)
resource.length: about 25 minutes for the introduction and cohort figures
resource.why: A secularization-theory account (its perspective named): the cohort charts show how generational replacement produces decline without anyone losing faith, the mechanism the lesson asks Logan to weigh against supply-side critics.
resource.verified_how: web search this session (an earlier pass of this build): citation confirmed (AJS 121(5): 1517-1556, March 2016, DOI 10.1086/684202) and an open-access copy indexed on DukeSpace, the repository of Duke University, where Chaves is on the faculty; not fetched.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Iran's Births Fell From More Than Six Per Woman to About Two in Roughly Fifteen Years - One of the Fastest Falls on Record.
days.concept: In the demographic transition, death rates fall first and birth rates follow, so population surges in between; why fertility falls - child survival, education, urbanization, contraception, changing norms - is weighted differently by different scholars.
days.focus: Teaches the four-stage transition model, total fertility rate and replacement level, and population momentum, then the contested causes of fertility decline. Angle: an Islamic republic produced one of history's fastest fertility falls, which embarrasses simple economic and secularization explanations alike.
days.model_or_equation: Population growth rate = crude birth rate - crude death rate (+ net migration); the transition opens a gap when deaths fall first and closes it when births follow. Replacement TFR is about 2.1 where child mortality is low, higher where it is high.

story.title: Iran's census shock
story.hook: After the 1979 revolution Iran's leaders encouraged large families, and the 1986 census counted about 49 million people growing at roughly 3.9% a year (a figure inflated by Afghan refugees), a pace that would double the population in under two decades. In 1988-89 the government reversed course, relaunching family planning through a network of rural 'health houses', premarital contraception classes and free contraceptives, with clerical endorsement. The total fertility rate, around 6.5-7 children per woman in the early-to-mid 1980s, fell to about 2 by around 2000.
story.puzzle: Iran was not rich, not secular and still largely rural in places - so how did its fertility fall in about fifteen years by as much as Western Europe's had fallen over several generations?
story.payoff: Most preconditions of the transition were already in place: child mortality had fallen, girls' schooling and literacy had surged, and couples wanted fewer, better-educated children; the programme supplied the means and the clerical blessing removed a normative barrier. The case shows that no single cause - income, secularization or contraception - suffices; they compound.
sources: Abbasi-Shavazi, McDonald & Hosseini-Chavoshi, The Fertility Transition in Iran: Revolution and Reproduction (Springer, 2009)
UN World Population Prospects (Iran TFR series)
Statistics Korea, 2023 and 2024 births data

days.application: South Korea's total fertility rate fell to 0.72 in 2023, the lowest of any country, before a small rise to about 0.75 in 2024 (the routine should check Statistics Korea's latest release). At that level each generation is roughly a third the size of its parents', so the working-age population shrinks while the over-65 share climbs - a population still being shaped by momentum from its earlier transition, with consequences for pensions, the military and regional towns.

builds_on.why: The mortality revolution: the transition's first stage is the collapse of child mortality that lesson explained.
Logistic growth: the transition's population curve and the fertility fall itself trace S-shapes, and Pearl and Reed's mistaken ceiling is a warning about projections.

across.link: The Matlab project in Bangladesh (from 1977, run by icddr,b) gave half a rural area intensive door-to-door family-planning services; fertility there fell well below the comparison area, evidence that access to contraception can lower fertility even before incomes rise.

days.apply_question: Nigeria's fertility remains around five children per woman while its child mortality has been falling; using the demographic transition, what would you expect to happen to its population growth and age structure over the next generation, and which single factor would you watch to judge how fast fertility will follow?
days.evidence_note: Settled: mortality decline precedes fertility decline in almost every transition, and below-replacement fertility produces ageing. Debated: the relative weight of economic incentives (Becker), child survival, female education, contraception access, and ideas spreading through culture and language (the Princeton European Fertility Project; Caldwell's wealth flows); whether pronatalist policy can raise fertility much. Value judgment: whether low fertility is a problem to fix or a choice to respect.

resource.title: Fertility Rate
resource.creator: Max Roser, Our World in Data
resource.why: Interactive long-run charts of fertility for every country, including how fast the fall happened in different places - the data behind the transition, with sources shown.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before both the drafting and the verification pass reached this lesson, and reference sites cannot be fetched from this environment; Our World in Data's long-standing fertility article is cited from established knowledge without a URL. days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: The First Immigrant Through Ellis Island Got a $10 Gold Coin. For Decades, Her Life Story Was Told Wrong.
days.concept: Assimilation is measured across generations - language, intermarriage, residence and earnings - and newly linked census records let researchers follow millions of immigrant families and their children over time.
days.focus: Teaches assimilation as a measurable, multi-generational process, the classic and segmented-assimilation models, and how record linkage changed the evidence. Angle: Annie Moore's misidentified life is a miniature of the measurement problem - and Abramitzky and Boustan's linked data answer it at scale.

story.title: Annie Moore, 1 January 1892
story.hook: On New Year's Day 1892 Annie Moore of County Cork, Ireland, about 17 (contemporary reports said 15), stepped off the steamship Nevada and became the first immigrant processed at the new Ellis Island station, with her younger brothers Anthony and Philip. Officials gave her a $10 gold coin. For decades she was believed to have gone west and died in Texas; in 2006 the genealogist Megan Smolenyak showed that woman was someone else. The real Annie Moore married, lived her life on Manhattan's Lower East Side, raised a large family in tenements and died in 1924, buried in Calvary Cemetery, Queens.
story.puzzle: If historians could lose track of the single most famous immigrant of the era, how could anyone know whether the millions who followed her - or their children - actually got ahead?
story.payoff: Single stories mislead in both directions; only following whole families across records answers the question. Linking millions of census entries by name, age and birthplace, Abramitzky and Boustan found that immigrants in the Age of Mass Migration climbed the occupational ladder at about the same pace as the US-born, so those who started behind largely stayed behind - but their children rose faster than the children of US-born parents who started at the same income rank - and the pattern holds for immigrants today.
sources: Ellis Island Foundation and National Park Service accounts of 1 Jan 1892
Smolenyak's 2006 identification (reported in the New York Times, Sept 2006)
Abramitzky & Boustan, Streets of Gold (PublicAffairs, 2022)
Abramitzky, Boustan & Eriksson, Journal of Political Economy 2014
Abramitzky, Boustan, Jacome & Perez, 'Intergenerational Mobility of Immigrants in the United States over Two Centuries', American Economic Review 111(2), 2021

days.application: Streets of Gold (2022): using linked historical censuses and modern tax records, Abramitzky and Boustan show that children of poor immigrants from almost every origin country, then and now, are more upwardly mobile than children of US-born parents at the same income rank, partly because immigrants settle where opportunity is and start below their skills; and that cultural markers such as English use, intermarriage and less 'foreign' baby names advance with time in the country.

builds_on.why: Mobility and opportunity: immigrants' children are measured with the same rank-based mobility tools and the same place effects.
Sampling: linked records are a sample of those who could be matched - who drops out of the linkage biases the answer.

across.link: The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed) capped arrivals with national-origin quotas of 2% of each nationality's count in the 1890 census, chosen to favour northern and western Europeans - a legal design premised on the claim that southern and eastern Europeans would not assimilate, which the linked-data evidence on their children's mobility does not support.

days.apply_question: Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers in 2015-16; using today's measures of assimilation, which outcomes would you track across the first and second generation to judge integration, and why would looking only at the arrivals' own earnings after five years mislead you?
days.evidence_note: Settled: immigrants' children in the US show strong upward mobility relative to children of the US-born at the same parental income. Debated: segmented assimilation (Portes & Zhou 1993) versus a broad mainstream model (Alba & Nee 2003); immigration's wage effects on natives (Card's Mariel study versus Borjas) belong to economics. Value judgment: how many and whom a country should admit.

resource.title: Streets of Gold: America's Untold Story of Immigrant Success
resource.creator: Ran Abramitzky and Leah Boustan (PublicAffairs, 2022)
resource.length: introduction and first chapter, about 30 minutes
resource.why: Explains, for general readers, how linked census records were built and what they show about immigrants' children then and now - the method behind the lesson's main claim.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: Robert Moses Built 627 Miles of Roads. A Writer With No Planning Degree Helped Stop the Expressway Through SoHo.
days.concept: Cities concentrate people so that ideas, jobs and services meet, producing more per head than smaller places - but density also brings costs, and planning can either kill or feed the street life that makes it work.
days.focus: Teaches agglomeration and Jacobs's account of how mixed use, short blocks, old buildings and concentration create safe, lively streets, then urban scaling as the quantitative version. Angle: a fight over one expressway as a test of two theories of what a city is.
key_concepts: mixed use and 'eyes on the street'
days.model_or_equation: Urban scaling law: Y = Y0 x N^beta, where N is city population. For wages, patents and GDP beta is about 1.1-1.3 (typically about 1.15: doubling N multiplies Y by about 2.2, roughly 11% more per head - popular accounts round this to '15%'); for road surface and petrol stations about 0.85 (sublinear: about 10% less per head); for household needs about 1 (Bettencourt et al. 2007).

story.title: The Lower Manhattan Expressway hearing, 1968
story.hook: Robert Moses, who built bridges, parkways and expressways across New York for four decades, wanted a ten-lane elevated Lower Manhattan Expressway along Broome Street, cutting through what is now SoHo and Little Italy; by common estimates it would have displaced roughly 2,000 families and 800 businesses. Jane Jacobs, a former Architectural Forum writer with no planning degree, had published The Death and Life of Great American Cities in 1961, arguing that busy, mixed sidewalks - 'eyes on the street' - made neighbourhoods safe and alive. At a state hearing in April 1968 she led protesters onto the stage, the stenographer's record was torn up, and she was arrested. Mayor John Lindsay's administration declared the expressway dead in 1969, and it was formally removed from the city map in 1971.
story.puzzle: Planners had the data on traffic and the authority; why did a neighbourhood of old lofts and walk-ups look like a slum to them and like a working organism to her - and who was right about what makes a city productive?
story.payoff: Jacobs saw the city as 'organized complexity': value comes from dense, diverse, overlapping use of the same streets, which an expressway would sever. Scaling research later measured what she described - per-head output rises with size and interaction - while the old lofts she defended became one of the most valuable districts in the city.
sources: Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (Random House, 1961)
Caro, The Power Broker (1974), on Moses's 627 miles of roads
Gratz, The Battle for Gotham (2010), on the April 1968 hearing
Bettencourt, Lobo, Helbing, Kuhnert & West, PNAS 104(17), 2007

days.application: Urban scaling: Bettencourt and colleagues (PNAS 2007) found that across hundreds of cities in several countries, wages, patents and GDP scale with population at exponents of about 1.1-1.3, so output per head rises with city size, while infrastructure scales at about 0.85, so bigger cities need less of it per head. Critics (Arcaute et al., Journal of the Royal Society Interface 2015) showed the exponents depend heavily on where city boundaries are drawn, and crime and disease also scale superlinearly - density's costs grow with its benefits.

builds_on.why: Scaling and power laws: urban scaling is a power law read as a straight line on a log-log plot, like Kleiber's law.
Emergence: Jacobs's 'sidewalk ballet' is order no planner designed, arising from many local choices.

across.link: Kleiber's law makes an animal's metabolic rate scale as mass to the 3/4 power - sublinear, so bigger organisms run slower per cell - whereas cities' socioeconomic output scales superlinearly; Geoffrey West uses the contrast to argue cities, unlike organisms, can speed up as they grow (a structural analogy that breaks because cities are not bounded bodies).

days.apply_question: Many US downtowns lost office workers after 2020 as remote work spread; using agglomeration and Jacobs's account of mixed use, what would you predict for the street life and safety of a downtown zoned almost entirely for offices, and what change in land use would most directly counter it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: larger, denser cities have higher average productivity and wages. Debated: how much is causal agglomeration versus sorting of skilled workers, how robust scaling exponents are to city definitions, and whether Jacobs's preservationism raised housing costs (Glaeser, Triumph of the City, 2011). Value judgment: whose interests planning should weigh - commuters, residents, future residents.

days.topic: Organizations and the normalization of deviance
days.headline_hint: The Night Before Challenger, an Engineer Was Told to 'Take Off Your Engineering Hat and Put On Your Management Hat.'
days.concept: Organizations can gradually redefine warning signs as acceptable when nothing bad happens, so that risky decisions feel normal from inside - Diane Vaughan's normalization of deviance.
days.focus: Teaches how a culture of production pressure, past success and incremental evidence can turn anomalies into accepted risk without anyone breaking rules - Vaughan's correction of the 'amoral managers' story. Angle: the same organization repeats the pattern seventeen years later with foam instead of O-rings.

story.title: The teleconference of 27 January 1986
story.hook: On the evening before Challenger's launch, engineers at Morton Thiokol in Utah, Roger Boisjoly and Arnie Thompson among them, argued on a teleconference with NASA that the shuttle should not fly below 53 degrees F, the coldest previous launch, after which they had found O-ring erosion and blow-by. An overnight freeze was forecast at Cape Canaveral. NASA managers pushed back; in an offline caucus, Thiokol senior vice president Jerald Mason told engineering vice president Robert Lund to 'take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat'. Thiokol reversed and recommended launch. At about 36 degrees F the next morning, 28 January, Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew.
story.puzzle: NASA had seen O-ring damage on many earlier flights and had written it up; why did intelligent, careful people keep accepting it - and was this simply managers overruling engineers for schedule?
story.payoff: Vaughan's archive work showed that each earlier anomaly had been analysed and formally judged an acceptable risk, so by 1986 erosion was 'normal' and the burden of proof had quietly flipped to those who wanted to stop. The decision was produced by an organizational culture following its own rules, not mainly by rule-breaking villains - which is why it recurred.
sources: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission, June 1986)
Vaughan, The Challenger Launch Decision (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Vol. 1 (August 2003), Chapter 8

days.application: Columbia, 2003: foam had struck the orbiter on many earlier launches and been reclassified from a safety issue to a maintenance 'turnaround' item. When a briefcase-sized piece hit Columbia's left wing on 16 January 2003, requests for imagery were not pursued; the shuttle broke up on re-entry on 1 February. The Columbia Accident Investigation Board, which consulted Vaughan, titled a chapter 'History as Cause' and found 'echoes of Challenger'.

builds_on.why: Normal accidents and high-reliability organizations: Vaughan's account is the organizational side of the Perrow-versus-HRO debate.
Values in science (inductive risk): the flipped burden of proof - 'prove it is unsafe' - is a choice about which error to risk.

across.link: The NTSB found that the crew of a Gulfstream IV that crashed on take-off at Bedford, Massachusetts, on 31 May 2014 (seven killed) had skipped complete flight-control checks on 98% of their previous 175 take-offs - a routine deviation that became normal until the night the gust lock was left on.

days.apply_question: A hospital ward has silenced or ignored its frequent false monitor alarms for months without harm; using the normalization of deviance, describe how this could end in a missed real alarm, and what organizational change - rather than telling nurses to try harder - would break the pattern.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the O-ring and foam histories and the Thiokol reversal are documented by two official inquiries. Debated: how much weight to give culture versus individual decisions and political pressure; some engineers and historians think Vaughan's account underplays managerial responsibility.

resource.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I, Chapter 8: History as Cause: Columbia and Challenger
resource.creator: Columbia Accident Investigation Board (NASA / US Government Printing Office, August 2003)
resource.why: An official inquiry, written with Vaughan's input, laying the two accidents side by side to show how the same organizational pattern produced both.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before both the drafting and the verification pass reached this lesson, and reference sites cannot be fetched from this environment; chapter title cited from established knowledge of the public report (the chapter discusses the normalization of deviance by name).
