days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Slavery and capitalism: did profit end the trade?
days.headline_hint: Parliament Voted 283 to 16 to Kill a Trade That Was Still Making Money. Was It Conscience or Capitalism?
days.concept: The slavery-and-capitalism debate: Eric Williams (1944) argued that Britain abolished the slave trade and slavery once they had become economically obsolete; Seymour Drescher (1977) showed that abolition came while the British slave system was still growing and profitable ('econocide'); and historians still dispute how central slavery was to industrial capitalism.
days.focus: Teaches the argument as a test of evidence. Williams makes two claims: that slavery's profits financed industrialization, and that economic decline caused abolition. Drescher's trade data put the British West Indies near their peak around 1800. The 'new history of capitalism' (Baptist 2014; Beckert 2014) faces economic historians' critiques (Olmstead & Rhode 2018; earlier, Engerman 1972 and O'Brien 1982 on profits too small to finance industrial investment). Logan should end able to say what each side claims and which data decide it.

story.title: 283 to 16, House of Commons, February 1807
story.hook: On 23 February 1807, after a long debate, the House of Commons voted 283 to 16 to give a second reading to the bill abolishing Britain's slave trade. In 1791, William Wilberforce's first motion for abolition had lost by 163 votes to 88. During the 1807 debate the Solicitor-General, Sir Samuel Romilly, contrasted Napoleon on his throne with Wilberforce returning home to his family, and the House rose to cheer while Wilberforce sat, head in hands, in tears. The act received royal assent on 25 March 1807. Britain had been the largest slave-carrying nation of the 18th century, more than three million Africans had been embarked on British ships over the history of the trade, and its Caribbean sugar colonies were among its most valuable possessions.
story.puzzle: If the trade was profitable and the planters' lobby powerful, why did the Commons vote 283 to 16 to destroy it? Was this conscience, or capitalism discarding a system it no longer needed?
story.payoff: Williams said the system was declining and capitalists no longer needed it. Drescher's trade figures show it was near its peak, so abolition destroyed value ('econocide') and needs a political and moral explanation: a mass petitioning movement, Quaker and evangelical conviction (Day 227), wartime politics and a shrewd 1806 measure that first cut the trade to foreign colonies. Today's dispute is narrower: not whether profit ended the trade, but how central slavery was to building industrial capitalism.
sources: Hansard, House of Commons debate on the Slave Trade Abolition Bill, 23 February 1807
Seymour Drescher, Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (1977; 2nd ed., UNC Press, 2010)
Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (UNC Press, 1944)
SlaveVoyages (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database)

days.application: Britain's Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 paid £20 million (commonly put at about 40% of annual government spending) to slave-owners, not to the enslaved, who were also bound to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' that ended only in 1838. University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database traces the compensation claims and where the money went, a link between slavery and British wealth that historians can follow pound by pound.

builds_on.why: The scale and mechanics of the Atlantic trade are the data Williams and Drescher argue over.
British abolitionism is often counted among the first modern social movements: mass petitions, boycotts and organized lobbying, the organization-and-openings model of that lesson.

across.link: Gregson v Gilbert (1783), the Zong case: the owners of a Liverpool slave ship, whose crew had thrown well over a hundred captive Africans overboard in 1781, sued their insurers for the lost 'cargo', and Lord Mansfield's court treated it as an insurance dispute. Slavery was written into the commercial law of marine insurance, a link between slavery and British capitalism that Granville Sharp and other abolitionists publicized.

days.apply_question: Brazil, the largest single destination of enslaved Africans, ended its slave imports in 1850 under British naval pressure and abolished slavery only in 1888, while its coffee economy was booming. Does Brazil's case fit Williams's decline thesis or Drescher's econocide better?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Britain's slave trade was large and profitable up to 1807, and the British Caribbean was not in steep economic decline when the trade was abolished; most economic historians now side with Drescher against Williams's decline claim. Debated: how much slavery contributed to British and American industrialization. Williams and the 'new history of capitalism' (Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told, 2014; Beckert, Empire of Cotton, 2014) say centrally. Olmstead & Rhode (Explorations in Economic History 2018) dispute Baptist's evidence, and many estimates (Engerman 1972; O'Brien 1982) find slave-trade profits too small to finance industrial investment by themselves. Value judgment: that compensation went to owners and not to the enslaved was unjust is a moral judgment, now widely shared.

resource.creator: Seymour Drescher (1977; 2nd ed., University of North Carolina Press, 2010)
resource.length: about 30-40 pages; skim the tables (about 30 minutes)
resource.why: The book that overturned the decline thesis, with the trade data laid out. It answers Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) directly, so read it knowing which claim it targets.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Abolition: Christian arguments on both sides
days.headline_hint: Nine of the Twelve Men Who Founded Britain's Abolition Society Were Quakers. Slavery's Defenders Quoted the Same Bible.
days.concept: Christian conviction powered much of the antislavery movement, and Christian argument also defended slavery from scripture. An honest history counts both as Christian, then asks what else moved abolition: the enslaved's own resistance, Enlightenment critics, and the interests and self-image of a rising class.
days.focus: Lays out the evidence on both sides. On one side, Quaker and evangelical organizing (Anstey 1975; Christopher Leslie Brown, Moral Capital, 2006, on antislavery as a way for Britons to recover moral standing after the American war). On the other, the proslavery biblical case in the American South (Noll 2006). Alongside both sit David Brion Davis's argument about interests and ideology, and the enslaved's own agency: Haiti (Day 225) and Jamaica's 1831-32 Baptist War led by the Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe. It names the No True Scotsman fallacy and shows how a historian defines 'Christian influence' before counting outcomes.

story.title: Twelve men in a Lombard Street print shop, 22 May 1787
story.hook: On 22 May 1787, twelve men met at 2 George Yard, Lombard Street, in the City of London, the premises of the Quaker printer and bookseller James Phillips, and formed the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. Nine were Quakers, members of a small sect that had already petitioned Parliament against the trade in 1783. The others included the veteran campaigner Granville Sharp and the young Anglican Thomas Clarkson, who would ride thousands of miles gathering evidence. That year the potter Josiah Wedgwood had his works produce a medallion of a kneeling, chained African under the words 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?', which Clarkson recalled being worn on bracelets and hairpins. Across the Atlantic, over the following decades, many Southern ministers would preach from the same Bible that slavery was sanctioned by God.
story.puzzle: If Christian conviction drove the founders, how could equally devout Christians defend slavery from the same scriptures, and which side, if either, was the 'real' Christianity?
story.payoff: Both sides were Christian in the historian's sense: both drew sincerely on Christian scripture and churches. The historical question is which readings, traditions and circumstances produced which side. Quaker discipline and evangelical revival supplied conviction and organization; a literalist reading inside a slave society supplied the defence (Noll); and interests, self-image (Davis, Brown) and the resistance of the enslaved shaped when either side won. Whether antislavery was the truer reading of Christianity is a legitimate theological and moral judgment, but not one that historical counting can settle.
sources: Thomas Clarkson, The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade (1808)
Adam Hochschild, Bury the Chains (Houghton Mifflin, 2005)
Mark A. Noll, The Civil War as a Theological Crisis (UNC Press, 2006)

days.application: Frederick Douglass's Narrative (1845) ends with an appendix that distinguishes the slaveholding 'Christianity of this land', which he condemns, from 'the Christianity of Christ', which he embraces. It is an enslaved man's own theological answer to the No True Scotsman problem, and a test of how a historian should classify it: as a Christian argument about which reading is faithful, not as evidence that slaveholders were not Christians.

builds_on.why: Drescher's econocide leaves a political and moral explanation to be found, and this lesson examines its religious part.
Motivated reasoning: readers in a slave society found in scripture what their interests needed, and the same mechanism can operate on any side.

across.link: Antony Flew named the 'No True Scotsman' move in Thinking About Thinking (1975): rescuing a generalization by redefining the group to exclude counterexamples. Crediting Christianity with Wilberforce while declaring proslavery Christians not really Christian is that move, a hidden-premise problem of the kind Day 37 taught.

days.apply_question: In the US civil-rights movement of the 1950s-60s, Black churches and ministers such as Martin Luther King Jr. led the campaign, while many white Southern churches defended segregation, some from scripture. How would you define 'Christian influence' in advance so that you could fairly measure religion's net role in that movement?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Quakers and evangelicals were heavily over-represented among British and American abolitionists, and Christian ministers in the American South produced an extensive biblical defence of slavery (Noll 2006). Debated: how much religion caused abolition compared with economic change (Williams), the interests and self-image of a rising class (Davis, The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution, 1975), the politics of moral capital (Brown 2006) and resistance by the enslaved; Anstey (1975) gives religion the leading role. Value judgment: whether antislavery was the faithful reading of Christianity is a theological claim, while that slavery was a grave wrong is a near-universal moral judgment.

resource.title: The Civil War as a Theological Crisis, the chapter 'The Crisis over the Bible'
resource.creator: Mark A. Noll (University of North Carolina Press, 2006)
resource.why: Noll, a leading evangelical historian, shows how proslavery and antislavery Americans argued from the same Bible and why a literal reading favoured slavery's defenders. It is the strongest short treatment of the side of the story that Christian accounts often leave out.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Italy Became a Country in 1861. By One Famous Estimate, Only About 2.5% of Its People Spoke Italian.
days.concept: Nations are in large part modern constructions, built in the 19th and 20th centuries by states, schools, print, railways, conscript armies and mass politics, though 'ethnosymbolists' argue they rest on older ethnic ties, myths and memories.
days.focus: Contrasts the modernist account with its critics. Gellner (1983) argued that industrial society needs a standardized literate culture, so states make nations; Anderson (1983) described 'imagined communities' created by print capitalism; and Hobsbawm & Ranger (1983) wrote of invented traditions. Against them stand Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism and Adrian Hastings's emphasis on vernacular Bibles. The lesson separates nation from state and treats nationalism as the principle that the two should coincide, which drove unifications, secessions and, later, expulsions.
key_concepts: nation-building through schools, language and conscription

story.title: A kingdom proclaimed in Turin, 17 March 1861
story.hook: On 17 March 1861 the first parliament of a united Italy, meeting in Turin, proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia King of Italy. The new kingdom's people spoke Piedmontese, Venetian, Neapolitan, Sicilian, Sardinian and many other tongues. By the linguist Tullio De Mauro's famous estimate, only about 2.5% spoke the Tuscan-based literary language that would become standard Italian; others, such as Arrigo Castellani, put it nearer 10%. The statesman Massimo d'Azeglio is credited with the line 'We have made Italy; now we must make Italians', though what he wrote in his memoirs (1867) was more rueful, and the polished slogan seems to have been coined later.
story.puzzle: If most 'Italians' could not understand one another's speech, in what sense was Italy a nation in 1861? Did the nation make the state, or the state make the nation?
story.payoff: On the modernist account, Italy in 1861 was a state in search of a nation. Schools, conscription, railways and newspapers, and later radio and television, made Italians, and standard Italian became most people's everyday speech only in the 20th century. Ethnosymbolists reply that the project worked because older shared materials (Dante's language, the memory of Rome, Catholic culture) gave it something to build on. Both agree that 1861 was a beginning, not an end.
sources: Tullio De Mauro, Storia linguistica dell'Italia unita (1963)
Massimo d'Azeglio, I miei ricordi (1867)
Christopher Duggan, The Force of Destiny: A History of Italy since 1796 (2007)

days.application: Eugen Weber's Peasants into Frenchmen (1976). A French government survey of 1863 found that millions of citizens, roughly a fifth of the population, did not speak French. Weber argued that roads, railways, compulsory primary schooling (the Ferry laws of 1881-82) and military service turned rural people into Frenchmen only between about 1870 and 1914. Critics have argued that he exaggerated rural isolation.

builds_on.why: Anderson's 'print capitalism': printing in vernacular languages created reading publics that could imagine themselves as one people.
The sovereign territorial state came first; nationalism later claimed that each state should match one nation.

across.link: Henri Tajfel's minimal-group experiments (Bristol, early 1970s): schoolboys divided by a trivial criterion, such as preferring Klee or Kandinsky, favoured their own group when allocating rewards. In-group loyalty needs very little to start, and nation-builders can amplify it. The analogy breaks because nations add institutions, memories and stakes that no laboratory group has.

days.apply_question: After independence, India kept English alongside Hindi for official purposes and in 1956 redrew its states along linguistic lines rather than imposing one national language. Using the modernist account of nation-building, explain why that choice might have strengthened rather than weakened Indian national identity.
days.evidence_note: Settled: most European national languages became the everyday speech of most citizens only in the 19th and 20th centuries, through schooling, conscription and media. Debated: whether nations are essentially modern inventions (Gellner, Anderson, Hobsbawm) or modern forms of older ethnic communities (Anthony D. Smith; Adrian Hastings, The Construction of Nationhood, 1997, who gives vernacular Bibles and Christianity a central role, especially in England); and whether Weber overstated rural isolation. Value judgment: whether nationalism has been, on balance, a force for self-government or for exclusion and war is a moral-political judgment.

resource.title: Imagined Communities, chapter 3, 'The Origins of National Consciousness'
resource.creator: Benedict Anderson (Verso, 1983; revised edition 1991)
resource.why: Anderson's short, famous argument that print in vernacular languages created communities of readers who could imagine themselves a nation. It is the modernist case, which Smith and Hastings dispute.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: A Missionary Photographed a Father Looking at His Daughter's Severed Hand and Foot. A Century Later, Economists Still Find the Rubber Regime in the Data.
days.concept: Colonial rule was often built to extract labour and resources, and economists find that some of its institutions left measurable marks on outcomes today. But persistence findings vary in robustness and must be tested as hard as any other result.
days.focus: Teaches the mechanics of extraction (concessions, forced labour, quotas enforced by violence) and how persistence studies work: comparing places inside and outside a colonial institution's boundary (Dell's 2010 study of Peru's mita; Lowes & Montero on Congo's rubber concessions). It then teaches the critiques (Albouy 2012 on settler-mortality data; Kelly 2019 on spatial noise inflating persistence results) and applies one evidence standard to findings that flatter Christianity, such as Woodberry's missionaries, and to those that indict empire.

story.title: A photograph on a mission veranda, Baringa, May 1904
story.hook: In May 1904, at the Congo Balolo Mission station at Baringa in King Leopold II's Congo Free State, a man named Nsala of Wala came to the missionaries carrying a small bundle: the severed hand and foot of his five-year-old daughter, Boali. He said she had been killed by sentries of the Anglo-Belgian India Rubber Company when his village fell short of its rubber quota. Alice Seeley Harris, an English Baptist missionary, photographed him sitting on the veranda, looking at what remained of his child. Her photographs, shown at many lantern-slide meetings in Britain and America, joined the British consul Roger Casement's report (published in February 1904) and E. D. Morel's Congo Reform Association in a campaign that helped force Leopold to hand the territory to the Belgian state in 1908.
story.puzzle: The Congo Free State ended in 1908. Can a regime that lasted barely two decades still shape how people live in the same villages more than a century later, and how would anyone know?
story.payoff: Persistence studies compare places inside and outside the old rubber concessions. Lowes & Montero (Quarterly Journal of Economics 2021) report lower education, wealth and health today inside the former concession areas, and link the gap partly to the way the concessions ruled through coercive local chiefs. Results like this show how extractive institutions can outlive their makers. Each one must also survive re-analysis, because data choices, borders and spatial noise can manufacture effects, as Albouy and Kelly have shown for other famous findings.
sources: Roger Casement's consular report on the Upper Congo, published as a British parliamentary paper, February 1904
Anti-Slavery International archive: Alice Seeley Harris photographs
Adam Hochschild, King Leopold's Ghost (Houghton Mifflin, 1998)
Sara Lowes & Eduardo Montero, 'Concessions, Violence, and Indirect Rule: Evidence from the Congo Free State', Quarterly Journal of Economics (2021)

days.application: Robert Woodberry's 'The Missionary Roots of Liberal Democracy' (American Political Science Review, 2012) found that places with more historic Protestant missionary activity are more democratic today, a result many Christians welcomed. Nikolova & Polansky's re-analysis (British Journal of Political Science, 2021) argued that the effect is not robust to alternative data and specifications. That is the same scrutiny Albouy (American Economic Review, 2012) applied to the colonial-origins evidence for institutions, now applied to a flattering result.

builds_on.why: Colonial extraction is the purest case of extractive institutions, and colonial origins are the main evidence for Acemoglu and Robinson's thesis.
Replication and re-analysis: persistence findings, flattering or damning, stand only if they survive independent re-analysis.

across.link: Lowes & Montero, 'The Legacy of Colonial Medicine in Central Africa' (American Economic Review, 2021): French colonial campaigns against sleeping sickness (1921-56), which forcibly examined and injected millions of people, are associated with lower trust in medicine and lower vaccination uptake today. An empire's legacy can run through public health (Days 141-145).

days.apply_question: Melissa Dell found that Peruvian districts just inside the boundary of the mita, a colonial forced-labour draft for the Potosí silver mines abolished in 1812, are poorer today than districts just outside it. What alternative explanation would you have to rule out before accepting that the mita itself caused the gap?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Congo Free State's rubber regime used forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation, documented by Casement, missionaries and others, and many colonial regimes were designed for extraction. Debated: the Congo death toll (estimates vary widely, and the frequently cited figure of about ten million is contested); and how much colonial institutions explain development today. Strong persistence findings (Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson 2001; Nunn 2008; Dell 2010) face robustness critiques (Albouy 2012; Kelly 2019), and Woodberry (2012) faces Nikolova & Polansky (2021). Value judgment: the atrocities were grave wrongs, a near-universal judgment, while whether particular empires did net good or harm depends on counterfactuals no one can observe.

resource.title: King Leopold's Ghost: A Story of Greed, Terror, and Heroism in Colonial Africa (the chapter on Roger Casement's 1903 journey up the Congo)
resource.creator: Adam Hochschild (Houghton Mifflin, 1998)
resource.why: A gripping, well-documented narrative of how the rubber regime worked and how missionaries, Casement and Morel exposed it. Hochschild's death-toll estimate is disputed, so treat that figure as one estimate.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Britain Fired About 1.5 Million Shells to Clear the Way. On 1 July 1916, 19,240 of Its Soldiers Died Anyway.
days.concept: World War I was the first fully industrial war. Factories, railways and science multiplied firepower far faster than armies could move, so defence beat attack and victory went to whichever side could mobilize the most men, money, materials and science for longest: total war.
days.focus: Explains why firepower outran mobility: machine guns, quick-firing artillery and barbed wire against men on foot, and railways that moved defenders' reserves to a breach faster than attackers could exploit it, leaving attrition as the result. It then covers total war: conscription, state control of industry, women's munitions work, rationing and propaganda, plus science conscripted into gas, aircraft and tanks (first used at Flers-Courcelette on the Somme, 15 September 1916). Theories of why wars happen belong to International Relations; this lesson is the industrial history.
days.model_or_equation: Lanchester's square law (Frederick Lanchester, 1916): dA/dt = −b·B and dB/dt = −a·A, so a·A² − b·B² stays constant throughout a battle. Symbols: A and B are the two forces' sizes, and a and b are each side's effectiveness per unit (kills per unit time). Under aimed fire, fighting strength grows with the square of numbers times effectiveness, so in attrition, industrial output of men and guns, not élan, decides. The law ignores terrain and entrenchment, which is exactly where the Western Front broke it in the defender's favour.

story.title: Zero hour on the Somme, 7:30 a.m., 1 July 1916
story.hook: For about a week from 24 June 1916, British guns fired something like 1.5 million shells at the German lines north of the River Somme, on the assumption that the barbed wire would be cut and the defenders killed or stunned. At 7:30 a.m. on 1 July the whistles blew, and roughly 100,000 British soldiers climbed out of their trenches along a front of some fifteen miles, many walking forward under heavy loads. German machine-gunners, who had sheltered in deep dugouts, came up and opened fire, and in many places the wire was still intact. By nightfall the British Army had suffered 57,470 casualties, 19,240 of them killed, the worst day in its history.
story.puzzle: How could the heaviest bombardment the British Army had ever fired fail to clear the way, and why did generals on both sides keep attacking against defences like these for four years?
story.payoff: Industrial war had made defence far stronger than attack. Deep dugouts survived the shelling, a few machine guns could stop a battalion, and railways brought reserves to a threatened sector faster than infantry could walk across torn ground. With no decisive breakthrough possible, the war became attrition, a contest of whole economies in manpower, shells and science. Until combined arms, tanks and more accurate artillery restored some mobility in 1918, attacking was both the only way to win and the most costly way to fight.
sources: Sir James Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1916, vol. 1 (British Official History, 1932)
Martin Middlebrook, The First Day on the Somme (1971)
Imperial War Museums, 'The Battle of the Somme'

days.application: Fritz Haber's chlorine attack at Ypres on 22 April 1915. German troops released roughly 150-170 tonnes of chlorine from several thousand cylinders and opened a gap they lacked the reserves to exploit. Haber, who directed the gas programme, was the chemist whose ammonia synthesis (Day 86) gave Germany the nitrates for explosives once the blockade cut imports: science conscripted twice over. His wife, the chemist Clara Immerwahr, shot herself on 2 May 1915; how far his gas work drove her to it is debated.

builds_on.why: Haber-Bosch nitrates kept German explosives flowing despite the blockade, and Haber himself led gas warfare, the History link that the Haber-Bosch case previewed.
Lanchester's 1916 attrition model is a pair of coupled differential equations, rules for change of exactly the kind that lesson taught.

across.link: 'Shell shock': Charles Myers introduced the term in The Lancet in February 1915 to describe soldiers' breakdowns under bombardment. Industrial war created a mass psychiatric problem whose diagnosis and treatment were argued over for decades, a case of how diagnostic categories are built (Day 166).

days.apply_question: In the war in Ukraine since 2022, cheap drones, mines and artillery have made massed attacks very costly, and front lines have moved little for long periods. Using the firepower-versus-mobility logic of 1914-18, explain why the capacity to produce shells and drones has become as decisive as battlefield tactics.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the casualty figures for 1 July 1916 (British Official History) and the basic tactical problem of defensive firepower and rail-moved reserves outmatching attackers on foot. Debated: whether British commanders, Haig above all, learned and adapted (the 'learning curve' school: Gary Sheffield, William Philpott) or squandered lives ('lions led by donkeys'); and how much of the outcome came from attrition, blockade or the 1918 offensives. Value judgment: whether the war was worth its cost, and whether gas was uniquely wrong compared with shells, are moral judgments (Day 270 covers just war).

resource.creator: John Green, Crash Course (2012)
resource.why: A brisk overview of why the war started and why it became a static industrial slaughter. It is a survey, useful for context but not for the Somme's details.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Totalitarian rule and the Great Leap famine
days.headline_hint: China's Defence Minister Warned Mao in a Private Letter That the Harvest Numbers Were False. He Was Purged, and the Famine Got Worse.
days.concept: Totalitarian planning destroys the information it depends on. When officials are rewarded for meeting targets and punished for bad news, reports inflate, decisions rest on false numbers and errors compound into catastrophe, as in China's Great Leap famine of 1959-61.
days.focus: Walks the mechanism: Goodhart's law plus terror. Inflated grain reports set state procurement from fictional harvests; grain was taken and exported while villages starved; and punishing truth-tellers at Lushan removed the correction loop. This is set against Amartya Sen's claim that famines do not occur in functioning democracies with a free press, because bad news reaches voters and costs rulers, a strong regularity with debated edge cases.
days.model_or_equation: A broken control loop, described: reported harvest (inflated) → procurement quota → grain left in villages = true harvest − procurement → hunger and deaths. The correcting channel is honest reports of shortfall. When reporting a shortfall is punished, the controller acts on a false sensor and steers the system further off course, the failure mode of Day 92's feedback control with a corrupted measurement.

story.title: A private letter at Lushan, July 1959
story.hook: In July 1959 China's leaders gathered at the mountain resort of Lushan, in Jiangxi, to review the Great Leap Forward, the crash campaign launched in 1958 to overtake Britain in steel and multiply grain output through people's communes. On 14 July the defence minister, Marshal Peng Dehuai, a peasant's son and veteran of the Long March and Korea, sent Mao Zedong a private letter. It warned of exaggerated harvest figures, wasted backyard-furnace steel and 'petty-bourgeois fanaticism'. Mao circulated the letter and denounced Peng on 23 July, and at the plenum that followed Peng was condemned as leader of an 'anti-Party clique' and removed. A campaign against 'right opportunists' swept the country, and the famine, already under way, reached its worst in 1960; estimates of excess deaths for 1959-61 range from about 15 million to 45 million or more, with many scholars near 30 million.
story.puzzle: The leadership had been warned by one of its own marshals before the worst year. Why did the warning make things worse rather than better?
story.payoff: Punishing Peng taught every official that reporting shortfalls was dangerous, so provinces kept reporting inflated harvests. Procurement was set from those numbers, grain was taken from starving villages and exports continued. The leaders' information got worse just when they most needed it, because totalitarian rule had cut its own feedback loop.
sources: Yang Jisheng, Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine, 1958-1962 (English ed., 2012)
Frank Dikötter, Mao's Great Famine (2010)
Basil Ashton, Kenneth Hill, Alan Piazza & Robin Zeitz, 'Famine in China, 1958-61', Population and Development Review 10:4 (1984)
Roderick MacFarquhar, The Origins of the Cultural Revolution, vol. 2 (1983)

days.application: Stalin's suppression of the 1937 Soviet census. It counted about 162 million people, millions fewer than the leadership's public claims implied after the famine of 1932-33. The census was declared defective, its leading statisticians were arrested and several were shot, and its results stayed secret until the archives opened: a state destroying a measurement because it revealed famine deaths.

builds_on.why: Goodhart's law: once grain output became a political target, reported output stopped measuring the harvest.
Feedback control needs an honest sensor. Lushan corrupted the sensor, so the controller drove the system further from its goal.

across.link: Lysenkoism: at the August 1948 session of the Soviet Lenin Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Trofim Lysenko's rejection of genetics was endorsed with Stalin's approval, and geneticists lost their posts. Great Leap directives for 'close planting' and 'deep ploughing' drew partly on similar Soviet pseudo-agronomy (Jasper Becker, Hungry Ghosts, 1996). It was the same suppression of inconvenient evidence, applied to science itself.

days.apply_question: Sen points out that India, a poor democracy with a free press, averted famine in severe droughts such as Maharashtra's in 1970-73. Using today's concept, explain which feedback channel elections and a free press provided there that China's leadership lacked in 1959-60.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Great Leap famine of 1959-61 was among the deadliest in recorded history and was driven largely by policy (excessive procurement based on inflated reports, labour diverted to steel and irrigation, communal mess halls), not by weather alone. Debated: the death toll, about 15 to 45 million or more, depending on methods and baseline assumptions (Ashton et al. 1984; Yang 2012; Dikötter 2010); how much Mao knew and when; and the exact scope of Sen's democracy-famine claim, where critics point to edge cases in weak or partial democracies. Value judgment: assigning responsibility for the deaths is a moral judgment, though one the evidence strongly informs.

resource.creator: Amartya Sen, Journal of Democracy 10:3 (July 1999)
resource.why: Sen's own short statement of the argument that free elections and a free press prevent famine, drawing on the Chinese famine of 1958-61 and India's record. It argues for a thesis, so note where critics press its edge cases.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Holocaust: bureaucracy and ordinary people
days.headline_hint: Fifteen Officials Met at a Lakeside Villa for About Ninety Minutes. Their Minutes Listed 11 Million Jews.
days.concept: The Holocaust was organized through the ordinary machinery of a modern state (bureaucratic division of labour, paperwork, railways and coordination between agencies) and carried out by many ordinary people as well as committed ideologues; how much each factor explains is debated.
days.focus: Teaches Raul Hilberg's 'machinery of destruction' (definition, expropriation, concentration, annihilation) and the role of officials who never killed directly. Then Christopher Browning's Reserve Police Battalion 101, in which most men shot Jews though a minority refused without punishment, set against Daniel Goldhagen's 'eliminationist antisemitism' (1996), and Zygmunt Bauman's argument (1989, debated) that modern rationality made it possible. The application turns to Christian antisemitism and Christian responses on both sides; WWII campaign history is deliberately left out.
key_concepts: Christian anti-Judaism and the Church struggle

story.title: A lakeside villa in Berlin, 20 January 1942
story.hook: At midday on 20 January 1942, fifteen men met at a villa on the Wannsee lake in Berlin at the invitation of Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office. They included state secretaries and other senior officials from the interior, justice and foreign ministries, the Four-Year Plan, the Reich Chancellery and the occupied territories, along with Nazi Party and SS officers. The meeting lasted about ninety minutes. Adolf Eichmann's minutes, written in euphemism ('evacuation to the East'), listed some 11 million Jews of Europe country by country, including those in Britain, Ireland and neutral states. By then mobile killing units had already shot hundreds of thousands of Jews in the occupied Soviet Union and gassing had begun at Chełmno; only one of the thirty copies of the minutes survived, found in German Foreign Office files in 1947.
story.puzzle: If the killing had already begun, why did it need a meeting of civil servants? And how could a room of educated officials agree within ninety minutes, with no recorded objection to the goal, to coordinate the murder of a continent's Jews?
story.payoff: Genocide on this scale was a coordination problem across agencies: who counted as a Jew, what happened to property, trains, labour and jurisdiction. Wannsee settled that under Heydrich's authority. The participants were lawyers and administrators applying routine methods to an unprecedented goal, and their agreement reflects ideology, ambition and conformity, not ignorance. Bureaucracy did not cause the Holocaust, but it let the killing proceed at that speed and scale, and it divided the work so that many contributed without pulling a trigger.
sources: House of the Wannsee Conference, memorial and educational site, Berlin
Mark Roseman, The Villa, the Lake, the Meeting: Wannsee and the Final Solution (2002)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (1961; 3rd ed. 2003)
US Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia, entry on the Wannsee Conference

days.application: Christian responses on both sides. Centuries of Christian anti-Judaism, including Martin Luther's 1543 tract On the Jews and Their Lies, gave Nazi propaganda material to exploit, and the pro-Nazi 'German Christians' won church elections in 1933. Against them stood the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (May 1934), which defended the church's independence but did not speak for the Jews, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer, executed at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945. In the Protestant village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, pastors André Trocmé and Édouard Theis, Magda Trocmé and their neighbours sheltered several thousand refugees, many of them Jewish children; Yad Vashem honours the village as Righteous Among the Nations.

builds_on.why: Obedience and the power of situations: Milgram began his experiments in 1961, months after the Eichmann trial opened, and Browning draws on them, with their debated validity, to explain Battalion 101.
Conformity: Browning found that not wanting to break ranks with comrades kept many reservists shooting.

across.link: Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer, coined the word 'genocide' in Axis Rule in Occupied Europe (1944), and the UN adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on 9 December 1948. This turned the Holocaust's lessons into international law, which the Law and International Relations blocks cover.

days.apply_question: In the 1994 Rwandan genocide, identity cards recording each person's ethnicity, together with the state's local administrative structure, were used to identify and organize victims. Using today's concept, explain how such ordinary administrative tools could make mass killing faster and wider.
days.evidence_note: Settled: about six million Jews were murdered. The killing was organized by the German state with the participation of ministries, railways, police and many ordinary people, and the Wannsee minutes are authentic. Debated: the weight of ideology and antisemitism (Goldhagen 1996) against situational pressures (Browning 1992) in explaining perpetrators; Bauman's (1989) claim that modern bureaucratic rationality was itself a precondition; and how far Christian anti-Judaism prepared the ground for racial antisemitism, which historians distinguish from it while tracing the links. Value judgment: that the Holocaust was a supreme moral evil is a near-universal judgment, while judging the churches' failures and the rescuers' virtue is moral evaluation built on this record.

resource.why: Browning's concluding analysis of why most of about 500 middle-aged reservists became killers and a minority refused. It is the core evidence for the 'ordinary people' half of today's concept; later editions add an afterword answering Goldhagen.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Cold War: a contest of systems
days.headline_hint: 'No One Intends to Build a Wall,' East Germany's Leader Said in June 1961. Two Months Later One Went Up, to Keep His Own People In.
days.concept: The Cold War was a rivalry between two political-economic systems as well as two superpowers, and its divisions of Germany and Korea created rare natural experiments in what systems do to the same people.
days.focus: Covers what the rivalry was about (central planning and one-party rule against markets and pluralism; deterrence and alliances are left to International Relations) and how its natural experiments are read. East and West Germany and North and South Korea are the cases, with pre-existing differences and outside aid (the Marshall Plan, Soviet reparations) as confounders. It also covers the data problem: planned economies' statistics were unreliable, and Western estimates misjudged the Soviet economy.
key_concepts: contest of systems: planning versus markets

story.title: Barbed wire across Berlin, Sunday 13 August 1961
story.hook: On 15 June 1961, East Germany's leader Walter Ulbricht told a press conference: 'No one has the intention of building a wall.' In the early hours of Sunday 13 August, East German police and troops strung barbed wire and blocked streets along the 43-kilometre line between East and West Berlin, and concrete followed within days. Since 1949 roughly 2.7 million people had left East Germany for the West, many of them young and skilled and many through Berlin's open sector border, and that summer the flow had swollen to tens of thousands a month. On 22 August Ida Siekmann, a 58-year-old nurse whose building on Bernauer Strasse stood in the East while its pavement lay in the West, died after jumping from her window, the first of at least 140 people to die at the Wall. It stood until the night of 9 November 1989.
story.puzzle: Why would a state that called itself a workers' and peasants' state have to wall its own citizens in, and what did splitting one nation in two reveal about the two systems?
story.payoff: Germany's division was a natural experiment: one people, one language and comparable pre-war industry, assigned by the war's end to two systems. East Germans voted with their feet ('exit', in Albert Hirschman's terms) because the planned economy and one-party state offered less freedom and an increasingly lower standard of living, and the Wall was the system's admission that it could keep people no other way. The experiment is imperfect, because the East bore heavy reparations to the Soviet Union and received no Marshall aid, so careful comparisons adjust for that. Even so, the gap that opened was large.
sources: Berlin Wall Memorial (Stiftung Berliner Mauer), research on the victims of the Wall
Hope M. Harrison, Driving the Soviets up the Wall: Soviet-East German Relations, 1953-1961 (Princeton UP, 2003)
Frederick Taylor, The Berlin Wall: A World Divided, 1961-1989 (2006)

days.application: The Soviet collapse of 1991 and the data it exposed. In 1987 Vasily Selyunin and Grigory Khanin's article 'Lukavaya tsifra' ('The Cunning Figure', Novy Mir) argued that official Soviet growth statistics were greatly inflated. After 1991, archival work and new estimates led many economists to conclude that Western estimates, the CIA's included, had overstated the Soviet economy's size, though by how much is debated: a lesson in measuring a system that controls its own statistics.

builds_on.why: Divided Germany and Korea are the natural-experiment design of that lesson, applied to whole political-economic systems.
Apollo was a prestige project inside this contest of systems, and the Moon race was the Cold War's showcase.

across.link: Alesina & Fuchs-Schündeln, 'Good-Bye Lenin (or Not?)' (American Economic Review, 2007), used reunification as a natural experiment in values. After four decades of communism, East Germans were markedly more in favour of state provision than West Germans, and the authors estimated that convergence would take one to two generations: systems shape norms (Day 202).

days.apply_question: North and South Korea were divided in 1945, and today South Korea's income per head is many times the North's. Which pre-1945 or outside-aid difference between the two halves would you have to check before treating that gap as a clean measure of the effect of the two systems?
days.evidence_note: Settled: East and West Germany, and North and South Korea, diverged sharply in income and freedom after division, and Soviet-type economies' official statistics were unreliable. Debated: how much of each gap reflects the economic system rather than starting conditions, aid and geopolitics; how far Western intelligence overestimated the Soviet economy; and the Cold War's causes and responsibility (orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist historians). Value judgment: that walling in a population violates basic freedom is a widely shared moral judgment, while which system was 'better' depends on how one weighs freedom, security and equality.

resource.why: A fast overview of the Cold War as a global contest between two systems, including the proxy wars and decolonization that this lesson leaves to International Relations. It is a survey, not a natural-experiment analysis.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: The World Bank Moved Its Poverty Line, and 125 Million More People Counted as Extremely Poor. No One's Income Fell.
days.concept: Every measure of progress (GDP, poverty counts, the Human Development Index, life expectancy, capabilities, life satisfaction) embeds choices about what to count and where to set lines, so disputes about whether the world is getting better are often disputes about those choices.
days.focus: Shows how the international poverty line is built (the median of the poorest countries' national lines, converted with PPPs) and why updating it moved the count. It covers the HDI (UNDP 1990, Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen) and its built-in weights, Sen's capabilities approach and subjective well-being (Day 168). The Rosling-Pinker versus Hickel dispute is then read as partly a dispute over lines and baselines. Logan learns to ask of any progress claim: measured how, against which line, and chosen by whom?
days.model_or_equation: HDI = (I_health × I_education × I_income)^(1/3): the geometric mean of three dimension indices, each computed as I = (actual − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum), with income entered as a logarithm. Symbols: I_health from life expectancy at birth, I_education from mean and expected years of schooling, I_income from gross national income per head (PPP). Every minimum, maximum, the log on income and the equal weighting are choices someone made.

story.title: A line moved in Washington, June 2025
story.hook: In June 2025 the World Bank raised its international poverty line, the threshold behind the world's count of people in 'extreme poverty', from $2.15 a day in 2017 prices to $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing-power-parity prices. The reason was technical: new price comparisons across countries, and newer national poverty lines in the poorest countries, whose median sets the international line. The effect was not technical. By the Bank's own estimates, the update added roughly 125 million people to the global count of the extremely poor, though no one's income had fallen.
story.puzzle: If the number of extremely poor people can jump by more than a hundred million without anyone becoming poorer, what is a poverty count actually measuring, and can a figure like that settle whether the world is getting better?
story.payoff: A poverty count measures people below a line, and the line is a convention. It is chosen to reflect what the poorest countries themselves treat as poverty and converted with price indexes that get revised. The 2025 update did not change the world; it changed the ruler. The long-run fall in extreme poverty survives any reasonable line, but its size, and the number of people left behind, depend on where the line sits. That is why Rosling and Pinker and their critic Hickel can read the same data and tell different stories.
sources: World Bank, June 2025 update of the International Poverty Line (Poverty and Inequality Platform)
UNDP, Human Development Report 1990
Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen & Jean-Paul Fitoussi, Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress (2009)

days.application: The Preston curve (Day 145). Samuel Preston (Population Studies, 1975) showed that life expectancy rises steeply with income at low incomes and flattens at high ones, and that the whole curve shifted upward over the 20th century, so health improved even at a given income. Sullivan & Hickel (World Development, 2023) use real wages, human height and mortality since the 16th century to argue that extreme poverty was not the historical norm and worsened under colonial capitalism. That challenges the standard 'everyone was poor before 1800' story, and others, including Max Roser and Robert Allen's basic-needs work, contest it.

builds_on.why: Life expectancy is a period statistic, a definition rather than a lifespan, and the Preston curve built on it is a measurement choice like any other.
Well-being has several measures (life evaluation and moment-to-moment feelings) that move differently with income, the same lesson applied to progress.

across.link: Amartya Sen's capabilities approach (Commodities and Capabilities, 1985; Development as Freedom, 1999), extended in Martha Nussbaum's list of central capabilities (Women and Human Development, 2000), defines progress as expanding what people are able to do and be. It is a philosophical answer to 'progress toward what?' that the HDI tries to put into numbers; Philosophy II takes up the idea of progress itself.

days.apply_question: The OECD's Better Life Index lets each user set their own weights across eleven dimensions, from income and housing to life satisfaction and work-life balance, and re-ranks countries accordingly. Is that design an honest answer to the weighting problem or a way of avoiding it? Separate what you would need to know from what you would need to value.
days.evidence_note: Settled: on any widely used absolute line, the share of humanity in extreme poverty has fallen enormously since 1820, and especially since 1990, and life expectancy has more than doubled. Debated: the size of the fall and the number still poor, which depend on the line (the World Bank's $3.00, its higher lines, or Hickel's proposed 'ethical' lines), on PPP conversions and on pre-1820 baselines. Rosling (Factfulness, 2018) and Pinker (Enlightenment Now, 2018) stand on one side and Hickel (2019; Sullivan & Hickel 2023) on the other, with a further dispute over whether GDP, the HDI or well-being should anchor the story. Value judgment: what counts as a good life, and therefore which metric measures 'progress', is a value question, which is why the choices should be stated rather than hidden.

resource.title: Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress (Executive Summary)
resource.creator: Joseph E. Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi (Paris, September 2009)
resource.why: The canonical statement that metric choices matter. Commissioned by the French government and led by two Nobel laureates and Fitoussi, it sets out why GDP misleads as a welfare measure and recommends a dashboard of income, distribution, well-being and sustainability.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified. The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this block was written and again before verification, and direct page fetches failed. Report cited from knowledge; its original site is no longer reliable, so confirm where the executive summary is hosted before linking.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 14: The cotton gin, slavery and abolition
days.headline_hint: Eli Whitney Built a Machine to Save Labour. Within Seventy Years America's Enslaved Population Had Grown More Than Fivefold.
days.concept: Why did a labour-saving machine expand slavery, and what ended it? The cotton gin as a loop in which an invention created demand for coerced labour, credit and law reinforced it, and moral, political and military conflict finally broke it.
days.focus: Walks the gin through Logan's chain as a loop, not a pipeline: invention before need (Kranzberg), British demand (Day 219), biological and land constraints, credit secured on human beings (named at CFA level), law that protected and then ended slavery (previews), adoption as an S-curve, the domestic slave trade, and feedback through theology, abolition, war and Reconstruction's reversal. It is a harm-and-repair case, and the ledger asks who gained, who paid and who consented.
key_concepts: invention is the mother of necessity (Kranzberg)
the domestic slave trade ('Second Middle Passage')
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, the cotton boom (reinforcing): the gin cut cleaning costs, cheaper cotton fed British demand, high prices drove more planting, and more enslaved people were bought and moved west to grow more cotton. R2, credit (reinforcing): rising prices for enslaved people raised their value as collateral, which supported more borrowing for land and more purchases. B1, land and soil (balancing, with a delay): soil exhaustion pushed planters west, and westward expansion turned each new territory into a political fight over slavery. B2, moral-political (balancing, long delay): expansion fed abolitionist and free-soil opposition, which led to secession, war and emancipation, some seventy years after the gin. Documented reversals: the invention created the 'need' for more labour (Kranzberg's second law); the 1808 import ban, meant to restrict slavery, made the domestic trade more lucrative; and emancipation was answered at once by the Black Codes of 1865-66 and, after Reconstruction ended in 1877, by sharecropping's debt peonage, convict leasing and Jim Crow, an extractive institution re-forming.

story.title: A plantation workshop near Savannah, 1793
story.hook: In 1793 at Mulberry Grove, a plantation near Savannah, Georgia, owned by Catharine Greene, widow of the Revolutionary general Nathanael Greene, a 27-year-old Yale graduate named Eli Whitney built a small machine. Wire teeth on a turning cylinder pulled cotton fibre through slots too narrow for the seeds, and a brush swept the lint away. Upland 'green-seed' cotton, which grew almost anywhere in the inland South, had been nearly worthless because a worker could clean only about a pound of fibre a day by picking out its sticky seeds. Whitney received his patent on 14 March 1794 and, with his partner Phineas Miller, planned to gin planters' cotton for a share of the crop; instead, copies appeared across Georgia and the Carolinas, and he spent years in lawsuits. The first US census, in 1790, had counted about 700,000 enslaved people; in 1860 the census counted about 3.95 million.
story.puzzle: How did a machine that saved labour in one task end up multiplying the number of people held in slavery, and what, in the end, broke the system it fed?
story.payoff: The gin removed the bottleneck in cleaning, so the binding constraints became picking and land, both supplied by enslaved people forced west. British demand, credit secured on enslaved people and the 1808 import ban (which made the domestic trade lucrative) closed the loop. Ending it took moral and religious argument, the resistance of the enslaved, political conflict and finally a war that killed roughly 620,000 to 750,000 people, and Reconstruction's reversal showed that the loop could reassert itself in law.
sources: Angela Lakwete, Inventing the Cotton Gin: Machine and Myth in Antebellum America (Johns Hopkins UP, 2003)
Eli Whitney's cotton gin patent, 14 March 1794 (US National Archives)
US Census of 1790 and 1860, enslaved population
J. David Hacker, 'A Census-Based Count of the Civil War Dead', Civil War History 57:4 (2011)

days.application: The US cotton economy from 1793 to 1877 as one system: Lancashire mills, Southern plantations, Northern and British finance, federal law and the war that broke it. The case touches every link of Logan's chain, with need, invention, constraints, financing, adoption and consequences taught deep and the legal links previewed.

builds_on.why: British mechanized spinning was the demand side of the loop; induced innovation in Lancashire created the need the gin met.
The slavery-and-capitalism debate (Williams, Drescher, Baptist, Olmstead & Rhode) frames how central cotton slavery was to industrial capitalism.
The proslavery and antislavery biblical arguments were the moral feedback loop that cotton wealth intensified.
Slavery was an extractive institution, and its re-formation after Reconstruction illustrates the 'iron law of oligarchy'.

across.link: In the Senate on 4 March 1858, James Henry Hammond declared that no power on earth dared make war on cotton: 'Cotton is king.' The Confederacy's informal cotton embargo of 1861 tried to force British recognition and failed, as Britain drew down its stocks and turned to Indian and Egyptian cotton. It was an early test of economic leverage over a chokepoint commodity, a subject of the International Relations block.

days.apply_question: The mechanical cotton picker, made commercially by International Harvester from the late 1940s, could do the work of dozens of hand pickers. Trace one loop, through labour, migration or law, by which that labour-saving machine changed the society that adopted it, as the gin had 150 years earlier.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the enslaved population rose from about 700,000 (1790) to about 3.95 million (1860); cotton became the leading US export; and the Civil War killed at least 620,000 people (Hacker estimates about 750,000). Debated: how far the gin itself, rather than land, British demand and policy, caused slavery's expansion; whether rising picking productivity came mainly from seed varieties (Olmstead & Rhode) or from violence (Baptist); how central cotton slavery was to US and British industrialization (the new history of capitalism against its critics); and how new Whitney's gin really was (Lakwete). Value judgment: the enslaved paid and did not consent, while planters, merchants, financiers, manufacturers and consumers gained. That slavery was a grave wrong is a near-universal judgment. Weighing the war's costs and Reconstruction's failures draws on consequentialist, Kantian rights-based and Christian natural-law readings, and whether slavery would have ended without war is an unknowable counterfactual.

chain.point: Lancashire's mechanized spinning (Day 219) created an exploding demand for raw cotton in the 1780s-90s. Meanwhile upland 'green-seed' cotton, the only kind that grew across the inland South, was nearly worthless because one worker could clean only about a pound a day by hand. The need was British; the bottleneck was American.

Whitney's gin (1793; patent 14 March 1794) pulled lint through slots with wire teeth on a cylinder. Roller gins such as India's churka had long cleaned long-staple cotton, Hodgen Holmes's saw gin (patented 1796) soon displaced Whitney's design, and Lakwete (2003) argues the gin was an adaptation more than a breakthrough. This is invention as combination, and the 'heroic inventor' as partly myth (the same Whitney staged the musket demonstration of Day 96).

Upland cotton needs a long frost-free season and fertile soil, which confined it to a belt from the Carolinas to Texas and pushed planters west as soils wore out. New varieties (Mexican seed from 1806, later 'Petit Gulf') raised daily picking rates roughly fourfold by 1860 (Olmstead & Rhode, Journal of Economic History 2008). They call this biological innovation; Baptist (2014) attributes the rise mainly to violent 'pushing' of enslaved pickers.

Gins grew from hand-cranked boxes to horse- and later steam-driven gin houses with screw presses for baling, and steamboats on western rivers from the 1810s cut the cost of moving bales to New Orleans. Picking stayed by hand until mechanical pickers spread after the late 1940s, so the engineering freed one bottleneck and moved the constraint onto human labour.

Named at CFA level. Planters borrowed through cotton factors and bills of exchange drawn on Liverpool and London houses, with enslaved people as the main collateral (Bonnie Martin, Journal of Southern History 2010). Louisiana's property banks of the late 1820s and 1830s sold bonds in Europe backed partly by mortgages on enslaved people. By 1860 the enslaved were valued at roughly $3 billion, by common estimates more than US railroad and manufacturing capital combined, though that comparison is debated.

Whitney's patent under the Patent Act of 1793 was copied across the South. He won a key infringement case only in 1807, and Congress declined to renew the patent. Whether patents spur or slow the spread of a technology is the Law block's intellectual-property question (Day 256).

The Constitution protected the import trade until 1808 and counted three-fifths of the enslaved for representation. The 1807 Act banned imports from 1 January 1808, which raised the value of enslaved people already in the US and fed the domestic trade. The Fugitive Slave Act (1850), Dred Scott (1857) and the Thirteenth Amendment (ratified 6 December 1865) are taught in the Government and Law blocks.

US cotton output rose from a few million pounds around 1790 to roughly 2 billion pounds (some 4-5 million bales) by 1860. It followed an S-curve (Day 7), spreading by copying and imitation (Day 213), and by the 1850s the US supplied roughly three-quarters of Britain's raw cotton.

The enslaved population rose from about 700,000 (1790) to about 3.95 million (1860), after 1808 by natural increase. Roughly a million people were moved from the Upper South to the cotton states by sale and forced migration, the 'Second Middle Passage' (Ira Berlin, Generations of Captivity, 2003), which broke up families on a vast scale.

Cotton wealth hardened proslavery politics and the biblical defence of slavery, while abolitionists answered from the same Bible (Day 227). Expansion into new territories split the parties and led to secession. The Civil War killed about 620,000 by the traditional count and about 750,000 by Hacker's (2011) census-based estimate, and it ended slavery. In Lancashire, the cotton famine of 1861-65 pushed Britain toward Indian and Egyptian supply.

The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) was answered at once by Southern Black Codes (1865-66). The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments (1868, 1870) followed, but after Reconstruction ended in 1877 came sharecropping's debt peonage, convict leasing and Jim Crow, and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld segregation. An extractive institution re-formed in new legal dress (the pattern of Day 222); the law of it is taught in the Government and Law blocks.

resource.title: Empire of Cotton: A Global History, chapter 5, 'Slavery Takes Command'
resource.creator: Sven Beckert (Knopf, 2014)
resource.why: A vivid global account of how British mills, American slavery and transatlantic credit fused after the gin. It represents the 'new history of capitalism' side, which Olmstead & Rhode criticize, so read it as one argument.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Why obey? Legitimacy from Hobbes to Weber
days.headline_hint: Max Weber Told Munich What Makes a State in January 1919. By April, Bavaria Had Two Governments and No State.
days.concept: A state is the organization that successfully claims a monopoly of legitimate force over a territory. Its rule lasts when people accept that force as rightful, through tradition, a leader's charisma or lawful procedure (Weber), and not merely because it has the guns.
days.focus: Teach legitimacy as the difference between power and authority. Hobbes (1651) and Locke (1689) give the social-contract answers to why we should obey (normative legitimacy), and Weber gives the three grounds on which people actually do obey (descriptive legitimacy). The angle: in Weber's definition force is necessary but never sufficient, so a state whose legitimacy collapses becomes one armed party among several.
key_concepts: monopoly of legitimate force (Weber's definition of the state)
social contract: Hobbes's obedience in exchange for protection; Locke's consent, with a right of resistance
Weber's three types of authority: traditional, charismatic, legal-rational
days.model_or_equation: Weber's typology as a three-row table. Traditional authority: obeyed because it has always been so (a hereditary monarch). Charismatic authority: obeyed because of a leader's extraordinary personal qualities (a revolutionary leader). Legal-rational authority: obeyed because the office was filled by lawful procedure (an elected government and its civil service). Beside it, Hobbes's logic as a game: without a sovereign, striking first is each person's best reply, and the sovereign changes the payoffs (Day 14).

story.title: A lecture on the state, in a city about to have none
story.hook: On Tuesday 28 January 1919 Max Weber, 54 and Germany's best-known social scientist, lectured to the Free Students' association in Munich, reportedly in the hall of the bookseller Carl Georg Steinicke. Bavaria's king had fled in November 1918, when Kurt Eisner proclaimed a republic. In Berlin, Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht had been murdered thirteen days earlier, after the Spartacist rising. Weber gave his young audience a cold definition: a state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. Within weeks Munich tested it. Eisner was shot dead on 21 February. In April a Soviet Republic was proclaimed in Munich, and the elected government of Johannes Hoffmann fled to Bamberg. In early May Freikorps troops stormed the city, and hundreds died.
story.puzzle: Every faction in Munich had guns, and each claimed to be the government. If a state is just the strongest armed group, why did Weber insist on the word 'legitimate'? And what besides force decides which group is the state?
story.payoff: Weber's answer is that force is necessary but not sufficient. A state exists where its claim to rightful force is accepted, and that acceptance rests on tradition, charisma or lawful procedure. In spring 1919 all three failed at once in Bavaria. The monarchy's tradition was gone, Eisner's charisma died with him, and the new legal order had not yet won acceptance. So there were rival claimants and no monopoly. The Weimar constitution, adopted that summer, was an attempt to rebuild legal-rational legitimacy.
sources: Max Weber, 'Politik als Beruf' (lecture of 28 Jan 1919, published 1919); English translation in H. H. Gerth & C. Wright Mills (eds.), From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology (1946)
Allan Mitchell, Revolution in Bavaria, 1918-1919: The Eisner Regime and the Soviet Republic (1965)
Wolfgang J. Mommsen, Max Weber and German Politics, 1890-1920 (English ed. 1984)

days.application: Somalia after January 1991, when Siad Barre's regime fell. For about two decades there was no functioning central government (a federal government was formed in 2012). Meanwhile self-declared Somaliland (May 1991) built a working order by grafting clan elders' traditional authority onto elected institutions: Weber's types at work. It is also a test of what happens to security and welfare when the monopoly of force disappears. Leeson (2007) argued that several welfare indicators improved compared with Barre's predatory state; critics reject that comparison.

builds_on.why: Hobbes's state of nature is often modelled as a many-player prisoner's dilemma (some theorists prefer an assurance game). Without a sovereign, attacking first is each person's best reply; the Leviathan changes the payoffs so that keeping the peace becomes rational.

Day 198's settlements of the wars of religion strengthened territorial sovereignty (while the '1648 founded the state system' story is partly myth). Hobbes wrote Leviathan (1651) amid the English Civil War, a conflict over religion and authority, to argue for an undivided sovereign: the claim to obedience this lesson examines.

across.link: In The Concept of Law (1961), H. L. A. Hart attacked John Austin's command theory of law as 'the gunman situation writ large'. A robber's order obliges you to hand over your money but creates no obligation to do so, so law needs accepted rules (a 'rule of recognition'), not just threats. This is Weber's line between power and legitimate authority, drawn inside jurisprudence.

days.apply_question: Since Myanmar's military seized power on 1 February 2021, the junta and the exiled National Unity Government have both claimed to be the country's government, while armed groups hold large parts of its territory. Using Weber's definition and his three grounds of legitimacy, what would you need to observe before saying that Myanmar has a state again?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Weber's definition and typology are standard tools of political science, and the events in Munich in 1918-19 are well documented. Debated: whether stateless Somalia fared better or worse than under Barre (Leeson 2007 against his critics), and how much obedience in practice comes from legitimacy rather than coercion and patronage. Value judgment: whether, and when, citizens are obliged to obey. Hobbes, Locke and philosophical anarchists such as A. John Simmons answer differently. Christian readings range from Romans 13 ('be subject to the governing authorities') to Acts 5:29 ('we ought to obey God rather than men') and Augustine's question: if justice is removed, what are kingdoms but great robberies (City of God IV.4)?

resource.title: Politics as a Vocation: the opening section (the definition of the state and the three inner justifications of domination)
resource.creator: Max Weber; English translation in H. H. Gerth & C. Wright Mills (eds.), From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology (Oxford University Press, 1946)
resource.length: about 15-20 minutes for the opening pages; the whole lecture is about 50 pages
resource.why: Weber's own words from the lecture in today's story. He defines the state, calls it a relation of domination resting on violence that is considered legitimate, and gives his three grounds of legitimacy in their original compressed form.
resource.verified_how: Writer's web search this session confirmed the lecture's date, the Free Students' association and (single-sourced, archive.org) the Steinicke venue. The Gerth & Mills edition (OUP 1946, about 50 pages for the lecture) is from prior knowledge.
