days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: State capacity: the power to count, tax and deliver
days.headline_hint: Sweden Counted Its People Half a Century Before Britain Did. It Borrowed the Church to Do It.
days.concept: State capacity is a government's practical ability to know its population, raise revenue, enforce its rules and deliver services across its territory (Michael Mann's 'infrastructural power'). It is built through cumulative investment, often on top of older institutions.
days.focus: Teach state capacity as something separate from regime type and from despotic power. The tools are Besley and Persson's fiscal and legal capacity, Mann's infrastructural power, and the information base beneath both (Scott's 'legibility'). The angle: capacity is built up and often borrowed, as when Sweden based the world's oldest continuous population statistics on its Lutheran parish registers, and legibility cuts both ways, enabling welfare and surveillance alike.
key_concepts: leakage: benefits lost between the state and the intended recipient

story.title: A kingdom that counted itself before anyone else
story.hook: In 1749 Sweden created Tabellverket, a system of standard tables on which every parish reported its births, marriages, deaths and population. Sweden had shrunk after losing its Baltic provinces in the Great Northern War, and the first published figures (1764) counted 2,383,113 people for 1760, Finland included. Statistics Sweden calls Tabellverket the world's oldest regular national population statistics, and the series has never stopped. Britain, far richer, held its first census only in 1801, and England began civil registration of births only in 1837. Sweden had no army of census-takers. The tables were filled in by parish clergy. Under the Church Law of 1686 they already kept rolls of every household and held yearly examinations (husförhör) of every household's members on reading and the catechism.
story.puzzle: How did a poor, sparsely settled, mostly rural kingdom do what wealthier and more powerful states did not? And why would an eighteenth-century government want to count every person at all?
story.payoff: State capacity is built, and often borrowed. The Swedish state turned an existing church infrastructure into a counting machine at almost no new cost: a literate registrar in every parish, under a legal duty to keep household rolls. Counting mattered because mercantilist governments saw population as the wealth and military strength of the realm, and a state cannot tax, conscript or plan for people it cannot see. Legibility came first. Taxation, conscription and, much later, welfare were built on it. Legibility was also political: in 1753 a British bill for an annual count passed the Commons but failed in the Lords, after opponents warned it would subvert English liberty.
sources: Statistics Sweden (SCB), 'History of Statistics Sweden' (Tabellverket 1749; first publication 1764; 2,383,113 inhabitants in Sweden and Finland in 1760)
Swedish Church Law of 1686 (household examination rolls, husförhörslängder)
Umeå University, Centre for Demographic and Ageing Research, Tabellverket / TABVERK database documentation

days.application: India's Aadhaar biometric ID. Since the first number was issued in September 2010, it has enrolled more than 1.3 billion people and is used to route welfare payments and food rations. A large randomized rollout in Jharkhand, evaluated by Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar, found that biometric checks alone did not reduce leakage; leakage fell only once electronic reconciliation was added, and roughly 1.5 to 2 million people lost benefits at some point during the transition. Drèze, Khera and Somanchi dispute parts of that reading. On 26 September 2018 India's Supreme Court (4-1) upheld Aadhaar for welfare but struck down its compulsory use by private companies (Section 57).

builds_on.why: Writing began as state accounting (Uruk's tablets). Tabellverket is the same technology, standardized records, scaled up to a whole population.
The Reformation's push for lay Bible reading helps explain why Lutheran Sweden's church examined every household on its reading. That gave the state a ready-made registrar in every parish.

across.link: The Human Mortality Database's series for Sweden starts in 1751, the longest national series in the database, and its early years rest on Tabellverket's parish counts. The state's counting is what lets demographers measure the mortality revolution at all.

days.apply_question: The United States began withholding income tax from wages in 1943. Using the idea of legibility, explain why making employers report and withhold tax raised the state's fiscal capacity more than simply raising tax rates would have.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Tabellverket's dates and Sweden's lead in continuous population statistics. The link between state capacity and development is a strong, widely replicated correlation. Debated: the direction of causation (Besley and Persson model capacity and growth as determined jointly), and Aadhaar's net effect on welfare delivery (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar against Drèze, Khera and Somanchi). Value judgment: how legible a free society should make its people. Scott warns that 'seeing like a state' flattens local knowledge, and India's Supreme Court recognized privacy as a fundamental right (Puttaswamy, 2017); both weigh against the efficiency gains.

resource.title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed (Introduction)
resource.creator: James C. Scott (Yale University Press, 1998)
resource.why: The classic statement of 'legibility'. It explains why states standardize names, measures and land records in order to see their subjects, and why ambitious state schemes fail when legibility replaces local knowledge. It is the critical counterweight to today's lesson.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge: a standard, widely cited book; its Introduction is about ten pages. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Constitutions and checks: ambition against ambition
days.headline_hint: The Day Massachusetts Ratified by 19 Votes, Madison Explained Why a Government Should Fight Itself.
days.concept: Separation of powers with checks and balances gives each branch both the means and the motive to resist the others ('ambition must be made to counteract ambition'), so liberty does not depend on rulers' virtue. Every added veto point protects against abuse and also raises the cost of change.
days.focus: Teach constitutional design as the design of incentives: the logic of Federalist No. 51 (divide power and give each part a personal stake in defending its ground), and its modern form as veto players (Tsebelis 2002). The angle: more veto players with differing preferences make policy stable, which protects liberty and blocks reform alike. Contrast Germany's post-Weimar answer to the opposite problem, governments that were too easy to topple.
key_concepts: policy stability (the institutional status quo bias)
days.model_or_equation: Tsebelis's veto-player model, in words and one picture. Each veto player is a point in policy space, with a circle of outcomes it prefers to the status quo. A change can pass only inside the area where all the circles overlap (the 'winset' of the status quo). Add a player, or move the players farther apart, and the winset shrinks, so policy becomes more stable.

story.title: A newspaper essay and a 19-vote margin
story.hook: On Wednesday 6 February 1788, readers of New York's Independent Journal found essay No. 51 of The Federalist, signed 'Publius'. Most scholars attribute it to James Madison, though Hamilton's side later claimed it. On the same day in Boston, Massachusetts' ratifying convention approved the new Constitution by 187 votes to 168, a margin of 19. The Anti-Federalists' fear was concrete: a distant national government with a strong executive and a standing army would become the tyranny the Revolution had fought. Madison's reply did not promise good rulers. 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary,' he wrote. 'If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary.' His remedy was to give 'those who administer each department the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others.' In short: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
story.puzzle: Madison deliberately designed a government that would fight itself and move slowly. Why would anyone build friction into the machine? And how could selfish officeholders produce a safer government than virtuous ones?
story.payoff: Because the design does not rely on virtue. By giving each branch its own power base and a self-interested reason to guard it, the Constitution turns officeholders' ambition into a balancing force. The cost is the friction itself. In veto-player terms, every independent institution whose consent is needed shrinks the set of changes that can pass, protecting against abuse and against reform alike.
sources: The Federalist No. 51, New York Independent Journal, 6 Feb 1788 (Documentary History of the Ratification of the Constitution, Center for the Study of the American Constitution)
Massachusetts ratifying convention, vote of 6 Feb 1788 (187-168)
George Tsebelis, Veto Players: How Political Institutions Work (2002)

days.application: Germany's 'constructive vote of no confidence' (Basic Law Article 67, 1949): the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote. Weimar's parliament could bring down governments with a purely negative majority, and Weimar went through some twenty cabinets in fourteen years. Under Article 67 there have been only two attempts. On 27 April 1972 the attempt against Willy Brandt failed by two votes; the Stasi appears to have bribed at least one opposition deputy. On 1 October 1982 the second attempt succeeded, replacing Helmut Schmidt with Helmut Kohl. This is a check designed for stability rather than against tyranny.

builds_on.why: Day 14 showed that changing the rules of a game changes which behaviour is an equilibrium. Madison sets the payoffs so that each self-interested branch's best reply is to resist encroachment, so the safe outcome does not depend on anyone's virtue.
The Age of Revolutions made consent and rights the test of legitimate government. The 1787 Constitution was one of its experiments, written after the weak Articles of Confederation.

across.link: Saltzer and Schroeder's 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems' (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975) sets out the principle of 'separation of privilege': a protection mechanism that needs two keys is more robust than one that needs only one. That is the logic of requiring two chambers and a president to agree. The analogy breaks because Madison's design relies on the keyholders' rival ambitions, and software keys have none.

days.apply_question: The US federal government was partly shut down for 35 days, from 22 December 2018 to 25 January 2019, because the President and the House could not agree on border-wall funding. Using the veto-player idea, explain why that outcome is a predictable cost of Madison's design rather than a malfunction.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the texts and dates; the veto-player logic is a standard formal result. Debated: whether presidential systems, with their many veto points, are more prone to breakdown than parliamentary ones (Juan Linz, 'The Perils of Presidentialism', 1990, against Cheibub's 2007 evidence that many presidential democracies inherited a military legacy, which explains much of their fragility). Also debated: how much Madison's view of human nature owes to Reformed theology (he studied at Princeton under the Presbyterian John Witherspoon) rather than to Hume and the Scottish Enlightenment. Value judgment: how much gridlock is a fair price for protection against abuse.

resource.title: The Federalist No. 51
resource.creator: 'Publius' (James Madison), New York Independent Journal, 6 February 1788; text as published by the Center for the Study of the American Constitution, University of Wisconsin-Madison
resource.why: The primary text behind today's lesson, short enough to read whole. It is Madison's own argument for dividing power and arming each part against the others, including the 'angels' passage and his case that a large republic of many interests protects minorities.
resource.verified_how: The writer's web search this session returned this exact URL on csac.history.wisc.edu (the Center for the Study of the American Constitution, editors of the Documentary History of the Ratification), titled 'DC6 04 51 Federalist 51 6Feb88'. days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Voting rules and social choice: why no rule is perfect
days.headline_hint: Four in Five French Voters Rejected Le Pen. On 21 April 2002 He Still Made the Final Two.
days.concept: With three or more options, no rule for combining voters' rankings can turn every possible set of rankings into a consistent group ranking while meeting a short list of fairness conditions (Arrow's impossibility theorem, 1951). So the choice of rule, and not only the voters, shapes who wins.
days.focus: Teach Arrow's theorem through its ingredients: Condorcet's paradox (majorities can go round in a cycle, 1785), Arrow's conditions (unanimity, independence of irrelevant alternatives, no dictator, a consistent group ranking), and the practical results: spoilers, centre squeezes and strategic voting (Gibbard-Satterthwaite). The angle: every real rule, whether plurality, two-round, ranked-choice or Borda, breaks some condition, so the honest question is which flaw you can live with.
key_concepts: independence of irrelevant alternatives (the spoiler effect)
days.model_or_equation: Condorcet's three-voter cycle. Voter 1 ranks A>B>C, voter 2 ranks B>C>A, voter 3 ranks C>A>B. Then A beats B 2-1, B beats C 2-1, and C beats A 2-1, so the majority 'prefers' A to B to C to A. Arrow's theorem: with three or more options, any rule that accepts every possible set of rankings (unrestricted domain), respects unanimity (Pareto), satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives and always produces a consistent ranking must be a dictatorship.

story.title: Eight o'clock on 21 April 2002
story.hook: At 8 p.m. on Sunday 21 April 2002, French television showed the two candidates who would contest the presidential run-off. One was the incumbent, Jacques Chirac, with 19.9% of the first-round vote. The other was not the Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin, as almost everyone had expected, but the far-right Jean-Marie Le Pen: 16.86% to Jospin's 16.18%, a gap of about 195,000 votes out of more than 28 million. Sixteen candidates had stood, and the left's vote had scattered among several of them, including Jean-Pierre Chevènement (5.33%) and Christiane Taubira (2.32%). Jospin announced his retirement from politics that night. Two weeks later, on 5 May, Chirac beat Le Pen with about 82% of the vote.
story.puzzle: A candidate whom roughly four voters in five rejected in the run-off reached it, while a candidate who would very probably have beaten him head to head was eliminated. Was the electorate confused, or did the counting rule itself produce a result most voters did not want?
story.payoff: The rule did it. In a two-round system, minor candidates who cannot win can still decide who reaches the final. That breaks the condition Arrow called independence of irrelevant alternatives: whether Jospin or Le Pen advanced depended in part on how many other left-wing candidates split the first-round vote, not only on how voters ranked Jospin against Le Pen. Arrow proved that every rule must break one of his fairness conditions somewhere; France's rule broke this one in public.
sources: Conseil constitutionnel, official first-round results of 21 Apr 2002 (Le Pen 4,804,713 votes, 16.86%; Jospin 4,610,113, 16.18%)
Kenneth J. Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951)
Condorcet, Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions rendues à la pluralité des voix (1785)

days.application: Ranked-choice voting in Alaska, adopted narrowly by referendum in 2020 (Maine had adopted it by referendum in 2016). In the August 2022 special election for Alaska's US House seat, the cast-vote records show that Republican Nick Begich would have beaten both Sarah Palin and Mary Peltola head to head. Yet he had the fewest first preferences and was eliminated first, and Peltola then beat Palin by about 51.5% to 48.5%. This 'centre squeeze' is ranked-choice voting's version of an Arrow failure. A 2024 ballot measure to repeal ranked-choice voting failed by roughly 740 votes out of about 321,000 cast.

builds_on.why: Arrow's theorem is a proof. From a few axioms it shows that no rule can satisfy them all, a certainty that no amount of experience with elections could give.
Once a rule is in place, voters and candidates play a game. Strategic voting and strategic entry (Gibbard-Satterthwaite) follow from best responses, as in game theory.

across.link: Conitzer and colleagues' position paper 'Social Choice Should Guide AI Alignment in Dealing with Diverse Human Feedback' (ICML 2024) argues that training language models on many people's pairwise preferences is an aggregation problem of exactly Arrow's kind, cycles and impossibility results included.

days.apply_question: In the 2000 US presidential election, Ralph Nader won 97,488 votes in Florida while George W. Bush carried the state by 537 votes over Al Gore. Using the idea of independence of irrelevant alternatives, explain how a third-party candidate with no chance of winning can still decide the winner under plurality rule.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Arrow's theorem and the Condorcet paradox are proofs, and the 2002 and 2022 results are official. Debated: how often cycles and spoilers occur in real elections (studies find Condorcet cycles rare; spoilers and centre squeezes are less rare), and which rule works best in practice. Supporters of ranked-choice, approval and STAR voting all cite Alaska 2022: Jeanne Clelland's analysis finds Begich was the Condorcet winner, that approval voting would probably still have elected Peltola, and that STAR voting would probably have elected Begich. Value judgment: which of Arrow's conditions to give up is a choice about fairness, not a mathematical fact.

resource.title: Why Democracy Is Mathematically Impossible
resource.creator: Veritasium (Derek Muller), YouTube, 2023
resource.why: Animates Condorcet's cycle and walks through the logic of Arrow's proof, then shows how other approaches, such as single-peaked preferences and approval voting, step around it. It supplies the proof's machinery, which the brief can only state.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the Veritasium channel (uploaded 2023; about 24 minutes, over the ~20-minute guide). Beware same-title re-uploads by other channels. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: The Reichstag Voted 444 to 94 to Give Away Its Own Power. Each Step Was Dressed as Law.
days.concept: Modern democracies usually die not by coups but by legal steps: emergency powers, captured referees, sidelined opponents and rewritten rules. These steps succeed once the unwritten norms that restrain the use of legal power, mutual toleration and institutional forbearance, have worn away (Levitsky & Ziblatt 2018).
days.focus: Teach democratic breakdown as a process, using Levitsky and Ziblatt's toolkit: capture the referees, sideline the players, change the rules, plus the 'fateful alliance' in which established politicians think they can control an outsider. The angle: written rules are necessary but not sufficient, and measuring 'backsliding' requires judgment, as the 2024 dispute over expert-coded indices shows.
key_concepts: capturing the referees (courts, prosecutors, election bodies, media regulators)
days.model_or_equation: Levitsky and Ziblatt's four warning signs, as a <dl>: (1) rejection, in words or action, of the democratic rules of the game; (2) denial of the legitimacy of political opponents; (3) toleration or encouragement of violence; (4) readiness to curtail the civil liberties of opponents, including the media. Add their three moves of subversion: capture the referees, sideline the players, rewrite the rules.

story.title: A parliament votes in an opera house
story.hook: On Thursday 23 March 1933 the Reichstag met in Berlin's Kroll Opera House, because its own building had been gutted by fire nearly four weeks earlier. A decree issued the day after the fire had suspended civil liberties. Most of the 81 Communist deputies had been arrested or had fled, some Social Democrats were missing too, and SA stormtroopers lined the hall. The Enabling Act before the deputies would let the government issue laws for four years without parliament, including laws that departed from the constitution. It needed a two-thirds majority. The Catholic Centre Party, promised protection for the Church, voted yes. Only the Social Democrats voted no. Their leader, Otto Wels, told the chamber: 'Freedom and life can be taken from us, but not our honour.' The result was 444 to 94, and President Hindenburg signed the Act the next day. Since 1930 Germany had already been governed largely by presidential emergency decrees under Article 48 of the Weimar constitution.
story.puzzle: No tanks surrounded the parliament. The Act passed by more than the supermajority the constitution demanded, and each step was given legal form, even though the arrests that cleared the way were of doubtful legality. How can a democracy end by following its own rules?
story.payoff: Because rules are only as strong as the norms and referees behind them. By 1933 Weimar's referees had been captured: the president ruled by decree and appointed the chancellor. Its strongest opponents had been sidelined: Communist deputies were arrested under the fire decree, and the rules of procedure were reportedly altered so that unexcused absentees counted as present. Its conservative elites had made a 'fateful alliance', believing they could tame Hitler. Each step wore a legal form; together they removed the guardrails. That is the pattern Levitsky and Ziblatt find again and again.
sources: Reichstag proceedings, 23 Mar 1933: the Enabling Act passed 444-94
Otto Wels's speech against the Enabling Act, 23 Mar 1933 (historical materials of the German Bundestag)
Richard J. Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich (2003)
Steven Levitsky & Daniel Ziblatt, How Democracies Die (2018)

days.application: Hungary since 2010. Fidesz won two-thirds of parliament's seats with about 53% of the party-list vote, then used that legal supermajority to write a new constitution (2011), enlarge and refill the Constitutional Court, centralize media regulation and redraw the electoral rules. V-Dem has classified Hungary as an 'electoral autocracy' since its 2020 report, and in 2022 the European Parliament described it as a 'hybrid regime of electoral autocracy'. Hungary's government rejects both judgments. Before writing about Hungary's present, the routine must check the outcome of the April 2026 parliamentary election and V-Dem's latest classification: an incumbent's defeat at the polls would itself be evidence in the measurement dispute.

builds_on.why: Forbearance and mutual toleration are social norms, self-enforcing expectations. Like the norms of Day 202, they can collapse quickly once enough players stop expecting others to keep them.

Motivated reasoning and identity-protective cognition help explain why voters excuse their own side's norm-breaking. In Graham and Svolik's experiments (APSR 2020), only a small minority of US voters (a few per cent) punished a candidate for undemocratic positions when doing so meant voting against their own party.

across.link: Germany's Basic Law (1949) answered the Enabling Act with 'militant democracy'. Article 79(3), the 'eternity clause', puts human dignity, democracy and federalism beyond amendment. Article 21(2) lets the Federal Constitutional Court ban parties that seek to abolish the democratic order: it banned the SRP in 1952 and the KPD in 1956, and in 2017 it declined to ban the NPD as too insignificant to succeed.

days.apply_question: In 2004 Venezuela's National Assembly, controlled by Hugo Chávez's supporters, enlarged the Supreme Tribunal of Justice from 20 to 32 justices and filled the new seats with allies. In Levitsky and Ziblatt's framework, why can a step that was legal on its face still count as evidence of democratic erosion?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Weimar sequence (rule by Article 48 decree from 1930, the fire decree, the 444-94 vote) and Hungary's institutional changes after 2010 are documented. Debated: how much of Weimar's collapse came from institutional design (Article 48, proportional representation) rather than the Depression and elite choices. Also debated: whether expert-coded indices such as V-Dem overstate global backsliding. Little and Meng (PS: Political Science & Politics, 2024) find little decline in objective indicators, while Knutsen and colleagues (2024) defend expert coding. Check Hungary's April 2026 election result and V-Dem's current classification before describing Hungary's present. Value judgment: what counts as democracy at all, majority rule alone or majority rule bounded by rights and fair competition.

resource.title: How Democracies Die, Chapter 4: 'Subverting Democracy'
resource.creator: Steven Levitsky & Daniel Ziblatt (Crown, 2018)
resource.why: The chapter that sets out the three legal moves (capturing the referees, sidelining the players, changing the rules) with cases from Peru, Venezuela, Hungary and Turkey. It is the mainstream political-science account the brief summarizes; the 2024 measurement dispute questions it mainly at the global scale.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book: Chapter 1 is 'Fateful Alliances' and Chapter 4 'Subverting Democracy'. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: Switzerland Gave Women the Vote in 1971. One Canton Held Out Until Judges Ruled in 1990.
days.concept: Federalism divides authority between levels of government so that decisions can be made close to the people they affect and states can experiment. Subsidiarity, from Catholic social teaching, adds that a higher level should neither take over what a lower one can do well nor abandon it when it cannot, so the weight falls on the qualifier in 'the lowest competent level'.
days.focus: Teach the allocation question, who decides what, through federalism's benefits (local knowledge, fit to local preferences, experiments, the option to leave) and its costs (spillovers, races to the bottom, local majorities oppressing local minorities), together with Quadragesimo Anno's (1931) principle of subsidiarity, which runs in both directions. The angle: subsidiarity is often quoted as 'smaller is better', but its own text says the higher level exists to help (subsidium), which is how Swiss federal judges could rightly overrule a canton.
key_concepts: spillovers and races to the bottom

story.title: The last canton
story.hook: On Sunday 7 February 1971 Swiss men voted, by about two to one, to give women the vote in federal elections. Each canton still controlled its own franchise, and one by one the holdouts followed. The exception was Appenzell Innerrhoden, a small Catholic half-canton that still makes its laws at the Landsgemeinde, an open-air assembly where citizens vote by raising their hands in the square of the town of Appenzell. As late as April 1990 its men voted again to keep women out. Women of the canton, Theresa Rohner among them, took the case to the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne. On 27 November 1990 the judges ruled that the cantonal constitution violated the guarantee of equal rights for men and women that had been added to the federal constitution in 1981. In April 1991 the women of Appenzell Innerrhoden stood in the square and voted for the first time.
story.puzzle: Switzerland prizes local self-government and direct democracy more than almost any other country. Was the court defending democracy or overriding it? And who should decide which questions belong to the canton and which to the nation?
story.payoff: Federalism and subsidiarity say 'decide at the lowest level' only with a qualifier: the lowest competent level, within guarantees the higher level owes to everyone. Appenzell's assembly was competent to set its taxes and school calendar. But the federal constitution had made equal political rights a national guarantee, so a canton that denied them was not exercising autonomy; it was failing a duty. In subsidiarity's own terms, that is when the higher body steps in.
sources: Swiss Federal Supreme Court, judgment of 27 Nov 1990, BGE 116 Ia 359 (Rohner and others v. Appenzell Innerrhoden)
Federal popular vote of 7 Feb 1971 on women's suffrage (Swiss Federal Chancellery)
Pius XI, Quadragesimo Anno (15 May 1931), §79

days.application: US states' differing traffic-safety laws as Brandeis's 'laboratories'. Dissenting in New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann (1932), Brandeis wrote that 'a single courageous State may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory'. New York passed the first mandatory seat-belt law in 1984; New Hampshire still has none for adults. Some states let police stop drivers for being unbelted (primary enforcement); others can cite it only after another offence. Because states adopted their laws at different times, researchers can compare them as natural experiments. Cohen and Einav (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2003) found that mandatory belt laws raised belt use and cut occupant deaths, with no measurable offsetting risk-taking. In Logan's chain this sits at the regulation link for the car.

builds_on.why: States that adopt a law at different times create natural experiments. Difference-in-differences across states is how 'laboratories of democracy' actually produce knowledge.
One of Ostrom's design principles is 'nested enterprises', governance in layers with each layer handling what it can. That is the commons version of federalism and subsidiarity.

across.link: The 'end-to-end argument' (Saltzer, Reed & Clark, ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, 1984) says a network's core should not perform functions that the endpoints can perform completely and correctly. It is a rule for where to place functions, with the same shape as subsidiarity. The analogy breaks because subsidiarity rests on the dignity and freedom of persons and communities, which packets do not have.

days.apply_question: Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union lets the EU act only where member states cannot sufficiently achieve an objective on their own. Using both directions of subsidiarity, should limits on power-plant carbon emissions be set in Brussels or by each member state, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Swiss dates and the court's ruling; the text of Quadragesimo Anno. Debated: whether competition between states produces useful experiments or races to the bottom, and how far successful policies actually spread from state 'laboratories' (the evidence is mixed by policy area). Value judgment: which questions are local and which are rights owed everywhere. Subsidiarity (Catholic social teaching), Kuyper's Protestant 'sphere sovereignty' and liberal federalism give different answers, and the Appenzell case shows the same principle of local self-rule being invoked on both sides.

resource.title: Federalism
resource.creator: Andreas Føllesdal, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (online entry, revised edition)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the sections on the arguments for and against federal arrangements
resource.why: A philosopher's map of why authority is divided at all: the arguments from liberty, local knowledge, minority protection and experimentation, and the objections to each. Its author is a leading scholar of subsidiarity, and it gives the concept a structure the brief can only sketch.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the SEP entry and its author. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Bureaucracy and the merit civil service
days.headline_hint: A Man Who Wanted a Government Job Shot the President. Congress Answered With an Exam.
days.concept: A Weberian bureaucracy, with offices defined by written rules, files, expertise, and hiring and promotion on merit, all kept separate from the officeholder's private interests, replaced patronage. It bought competence and impartiality at the price of responsiveness, and the principal-agent problem of controlling officials never goes away.
days.focus: Teach why merit bureaucracy outperforms patronage, and why patronage's responsiveness keeps tempting reformers back, using Weber's ideal type, the principal-agent problem, and evidence from Evans and Rauch (1999) and Xu (2018). The angle: reform came when politicians had reasons to tie their own hands, and a bureaucracy's virtues (rules, impersonality, obedience to procedure) are also its pathologies.
key_concepts: Weberian bureaucracy (rules, files, expertise, merit, career)
tenure protection and political neutrality of the civil service
days.model_or_equation: The principal-agent problem in one line. The principal (the public, acting through elected leaders) wants outcome X. The agent (an official) knows more and has interests of her own. Patronage ties the agent to her patron; merit hiring and a protected career tie her to the rules and the job. Each solves one problem and opens another.

story.title: A disappointed office-seeker at the railroad station
story.hook: At about 9:30 on the morning of Saturday 2 July 1881, President James Garfield walked through the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington, on his way out of the city for the summer. Charles Guiteau had spent months pestering the White House and the State Department for a consulship in Paris. He shot the president twice from behind and reportedly declared, 'I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts... Arthur is President now.' Garfield lingered for eleven weeks while his doctors probed the wound with unwashed fingers, and he died at Elberon, New Jersey, on 19 September. At the time almost every federal job, from postmaster to customs clerk to consul, was a party reward, handed out by the winners after each election. On 16 January 1883 President Chester Arthur, once the patronage boss of the New York Custom House, signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act. It required competitive examinations for about one federal job in ten.
story.puzzle: Patronage was the fuel of nineteenth-century party machines: it rewarded party workers and won elections. Why would the politicians who lived off it vote to give it up, and why did they start with only a tenth of the jobs?
story.payoff: Outrage at the assassination turned the spoils system into a national scandal, and the 1882 midterm elections punished the Republicans. With their hold on the presidency in doubt, they also had a reason to lock their own appointees into protected posts before a Democratic president could fire them. Historians weigh public pressure (Theriault 2003) against this partisan insurance. Either way, merit protection began small and spread as outgoing administrations 'blanketed in' their own people. Over time it built Weber's bureaucracy: officials chosen for competence and protected from the next election's spoils.
sources: Candice Millard, Destiny of the Republic (2011)
Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, 16 Jan 1883 (US Office of Personnel Management, history of the civil service)
Sean M. Theriault, 'Patronage, the Pendleton Act, and the Power of the People', Journal of Politics 65 (2003)

days.application: Governors in the British Empire. Guo Xu ('The Costs of Patronage: Evidence from the British Empire', American Economic Review, 2018) found that colonial governors with social ties to the Secretary of State for the Colonies received more lucrative postings and honours yet performed worse, notably in collecting revenue, and that these effects faded once their patrons left office. The costs of patronage show up in the accounts.

builds_on.why: Hilberg, and more controversially Bauman, argued that the machinery that makes bureaucracy competent, files, rules and divided labour, also made mass murder administrable. That is the dark side of Weber's ideal type.
Bureaucracies run on rules and measured targets, so Goodhart's law is a constant hazard: officials optimize the metric they are judged by, as with the NHS waiting-time targets of Day 23.

across.link: Robert K. Merton's 'Bureaucratic Structure and Personality' (Social Forces, 1940) named 'goal displacement': officials trained to follow rules come to treat the rules as ends in themselves. It is sociology's account of red tape, the counterpart to Weber's praise of rule-bound administration.

days.apply_question: For about 1,300 years, until 1905, imperial China recruited many of its officials through written civil-service examinations. Using the principal-agent problem, why might an emperor prefer officials chosen by examination to officials chosen by noble birth, even though the exam-chosen owed him no personal loyalty?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the facts of Garfield's assassination and the Pendleton Act. Debated: why Congress passed the Act (public outrage, as Theriault 2003 argues, or partisan insurance), and how large the performance gains from merit systems are. Cross-national evidence, such as Evans and Rauch (1999) on 'Weberian' bureaucracies and economic growth, is correlational; Xu (2018) comes closer to a causal estimate. Value judgment: the right balance between a neutral, protected civil service and elected leaders' control over the officials who carry out their policies.

resource.title: Political Order and Political Decay, Part I: the chapters 'The United States Invents Clientelism' and 'The End of the Spoils System'
resource.creator: Francis Fukuyama (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2014)
resource.why: Places the Pendleton Act within a comparative history of how states moved from patronage to merit (Prussia, Britain, Greece, Italy and the US), and argues that clientelism is an early form of democratic politics rather than simply corruption.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: How regulation works: rules, prices and disclosure
days.headline_hint: The 1952 Smog Killed Perhaps 12,000 Londoners. Much of the Smoke Came From Their Own Fireplaces.
days.concept: Governments change behaviour with a small toolkit: commands (standards and bans), prices (taxes, subsidies and tradable permits) and information (disclosure). The right tool depends on what the regulator can observe, how many sources there are, and how much the cost of compliance differs among them.
days.focus: Teach the regulatory toolkit and how to choose among its instruments: technology versus performance standards, Pigouvian taxes and cap-and-trade (the economics is assumed at CFA level), subsidies, and disclosure such as restaurant hygiene grade cards, plus cost-benefit analysis as government's own test. The angle: Britain's 1956 Clean Air Act worked through zones, bans and grants because the polluters were millions of households, not a few smokestacks.
days.model_or_equation: A choice table rather than an equation, listing for each tool what the regulator must observe and when it works best. Standard: the technology or the emission rate; works with few, similar sources that are easy to inspect. Tax: emissions; fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain; suits cases where marginal damage is flat. Cap-and-trade: emissions; fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain; suits sources whose abatement costs differ widely. Disclosure: only that the information is true; works when buyers or neighbours can act on it. Weitzman's 'Prices vs. Quantities' (1974) formalizes the choice between tax and cap under uncertainty.

story.title: Five days when London could not see its feet
story.hook: On Friday 5 December 1952 a high-pressure system settled over London. Cold, windless air trapped smoke from power stations and from millions of household coal fires beneath a lid of fog. For five days visibility fell to a few metres. Buses crawled behind men carrying flares, a performance at Sadler's Wells was reportedly halted because the audience could no longer see the stage, and prize cattle at the Smithfield Show reportedly choked. Undertakers ran short of coffins. Officials first counted about 4,000 extra deaths; later re-analysis of the mortality records puts the toll at about 12,000. Londoners had complained about coal smoke at least since John Evelyn's Fumifugium of 1661. Even so, the government moved cautiously. It took a committee chaired by Sir Hugh Beaver, and a private member's bill pressed by the MP Gerald Nabarro, before Parliament passed the Clean Air Act in 1956.
story.puzzle: The smoke came from a vast number of small sources: ordinary families' grates, each one trivial, burning cheap coal to keep warm. A tax on smoke would need a meter on every chimney, and a simple ban would leave poor families cold. How do you regulate a fireplace?
story.payoff: You choose the tool that fits what you can observe. The 1956 Act let local councils declare smoke control areas, where burning smoky fuel was banned, which inspectors could enforce by sight. It also paid most of the cost of converting old grates to smokeless fuel, gas or electricity, so compliance did not fall on poor households alone. A command plus a subsidy worked where a price would not, because the regulator could see smoke but could not meter it.
sources: Met Office, 'The Great Smog of 1952'

Michelle L. Bell, Devra L. Davis & Tony Fletcher, 'A retrospective assessment of mortality from the London smog episode of 1952: the role of influenza and pollution', Environmental Health Perspectives 112 (2004)
Clean Air Act 1956 (UK)

days.application: The US Clean Air Act's own cost-benefit test. In 2011 the EPA's retrospective study, 'The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020', estimated benefits of about $2 trillion in 2020 against compliance costs of about $65 billion, roughly 30 to 1. Most of the benefit came from avoiding some 230,000 early deaths in 2020 alone through lower fine-particle pollution. Critics question both the fine-particle mortality estimates and the dollar value placed on each statistical life. The example shows how regulation is justified, and where its numbers are softest.

builds_on.why: In Meadows's terms, a standard changes a parameter, while a tradable permit changes the rules and the information flows (the 1990 sulfur-dioxide market of Day 33). Choosing a tool means choosing a leverage point.
City air is an open-access commons. Each household's smoke harms everyone, which is why voluntary restraint failed and a rule or a price was needed.

across.link: Wang and colleagues ('Persistent sulfate formation from London Fog to Chinese haze', PNAS, 2016) reproduced the 1952 fog's chemistry: nitrogen dioxide in fog droplets rapidly turned coal's sulfur dioxide into sulfuric acid, the same pathway they found in Beijing's winter haze. Knowing the chemistry is what tells a regulator which pollutant, and which source, to target.

days.apply_question: Since 1998 Los Angeles County has required restaurants to display A, B or C hygiene grade cards in their windows. Using the regulatory toolkit, explain why disclosure can improve kitchen hygiene even though it adds no new rule or fine.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the smog's dates, the Clean Air Act 1956, and the basic properties of each instrument. Debated: the size of the 1952 death toll, between about 4,000 and 12,000; the higher figure comes from re-analysis that attributes deaths to pollution rather than influenza. Also debated: the EPA's roughly 30-to-1 ratio of benefits to costs, which rests heavily on fine-particle mortality estimates and on how statistical lives are valued. Value judgment: how to weigh lives against costs, and who should bear the costs; and whether a government should put a price on pollution (accepting some in exchange for money) or forbid it.

resource.title: Policy Evolution under the Clean Air Act
resource.creator: Richard Schmalensee & Robert N. Stavins, Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(4), Fall 2019
resource.length: about 40 minutes for the whole paper; the first half covers the choice of instruments
resource.why: Two leading environmental economists trace fifty years of the US Clean Air Act, showing where it used standards, where it used trading, and why the choice changed. It is the toolkit applied to a real statute, and it is free from the American Economic Association.
