days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: A Railroad Lawyer Told a Railroad Boss to Keep His Regulator. It Could Be 'of Great Use to the Railroads.'
days.concept: Concentrated interests organize more easily than diffuse ones (Olson's logic of collective action), so regulators can drift toward serving the industries they oversee (Stigler's capture theory). But capture is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a law of nature, and institutions can be designed against it (Carpenter & Moss).
days.focus: Teach public choice's core move, treating officials and interest groups as self-interested actors, through Olson (1965) and Stigler (1971). Then teach the corrective: Carpenter and Moss insist on evidence and on degrees of capture (strong versus weak, plus 'cultural capture'). The angle: the 737 MAX shows how delegation, thin resources and close relationships can produce failures that look like capture with no bribes involved.
key_concepts: the logic of collective action (concentrated benefits, diffuse costs)
days.model_or_equation: Olson's asymmetry in numbers. A rule worth $100 million to 10 firms is worth $10 million to each, enough to hire lobbyists. If the same $100 million is spread across 100 million consumers, it costs each of them $1, not worth a phone call. Organized effort follows the concentrated stake, not the total.

story.title: A letter between railroad men
story.hook: In 1887 Congress created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first major federal regulatory agency, in response to farmers' and shippers' fury at railroad rate discrimination. The courts soon began trimming its powers, and Charles E. Perkins, president of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, wanted it abolished altogether. He sought the advice of Richard Olney, a Boston lawyer long retained by railroads, who in March 1893 became Grover Cleveland's Attorney General. Olney's reply, usually dated 28 December 1892, advised against abolition. 'The Commission, as its functions have now been limited by the courts, is, or can be made, of great use to the railroads,' he wrote. 'It satisfies the popular clamor for a government supervision of railroads, at the same time that that supervision is almost entirely nominal.' And: 'the older such a commission gets to be, the more inclined it will be found to take the business and railroad view of things.' The ICC lasted until Congress abolished it at the end of 1995.
story.puzzle: The commission was created to restrain the railroads. Why would a railroad insider want to keep it? And what would have to be true for a regulator to end up serving the industry it was meant to police?
story.payoff: The railroads were few, highly organized, and had far more at stake in each of the commission's decisions than the scattered shippers and farmers did. So they could watch it, argue before it, staff it and shape it: Olson's logic. A commission that looked like protection but leaned the industry's way was more useful to them than no commission at all, because it absorbed public anger while the industry kept its influence. That is capture as Stigler later theorized it. Whether the ICC was in fact captured is still debated by historians.
sources: Richard Olney to Charles E. Perkins, 28 Dec 1892, quoted in Gabriel Kolko, Railroads and Regulation, 1877-1916 (1965)
Interstate Commerce Act (1887); ICC Termination Act (1995)
George J. Stigler, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation', Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2 (1971)

days.application: The Boeing 737 MAX. Under the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization program, Boeing employees did much of the certification work on the agency's behalf. The FAA was not fully informed of how much MCAS had changed, and two crashes killed 346 people (Day 93). The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's 2020 report found failures of FAA oversight and a 'culture of concealment' at Boeing, and Congress passed the Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act in December 2020. The live question is whether this was capture, chronic under-resourcing of the FAA (Congress had pressed the FAA to delegate more, partly to stretch limited staff and budgets), or both.

builds_on.why: The 737 MAX's MCAS design, which relied on a single sensor, is the engineering failure of Day 93. Today's lesson asks why the regulatory check that should have caught it was weak.
Olson's logic is an n-person prisoner's dilemma. Each diffuse consumer's best reply is to free-ride on others' lobbying, so the concentrated side wins by default.

across.link: James Kwak's chapter 'Cultural Capture and the Financial Crisis' (in Carpenter & Moss, eds., Preventing Regulatory Capture, 2014) argues that regulators can be captured without bribes, through shared identity, status and social networks with the people they regulate. It applies conformity and in-group psychology to the financial regulators before 2008.

days.apply_question: The US sugar program keeps domestic sugar prices well above world prices through import quotas and price supports, which benefit relatively few growers and processors while costing consumers more in total. Using Olson's logic, explain why the program has survived decades of criticism from economists across the political spectrum.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the arguments of Olson and Stigler, the text of the Olney letter, and the 737 MAX facts as found by investigators. Debated: how often capture actually happens. Stigler treated it as the rule; Carpenter and Moss (2014) find it is often asserted without evidence and comes in degrees. Historians still argue whether the ICC was captured (Kolko 1965) or merely weak, and analysts disagree whether the FAA's failures on the 737 MAX were capture or under-resourcing. Value judgment: how far to trust expert agencies at all. Public-choice scholars stress government failure as much as market failure; defenders of the administrative state stress the cost of leaving harms unregulated.

resource.title: Preventing Regulatory Capture: Special Interest Influence and How to Limit It (Introduction)
resource.creator: Daniel Carpenter & David A. Moss (eds.), Cambridge University Press / The Tobin Project, 2014
resource.why: The best short corrective to 'capture is everywhere'. It defines capture precisely, distinguishes strong from weak capture, sets out what evidence would show it, and surveys how institutions can be designed to resist it.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge; the Tobin Project has offered the volume's chapters as free PDFs, which was not re-checked. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: Mexico's New President Kept His Rivals' Anti-Poverty Programme. A Randomized Trial Had Made It Hard to Kill.
days.concept: Governments can learn what works by testing policies with randomized and natural experiments. But a result shows what worked there and then; whether it transfers to another place, scale or time (external validity) is a separate question that needs its own evidence.
days.focus: Teach evidence-based policy as applied causal inference: internal versus external validity, the problem of scaling up, and the politics of evidence. The angle: PROGRESA's built-in randomized evaluation helped it survive Mexico's first opposition victory in 71 years, yet did not save it in 2019; and trials run by nudge units show that published effects shrink at scale (DellaVigna & Linos 2022).

story.title: An anti-poverty programme with a control group
story.hook: In 1997 Mexico's deputy finance minister, Santiago Levy, launched PROGRESA. It paid poor rural mothers cash every two months, on condition that their children attended school and the family kept up its clinic visits. Mexican governments had a habit: each new president replaced his predecessor's flagship anti-poverty programme with his own. Levy, by his own later account, built in a defence. There was not enough money to start everywhere at once, so the first rollout was randomized. Of 506 eligible villages, about 320 began receiving payments and about 186 waited, while independent researchers at the International Food Policy Research Institute compared the two groups. In July 2000 Vicente Fox won the presidency, ending 71 years of rule by the PRI, the party that had created PROGRESA.
story.puzzle: Fox's new government had every political reason to scrap a PRI programme. Instead it kept PROGRESA, renamed it Oportunidades in 2002 and extended it to the cities, and many countries copied it. Then in 2019 a later government ended it anyway. What protected the programme for nearly two decades, and why was that protection not permanent?
story.payoff: Credible, public evidence. Because villages had been assigned at random, the evaluation could show that the transfers raised school enrolment, especially for girls in secondary school, and improved health, and that finding belonged to no party. The evidence raised the political cost of killing a programme that demonstrably worked. But evidence answers 'what works'. Whether to fund it is also a question of values and priorities, and a government that weighed them differently could still end it: Hume's gap between is and ought, in budget form.
sources: Santiago Levy, Progress Against Poverty: Sustaining Mexico's Progresa-Oportunidades Program (Brookings, 2006)
T. Paul Schultz, 'School subsidies for the poor: evaluating the Mexican Progresa poverty program', Journal of Development Economics 74 (2004)
International Food Policy Research Institute, PROGRESA evaluation reports (1998-2000)

days.application: The UK Behavioural Insights Team's 2011 tax-letter trial with HM Revenue and Customs. Letters telling late payers that nine out of ten people pay their tax on time, especially when the comparison named the recipient's local area, raised the share who paid within 23 days by several percentage points over the standard letter (Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe & Vlaev, Journal of Public Economics, 2017). The effect was cheap and real, and it also tests scaling: DellaVigna and Linos (Econometrica, 2022) found that trials run by government nudge units average an effect of about 1.4 percentage points, against about 8.7 points in published academic studies. They attribute the gap largely to publication bias and small samples.

builds_on.why: PROGRESA's phased rollout is a randomized controlled trial run by a government: chance, not officials, decided which villages went first, so the difference between groups estimates the programme's effect.
Nudge effects shrink between academic papers and nudge-unit trials because of publication bias, the same mechanism that inflated the published literatures of Day 22.

across.link: Evidence-based policy borrowed its methods from evidence-based medicine. Archie Cochrane's Effectiveness and Efficiency (1972) inspired the Cochrane Collaboration (1993), and the Campbell Collaboration (2000) carried its model of systematic reviews into education, crime and social welfare.

days.apply_question: In 2017-18 Finland ran a randomized basic-income experiment, paying 2,000 unemployed people €560 a month with no conditions. Using the idea of external validity, explain why its results could not settle what would happen if Finland paid a basic income to every adult.
days.evidence_note: Settled: random assignment gives credible estimates of effects in the population tested, and PROGRESA's evaluation is among the most cited in development economics. Debated: how far such results generalize. Deaton and Cartwright (2018) and Vivalt (2020) stress weak external validity; advocates such as Banerjee and Duflo (Nobel 2019) argue that repeated trials across settings build knowledge that transfers. Also debated: how large nudge effects are at scale (DellaVigna & Linos 2022). Value judgment: whether a programme that works should be funded is a separate question of priorities, and conditional transfers raise their own dispute between paternalism and unconditional aid.

resource.title: Social experiments to fight poverty
resource.creator: Esther Duflo, TED2010
resource.why: The future Nobel laureate makes the case for testing anti-poverty policies with randomized trials, using examples from health and education. It is an advocate's account, to set against the brief's critique based on external validity.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the TED talk (about 17 minutes). Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Corruption and how countries escape it
days.headline_hint: A Hong Kong Police Superintendent Couldn't Explain More Than HK$4 Million. He Fled, and the Colony Reset What Everyone Expected.
days.concept: Systemic corruption is an equilibrium of expectations: when everyone expects officials to take bribes, honesty does not pay for any one person. So lasting escapes usually come from 'big bang' changes that reset everyone's expectations at once, not from punishing a few individuals.
days.focus: Teach corruption as a collective-action and coordination problem (Persson, Rothstein & Teorell 2013), not only as a principal-agent problem, with Klitgaard's formula (monopoly plus discretion minus accountability) for the mechanics at the level of a single official. The angle: Hong Kong's ICAC, Georgia's police and nineteenth-century Sweden show that credible, simultaneous change can flip the equilibrium, and that an amnesty for the past may be part of the price.
key_concepts: systemic corruption as a coordination equilibrium
principal-agent versus collective-action views of corruption
days.model_or_equation: Klitgaard's formula, C = M + D − A. Corruption (C) grows with an official's monopoly over a decision (M) and with the discretion in making it (D), and shrinks with accountability (A). Read it as a heuristic, not an equation with units. The coordination view adds that A itself depends on what officials expect their colleagues to do.

story.title: Chief Superintendent Godber's flight
story.hook: In June 1973, after an investigation by Hong Kong's anti-corruption office, at the time a branch of the police force itself, the authorities gave Chief Superintendent Peter Godber a week to explain how he had accumulated more than HK$4 million, several times all the salary he had ever earned. On 8 June he used his airport pass to get past the checks at Kai Tak and flew to England. Hong Kong erupted, and students rallied under the slogan 'Fight Corruption, Catch Godber'. The bribery was not one officer's vice. Syndicates within the police collected regular payments from gambling dens, drug dealers and street hawkers and passed the money up the ranks. Governor Murray MacLehose appointed a commission of inquiry, and on 15 February 1974 created the Independent Commission Against Corruption, answerable to him alone. Godber was extradited in January 1975 and jailed for four years.
story.puzzle: Anti-corruption laws had existed for decades, and the police already had an anti-corruption branch. Why had nothing worked? And how did a colony whose police were among the most corrupt anywhere become, within a generation, one of Asia's cleanest administrations?
story.payoff: Because the problem was an equilibrium, not a few bad apples. Where everyone takes a cut, an honest officer gains nothing and risks his career, and an anti-corruption unit staffed by the same police is part of the system. The ICAC changed expectations all at once: it was independent of the police, well funded, and combined investigation, prevention and public education, so honesty became the safe strategy. When police protests in October 1977 threatened the whole effort, MacLehose granted a partial amnesty for most offences committed before 1977, pardoning the past to make the new expectations credible.
sources: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong), official history of the ICAC
Leslie Palmier, The Control of Bureaucratic Corruption: Case Studies in Asia (1985)
Bo Rothstein, 'Anti-corruption: the indirect "big bang" approach', Review of International Political Economy 18 (2011)

days.application: Georgia after the Rose Revolution. In 2004 the new government dismissed the entire traffic police, a force notorious for roadside bribes (it is often reported at around 15,000 officers, though figures vary), and replaced it with a smaller, better-paid, newly trained patrol police. In later surveys the share of Georgians reporting bribes to public officials was among the lowest in the former Soviet Union. It is a textbook big bang, with a caution: petty bribery fell much more than concerns about elite corruption and political control, which persisted.

builds_on.why: Corruption is a norm in Day 202's sense, a self-enforcing expectation about what others do. Like footbinding or drunk driving, it changes when expectations shift together, not person by person.
Honest and corrupt administration are two equilibria of the same coordination game: each official's best reply depends on what the others do.

across.link: Gächter and Schulz ('Intrinsic honesty and the prevalence of rule violations across societies', Nature, 2016) gave the same die-rolling honesty test to 2,568 young people in 23 countries. They found more dishonest reporting where an index of corruption, tax evasion and electoral fraud was higher, evidence that institutional corruption shapes individual honesty.

days.apply_question: Since August 2016 Ukraine has required its public bodies to buy through ProZorro, an open online procurement system that publishes every government tender and bid. Using the equilibrium view of corruption, explain why making every contract public at once might work better than prosecuting a few corrupt procurement officials.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the reform sequences in Hong Kong and Georgia; corruption is strongly correlated with poverty and weak institutions. Debated: whether corruption is better modelled as a principal-agent problem (monitor and punish individuals) or a collective-action problem (Persson, Rothstein & Teorell 2013); whether gradual reform can work where a big bang is politically impossible; and how lasting Georgia's gains are. Indices such as Transparency International's measure perceptions, not bribes paid. Value judgment: whether an amnesty for past corruption is a fair price for future honesty.

resource.title: Fighting Corruption in Public Services: Chronicling Georgia's Reforms
resource.creator: World Bank (Directions in Development series, 2012)
resource.length: about 25 minutes for the chapter on the patrol police
resource.why: A detailed, sourced account of how Georgia dismissed and rebuilt its traffic police, cut red tape and changed expectations: the mechanics of a 'big bang' that the brief can only summarize. It is an official and largely sympathetic account, written before later concerns about elite corruption.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the World Bank report, which is free from the World Bank's Open Knowledge Repository. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: She Held Up a 'No War' Sign on Russia's Evening News. The State's First Answer Was a Fine.
days.concept: Most modern autocrats survive less by mass terror than by manipulating information: selective censorship, propaganda that projects competence, co-opting elites and staging elections, with violence held in reserve. Guriev and Treisman (2022) call this 'spin dictatorship'.
days.focus: Teach the shift from 'fear dictators' to 'spin dictators' and their toolkit: censorship aimed at collective action rather than at criticism, co-optation, legitimacy earned by performance, and managed elections, together with the evidence for it (King, Pan & Roberts 2013). The angle: spin is a strategy, not a permanent condition. Under the strain of war, Russia moved back toward fear, criminalizing 'fakes' about its army in March 2022.

story.title: Live on Channel One
story.hook: On the evening of Monday 14 March 2022, less than three weeks into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Marina Ovsyannikova, an editor at the state broadcaster Channel One, stepped behind the presenter of Vremya, the country's most-watched news programme. She held a hand-lettered sign: 'NO WAR. Stop the war. Don't believe the propaganda. They are lying to you here.' Ten days earlier Russia had made spreading 'knowingly false information' about its armed forces a crime punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Ovsyannikova was detained and questioned for about 14 hours, then fined 30,000 rubles, a few hundred dollars, for an online video calling for protests. Months later, after a one-woman street protest, she was charged under the new law and placed under house arrest. She escaped with her daughter, and in 2023 she was sentenced in absentia to eight and a half years.
story.puzzle: A regime that had just made criticism of its war a serious crime answered the most visible protest against that war, broadcast on its own flagship channel, with a fine. Why the light touch, and why did it not last?
story.payoff: Spin dictators prefer to avoid visible, dramatic repression, which creates martyrs and damages the image of a popular, competent government. They rely instead on controlling what most people see and on quiet, targeted pressure, and the fine fitted that playbook. The later criminal case fitted the other playbook. As the war raised the stakes, Russia moved back toward fear, with mass arrests and long sentences for dissent: a shift that many analysts, Guriev and Treisman among them, have described since the invasion.
sources: News reports of 14-15 Mar 2022 (for example BBC News and Reuters) on Ovsyannikova's protest and fine
Russian federal law of 4 Mar 2022 adding Article 207.3 to the Criminal Code
Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Spin Dictators: The Changing Face of Tyranny in the 21st Century (2022)

days.application: China's internet censorship. King, Pan and Roberts (American Political Science Review, 2013) collected millions of posts from Chinese social-media sites before the censors could act. Posts criticizing the state, its leaders and its policies were not especially likely to be deleted. Posts with collective-action potential, calling for or reporting on protests whatever their politics, were deleted far more often. A follow-up (APSR, 2017) estimated that the government fabricates about 448 million social-media posts a year, mostly cheerleading and distraction rather than argument.

builds_on.why: The Great Leap famine showed fear-based rule destroying the information its rulers needed. Spin dictators try to keep accurate information flowing to themselves while controlling what the public sees.

Granovetter's threshold model (Day 28) explains why censors target collective action. A protest can tip from a few people to many, so the regime suppresses the signals that let people see how many others would join.

across.link: China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, in force from 15 August 2023, require generated content to 'adhere to core socialist values'. The censorship apparatus now reaches from posts written by people to text written by models.

days.apply_question: Before Russia's 2024 presidential election, the authorities barred the anti-war candidate Boris Nadezhdin from the ballot over alleged flaws in his supporters' signatures, after long public queues had formed to sign for him. Using the spin-dictator toolkit, explain why a regime certain of winning would still keep him off the ballot rather than let him lose.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the facts of Ovsyannikova's case and of Russia's March 2022 law. King, Pan and Roberts's findings were supported by their later experimental work (Science, 2014). Debated: how large the shift from fear to spin really is (Guriev and Treisman's coding of regimes is contested); whether Russia since 2022 is best described as a spin dictatorship under strain or as a return to fear; and how much performance legitimacy explains in China. Value judgment: whether a regime that delivers growth and order but denies free expression can be legitimate. That is the gap between descriptive and normative legitimacy from Day 236.

resource.title: Informational Autocrats
resource.creator: Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(4), Fall 2019
resource.why: The authors' own compact statement of the spin-dictator model and the evidence for it: the falling share of autocrats who resort to mass killing, and the rise of co-optation and media manipulation. It is free from the American Economic Association; their book Spin Dictators (2022) expands it.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge: JEP 33(4), Fall 2019, the same issue as Day 243's resource; free from the American Economic Association. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: On the Day Baptists Gave Jefferson a 1,235-Pound Cheese, He Wrote Baptists About a 'Wall of Separation.'
days.concept: States arrange their relation to religion along a spectrum: establishment, cooperation, separation and laïcité. The modern idea of religious liberty grew substantially, alongside Enlightenment arguments, from Christian dissenters' argument that coerced faith is not faith, an argument the Catholic Church formally adopted in Dignitatis Humanae (1965).
days.focus: Teach the church-state spectrum through real cases (England's established church, Germany's church tax, the US First Amendment, France's 1905 law) and the theology behind religious liberty, from Roger Williams's 'hedge or wall of separation' (1644) to Dignitatis Humanae. The angle: devout Baptists asked for the 'wall' to protect religion from the state, and its legal meaning in the US is still moving (Everson 1947, Lemon 1971, Kennedy v. Bremerton 2022).
key_concepts: incorporation (applying the First Amendment to the states)
Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom as a right of the person)
days.model_or_equation: The spectrum as a <dl>. Establishment: an official state church (England, Denmark). Cooperation: the state recognizes churches and collects taxes for them, and the churches govern themselves (Germany). Separation, whether accommodating or strict: no established church, with free exercise protected (the US). Laïcité: the republic recognizes, pays and subsidizes no religion and keeps religion out of public institutions (France since 1905).

story.title: A cheese, a letter and a sermon
story.hook: On New Year's Day 1802 the Baptist preacher John Leland presented President Thomas Jefferson with a 'Mammoth Cheese' of about 1,235 pounds, made by the farmers of Cheshire, Massachusetts, in thanks for his defence of religious liberty. The same day Jefferson signed a reply to another group of Baptists, the Danbury Baptist Association of Connecticut. In October 1801 they had written to him as a persecuted minority. Connecticut still had an established Congregational church, and they complained that the religious privileges they enjoyed were treated 'as favors granted, and not as inalienable rights'. Jefferson answered that the First Amendment had built 'a wall of separation between Church & State'. Two days later, on Sunday 3 January, he attended a service in the chamber of the House of Representatives at which Leland preached.
story.puzzle: The 'wall of separation' is now quoted mostly to keep religion out of public life. Why did devout Baptists ask for it? Why did Connecticut keep its established church until 1818, decades after the First Amendment? And how could the man who coined the phrase go to church in the Capitol?
story.payoff: Because the wall was built to protect religion from the state as much as the state from religion. Dissenting Protestants, from Roger Williams to the Baptists and Quakers, argued that faith under compulsion is not faith, so a government that funds and polices one church wrongs all the others. The First Amendment originally bound only Congress, so state establishments survived (Massachusetts kept its church until 1833) until the Supreme Court applied the Amendment to the states in the 1940s. And separation never meant that officials must not worship. It meant the government may not establish or coerce religion; where that line falls is what the courts still argue about.
sources: Danbury Baptist Association to Thomas Jefferson, 7 Oct 1801, and Jefferson's reply, 1 Jan 1802 (Library of Congress)
James H. Hutson, ''A Wall of Separation': FBI Helps Restore Jefferson's Obliterated Draft', Library of Congress Information Bulletin (June 1998)
Library of Congress exhibition 'Religion and the Founding of the American Republic' (the Cheshire cheese and Leland's sermon)

days.application: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (27 June 2022). By 6 votes to 3, the Supreme Court held that a public-school football coach's brief prayer at midfield after games was protected by the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses. The Court said it had 'long ago abandoned' the Lemon test of 1971 (which asked about secular purpose, primary effect and excessive entanglement) in favour of reading the Establishment Clause by 'historical practices and understandings'. The dissent argued that the ruling let a school endorse prayer and pressure students. It is a live case of where the wall now stands.

builds_on.why: The wars of religion ended in settlements that slowly produced toleration. Roger Williams's Rhode Island and Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (Day 198) are the direct ancestors of the Danbury Baptists' argument.

Religious-market theorists (Stark and Finke, Day 207) argue that America's disestablished churches competed and grew while state churches stagnated. That is a claim about the consequences of the church-state model itself.

across.link: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948) includes the freedom to change one's religion. Saudi Arabia, objecting partly to that clause, was among the eight states that abstained, so religious liberty became both an international norm and a fault line in the same text.

days.apply_question: Sweden's Lutheran church ceased to be the state church on 1 January 2000. Using the dissenters' argument for religious liberty, what case could a committed Swedish Lutheran make that disestablishment was good for the church itself?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the dates and texts (the Danbury exchange, the 1905 French law, Dignitatis Humanae, the holding in Kennedy v. Bremerton). Debated: what the Establishment Clause originally meant. Separationists, following Everson (1947), read the wall broadly; accommodationists argue it barred a national church and coercion, not public religious expression. Also debated: whether disestablishment strengthens religion (Stark and Finke) or simply accompanies its decline. Value judgment: how much public space religion should have. Christian traditions disagree among themselves, from established churches to the Baptist and Anabaptist insistence on separation, while Catholic teaching since 1965 grounds religious freedom in the dignity of the person.

resource.title: 'A Wall of Separation': FBI Helps Restore Jefferson's Obliterated Draft
resource.creator: James H. Hutson, Library of Congress Information Bulletin (June 1998)
resource.why: The Library of Congress's manuscripts chief uses the restored draft to show what Jefferson deleted from the Danbury letter and why, evidence that the 'wall' was also a political move. It sets the Baptists' letter and Jefferson's reply side by side.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the Library of Congress article. Not re-checked in the verifier pass: the shared web-search budget was exhausted and WebFetch could not reach any host. No URL; cite without a link.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 15: The FDA, drug regulation built by disasters
days.headline_hint: A Raspberry-Flavoured Medicine Killed More Than 100 People in 1937. The Law Could Only Charge a Misleading Word.
days.concept: How does a society decide when a medicine is safe and effective enough to sell? In the US the answer was written mostly by disasters and protests, each of which tightened or loosened the rules, so drug regulation behaves like a balancing loop with long delays.
days.focus: Walk the US drug-regulation system through the chain as a loop. A sulfa drug in a toxic solvent (1937) produced the 1938 safety law; thalidomide and Frances Kelsey (1961-62) produced the 1962 efficacy law; AIDS activists (1988) produced accelerated approval; user fees (1992) bought faster reviews; Vioxx (2004) tightened the rules after approval. The angle: the FDA is both gatekeeper and promoter, and its two kinds of error differ in visibility. The victims of a bad approval have names; the victims of a delayed good drug mostly do not.
key_concepts: two kinds of regulatory error (the 'invisible graveyard')
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. B1, the safety loop (balancing): a drug disaster brings public outrage, then stricter pre-market rules, so fewer harmful drugs reach patients and disasters become rarer. It acts with a delay of years. B2, the access loop (balancing in the opposite direction): stricter rules mean slower, costlier approvals; patients die waiting, mostly unseen; organized patients and industry push back; faster pathways follow (accelerated approval in 1992, breakthrough-therapy designation in 2012). R1, the funding loop (reinforcing, with capture risk): user fees pay for more reviewers and firm deadlines, approvals speed up, industry supports renewing the fees every five years, and the agency's budget comes to depend more on the industry it regulates. B1 and B2 together, with their delays, produce oscillation (Day 27): the rules tighten after each scandal and loosen after each era of frustration. Documented reversal: regulation followed disasters instead of anticipating them, and in 1937 the government could prosecute only under a labelling rule.

story.title: Taste of raspberries
story.hook: In September 1937 the S. E. Massengill Company of Bristol, Tennessee, began shipping 'Elixir Sulfanilamide', a liquid form of the new sulfa antibacterial that children could swallow. The company's chief chemist, Harold Cole Watkins, had found that the drug dissolved in diethylene glycol, a sweet-tasting solvent closely related to the ethylene glycol in antifreeze, and added raspberry flavouring. The firm tested the mixture for flavour, appearance and fragrance but not for toxicity, and no law required it to. Within weeks people in Tulsa and across the South were dying of kidney failure. FDA inspectors fanned out to trace every shipment and recovered most of the roughly 240 gallons, but more than 100 people died, many of them children. A Tulsa mother, Maise Nidiffer, wrote to President Roosevelt describing her daughter's death. Watkins later killed himself. The only charge the government could bring was misbranding: an 'elixir' was supposed to contain alcohol, and this one contained none.
story.puzzle: A company had sold a lethal medicine across the country, and the law could punish it only for a misleading word on the label. How does a society decide when a medicine is safe and effective enough to sell, and why were America's rules written, again and again, by disasters?
story.payoff: Because political attention follows visible catastrophe. Within a year Congress passed the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, signed on 25 June 1938, which required evidence of safety before a drug could be sold. Thalidomide did the same for efficacy in 1962, AIDS activists for speed in 1988-92, and Vioxx for monitoring after approval in 2007. Each disaster tightened one loop, and each period of delay loosened another. Today's rules are the residue of that oscillation, not the product of a single design.
sources: Carol Ballentine, 'Taste of Raspberries, Taste of Death: The 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide Incident', FDA Consumer (June 1981)
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 25 June 1938
Daniel Carpenter, Reputation and Power: Organizational Image and Pharmaceutical Regulation at the FDA (2010)

days.application: The system itself: US drug regulation from Elixir Sulfanilamide (1937) to the FDA's 2021 accelerated approval of aducanumab. For contrast, The Gambia in 2022, where cough syrups contaminated with diethylene glycol were linked to the deaths of about 70 children (WHO alert, October 2022): the 1937 chemistry recurring where testing capacity was thin.

builds_on.why: The 1962 amendments' demand for 'adequate and well-controlled investigations' made the randomized controlled trial the legal standard for proving efficacy.
How much evidence is enough before approval depends on the cost of each kind of error: inductive risk, which Day 42 applied to the FDA's 2021 approval of aducanumab.
Frances Kelsey's refusal to approve thalidomide is Weberian bureaucracy at its best: a protected, expert official applying the rules against company pressure.
Since 1992 user fees have made the agency's drug-review budget depend partly on the regulated industry, the structural setup capture theory warns about.

across.link: Product-liability litigation acts as a second regulator. Merck withdrew Vioxx in September 2004 and in November 2007 agreed to a $4.85 billion settlement of US claims: tort law putting a price on a risk the approval system had missed.

days.apply_question: Was the FDA's December 2020 emergency authorization of the first COVID-19 vaccines, after trials lasting months rather than years, a defensible move of the evidence bar? What would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to answer?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the disasters and the laws they produced (1937-38, 1961-62, 2004-07); the toxicity of diethylene glycol and thalidomide; PDUFA shortened review times. Debated: whether FDA stringency costs more lives through delay than it saves through screening, with Peltzman (1973) and later 'drug lag' critics on one side and defenders such as Carpenter, who credit the agency's reputation for the public trust that makes new drugs usable, on the other. Also debated: whether user fees compromise safety (Carpenter, Zucker & Avorn, NEJM 2008), and how much accelerated approval on surrogate endpoints actually helps patients. Value judgment: whose risk it is to take, patients' autonomy (the 2018 Right to Try Act) or protection of the vulnerable. Consequentialists count total lives, deontologists stress consent, and Christian traditions (natural law, Catholic social teaching's common good) emphasize protecting the weakest. Ask who gained (patients, firms), who paid (victims, taxpayers, those left waiting) and who consented. The counterfactual, how many would have died under looser or tighter rules, cannot be observed.

chain.point: Bacterial infections were leading killers. Sulfanilamide, the active part of Prontosil (Gerhard Domagk's discovery that it fights bacteria was published in 1935), was among the first broadly effective antibacterial drugs, and doctors wanted a liquid form for children with streptococcal infections.

Sulfanilamide dissolves poorly in water. Watkins chose diethylene glycol as the solvent because it dissolved the drug, without testing whether it was toxic; the body breaks it down into compounds that destroy the kidneys. The same contamination has killed again and again wherever testing was weak, including in The Gambia in 2022 (about 70 children; WHO alert, October 2022).

Massengill's 'control laboratory' checked flavour, appearance and fragrance. Modern drug production runs under current Good Manufacturing Practice regulations (first issued in 1963), which require documented, tested control of every ingredient and every batch.

The 1938 Act required evidence of safety before sale. In 1960-62 the FDA medical officer Frances Kelsey refused to clear thalidomide, which caused severe birth defects in perhaps 10,000 children abroad. The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 10 October 1962 added proof of efficacy and a requirement of informed consent.

Efficacy must rest on 'substantial evidence' from 'adequate and well-controlled investigations', which in practice means randomized trials. Where to set the bar trades approving bad drugs against delaying good ones, as in the 2021 accelerated approval of aducanumab against its advisory committee's advice.

Named at CFA level, not taught: under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (1992), firms pay fees that fund reviewers in return for review-time goals, and median review times fell sharply. Developing a new drug is estimated to cost from about $1 billion to $2.6 billion, counting failures and the cost of capital (Wouters et al. 2020; DiMasi et al. 2016), so the evidence standard is also a cost standard.

On 11 October 1988 ACT UP's 'Seize Control of the FDA' demonstration brought more than a thousand protesters to the agency's headquarters in Rockville, Maryland, to demand faster access to AIDS drugs. The FDA created expedited procedures (1988) and accelerated approval on surrogate endpoints (1992).

The two kinds of error differ in visibility: the victims of thalidomide and Vioxx had faces, while patients harmed by delay mostly did not. Sam Peltzman (Journal of Political Economy, 1973) estimated that the 1962 amendments cut new-drug introductions by more than half with no measurable gain in quality, a claim others dispute. Vioxx, withdrawn on 30 September 2004, was estimated by the FDA scientist David Graham to have caused tens of thousands of excess heart attacks and strokes.

Each disaster tightened the rules (1938, 1962, and the 2007 FDA Amendments Act after Vioxx), and each era of frustration loosened them (1992, the 2012 breakthrough-therapy designation, the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016): a balancing loop with long delays, so it oscillates. Carpenter, Zucker and Avorn (NEJM, 2008) found that drugs approved just before PDUFA deadlines had more safety problems later.

Courts are a second regulator. Product-liability suits (such as Merck's 2007 Vioxx settlement) and judicial review of agency rules shape what the FDA can do; the Law block teaches tort and product liability, and administrative law.

Medicines and their ingredients cross borders faster than any national regulator can reach (the Gambian syrups were made in India), which is why the WHO issues global alerts and regulators harmonize standards. The International Relations block takes up international institutions.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: What is law? Legal positivism and natural law
days.headline_hint: In 1944 a German Wife Turned In Her Husband Under Nazi Law. In 1949 a Court Convicted Her. Which Was the Law?
days.concept: Legal positivism holds that whether a rule is law depends on its source (valid enactment under the rule of recognition a legal system actually uses) and not on its justice, while natural-law theory holds that a gravely unjust rule fails as law, either because it lacks law's inner morality (Fuller) or because its injustice is intolerable (the Radbruch formula).
days.focus: Teach positivism's separation of law from morality, and its rival, through the 1958 Hart-Fuller exchange in the Harvard Law Review, which used one postwar German case as its test. The angle: both men argued over what the Bamberg court had done, and H. O. Pappe (1960) showed that it had done something narrower. Check the facts before building a theory on them.
key_concepts: legal positivism and the separation thesis
the rule of recognition (Hart, The Concept of Law, 1961)
Fuller's inner morality of law (eight demands of legality, set out in The Morality of Law, 1964)
nulla poena sine lege (no punishment without a prior law)
days.model_or_equation: Two tests side by side. The positivist test: a rule is law if it was made in a way the system's rule of recognition accepts (passed by the legislature, laid down by the courts), whatever its merits. Whether to obey it is a separate moral question. Fuller's test (The Morality of Law, 1964): a system is law only to the degree that it meets eight demands of legality. Its rules must be general, public, prospective, clear, consistent with each other, possible to obey and reasonably stable, and officials must apply them as written. Radbruch's formula (1946): enacted law prevails even when unjust, unless its conflict with justice is so intolerable that it must yield.

story.title: A wife, a denunciation and a court in Bamberg
story.hook: In 1944 a German soldier home on leave from the army spoke bitterly to his wife about Hitler. His wife, who by the account later given in court wanted to be rid of him, reported his remarks to the authorities. The regime's statutes made such remarks a crime. A military court sentenced him to death, but the sentence was not carried out: after a time in prison he was sent back to the front. In 1949 the wife was convicted, in a judgment upheld by the regional court of appeal at Bamberg, of illegally depriving her husband of his liberty, under a provision of the 1871 Criminal Code that had never been repealed. A short note in the Harvard Law Review (1951) reported the case as though the court had declared the Nazi statutes void, as contrary to 'the sound conscience and sense of justice of all decent human beings'. In 1958 H. L. A. Hart and Lon Fuller both took it as their test case in a celebrated exchange in that journal.
story.puzzle: She had used the law exactly as the state of the day meant it to be used. If those statutes were valid law, what crime had she committed? And if they were not law, what had sent her husband to a death cell?
story.payoff: Hart answered as a positivist. The Nazi statutes were law, but law too wicked to obey. If Germany wanted to punish her, it should do so openly with a retroactive statute and admit the cost. Fuller answered from law's inner morality. A regime of secret, retroactive and arbitrary commands had stopped being a legal order at all, so restoring legality required treating its worst rules as not law. Then in 1960 Pappe read the Bamberg judgment itself. The court had not declared the statutes void. It upheld the conviction on narrower grounds: she had no legal duty to inform on her husband, and she had used the courts as a tool to get rid of him. The two theories tell you what each man needed the case to be, and the episode shows why the facts mattered.
sources: H. L. A. Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958): 593-629
Lon L. Fuller, 'Positivism and Fidelity to Law: A Reply to Professor Hart', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958): 630-672
Recent Cases note on the 1949 Bamberg judgment, Harvard Law Review 64 (1951): 1005
H. O. Pappe, 'On the Validity of Judicial Decisions in the Nazi Era', Modern Law Review 23 (1960)

days.application: The Nuremberg trial of the major war criminals (20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946). The London Charter of 8 August 1945 made 'crimes against humanity' punishable 'whether or not in violation of the domestic law of the country where perpetrated', and its Article 8 provided that acting on the orders of a government or a superior did not free a defendant from responsibility, though it could be weighed in mitigation. Defence counsel objected that the court was punishing acts, above all the waging of aggressive war, that no law had made crimes when they were done (nulla poena sine lege). The tribunal replied that the maxim is 'not a limitation of sovereignty, but is in general a principle of justice', and that it would be more unjust to let the aggressors go unpunished. It convicted 19 of the 22 defendants and sentenced 12 to death. This is the Hart-Fuller dispute in practice: a court refusing to let legality under national law settle whether an act was a crime. (The Nuremberg Code of 1947, from Day 46, is a different document, produced by a later trial of doctors.)

builds_on.why: Day 48's natural-law tradition is the moral root of today's legal dispute. In Birmingham, King cited Augustine ('an unjust law is no law at all') and Aquinas (an unjust law is 'a human law that is not rooted in eternal law and natural law'). Fuller and Radbruch restate a version of that view in legal terms; today asks what it means for a judge.

Weimar democracy was dismantled through steps that each had legal form, ending in the Enabling Act of March 1933. Positivism asks whether legal form is enough to make a rule law, and natural-law theory says it is not.

across.link: The London Charter's Article 8 refused 'superior orders' as a defence. In 1961, the year Adolf Eichmann was tried in Jerusalem, Stanley Milgram began his Yale obedience experiments, which asked how far ordinary people will follow an authority's orders (Day 161). Law asks whether obedience can excuse an act; psychology asks how often obedience happens. They are different questions about the same act, and a high rate of obedience in the experiments (itself debated, as Day 161 showed) does not answer the legal one.

days.apply_question: In the 1990s German courts, citing Radbruch's formula, upheld the convictions of East German border guards who had shot people fleeing over the Berlin Wall, even though East Germany's own border law had been read to permit the shootings. Would Hart's route, a retroactive statute openly declared as such, have been more honest than the courts' approach, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: what Hart, Fuller and Radbruch argued; the Nuremberg Charter's terms; Pappe's correction of how the Bamberg reasoning was reported. Debated: whether positivism or natural-law theory gives the better account of what law is. Hart's successors (Raz, Green) and natural lawyers (Finnis, who adopts much of Hart's method) still dispute it. Also debated: whether Nuremberg was retroactive justice. Value judgment: whether a judge should ever refuse to apply a valid but wicked statute. The Christian natural-law tradition (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II q.96 a.4, which calls unjust laws 'acts of violence rather than laws') is one voice; secular positivists and secular natural lawyers also take positions.

resource.title: Legal Positivism
resource.creator: Leslie Green and Thomas Adams, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (entry first published 2003, substantively revised 2019)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the opening sections
resource.why: A leading positivist states exactly what positivism claims and what it does not: it is not a theory that law ought to be obeyed. The entry discusses the natural-law challenges to positivism, and it gives the Hart side a precision a 15-minute lesson cannot. It is written from inside the positivist tradition.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Common law and precedent: how judges grow the law
days.headline_hint: No One Ever Proved There Was a Snail in May Donoghue's Ginger Beer. Her Case Still Rewrote the Law Across the Common-Law World.
days.concept: In the common law, judges decide new cases by reasoning from earlier decisions (stare decisis), so the binding part of each decision (its ratio decidendi) is extended, narrowed or distinguished case by case, and the law grows by analogy rather than from a code.
days.focus: Teach precedent as a method: binding and persuasive authority, ratio and obiter dicta, distinguishing and overruling, and Edward Levi's 'reasoning by example'. The angle: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) never established a single fact, because the case settled before trial. Its principle still governs negligence across the common-law world, and Lord Atkin built it partly from an American car-wheel case.
days.model_or_equation: Levi's three-step 'reasoning by example' (An Introduction to Legal Reasoning, 1949). First, a judge sees a similarity between the new case and earlier ones. Second, the judge announces the rule inherent in the earlier case. Third, the judge applies that rule to the new case. The rule changes as it is applied, because each new case decides which similarities count.

story.title: A snail in a bottle in Paisley
story.hook: On the evening of Sunday 26 August 1928 May Donoghue, a shop assistant of about thirty, sat in Francis Minchella's Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow. A friend bought her an ice-cream float, and Minchella poured ginger beer over the ice cream from a dark, opaque bottle. Mrs Donoghue drank some. When her friend poured out the rest, Mrs Donoghue later alleged, the decomposed remains of a snail floated out. She said she suffered shock and gastroenteritis. She could not sue the café, because she had bought nothing and so had no contract with it, and the courts had generally held that a manufacturer owed nothing to a consumer it had no contract with, unless the product was dangerous in itself. So her solicitor, Walter Leechman, sued the manufacturer, David Stevenson, for £500. Leechman had recently lost a similar case over dead mice in ginger-beer bottles. On 26 May 1932 the House of Lords held, by three votes to two, that she had a case.
story.puzzle: No statute gave her a claim, and the two dissenting law lords said no earlier case did either. Stevenson died before any trial, the claim was settled, and no court ever found that there had been a snail. How can a case with no proven facts become one of the most cited cases in the English-speaking world? And where did the judges get the rule they announced?
story.payoff: They got it from precedent, by analogy. Lord Atkin searched the scattered earlier cases, English and American, including Cardozo's 1916 judgment in MacPherson v. Buick. He looked for the principle that unified them and stated it as a rule: take reasonable care not to injure your 'neighbour', meaning anyone so closely and directly affected by your act that you ought to have them in mind. The facts did not need to be proved, because the Lords were deciding a question of law: if this happened, does she have a claim? That answer became the binding ratio, and judges have extended, narrowed and distinguished it ever since. That is how the common law grows.
sources: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (HL), decided 26 May 1932
Matthew Chapman, The Snail and the Ginger Beer: The Singular Case of Donoghue v Stevenson (Wildy, Simmonds & Hill, 2010)

days.application: The civil-law alternative: the French Civil Code of 21 March 1804, the Code Napoléon. The principle that took the House of Lords a long line of cases to reach, the Code stated as a general rule in one sentence, Article 1382 (renumbered 1240 in 2016): any act by which a person causes damage to another obliges the person at fault to repair it. Article 5 forbade judges to lay down general rules when deciding cases, to keep law-making with the legislature. In practice the contrast has softened. French judges built much of their liability law by interpreting a few short articles: the Cour de cassation's Jand'heur decision of 13 February 1930, over a girl run down by a lorry, made the 'guardian' of a thing such as a motor vehicle presumptively liable for the harm it does. Meanwhile common-law countries now legislate heavily. Yet the starting points still differ: in civil law the code comes first and cases apply it; in common law the cases come first and statutes are laid over them. On the car chain, the Jand'heur ruling sits at the liability side of regulation.

builds_on.why: Precedent is path dependence by design. Early decisions constrain later ones, which makes the law predictable but can lock in a bad rule until a court is willing to overrule it.

Reasoning from precedent generalizes from particular cases to a rule, so it shares induction's gap: no finite set of past cases fixes the rule, and nothing in the old cases alone tells the judge which of their features matter for the new one.

across.link: Lord Atkin made the link himself: 'The rule that you are to love your neighbour becomes in law, you must not injure your neighbour; and the lawyer's question, Who is my neighbour? receives a restricted reply.' The lawyer's question is from the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29). The analogy breaks at one point: the parable demands help, while the law's duty is only to avoid injuring, and English law still imposes no general duty to rescue.

days.apply_question: In Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990) a company bought shares relying on audited accounts that overstated profits, and the House of Lords held that the auditors owed no duty of care to investors at large. Using how the common law extends and limits a principle case by case, why might judges who accept Lord Atkin's neighbour principle still refuse to stretch it this far?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the doctrine of precedent and the holdings described. Debated: whether the common law tends towards efficient rules. Priest (1977) and Rubin (1977) argued that inefficient rules are litigated more often and so get replaced. Also debated: whether common-law countries have done better economically than civil-law ones. The 'legal origins' research (La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer, 2008) says yes; critics stress colonial history and other confounders. Little value judgment arises, apart from the standing trade-off between certainty and flexibility.

resource.title: An Introduction to Legal Reasoning: the section on case law
resource.creator: Edward H. Levi (University of Chicago Press, 1949; first published in the University of Chicago Law Review, 1948)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the section on case law
resource.why: The classic short account of reasoning by example. Levi follows one rule, the liability of makers of 'inherently dangerous' things, from Winterbottom v Wright (1842) to MacPherson v. Buick (1916), and shows how a rule shifts each time a court applies it. It works the method through real cases at a length the lesson cannot.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.headline_hint: One Man Chased the Fox. Another Killed It and Walked Off With It. New York's Supreme Court Had to Decide Whose It Was.
days.concept: Property is a bundle of rights over a thing (to use it, exclude others from it and transfer it) that the state stands ready to enforce. The rules that assign it, such as first possession, are chosen for the behaviour they produce, and rights tend to be defined more sharply once a resource becomes valuable enough to fight over (Demsetz 1967).
days.focus: Teach property as a bundle of enforceable rights, using Pierson v. Post's choice between rewarding the chase and rewarding the kill, then Demsetz's theory of why property rights emerge. The angle: a property rule is both an incentive and a signal to strangers (Carol Rose). The best evidence on what secure title does comes from a natural experiment in Buenos Aires, which supports the investment effects of title but not Hernando de Soto's promised credit boom.
key_concepts: the bundle of rights (use, exclusion, transfer)
first possession and the rule of capture
Demsetz's theory of the emergence of property rights
clear rules versus flexible standards ('crystals and mud', Rose 1988)
days.model_or_equation: Demsetz's condition, in words: property rights over a resource are worth creating when the gains from ending its overuse or underinvestment exceed the costs of defining, monitoring and enforcing them. A rise in the resource's value (Demsetz's example: the fur trade and beaver) or a fall in enforcement costs (Anderson and Hill's 1975 example: barbed wire on the American plains from the 1870s) tips the balance toward private rights.

story.title: A dead fox on a Southampton beach
story.hook: Around the turn of the nineteenth century, on a stretch of empty beach at Southampton on the eastern end of Long Island, Lodowick Post and his hounds were in full chase after a fox. Jesse Pierson, who, Post alleged, knew whose hunt it was, intercepted the fox, killed it and carried it off. A fox was worth very little, but Post sued and won before a local justice of the peace, and Pierson appealed. In 1805 New York's Supreme Court heard arguments that cited Justinian, Bracton, Grotius and Pufendorf. Justice Daniel Tompkins, for the majority, held for Pierson: chasing a wild animal, even with hounds and every hope of success, gave no ownership. Only capture, a mortal wound or a trap did. Justice Brockholst Livingston dissented. The fox, he wrote, was a 'wild and noxious beast', the hunter who rid farmers of it deserved protection, and the question should have been left to 'the arbitration of sportsmen'. Historians have since argued that the lawsuit also carried quarrels between the two families (Berger 2006; Fernandez 2018).
story.puzzle: Post did all the work; Pierson did almost none. Why should the man who merely finished the job own the fox?
story.payoff: Because a property rule is chosen for what it makes everyone else do, not to reward one person. A capture rule is crystal clear: anyone can see who holds the fox, so strangers know what not to take, and courts rarely have to judge a chase. Livingston's rule would reward the effort that kills more foxes, but every disputed chase would need a judge. Possession, as Carol Rose put it, is a message to the world. Demsetz explains why the court could live with a blunt rule: with foxes nearly worthless, nothing was gained by more refined rights. When a resource becomes valuable, people invest in sharper rights.
sources: Pierson v. Post, 3 Cai. R. 175 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1805)
Bethany R. Berger, 'It's Not About the Fox: The Untold History of Pierson v. Post', Duke Law Journal 55 (2006)
Angela Fernandez, Pierson v. Post, the Hunt for the Fox: Law and Professionalization in American Legal Culture (Cambridge University Press, 2018)

days.application: Land titles for squatters in Buenos Aires. In 1981 roughly 1,800 families occupied vacant land in San Francisco Solano, in the Quilmes district on the edge of Buenos Aires. In 1984 the provincial government expropriated the land to give the occupiers title. Some former owners accepted compensation; others fought in the courts for years. Whether a family got title therefore depended on the former owner's legal choices, not on the family: a natural experiment. Galiani and Schargrodsky (Journal of Public Economics, 2010) found that titled families invested more in their houses, had smaller households and invested more in their children's education. They gained little access to credit, contrary to Hernando de Soto's claim (The Mystery of Capital, 2000) that titling unlocks 'dead capital' through mortgages.

builds_on.why: The Buenos Aires evidence rests on Day 21's logic: an accident of the courts assigned title as if at random, so titled and untitled neighbours can be compared.
Property is one answer to Day 30's commons problem. Demsetz's private hunting territories and Ostrom's community rules are two ways of ending open access.

across.link: The Outer Space Treaty (1967, Article II) forbids any nation to claim the Moon or other celestial bodies. The US Space Resource Exploration and Utilization Act of 2015 nonetheless gives American citizens the right to 'possess, own, transport, use, and sell' resources they extract from an asteroid. In effect it applies Pierson v. Post's capture rule in space: no one may own the body, but whoever captures part of it owns that part. Luxembourg passed a similar law in 2017. The analogy breaks where the fox's did not: whether national laws like these are consistent with the treaty is disputed among states and international lawyers. Day 124's orbital commons shows what open access does there.

days.apply_question: Nineteenth-century whalers often followed the opposite rule to Pierson v. Post: in some fisheries the crew that first planted a harpoon owned the whale, even if another crew finished the kill (Ellickson, 1989). Using the idea that property rules are chosen for the behaviour they produce, why might whalers sensibly reward the chase when New York's court rewarded the kill?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the holding in Pierson v. Post, and the finding that more secure tenure raises investment in many settings. Debated: how much formal titling matters compared with informal security (de Soto against Galiani and Schargrodsky and others). Also debated: whether Demsetz's main example holds. He followed Eleanor Leacock's view that the Montagnais hunting territories arose with the fur trade; Frank Speck had argued that they were older. Value judgment: whether property is a natural right (Locke, and much of the Christian natural-law tradition, which qualifies it with the 'universal destination of goods') or a social convention justified by its results (Hume, Bentham).

resource.title: Possession as the Origin of Property
resource.creator: Carol M. Rose, University of Chicago Law Review 52 (1985)
resource.why: A short, much-cited essay that starts from Pierson v. Post and argues that possession matters because it communicates a claim to the world. It shows why clear acts of possession, not effort alone, ground property. It extends the lesson's central idea, in the author's own voice.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.headline_hint: A Carrier Delayed a Mill's Broken Crankshaft for Days. The Court Said the Lost Profits Weren't the Carrier's Problem.
days.concept: Contract law makes promises enforceable, so that strangers can rely on each other without trust or repeat dealing. It limits damages for breach to losses that were foreseeable when the deal was made (Hadley v Baxendale, 1854), which pushes each side to disclose unusual risks so they can be priced.
days.focus: Teach the enforceable promise as a commitment device that turns Day 14's one-shot dilemma into cooperation, along with expectation damages and Hadley's foreseeability rule, read as a default rule that forces information into the open (Ayres and Gertner, 1989). The angle: every contract is mostly gaps, which the law fills. The DAO's 'code is law' experiment of 2016 shows what happens when nobody can fill them.
days.model_or_equation: Gap-filling logic, in words. A carrier who charges every customer the same price cannot price a risk it does not know about. Under Hadley's rule the carrier pays the ordinary losses that arise naturally from a breach, plus any special loss the customer told it about when making the contract. So a customer facing an unusual loss has a reason to say so, and the carrier can then charge more, take extra care, or decline the job. A rule making carriers pay every loss would force them to charge every customer for the worst case.

story.title: A broken crankshaft in Gloucester
story.hook: In May 1853 the crankshaft of the steam engine at Joseph and Jonah Hadley's City Steam-Mills in Gloucester broke, and the mill stopped. The engine's makers, W. Joyce & Co. of Greenwich, needed the broken shaft as a pattern for a new one. The Hadleys sent a servant to the office of Pickford & Co., the great carriers, of which Joseph Baxendale was a partner. A clerk said that a parcel handed in by noon would be delivered in Greenwich the next day. Through the carrier's neglect, the shaft was delayed for several days, and the mill stood idle the whole time. The Hadleys sued for their lost profits, and a jury at the Gloucester assizes awarded them damages. In February 1854 the Court of Exchequer ordered a new trial. Baron Alderson held that a party who breaks a contract owes only the losses that arise naturally from the breach, or that both parties could reasonably have contemplated, when they made the contract, as its probable result.
story.puzzle: Pickfords broke its promise, and the Hadleys lost money as a direct result. Why should the Hadleys, not the carrier at fault, bear the cost of the idle mill?
story.payoff: Because the rule is a default that brings hidden risks into the open. Most mills, Alderson reasoned, would have had a spare shaft, and a carrier charging an ordinary fee could not know that this one meant a stopped mill. If carriers owed every unforeseeable loss, they would have to price every parcel as if it were the last crankshaft in England. Under Hadley, a customer with an unusual stake must say so, and the carrier can then price the risk, take extra care, or refuse. Enforceable promises let strangers deal with each other; the foreseeability limit lets them price what they are promising. One oddity remains: the reported facts say the clerk was told that the mill was stopped, which legal historians have puzzled over ever since (Danzig 1975).
sources: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341; 156 ER 145
Richard Danzig, 'Hadley v. Baxendale: A Study in the Industrialization of the Law', Journal of Legal Studies 4 (1975)
Ian Ayres and Robert Gertner, 'Filling Gaps in Incomplete Contracts: An Economic Theory of Default Rules', Yale Law Journal 99 (1989)

days.application: 'Code is law', tested. The DAO was an investment fund run by a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. In 2016 it raised ether worth about $150 million, and its stated terms said that nothing outside its code could add obligations to it. On 17 June 2016 an attacker used a flaw in the code: a withdrawal function could be called again before it had updated its own records. The attacker moved about 3.6 million ether, then worth roughly $50-60 million, into a separate contract. The code had run exactly as written. Ethereum's developers and most of its users answered not with a lawsuit but with a 'hard fork' on 20 July 2016, which rewrote the chain's history to return the funds; a minority kept the original chain, now called Ethereum Classic. A contract with no gap-filling, no foreseeability limit and no judge turned out to need all three, and they were supplied after the event by a community decision.

builds_on.why: A one-shot exchange between strangers is a prisoner's dilemma: each side does better by cheating. Enforceable contracts change the payoffs, so that keeping the promise becomes the rational choice.
The DAO failed the way Day 110 says software fails, through a design error (a re-entrancy flaw that no test caught) rather than wear, and the failure was sudden and total.

across.link: Avner Greif (1989; American Economic Review, 1993) argued that eleventh-century Maghribi traders in the Mediterranean enforced agreements with overseas agents without courts: a coalition shared information and boycotted any agent who cheated. Edwards and Ogilvie (Economic History Review, 2012) replied that the traders' own letters show heavy use of courts. The question is the same as today's: what makes a promise between distant strangers credible, a court or a community?

days.apply_question: On 19 July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike security update crashed millions of Windows computers; Delta Air Lines said the outage cost it about $500 million and sued, while CrowdStrike pointed to contract terms capping its liability. Using Hadley v Baxendale's logic, who is better placed to bear the risk of an airline's lost revenue from a vendor's faulty update, the airline or the vendor, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Hadley's rule and its place in common-law contract law. Debated: whether 'efficient breach', breaking a contract and paying damages when that is cheaper than performing, is acceptable. Economic analysts of law (Posner) defend it; promise-based theorists (Fried; Shiffrin, 'The Divergence of Contract and Promise', 2007) object. Also debated: whether reputation or courts did more to support long-distance trade in history (Greif against Edwards and Ogilvie). Value judgment: whether contract is at root a moral promise, as Fried argues, or a tool for allocating risk.

resource.title: Contract as Promise: A Theory of Contractual Obligation, chapter 2, 'The Promise Principle'
resource.creator: Charles Fried (Harvard University Press, 1981; 2nd edition, Oxford University Press, 2015)
resource.why: A short, influential argument that contract law rests on the morality of promising, not merely on economic efficiency. It is a clear foil to the risk-pricing reading of Hadley taught today, and it speaks directly to how law relates to moral obligation. It is one side of the debate, and it says so.
