days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Tort and product liability: who pays for an accident?
days.headline_hint: Donald MacPherson Bought His Buick From a Dealer, Not From Buick. In 1916 Buick Had to Pay Him Anyway.
days.concept: Tort law makes a person who carelessly causes harm pay for it (negligence: a duty of care, its breach, causation and damage). Product liability extends that duty from the buyer to everyone a dangerous product foreseeably reaches, and later makes manufacturers strictly liable for defects, so that the cost of accidents falls on those best placed to prevent them.
days.focus: Teach negligence's four elements, the Hand formula as the test of carelessness, and the twentieth-century move from privity of contract to strict product liability (MacPherson 1916; Greenman v. Yuba Power Products 1963). The angle: tort law is a private regulator that acts after the fact, and its two jobs, compensating victims and deterring careless design, can pull apart, as the Pinto verdict and its reduction show.
key_concepts: privity of contract and its fall
strict product liability (manufacturing, design and warning defects)
days.model_or_equation: The Learned Hand formula (United States v. Carroll Towing Co., 2d Cir. 1947): a party is negligent if B < P x L. B is the burden, or cost, of the precaution that would have prevented the accident; P is the probability of the accident without it; L is the size of the loss. Worked example: if a $50 inspection would remove a 1-in-100 chance of a $100,000 injury, then B = $50 and P x L = 0.01 x $100,000 = $1,000. Because B < PL, skipping the inspection is negligent.

story.title: A wooden wheel gives way
story.hook: In 1910 Donald MacPherson, a stonecutter in upstate New York, bought a new Buick runabout, not from Buick but from a dealer in Schenectady. In 1911, while he was driving it, one of the wooden wheels collapsed, its spokes crumbling, and he was thrown from the car and injured. Buick had not made the wheel. It bought wheels from a supplier, the Imperial Wheel Company, and there was evidence that a reasonable inspection would have found the defective wood. But MacPherson had no contract with Buick. Since Winterbottom v Wright (1842), when an English mail-coach driver lost his claim against the man who had contracted to maintain a coach that collapsed under him, the usual rule had been that a maker owed care only to the person it dealt with. On 14 March 1916 the New York Court of Appeals, in an opinion by Benjamin Cardozo, held Buick liable all the same.
story.puzzle: MacPherson had made no promise to Buick, and Buick none to him; Buick had not even built the wheel. On what principle could he recover from the manufacturer?
story.payoff: On a duty of care that arises from danger, not from contract. Cardozo held that a thing 'reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made' is a thing of danger. If its maker knows it will be used by people other than the buyer, without new tests, the maker owes them care 'irrespective of contract'. A car designed, as Cardozo noted, to go fifty miles an hour, and sold through dealers to drivers, fitted exactly. 'Precedents drawn from the days of travel by stage coach do not fit the conditions of travel to-day.' Buick was responsible for inspecting the parts it put in its cars. The loss fell on the party best able to prevent it, and that is the logic of product liability.
sources: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co., 217 N.Y. 382 (N.Y. 1916)
Winterbottom v Wright (1842) 10 M & W 109
James A. Henderson Jr., 'MacPherson v. Buick Motor Company: Simplifying the Facts While Reshaping the Law', in Robert L. Rabin and Stephen D. Sugarman (eds.), Torts Stories (Foundation Press, 2003)

days.application: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co. (California Court of Appeal, 1981). On 28 May 1972 a Ford Pinto driven by Lily Gray stalled on a California freeway and was struck from behind. The fuel tank ruptured and the car burned. Gray died, and her passenger, 13-year-old Richard Grimshaw, survived with terrible burns. Evidence at trial suggested Ford knew from crash tests that the tank's placement was vulnerable and that cheap fixes existed. In February 1978 the jury awarded about $2.5 million in compensatory damages to Grimshaw, about $560,000 to Gray's family, and $125 million in punitive damages. The trial judge cut the punitive award to $3.5 million, and the appeal court upheld that in 1981. On the car chain this is liability, the private twin of regulation: a court putting a price on a design choice after the fact. (As Day 45 showed, the famous 'Pinto memo' concerned an industry-wide fuel-leakage rule, not the Pinto's tank.)

builds_on.why: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle of 1932 drew on Cardozo's MacPherson judgment. Today's case is the same duty arriving first in America, by the same case-by-case extension of earlier rulings.

The Hand formula writes consequentialist cost-benefit reasoning into the legal definition of carelessness. That is why the Pinto case, where a cost-benefit memo was the famous exhibit, provoked such anger.

across.link: In mock-jury experiments, W. Kip Viscusi ('Corporate Risk Analysis: A Reckless Act?', Stanford Law Review, 2000) found that people awarded higher punitive damages when a company had done an explicit cost-benefit analysis of a safety decision than when it had not. Written down, the Hand formula's logic reads to jurors as callousness. This is Day 162's moral intuitions meeting legal doctrine: putting an explicit price on a life provokes condemnation that the same trade-off left implicit does not.

days.apply_question: Samsung said in January 2017 that the battery fires which forced it to recall and then abandon its Galaxy Note 7 phone in 2016 came from defects in batteries made by two outside suppliers: using MacPherson's duty and strict product liability, why should a buyer injured by one of those phones be able to recover from Samsung even if Samsung itself had not been careless?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the elements of negligence and the shift from privity to product liability. Debated: how far tort liability deters rather than merely compensates. The deterrent effect varies by field, and studies of US tort costs find that a large share of what defendants pay never reaches victims. Also debated: whether punitive damages are predictable enough to guide firms (Sunstein, Kahneman and Schkade's jury studies). Value judgment: whether a company may ever accept a known, small risk of death to save money. Every product design does so implicitly; this is Day 45's dilemma.

resource.title: The Engineer's Lament
resource.creator: Malcolm Gladwell, The New Yorker (May 2015)
resource.why: Gladwell revisits the Pinto through the eyes of Ford's recall coordinator of the time and contrasts how engineers and the public judge whether a car is 'defective', the question every product-liability case turns on. It is journalism with a point of view, not a legal treatise, and it is best read after the lesson.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: The corporation: a legal person with limited liability
days.headline_hint: Aron Salomon Owned 20,001 of His Company's 20,007 Shares. When It Failed, He Stood in Line Ahead of Its Creditors, and Won.
days.concept: Incorporation creates a separate legal person that owns its own assets and owes its own debts. Its shareholders can lose no more than they invested (limited liability), and its creditors look to the company's assets, not the owners'. That partition lets strangers pool capital without watching one another. Whose interests the company should serve is a separate, contested question.
days.focus: Teach separate legal personality, limited liability and asset partitioning (Hansmann and Kraakman, 2000) through Salomon v Salomon (1897), the case that confirmed that a one-man company is still a different person from the man. The angle: the question of purpose, shareholders or stakeholders, runs from Dodge v. Ford (1919) to the Business Roundtable's 2019 statement. Finance itself is assumed at CFA level.
days.model_or_equation: Two walls, described in words. The first, limited liability, keeps the company's creditors from reaching the shareholders' personal assets. The second keeps a shareholder's personal creditors from seizing the company's assets or forcing its liquidation (Hansmann and Kraakman's 'affirmative asset partitioning', 2000, later called 'entity shielding'). The second wall lets a company run as a going concern whatever happens to any one owner. The first lets an investor buy a share without checking every other shareholder's solvency or every risk the business runs.

story.title: Aron Salomon's boot business
story.hook: For about thirty years Aron Salomon ran a leather and wholesale boot-making business in Whitechapel, in London's East End. In 1892 he turned it into a limited company, A. Salomon and Company Limited. The Companies Act required at least seven members, so his wife and five of his children took one share each, and Salomon held the other 20,001 of the 20,007 shares issued. The company bought his business for about £39,000. It paid him partly in shares and partly with £10,000 of secured debentures, loans to the company that gave the lender first claim on its assets. Within about a year, after strikes and the loss of government boot contracts, the company failed. Its unsecured creditors were owed about £7,700, and once the debenture holders had been paid there was nothing left for them. The liquidator sued Salomon, and both the trial judge and the Court of Appeal held him responsible for the company's debts. In their view the company was a mere device: his agent, or his alias.
story.puzzle: Salomon owned virtually all of the company and ran it alone. How could a man be his own creditor, and be paid ahead of the tradesmen his own business owed?
story.payoff: Because the company was not Salomon. On 16 November 1896 the House of Lords unanimously reversed the Court of Appeal. In Lord Macnaghten's words, 'The company is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum.' The Companies Act said nothing about how many shares each member must hold or how independent they had to be. Seven subscribers, once registered, made a new legal person, with its own assets and its own debts. The unsecured creditors had dealt with a company whose name ended in 'Limited', and they could look only to its assets. That partition was hard on these creditors, but it is exactly what lets strangers invest in a business without risking their homes.
sources: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22 (HL), judgment of 16 November 1896
Henry Hansmann and Reinier Kraakman, 'The Essential Role of Organizational Law', Yale Law Journal 110 (2000)
Companies Act 1862 (UK)

days.application: Dodge v. Ford Motor Co. (Michigan Supreme Court, 7 February 1919). By 1916 Ford Motor had accumulated a surplus of more than $100 million. Henry Ford stopped its large special dividends and announced that he would put the profits into cheaper cars, more jobs and the giant River Rouge plant: 'My ambition is to employ still more men, to spread the benefits of this industrial system to the greatest possible number.' John and Horace Dodge, who owned about a tenth of the shares and were building their own car company, sued. The court ordered a special dividend of about $19 million, declaring that 'a business corporation is organized and carried on primarily for the profit of the stockholders'. But it refused to stop the expansion, deferring to the directors' business judgment. A century later, on 19 August 2019, 181 chief executives of the Business Roundtable signed a statement committing their firms to customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders alike. Whether either text changed what directors actually do is disputed (Stout, 2008; Bebchuk and Tallarita, 2020). On the car chain this is financing and production: who gets the profits a production revolution makes.

builds_on.why: Dodge v. Ford was a fight over the profits of the Highland Park system of Day 103: Ford wanted to put them back into cheaper cars and the River Rouge plant, and his minority shareholders wanted them paid out.

Incorporation by simple registration, open to anyone after Britain's mid-nineteenth-century Companies Acts, is an inclusive institution in Day 222's sense: an impersonal right to form a firm, no longer a privilege granted by the state.

across.link: On 16 February 2017 the European Parliament adopted a resolution on civil-law rules for robotics that invited the Commission to consider a specific legal status, 'electronic persons', for the most sophisticated autonomous robots. An open letter signed by more than 150 experts in AI, robotics, law and ethics opposed it in 2018, and the idea was dropped. Legal personhood is a legal technology, and it can be extended to non-humans, as it was to the company, if the separation it creates is useful. The question is whether separating an AI's liability from its makers' would help victims or shield the makers.

days.apply_question: Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty to federal crimes over its marketing of OxyContin, yet the Sackler family who owned it were not liable for its debts merely because they were its owners. Using the logic of separate legal personality and limited liability, in what circumstances, if any, should a court make the owners of a company answer personally for its harms?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the doctrines of separate personality and limited liability, and the holdings of Salomon and Dodge v. Ford. Debated: whether limited liability for torts, as opposed to debts people agree to, lets firms push risks onto victims who never chose to deal with them. Hansmann and Kraakman (Yale Law Journal, 1991) proposed unlimited pro-rata liability for shareholders in tort cases. Also debated: whether stakeholder pledges change behaviour (Bebchuk and Tallarita against defenders of stakeholder capitalism). Value judgment: whom a corporation should serve. Milton Friedman (1970) answered profit within the rules of the game; stakeholder theorists, and Catholic social teaching, which calls a business 'a community of persons' (Centesimus Annus 35, 1991), ask for more.

resource.title: The Company: A Short History of a Revolutionary Idea
resource.creator: John Micklethwait and Adrian Wooldridge (Modern Library, 2003)
resource.length: about 40 minutes for the introduction and the chapter on Victorian Britain's limited-liability reforms
resource.why: A brisk, readable history of the company, from merchant guilds and chartered trading companies to the general incorporation and limited-liability acts of the 1850s and 1860s that made Salomon's company possible. It gives the historical depth the lesson can only sketch. It is written by two Economist journalists sympathetic to the company as an institution.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Intellectual property: patents, copyright and the bargain
days.headline_hint: American Printers Reprinted Dickens Without Paying Him, and It Was Legal. When He Asked for Copyright in 1842, the Press Turned on Him.
days.concept: Intellectual property law grants creators a temporary exclusive right: a patent on an invention in return for publicly disclosing it, and a copyright on an original expression, though never on the idea behind it. Because anyone can copy an idea at almost no cost, the right lets ideas still repay the cost of creating them, and so every IP rule is a bargain between incentives to create and access to what is created.
days.focus: Teach why ideas need special property (they are non-rival and cheap to copy), the patent bargain (exclusivity for about 20 years in exchange for disclosure), copyright's line between idea and expression, and the cost that exclusivity imposes on users. The angle: each country strikes the bargain for its own interests (the United States refused copyright to foreign authors until 1891), and the bargain can be gamed, as George Selden's car patent was.
key_concepts: non-rival goods and the trade-off between incentive and access
the patent bargain: exclusivity for disclosure
patent term, novelty and prior art

story.title: Dickens asks for copyright, 1842
story.hook: Charles Dickens arrived in Boston on 22 January 1842, not yet thirty and the most popular novelist in the English-speaking world. Crowds followed him, and Boston gave him a grand public dinner. But American publishers had been reprinting his books for years without paying him, and doing so legally: the US Copyright Act of 1790 protected only citizens and residents, and expressly permitted reprinting foreigners' books. At dinners in Boston and Hartford in early February, Dickens told his hosts that an international copyright law would be just to British authors and good for American ones. Many newspapers turned on him, calling him mercenary and ungrateful for American hospitality, and some American friends urged him to drop the subject. He went home and satirized the country in American Notes (1842) and Martin Chuzzlewit. The United States did not protect foreign authors until the International Copyright Act of 1891. It joined the Berne Convention, the main international copyright treaty, only in 1989.
story.puzzle: The young republic took creators' rights seriously enough to write them into its Constitution: Congress may secure 'for limited Times to Authors and Inventors the exclusive Right to their respective Writings and Discoveries'. Why would the same country let its printers copy the most popular author alive for free? And why, half a century later, did it change its mind?
story.payoff: Because intellectual property is a bargain each society strikes for its own benefit. Exclusive rights reward creators, but they raise what everyone else pays. In 1842 the United States imported far more literature than it exported, so free reprints gave American readers cheap books while British authors bore the cost. The losers at home were American authors, whose books had to compete with free British ones. As American writing and publishing grew, the balance shifted, authors and publishers lobbied, and the 1891 Act passed, with a clause requiring protected foreign books to be typeset in the United States. Poorer countries strike the same bargain today in the argument over patents on medicines.
sources: Copyright Act of 1790 (1 Stat. 124), section 5
International Copyright Act of 3 March 1891 (the Chace Act)
K. J. Fielding (ed.), The Speeches of Charles Dickens (Oxford, 1960)
B. Zorina Khan, The Democratization of Invention: Patents and Copyrights in American Economic Development, 1790-1920 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)

days.application: George Selden's car patent. Selden, a patent lawyer in Rochester, New York, applied on 8 May 1879 for a patent on a 'road-engine', a carriage driven by a liquid-fuel internal-combustion engine. He then kept the application pending with amendments for some sixteen years, until a car industry existed, and the patent (No. 549,160) was granted on 5 November 1895. Its rights passed to a group that formed the Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers in 1903, which charged its licensed makers a royalty of 1.25 per cent of each car's price. Henry Ford refused to pay, and in 1909 a trial court upheld the patent against him. In January 1911 the Court of Appeals held the patent valid but not infringed: it covered only cars using the Brayton-type engine Selden had described, and Ford, like nearly every maker, used the Otto four-stroke. On the car chain this is where invention meets law. A patent meant to reward disclosure had become a toll on an industry its holder had not built.

builds_on.why: The printing press made copying cheap, and copyright was the legal answer. England's Statute of Anne (1710) gave authors, not just printers, a limited term of protection.

Day 35's innovation system, in which progress comes from many hands combining existing parts, is why the scope of a patent matters. Selden claimed a combination of existing parts and tried to tax the whole industry with it.

across.link: In Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics (13 June 2013) the US Supreme Court held unanimously that naturally occurring DNA sequences, including the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes linked to breast and ovarian cancer, cannot be patented merely because they have been isolated. Synthetic complementary DNA (cDNA) can be patented. The line between a discovery of nature (Day 135's code) and an invention decided who could offer the test, and competing labs began offering BRCA testing soon after.

days.apply_question: In June 2022 members of the World Trade Organization agreed to let developing countries authorize production of patented COVID-19 vaccines without the patent holders' consent. Using the patent bargain, what would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to judge whether that decision was right?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the legal structure of patents and copyright, and the US history from 1790 to 1891. Debated: how much patents actually spur innovation outside pharmaceuticals and chemicals. Surveys of firms (Levin et al., 1987; Cohen, Nelson and Walsh, 2000) find that most industries rely more on lead time and secrecy; Boldrin and Levine (Against Intellectual Monopoly, 2008) argue against patents altogether, and others defend them. Also debated: whether the 2022 WTO decision made any practical difference. Value judgment: whether access to life-saving medicine should override inventors' rights. Utilitarians, natural-rights theorists drawing on Locke's labour theory, and Catholic social teaching's 'universal destination of goods' give different answers.

resource.title: The Public Domain: Enclosing the Commons of the Mind, chapter 2, 'Thomas Jefferson Writes a Letter'
resource.creator: James Boyle (Yale University Press, 2008; also released free under a Creative Commons licence)
resource.why: A lively chapter built on Jefferson's 1813 letter arguing that ideas, once shared, cannot be owned like land, and on what that means for designing intellectual property. It sets out the economics of non-rival goods more fully than the lesson can. Boyle is a critic of IP expansion, and it shows.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Criminal law and punishment: the cabin boy and the custom of the sea
days.headline_hint: Four Men, a 13-Foot Dinghy, 24 Days Adrift. The Court Sentenced Two to Hang, Then the Crown Gave Them Six Months.
days.concept: A crime requires a guilty act (actus reus) done with a guilty mind (mens rea) and without a recognized justification or excuse. The state's right to punish it rests on contested justifications (retribution, deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation), which point to different punishments for the same act.
days.focus: Teach the elements of a crime, the difference between a justification (self-defence, necessity) and an excuse (duress, insanity), and the four rationales for punishment, through R v Dudley and Stephens (1884). The angle: the court declared the killing murder and the Crown then cut the sentence to six months, so law stated a principle and mercy tempered its application. The deterrence evidence (certainty of punishment matters more than severity; Nagin 2013) then tests the consequentialist rationale.
days.model_or_equation: Becker's deterrence model, in words (Gary Becker, 'Crime and Punishment: An Economic Approach', 1968). A would-be offender weighs the gain from a crime against its expected cost: the probability of being caught and punished (p) times the severity of the punishment (f). Expected cost = p x f. In the model, doubling p and doubling f deter equally. The evidence says they do not: people respond far more to p, partly because they heavily discount distant, uncertain punishments.

story.title: The Mignonette's dinghy, July 1884
story.hook: In May 1884 the yacht Mignonette, bought by an Australian lawyer, left Southampton for Sydney with a crew of four: Captain Tom Dudley, the mate Edwin Stephens, the seaman Edmund Brooks and Richard Parker, a 17-year-old cabin boy. On 5 July, in the South Atlantic, a wave stove in her side and she sank within minutes. The four got into a 13-foot dinghy with two tins of turnips and no fresh water. They caught a turtle and drank rainwater when they could. Parker drank seawater and fell gravely ill. On about the twentieth day, after Brooks had refused to take part, Dudley prayed and then killed Parker with a penknife. The three survivors lived on his body until a German barque, the Moctezuma, picked them up on 29 July. Landing at Falmouth in September, they told the whole story openly; sailors spoke of a 'custom of the sea'. Dudley and Stephens were charged with murder.
story.puzzle: Everyone agreed that without food all four would probably have died, and that Parker, the weakest, would probably have died first. The people of Falmouth were on the sailors' side. If killing Parker saved three lives, why was it murder? And if it was murder, why did the Crown let them go after six months?
story.payoff: On 9 December 1884 five judges of the Queen's Bench Division, led by Lord Coleridge, held that it was murder. There was a deliberate killing (the guilty act) done with intent to kill (the guilty mind), and necessity could not justify taking an innocent life: 'Who is to be the judge of this sort of necessity? By what measure is the comparative value of lives to be measured?' Coleridge pointed to 'the Great Example whom we profess to follow' as the model of self-sacrifice. The law required a death sentence; the Home Secretary commuted it to six months in prison. The court stated, in retributive and expressive terms, the principle that no one may choose whom to sacrifice. It left mercy to the executive, where pity, and the small deterrent value of hanging starving sailors, pointed the other way.
sources: R v Dudley and Stephens (1884) 14 QBD 273
A. W. Brian Simpson, Cannibalism and the Common Law: The Story of the Tragic Last Voyage of the Mignonette and the Strange Legal Proceedings to Which It Gave Rise (University of Chicago Press, 1984)

days.application: Hawaii's HOPE probation programme. In October 2004 Judge Steven Alm in Honolulu began answering every probation violation, such as a missed appointment or a positive drug test, with a swift, certain and short jail stay of a few days, instead of occasional long revocations. A randomized trial (Hawken and Kleiman, 2009) found HOPE probationers much less likely to be arrested again, use drugs or have their probation revoked. It looked like proof that certainty beats severity. Then a federally funded replication at four sites in other states (Lattimore and colleagues, Criminology & Public Policy, 2016) found no reduction in re-arrests. The general finding about certainty survives; whether this programme works outside Honolulu is unresolved.

builds_on.why: Deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation are consequentialist justifications: punish because of the crimes punishment prevents. Day 45's method is how they are tested, and the Mignonette shows its limit, since the arithmetic of three lives against one favoured the killers.

Retribution is Kant's answer: punish because the offender deserves it, never merely as a means to deter others. Coleridge's refusal to weigh lives against each other is the deontological side constraint of Day 46 written into law.

across.link: Carlsmith, Darley and Robinson ('Why Do We Punish?', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002) gave people crime scenarios that varied features relevant to deterrence (how likely detection was, how public the punishment) and features relevant to desert (how serious the crime was, the offender's motive). The sentences people chose tracked desert and largely ignored deterrence, even though many of them said they believed in deterrence. Moral intuitions (Day 162) shape punishment more than stated theory does.

days.apply_question: A city wants to cut speeding on a road where pedestrians keep dying. Using what deterrence research says about the certainty and severity of punishment, would doubling the speeding fine or installing automated speed cameras be more likely to work, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the elements of a crime and the rule in Dudley and Stephens; the finding that the perceived certainty of punishment deters more reliably than its severity (Nagin, 'Deterrence in the Twenty-First Century', Crime and Justice, 2013). Debated: whether the death penalty deters at the margin (the US National Research Council concluded in 2012 that existing studies cannot tell us), and whether swift, certain programmes like HOPE replicate. Value judgment: which rationale should govern punishment. Retributivists (Kant) say desert; consequentialists (Bentham) say crime prevention; many Christian traditions insist on both justice and mercy; restorative-justice advocates put repair and reconciliation first.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Evidence, burdens of proof and due process
days.headline_hint: Clarence Gideon Was Convicted Without a Lawyer in 1961. Retried With One in 1963, He Was Acquitted in About an Hour.
days.concept: Standards of proof are deliberate choices about which mistakes a society would rather make: preponderance of the evidence in most civil cases, clear and convincing evidence in some, beyond reasonable doubt in criminal trials. Due process (notice, counsel, the chance to confront and cross-examine witnesses) is the machinery that makes any standard mean something.
days.focus: Teach the burden of proof as a decision threshold applied to uncertain evidence (Blackstone's ratio; Justice Harlan's concurrence in In re Winship, 1970), and adversarial testing as the way evidence gets checked. The angle: Clarence Gideon was the same man facing the same chief witness in 1961 and in 1963, and what changed the verdict was a lawyer.
key_concepts: burden of proof (who must prove) and standard of proof (how much)
preponderance, clear and convincing, beyond reasonable doubt
false convictions and false acquittals (Blackstone's ratio)
due process and the right to counsel
days.model_or_equation: Thresholds as error trade-offs. Treat the fact-finder's belief that the defendant did it as a probability. A standard of proof is a threshold: decide against the defendant only if belief exceeds it. Preponderance is usually glossed as 'more likely than not', above 0.5. Courts refuse to put a number on 'beyond reasonable doubt', but it means far higher. Raising the threshold cuts false convictions and raises false acquittals; lowering it does the reverse. Blackstone's ratio ('better that ten guilty persons escape, than that one innocent suffer', 1769) states how much worse one error is than the other. It is the same trade-off as choosing a significance level (Day 17).

story.title: A pencilled petition from a Florida prison
story.hook: Early on the morning of Saturday 3 June 1961 someone broke into the Bay Harbor Poolroom in Panama City, Florida, and took coins from a cigarette machine and a jukebox, along with some drinks. Clarence Earl Gideon, a drifter of about fifty with little schooling and a record of petty crimes, was arrested on the word of a witness who said he had seen him inside. At his trial that August Gideon asked for a lawyer. The judge replied that Florida appointed counsel only in capital cases. Gideon defended himself, badly, and was sentenced to five years. From prison he wrote a petition to the US Supreme Court in pencil, arguing that a poor man had a right to a lawyer. The Court took the case, appointed Abe Fortas (a future justice) to argue it, and on 18 March 1963 ruled unanimously in Gideon v. Wainwright that states must provide a lawyer to anyone facing a felony charge who cannot afford one. On 5 August 1963 Gideon was tried again, in the same courthouse, on the same charge.
story.puzzle: The same man faced the same charge, in the same courthouse, with the same chief witness. In 1961 a jury convicted him; in 1963 a jury acquitted him after about an hour. What had changed?
story.payoff: The evidence had been tested. Gideon's lawyer, W. Fred Turner, prepared the case and cross-examined the prosecution's key witness, giving the jury reasons to doubt what the man claimed to have seen at dawn outside the poolroom. A standard of proof is only a threshold. It protects the innocent only when someone can show the fact-finder where the evidence is weak. Due process (counsel, confrontation, and a burden that stays on the state) is what turns 'beyond reasonable doubt' from words into a working filter on error.
sources: Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963)
Anthony Lewis, Gideon's Trumpet (Random House, 1964)
In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970)

days.application: O. J. Simpson's two trials. On 3 October 1995 a Los Angeles jury acquitted Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman; the state had to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. On 4 February 1997 a civil jury in Santa Monica, deciding on the preponderance of the evidence, found him liable for their deaths and awarded $33.5 million in damages. The verdicts do not contradict each other, because each answers a different question: did the evidence clear a very high bar, or did it tip the scale? The trials also differed in other ways (Simpson had to testify in the civil case, and the jury was different), so the gap does not come from the standard alone.

builds_on.why: Day 17's Type I and Type II errors are the statistical version of false convictions and false acquittals. A significance level and a standard of proof are both thresholds chosen by deciding which error is worse.
Day 42's inductive risk says that how much evidence is enough depends on the cost of being wrong. Standards of proof make that judgment explicit, and set it differently for liberty than for money.

across.link: Signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966) treats any yes-or-no judgment under uncertainty, whether a radiologist's, a radar operator's or a juror's, as a threshold on noisy evidence: moving the threshold trades misses for false alarms without improving accuracy. Applied to police line-ups, ROC analysis (Mickes, Flowe and Wixted, 2012) showed that a procedure once thought better, because it produced fewer false identifications, had mostly made witnesses more cautious rather than more accurate. The same distinction separates a stricter standard of proof from better evidence.

days.apply_question: Federal guidance for US colleges deciding sexual-misconduct complaints has swung between requiring 'preponderance of the evidence' (2011) and permitting 'clear and convincing evidence' (2020). Which errors does each standard risk more, and what would you need to value to choose between them?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the legal standards and the holdings in Gideon and Winship. Debated: how often innocent people are convicted. One careful estimate puts at least about 4 per cent of US death sentences as wrongful (Gross and colleagues, PNAS, 2014); rates for ordinary felonies are much harder to measure. Also debated: how well public defence works in practice, given documented underfunding in many states. Value judgment: the ratio itself, meaning how many guilty people should go free to spare one innocent. Blackstone said ten, others have proposed other numbers, and no evidence can settle it.

resource.title: Gideon's Trumpet: the final chapter, on the 1963 retrial
resource.creator: Anthony Lewis (Random House, 1964)
resource.why: The New York Times's Supreme Court reporter tells how a lawyer took apart the case that had convicted Gideon. It shows adversarial testing, the subject of today's lesson, happening in a small Florida courtroom.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.headline_hint: John Marshall Told William Marbury He Was Right, and That the Court Couldn't Help Him. Turning Him Away Made the Court Powerful.
days.concept: Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws and official acts that conflict with the constitution. It protects rights and enforces limits against majorities, but it also lets unelected judges overrule elected ones (Bickel's 'counter-majoritarian difficulty'), which makes how judges read a constitution (originalism or living constitutionalism) a political question as well.
days.focus: Teach Marbury's logic, the counter-majoritarian difficulty and the main camps of constitutional interpretation, with weak-form review (the UK's Human Rights Act 1998; Canada's notwithstanding clause) as the contrast. Marbury's logic runs: a written constitution is supreme law, courts must apply law, so courts must refuse to apply a statute that contradicts it. The angle: Marshall won the power by declining to use it against Jefferson. Gerald Rosenberg's 'hollow hope' then asks how much courts can change on their own.
days.model_or_equation: Marshall's syllogism (Marbury v. Madison, 1803). (1) The Constitution is supreme law, which ordinary acts cannot change. (2) 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' (3) So when a statute conflicts with the Constitution, a court deciding a case must apply the Constitution and treat the statute as void. The argument's hidden premise (Day 37) is that courts, not Congress or the President, have the last word on what the Constitution means. Jefferson denied exactly that.

story.title: The commission nobody delivered
story.hook: After losing the election of 1800, President John Adams and the outgoing Federalist Congress created dozens of new judicial posts and filled them with loyalists. On 3 March 1801, his last full day in office, Adams was still signing commissions for justices of the peace in the District of Columbia. One was for William Marbury, a Federalist businessman. Secretary of State John Marshall, already confirmed as Chief Justice, sealed it, but it was never delivered. Thomas Jefferson's new Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to hand it over. In December 1801 Marbury asked the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus ordering Madison to deliver it. The Jeffersonian Congress repealed the new circuit judgeships and rearranged the Court's sittings so that it did not meet again until February 1803. When the Court finally ruled, on 24 February 1803, Jefferson's administration was widely expected to ignore any order it gave, and Marshall himself was the official who had failed to deliver the commission.
story.puzzle: Marshall wrote that Marbury had a legal right to his commission and that withholding it violated that right. Then he wrote that the Court could do nothing to help him. How did a ruling that gave Marbury nothing make the Supreme Court one of the most powerful courts in the world?
story.payoff: The Court said it could not issue the writ because the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that seemed to authorize it added to the Court's original jurisdiction in a way Article III did not allow. That section was therefore unconstitutional and void. By refusing a power Congress had given it, the Court claimed a larger one: the power to declare Acts of Congress void. Jefferson had nothing to defy, because the ruling ordered him to do nothing. That resolves the puzzle, and it names the problem that has followed judicial review ever since. When judges say what the Constitution means, they can overrule majorities, but their authority depends on the other branches and the public obeying.
sources: Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803)
Alexander M. Bickel, The Least Dangerous Branch: The Supreme Court at the Bar of Politics (1962)
William W. Van Alstyne, 'A Critical Guide to Marbury v. Madison', Duke Law Journal (1969)

days.application: Brown v. Board of Education (17 May 1954). A unanimous Court held that state-mandated segregation of public schools violates the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection, rejecting for education the 'separate but equal' doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896). It is judicial review at its most celebrated. Yet Gerald Rosenberg (The Hollow Hope, 1991; second edition 2008) found that a decade later only about 1 per cent of Black children in the eleven former Confederate states attended school with white children. Desegregation came after Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and tied federal school money to compliance. Critics answer that Brown legitimized the civil-rights movement and set Congress's agenda. Which side is right decides how much a court can change on its own.

builds_on.why: Federalist 51 set ambition against ambition among the branches. Judicial review made the courts a check that Madison's essay did not spell out, and Marbury is its founding move.

Day 240 showed democracies eroding by capturing their referees, as in Hungary after 2010, where the governing majority changed how constitutional judges are chosen and enlarged the Constitutional Court. Judicial review protects anything only while the courts stay independent.

across.link: Doug McAdam's political-process model (Political Process and the Development of Black Insurgency, 1930-1970, 1982) explains the civil-rights movement by shifting political opportunities, indigenous organization (Black churches and colleges) and 'cognitive liberation'. It credits rulings such as Brown with signalling that change was possible. That is the mechanism Rosenberg doubts, and the same question as Day 212's: do movements make law, or does law make movements?

days.apply_question: On 1 January 2024 Israel's Supreme Court, by eight votes to seven, struck down a Knesset amendment to a Basic Law that had barred judges from reviewing government decisions for 'reasonableness'. Using the counter-majoritarian difficulty, what would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to judge whether the Court was right to strike it down?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the holdings in Marbury and Brown, and Rosenberg's figures on school desegregation as data. Debated: how much courts drive social change (Rosenberg against Klarman's backlash thesis and against movement scholars such as McAdam), and how far judges' votes follow ideology rather than law, as measured by voting patterns. Value judgment: whether unelected judges should strike down democratic laws, and by what method of interpretation. Originalists (Scalia; Barrett) argue that fixed original meaning restrains judges; living constitutionalists (Strauss, The Living Constitution, 2010) argue that meaning must develop through precedent.

resource.title: Marbury v. Madison (1803): Chief Justice Marshall's opinion, the closing section on judicial review
resource.creator: John Marshall, opinion of the US Supreme Court, 24 February 1803 (public domain; widely available, for example from the Library of Congress)
resource.length: about 15 minutes for the closing section
resource.why: The argument for judicial review in its author's own words, including 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' Reading the reasoning itself shows how much rests on that one premise, which a summary cannot.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Administrative law: who makes the rules?
days.headline_hint: Herring Boats Were Told to Pay About $710 a Day for Federal Monitors. Their Lawsuit Ended Forty Years of Deference to Agencies.
days.concept: Most binding rules in a modern state are written by agencies under power delegated by the legislature, through procedures such as notice-and-comment rulemaking. Administrative law decides how far courts defer to them: on facts and policy, and, until Loper Bright (2024), on the meaning of the statute itself.
days.focus: Teach delegation, notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (1946), 'arbitrary and capricious' review (State Farm, 1983) and the rise and fall of Chevron deference (1984-2024). The angle: a dispute over who pays for herring monitors ended forty years of judicial deference. Underneath is the question of who should settle the technical questions Congress leaves open, experts or judges, and both answers have costs.
days.model_or_equation: The rulemaking pipeline. A statute delegates power. The agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register. The public comments, usually for 30 to 60 days. The agency answers significant comments and publishes a final rule with its reasons. Anyone harmed can sue. The court then asks two things: whether the agency stayed within the statute (after Loper Bright, the court decides that question itself), and whether the agency's reasoning was 'arbitrary, capricious' (State Farm).

story.title: Herring boats and a $710-a-day monitor
story.hook: Federal fisheries law has long let managers require fishing boats to carry observers who count the catch and the bycatch. In 2020 the National Marine Fisheries Service went further for the Atlantic herring fleet. On trips selected for monitoring, boats would pay for the monitors themselves, at an estimated $710 a day, which the agency's own analysis said could cut a vessel's annual returns by up to 20 per cent. Family-run herring firms, Loper Bright Enterprises in New Jersey and Relentless Inc. in Rhode Island, sued. The Magnuson-Stevens Act said boats could be required to carry observers; for this fishery, it did not say who must pay them. The lower courts, following Chevron v. Natural Resources Defense Council (1984), deferred to the agency's reasonable reading of an ambiguous statute. On 28 June 2024 the Supreme Court overruled Chevron, by 6-3 in the Relentless case and 6-2 in Loper Bright, from which Justice Jackson recused.
story.puzzle: The case was about a few hundred dollars a day on a few dozen boats. Why did it end a doctrine that courts had cited in thousands of decisions on air, drugs, banks and the internet? And who now decides what an ambiguous statute means?
story.payoff: Because the fishermen were asking the general question: when Congress leaves a gap, does the agency fill it, or the court? Chevron said courts should accept any reasonable agency reading. Loper Bright held that the Administrative Procedure Act tells reviewing courts to 'decide all relevant questions of law' themselves. Judges must now find the best reading of the statute, and agencies' views get only the respect their reasoning earns (Skidmore, 1944). The agency still writes the rules, but the court has the last word on what the statute means. Supporters call this a restoration of the separation of powers; Justice Kagan, dissenting, called it judges seizing questions that belong to experts.
sources: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce (US Supreme Court, 28 June 2024)
Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, 467 U.S. 837 (1984)
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. sections 553 and 706

days.application: The airbag rule and State Farm (1983). In 1977 the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration required new cars to have 'passive restraints', airbags or automatic seatbelts, phased in from the early 1980s. In 1981, under a new administration, the agency rescinded the rule, arguing that carmakers would mostly fit detachable automatic belts that many drivers would simply unhook. Insurers sued. On 24 June 1983 the Supreme Court held the rescission arbitrary and capricious, because the agency had not considered simply requiring airbags and had not adequately explained its doubts about the belts. Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole's 1984 rule then required passive restraints unless states covering two-thirds of the population passed laws requiring seat-belt use. States hurried to pass them, beginning with New York in 1984, and Congress later required airbags in all new cars from the late 1990s. On the car chain this is regulation, with the courts checking the regulator's reasoning.

builds_on.why: Day 243's regulatory toolkit (standards, prices, disclosure) is what agencies write; administrative law is the procedure and review that every one of those tools must pass.

Capture and public choice (Day 244) are the main argument on each side. Deference to agencies worries those who fear capture, and judicial control worries those who fear judges captured by litigants or ideology.

across.link: Notice-and-comment assumes that comments come from real people. When the FCC proposed repealing net-neutrality rules in 2017, it received about 22 million comments. A May 2021 report by the New York Attorney General found that more than 18 million were fake, many generated by bots or submitted in real people's names without their knowledge. A procedure designed for paper letters met automated identity fraud.

days.apply_question: In January 2025, no longer deferring to the agency after Loper Bright, a federal appeals court struck down the FCC's 2024 net-neutrality rules, deciding for itself that broadband is an 'information service' under a 1996 statute. Who should decide what an ambiguous technical term in an old statute means, an expert agency or a court, and what does each choice risk?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the APA's procedures and the holdings in State Farm, Chevron and Loper Bright. Debated: whether ending Chevron will make law more stable (one judicial reading instead of a reading that changes with each administration) or less stable, with circuits splitting; whether courts are competent to settle technical questions; and how often agency rules are captured. Value judgment: how much law-making power an elected legislature may hand to unelected experts. Originalist critics of the administrative state and its defenders (Metzger, '1930s Redux', Harvard Law Review, 2017; Vermeule, Law's Abnegation, 2016, which argues that courts should defer) divide over it.

resource.title: A Guide to the Rulemaking Process
resource.creator: Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration
resource.why: The government's own plain-language walk through how a federal rule is proposed, commented on, finalized and reviewed. It shows how the machinery behind the herring rule works, step by step and without spin.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: International law: binding sovereigns without a sovereign
days.headline_hint: The US Navy Seized Two Cuban Fishing Boats in 1898. The Supreme Court Made the Government Pay, Citing a Custom Older Than Columbus.
days.concept: International law binds states without a world government. Its rules come from treaties, from custom (general practice accepted as law) and from general principles (Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice). States mostly comply because of reciprocity, reputation and the domestic courts and officials who absorb its rules: 'almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law ... almost all of the time' (Henkin, 1968).
days.focus: Teach the sources of international law, customary law's two elements (state practice and opinio juris, the belief that the practice is legally required), and why compliance happens without central enforcement. The angle: in 1900 the US Supreme Court made its own government pay for prizes because of a custom traced to medieval England, while in 2016 China rejected an arbitral award outright. International law is strongest where reciprocity is strong and weakest where a great power's core interests are at stake.
key_concepts: treaties, custom and general principles (ICJ Statute, Article 38)
customary international law: state practice plus opinio juris
reciprocity and reputation as compliance mechanisms
incorporation of international law into domestic law
days.model_or_equation: Compliance as a repeated game (Day 14), in words. A state keeps a rule when the long-run value of others' compliance, which its own compliance helps secure, exceeds the one-time gain from breaking it. The model predicts strong compliance where interactions repeat, breaches are visible and the stakes of any single breach are small (postal rules, aviation, diplomatic immunity). It predicts weak compliance where a single breach is worth a great deal (territory, survival).

story.title: Two fishing smacks off Havana
story.hook: In April 1898, at the start of the Spanish-American War, ships of the US blockading squadron off Cuba stopped two small fishing smacks, the Paquete Habana and the Lola, which were returning to Havana with their catch. Each carried a handful of fishermen. Neither was armed, and neither had tried to run the blockade. The navy took them to Key West as prizes of war, a federal court there condemned them, and they were sold at auction, for $490 and $800. Their owners appealed to the Supreme Court. No treaty and no Act of Congress exempted fishing boats from capture, and the government treated any such exemption as a courtesy that a nation at war was free to ignore.
story.puzzle: There was no treaty, no statute and a war to win. Why would the United States' own Supreme Court order the government to pay for two enemy fishing boats?
story.payoff: Because custom is law. On 8 January 1900 Justice Horace Gray, writing for a Court divided six to three, traced the practice of sparing coastal fishermen through centuries of state practice, back to orders of England's Henry IV in the early 1400s. He concluded that it had become a rule of international law, which nations accepted as binding and not merely as a courtesy. 'International law is part of our law,' he wrote, and where there is no treaty and no controlling executive or legislative act or judicial decision, courts must look to 'the customs and usages of civilized nations'. The Court ordered the sale proceeds restored, with damages and costs. The custom bound the United States because its own courts treated it as law, and because the United States would want its own fishermen spared in the next war.
sources: The Paquete Habana, 175 U.S. 677 (1900)
Louis Henkin, How Nations Behave: Law and Foreign Policy (1968; 2nd edition 1979)
Statute of the International Court of Justice (1945), Article 38(1)

days.application: The South China Sea arbitration (award of 12 July 2016). The Philippines brought a case against China under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which both countries had ratified. The tribunal, set up under the treaty's compulsory procedure, found that China's claim to 'historic rights' within its 'nine-dash line' had no legal basis under the Convention, and that none of the Spratly features in dispute could generate a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone. China refused to take part and declared the award 'null and void' with 'no binding force'. A decade on, China's island-building and patrols continue, while other states cite the award to support their own claims and naval transits. Compliance fails where a great power's core interest is at stake, yet the ruling still shapes everyone else's claims.

builds_on.why: Reciprocity in international law is Day 14's repeated game. TIT FOR TAT's logic (cooperate, retaliate against defection, forgive) explains why a navy spares enemy fishermen it would like its own fishermen spared.
Day 236 grounded obedience in a state with a monopoly of force. Here there is no such state, so the question of why anyone obeys must be answered without one.

across.link: John Mearsheimer's 'The False Promise of International Institutions' (International Security, 1994/95) argues the realist case that international rules and institutions mostly reflect the distribution of power and have little independent effect on how states behave. If he is right, the Paquete Habana custom held because breaking it was cheap to forgo, not because it was law. The International Relations block takes up the realist view next.

days.apply_question: On 16 March 2022 the International Court of Justice ordered Russia to suspend its military operations in Ukraine, and Russia ignored the order. Using reciprocity and reputation, why does international law bind so weakly in a case like this, while rules on mail, aviation and shipping are obeyed almost every day?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the sources of international law and the holdings and award described. Debated: why states comply. Rationalists stress reciprocity and reputation (Guzman, How International Law Works, 2008); managerial accounts stress capacity and ambiguity rather than defiance (Chayes and Chayes, The New Sovereignty, 1995); sceptics say states comply mainly when it costs them little (Goldsmith and Posner, The Limits of International Law, 2005). Compliance studies also struggle to separate law's effect from what states intended to do anyway. Value judgment: how far national sovereignty should yield to international obligations.

resource.title: International Law: A Very Short Introduction, opening chapters
resource.creator: Vaughan Lowe (Oxford University Press, 2015)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the first two chapters
resource.why: A former Chichele Professor of Public International Law at Oxford explains plainly how international law is made and why it works most of the time. It gives the practitioner's view of the same rules the lesson describes, and it is balanced rather than polemical.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Law and new technology: who is liable?
days.headline_hint: Prodigy Tried to Keep Its Message Boards Clean. A Court Said That Made It the Publisher of Every Post, and Congress Answered With 26 Words.
days.concept: Intermediary liability is the set of rules that decides who answers for harm flowing through a platform, network or autonomous system: the person who acted, the service that carried it, or the maker of the tool. Every such rule faces the Collingridge dilemma: a technology is easy to shape early, when its harms are unknown, and hard to shape later, when they are known but the technology is entrenched (Collingridge, 1980).
days.focus: Teach the distinction between publisher and distributor liability, Section 230's immunity (1996) and Europe's different choices, and the Collingridge dilemma. The angle: a 1995 New York ruling punished a service for moderating, Congress answered with 26 words that shaped the internet, and the EU's 2024 Product Liability Directive now treats software and AI as products. These are two strategies for the same dilemma.
key_concepts: Section 230 immunity and its 'Good Samaritan' clause

story.title: An anonymous post on 'Money Talk'
story.hook: In October 1994 an anonymous user of 'Money Talk', a finance bulletin board on the Prodigy online service, posted that a Long Island brokerage, Stratton Oakmont, and its president had committed 'criminal and fraudulent acts' in a share offering. Stratton Oakmont sued Prodigy for $200 million for libel. Prodigy had marketed itself as a family-friendly service: it published content guidelines, used software to screen out offensive language and employed 'Board Leaders' to enforce its rules. On 24 May 1995 Justice Stuart Ain of the New York Supreme Court held that this made Prodigy a publisher, responsible for its users' posts as a newspaper is for its letters page. Four years earlier a federal court had held that CompuServe, which did not review its forums, was merely a distributor, like a bookshop, liable only if it knew of the defamation (Cubby v. CompuServe, 1991).
story.puzzle: Prodigy was held liable because it tried to keep its boards clean, and CompuServe escaped because it did not try. What sort of rule makes a service that moderates more liable than one that does nothing, and what should replace it? (Stratton Oakmont was the firm founded by Jordan Belfort, who later pleaded guilty to securities fraud, so the anonymous poster may have had a point.)
story.payoff: The New York ruling followed a sound old principle, that whoever exercises editorial control takes responsibility for what is published. Applied to millions of posts, it rewarded ignorance. Representatives Chris Cox and Ron Wyden drafted what became Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, signed into law on 8 February 1996: 'No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider.' A second clause protected good-faith moderation. Congress chose early, while the harms were unknown, to put liability on the speaker, not the carrier. That was the early choice the Collingridge dilemma describes. The argument since has been about living with it now that the internet is entrenched.
sources: Stratton Oakmont, Inc. v. Prodigy Services Co. (N.Y. Sup. Ct., Nassau County, 24 May 1995)
Cubby, Inc. v. CompuServe Inc., 776 F. Supp. 135 (S.D.N.Y. 1991)
Jeff Kosseff, The Twenty-Six Words That Created the Internet (Cornell University Press, 2019)
David Collingridge, The Social Control of Technology (1980)

days.application: The EU's new Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853). Adopted in 2024 to replace a 1985 directive written for physical goods, it treats software, including AI systems and software updates, as a 'product'. Makers therefore face strict liability for defects that cause death, personal injury, damage to property or the destruction of data. It eases the claimant's burden of proof where technical complexity makes a defect hard to show, and it applies to products placed on the market from December 2026. For a self-driving car, the question of who pays after a crash shifts from the driver's negligence toward the maker's defect. On the car chain this is regulation: liability rules for the next car are being written before such cars are common. That is the Collingridge dilemma's early move, made in the opposite direction from Section 230.

builds_on.why: The EU directive extends Day 254's strict product liability, born with MacPherson's wooden wheel, to code: the same idea, that the maker is best placed to prevent defects, applied to software.

Collingridge's 'entrenchment' is Day 31's lock-in. Once a technology has users, complementary businesses and habits around it, the cost of changing its rules rises, as the long fight over Section 230 shows.

across.link: The UK's Automated Vehicles Act 2024 (Royal Assent on 20 May 2024) answers the liability question for self-driving cars. When an authorized self-driving feature is engaged, the person in the driving seat becomes a 'user-in-charge' who is not liable for how the car drives, and responsibility shifts to an 'authorised self-driving entity', usually the manufacturer or software developer. That is Section 230's question, who answers for what the system does, asked of Day 181's long-tail problem.

days.apply_question: Section 230 protects services that host what others post. Should it also protect an AI chatbot's answers, which the service's own model generates rather than merely carries? Using the logic of intermediary liability, argue which way a court should decide.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the text of Section 230, the holdings described, and the scope of the new EU directive. Debated: whether Section 230 enabled the internet's growth and free expression (Kosseff; the Electronic Frontier Foundation) or shields platforms from responsibility for harms such as harassment and exploitation (Citron and Wittes, 'The Internet Will Not Break', 2017); and whether strict liability for AI will slow innovation or make it safer. Value judgment: how to weigh free expression, innovation and redress for victims, and who should bear the cost of harms no one could foresee.

resource.title: The Twenty-Six Words That Created the Internet: the early chapters on Cubby, Stratton Oakmont and the drafting of Section 230
resource.creator: Jeff Kosseff (Cornell University Press, 2019)
resource.length: about 40 minutes for the early chapters
resource.why: A cybersecurity-law professor tells the story of the cases and the two congressmen behind Section 230, with interviews and court records, then traces what the law made possible. It shows how one early legal choice locked in a whole industry's structure, at a depth the lesson cannot reach. Kosseff is broadly sympathetic to Section 230 but presents its critics.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 16: Tobacco and manufactured doubt
days.headline_hint: In 1954 the Tobacco Companies Promised Smokers Honest Research in 448 Newspapers. It Took 44 Years and a $206 Billion Settlement to Make Them Pay.
days.concept: How did a product that kills up to half of its long-term users stay legal, popular and lightly regulated for decades after the science was clear, and what finally changed that?
days.focus: Walk the cigarette through the chain as a loop. Bonsack's machine made mass supply possible before there was mass demand. Nicotine's reward made demand self-reinforcing. Epidemiology found the harm in 1950-54. The industry's 'Frank Statement' and its research committee turned scientific uncertainty into a product. Then regulation, three waves of lawsuits, leaked internal documents and a racketeering judgment finally took hold. The angle: the law's tools worked only once litigation exposed what the companies knew, and the doubt playbook outlived the companies' defeat.
key_concepts: the three waves of tobacco litigation
the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003)
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, addiction (reinforcing): nicotine delivers a reward (Day 151), which brings dependence, steady consumption and more nicotine. R2, scale and marketing (reinforcing): Bonsack's machine and Duke's combination cut costs, which meant cheap cigarettes and heavy advertising, then more smokers and more revenue for advertising. B1, evidence and regulation (balancing, delayed by decades): rising lung cancer led to epidemiology (1950), the Surgeon General's report (1964), then warnings, advertising bans, taxes and smoke-free laws, and so fewer smokers. B2, doubt (a loop that weakens B1): each new study met industry-funded counter-research and public relations ('Doubt is our product', 1969), which kept the public and politicians uncertain and delayed regulation. R3, denormalization (reinforcing, the turn): fewer smokers made smoking look deviant, which brought smoke-free laws and social disapproval, and still fewer smokers. Delays: lung cancer follows smoking by two to three decades, so US men's lung-cancer death rates kept rising until about 1990, long after the share of men smoking had begun to fall. Unintended consequences: filters and 'light' cigarettes reassured smokers, who compensated by inhaling harder. The 1971 broadcast advertising ban also ended the free anti-smoking spots that the Fairness Doctrine had required broadcasters to run. The 1998 settlement made state budgets depend on continued cigarette sales. Documented reversals: invention came before need (the machine before mass demand), and science came before regulation by decades.

story.title: A Frank Statement in 448 newspapers
story.hook: On Monday 4 January 1954 readers of 448 newspapers in 258 American cities opened their papers to a full-page advertisement headed 'A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers'. Its sponsors were the leading tobacco manufacturers, joined by growers' and warehouse associations. Recent reports linking smoking to lung cancer, it said, had received wide publicity, but 'we believe the products we make are not injurious to health'. 'We accept an interest in people's health as a basic responsibility, paramount to every other consideration in our business.' The companies announced a Tobacco Industry Research Committee, to be led by a scientist of unimpeachable integrity. They had planned the campaign with the public-relations firm Hill & Knowlton at meetings at New York's Plaza Hotel in December 1953, weeks after Ernst Wynder and colleagues reported that cigarette tar painted on mice produced tumours. An estimated 43 million people saw it.
story.puzzle: The companies promised research and candour. Within a decade the US Surgeon General declared that smoking caused lung cancer. Yet cigarettes stayed legal, heavily advertised and, for years, barely regulated, and the industry did not lose a major lawsuit for decades. How did a product that kills up to half of its long-term users stay so popular and so protected for so long, and what finally changed that?
story.payoff: The research committee was a public-relations instrument. By funding doubt rather than answers, the industry kept the debate 'open' long after epidemiology (Doll and Hill, Wynder and Graham) had settled the central question, and juries kept finding that smokers had chosen their own risk. What changed was not new science but new evidence of what the companies knew. Internal documents, leaked in 1994 and forced into the open by the Minnesota trial of 1998, showed that the companies had long understood nicotine's addictiveness and smoking's dangers. That turned the smoker's 'assumed risk' into the company's fraud. The 1998 Master Settlement and Judge Gladys Kessler's 2006 racketeering judgment followed. The Frank Statement's promise had become evidence against its authors.
sources: 'A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers', advertisement of 4 January 1954 (UCSF Truth Tobacco Industry Documents)
Allan M. Brandt, The Cigarette Century: The Rise, Fall, and Deadly Persistence of the Product That Defined America (Basic Books, 2007)
United States v. Philip Morris USA Inc., 449 F. Supp. 2d 1 (D.D.C. 2006)
Naomi Oreskes and Erik M. Conway, Merchants of Doubt (Bloomsbury, 2010)

days.application: The system itself: the American cigarette from James Bonsack's rolling machine (1881) to the FDA's tobacco authority (2009) and the steady fall in the share of adults who smoke. The industry's growth in lower- and middle-income countries is the contrast that the International Relations block picks up.

builds_on.why: Doll and Hill's 1950 case-control study and Bradford Hill's viewpoints were the science the 'Frank Statement' set out to cast doubt on, and the industry's 'correlation is not causation' line was answered by exactly those criteria.

Tort and product liability were the main legal weapons. For forty years they failed against the defence that smokers knew the risk, until evidence of corporate knowledge and fraud changed what juries saw.

Burdens of proof shaped every wave of the litigation. An individual smoker had to prove that this cigarette caused this cancer, while states suing for Medicaid costs could rely on statistics across a whole population.
Administrative law decided the FDA's reach. In FDA v. Brown & Williamson (2000) the Supreme Court held that Congress had not given the agency power over tobacco, and only the 2009 Act did.

across.link: The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (adopted in 2003, in force from 2005) was the first treaty negotiated under the World Health Organization. The industry fought national controls through investment law as well: Philip Morris sued Uruguay over its large graphic health warnings and lost in July 2016 (an ICSID arbitration). The fight moved from courts and agencies to treaties and trade.

days.apply_question: In 2016 researchers (Kearns, Schmidt and Glantz, JAMA Internal Medicine) reported that a sugar-industry trade group had paid Harvard scientists in the 1960s for a review that played down sugar's role in heart disease. Using this case's loops, what evidence would you need before concluding that manufactured doubt, rather than honest scientific uncertainty, delayed action on sugar?
days.evidence_note: Settled: smoking causes lung cancer, heart disease, chronic obstructive lung disease and many other conditions. About half of persistent smokers die of their habit (the British Doctors Study's 50-year follow-up, Doll and colleagues, BMJ 2004). The companies' internal documents show that they knew of the risks and of addiction while publicly denying both, as the federal court found in 2006. Debated: how much each tool (taxes, advertising bans, smoke-free laws, litigation, warnings, changing norms) contributed to the decline; price increases have the strongest evidence. Also debated: whether e-cigarettes are a net public-health gain (the UK's harm-reduction stance against the more cautious US and WHO positions), and whether the Master Settlement protected the incumbent firms and made states dependent on tobacco revenue. Value judgment: autonomy against protection. Mill's harm principle, libertarians and the industry stress adult choice; public-health ethicists, Catholic social teaching (the common good and the protection of life) and many Protestant traditions stress addiction, children and deception. Who gained: the companies and their shareholders, and later state budgets. Who paid: smokers, their families, bystanders and taxpayers. Who consented: about nine in ten adults who smoke daily first tried a cigarette before 18 (CDC), when consent is weakest. The counterfactual, how many lives earlier action would have saved, cannot be known precisely.

chain.point: Nicotine reaches the brain within seconds of inhaling and triggers dopamine release in the reward system, so smoking is reinforced puff by puff and dependence follows. Most adult smokers began as teenagers, before they could weigh a risk that arrives decades later.

James Bonsack's cigarette-rolling machine (patented 1881) turned out roughly 200 cigarettes a minute, far more than a skilled hand-roller could make. James Buchanan Duke leased it on favourable terms in the mid-1880s, and his output outran demand, so he created demand with cheap packs, collectible cards and national advertising. His American Tobacco Company (1890) dominated the market until the Supreme Court ordered it broken up in 1911.

A burning cigarette is incomplete combustion, with the tip reaching roughly 800-900 degrees Celsius during a puff. Its smoke carries tar (thousands of compounds, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that damage DNA) and carbon monoxide. The mild flue-cured tobacco used in cigarettes made the smoke easy to inhale deep into the lungs, which pipe and cigar smoke mostly was not.

Doll and Hill's 1950 case-control study and Wynder and Graham's study the same year were followed by the British Doctors cohort from 1951. The Surgeon General's report of 11 January 1964 concluded that smoking causes lung cancer in men. The statistician R. A. Fisher, himself a smoker who had worked as a consultant to the industry, argued that a genotype might cause both smoking and cancer. That confounding objection was answered by dose-response, consistency across studies and falling risk in people who quit.

The Tobacco Industry Research Committee funded research that skirted the central question and publicized every uncertainty. A 1969 Brown & Williamson memo stated: 'Doubt is our product since it is the best means of competing with the "body of fact" that exists in the mind of the general public.' The strategy worked on how much evidence people demand before acting (Day 42) and on smokers' motivated reasoning (Day 163).

Cigarettes spread through advertising, wartime rations and social norms. On Easter Sunday 1929 Edward Bernays staged a march of young women smoking 'torches of freedom' in New York's Easter Parade, to break the taboo on women smoking in public. By 1965 about 42 per cent of American adults smoked. The reverse cascade came later, as smoke-free laws and disapproval made smoking a minority, stigmatized habit.

Warnings appeared on packs from 1966, and broadcast advertising was banned from 2 January 1971. The FDA's 1996 attempt to regulate cigarettes as nicotine-delivery devices was struck down in FDA v. Brown & Williamson (2000), because Congress had never given it that power. The Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act of 22 June 2009 finally did. Regulation followed the science by decades.

Lawsuits came in three waves. From 1954 into the 1970s the companies won almost every suit by arguing that smokers knew the risks. In the 1980s Rose Cipollone's family won a jury verdict that was overturned on appeal. In the 1990s states sued to recover Medicaid costs, and leaked and court-ordered documents showed what the companies knew. In the Master Settlement Agreement of 23 November 1998 the largest companies agreed with 46 states to pay about $206 billion over its first 25 years and to end cartoon characters and billboard advertising; four states had already settled separately.

In August 2006 Judge Gladys Kessler held the major manufacturers liable under the federal racketeering law (RICO) for a decades-long, coordinated scheme to deceive the public about smoking, nicotine and 'light' cigarettes. Court-ordered 'corrective statements' finally ran in newspapers and on television from November 2017, eleven years later.

Cigarettes are cheap to make and demand for them responds little to price, so the companies passed settlement payments on to smokers as price rises. Several states sold their future settlement income as 'tobacco bonds', tying public budgets to continued cigarette sales: a public-choice trap of the kind Day 244 describes.

US adult smoking fell from about 42 per cent in 1965 to about 11-12 per cent in the early 2020s. Men's lung-cancer death rates peaked around 1990 and have fallen since. Smoking still causes about 480,000 US deaths a year (CDC) and about 7-8 million worldwide (WHO), the textbook chronic disease of Day 148's epidemiological transition.

Oreskes and Conway (2010) traced the same tactics, and some of the same scientists, from tobacco to acid rain, the ozone hole and climate change. Day 49's leaded-gasoline case shows the earlier version of the same move: industry demanding proof of harm before any restriction.

As rich-country markets shrank, sales grew in Asia and Africa. The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003) and investor-state cases such as Philip Morris v. Uruguay (2016) carried the fight into international law. The International Relations block takes up treaties and global institutions.
Whether an addicted smoker chooses freely, and so who is responsible (smoker, seller or state), is a question for Philosophy II's lesson on free will and responsibility.

resource.creator: Allan M. Brandt, American Journal of Public Health 102(1) (January 2012)
resource.why: A Harvard historian of medicine, who served as an expert witness against the industry, traces the Frank Statement, Hill & Knowlton's strategy and the research committee from the industry's own documents. It shows manufactured doubt from the inside and how it spread to later industries. It is open access, and its author's role in the litigation is part of the story.
