days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: Tiny Melos Asked Only to Stay Neutral. Athens Replied That 'the Strong Do What They Can.' Why Did Greece's Greatest Sea Power Think Its Safety Required Crushing It?
days.concept: With no world government above them, states must provide their own security, and the arms and alliances one state builds to feel safe can make its neighbours less safe: the security dilemma at the heart of realism.
days.focus: Teaches realism as a lens built on anarchy (no authority above states), self-help and relative power, from Thucydides and Hobbes through Morgenthau (1948), Waltz's structural realism (1979) and Mearsheimer's offensive realism (2001), centred on the security dilemma (Herz 1950; Jervis 1978) and Jervis's point that it eases when defence is stronger than offence and the two can be told apart. Realism is taught as a powerful lens with a weak forecasting record, not as a law.
days.model_or_equation: Jervis's two-by-two (World Politics, 1978): whether offence or defence has the advantage, crossed with whether offensive and defensive forces can be told apart. Offence-advantaged and indistinguishable is 'doubly dangerous' (arms races spiral); defence-advantaged and distinguishable is 'doubly stable' (states can arm without threatening anyone). Underneath, the security dilemma has the payoff structure of a prisoner's dilemma (Day 14), or of a stag hunt (an assurance game) when both sides would prefer mutual restraint if each could trust the other.

story.title: Thirty-eight ships off a small island
story.hook: In the summer of 416 BC, the sixteenth year of the Peloponnesian War, Athens sent thirty-eight ships, about 2,700 hoplites (heavy infantry) and some 320 archers to Melos, a small Aegean island settled long before from Sparta (Thucydides 5.84). Thucydides says the Melians at first took no part in the war, until Athenian raids pushed them into open hostility. Before attacking, the Athenian envoys were heard not by the Melian assembly but by its magistrates and leading men. Thucydides' reconstruction of that meeting, the Melian Dialogue, is realism's founding text: 'right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' (5.89). The Melians appealed to justice, to the gods and to their Spartan kin, and asked to be left neutral. None of it helped. After a siege that ran into the winter they surrendered, and Athens killed the grown men, sold the women and children into slavery and sent out five hundred colonists of its own (5.116).
story.puzzle: Melos had no fleet worth fearing and asked to be 'friends instead of enemies, but allies of neither side' (5.94). Why did the greatest naval power in Greece believe its own safety required destroying it?
story.payoff: The Athenians answer in the dialogue itself: 'your hostility cannot so much hurt us as your friendship will be an argument to our subjects of our weakness' (5.95). Where no authority stands above states, safety rests on relative power and on a reputation for using it, so even a harmless neutral looks like a crack in the wall: that is the realist logic of anarchy and self-help. Thucydides also records realism's warning about itself: the next year Athens launched the Sicilian expedition, which ended in catastrophe in 413 BC. Expansion driven by fear can manufacture the threats it fears.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116 (trans. Richard Crawley, 1874)
Thucydides 1.22, on how the speeches were composed
Robert Jervis, 'Cooperation Under the Security Dilemma', World Politics 30(2), 1978
John H. Herz, 'Idealist Internationalism and the Security Dilemma', World Politics 2(2), 1950
R. Meiggs & D. Lewis, A Selection of Greek Historical Inscriptions, no. 67 (contributions to a Spartan war fund)

days.application: The Anglo-German naval race: HMS Dreadnought, launched at Portsmouth on 10 February 1906, made every existing battleship obsolete, including Britain's own large lead in them. Germany answered under Tirpitz's Navy Laws, Britain's 1909 naval scare ('We want eight and we won't wait') answered back, and by August 1914 Britain had about twenty dreadnought battleships in service to Germany's roughly thirteen (each side also had battlecruisers), each side's defence reading as the other's threat.

builds_on.why: Hobbes's state of nature (no common power, so each must secure itself) is realism's anarchy moved from individuals to states; Hobbes himself pictured sovereigns 'in the state and posture of gladiators' (Leviathan, ch. 13)

the security dilemma has a prisoner's-dilemma structure (arming is individually rational and collectively ruinous), and Day 14 showed how repetition can change such a game; Jervis also modelled the milder case as a stag hunt, an assurance game

across.link: Evolutionary arms races between predators and prey or parasites and hosts (Dawkins & Krebs, 'Arms races between and within species', Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 1979) share the security dilemma's logic of relative advantage that leaves neither side safer. The analogy breaks where states can talk: the Washington Naval Treaty (1922) negotiated capital-ship ratios of 5:5:3 for Britain, the United States and Japan, something no cheetah and gazelle can do.

days.apply_question: In December 2022 Japan adopted a strategy to raise defence spending to about 2 percent of GDP by 2027 and to acquire long-range 'counterstrike' missiles, and it soon agreed to buy several hundred US Tomahawk cruise missiles: using the security dilemma and Jervis's offense-defense distinction, what kind of Japanese capability would add most to Tokyo's security while looking least threatening to Beijing?
days.evidence_note: Lens, not law: realism's claims about the pressures of anarchy are widely accepted; its predictions are contested and grand theories have a weak forecasting record (Tetlock's experts, Day 167). The Melian Dialogue is Thucydides' literary reconstruction: he says his speeches give 'the general sense' of what was said (1.22), so tell it as his account, not a transcript. Melos's neutrality was less clean than the dialogue suggests: Thucydides himself says it had been openly hostile since Athenian raids (Nicias's attack of 426 BC), and an inscribed list of contributions to a Spartan war fund (Meiggs & Lewis no. 67, date disputed) includes Melians. Debated: whether the naval race helped cause the First World War; many historians argue Britain had effectively won it by 1912-13 and that the war's triggers lay elsewhere.

resource.title: The Melian Dialogue (History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, chapters 84-116)
resource.creator: Thucydides, translated by Richard Crawley (1874)
resource.why: Realism's founding text in its own words: the Athenians' case for power and the Melians' case for justice, argued point by point, so Logan can judge for himself whether the Athenians were right about their own safety.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.topic: Institutions and interdependence: the liberal lens
days.headline_hint: In 1910 Norman Angell Argued That War Could No Longer Pay, Even for the Victor. Four Years Later Europe Went to War Anyway. Was He Wrong?
days.concept: Liberal theories hold that trade, international institutions and democracy can make cooperation between states durable by raising the cost of war, lengthening the 'shadow of the future' and constraining leaders: strong tendencies, not guarantees.
days.focus: Teaches the liberal lens through its three legs: economic interdependence (Keohane & Nye 1977), institutions that make cooperation repeated and verifiable (Keohane 1984), and the democratic peace (Doyle 1983; Russett 1993). Names the weak spots: the democratic peace is a strong correlation whose cause is debated (Day 18), and trade alone did not stop 1914. The Schuman Plan shows the lesson Europe drew: bind trade inside institutions.
days.model_or_equation: Why institutions help, the shadow of the future (Axelrod & Keohane 1985, building on Day 14): in a repeated prisoner's dilemma with payoffs T > R > P > S (temptation, reward, punishment, sucker's payoff), cooperation backed by the threat of permanent retaliation is sustainable when delta >= (T - R)/(T - P), where delta is how much each side values the next round relative to this one. Institutions raise delta (regular meetings, rules and monitoring make the future count and cheating visible) and can lower T, the gain from cheating.

story.title: The best-seller that said war could not pay
story.hook: In 1909 Norman Angell, general manager of the Paris edition of Lord Northcliffe's Daily Mail, published a pamphlet called Europe's Optical Illusion; expanded in 1910 as The Great Illusion, it became one of the most discussed books in Europe and was translated into many languages. His argument: in an economy knit together by credit and trade, a conqueror cannot seize another nation's wealth without wrecking his own, so war cannot pay even the victor. Britain and Germany were among each other's largest trading partners. In August 1914 they went to war anyway, in a conflict that killed something like 15 to 20 million soldiers and civilians. Angell has been mocked ever since as the man who said war was impossible. He never said that. He said it was futile.
story.puzzle: If Angell was right that war could not pay, why did the most interdependent economies in Europe fight the most destructive war in their history, and does 1914 refute the idea that trade keeps the peace?
story.payoff: Angell was largely right about the economics (the war ruined victors and vanquished alike) and wrong to expect that being right would be enough. Leaders fought over security, status and fear of decline, and nothing institutional tied their hands or made their promises enforceable. Liberal theory's later answer is that interdependence raises the cost of war but does not by itself remove the reasons for it: it needs institutions that make cooperation repeated and verifiable, and governments answerable to the people who pay. Angell received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1933.
sources: Norman Angell, The Great Illusion (London: Heinemann, 1910)
Nobel Peace Prize 1933, Sir Norman Angell (Nobel Foundation)
Robert O. Keohane & Joseph S. Nye, Power and Interdependence (1977)
Michael W. Doyle, 'Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs', Philosophy & Public Affairs 12, 1983

days.application: The Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950: French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed placing French and German coal and steel, the sinews of war, under a common High Authority so that war between the two would become 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. The Treaty of Paris (18 April 1951) created the European Coal and Steel Community of six states, the seed of today's European Union: interdependence deliberately wrapped in institutions.

builds_on.why: the democratic peace is a strong correlation (established democracies have very rarely, if ever, fought each other) with candidate confounders such as wealth, alliances and trade (Farber & Gowa 1995; Gartzke 2007)
Axelrod's repeated prisoner's dilemma is the engine of liberal institutionalism: rules and monitoring lengthen the shadow of the future so that cooperation pays

across.link: Kant's Toward Perpetual Peace (1795) proposed republican constitutions, a federation of free states and 'cosmopolitan right'; Russett and Oneal's Triangulating Peace (2001) tested those three legs (democracy, international organizations and trade) statistically and called them the 'Kantian triangle'.

days.apply_question: For two decades German governments defended deep energy trade with Russia, including the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, as 'Wandel durch Handel' (change through trade): using the liberal lens's three legs of trade, shared institutions and democracy, why did that interdependence fail to deter Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022?
days.evidence_note: Settled as a pattern: wars between established democracies have been very rare. Debated: why (shared norms and institutions, per Doyle and Russett, versus a 'capitalist peace', Gartzke 2007, Cold War alliance, Farber & Gowa 1995, or definitional choices, Rosato 2003); and whether trade reduces conflict (Russett & Oneal 2001) or can raise it (Barbieri, The Liberal Illusion, 2002; Copeland 2015 on expectations of future trade). Realists (Mearsheimer, 'The False Promise of International Institutions', 1994-95) argue institutions only reflect power. Teach liberalism as a lens and label only these disputed claims.

resource.title: Toward Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch, Second Section (the three 'definitive articles')
resource.creator: Immanuel Kant (1795); many translations, including public-domain ones
resource.why: The source of liberal international thought in its own words: why Kant thought republican government, a federation of free states and a right of hospitality to strangers would make peace more likely, and why he treated peace as something to be built rather than a natural state.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: North Korea's First Nuclear Test Was a Fraction of Hiroshima's. Britain's Arsenal Was Vastly More Powerful. Only One of Them Alarmed Washington.
days.concept: Constructivism holds that what states fear and want depends on shared ideas (identities, norms and the meanings they give one another's power), so the same weapon can be a threat or a reassurance: 'anarchy is what states make of it' (Wendt 1992).
days.focus: Teaches the third lens: material facts matter through the meanings states give them. Covers Wendt's three 'cultures of anarchy', norms as shared expectations that constitute identities as well as constrain behaviour, and how such norms change (Day 202). Pairs it honestly with realism's reply: Walt's balance-of-threat theory (1987) also weighs intentions, so constructivism's distinctive contribution is explaining where intentions and identities come from and how they shift.
days.model_or_equation: Wendt's three cultures of anarchy (Social Theory of International Politics, 1999): Hobbesian, where the other is an enemy and violence has no limits; Lockean, where the other is a rival whose survival is accepted and whose conflicts are limited; Kantian, where the other is a friend, disputes are settled without war and security is pursued together. The same distribution of power can sit inside any of the three.

story.title: Five days, fifteen votes, one small bomb
story.hook: On 9 October 2006 North Korea set off its first nuclear device under a mountain at Punggye-ri. Seismographs registered a tremor of about magnitude 4, and most outside estimates put the yield below one kiloton, less than a tenth of Hiroshima's. Five days later the UN Security Council voted 15 to 0 for sanctions (Resolution 1718). Britain at the time kept fewer than 200 operationally available warheads on its Trident missiles, each estimated at around 100 kilotons, and no one in Washington treated them as a threat. Eleven years earlier, before North Korea had tested any weapon, the political scientist Alexander Wendt had written that '500 British nuclear weapons are less threatening to the United States than 5 North Korean nuclear weapons, because the British are friends of the United States and the North Koreans are not.'
story.puzzle: By any material measure, Britain's arsenal could do thousands of times more damage to the United States than North Korea's single test device. Why did the tiny one cause the alarm?
story.payoff: Threat is not capability alone; it is capability read through identity. The United States and Britain share a history, an alliance and settled expectations about each other (a Kantian culture in Wendt's terms), while the United States and North Korea have treated each other as enemies since 1950. Wendt's sentence goes on: 'amity or enmity is a function of shared understandings.' Those understandings were made, and can be unmade, which is why constructivists study how identities change.
sources: Alexander Wendt, 'Constructing International Politics', International Security 20(1), 1995
Alexander Wendt, 'Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics', International Organization 46(2), 1992
UN Security Council Resolution 1718 (14 October 2006)
UK Ministry of Defence, The Future of the United Kingdom's Nuclear Deterrent (Cm 6994, December 2006)

days.application: The nuclear taboo: no nuclear weapon has been used in war since Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, including in wars nuclear powers fought against non-nuclear opponents (the United States in Korea and Vietnam, the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, Britain in the Falklands, China against Vietnam in 1979). Nina Tannenwald (International Organization, 1999; The Nuclear Taboo, 2007) argues a norm against use grew up that made it 'unthinkable' to leaders, documenting 1950s officials, among them Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, who complained of the 'taboo' as an obstacle; T.V. Paul (2009) calls it a 'tradition' kept for reputational reasons; deterrence explains part of it.

builds_on.why: norms are self-enforcing expectations that can shift suddenly once enough actors move together; constructivism applies the same idea to states, and the nuclear taboo is such a norm
Durkheim's social facts, patterns that exist at the level of the group and constrain individuals, are the sociological root of constructivism's 'intersubjective' structures

across.link: John Searle's The Construction of Social Reality (1995) explains institutional facts with the formula 'X counts as Y in context C': a piece of paper counts as money, a line on a map counts as a border. Constructivists in IR build on this account of facts that exist only because people collectively accept them.

days.apply_question: Japan has advanced nuclear technology and tonnes of separated plutonium, yet it has kept Prime Minister Eisaku Sato's 1967 Three Non-Nuclear Principles (not possessing, not producing and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons): what evidence would help you decide whether a constructivist account (an identity shaped by Hiroshima and Nagasaki) or a realist one (security under the US nuclear umbrella) does more to explain that restraint?
days.evidence_note: Lens, not law: constructivism explains change and meaning well and predicts poorly, like the other lenses. Settled: no nuclear use in war since 9 August 1945. Debated: why (a normative taboo, per Tannenwald; a reputational tradition, per T.V. Paul 2009; or deterrence and luck); survey experiments find many Americans would approve nuclear use under some conditions (Press, Sagan & Valentino, APSR 2013; Sagan & Valentino, International Security 2017), which challenges a public taboo while leaving leaders' restraint to explain. The 2006 test's yield is an estimate (below about one kiloton).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: Serbia's Reply Seemed to Accept Almost Every Demand. Even the Kaiser Wrote That 'Every Reason for War Drops Away.' Austria Declared War the Same Day.
days.concept: Because war destroys value, there is always some deal that both sides should prefer to fighting, so wars happen when bargaining fails: through private information and the incentive to bluff, through commitment problems when power is shifting, or over stakes that cannot be divided (Fearon 1995).
days.focus: Teaches the bargaining model of war, the mainstream rationalist account, built from expected value (Day 11) and game theory (Day 14): costs create a bargaining range, and war breaks out when leaders cannot credibly reveal their strength or resolve, cannot credibly promise not to exploit future power, or treat the stake as indivisible. Names the model's limits (unitary-state assumptions, misperception, domestic politics, leaders' private interests; Blattman 2022) and shows that fighting itself reveals information.
key_concepts: private information and incentives to misrepresent
days.model_or_equation: Fearon's bargaining range. A prize worth 1 is disputed; state A would win a war with probability p; fighting costs A c_A and B c_B, both greater than zero, measured as shares of the prize. A's expected payoff from war is p - c_A; B's is (1 - p) - c_B. Any peaceful split that gives A a share x with p - c_A <= x <= p + c_B leaves both at least as well off as war, and this range is never empty because c_A + c_B > 0. So war needs an explanation: the sides disagree about p (private information), cannot trust a deal to last (commitment), or cannot divide the prize.

story.title: Forty-eight hours in Belgrade
story.hook: At six in the evening on 23 July 1914, nearly four weeks after a Bosnian Serb assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary's minister in Belgrade, Baron Wladimir Giesl, handed Serbia an ultimatum of ten demands with 48 hours to reply. Vienna's leaders had drafted it hoping it would be refused. Shortly before the deadline on 25 July, Prime Minister Nikola Pasic delivered Serbia's answer in person. Conciliatory in tone, it seemed to accept almost everything, rejecting outright only the demand that Austro-Hungarian officials take part in the investigation on Serbian soil, though it hedged several other points. Giesl broke off relations at once and left on the evening train. When Kaiser Wilhelm II read the reply on 28 July he wrote that it was 'a brilliant performance for a time limit of only 48 hours' and that with it 'every reason for war drops away'. That same day Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; within a week Germany, Russia, France and Britain were at war too.
story.puzzle: Serbia appeared to have conceded nearly everything, and even the Kaiser thought the quarrel was settled. Why could no deal be struck that left every government better off than a war that would kill millions?
story.payoff: Fearon's mechanisms were all present. Commitment: Vienna believed no Serbian promise to suppress nationalist agitation could be trusted as Serbia grew stronger with Russian backing, so a deal now looked worse than war now; Germany's generals reasoned the same way about Russia's rearmament programme, due to be completed around 1917. Private information: each capital guessed at the others' resolve (Berlin hoped Russia would back down and Britain stay out), and each had reasons to bluff; even the Serbian reply was hard to read, since Christopher Clark argues it conceded far less than its tone suggested. Bargaining failed not because no better deal existed but because no one could credibly reveal or promise what a deal required. Historians still argue over how much was design and how much 'sleepwalking'.
sources: James D. Fearon, 'Rationalist Explanations for War', International Organization 49(3), 1995
Imanuel Geiss, ed., July 1914: The Outbreak of the First World War: Selected Documents (1967), including Wilhelm II's note of 28 July 1914
Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers (2012)
Margaret MacMillan, The War That Ended Peace (2013)

days.application: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, read through competing bargaining accounts: a commitment problem (Moscow feared that a Ukraine drifting into Western alignment could not be held to any promise of neutrality, and by many accounts Kyiv in turn saw no Russian guarantee as credible, one reason offered for the failure of the spring-2022 Istanbul talks, whose collapse is itself disputed) versus private information and misperception (Russian planners appear to have expected Kyiv to fall within days and badly underestimated Ukrainian resistance). Present these as the explanations scholars argue over, not as a verdict.

builds_on.why: the bargaining range is an expected-value calculation: each side's war payoff is its probability of winning times the prize, minus its costs
commitment problems and bluffing are game-theory ideas: a promise is credible only if keeping it will still be in the promiser's interest when the time comes

across.link: The Priest-Klein model of litigation (Journal of Legal Studies, 1984) applies the same logic to lawsuits: trials are costly, so most disputes settle, and the cases that go to trial are disproportionately those where the parties' private estimates of winning diverge, the courtroom version of war through private information.

days.apply_question: On 2 April 1982 Argentina's military junta seized the Falkland Islands, and Britain sent a task force; the war killed about 900 people and Argentina lost: which of Fearon's three mechanisms best explains why the two governments failed to reach a negotiated deal that both would have preferred to fighting?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the bargaining framework is the field's mainstream starting point. Debated: responsibility for 1914 (Fischer's thesis that German leaders sought the war versus Clark's account of shared misjudgment, with MacMillan in between) and how much the Serbian reply really conceded (Clark reads it as a masterpiece of equivocation; others as a genuine climb-down); explanations of 2022, where commitment, misperception and ideological or imperial motives are all argued and much evidence is still closed. Critics note the model assumes unitary, rational states and stress leaders' private interests and emotions (Blattman, Why We Fight, 2022). Explain; do not assign blame.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: A Sweltering Soviet Submarine, a Nuclear Torpedo and One Officer's Reported 'No': In October 1962 Deterrence Ran on Chance
days.concept: Nuclear deterrence prevents attack by making retaliation certain enough and terrible enough, which requires a second-strike force that can survive a first strike, and its threats can be credible even when no sane leader would carry them out, because a crisis creates 'the threat that leaves something to chance' (Schelling 1960).
days.focus: Teaches deterrence by punishment: Brodie's 1946 insight that the bomb's chief purpose is to avert wars, Wohlstetter's 'delicate balance of terror' (1959) and the secure second strike, mutual assured destruction, and Schelling's answer to the credibility problem: manipulate shared risk rather than promise deliberate suicide. Its dark side is the same chance: organizations, accidents and false alarms (Sagan 1993, drawing on Day 94).
key_concepts: the threat that leaves something to chance
days.model_or_equation: Two conditions. Deterrence: an attack is deterred when the attacker's expected cost of retaliation, P(retaliation) x damage, exceeds its expected gain, which requires forces that survive a first strike. Schelling's risk manipulation: if staying in a crisis carries a probability q each round that events slip out of anyone's control into catastrophe D, each side bears an expected cost of q x D for every round it holds out, so a side can coerce by raising q (moving forces, delegating authority) without ever deciding to fire.

story.title: Practice depth charges over B-59
story.hook: On 27 October 1962, the most dangerous day of the Cuban Missile Crisis (an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba that day), the Soviet diesel submarine B-59 was cornered by US Navy destroyers in the Atlantic. The Americans dropped practice depth charges to signal it to surface. Washington had told Moscow what the signals meant, but the message never reached the submarines, and the crew, who had not heard from Moscow for days, could not know they were signals. Inside, with batteries failing and temperatures reported above 45 C, Captain Valentin Savitsky, by the later account of the signals-intelligence officer aboard, Vadim Orlov, ordered the boat's nuclear torpedo readied: 'We're going to blast them now! We will die, but we will sink them all.' The brigade chief of staff aboard, Vasili Arkhipov, is reported to have talked him down, and B-59 surfaced and turned for home. The story became public only in 2002, and its details are debated.
story.puzzle: The whole point of deterrence is that no rational leader would start a nuclear war. Yet here the decision sat with an exhausted captain under the sea. Was deterrence working in October 1962, or failing?
story.payoff: Both, and that is Schelling's insight. Kennedy and Khrushchev each had reason to back down precisely because neither fully controlled what would happen next: quarantine lines, armed submarines and jittery commanders put a real probability of catastrophe on the table, and that shared risk is what coerced. Deterrence did not depend on anyone deciding to fire; it depended on the chance that someone might. The same fact makes it fragile: a threat that leaves something to chance can come true by chance.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict (1960), ch. 8, 'The Threat That Leaves Something to Chance'
National Security Archive (George Washington University), briefing book on Soviet submarines in the Cuban Missile Crisis (2002), including Vadim Orlov's account
Svetlana Savranskaya, 'New Sources on the Role of Soviet Submarines in the Cuban Missile Crisis', Journal of Strategic Studies 28(2), 2005

days.application: The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972: the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to limit missile defences to two sites each (one after a 1974 protocol), deliberately leaving their cities open to retaliation so that neither could hope to strike first and escape. Mutual vulnerability was written into law. The United States withdrew in 2002 to build limited defences, and the argument over whether defences undermine deterrence continues.

builds_on.why: deterrence is a game of commitment and credibility in which each side's best move depends on the other's, and Schelling, a game theorist, built it from the strategic reasoning of Day 14
Perrow's normal accidents in tightly coupled systems are the 'chance' in Schelling's threat; Scott Sagan's The Limits of Safety (1993) applied Perrow's argument to US nuclear forces

across.link: Permissive action links, coded locks fitted to US nuclear weapons under a 1962 presidential directive (NSAM 160), and the 'two-person rule' are engineering controls built to remove the unauthorized-use risk on which Schelling's chance depends; the reported need for B-59's senior officers to agree is the human version of the same redundancy.

days.apply_question: Just after midnight on 26 September 1983, Soviet early-warning satellites told Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov that US Minuteman missiles were inbound, first one and then five, and he judged it a false alarm, rightly (sunlight glinting off high clouds): using second-strike logic, why do missile submarines hidden at sea make such a false alarm less dangerous than a force that can survive only by launching on warning?
days.evidence_note: Settled: no nuclear use since 1945; the logic of second-strike stability is mainstream strategy. Debated: the B-59 story rests largely on later recollections, and whether launch needed three officers' consent and how close it came are disputed; whether deterrence kept the long peace or luck did (Sagan 1993; Lebow & Stein, We All Lost the Cold War, 1994); whether missile defence is destabilizing. Value judgment: whether threatening cities can be moral; the US Catholic bishops' pastoral letter 'The Challenge of Peace' (1983) gave deterrence only 'strictly conditioned moral acceptance', while others hold that intending even a conditional massacre is wrong.

resource.why: Schelling's own readable account of brinkmanship as the deliberate creation of shared risk, the idea behind 'the threat that leaves something to chance', written with the Berlin and Cuba crises fresh in mind.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: A Quaker Ambulance Driver Sorted More Than a Century of Wars by Size. They Looked Like Earthquakes, and That Makes Peace Very Hard to Prove.
days.concept: Because war sizes follow a fat-tailed, power-law distribution in which a few enormous wars dominate the total, seven decades without a war between great powers is weak evidence that the underlying risk of a catastrophic war has fallen, so whether war has declined depends on which measure and how long a window you trust.
days.focus: Teaches how to judge a trend claim when events are fat-tailed (Day 12): Richardson's power law of 'deadly quarrels', Gaddis's 'Long Peace' (1986), Pinker's case that violence has declined (2011), and the statistical challenges from Cirillo & Taleb (2016), Clauset (2018) and Braumoeller (2019). Separates the measures that clearly fell (battle deaths per head after 1945; war between great powers) from the question that stays open (the risk of a very large war).
days.model_or_equation: Richardson's finding in modern form: the probability that a war kills more than x people falls as a power of x, P(X > x) proportional to x^(-alpha), with alpha estimated at roughly one-half for interstate wars (Clauset 2018; Cirillo & Taleb 2016). With alpha below 1 the average war size is dominated by the rare largest wars, so decades of smaller wars barely move the estimate; and if outbreaks arrive at random (a Poisson process), long gaps between great wars are expected even when nothing has changed.

story.title: Deadly quarrels, measured like earthquakes
story.hook: Lewis Fry Richardson, a Quaker physicist, spent 1916 to 1919 with the Friends' Ambulance Unit on the Western Front, where between shifts he worked out by hand the first numerical weather forecast. After the war he turned the same habit of measurement on war itself. He catalogued every 'deadly quarrel' he could find from 1820 to the mid-twentieth century, from murders to world wars, and gave each a magnitude: the base-10 logarithm of its dead, so a quarrel killing 1,000 scored 3 and one killing ten million scored 7, a class only the two world wars reached. Small quarrels were many and great ones rare, falling off in a regular pattern, and wars broke out as if at random, with no clear trend up or down. Richardson died in 1953; his Statistics of Deadly Quarrels was published in 1960.
story.puzzle: Since the Korean War no two great powers have fought each other in a full-scale war: the 'Long Peace'. Is that a real decline in war, or the kind of quiet stretch Richardson's random, fat-tailed pattern would produce anyway, and how long would you have to wait to tell?
story.payoff: In a fat-tailed world a long quiet spell is weak evidence. Aaron Clauset (2018) tested the post-1945 record against Richardson's unchanging process and found it statistically consistent with no change; on his estimate the Long Peace would need to last roughly another century or more before it became clearly distinguishable from chance. That does not prove Pinker wrong (battle deaths per head of population did fall sharply after 1945); it shows which claims the data can carry: fewer deaths from smaller wars, yes; a lower risk of a catastrophic one, not yet knowable.
sources: Lewis F. Richardson, Statistics of Deadly Quarrels (1960)
Aaron Clauset, 'Trends and fluctuations in the severity of interstate wars', Science Advances 4(2), 2018
Pasquale Cirillo & Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 'On the statistical properties and tail risk of violent conflicts', Physica A 452, 2016
Steven Pinker, The Better Angels of Our Nature (2011)
Bear F. Braumoeller, Only the Dead (2019)
John Lewis Gaddis, 'The Long Peace', International Security 10(4), 1986

days.application: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program's count for 2022: by its estimates roughly 237,000 people died in organized violence, about double 2021 and the most since 1994, the year of the Rwandan genocide, driven above all by Ethiopia's Tigray war (over 100,000 deaths) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine (over 80,000); and for 2024 UCDP recorded about 60 active state-based conflicts, the most in its series since 1946. Read with today's concept, one terrible year neither proves the decline was an illusion nor shows that it has reversed.

builds_on.why: power laws and fat tails are the mathematics here: in a fat-tailed world the largest events dominate the total and the record so far understates what can come next
asking whether the Long Peace is a real change is a significance question: how surprising would seven quiet decades be if nothing had changed?

across.link: Cirillo and Taleb applied the same tail statistics to epidemics ('Tail risk of contagious diseases', Nature Physics, 2020) and found pandemic death tolls fat-tailed as well, so long quiet spells between great pandemics say little about the risk of the next one.

days.apply_question: No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 9 August 1945, more than 80 years ago: using today's reasoning about rare, fat-tailed events and observation windows, why can that record alone not show that the annual risk of nuclear use is now very low?
days.evidence_note: Settled: battle deaths per head fell sharply after 1945, and great powers have not fought a full-scale war against each other since Korea (1950-53). Debated: whether this is a durable decline (Pinker 2011; Goldstein 2011; Gaddis 1986) or a lull consistent with unchanged underlying risk (Cirillo & Taleb 2016; Clauset 2018; Braumoeller 2019, who finds no decline in the rate at which states start conflicts); historians in The Darker Angels of Our Nature (Dwyer & Micale, eds., 2021) also dispute Pinker's use of sources. UCDP figures are estimates with wide ranges. Keep the empirical question apart from the value question of whether modern societies are morally better.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: Oxford Wanted to Honour Harry Truman. A Catholic Philosopher Who Was No Pacifist Stood Up to Call the Atomic Bombings Murder.
days.concept: Just war theory holds that war can be justified only under strict conditions (just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort) and must be fought with discrimination and proportionality, with the doctrine of double effect separating harm to civilians that is intended, which is forbidden, from harm that is foreseen but unintended, which is sometimes permitted.
days.focus: Teaches the just war tradition as the main Western framework for the ethics of war, from Augustine and Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.40; double effect in q.64 a.7) through Grotius to Walzer's secular Just and Unjust Wars (1977), placed among its rivals: realists who deny that morality binds states, consequentialists who weigh outcomes alone, and Christian pacifists (Yoder, The Politics of Jesus, 1972; Hauerwas) who reject the frame. Keeps empirical questions (would Japan have surrendered without the bombs?) apart from moral ones (may one intend civilian deaths?).
key_concepts: jus ad bellum (justice of going to war)
jus in bello: discrimination (noncombatant immunity) and proportionality
days.model_or_equation: Double effect in its classic four conditions, as later Catholic moral theology systematized it: an act with a good and a bad effect may be permitted if (1) the act itself is not wrong; (2) the agent intends only the good effect; (3) the bad effect is not the means to the good effect; (4) there is a proportionate reason for allowing the bad effect. Anscombe's charge against Hiroshima turns on conditions (2) and (3): the civilians' deaths were the means of breaking Japan's will.

story.title: A dissent at Oxford, 1956
story.hook: In the spring of 1956 the University of Oxford proposed an honorary Doctorate of Civil Law for Harry S. Truman, who as president had ordered the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing well over 100,000 people, most of them civilians. Elizabeth Anscombe, a 37-year-old Catholic philosopher at Somerville College and the translator of Wittgenstein, rose in the university's assembly to oppose it, forcing a vote. She lost; the degree was conferred that June. She then published a pamphlet, Mr Truman's Degree, arguing that 'for men to choose to kill the innocent as a means to their ends is always murder.' Anscombe was no pacifist: she held that some wars are just, and in 'War and Murder' (1961) she argued that pacifism had helped erode respect for the line between killing combatants and murdering the innocent.
story.puzzle: If Anscombe accepted that a war can be just, and the bombs plausibly hastened the end of the most destructive war in history, how could she call them murder?
story.payoff: Because just war theory judges how a war is fought separately from why it is fought. Even in a just war, discrimination forbids making noncombatants the target, and double effect explains the line she drew: a commander may sometimes foresee civilian deaths as a side effect of striking a military target, but at Hiroshima and Nagasaki the civilians' deaths were the means, the intended path to surrender. On that tradition's terms good consequences cannot make the intended killing of the innocent permissible. A consequentialist reading, which weighs lives lost against lives saved, reaches a different verdict, and that disagreement is what the lesson maps.
sources: G.E.M. Anscombe, 'Mr Truman's Degree' (pamphlet, 1956/57), in Collected Philosophical Papers, vol. III: Ethics, Religion and Politics (1981)
G.E.M. Anscombe, 'War and Murder' (1961), in the same volume
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.40 and q.64 a.7
Michael Walzer, Just and Unjust Wars (1977)

days.application: NATO's 78-day air campaign against Yugoslavia over Kosovo (24 March to 10 June 1999), launched without Security Council authorization, which the Independent International Commission on Kosovo (2000) judged 'illegal but legitimate'. In bello it raised double-effect questions in practice, such as the strike on a passenger train crossing the Grdelica gorge bridge (12 April 1999) and the bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade (7 May 1999); Human Rights Watch counted roughly 500 civilian deaths from the campaign.

builds_on.why: just war theory and double effect come from the natural-law tradition of Aquinas taught on Day 48, and Anscombe argued from within it
the case for Hiroshima is consequentialist (more lives saved by ending the war than taken by the bombs), so the dispute is consequentialism against an absolute constraint

across.link: Double effect governs end-of-life care: a doctor may give doses of opioids or sedation that foreseeably hasten death if the aim is relieving suffering rather than killing, and the US Supreme Court relied on that distinction of intent in Vacco v. Quill (1997) when it upheld New York's ban on assisted suicide.

days.apply_question: On 13 February 1991, during the Gulf War, US aircraft destroyed the Amiriyah shelter in Baghdad, which American planners believed was a military command bunker, and hundreds of civilians sheltering inside were killed: using double effect and the jus in bello principles, what would you need to know about what the planners knew and intended, and what would you need to value, to judge whether the strike was permissible?
days.evidence_note: Value judgment throughout: whether intention matters morally (defended by the Thomist tradition, Anscombe and, in modified form, Walzer; doubted by consequentialists and by some deontologists, such as Judith Jarvis Thomson), and whether Christians may take part in war at all (Augustine and Aquinas: yes, under conditions; Yoder and Hauerwas: no). Debated empirically: whether the atomic bombings were needed to end the war without an invasion (Gar Alperovitz argues not; Richard Frank, Downfall, 1999, argues they were decisive; Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy, 2005, stresses Soviet entry into the war). Present the Christian positions among the others, attributed, never as the house verdict.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: In 1973 Arab Producers Embargoed America. Tankers Rerouted Around It, Yet Oil Prices Quadrupled and Washington Rewrote the Rules for Its Cars.
days.concept: Interdependence is never symmetrical, and a state that controls a node others cannot route around (a commodity with no substitute, a financial hub, a unique machine) can turn that dependence into coercion; Farrell and Newman call this weaponized interdependence.
days.focus: Teaches economic statecraft as a question of network position: Hirschman's insight (1945) that trade creates asymmetric dependence, Keohane & Nye's distinction between sensitivity and vulnerability (1977), and Farrell & Newman's 'chokepoint' and 'panopticon' effects (2019). Shows why fungible commodities make leaky weapons and network hubs (dollar clearing, SWIFT, extreme-ultraviolet lithography) sharp ones, and how targets respond by stockpiling, substituting and building alternatives, including Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou as hedges against dependence on GPS (Day 131). Trade and sanctions economics are assumed at CFA level.
days.model_or_equation: A rough rule for leverage, drawn from Farrell & Newman and Keohane & Nye: coercive power over a target grows with (1) how central the node you control is, meaning how many flows must pass through it; (2) how hard it is for the target to substitute or reroute; and (3) how long the target needs to adjust. Oil fails test (2) because it is fungible; ASML's EUV machines and dollar clearing pass all three, for now, since every use of a chokepoint raises the target's incentive to build around it.

story.title: A barrel of oil can change its address
story.hook: On 17 October 1973, eleven days into the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil ministers meeting in Kuwait agreed to cut production month by month; within days, after President Nixon asked Congress for $2.2 billion in emergency aid for Israel, Saudi Arabia and its partners embargoed oil sales to the United States and the Netherlands. The posted price of Saudi light crude went from about $3 a barrel before the war to $11.65 by January 1974. Americans queued at gas stations, Congress imposed a national 55-mph speed limit, and in December 1975 the Energy Policy and Conservation Act created both fuel-economy standards for cars and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Yet the embargo itself leaked: oil companies reshuffled cargoes so that non-Arab crude flowed to the embargoed countries and Arab crude to everyone else.
story.puzzle: If oil could simply be rerouted around the embargo, where did the Arab producers' leverage come from, and why did it reshape American law for decades?
story.payoff: From the production cut, not the targeting. Oil is fungible, so a ban on particular buyers is easy to evade, but removing barrels at the source raises the price for every importer at once: the world market itself carried the shock to the targets. That makes oil a blunt chokepoint, one that hits friends and foes alike and that cost the producers market share as consumers adapted. America's response (a strategic reserve, efficiency standards and, with its allies, the International Energy Agency's oil-sharing scheme of 1974) is the textbook way to blunt a chokepoint: stockpile, substitute, reduce dependence. Precise chokepoints are the network hubs a target cannot route around.
sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Oil Embargo, 1973-1974'
Daniel Yergin, The Prize (1991)
Energy Policy and Conservation Act, Pub. L. 94-163 (22 December 1975)
Henry Farrell & Abraham L. Newman, 'Weaponized Interdependence', International Security 44(1), 2019

days.application: The US export controls of 7 October 2022, which barred sales to China of the most advanced AI chips and of the tools to make them, later reinforced by Dutch and Japanese rules in 2023 (ASML's EUV machines had been kept from China since 2019): a precise chokepoint, because only ASML builds the extreme-ultraviolet lithography machines needed for the smallest chips (Day 106). China answered with export licensing on gallium and germanium from August 2023, later extended to other critical minerals, and with a drive to build its own tools; Huawei's Mate 60 Pro (August 2023) carried a 7-nanometre chip made by SMIC without EUV.

builds_on.why: a chokepoint is a hub in a network: Farrell and Newman's argument is network theory applied to the world economy, in which whoever controls the high-degree nodes controls the flows
the 2022 export controls target the transistor-scaling frontier, where ASML's EUV machines are the only way to print the smallest chips

across.link: In the first days of the First World War Britain cut Germany's undersea telegraph cables, exploiting London's place at the hub of the world's cable, shipping, insurance and credit networks; Nicholas Lambert's Planning Armageddon (2012) shows the Admiralty had planned this economic warfare in advance, weaponized interdependence a century before the term.

days.apply_question: In 2021 Russia supplied about 45 percent of the European Union's gas imports, nearly 40 percent of the gas it consumed, most of it by pipeline, and in 2022 it cut those flows sharply: using today's concept, why did pipeline gas give Russia a sharper but self-limiting weapon against Europe than oil gave the Arab producers in 1973?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the 1973 production cuts and price rise, and the US laws that followed. Debated: how much of the American shortage came from the embargo itself rather than from production cuts and US price and allocation controls; whether chip export controls durably slow China's AI and chipmaking or speed its self-sufficiency (Huawei's 2023 phone is cited on both sides). Value judgment: when economic coercion is a legitimate alternative to force, given that its costs fall heavily on civilians; some ethicists apply the just-war criteria of Day 270 to sanctions.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: Twelve of Sixteen Rising-Power Rivalries Ended in War, Says a Harvard Study. Xi Jinping Says There Is No Trap. What Does That Base Rate Really Tell You?
days.concept: Power-transition theory holds that the risk of war rises when a rising state approaches the strength of a dominant one, especially if the riser is dissatisfied with the existing order and the declining power fears a worse bargain later, though how often transitions end in war depends heavily on which cases are counted.
days.focus: Teaches power transitions (Organski 1958; Gilpin 1981) and their modern mechanism, the commitment problem of shifting power (Day 267): a declining power cannot trust a rising one's promises, which tempts preventive war (Copeland 2000). Uses Allison's 'Thucydides Trap' count as a lesson in base rates and case selection (Days 15-16), sets it beside peaceful transitions such as Britain's to the United States (Schake 2017), and applies it to Taiwan's semiconductor 'silicon shield'.
days.model_or_equation: Organski's claim in one line: the probability of war is highest when the challenger's power approaches parity with the dominant state's and the challenger is dissatisfied with the status quo. Allison's base rate: 12 wars in 16 cases is 75 percent, but a rate is only as good as its denominator: who counts as 'rising', which pairs enter the list, and whether cases were chosen because they are famous (and famous because they ended in war).

story.title: A dinner in Seattle, an essay in The Atlantic
story.hook: On the evening of 22 September 2015, at the first stop of his state visit to the United States, Chinese President Xi Jinping told a dinner audience in Seattle: 'There is no such thing as the so-called Thucydides trap in the world. But should major countries time and again make the mistakes of strategic miscalculation, they might create such traps for themselves.' He was answering a phrase coined by Harvard's Graham Allison from Thucydides' explanation of the Peloponnesian War, which Allison renders as 'It was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable.' That week The Atlantic published Allison's essay 'The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?' His team had found sixteen cases over the past 500 years in which a rising power challenged a ruling one; twelve had ended in war.
story.puzzle: If three in four such rivalries have ended in war, should you expect a war between the United States and China, or is the number less informative than it looks?
story.payoff: Treat 12 of 16 as a base rate and the questions of Days 15 and 16 arrive at once: the cases were assembled after the fact, famous rivalries are famous partly because they ended in war, and redefining 'rising' or 'ruling' changes the count. Critics, among them historians of ancient Greece, dispute both Allison's list and Thucydides' explanation. The mechanism underneath is sturdier than the number: a declining power fears that any bargain struck today will be reopened tomorrow by a stronger rival (the commitment problem of Day 267), and transitions stay peaceful when the riser can credibly reassure or the incumbent accepts the change, as Britain largely did with the United States around 1900.
sources: Graham Allison, 'The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?', The Atlantic, September 2015
Graham Allison, Destined for War (2017)
Xi Jinping, speech in Seattle, 22 September 2015 (reported by Xinhua)
Kori Schake, Safe Passage: The Transition from British to American Hegemony (2017)
A.F.K. Organski, World Politics (1958)

days.application: Taiwan and TSMC: by common industry estimates Taiwan makes around 90 percent of the world's most advanced logic chips, most of them at TSMC. The 'silicon shield' argument (Craig Addison, Silicon Shield, 2001) holds that the world's dependence on those fabs deters a Chinese attack and commits the United States to Taiwan's defence; critics answer that it makes Taiwan a prize, that a war would destroy the fabs anyway, and that TSMC's new plants in Arizona and Japan may thin the shield (Day 106).

builds_on.why: power transitions are the leading example of Fearon's commitment problem: shifting power makes today's bargain untrustworthy and tempts preventive war
Allison's 12 of 16 is a sample, and a sample's value comes from how it was drawn; a list built from famous rivalries is selected on the outcome

across.link: Charles Kindleberger's The World in Depression, 1929-1939 (1973) argued the slump deepened because Britain could no longer, and the United States would not yet, stabilize the world economy; Joseph Nye's 'Kindleberger Trap' (2017) applies that to China, so a transition can fail through under-provided public goods as well as through war.

days.apply_question: Between the 1895-96 Venezuela boundary crisis and the 1901 Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, in which Britain gave up its claim to a joint role in any canal across Central America, Britain repeatedly yielded to the rising United States in the Americas: using power-transition theory and the commitment problem of shifting power, why did this transition stay peaceful when the Anglo-German rivalry did not?
days.evidence_note: Debated: Allison's case list and coding (critics, including political scientists and historians of Greece, find many transitions ended peacefully or were miscounted); whether rising or declining powers start such wars (Organski versus Copeland 2000); and the silicon-shield argument. Power-transition theory has mixed statistical support. US-China relations are a live policy question: present the competing readings without a verdict and label forecasts as forecasts.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: The Soviet Chair Was Empty When the Security Council Sent Forces to Korea. Why Would a Superpower Skip a Vote It Could Have Vetoed?
days.concept: International organizations are built by great powers to be useful without binding the great powers themselves, which is why the UN Security Council gives its five permanent members a veto: it keeps them inside the institution at the price of paralysing it whenever their interests collide.
days.focus: Teaches the institutional bargain of 1945 (Ikenberry, After Victory, 2001): the League of Nations failed partly because great powers stayed out or walked out, so the UN Charter traded equality for participation through Article 27(3). Shows what the veto blocks (Syria, Ukraine), the workarounds (Uniting for Peace, the General Assembly's 2022 'veto initiative'), and the same bargain elsewhere, such as the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003), which the United States signed but never ratified (Day 263).
days.model_or_equation: The Security Council's rule (UN Charter, Article 27(3)): a substantive decision needs at least nine of fifteen votes (seven of eleven before 1965) and no negative vote from a permanent member (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States); by settled practice an abstention or absence is not a veto. The bargain it encodes: the most powerful states are guaranteed that the institution can never be turned against their vital interests, in exchange for staying in.

story.title: An empty chair at Lake Success
story.hook: On 25 June 1950 North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel. That day the Security Council met at its temporary home at Lake Success, New York, and by nine votes to none, with Yugoslavia abstaining, called on North Korea to withdraw (Resolution 82). Two days later it recommended that members help South Korea repel the attack, and on 7 July it placed their forces under a unified command led by the United States. The Soviet Union could have vetoed every word. Its seat was empty: Ambassador Yakov Malik had walked out in January 1950 in protest that China's seat was still held by the Nationalist government on Taiwan rather than the new People's Republic. Malik returned on 1 August, as the Council's rotating president. The Soviets never boycotted the Council again.
story.puzzle: Why would a great power holding a veto stay out of the room, and why had the founders given great powers a veto at all, if it could paralyse the very institution meant to stop aggression?
story.payoff: The veto was the price of membership. The League of Nations had failed partly because the United States never joined and Japan, Germany and Italy walked out, so the UN's designers made sure no great power would ever face Council action against its vital interests. Korea in 1950 showed the bargain's other side: a great power that steps outside the institution lets the others use it against it. Whether Stalin blundered or meant to draw the United States into an Asian war is still debated (a letter he sent the Czechoslovak leader Klement Gottwald on 27 August 1950, published after the Cold War, claims the absence was deliberate), but Moscow drew the lesson and stayed in the room.
sources: UN Security Council Resolutions 82 (25 June 1950), 83 (27 June 1950) and 84 (7 July 1950)
Charter of the United Nations (1945), Article 27
G. John Ikenberry, After Victory (2001)
Stalin to Gottwald, 27 August 1950, as published by the Cold War International History Project

days.application: Vetoes over Syria and Ukraine: since 2011 Russia, often joined by China, has vetoed well over a dozen draft resolutions on Syria, and on 25 February 2022 Russia vetoed a draft deploring its own invasion of Ukraine (11 in favour, with China, India and the UAE abstaining). The Council then used a procedural vote, which cannot be vetoed, to send the issue to an emergency special session of the General Assembly under Uniting for Peace, which on 2 March 2022 demanded Russia's withdrawal by 141 votes to 5: a recommendation, not a binding order. The United States has used the same veto on Israeli-Palestinian drafts, including several Gaza ceasefire texts in 2023-24.

builds_on.why: international law's compliance logic (reciprocity and reputation rather than enforcement) explains why a body that cannot coerce its strongest members still matters
veto points: like the separation of powers, the Council's veto protects the powerful from being overridden and slows or blocks action, the same trade-off between protection and paralysis

across.link: The WHO's International Health Regulations (2005) oblige states to notify the organization of potential international health emergencies but give it no power to enter a country to investigate without consent, the same 'useful but not binding on the powerful' design, tested when the speed of China's early reporting of COVID-19 in January 2020 was disputed.

days.apply_question: Unlike the Security Council, the World Trade Organization's Appellate Body could rule against great powers, and it often ruled against the United States; from 2017 Washington blocked every new appointment until, on 11 December 2019, the body lost its quorum and stopped deciding appeals: using today's concept, why did the United States disable an institution that could bind it while keeping the Security Council, which never can?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Charter's voting rule and the veto record. Debated: how much the UN reduces war (studies find peacekeeping substantially lowers the risk that civil wars restart, Fortna, Does Peacekeeping Work?, 2008, and that more UN troops reduce the killing of civilians, Hultman, Kathman & Shannon, American Journal of Political Science 2013, and battlefield deaths, APSR 2014, while the failures in Rwanda in 1994 and Srebrenica in 1995 are equally real); whether Stalin's 1950 absence was a blunder or a ploy. Value judgment: whether a veto for five states is a legitimate price for keeping them in the system.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: A Former Dictator Recovering From Back Surgery in London Was Arrested on a Spanish Judge's Warrant. Sovereign Immunity Was Supposed to Make That Impossible.
days.concept: Human-rights norms spread through 'norm cascades', in which moral entrepreneurs persuade a critical mass of states and adoption then accelerates, but they are enforced weakly, through foreign and international courts, universal jurisdiction, publicity and domestic pressure, so whether rights treaties change states' behaviour is genuinely debated.
days.focus: Teaches the human-rights regime as a case of norms changing state behaviour (Finnemore & Sikkink's norm life cycle, 1998: emergence, tipping point, cascade, internalization) and of the enforcement gap: universal jurisdiction, the 'boomerang' of transnational activism (Keck & Sikkink 1998) and courts. States the central evidence dispute fairly: Hathaway (2002) found ratification often unrelated to, or even associated with, worse practices; Simmons (2009) found treaties matter most where citizens can use them. Ties to the rights tradition of Day 225 and the tipping points of Day 28.
days.model_or_equation: Finnemore & Sikkink's norm life cycle (1998): (1) emergence, in which norm entrepreneurs (activists, lawyers, a few states) persuade early adopters; (2) a tipping point, once a critical mass of states has adopted (they suggested roughly a third of states, including critical ones); (3) a cascade, as adoption spreads by socialization, reputation and imitation; (4) internalization, when the norm is taken for granted. Enforcement is a separate question at every stage.

story.title: A warrant at the London Clinic
story.hook: Late on the night of 16 October 1998, Scotland Yard officers entered the London Clinic, where General Augusto Pinochet, 82, was recovering from back surgery, and arrested him on a provisional warrant requested by the Spanish investigating judge Baltasar Garzon. Pinochet had ruled Chile from the coup of 1973 until 1990; Chile's later official commissions recognized about 40,000 victims of killing, disappearance, political imprisonment and torture under his rule, some 3,000 of them dead or disappeared. He was now a senator-for-life, shielded at home by a 1978 amnesty, and his lawyers claimed immunity as a former head of state. On 24 March 1999 the House of Lords ruled, six to one, that he had no immunity from extradition for torture committed after the UN Convention Against Torture bound Britain, Spain and Chile.
story.puzzle: For centuries rulers and former rulers had been immune from foreign courts for what they did in office at home. How did a Spanish judge's warrant put one under police guard in London, and why did he still never stand trial abroad?
story.payoff: A norm had cascaded. From the Universal Declaration of 1948 through the Convention Against Torture of 1984 and the campaigns of groups such as Amnesty International, state after state had signed up to the idea that torture is everyone's business, and the treaty's universal-jurisdiction clauses gave courts a handle. But enforcement stayed weak and political: after more than sixteen months the Home Secretary, Jack Straw, released Pinochet on medical grounds in March 2000, and he died in Chile in 2006 without being convicted, though Chilean courts had stripped his immunity in several cases. The norm moved; its teeth were partial.
sources: R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex parte Pinochet Ugarte (No. 3) [2000] 1 AC 147 (House of Lords, 24 March 1999)
Martha Finnemore & Kathryn Sikkink, 'International Norm Dynamics and Political Change', International Organization 52(4), 1998
Kathryn Sikkink, The Justice Cascade (2011)
Chile's National Commission on Political Imprisonment and Torture (Valech Commission), reports of 2004 and 2011

days.application: The Responsibility to Protect, endorsed at the 2005 World Summit (Outcome Document, paragraphs 138-139): every state must protect its people from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, and if a state manifestly fails, the international community may act through the Security Council. Its first major test was Libya: Resolution 1973 (17 March 2011, adopted 10 to 0 with Brazil, China, Germany, India and Russia abstaining) authorized 'all necessary measures' to protect civilians; NATO's campaign ended with Gaddafi's fall and death, and Russia and China, saying protection had become regime change, blocked comparable action on Syria.

builds_on.why: the Atlantic revolutions made universal rights the test of legitimate government while denying them to many; the human-rights regime is that language internationalized, and its origins are debated in the same terms (Tierney, Hunt, Moyn)
a norm cascade is a threshold process: once enough states adopt, the rest follow quickly, like the tipping points and Granovetter thresholds of Day 28

across.link: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, adopted on 17 July 1998 (three months before Pinochet's arrest) by 120 votes to 7 with 21 abstentions, created a permanent court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes; the United States, China, Russia and India remain outside it, the same uneven reach seen in the Pinochet case.

days.apply_question: On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the deportation of Ukrainian children, yet when he visited Mongolia, an ICC member, in September 2024 he was not arrested: using today's concept, why was Pinochet arrested in London in 1998 when Putin was not arrested in Ulaanbaatar?
days.evidence_note: Debated: whether human-rights treaties improve behaviour (Hathaway, Yale Law Journal 2002, found ratification often unrelated to, or associated with, worse practices; Simmons, Mobilizing for Human Rights, 2009, found positive effects where domestic actors can mobilize); where rights talk came from (Day 225). Debated: Libya 2011 (supporters credit the intervention with preventing a massacre in Benghazi; Kuperman, International Security 2013, argues it prolonged the war and the threat was overstated). Value judgment: universal jurisdiction against sovereignty and a nation's own settlement, such as Chile's 1978 amnesty.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.topic: Global commons: from ozone to climate
days.headline_hint: Three British Scientists With an Old-Fashioned Instrument Found a Hole in the Sky. Two Years Later the World Had a Treaty Every Nation Would Ratify. Why Can't Climate Do That?
days.concept: States solve global collective-action problems when acting is cheap and concentrated among a few producers, substitutes exist, and the treaty can reward joiners and punish free riders through side payments and trade measures: conditions the ozone problem met and climate change largely does not.
days.focus: Teaches the global commons as Day 30's tragedy at planetary scale, with no Ostrom-style community to govern it, and Scott Barrett's analysis (Environment and Statecraft, 2003) of why most environmental treaties achieve little and the Montreal Protocol worked: a handful of chemical makers, available substitutes, a Multilateral Fund that paid developing countries' costs, and Article 4's trade ban on non-parties. Then sets Paris's pledge-and-review design (2015) against the problem it faces: CO2 comes from nearly every economic activity (Day 85).
days.model_or_equation: Four conditions for a self-enforcing environmental treaty, after Barrett: (1) concentrated abatement, with few producers to regulate; (2) cheap substitutes, so acting costs little relative to the benefit; (3) side payments that make joining worthwhile for poorer countries; (4) a credible penalty on non-parties, such as a trade ban. Montreal had all four; Kyoto (1997) set binding targets with none of the enforcement; Paris (2015) traded bindingness for near-universal participation.

story.title: An old instrument at Halley Bay
story.hook: On 16 May 1985 Nature published a short paper by Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey. Using a Dobson spectrophotometer, an instrument of 1920s design, at Halley Bay on the Antarctic coast, they reported that springtime ozone overhead had fallen by roughly a third or more since the 1960s, and they pointed to chlorine from chlorofluorocarbons, the refrigerants Thomas Midgley had introduced around 1930. Satellite records soon mapped the loss across the whole Antarctic. In 1986 a 30-year-old NOAA chemist, Susan Solomon, led an expedition to McMurdo Station whose measurements helped pin the chemistry on chlorine activated on polar clouds. On 16 September 1987, little more than two years after the paper, governments signed the Montreal Protocol.
story.puzzle: Climate change was understood in outline decades earlier (Day 85), yet after three decades of negotiation the world's emissions are still near record highs. Why could governments agree to phase out CFCs within two years, and why did the Montreal Protocol and its parent Vienna Convention become, in 2009, the first treaties in UN history ratified by every member state?
story.payoff: Because ozone met the conditions climate lacks. A few firms, DuPont the largest, made most of the world's CFCs, and once substitutes were in reach DuPont announced in March 1988 that it would stop making them; the costs were small next to the benefits, even by the US government's own analysis of acting alone; a Multilateral Fund (1990) paid poorer countries' costs of switching; and Article 4 banned trade in controlled substances with non-parties, so staying out was costly. Climate's emissions come from nearly every factory, field, car and power station, the costs fall now while the benefits come later and elsewhere, and no trade penalty has been agreed. The ozone layer is projected to recover to 1980 levels over Antarctica around 2066.
sources: J.C. Farman, B.G. Gardiner & J.D. Shanklin, 'Large losses of total ozone in Antarctica reveal seasonal ClOx/NOx interaction', Nature 315, 207-210 (1985)
Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer (1987)
Scott Barrett, Environment and Statecraft (2003)
WMO/UNEP, Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion: 2022

days.application: The Paris Agreement (adopted 12 December 2015): instead of binding targets, each country sets its own nationally determined contribution and the parties review progress in a global stocktake every five years (the first in 2023), a design that bought near-universal participation by giving up enforcement. UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2023 found current pledges and policies consistent with roughly 2.5 to 2.9 C of warming this century, against the agreement's 'well below 2 C' goal, and the United States has withdrawn twice, the second withdrawal taking effect in January 2026.

builds_on.why: the ozone layer and the atmosphere's capacity to absorb carbon are open-access commons in Hardin's sense, but with no local community to apply Ostrom's design principles, treaties must supply the monitoring and sanctions

Thomas Midgley, who put lead in gasoline, also introduced CFC refrigerants, and Montreal answers Day 49's burden-of-proof question the other way: governments acted before the chemistry was fully confirmed

across.link: Stratospheric ozone filters the UV-B radiation that causes skin cancers and cataracts; the US EPA's model of the Protocol's effects estimates that it will prevent on the order of 400 million skin-cancer cases and tens of millions of cataracts among Americans born between 1890 and 2100, a public-health payoff measured with the epidemiological methods of Day 143.

days.apply_question: Negotiations for a global treaty on plastic pollution broke up without agreement in Busan in 2024 and again in Geneva in 2025, split over whether to cap plastic production: using the four conditions from today's lesson, why does plastic pollution look more like climate than like ozone as a collective-action problem?
days.evidence_note: Settled: CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone (Molina, Rowland and Crutzen, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1995), the Protocol has phased out about 99 percent of ozone-depleting substances, and the greenhouse physics of CO2 (Day 85). Debated: how far Montreal's success transfers (Barrett stresses treaty design; others stress the availability of substitutes and US and corporate leadership); how effective Paris's pledge-and-review proves to be. Value judgment: how to share the burden between rich countries that emitted first and poorer ones still growing ('common but differentiated responsibilities'), and how much present people owe future ones.
