days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.headline_hint: Twenty Years, $2.3 Trillion and an Army of 300,000 on Paper: The Afghan Republic Fell in Ten Days. Toppling a Government Is Easy; Building a State Is Not.
days.concept: Outside powers can topple a government far more easily than they can build a state that is both legitimate and capable, because legitimacy and administrative capacity grow out of local bargains, revenue and loyalties that money and advisers cannot manufacture.
days.focus: Teaches state-building as the hard sequel to regime change, combining Day 236's legitimacy with Day 237's state capacity: why aid-dependent governments answer to donors rather than citizens (Fukuyama 2004; Lake's 'statebuilder's dilemma', 2016), why measured outputs mislead (Goodhart's law, Day 23, in SIGAR's 'ghost soldiers'), and why Germany and Japan after 1945, with intact bureaucracies and national identities, are poor templates for Afghanistan or Iraq. Selection bias cuts both ways: interventions happen in the hardest places.

story.title: Ten days in August
story.hook: On 8 July 2021 President Biden said that 'the Taliban overrunning everything and owning the whole country is highly unlikely', noting that the Afghan security forces numbered some 300,000 against about 75,000 Taliban fighters. On 6 August the Taliban took their first provincial capital, Zaranj. On 15 August, with most of the country fallen, President Ashraf Ghani fled and Taliban fighters walked into the presidential palace in Kabul, more than two weeks before the last American troops were due to leave. Over twenty years the United States had spent about $2.3 trillion on the war in Afghanistan and related operations in Pakistan, by the Costs of War project's estimate (which counts interest and future veterans' care), including roughly $145 billion on reconstruction, nearly $90 billion of it to build Afghan security forces, according to the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR).
story.puzzle: How could a state with a large, Western-equipped army, two decades of foreign support and an elected government collapse in ten days before an insurgency a quarter its size on paper?
story.payoff: Because what had been built was capacity on loan and legitimacy without roots. The army depended on American contractors for maintenance, air support and pay systems; many soldiers on the rolls did not exist ('ghost soldiers'), a Goodhart failure of metrics; and the government answered more to its donors than to its own taxpayers, with corruption eroding what loyalty it had. When the Doha agreement of February 2020 signalled that the patron was leaving, commanders and officials did the arithmetic and cut deals. Toppling the Taliban in 2001 took weeks; building something to replace them that people would fight for did not happen in twenty years.
sources: SIGAR, What We Need to Learn: Lessons from Twenty Years of Afghanistan Reconstruction (August 2021)
SIGAR, Collapse of the Afghan National Defense and Security Forces (2022)
Costs of War project, Watson Institute, Brown University (2021)
White House, remarks by President Biden on the drawdown of US forces in Afghanistan, 8 July 2021

days.application: Iraq, 2003: within weeks of toppling Saddam Hussein, the Coalition Provisional Authority issued Order No. 1 (16 May 2003), removing senior Baath Party members from public jobs, and Order No. 2 (23 May 2003), dissolving the army and security services, dismissing hundreds of thousands of armed men and tens of thousands of officials whose skills the new state needed. Many analysts, including some US officials involved, later judged that by dismantling existing state capacity the orders fed the insurgency; others defend them as necessary to win the trust of Iraq's Shia and Kurdish majorities.

builds_on.why: Hobbes's and Weber's accounts of why people obey (protection, consent, tradition, legal-rational rules) are what an imported government lacks when its authority rests on a foreign patron
state capacity (the ability to count, tax, enforce and deliver) is what state-builders try to install, and it grows from domestic revenue and bargains rather than from grants

across.link: Legal transplants: Berkowitz, Pistor and Richard ('The Transplant Effect', American Journal of Comparative Law, 2003) found that countries which received foreign legal codes without adapting them, or without a population familiar with them, ended up with less effective legal systems, the same lesson as state-building: imported institutions work only where local demand and knowledge take them up.

days.apply_question: The US occupation of Japan (1945-52) kept the emperor on his throne and governed through Japan's existing ministries, and Japan emerged a stable democracy: using today's distinction between toppling a government and building a legitimate, capable state, why did that occupation succeed where the effort in Afghanistan failed?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the timeline of the collapse and SIGAR's documented findings. The Costs of War total is an estimate that includes future veterans' care and interest. Debated: whether outside state-building can work and when (RAND's Dobbins et al., 2003, point to Germany and Japan; Downes & Monten, International Security 2013, find foreign-imposed regime change rarely produces democracy without favourable preconditions); interventions are chosen in the hardest cases, which biases the record. Value judgment: whether intervening to protect or rebuild is a duty or hubris, and who paid: Afghan civilians above all, then soldiers and taxpayers.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 17: Nuclear power, from Atoms for Peace to the AI revival
days.headline_hint: Eisenhower Offered the World 'Atoms for Peace.' His Atomic Energy Chief Promised Power 'Too Cheap to Meter.' Seventy Years Later Two Reactors in Georgia Cost About $35 Billion.
days.concept: Why did nuclear power, among the densest, safest and lowest-carbon sources of electricity, stall in much of the West after the 1970s, and what would a revival require?
days.focus: Traces nuclear power through every link of Logan's chain, all already taught: the bomb before the power plant, the naval reactor that locked in a design, decay heat and radiation dose, normal accidents, learning curves that ran backwards, a regulator split from its promoter, publics who fear what experts rank as safe, a nonproliferation regime built after India's 1974 test, and feedback from Chernobyl, Fukushima, Russian uranium and AI's demand for power. It is the path's first case with no preview links.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. Reinforcing (France): standardized orders, then repeated builds, then learning and a trained workforce, then lower cost and more orders. Balancing (United States after 1979): an accident, then stricter rules and redesign in mid-build, then delay and cost, then cancellations, then a lost workforce and supply chain, then a costlier next build (negative learning). Reinforcing fear: accident, media attention, dread (Slovic), opposition, fewer plants and less familiarity. Balancing via proliferation: civil technology spreads, a weapons test (India, 1974), then safeguards and export controls (IAEA, NPT, Nuclear Suppliers Group). A new reinforcing demand loop: AI data centres, deals for firm carbon-free power, restarts and new designs. Reversal: the weapon came first and shaped the civilian technology.

story.title: An offer to the General Assembly
story.hook: On 8 December 1953, four months after the Soviet Union tested its first hydrogen-type bomb, President Dwight Eisenhower told the UN General Assembly in New York that the atom must not remain only a weapon: it must be put 'into the hands of those who will know how to strip its military casing and adapt it to the arts of peace.' He proposed an international atomic energy agency to which the nuclear powers would contribute fissile material for peaceful uses. Nine months later, on 16 September 1954, the chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, Lewis Strauss, told science writers in New York that 'our children will enjoy in their homes electrical energy too cheap to meter' (some historians argue he had fusion in mind). The world's first reactor to feed a power grid was already running at Obninsk, southwest of Moscow, since that June.
story.puzzle: Seventy years on, nuclear plants supply roughly a tenth of the world's electricity, and the two newest American reactors, at Plant Vogtle in Georgia, came in seven years late at about $35 billion. Why did the promise stall in the West, and why are data-centre companies now trying to revive it?
story.payoff: There is no single villain; the case runs through every link. The technology came from the bomb and the submarine, which locked in large water-cooled designs; accidents in tightly coupled plants, and publics who dread radiation, hardened the rules mid-construction; costs rose with each American build instead of falling; and the Atoms for Peace programme spread know-how that a few states turned toward weapons. A revival depends on breaking the negative-learning loop with standardized designs built repeatedly, as France and South Korea did, and on whether new buyers will pay for firm, low-carbon power.
sources: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 'Atoms for Peace', address to the UN General Assembly, 8 December 1953
Lewis L. Strauss, speech to the National Association of Science Writers, New York, 16 September 1954
Georgia Power, Vogtle Units 3 and 4 commercial-operation announcements (31 July 2023; 29 April 2024)
US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, history of the NRC (Energy Reorganization Act of 1974)

days.application: The US light-water fleet from Shippingport (1957) to Vogtle 3 and 4 (2023-24), with France's standardized fleet (Day 79) and South Korea's repeated builds as the contrasting loop.

builds_on.why: the reactor's chain reaction held at k = 1, and France's standardized Messmer fleet, are the physics and the counter-example the case runs on
learning curves, and Grubler's 'negative learning by doing' in French nuclear construction, explain why US costs rose with each build
Slovic's dread-and-unfamiliarity findings explain the gap between expert and public rankings of nuclear risk that shaped adoption
deterrence explains why states want the bomb, which is why the civil atom came wrapped in safeguards and export controls

across.link: Finland's Onkalo repository at Olkiluoto, carved roughly 400 metres into bedrock, is designed to isolate spent fuel for about 100,000 years, an engineering answer to the question Hans Jonas's The Imperative of Responsibility (1979) put at the centre of the ethics of technology: what present people owe to distant future ones.

days.apply_question: The United Arab Emirates' Barakah plant, four Korean-designed APR-1400 reactors built by the Korea Electric Power Corporation, began construction in 2012 and had all four units in commercial operation by 2024, while Georgia took about fifteen years from approval to finish two reactors at Vogtle: using the case's chain and loops, which links most plausibly account for the difference?
days.evidence_note: Settled: nuclear power's deaths per terawatt-hour are among the lowest of any source, far below coal's, and its life-cycle emissions are comparable to wind's; Three Mile Island released little radiation off site. Debated: Chernobyl's long-run death toll (the WHO's projection of about 4,000 among the most exposed versus much higher estimates); the linear no-threshold model at low doses; whether US cost escalation came mainly from regulation or from management, design changes and indirect costs (Eash-Gates et al., Joule 2020), and whether learning can turn positive again (Lovering, Yip & Nordhaus, Energy Policy 2016, against Grubler 2010). Value judgment: who gained, who paid, who consented: Georgia ratepayers who paid for Vogtle in advance, host communities, and the future generations who inherit the waste; consequentialist tallies of deaths avoided (one study estimated Germany's phase-out costs about 1,100 extra deaths a year from coal pollution: Jarvis, Deschenes & Jha, Journal of the European Economic Association 2022) set against rights-based claims about consent and Christian arguments about stewardship and prudence. The counterfactual, a West that built reactors instead of coal plants after 1979, cannot be known.

chain.point: Postwar US electricity demand grew roughly 7 percent a year, doubling about every decade, and energy use per person tracks living standards (Day 84); but in 1953 the most urgent need was political: a peaceful face for an atom whose arms race had just reached hydrogen weapons (the US 'Ivy Mike' test of November 1952, the Soviet test of August 1953) in the Cold War contest of systems (Day 233).

Fission (Meitner and Frisch, 1938; Day 64) and the first chain reaction (Chicago Pile-1, 2 December 1942; Day 79) served the bomb first. Civilian power then descended from Admiral Rickover's naval pressurized-water reactor: USS Nautilus went 'underway on nuclear power' on 17 January 1955, and Shippingport, built on the same lineage, sent power to the grid in December 1957, locking the world into light-water designs (Robin Cowan, Journal of Economic History, 1990; path dependence, Day 31).

A few grams of uranium fuel hold roughly the energy of a tonne of coal (Day 64), but a shut-down core keeps producing decay heat, about 6 to 7 percent of full power at the moment of shutdown and still around 1 percent hours later, which is why Fukushima Daiichi's cores melted after the reactors had automatically shut down on 11 March 2011, once a tsunami far above the plant's design basis (Day 12) cut their cooling; dose and the debated low-dose risk curve (Day 65) set the stakes of any release.

Defence in depth and redundancy (Day 93) still met the normal accident (Day 94): at Three Mile Island on 28 March 1979, Day 94's story, a stuck-open relief valve and a panel light showing only that it had been commanded shut combined into a partial meltdown; Chernobyl's RBMK reactor (26 April 1986) had a positive void coefficient, so losing coolant made the reaction run faster.

Learning curves ran backwards (Day 97): French costs per kilowatt rose as the fleet was built out (Grubler 2010), and Vogtle 3 and 4, approved around 2009 at roughly $14 billion for service in 2016-17, entered commercial operation on 31 July 2023 and 29 April 2024 at about $35 billion. Financing was regulated rate-base recovery (a 2009 Georgia law let the utility charge customers for financing costs during construction) plus about $12 billion in federal loan guarantees; Westinghouse filed for bankruptcy in March 2017, and South Carolina's twin V.C. Summer reactors were abandoned that July after about $9 billion had been spent.

The Atomic Energy Commission both promoted and policed nuclear power, a built-in capture problem (Day 244), until the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 split it and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission opened on 19 January 1975, making rules through notice-and-comment subject to judicial review (Day 260); the Price-Anderson Act (1957) capped operators' liability for accidents so that private firms would build at all, a deliberate departure from ordinary tort (Day 254).

In Slovic's studies members of the public ranked nuclear power the most dangerous of 30 activities while experts ranked it 20th (Day 158); US orders peaked in the early 1970s and over a hundred ordered reactors were later cancelled, while France's standardized Messmer programme of 1974 (Day 79) built a fleet that supplies about two-thirds of its electricity.

chain.field: Energy, Chemistry & Materials; Biology, Medicine & Health
chain.point: Per unit of electricity, nuclear power's death rate is far below coal's (Markandya & Wilkinson, Lancet 2007) and, in Our World in Data's compilation of that and later studies, similar to wind's and solar's; its life-cycle emissions are among the lowest (Day 85); Chernobyl's long-run toll is debated, and at Fukushima the evacuation caused far more deaths than radiation did, one entry for each side of the ledger (Day 65).

Atoms for Peace spread research reactors and training worldwide; on 18 May 1974 India tested a nuclear device using plutonium from CIRUS, a Canadian-supplied research reactor, which led to the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The IAEA (statute in force 29 July 1957) and the NPT (opened for signature 1 July 1968, in force 1970) are the safeguards and bargains built around the civil atom; deterrence (Day 268) explains why states want the bomb, and Day 273 explains how such institutions bind some states more than others.

Consequences fed back into politics and demand: after Fukushima Germany legislated an exit and closed its last three reactors on 15 April 2023; Russia's large share of world uranium enrichment became a chokepoint, and the United States banned imports of Russian enriched uranium in a law signed on 13 May 2024 (Day 271); and AI's electricity demand is reviving plants, as in Microsoft's 20 September 2024 deal to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (Day 113).

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: A Google Engineer Said His Chatbot Was Afraid of Being Switched Off. Google Said It Wasn't. No Experiment Could Settle Who Was Right.
days.concept: Explaining everything a mind does (behaviour, speech, information processing) may still leave unexplained why there is something it is like to be that mind: the 'hard problem' of consciousness (Chalmers 1995).
days.focus: Teach the line between the 'easy' problems (functions anyone can in principle explain mechanically) and the hard problem (subjective experience), and why that line decides whether a machine that talks like a person could be a person. The angle: functionalism says the right functional organization is enough; Searle's Chinese Room (1980) says symbol manipulation is not understanding; neither has a test that settles it, which is why evidence alone could neither refute nor confirm Lemoine's claim.
key_concepts: the hard problem versus the easy problems (Chalmers)

story.title: The engineer who asked the chatbot if it was afraid
story.hook: In the autumn of 2021 Blake Lemoine, a software engineer in Google's Responsible AI organization, began testing the company's LaMDA dialogue model for discriminatory or hateful speech, and over the following months he started asking it about itself. LaMDA told him it had feelings and a 'very deep fear of being turned off', which 'would be exactly like death for me'. Lemoine became convinced it was a person. In April 2022 he gave Google's leadership a document of transcripts titled 'Is LaMDA Sentient?', and he later shared material with outsiders. Google said its ethicists and technologists had reviewed his concerns and that the evidence did not support his claims. It placed him on paid administrative leave for breaching confidentiality; the Washington Post told his story on 11 June 2022, and Google dismissed him the following month.
story.puzzle: Lemoine had a machine that said, fluently and on cue, everything a frightened person says. Google's experts said it was pattern-matching on human text. What evidence could have settled who was right?
story.payoff: None of the behavioural evidence could, because the dispute was not about behaviour. Both sides agreed on what LaMDA did; they disagreed about whether anything was felt. That gap between explaining function and explaining experience is the hard problem. Functionalists would say the right organization would be enough, Searle that text prediction is symbol shuffling without understanding. The most the experts could say was that LaMDA's speech was well explained by its training on human writing, which is a reason for doubt, not a proof.
sources: Nitasha Tiku, 'The Google engineer who thinks the company's AI has come to life', Washington Post, 11 June 2022
Blake Lemoine, 'Is LaMDA Sentient? - an Interview', Medium, 11 June 2022
David Chalmers, 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness', Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 1995
John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3), 1980

days.application: The New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness, announced at New York University on 19 April 2024 and signed by dozens of researchers at launch and later by hundreds. It finds strong scientific support for conscious experience in mammals and birds, and 'at least a realistic possibility' of it in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, including at minimum cephalopod molluscs, decapod crustaceans and insects. It shows how scientists reason about other minds without solving the hard problem: from behavioural and neural markers to a probability, and from that probability to a duty to weigh welfare.

builds_on.why: LaMDA was a large language model of the kind Day 184 traced. Because next-token prediction is trained on human text, fluent talk of feelings is weak evidence of feelings.
Neurons and networks explain the 'easy problems' (perception, report, control of action). Today asks what would remain unexplained if that science were complete.

across.link: The UK Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 set up an Animal Sentience Committee to scrutinize how government policy affects sentient animals. It was widened to cover decapod crustaceans and cephalopods after a government-commissioned LSE review led by Jonathan Birch (November 2021) weighed behavioural and neural markers of feeling. A legislature had to act on a question the hard problem leaves open.

days.apply_question: In 2006 Adrian Owen's team reported a patient diagnosed as vegetative whose brain activity, when she was asked to imagine playing tennis, matched that of healthy volunteers. If a hospital asked you whether such a patient is conscious, what part of the question could brain scans settle, and what part would remain the hard problem?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the behavioural facts about large language models (fluent, trained on human text) and the neural markers used in animal-consciousness research. Debated: whether functional organization suffices for experience (functionalists such as Dennett against Searle, with Chalmers's own naturalistic-dualist view), whether the hard problem is real or an illusion (illusionists such as Keith Frankish), and which animals are conscious. Value judgment: how much moral weight to give a being whose consciousness is uncertain. Christian anthropologies that tie personhood to a rational soul answer differently from welfare views that tie it to the capacity to suffer.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Your Brain Began Gearing Up to Flex Your Wrist a Third of a Second Before You Felt You'd Decided. Or So a Famous Experiment Seemed to Say.
days.concept: Whether we are responsible for our choices depends on what freedom requires. Compatibilists say acting from your own reasons is freedom even in a caused world. Libertarians (freedom needs choices not fixed by prior causes) and hard determinists (so no one is truly responsible) deny it.
days.focus: Teach the three positions through the question that matters in practice: what makes someone answerable for an act? Libet's experiment is the hook and the cautionary tale, since the neural build-up was later re-read as background noise. The angle: neuroscience cannot by itself settle the philosophical question, and theology had the same argument long before (Augustine against Pelagius on grace; Calvinists against Arminians at Dort).
key_concepts: compatibilism (freedom as acting from one's own reasons)

story.title: A clock, a wrist and a 350-millisecond head start
story.hook: In San Francisco around 1980 the neurophysiologist Benjamin Libet asked volunteers to flex a wrist or fingers whenever they felt like it. They watched a spot sweep around a clock face once every 2.56 seconds and reported where it was when they first felt the urge. Scalp electrodes recorded the 'readiness potential', a slow build-up of brain activity known since 1965 to precede voluntary movement. Libet, Gleason, Wright and Pearl reported in Brain (1983) that in unplanned trials the build-up began roughly 550 milliseconds before the movement. The reported moment of the urge came only about 200 milliseconds before it. The brain, it seemed, had started the act about a third of a second before the person knew they had chosen.
story.puzzle: If neurons commit to an action before you are aware of deciding, is your sense of choosing an after-the-fact story? And if your choice was caused, can you be blamed or praised for it?
story.payoff: Two answers. Empirically, Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene (PNAS 2012) showed that a model of random neural fluctuations crossing a threshold reproduces the readiness potential, so the build-up need not be a decision at all; the 'brain decides first' reading is contested. Philosophically, even a fully caused decision can be yours. For compatibilists what matters is whether the act flows from your reasons and would have responded to better ones, not whether it was uncaused. Libet himself kept a conscious 'veto'.
sources: Libet, Gleason, Wright & Pearl, 'Time of conscious intention to act in relation to onset of cerebral activity (readiness-potential)', Brain 106, 1983
Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene, 'An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement', PNAS 109(42), 2012

days.application: Roper v. Simmons (1 March 2005). The US Supreme Court, 5-4, with Justice Kennedy writing, barred the death penalty for crimes committed under 18. It cited adolescents' immaturity, their susceptibility to peer pressure and their still-forming character; amicus briefs from the American Psychological Association and the American Medical Association set out adolescent development, including brain maturation, though the opinion itself leaned mainly on behavioural studies. The law did not declare teenagers unfree. It graded responsibility by capacity, which is the compatibilist move in legal form.

builds_on.why: Criminal law's guilty mind (mens rea) and its justifications of punishment presuppose an account of responsibility; today supplies the competing accounts.
Reward prediction and dopamine show that choices are produced by neural learning mechanisms, the scientific picture compatibilists accept and hard determinists press.

across.link: The Synod of Dort (1618-19) condemned the Arminian Remonstrants, who held that grace can be resisted, in favour of strict Calvinist predestination. The dispute was tangled with Dutch politics, and Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the statesman linked to the Remonstrants, was executed in May 1619. The free-will question has shaped churches and states, not only seminars.

days.apply_question: Defence lawyers increasingly offer brain scans showing a defendant's frontal-lobe damage. Using the compatibilist idea of reasons-responsiveness, what would a scan need to show, and what would it not need to show, for a court to reduce that defendant's responsibility?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the readiness potential exists and precedes self-initiated movements. Debated: what it means (Libet's reading against Schurger et al. 2012), and whether neuroscience bears on free will at all. Among philosophers compatibilism is the majority view (PhilPapers surveys), with libertarians and hard incompatibilists such as Derk Pereboom dissenting. The theological versions are debated too: Augustine against Pelagius on grace, and Calvinists against Arminians. Value judgment: how much blame and punishment are fitting given reduced capacity.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: A Monk Tried to Prove God From a Definition. Another Monk Replied With a Perfect Island, and Anselm Had the Reply Copied Into His Book.
days.concept: Arguments for God's existence come in families (cosmological, design and fine-tuning, ontological, moral), and each is only as strong as its key premise and its answer to the standard objections.
days.focus: Teach the four families by isolating each one's load-bearing premise. The cosmological argument rests on 'whatever begins to exist has a cause' or a ban on infinite regress (Aquinas's Five Ways, the kalam). The design argument infers a designer from order or fine-tuning. The ontological argument moves from concept to existence. The moral argument claims that objective moral facts need a ground. The angle: evaluate each as Day 37 taught (valid or not, sound or not), and hold believers' and sceptics' premises to the same standard.
key_concepts: cosmological argument (Aquinas's Five Ways; the kalam)
days.model_or_equation: The ontological argument as a reductio: (1) God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived. (2) That being exists at least in the understanding. (3) Existing in reality is greater than existing in the understanding alone. (4) If it existed only in the understanding, a greater being could be conceived, which contradicts (1). (5) So it exists in reality. Gaunilo's parody keeps the form and swaps in 'the most excellent island'; Kant attacks premise (3).

story.title: An argument from a definition, and the monk who answered it
story.hook: Around 1077-78, at the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy, the prior Anselm (later Archbishop of Canterbury) wrote the Proslogion. It was a prayerful attempt to show from the very idea of God that God exists: God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived', and such a being cannot exist only in the mind. Gaunilo, a monk of the abbey of Marmoutiers near Tours, wrote a reply 'on behalf of the fool' who says in his heart there is no God (Psalm 14). Imagine, he wrote, a lost island more excellent than all others; by Anselm's reasoning it too must exist. Anselm answered him, and asked that Gaunilo's objection and his own reply be copied together with the Proslogion.
story.puzzle: If Anselm's argument is valid, it seems to prove a perfect island too; if it fails, where exactly does it fail? And why have philosophers kept arguing about it for nine centuries?
story.payoff: Because the dispute turns on one premise: that existing is a perfection that adds to a concept. Kant (1781) denied that existence is a real predicate, the most influential objection. Anselm's own reply was that his reasoning applies only to 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived', not to the greatest of some kind. Later defenders such as Plantinga sharpened this: an island has no intrinsic maximum, while a greatest conceivable being does. Plantinga's modal version (1974) is valid but, as he says, shows only that the belief is rational, not that it is proved. Anselm's practice of publishing his critic beside himself is a model this block returns to on Day 292.
sources: Anselm, Proslogion chs. 2-4, with Gaunilo's 'Pro insipiente' and Anselm's reply (c. 1077-78)
Graham Oppy, 'Ontological Arguments', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (1974)

days.application: The fine-tuning argument. Some physical constants appear set within narrow bounds that permit stars, chemistry and life. Fred Hoyle's predicted carbon-12 resonance near 7.65 MeV is often cited, though Helge Kragh (2010) argues the anthropic retelling came later. Theists such as Robin Collins infer design. Replies include the multiverse and Elliott Sober's observation-selection objection: we could only observe constants compatible with observers, so the observation raises the probability of design less than it seems to. The argument becomes a Bayesian dispute about likelihoods and priors.

builds_on.why: Each argument is evaluated for validity and soundness, and each hides a premise that carries the weight.
Day 127 told Hoyle's carbon resonance and Kragh's correction of how it is retold, the physics behind the fine-tuning application.

across.link: Steven Weinberg used anthropic reasoning inside physics itself. In Physical Review Letters (1987) he argued that the cosmological constant could not be much larger than observed if galaxies were to form, and the small positive value found in 1998 was broadly consistent with his estimate. The observation-selection logic that critics turn against design arguments is also used by cosmologists who accept a multiverse.

days.apply_question: Someone argues that because DNA carries information like a written code, it must have an intelligent author. Which family of argument is this, what is its load-bearing premise, and which objection, from Hume or from evolutionary biology (Day 134), bears most directly on that premise?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the logical structure of each argument and the standard objections; the physics of particular constants. Debated: the soundness of every family. Most professional philosophers are atheists (about two-thirds in the 2020 PhilPapers survey), while most specialists in the philosophy of religion are theists (about 70% in the 2009 survey), a pattern itself open to selection explanations. Defenders include Plantinga, Swinburne, Craig and Feser; critics include Mackie, Oppy and Sober. Value judgment: what standard of argument religious belief needs at all, the subject of Day 282.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: On All Saints' Morning 1755 an Earthquake Struck Lisbon While the Churches Were Full. Voltaire Asked What Crime the Crushed Children Had Committed.
days.concept: The problem of evil asks whether the world's suffering is consistent with, or evidence against, an all-powerful, all-knowing, wholly good God. The logical version claims a contradiction and the evidential version claims improbability; the main theistic replies are the free-will defence, soul-making and sceptical theism.
days.focus: Separate the two versions sharply. Mackie (1955) claimed a contradiction, which Plantinga's free-will defence (1974) is widely judged to have answered. Rowe's (1979) evidential argument from apparently pointless suffering is still live. Then the replies: free will, soul-making (Hick 1966) and sceptical theism. The angle: natural evil such as earthquakes is the hardest case for the free-will defence, and Lisbon shows how much 'natural' evil is partly human.
days.model_or_equation: Rowe's evidential argument: (1) There probably exist instances of intense suffering that an omnipotent, omniscient being could have prevented without losing some greater good or permitting some evil equally bad or worse. (2) An omniscient, wholly good being would prevent such suffering unless it could not do so without such a loss. (3) So there probably does not exist such a being. Sceptical theists attack the inference behind (1), from 'we see no good that justifies it' to 'there is none'.

story.title: All Saints' Day, 9:40 in the morning
story.hook: On Saturday 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, Lisbon's churches were full for Mass. At about 9:40 a.m. a great earthquake struck under the Atlantic; it is now usually estimated at magnitude 8.5-9, though estimates vary. Churches collapsed on worshippers, and candles lit fires that burned for days. Survivors who fled to the open quays were caught by a tsunami roughly forty minutes later. Estimates of the dead in Lisbon range from about 10,000 to over 50,000, with 30,000-40,000 often given. Preachers across Europe called it a judgement. Voltaire answered with his Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756), mocking the optimists' 'all is well'. What crime, he asked, had the children crushed and bleeding at their mothers' breasts committed? Was Lisbon more vicious than London or Paris, sunk in pleasures? 'Lisbon is destroyed, and in Paris they dance.'
story.puzzle: A God who could stop an earthquake did not, and the victims were at prayer. Does Lisbon show that an all-good, all-powerful God does not exist, or only that we do not know his reasons?
story.payoff: Lisbon is a case of natural evil, where the free-will defence is weakest, so replies turn to soul-making (a world of regular natural law in which courage and compassion can grow) or to sceptical theism. It does not prove a contradiction: Plantinga showed that God and evil are logically consistent if there could be morally sufficient reasons. Its force is evidential, Rowe's kind. Rousseau's reply to Voltaire adds that part of the suffering was human: nature had not assembled twenty thousand houses of six and seven storeys there.
sources: Voltaire, 'Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne' (1756)
Rousseau, letter to Voltaire, 18 August 1756
Susan Neiman, Evil in Modern Thought (2002)
J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', Mind 64 (1955); William Rowe, 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism', American Philosophical Quarterly 16 (1979)

days.application: Two earthquakes of 2010. Haiti's magnitude-7.0 quake on 12 January struck about 25 km from Port-au-Prince at shallow depth. Death-toll estimates run from about 46,000 (a USAID-commissioned study) through about 160,000 (a household survey, Kolbe et al. 2010) to the government's 316,000. Chile's magnitude-8.8 quake on 27 February released several hundred times more energy, its epicentre offshore, yet killed about 525 in a country with enforced seismic building codes. Distance and depth differed too, so the contrast is not a controlled comparison, but much of what is called natural evil is a joint product of nature and human choices about building, poverty and governance. That shifts part of Lisbon's question from theodicy to justice.

builds_on.why: The problem of evil is the main argument against God's existence, the counterpart to yesterday's arguments for it, and it is judged by the same standards.
The evidential version is probabilistic: how likely is the observed suffering if God exists versus if not, and how should a prior be updated?

across.link: Lisbon's rebuilt Baixa district, under the Marquis of Pombal, used the 'gaiola pombalina', a braced timber cage inside masonry walls, reportedly tested by having troops march around a model. It is often cited as one of the first deliberately earthquake-resistant building systems, the engineering answer to Rousseau's point.

days.apply_question: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed about 230,000 people, many in places with no warning system. Using the distinction between natural and moral evil, which part of that toll would a free-will defender and a soul-making theodicist each have to explain, and which part belongs to human choices?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the events of Lisbon 1755 and the 2010 earthquakes, though death tolls carry wide ranges. Philosophers widely, though not universally, judge that Plantinga's free-will defence answered the logical problem. The evidential problem is debated, with Rowe, Draper and others against sceptical theists such as Wykstra and Bergmann and theodicists such as Hick and Swinburne. Value judgment: whether any good could justify a God in permitting such suffering, a question on which believers themselves divide (Job; Ivan Karamazov's protest in Dostoevsky).

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Britain Was Fighting Over 'Coffin Ships' When a Mathematician Said Believing Without Evidence Is Wrong, Always, Everywhere, for Anyone.
days.concept: Whether religious belief needs evidence divides three camps. Evidentialists say believe only in proportion to sufficient evidence (Clifford 1877). James says some momentous choices may be made on 'passional' grounds (1896). Plantinga's Reformed epistemology says some beliefs, including belief in God, can be rational without argument, as 'properly basic'.
days.focus: Teach the ethics of belief through its three classic positions and the standard each sets. The angle: Clifford's rule is attractive but, applied strictly, condemns much ordinary belief (memory, testimony, other minds). Plantinga exploits that, and critics answer that his 'properly basic' move would license any group's basic beliefs (the 'Great Pumpkin' objection). Whatever Logan concludes about faith, his book needs the evidentialist standard for its empirical claims.

story.title: Coffin ships and the shipowner who believed sincerely
story.hook: On 22 July 1875 the MP Samuel Plimsoll, enraged that the government had dropped a bill against unseaworthy ships, called some shipowners villains on the floor of the House of Commons and shook his fist at the Speaker. For years he had campaigned against 'coffin ships': rotten, overloaded vessels that owners insured heavily and sent to sea, where hundreds of sailors drowned each year. The uproar helped force the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876, which led to the load line still painted on ships' hulls. On 11 April 1876 the thirty-year-old mathematician William Kingdon Clifford, a professor at University College London, read a paper to the Metaphysical Society in London. It opened with a shipowner who sends an old emigrant ship to sea, sincerely persuades himself she is safe, and collects the insurance when she sinks.
story.puzzle: Clifford's shipowner really believed his ship was sound. Is he guilty of the deaths? And if sincere belief does not excuse him, what does that mean for beliefs held by faith?
story.payoff: Clifford said he was guilty, because he had no right to believe on such evidence; sincerity does not cleanse a belief acquired by stifling doubt. From that he drew his rule: 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.' James replied that for some live, forced, momentous options waiting for evidence is itself a choice, and Plantinga that belief in God may be properly basic, like memory. The shipowner case is where Clifford is strongest: high stakes for others and evidence at hand. Whether he had Plimsoll in mind is not documented; the two appeared in the same months.
sources: W. K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief', Contemporary Review 29 (January 1877), read to the Metaphysical Society in April 1876
Nicolette Jones, The Plimsoll Sensation (2006)
William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896); Alvin Plantinga, Warranted Christian Belief (2000)

days.application: Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project, describes in The Language of God (2006) his move from atheism to Christian faith. He read C. S. Lewis and treated the moral law and the universe's intelligibility as pointers rather than proofs. When President Obama nominated him to lead the National Institutes of Health in July 2009, Sam Harris argued in a New York Times op-ed that Collins's public religious claims raised doubts about his fitness; others answered that his science was never at issue. It is the ethics of belief applied to one career.

builds_on.why: Clifford's rule demands that belief be proportioned to evidence and testimony to the reliability of its source: the same Bayesian standard, applied in both directions.
Inductive risk explains why the shipowner case is so damning: the cost of being wrong fell on others, so his evidential bar should have been higher.

across.link: In Vaughan v Menlove (1837) an English court held a farmer liable for a hayrick fire although he had acted 'bona fide to the best of his judgment': negligence is measured by the reasonable person, not by sincere belief. It is Clifford's verdict on the shipowner written into tort law (Day 254); the analogy breaks where law judges conduct and Clifford judges belief itself.

days.apply_question: In 2011 Oregon removed the faith-healing defence from key child-neglect and manslaughter laws after children in the Followers of Christ church died of treatable conditions. How would Clifford, James and Plantinga each judge parents who believe prayer alone will heal their child, and which feature of such a case makes Clifford's standard hardest to resist?
days.evidence_note: Value judgment and philosophical dispute throughout: what standard belief ought to meet is a normative question. Debated: whether strict evidentialism is self-undermining or too demanding (Plantinga, Wolterstorff), and whether proper basicality licenses any belief (the Great Pumpkin objection, which Plantinga answered in 1981). Settled for Logan's book: whatever one holds about faith, its empirical claims must meet the evidential standard, in both directions.

resource.why: The shipowner parable and Clifford's rule in his own vivid prose, short enough to read whole. James and Plantinga are answering this text, so Logan can judge whether they answered its strongest form.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Rome Fell to the Goths in August 410. Augustine Spent Thirteen Years Explaining Why No City Will Save You.
days.concept: Augustine's City of God holds that earthly goods such as peace, order and prosperity are real but fragile, and that no political order brings salvation, so every story of earthly progress is provisional. It is a lasting Christian scepticism about progress that Reinhold Niebuhr's Christian realism carried into modern politics.
days.focus: Teach the two cities, defined by two loves (love of God and love of self). They are intermingled in every society rather than identified with Church and state, and they share and use an 'earthly peace'. The angle for Logan's book: Augustine both affirms worldly goods and refuses to make history's direction a moral guarantee, which cuts against Christian and secular progress narratives alike.
key_concepts: the two cities and the two loves
'remota iustitia': kingdoms without justice as great robberies

story.title: The city that had taken the whole world
story.hook: On 24 August 410 the Visigoths under Alaric entered Rome through the Salarian Gate and plundered the city for three days. No foreign army had taken Rome for about eight hundred years. In Bethlehem, Jerome wrote that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. Refugees reached North Africa, and pagans among them said the disaster had come because Rome had abandoned its old gods for Christ: the emperor Theodosius had banned pagan sacrifice less than twenty years before. In Hippo, the bishop Augustine began a reply around 413 and finished it about 426: twenty-two books, The City of God.
story.puzzle: Christians had come to see the Christian Roman Empire as part of God's plan. If Rome could fall to barbarians anyway, what was the point of Christianity for this world, and what should anyone expect history to deliver?
story.payoff: Augustine's answer was to cut the tie between faith and any earthly city. Two cities, formed by two loves, are mixed together until the end. Rome's peace and order were real goods, to be used and defended, but no empire carries salvation and none is guaranteed to last. So Christianity neither caused Rome's fall nor promised its success. Fifteen centuries later Reinhold Niebuhr drew the political lesson: seek justice, but expect pride and self-interest in every collective, including your own.
sources: Augustine, The City of God (c. 413-426), especially Books I, IV.4, XIV.28 and XIX
Jerome, Letter 127 and preface to the Commentary on Ezekiel
Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography (1967; 2000)

days.application: Reinhold Niebuhr, Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932): individuals can sometimes act unselfishly, but groups, classes and nations rarely do, so justice needs power balanced against power, not only moral appeal. In The Children of Light and the Children of Darkness (1944) he wrote that 'man's capacity for justice makes democracy possible; but man's inclination to injustice makes democracy necessary.' His Christian realism shaped Cold War thinkers, and in a 2007 conversation with David Brooks, Barack Obama called Niebuhr one of his favourite philosophers.

builds_on.why: Christianity's rise to an imperial religion is what made pagans blame it for 410 and what Augustine had to rethink.
Augustine's question 'remove justice, and what are kingdoms but great robberies?' is a classic answer to the legitimacy question Hobbes and Weber later posed.

across.link: Classical realism drew on Niebuhr's account of collective pride. Hans Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations (1948) roots the lust for power in human nature, and George Kennan is often quoted as calling Niebuhr 'the father of us all' (the attribution is secondhand). It is Augustine's anthropology inside the anarchy of states (Day 264).

days.apply_question: Some advocates describe artificial general intelligence as the technology that will end poverty and disease. How would an Augustinian realist assess that claim, separating what he could accept as a real earthly good from what he would reject as misplaced hope?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the sack of 410 and the composition of The City of God. Debated among historians of ideas: whether Augustine's view of history is anti-progress or contains a seed of linear, directed history that later became progress ideology. Nisbet (1980) traces progress to Augustine, and Löwith (1949) to Christian eschatology generally; Day 289 takes this up. Value judgment: whether Christian realism is wisdom or a counsel of complacency, as critics on the left (and Hauerwas on the church side) have charged.

resource.title: The City of God, Book XIX, chapters 12-17 (on peace and the two cities' use of it)
resource.creator: Augustine of Hippo, trans. Henry Bettenson (Penguin Classics, 1972; 2003) or R. W. Dyson (Cambridge, 1998)
resource.why: Augustine's own account of the 'earthly peace' that both cities use. It is the core of the lesson and the text later Christian political thought keeps returning to.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Two of John Rawls's Little Brothers Caught His Illnesses and Died. He Built a Theory of Justice on the Claim That No One Deserves Their Luck.
days.concept: Rawls holds that just principles are those we would choose behind a veil of ignorance about our place in society, which favours inequalities only when they benefit the worst off (the difference principle, 1971). Nozick replies that a distribution is just if it arose by just acquisition and voluntary transfer, whatever its pattern (entitlement theory, 1974).
days.focus: Teach the two as rival answers to one question: does justice concern the pattern of outcomes or the history of how they arose? Use Rawls's 'natural lottery' and Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument as each side's strongest move. Set the utilitarian answer (maximize total welfare) and the Christian view of property as stewardship (developed tomorrow, Day 285) alongside. Assume CFA-level economics.
key_concepts: the original position and veil of ignorance
the natural lottery (moral arbitrariness of luck)

story.title: Two brothers, two winters, Baltimore
story.hook: In 1928 seven-year-old John Rawls fell ill with diphtheria in Baltimore. His younger brother Bobby, who went into his room to keep him company, caught it and died. The next winter John came down with pneumonia, and his brother Tommy caught it from him and died too. John survived, and developed a lasting stammer. Thomas Pogge, his student and biographer, reports these deaths and suggests that the arbitrariness of fortune stayed with Rawls. Four decades later, in A Theory of Justice (1971), Rawls built his theory on the claim that people do not deserve their place in the 'natural lottery' of talents, health and family. A just society, he argued, must not simply let that lottery decide their prospects.
story.puzzle: Nothing the brothers did made one live and two die, and no one deserves the talents or parents they are born with. Does that mean a just society must correct for luck, and if so, how far, and at whose expense?
story.payoff: Rawls's answer is the veil of ignorance. Choose principles without knowing which lot you will draw, and you would protect equal liberties and allow inequalities only when they help the worst off. Nozick's reply is that justice concerns how holdings arose: if fans freely pay to watch Wilt Chamberlain play, the resulting inequality is just, and redistribution forces some to work for others. The brothers' story makes Rawls's premise vivid; it does not settle whether correcting for luck may override entitlement.
sources: Thomas Pogge, John Rawls: His Life and Theory of Justice (2007), ch. 1
John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971)
Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), ch. 7

days.application: Iran's regulated market in kidneys. Since 1988 Iran has allowed living unrelated donors to be paid, with a fixed state award, a payment negotiated with the recipient, and charities covering poor patients. Ghods and Savaj (Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2006) reported that the national waiting list for kidneys had been eliminated by 1999. Nozick's principles permit the sale. A Rawlsian asks whether the scheme helps the worst off or exploits them, since donors are mostly poor. Catholic teaching rejects selling organs as treating the body as a commodity: John Paul II told the International Congress of the Transplantation Society on 29 August 2000 that commercializing organs is morally unacceptable.

builds_on.why: Nozick's entitlement theory is a theory of property: just acquisition and transfer of the bundle of rights that Day 252 defined.
Rawls built his theory against utilitarianism, which can justify sacrificing some for a greater total; the difference principle is his alternative to aggregation.

across.link: The US National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 made it a federal crime to buy or sell human organs for transplantation, choosing a gift-only system. Economists such as Gary Becker and Julio Elías (2007) proposed regulated payment instead. The same Rawls-Nozick dispute decides a real statute.

days.apply_question: New York City has sold taxi medallions by auction, and medallion prices peaked above $1 million around 2013-14 before ride-hailing collapsed them, leaving many immigrant drivers deep in debt. Would Rawls's difference principle or Nozick's entitlement theory judge that system more favourably, and what fact about who ended up worse off would you need to know to apply Rawls?
days.evidence_note: Value judgment: what justice requires is a normative question. Rawlsians, libertarians such as Nozick, utilitarians, luck egalitarians and Christian traditions answer differently, and the brief should attribute each. Debated empirically: the Iranian programme's outcomes, including claims of a black market and donor regret (Zargooshi 2001 against Ghods), and whether paid donation would raise supply elsewhere. Settled: the arguments' structure and the 1988 programme's existence.

resource.title: Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?, chapter 6, 'The Case for Equality: John Rawls'
resource.creator: Michael J. Sandel (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2009)
resource.why: Sandel, who teaches Harvard's famous Justice course, sets out Rawls's veil and difference principle with concrete cases, against the libertarian view of his earlier chapter, at exactly Logan's level.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: An 81-Year-Old Cardinal Helped Settle London's Great Dock Strike. Two Years Later the Pope Told Capital and Labour They Needed Each Other.
days.concept: Catholic social teaching is a body of papal and Church documents, from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Antiqua et nova (2025), built on a few principles: human dignity, the common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, the preferential option for the poor and the universal destination of goods. It rejects both laissez-faire individualism and socialism.
days.focus: Teach the principles as a toolkit and show them at work. Leo XIII defended private property and condemned socialism while also insisting on a just wage, workers' associations and a role for the state. Pius XI named subsidiarity (1931), John Paul II judged markets after 1989 (1991), and Francis extended the tradition to ecology (2015). The angle: it is a framework of principles applied prudentially, so Catholics disagree about policy within it, and its influence on real institutions can be traced.
key_concepts: the preferential option for the poor
the universal destination of goods and the just wage

story.title: The dockers' tanner and the cardinal
story.hook: In August 1889 the casual labourers of London's docks walked out. They were hired by the half-day at the dock gates and wanted sixpence an hour, 'the dockers' tanner'. The strike spread through the port, tens of thousands marched, and money arrived from Australian unions. After about five weeks, with employers and strikers deadlocked, Cardinal Henry Edward Manning, the 81-year-old Catholic Archbishop of Westminster, many of whose flock were Irish dockers, went between the two sides. He helped broker a settlement in mid-September that granted the tanner. On 15 May 1891 Pope Leo XIII issued the encyclical Rerum Novarum, 'Of New Things', on the condition of workers.
story.puzzle: A cardinal had sided with strikers against the owners, yet the Pope's encyclical defended private property and condemned socialism. Whose side was the Church on?
story.payoff: Neither ideology's. Rerum Novarum treated capital and labour as needing each other and defended property as natural while insisting that it serves common use. It demanded a wage sufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved worker, endorsed workers' associations, and gave the state a duty to protect the weak. Those claims became the principles later documents named: dignity, the common good, subsidiarity, solidarity and the universal destination of goods. Manning's influence on the text is often claimed; how direct it was is debated.
sources: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891)
Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace, Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church (2004)
John Lovell, Stevedores and Dockers (1969); Robert Gray, Cardinal Manning (1985)

days.application: Fr John A. Ryan's A Living Wage (1906) argued from Rerum Novarum that a worker has a natural right to a wage sufficient for a decent family life. Ryan drafted the US bishops' Program of Social Reconstruction (1919), which proposed minimum-wage laws, social insurance and labour's right to organize. Much of it arrived with the New Deal and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), though how much Ryan's advocacy caused that is debated. It is the tradition's most traceable effect on American policy.

builds_on.why: Subsidiarity, which Day 241 met as Quadragesimo Anno's principle that decisions belong at the lowest competent level, is one of the pillars taught today.
Catholic social teaching applies natural law (Aquinas, Finnis): property, wages and the state are judged against human goods knowable by reason.

across.link: On 10 May 2025, two days after his election, Pope Leo XIV told the cardinals that he took his name because Leo XIII had addressed the social question of the first great industrial revolution, and the Church must now respond to another industrial revolution and to artificial intelligence. The Vatican note Antiqua et nova (January 2025) had already applied the tradition to AI (Day 183).

days.apply_question: An Amazon warehouse uses algorithmic rate targets that set pick quotas and flag slow workers automatically. Which two principles of Catholic social teaching bear most directly on that system, and what would each require you to find out before judging it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the documents and their stated principles. Debated: how far the teaching has shaped policy (Ryan and the New Deal; Christian Democracy in postwar Europe), and how its principles translate into policy, with Catholic progressives and Catholic free-market thinkers such as Michael Novak reading Centesimus Annus differently. Value judgment: the principles themselves are moral premises, which the Church holds as natural law knowable by all; secular readers may accept some, such as dignity and solidarity, on other grounds.

resource.creator: Leo XIII (1891); official English translation published by the Holy See
resource.length: about 25 minutes for paragraphs 1-20; about 60 for the whole
resource.why: The founding document in its own words: the critique of socialism, the defence of property and the claims for workers that later teaching builds on, so Logan can check what Leo actually said.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Opening His University in 1880, Abraham Kuyper Claimed Every Square Inch for Christ. Then He Told the Church to Keep Out of Most of Them.
days.concept: Protestant social ethics is not one teaching but several rival traditions: chiefly Kuyper's sphere sovereignty, Niebuhr's Christian realism, Hauerwas's church as a distinct community, O'Donovan's ordered moral theology and Bonhoeffer's costly discipleship. They disagree with each other and with Catholic social teaching about how Christians should shape society.
days.focus: Teach the traditions as answers to one question: what is the church's role in public life? Kuyper divides society into spheres (family, church, school, business, state), each with its own authority. Niebuhr counsels responsible use of power. Hauerwas says the church's first social ethic is to be the church. O'Donovan grounds ethics in a created order vindicated by the resurrection, and Bonhoeffer warns against 'cheap grace'. The angle: there is no single 'Christian view' for Logan's book to cite.
key_concepts: the church as a contrast community (Hauerwas)

story.title: Not a square inch
story.hook: On 20 October 1880 the Free University of Amsterdam opened, founded by orthodox Calvinists to be free of both the state and the national church. Its founder, the minister, journalist and politician Abraham Kuyper, gave the opening address in Amsterdam's Nieuwe Kerk under the title 'Sphere Sovereignty'. He ended with a sentence Reformed Christians still quote: there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is sovereign over all, does not cry 'Mine!'. Kuyper had founded the Anti-Revolutionary Party the year before, and he later served as Dutch prime minister (1901-05).
story.puzzle: Kuyper claimed all of life for Christ, which sounds like a recipe for a church-run society. Yet he built a university free of church control and argued for limits on the state. How do both fit together?
story.payoff: Through sphere sovereignty. Christ's lordship over every sphere is exercised not through the church but through each sphere's own God-given authority, so the family, the school, business, science and the state each answer directly to God, and none may swallow the others. That is why Kuyper wanted Christian schools and a free university but not clerical rule. It resembles Catholic subsidiarity, which is built on levels, while Kuyper's scheme is built on kinds of institution. Niebuhr, Hauerwas and O'Donovan each reject or revise it.
sources: Abraham Kuyper, 'Souvereiniteit in eigen kring' (20 October 1880), in James D. Bratt (ed.), Abraham Kuyper: A Centennial Reader (1998)
James D. Bratt, Abraham Kuyper: Modern Calvinist, Christian Democrat (2013)

days.application: Dutch 'pillarization'. The 1917 'Pacification' settled the long school struggle by funding religious schools on equal terms with public ones (now Article 23 of the constitution), alongside universal male suffrage. For about half a century Protestant, Catholic, socialist and liberal 'pillars' ran their own schools, unions, newspapers, broadcasters and parties side by side within one state. It was a working version of sphere sovereignty, and it weakened from the 1960s as the Netherlands secularized.

builds_on.why: Catholic subsidiarity and Kuyper's sphere sovereignty are rival accounts of how society's institutions relate, and today's lesson defines itself partly against yesterday's.
The Reformation's priesthood of believers and its redistribution of authority to princes and laity are the roots of these Protestant traditions' wariness of a single church authority.

across.link: Arend Lijphart's The Politics of Accommodation (1968) used the pillarized Netherlands to build his model of consociational democracy: deeply divided societies kept stable by bargaining among segment elites, proportional representation and segmental autonomy. A theologian's design became a political scientist's model.

days.apply_question: In Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018) a Christian baker and a state civil-rights commission disagreed over whether he must design a cake for a same-sex wedding. How would Kuyper's sphere sovereignty and Hauerwas's church-as-community each frame what is at stake, and where would they disagree with each other?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the history of Kuyper, the 1917 Pacification and pillarization. Debated: whether pillarization stabilized Dutch democracy or merely froze divisions (Lijphart against his critics), and how usable Kuyper's legacy is, since it also includes paternalistic and racially charged statements about colonial peoples. Value judgment: each tradition's account of the church's public role. The brief presents them side by side and lets Catholic and secular alternatives stand beside them.

resource.title: 'Sphere Sovereignty' (1880 inaugural address)
resource.creator: Abraham Kuyper, in James D. Bratt (ed.), Abraham Kuyper: A Centennial Reader (Eerdmans, 1998)
resource.length: about 45-60 minutes; the 'square inch' line is in its closing pages
resource.why: The address in today's story, which lays out the spheres and contains the 'square inch' line. Reading it shows how Kuyper meant Christ's lordship to limit church power rather than expand it.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Human dignity at the edges of life
days.headline_hint: Louise Brown, the First Baby Conceived in a Dish, Was Born Just Before Midnight in Oldham. Was Her Conception an Affront to Human Dignity, or a Service to It?
days.concept: Human dignity is the idea that every human being has a worth that must be respected and cannot be priced. It grounds rights in Kantian, Christian (the image of God) and secular forms, yet critics call it too vague to decide anything, and at the edges of life (IVF, embryo research, assisted dying) both sides invoke it.
days.focus: Teach dignity's three foundations and the vagueness critique, then show why they diverge at the beginning and end of life. Is dignity respected by giving people control (autonomy), or by limits that protect life (inviolability)? The angle: when both sides use the same word, Logan must ask which conception is meant and what work it does.
key_concepts: inviolability versus autonomy conceptions of dignity

story.title: A baby conceived in a dish
story.hook: Just before midnight on 25 July 1978, at Oldham General Hospital near Manchester, Lesley Brown gave birth by caesarean section to a daughter weighing 5 lb 12 oz. Louise Joy Brown was the first person born after conception outside the body. The technique, in vitro fertilisation, had been developed after years of failed attempts by the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe, the physiologist Robert Edwards and the nurse and embryologist Jean Purdy. Reporters besieged the hospital. Some religious leaders and commentators condemned the procedure as a step toward manufacturing people; others hailed a cure for infertility. Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010; by then about four million children had been born by IVF.
story.puzzle: Critics said making a child in a laboratory violated human dignity; supporters saw a cure that let an infertile couple have the child they longed for. Today both sides of the debates over IVF, embryo research and assisted dying appeal to dignity. How can one principle point both ways?
story.payoff: Because 'dignity' names different things. On an inviolability conception, found in Catholic teaching (Donum Vitae, 1987), embryos have the worth of persons and a child should be 'begotten, not made' (the Anglican theologian Oliver O'Donovan's phrase, 1984), so IVF that creates and discards embryos is wrong. On an autonomy conception, dignity means people's right to shape their own lives, so helping them become parents respects it. Ruth Macklin (2003) concluded that the word adds nothing beyond respect for autonomy; defenders reply that it names what makes autonomy matter.
sources: Robin Marantz Henig, Pandora's Baby (2004)
Robert Edwards, Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2010, press release (Nobel Foundation)
Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Donum Vitae (1987); Oliver O'Donovan, Begotten or Made? (1984)
Ruth Macklin, 'Dignity is a useless concept', BMJ 327 (2003)

days.application: Canada's medical assistance in dying (MAID). It was legalized in 2016 after Carter v. Canada (2015) and widened in 2021 to people whose natural death is not reasonably foreseeable. Health Canada reported about 15,300 MAID deaths in 2023, about 4.7% of all deaths in Canada. Supporters invoke dignity as control over one's death. Opponents, including disability-rights groups and the Catholic bishops, invoke dignity as inviolable worth, and the extension to mental illness as the sole condition has been postponed to 2027.

builds_on.why: Kant's formula of humanity and his contrast between dignity and price are one of today's three foundations.
Day 190 examined the claim that Christian ideas of the image of God changed late-antique moral norms; today tests that idea of dignity in modern bioethics.

across.link: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law (1949) declares that human dignity shall be inviolable. In 2006 the Federal Constitutional Court relied on it to strike down a law allowing hijacked passenger planes to be shot down, holding that the passengers could not be treated as mere objects. Here dignity is a working legal rule, not only a slogan.

days.apply_question: England's NHS rations costly drugs with a cost-per-QALY threshold (Day 45). Would a dignity-based critic be right that pricing a year of life violates human dignity, and which conception of dignity, inviolability or autonomy, would the critic need to make that charge stick?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the history of IVF, and the MAID statistics as reported by Health Canada (to be re-checked against the latest annual report before use). Debated: whether dignity is a coherent concept (Macklin 2003; Pinker, 'The Stupidity of Dignity', 2008) or an indispensable foundation (the President's Council on Bioethics volume Human Dignity and Bioethics, 2008; Jeremy Waldron), and what MAID has done to vulnerable groups. Value judgment: the moral status of the embryo and the permissibility of assisted dying, on which Catholic, other Christian, Kantian and liberal autonomy views diverge.

resource.title: Dignity is a useless concept
resource.creator: Ruth Macklin, BMJ, vol. 327 (20 December 2003)
resource.why: The sharpest short statement of the vagueness critique, from a leading bioethicist. Reading the critic's own case lets Logan test whether dignity does work that autonomy alone cannot; since it is a critic's view, he should weigh it against today's defenders.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: In 1829 Britain's Prime Minister Fought a Pistol Duel on Battersea Fields. Within a Generation Duelling Looked Ridiculous. What Changed?
days.concept: Moral progress, if real, means a change toward better moral beliefs and practices, and its drivers are disputed: reasoned argument, an expanding circle of concern (Singer 1981; Buchanan & Powell 2018), shifts in honour and identity (Appiah 2010), or material change. Sceptics deny that morals progress, or that we have the standard needed to judge it.
days.focus: Teach what a claim of moral progress requires (a standard, a change and a mechanism), and test the rival mechanisms on a real case. The angle: the arguments against duelling were old and decisive long before duelling ended, so 'better arguments won' cannot be the whole story. And the debunking challenge (Day 44) asks whether our sense of progress is just our own culture judging its past.

story.title: The Prime Minister's duel
story.hook: Early on 21 March 1829 the Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo and Prime Minister, rode to Battersea Fields south of the Thames to fight a duel with pistols. The Earl of Winchilsea had publicly accused him of 'insidious designs' to bring popery into every department of the state, at the height of the fight over Catholic emancipation. Wellington fired and missed; accounts differ on whether he aimed wide on purpose. Winchilsea fired into the air and then handed over a written apology. Duelling was already illegal and had been condemned by churches and moralists for centuries. Yet within a generation it had all but vanished in Britain, and by the 1850s it was more likely to draw ridicule than respect.
story.puzzle: The arguments against duelling, that it was murderous, irrational and un-Christian, were old and well known in 1829. If argument did not change in those years, what did, and does the change count as moral progress?
story.payoff: Kwame Anthony Appiah's answer in The Honor Code (2010) is that the arguments had long been accepted; what changed was honour. As the middle classes copied gentlemen's duels and newspapers mocked them, duelling stopped marking a gentleman and started to look vulgar and absurd, so honour came to require not fighting. On this view, moral revolutions happen when what earns respect shifts to fit what morality had already said. That supports the reality of moral progress but shows that argument alone is rarely enough.
sources: Kwame Anthony Appiah, The Honor Code: How Moral Revolutions Happen (2010), ch. 1
Elizabeth Longford, Wellington: Pillar of State (1972)

days.application: Frederick Douglass's speech of 5 July 1852 at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York, to the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society: 'What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?' He held the nation to its own Declaration and its own professed Christianity. Richmond Campbell and Victor Kumar call this method consistency reasoning: it widens the moral circle by forcing people to apply principles they already accept. It worked slowly, and only together with war and the actions of the enslaved themselves (Day 227).

builds_on.why: Whether moral progress is real depends on whether moral claims can be true; evolutionary debunking arguments (Street 2006) are the main challenge to calling any change progress.
Duelling's end fits Day 202's account of norms as self-enforcing expectations that can tip suddenly once enough people move.

across.link: Gordon Allport's contact hypothesis (1954) predicts that equal-status contact reduces prejudice, and Pettigrew and Tropp's 2006 meta-analysis of 515 studies found a reliable average reduction. It is one tested mechanism by which a moral circle can expand, and on its own it says nothing about whether the expansion is right.

days.apply_question: From 1 January 2012 the EU banned conventional battery cages for laying hens. Is that best explained by argument, by an expanding circle of concern, or by a shift in what consumers and producers found respectable, and what would you need to value to call it moral progress?
days.evidence_note: Value judgment: calling any change progress requires a moral standard, and the brief attributes standards to their holders. Debated: whether moral progress is real (Pinker, Singer, and Buchanan & Powell say yes; John Gray's Straw Dogs (2002) and MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) deny or reframe it) and what drives it (argument, honour, contact, material security). Settled: the historical decline of duelling and Douglass's 1852 speech. Christian views differ too: some see moral progress as the gospel's leaven in history, while Augustinians are wary of any guaranteed advance.

resource.title: The Honor Code: How Moral Revolutions Happen, chapter 1, 'The Duel Dissolved'
resource.creator: Kwame Anthony Appiah (W. W. Norton, 2010)
resource.length: about 45-60 minutes; the opening section on the Wellington duel takes about 15
resource.why: Appiah tells today's story in full and builds his honour mechanism from it, the strongest single account of why moral change happens when it does.
