days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Hiding From the Terror, Condorcet Wrote That Humanity Was Perfectible Without Limit. He Died in a Prison Cell Before It Was Published.
days.concept: Belief in progress, that history moves toward a better human condition, is itself an idea with a history. Scholars dispute whether it is secularized Christian hope (Löwith 1949) or a genuinely modern achievement (Blumenberg 1966), and writers from Bury (1920) to Lasch (1991) have examined or questioned it.
days.focus: Teach progress as an idea to be examined, not a fact to be assumed: its Enlightenment form (Condorcet's indefinite perfectibility), the debate over its origins (Löwith against Blumenberg, with Nisbet tracing it to Augustine), and its critics. The angle for Logan's book: measured improvement (Day 234) and belief in Progress as a law of history are different claims, and the second does not follow from the first.
key_concepts: the legitimacy of the modern age (Blumenberg)
progress as fact versus progress as faith

story.title: A book about perfectibility, written in hiding
story.hook: In July 1793 the mathematician and philosopher Nicolas de Condorcet, a leading figure of the French Revolution's early years, was denounced after opposing the Jacobins' constitution, and that October he was outlawed. He hid for about eight months in a widow's house in the rue Servandoni in Paris. There he wrote the Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind: ten epochs of human history, the last a future of equality among nations, universal education and the 'indefinite perfectibility' of the human species. Fearing for his hostess, he left in late March 1794 and was arrested at an inn at Clamart. He was found dead in his cell at Bourg-la-Reine on 29 March; the cause is unknown. The Sketch was published in 1795.
story.puzzle: Condorcet was being destroyed by the revolution he had helped make, and he responded by writing history's most confident hymn to human progress. Was his faith in progress an observation about history, or something closer to a religion?
story.payoff: J. B. Bury (1920) argued that progress is an idea that cannot be proved, only believed, and that it arose late, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Karl Löwith (1949) said it was Christian eschatology, history moving to a fulfilment, with God removed. Hans Blumenberg (1966) replied that it grew instead from modern science's open-ended accumulation of knowledge. Either way, Condorcet's book shows progress working as a hope that survives contrary evidence, which is why Logan must keep it apart from measured improvements.
sources: Condorcet, Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrès de l'esprit humain (1795)
Keith Michael Baker, Condorcet: From Natural Philosophy to Social Mathematics (1975)
J. B. Bury, The Idea of Progress (1920); Karl Löwith, Meaning in History (1949); Hans Blumenberg, The Legitimacy of the Modern Age (1966; trans. 1983)

days.application: Steven Pinker's Enlightenment Now (2018) argues from data on life expectancy, poverty, violence and knowledge that reason, science and humanism have produced progress and should be defended. Critics such as John Gray (New Statesman review, 2018) call it a faith in progress dressed as data, and others, such as Jason Hickel on poverty, dispute particular series; defenders answer that the trends are measured, not believed. It is Condorcet's argument rerun with better statistics, and part of the dispute is whether the trends license the larger claim.

builds_on.why: Measuring progress beyond GDP showed that every metric embeds choices; today asks the further question of whether improving metrics add up to Progress.
Augustine's refusal to make any earthly city the bearer of salvation is the background to Löwith's thesis and to Nisbet's claim that progress begins with Christian linear history.

across.link: Condorcet's jury theorem (1785) shows that if each voter is more likely right than wrong and votes independently, the chance that the majority is right approaches certainty as the group grows. It underwrote his faith that enlightened, educated majorities would make progress. The theorem is valid, and its conditions (competence above one half, independence) are exactly where real progress can fail.

days.apply_question: Global life expectancy rose from roughly 32 years in 1900 to over 70 today. What does that measured fact establish, and what further premises would you need before concluding that history is progressing?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Condorcet's life, and the measured long-run trends in health and income (Days 145, 218). Debated: the origin of the idea of progress (Löwith against Blumenberg; Nisbet; Bury), and whether Pinker's data support his larger thesis (Pinker against Gray, Hickel and others). Value judgment: whether recent centuries are better overall. That requires weighing measurable goods against goods such as meaning, virtue and community that resist measurement (Lasch 1991).

resource.title: The Idea of Progress: An Inquiry into Its Origin and Growth, Introduction
resource.creator: J. B. Bury (Macmillan, 1920)
resource.why: The classic statement that progress is an idea with a history and cannot be proved. It sets up the Löwith-Blumenberg debate and gives Logan the distinction his book needs between measured improvement and faith in Progress.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: A Famous Story Says Robert Moses Built Bridges Too Low for Buses to Keep the Poor Off His Beaches. The Story Is Shakier Than the Bridges.
days.concept: Technologies are not neutral tools: they can embody political choices and reshape the people who use them (Winner 1980; Ellul 1954; Borgmann 1984). How far design determines outcomes, rather than society shaping technology, is disputed.
days.focus: Teach the spectrum from instrumentalism (tools are neutral, and only their uses are good or bad) through social shaping to technological determinism. Use Winner's two senses of artifacts having politics: designed to settle an issue, or inherently suited to a form of power. The angle: the most famous example is contested, which teaches both the idea and the evidence standard for using it.

story.title: Nine feet of clearance
story.hook: In The Power Broker (1974), Robert Caro reported that Robert Moses, who built New York's parkways and Jones Beach, had the overpasses on the Long Island parkways built low, some with as little as nine feet of clearance at the curb, so that buses could not use them. Caro quoted Moses's associate Sidney Shapiro as saying that Moses wanted to keep poor and Black New Yorkers, who depended on buses, away from his beaches. In 1980 the political theorist Langdon Winner opened his essay 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?' with the bridges as his lead example: concrete that carried out a social policy for decades after its builder's intentions were forgotten. In 1999 the sociologist Bernward Joerges challenged the story.
story.puzzle: Can a bridge be racist? And if the story behind the most famous example is doubtful, does the idea that artifacts carry politics fall with it?
story.payoff: Joerges pointed out that commercial vehicles, buses included, were barred from the parkways by regulation anyway, and that Jones Beach could be reached by bus on other roads; whether Moses designed the bridges to exclude anyone remains disputed. But Winner's thesis does not depend on one case. Artifacts can settle political questions by design (whatever Moses intended, low bridges excluded buses), and some technologies suit particular power structures. The story's fate shows that the idea is sound but its best-known example needs a hedge.
sources: Robert A. Caro, The Power Broker (1974)
Langdon Winner, 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?', Daedalus 109(1), 1980
Bernward Joerges, 'Do Politics Have Artefacts?', Social Studies of Science 29(3), 1999

days.application: The Old Order Amish and the telephone. Around 1910 Old Order Amish communities in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, decided against telephones in the home, judging that the device would weaken face-to-face visiting and pull members into outside affairs. Later, shared phones in shanties at the end of lanes were allowed for business and emergencies (Diane Zimmerman Umble, Holding the Line, 1996). The Amish treat technologies as non-neutral and decide case by case, the reverse of determinism: a community shaping its tools instead of being shaped by them.

builds_on.why: Path dependence and lock-in explain how a design choice, once built in concrete or code, keeps acting for decades, which is part of how artifacts carry politics.
Day 210's Jacobs-Moses fight showed Moses's planning remaking city life; today asks whether his structures themselves carried his politics.

across.link: Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace (1999) argued that software architecture regulates behaviour alongside law, norms and markets: 'code is law'. It is Winner's thesis applied to the internet, and Day 253's DAO hack (2016) shows code enforcing an outcome no court intended.

days.apply_question: Many US cities have installed benches with armrests dividing the seat, which critics call 'hostile architecture' aimed at homeless people. Using Winner's two senses of artifacts having politics, what evidence would you need to call those benches political by design rather than merely by effect?
days.evidence_note: Settled: design choices can constrain behaviour, and Moses's parkways had low overpasses. Debated: Moses's intent and the bridges' actual effect (Caro and Winner against Joerges, with Woolgar and Cooper, 1999), and how much technology drives social change (determinists such as Ellul against social-shaping scholars such as Bijker and Pinch). Value judgment: which technologies a good society should adopt. Here Christian critics such as C. S. Lewis (The Abolition of Man, 1943: what we call man's power over Nature turns out to be a power exercised by some men over other men) and Ellul join secular critics such as Borgmann.

resource.title: Do Artifacts Have Politics?
resource.creator: Langdon Winner, Daedalus 109(1), Winter 1980; reprinted in The Whale and the Reactor (University of Chicago Press, 1986), ch. 2
resource.why: The essay in today's story and the field's most cited paper, with both of Winner's senses of artifacts having politics. Reading it after the Joerges challenge lets Logan judge the argument apart from its famous example.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: In 1967 a Christian Historian Told Science Readers That Christianity Bore 'a Huge Burden of Guilt' for the Ecological Crisis. Fifty Years of Surveys Checked.
days.concept: Environmental ethics runs from human-centred views (nature matters for us) through stewardship (humans hold creation in trust) to nature-centred views (nature matters in itself). Lynn White's thesis that Christian dominion theology caused the ecological crisis has met mixed empirical tests.
days.focus: Teach the three positions, and treat White's historical claim as a testable hypothesis. Then show what the tests found: Christian belief in the US is not associated with greater environmental concern, and the 'greening of religion' is weak, but that does not show Christianity caused the crisis, which arose in many cultures. The angle: one evidence standard for a thesis that indicts Christianity and for replies that flatter it.

story.title: A Christian historian accuses his own tradition
story.hook: On 26 December 1966, at the meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in Washington, the medieval historian Lynn White Jr., a Presbyterian, gave a lecture published in Science on 10 March 1967 as 'The Historical Roots of Our Ecologic Crisis'. Western science and technology, he argued, grew out of a Christian view of nature in which man was made in God's image and given dominion, and nature existed to serve him. Christianity, he wrote, 'bears a huge burden of guilt'. He proposed Francis of Assisi, who spoke of Brother Sun and Sister Moon, as a patron saint for ecologists. In 1979 Pope John Paul II named Francis patron of ecology.
story.puzzle: Was White right that a religious idea, dominion, drove humanity's assault on nature? If so, should Christians today be measurably less green than others, or measurably greener after half a century of response?
story.payoff: Bron Taylor, Gretel Van Wieren and Bernard Zaleha reviewed the evidence (Conservation Biology, 2016) and found no clear 'greening' of Christian environmental attitudes or behaviour. In the US, Christians, especially conservative Protestants, showed on average less environmental concern than the non-religious. That is consistent with part of White's thesis but does not prove his causal history: deforestation and extinctions occurred under many religions, and theologians answer that dominion means stewardship (Genesis 2:15, 'to work it and keep it').
sources: Lynn White Jr., 'The Historical Roots of Our Ecologic Crisis', Science 155 (1967): 1203-1207
Bron Taylor, Gretel Van Wieren & Bernard Zaleha, 'Lynn White Jr. and the greening-of-religion hypothesis', Conservation Biology 30(5), 2016
John Paul II, Inter Sanctos (29 November 1979)

days.application: Laudato si', Pope Francis's encyclical dated 24 May 2015 and published that June, the first devoted to ecology. It rejects a 'tyrannical anthropocentrism', calls the climate a common good, and treats care for nature and for the poor as one 'integral ecology'. Its measured effects on opinion appear modest and polarized. One US survey study (Li et al., Climatic Change, 2016) found that awareness of the encyclical went with more concern about climate change among liberals and, if anything, less among conservatives.

builds_on.why: Lynn White was also Day 193's historian of medieval technology; his ecology thesis extends his claim that medieval Christian culture drove Western technological dynamism.
The greenhouse effect is the settled science behind the climate part of the ecological crisis; today's question is about attitudes and values toward it.

across.link: In TVA v. Hill (1978) the Supreme Court read the US Endangered Species Act (1973) to halt a nearly finished dam to protect the snail darter, finding that Congress had meant to halt and reverse the trend toward extinction 'whatever the cost'. A nature-centred value was written into statute and enforced against human benefit.

days.apply_question: Evangelical leaders launched the Evangelical Climate Initiative in 2006, and polls continue to show white evangelicals among the Americans least likely to call climate change a serious problem. What would you need to know to decide whether theology, politics or something else explains that gap?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the greenhouse physics, and the survey findings that US Christians are on average not more environmentally concerned than the non-religious. Debated: White's causal history (critics include historians who note ecological damage under non-Christian civilizations, and theologians who read dominion as stewardship), and how far religious attitudes drive environmental behaviour at all, given confounding by politics. Value judgment: whether nature has value in itself, and humanity's place in it, where Christian, secular anthropocentric and ecocentric views differ.

resource.title: The Historical Roots of Our Ecologic Crisis
resource.creator: Lynn White Jr., Science, vol. 155, no. 3767 (10 March 1967), pp. 1203-1207
resource.why: The five-page essay itself, which is more nuanced than its reputation. White argues as a Christian, proposes Francis as a Christian alternative, and frames a hypothesis Logan can test against the evidence in today's lesson.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Arguing fairly: steelmanning and the ideological Turing test
days.headline_hint: A Neuroscientist Bet a Philosopher a Case of Wine in 1998. Twenty-Five Years Later He Paid Up, After an Experiment Designed by Rival Camps Bruised Both Their Theories.
days.concept: To know your own case you must know the other side at its strongest. That is Mill's principle (On Liberty, 1859), and steelmanning, Bryan Caplan's ideological Turing test (2011) and adversarial collaboration turn it into practices.
days.focus: Teach fair argument as an evidence method, not a courtesy. You cannot know whether you are right until you can state the opposing view so well that its holders accept it, and rivals who agree in advance what would count against them can make a dispute decidable. The story tests the theories of consciousness from Day 278. The angle for Logan's book: pre-register theses with what would disconfirm them, and pass an ideological Turing test on his strongest critics.
key_concepts: Mill's principle: 'He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that'

story.title: A case of wine, twenty-five years late
story.hook: In 1998, at a consciousness conference in Bremen, the neuroscientist Christof Koch bet the philosopher David Chalmers a case of fine wine that within twenty-five years science would have clearly identified the neural signature of consciousness. In 2019 a group of rival labs, later called the Cogitate Consortium, began an unusual experiment. Proponents of two leading theories, integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory, agreed in advance and in public on predictions where their theories conflicted, and theory-neutral labs ran the tests. In June 2023, at a meeting in New York, the first results were presented; neither theory came through cleanly, and Koch conceded the bet and handed Chalmers the wine. Within months more than a hundred researchers signed an open letter calling integrated information theory pseudoscience, and others protested the letter.
story.puzzle: An experiment designed jointly by rivals to settle their dispute left both theories bruised and the field angrier than before. Did adversarial collaboration fail, or is this what fair argument looks like when it works?
story.payoff: It worked in the way Mill describes. Because the rivals had stated each other's predictions in forms both accepted, the results could count against both, and they did (Nature, 2025). No one could dismiss the data as a strawman test. The anger came from what followed, not from the method. Fair argument does not guarantee agreement; it makes disagreement precise, and it shows each side where it is weakest.
sources: Cogitate Consortium, 'Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness', Nature (2025)
News coverage of the Koch-Chalmers bet, June 2023 (e.g. Nature news; Science)
J. S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), ch. 2

days.application: Leah Libresco's ideological Turing tests (2011-2013). On her blog Unequally Yoked, then hosted by Patheos, Libresco, at the time an atheist in a relationship with a Catholic, invited atheists and Christians to answer questions about their beliefs both honestly and while impersonating the other side. Readers tried to tell the real answers from the fakes; many impostors were hard to spot, and some sides were easier to fake than others. She announced her own conversion to Catholicism in 2012. It is Caplan's test run on exactly the divide Logan's book crosses.

builds_on.why: Motivated reasoning is the failure fair argument is meant to correct: people evaluate evidence through what their side needs, so you must deliberately build the other side's best case.
Day 168's Kahneman-Killingsworth study was itself an adversarial collaboration; today generalizes the method.

across.link: From 1587 the Catholic Church's canonization process included an official 'Promoter of the Faith', popularly the devil's advocate, whose job was to argue against a candidate's sainthood; John Paul II's 1983 reforms reduced the office's role. Institutions as well as individuals can build in the strongest opposing case, as adversarial trials do.

days.apply_question: Jonathan Haidt and Candice Odgers disagree over whether social media caused the rise in teenage depression (Day 169). Write, in one sentence, the strongest version of the side you find less convincing, then say what result from a pre-registered study would change your mind.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Cogitate results were published and challenged both theories, and Mill's argument and Caplan's test are as stated. Debated: whether adversarial collaborations change minds (Kahneman's experience suggests rarely; their value is in sharpening disputes), and the standing of integrated information theory. Value judgment: how much charity opponents are owed. Mill's case is partly epistemic (you cannot otherwise know you are right) and partly moral, and Christian ethics of truth-telling and love of neighbour bear on it too.

resource.title: On Liberty, chapter 2, 'Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion': the passage from 'He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that' to the end of that argument
resource.creator: John Stuart Mill (1859)
resource.length: about 15 minutes for the passage; about 60 for the whole chapter
resource.why: Mill's own case for knowing the opposing view at its strongest, including his point that a truth held without facing objections becomes 'dead dogma', the reason Logan's book needs its critics.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 18: Car IV, the full loop: was the car progress?
days.headline_hint: Bridget Driscoll Was Killed in 1896 by a Car Its Driver Said Was Doing Four Miles an Hour. The Coroner Hoped It Would Never Happen Again. Cars Have Since Killed Tens of Millions.
days.concept: Was the automobile, on balance, morally beneficial progress? Answering requires every link of the chain (need, invention, constraints, engineering and production, financing, regulation, adoption, consequences, feedback) as a loop, then an explicit moral standard, because the facts alone cannot deliver the verdict.
days.focus: The capstone of the path and of Logan's book question. First the full chain, deep on every link, redrawn as the loop it was. Then the evaluation: measured goods (mobility, access, rural connection, emergency care, freedom) and harms (about 1.19 million road deaths a year, pollution and lead, climate, sprawl), and the counterfactual that cannot be known. Then how consequentialist, Kantian, virtue, natural-law and Catholic social teaching, Augustinian and philosophy-of-technology frameworks weigh them, and finally whether 'beneficial' can be true at all (Day 44).
key_concepts: the socio-technical system and its loops
who gained, who paid, who consented
Kranzberg's first law: technology is neither good nor bad, nor is it neutral
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, car dependence (reinforcing): more cars bring roads and parking, then low-density development, longer trips and weaker transit, then more need for cars (Day 216). B1, induced demand (balancing on congestion): more lane-miles cut travel time, driving rises roughly one-for-one, and congestion returns (Duranton & Turner 2011). B2, safety, with a delay of decades: deaths bring advocacy, law, liability and design (MacPherson 1916; Nader 1965; the 1966 Act; Haddon), and the death rate per mile falls. Coupled loop, lead: leaded fuel, then Patterson's measurements and the 1970 Clean Air Act, then catalytic converters that needed unleaded fuel, removing lead; the last leaded petrol was sold in Algeria in 2021 (Day 49). Geopolitical loop: the fleet raises oil imports, then the 1973 embargo, then fuel-economy rules, cheaper miles and rebound (Days 271, 83). Reversals: regulation before the car (Britain's 1865 Locomotive Act), roads demanded before the car (the League of American Wheelmen, founded 1880, and the Good Roads movement), credit before demand (GMAC, 1919). Closure: consequences become new needs, as deaths and climate create demand for electric and automated cars, the next loop.

story.title: Crystal Palace, 17 August 1896
story.hook: On 17 August 1896, in the grounds of the Crystal Palace in south London, Bridget Driscoll, a 44-year-old woman from Croydon, stepped into the path of a car giving demonstration rides for the Anglo-French Motor Carriage Company. The driver, Arthur Edsall, said he was going about four miles an hour; a witness described a 'reckless pace'. She died within minutes, the first pedestrian known to have been killed by a car in Britain. At the inquest the jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and the coroner is reported to have said he hoped such a thing would never happen again. On 14 November 1896 the Locomotives on Highways Act raised the speed limit for light motor cars from 4 miles an hour (2 in towns) to 14, which the Local Government Board promptly set at 12.
story.puzzle: Since 1896 cars have killed tens of millions of people and given billions a freedom of movement no earlier generation had. Was the automobile, on balance, progress, and what would it even take to answer?
story.payoff: It takes three kinds of knowledge kept apart. First, the facts: the chain, measured as well as the evidence allows. Second, the counterfactual: what the world would have been without the car, or with a different car system (the Dutch turn of the 1970s, or electric cars winning around 1905). It cannot be observed and must be marked as unknowable. Third, a moral standard that weighs goods against harms and asks who gained, who paid and who consented; different frameworks weigh them differently. Driscoll's death, accepted as 'accidental' and followed within months by a higher speed limit, shows society making that trade from the start, mostly without deciding to.
sources: Inquest reports, e.g. The Times (London), August 1896; Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents historical notes
Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 (in force 14 November 1896)
WHO, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023

days.application: The system itself: the automobile from Benz's 1886 patent to today's roughly 1.19 million road deaths a year worldwide (WHO 2023, for 2021) and the electric transition, evaluated through the full chain and then through the frameworks. For contrast within the case, the Netherlands, where the 'Stop de Kindermoord' protests (1972-73) helped turn street design toward cyclists and children, a documented case of the loop being redirected (Day 216).

builds_on.why: Car I set out the car by the numbers (energy density, the Model T's price on a log scale, the S-curve, death rates); Car IV closes the spiral with the moral evaluation those numbers could not supply.
Consequentialism supplies one evaluation: add up measured benefits and harms, which forces explicit trade-offs such as the value of a statistical life.
Philosophy of technology asks whether the car was a neutral tool or a system that reshaped people and cities in ways no one chose, which changes what 'progress' means here.
Whether 'the car was morally beneficial' can be true at all is a metaethical question: realists say yes, while anti-realists say it expresses or constructs a standard.

across.link: Automated driving is the newest turn of the same loop. The Uber test-car death of Elaine Herzberg in Tempe (18 March 2018) and Waymo's paid driverless rides (Day 181) replay the 1896 questions of who is liable, what risk is acceptable and who consented, for a machine that now also makes the driving decisions.

days.apply_question: Using the same three-part method (the facts of the chain, the counterfactual you cannot observe, and the moral standard you would need), how would you begin to judge whether the smartphone has been progress, and on which link of its chain do you think the evidence is weakest?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the measured facts in the chain (registrations, road deaths, lead exposure and its fall, induced demand, the Model T's price path) and the dates of the laws. Debated: the size of particular effects (the lead-crime link; how much safety law, rather than other factors, cut death rates; risk compensation, Peltzman 1975), and whether a different car system was feasible. Value judgment: whether the car was progress, which no data settle. Consequentialists weigh total welfare (mobility gains against deaths and climate harm). Kantians ask whether third parties, such as pedestrians, children and future generations, were used without consent. Natural-law and Catholic social teaching traditions weigh the common good, the universal destination of goods and the preferential option for the poor (most road deaths fall in low- and middle-income countries). Augustinians distrust a verdict of Progress itself, and philosophers of technology ask what the car did to community and practice. Who gained: drivers and economies. Who paid: pedestrians, the poor, children exposed to lead, future climates. Who consented: few were asked. The counterfactual is unknowable, and the verdict belongs to Logan, in the book.

chain.point: One car serves several needs at once (autonomy, access to work and markets, status), so 'need' is not a single first cause. Needs were also partly built: cyclists' League of American Wheelmen, founded in 1880, demanded paved roads before cars existed.

chain.field: History of technology and Systems Thinking
chain.point: The car combined earlier inventions (Otto's four-stroke engine of 1876, bicycle wheels and bearings, Dunlop's 1888 pneumatic tyre), assembled in parallel by Benz in Mannheim and by Daimler and Maybach in Cannstatt. It is a textbook case of invention as a chain-linked system rather than a pipeline.

Gasoline's energy density (about 12 kWh per kilogram) beat early batteries by a wide margin, while the Carnot limit and engine losses mean only about 12-30% of fuel energy reaches the wheels. That combination decided the petrol car's victory and its emissions.

Highland Park's moving line (1913-14) cut chassis assembly from about 12.5 hours to about 1.5, and learning curves drove the Model T's price from about $850 (1908) to about $260 by the mid-1920s; the same curve now drives battery costs.

Instalment credit built demand. GM founded GMAC in 1919, and by the mid-1920s roughly two-thirds or more of new cars were bought on instalment loans, typically over 12-18 months (Martha Olney, Buy Now, Pay Later, 1991; estimates vary). Credit, not only falling prices, made the car a mass good.

Liability came early: MacPherson v. Buick (1916) made makers answerable to the people who used their cars, not only to the dealers who bought them. Administrative rules followed: the 1966 Safety Act, then NHTSA's passive-restraint rule, whose rescission the Supreme Court struck down in Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm (1983). Leaded petrol showed how a burden-of-proof rule can delay a fix for decades.
US registrations went from 8,000 vehicles in 1900 to about 23.1 million passenger cars in 1929 along an S-curve, spreading through neighbours, status and credit as diffusion theory predicts.

chain.field: Sociology, Energy, Chemistry & Materials, and Biology, Medicine & Health
chain.point: About 1.19 million road deaths a year worldwide (WHO 2023); suburbs, induced demand and weaker social ties; lead exposure; and road vehicles' CO2, roughly three-quarters of transport's emissions, whose warming effect is settled physics.

A large fleet made oil a strategic chokepoint. The October 1973 embargo quadrupled prices and produced US fuel-economy rules and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; today China's lead in battery supply chains is the electric car's chokepoint.

The frameworks weigh the same facts differently: consequentialist totals, the Kantian question of third parties' consent, virtue and practice, natural law and Catholic social teaching's common good and option for the poor, Augustinian distrust of Progress itself, and the philosophy of technology's question of what the system did to us. Moral progress needs a standard, and metaethics asks whether we can have one.

resource.title: Technology and History: 'Kranzberg's Laws'
resource.creator: Melvin Kranzberg, Technology and Culture 27(3), July 1986, pp. 544-560
resource.why: A historian of technology's six 'laws', beginning 'Technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral', are the best short frame for the capstone question. They refuse both the triumphal and the dismissive verdict and insist that the answer depends on context, which is exactly the method the case asks Logan to apply.
